Patient: OKKES REILLY
Occupation: Writer
Home address: 22 De Ferrers Drive, Aylesbury, HP19 0FA
Contact email: okkes.reilly50@gmail.com
Employer: Brownroyd Hill Secondary School

Review – hypothyroidism

Reports several months of reduced energy, feeling unusually cold and constipation. No chest pain, breathlessness, palpitations or unexplained weight loss. Appetite unchanged. Sleep is adequate, although she feels unrefreshed in the mornings. No neck swelling, dysphagia or voice change. Takes levothyroxine each morning with water, usually before breakfast; occasionally forgets a dose at weekends. No other regular medicines reported.

Examination: alert and orientated, communicating normally. Pulse 64 bpm and regular; BP 118/72 mmHg. Weight stable by history. Skin mildly dry. No tremor or peripheral oedema. Thyroid not enlarged or tender. Chest clear and heart sounds normal. Abdomen soft, non-tender, with no palpable masses.

Assessment

Symptoms may reflect suboptimal thyroid replacement, with adherence and administration timing also relevant. No clinical features of significant thyrotoxicosis or myxoedema.

Plan

Continue levothyroxine at the current prescribed dose of 75 micrograms once daily. Take consistently on an empty stomach, at least 30 minutes before food, and separate from calcium or iron supplements by four hours. Arrange thyroid function tests, including TSH and free T4, before the next review. Discussed regular fluids, dietary fibre and gentle activity for constipation; seek advice sooner if abdominal pain, vomiting or failure to pass stool.

If blood results remain abnormal, dose adjustment will be considered. If results are satisfactory but fatigue persists, review sleep, mood, diet and other possible causes rather than increasing levothyroxine empirically.

Follow-up planned in about 8 weeks, with earlier GP review for worsening symptoms, marked drowsiness, palpitations or new neck swelling. Patient is agreeable to the plan and will receive results through the usual practice contact route.

Discharge summary for RENU BLACKWELL
NHS number: 000 161 4780

You were admitted to Aberdeen Royal Infirmary with worsening heart failure. Before admission you had increasing breathlessness when lying flat (orthopnoea), swelling around both ankles and a noticeable reduction in how far you could walk or exercise. Examination and chest imaging were consistent with fluid building up in and around the lungs. Your blood tests showed reduced kidney function on arrival, which improved with treatment. The ECG showed sinus rhythm, and there was no evidence of an acute heart attack.

During your admission, you were treated with intravenous diuretic medicine to remove excess fluid. Your breathing and ankle swelling improved, and you were able to walk on the ward without significant breathlessness. The diuretic was changed back to tablets before discharge. Kidney function and potassium levels remained satisfactory on the final blood test.

Please continue your discharge medicines as listed below:

• furosemide 40 mg once daily  
• bisoprolol at your usual prescribed dose

Do not stop bisoprolol suddenly. Take furosemide in the morning where possible, as it increases urine production. Weigh yourself regularly, ideally at the same time each morning. Contact your GP surgery if your weight increases by more than 2 kilograms over three days, or if your ankle swelling or breathlessness starts to worsen. Seek urgent help through NHS 111 or A&E if you are severely breathless at rest, develop chest pain, become faint or confused, or cannot lie flat despite using extra pillows.

Please arrange a medication and fluid-status review with your GP. A repeat U&E blood test should be taken within one week of discharge, with the result reviewed by the GP or heart-failure team. Your heart-failure clinic follow-up is booked for 29th February 1996. Please bring an up-to-date list of all medicines and, if available, your daily weight record.

With your consent, your relative A. Bryant in Poolewe was informed that you were leaving hospital and was given general advice about watching for worsening breathlessness or swelling. They should not alter your medicines, but may help you contact the GP or NHS 111 if you become unwell.

At discharge you were clinically improved, eating and drinking, passing urine normally and mobilising independently. Continue to limit added salt, avoid over-the-counter anti-inflammatory painkillers unless specifically advised, and follow the fluid allowance discussed with the ward team.

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT ASSESSMENT
NHS number: 0007267674

Patient: Elis, a 42-year-old African American male patient
MRN: 0466356
Home address: 151 Padeswood Lake Road, Tref-y-Clawdd / Knighton, LD7 1AA
Preferred contact detail: elis.hogg40@gmail.com

Presenting complaint
Two days of frequent watery diarrhoea with four episodes of vomiting since yesterday evening. Associated colicky lower abdominal cramps and reduced oral intake. No blood or mucus reported. Felt feverish overnight but no measured temperature. No recent antibiotics, foreign travel or known contact with diarrhoeal illness. Passing urine, although less often than usual. No chest pain, breathlessness or urinary symptoms.

Background
No significant past medical history disclosed. Not taking regular medicines. No known drug allergies. Has tried small amounts of water at home but has not yet used oral rehydration solution.

Assessment
Alert and appropriately responsive, mildly uncomfortable but not toxic. Airway clear; respiratory rate 16/min, oxygen saturations 98% on air. Pulse 96/min, regular; blood pressure 112/70 mmHg; temperature 37.6°C. Capillary refill 2 seconds. Oral mucosa slightly dry. Heart sounds normal, chest clear.

Abdomen soft with mild, diffuse lower abdominal tenderness and audible bowel sounds. No guarding, rebound tenderness or palpable mass. No calf tenderness or rash. Current abdominal pain rated 5/10.

Investigations
Urinalysis: concentrated urine, otherwise negative for blood, ketones and nitrites. Capillary glucose 5.8 mmol/L. Blood samples sent for full blood count, urea and electrolytes, C-reactive protein and liver function; results show mild haemoconcentration with preserved renal function and no significant inflammatory response. Stool sample requested if diarrhoea persists or becomes bloody.

Clinical impression
Most consistent with acute infectious gastroenteritis, currently without evidence of peritonism, significant sepsis or clinically important dehydration. No indication for abdominal imaging or antibiotics at this stage.

Treatment in department
Ondansetron administered for nausea, with improvement and no further vomiting during observation. Oral rehydration solution commenced in frequent small volumes and tolerated. Advice given to continue oral rehydration solution at home, taking small sips after each loose stool, and to resume light food as tolerated. Ondansetron prescribed as required.

Disposition and safety-netting
Suitable for discharge with a responsible adult. Return to A&E urgently for inability to retain fluids, markedly reduced urine output, fainting, worsening or localised abdominal pain, blood in stool, persistent high fever or increasing drowsiness. Avoid preparing food for others until 48 hours after the last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting. GP review advised if not clearly improving within 48–72 hours.

Referral to Haematology

Patient: EDMOND NEEDHAM

Referring organisation: Ulster Hospital
Referring locality: BALLYHORNAN

Clinical question
Please assess this patient urgently for suspected Hodgkin lymphoma and advise on definitive tissue diagnosis and staging.

History
There is a six-week history of painless left cervical lymphadenopathy, with progressive enlargement despite no infective symptoms. The patient reports drenching night sweats on most nights and unintentional weight loss of approximately 6 kg over two months. There has been no documented fever, pruritus or abdominal pain. No recent dental infection or antibiotic course.

Examination and investigations
Several firm, non-tender left cervical nodes are palpable, the largest approximately 3 cm, with a smaller supraclavicular node. No axillary or inguinal lymphadenopathy was identified. Chest is clear and there is no hepatosplenomegaly on examination.

FBC shows mild normocytic anaemia and a raised ESR. CRP is mildly elevated; renal and liver profiles are within reference ranges. A chest radiograph demonstrates subtle left hilar fullness. Ultrasound of the neck confirms abnormal, hypoechoic lymph nodes with loss of normal fatty hila. An urgent CT neck, thorax, abdomen and pelvis has been requested; the report is pending.

Management to date
The patient is receiving supportive care pending tissue diagnosis. Paracetamol as required has been advised for discomfort. No corticosteroids have been commenced, to avoid compromising subsequent biopsy interpretation. The patient has been given safety-net advice regarding worsening breathlessness, fever or rapidly increasing swelling and understands the need to attend the emergency department if these occur.

Requested action
I would be grateful for prompt review, consideration of excision or image-guided biopsy, and further staging investigations as indicated. Please advise whether any additional blood tests should be arranged before clinic review.

Yours faithfully,

J. Payne
GMC number: 0987216
Referring clinician
BALLYHORNAN

LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: moyosola fitzpatrick
MRN: 0129927
Requesting organisation: Skin Hospital
Specimen/report date: 06/04/2018
Clinical details: Essential hypertension; intermittent headache and light-headedness. Current treatment recorded as amlodipine and ramipril.

Specimens
Serum, EDTA plasma and random urine received for hypertension monitoring. Sample integrity acceptable. A preliminary data-quality entry recorded the specimen date as 31/04/2025; this is not a valid calendar date and was rejected. The report date above is the verified encounter date.

Results

Renal profile
Sodium 139 mmol/L (133–146)
Potassium 4.6 mmol/L (3.5–5.3)
Urea 5.8 mmol/L (2.5–7.8)
Creatinine 79 µmol/L (45–90)
eGFR (CKD-EPI) 82 mL/min/1.73 m² (>60)

Liver profile
ALT 24 U/L (0–40)
ALP 86 U/L (30–130)
Bilirubin 11 µmol/L (0–21)
Albumin 43 g/L (35–50)

Lipid profile
Total cholesterol 5.4 mmol/L
HDL cholesterol 1.32 mmol/L
Non-HDL cholesterol 4.08 mmol/L
Triglycerides 1.6 mmol/L
LDL cholesterol 3.36 mmol/L

Urine albumin:creatinine ratio
3.1 mg/mmol (<3.0)

Interpretation
Renal function and serum electrolytes are within the stated limits. There is a borderline increase in urine ACR, without evidence in this sample of significant albuminuria. Lipid concentrations should be interpreted alongside overall cardiovascular risk and treatment goals; no fasting status was provided.

Clinical comment
Please continue routine monitoring of creatinine, potassium and urine ACR while taking ramipril. A repeat early-morning urine ACR may be considered if clinically indicated, particularly if hypertension remains difficult to control. Correlate the light-headedness with seated and standing blood pressure readings and medication timing. Seek urgent clinical assessment for severe or sudden headache, neurological deficit, chest pain or marked blood-pressure elevation.

Nursing progress note

Patient: N. Whitfield, 79-year-old African American female patient  
Clinical lead: Aryaz Khalid

Assessment
Alert and orientated, conversing appropriately. Reports mild aching from the plantar ulcer when mobilising, rated 3/10, with no pain at rest. Reduced protective sensation to the affected foot. Ulcer remains clean-based with a small amount of yellow local discharge; surrounding skin mildly erythematous, warm and tender, with no spreading cellulitis observed. No malodour. Temperature 37.2°C, pulse 86 bpm, BP 128/74 mmHg, respirations 18, SpO₂ 98% on air. NEWS2 0.

Mobility and intake
Mobilised short distances to the bathroom using a frame and supervision. Reinforced non-weight-bearing through the affected forefoot and advised to use the heel only for essential transfers. Tolerated mobilisation without dizziness. Ate approximately three-quarters of lunch and drank 900 mL during the shift. Passed urine; bowels opened yesterday.

Care delivered
Wound cleansed with sterile saline, gently dried and redressed as per tissue viability plan. Co-amoxiclav administered as prescribed; no adverse reaction noted. Foot elevated intermittently. Blood glucose monitored before meals, readings 8.9 and 10.7 mmol/L; diabetes team guidance followed. Patient educated not to walk barefoot and to report increased pain, spreading redness, fever or offensive drainage.

Risk and escalation
Falls risk remains increased due to altered gait and reduced sensation. Call bell left within reach and footwear checked before transfer. Escalate promptly for fever, tachycardia, worsening erythema, increased discharge or signs of systemic infection. BOJIDAR PRINCE updated by telephone regarding the need for supervised mobility and dressing review.

Plan for next shift
Repeat observations and capillary glucose monitoring. Inspect wound and document drainage, size and surrounding skin. Continue prescribed co-amoxiclav and dressing regimen, maintain pressure off-loading, encourage fluids and liaise with podiatry/tissue viability if deterioration occurs. Follow-up review booked for 1 Dec 2019, in about 9 weeks.

Date: 28 May 2020
NHS number: 0005218732

Patient: Raheemah ALDRIDGE  
This is a 41-year-old African-American male patient reviewed in the surgery for recurrent headaches. She reports a six-month history of episodic, left-sided throbbing pain, usually centred behind the eye and extending to the temple. Attacks occur approximately twice monthly and last between six and twelve hours if untreated. She often feels nauseated and has vomited on two occasions. Bright light is particularly uncomfortable during an attack, and she prefers to lie in a quiet, dark room. There is no associated limb weakness, facial droop, speech disturbance, collapse or persistent visual loss.

The headaches are more likely after missed meals and during periods of poor sleep. She has noticed no clear relationship with her menstrual cycle. She denies fever, neck stiffness, recent head injury or unexplained weight loss. Simple paracetamol has provided little benefit. She has used sumatriptan on three occasions, with partial relief, and takes naproxen with food when the pain begins. She is not taking these medicines on a daily basis.

She appeared well between attacks and was alert and appropriately conversational. Blood pressure was 124/78 mmHg and pulse 72 bpm, regular. Cranial nerves were intact, with normal pupils, eye movements and visual fields to confrontation. There was no facial asymmetry. Power, tone, sensation and coordination were normal in all four limbs, and gait was steady. Fundoscopy was unremarkable bilaterally. There was no scalp tenderness or neck rigidity.

We discussed that the pattern is most consistent with migraine without aura. There are no current red-flag features or examination findings to suggest raised intracranial pressure, although she was advised to seek urgent assessment through A&E if a sudden maximal headache, new neurological symptom, persistent vomiting, fever with neck stiffness or significant visual change develops.

Assessment

Recurrent migraine without aura, with nausea and photophobia. Current frequency does not suggest medication-overuse headache.

Plan

She will continue sumatriptan at the onset of a typical attack, following the prescribed dose instructions, and may take naproxen with food if required. She understands not to combine naproxen with other anti-inflammatory painkillers and to avoid using acute medicines on more than ten days per month. A headache diary was recommended, including possible triggers, duration, menstrual timing and response to treatment. Regular meals, adequate fluids, consistent sleep and limiting excess caffeine were discussed.

A routine blood test request has been made to exclude anaemia and thyroid dysfunction; no urgent imaging is indicated at present. The report/accession ID is 26/351462. If attacks become more frequent, prolonged or less responsive, she will arrange review to consider preventive treatment and possible referral to a consultant neurologist.

She will contact the surgery with an update in six to eight weeks. The preferred contact number recorded is 07700 900547.

Discharge summary

Patient: amita harding
Discharging organisation: Ulster Hospital
Report/accession ID: 0696351994

Reason for admission

amita harding was admitted with a five-day history of worsening lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge and deep dyspareunia. She had also reported urinary frequency but no dysuria, haematuria or gastrointestinal bleeding. There was no history of vomiting or collapse. Pregnancy testing was negative.

Assessment and hospital course

On arrival she was haemodynamically stable and afebrile. Abdominal examination demonstrated suprapubic and bilateral iliac fossa tenderness without guarding or rebound. Pelvic examination identified mucopurulent cervical discharge and cervical excitation. Initial blood tests showed a mildly raised C-reactive protein and white cell count; renal and liver profiles were satisfactory. Urinalysis did not suggest a urinary tract infection. A pelvic ultrasound showed no tubo-ovarian abscess or significant free fluid.

The clinical picture was consistent with pelvic inflammatory disease. Vaginal and endocervical samples were taken before treatment. The microbiology report subsequently showed no gonorrhoea or chlamydia detected; this does not exclude polymicrobial pelvic inflammatory disease. Report/accession ID 0696351994 was used for the associated laboratory result.

She received ceftriaxone at presentation, followed by doxycycline and metronidazole. Analgesia was provided with regular paracetamol and short-term oral ibuprofen, with good improvement in pain and mobility. She remained clinically stable, tolerated oral medication and was able to eat and drink. There was no indication for surgical intervention or inpatient drainage.

Discharge treatment

Continue doxycycline 100 mg twice daily to complete a 14-day course and metronidazole 400 mg twice daily to complete the same course. Avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole and for 48 hours after the final dose. Simple analgesia may be taken as directed on the packet, provided there is no contraindication. Ceftriaxone was given in hospital and does not require continuation.

She was advised to avoid sexual intercourse until treatment is complete, symptoms have resolved and any partners have been assessed and treated where appropriate. Condoms should be used thereafter. The importance of completing both antibiotic courses was discussed.

Follow-up and safety-netting

A sexual health clinic review has been requested in about 9 weeks, with earlier assessment if symptoms persist. She should contact her GP surgery or the sexual health service if pain, discharge or dyspareunia has not substantially improved within 72 hours. She should attend A&E urgently for increasing abdominal pain, fever, persistent vomiting, fainting or heavy vaginal bleeding.

Discharged home in a stable condition. The summary was reviewed by cecilia-rose turnbull, consultant physician, GMC number 0017097.

Emergency Department Handover – 2022-07-02

Patient: Brogun
Report/accession ID: 06480969
Healthcare organisation: The Royal London Hospital Whitechapel Rd

Presenting problem
Several days of worsening lower abdominal pain, now bilateral and constant, with abnormal offensive vaginal discharge and deep dyspareunia. No collapse or heavy vaginal bleeding. Mild nausea, no vomiting. Reports urinary frequency but no dysuria. Last menstrual period not documented at triage. C. Daniel, her relative, is available by telephone if needed.

Assessment
Alert and communicating appropriately. Temperature 37.8°C, pulse 96 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturations 99% on air. Current pain 5/10. Abdomen soft, with suprapubic and bilateral lower-quadrant tenderness; no guarding or rebound. No costovertebral-angle tenderness.

Speculum examination: mucopurulent discharge from the cervical os, cervix friable. Bimanual examination produces cervical excitation and bilateral adnexal tenderness, without a definite mass. Chaperone present. Pregnancy test negative. No clinical features of shock or acute abdomen.

Investigations
FBC: mild neutrophilia; haemoglobin satisfactory. CRP mildly raised. U&Es and liver profile acceptable. Urinalysis with trace leucocytes, no convincing urinary infection. Vaginal and endocervical swabs taken for gonorrhoea and chlamydia NAAT, microscopy and culture. Results pending; report linked to accession ID above.

Working diagnosis and plan
Clinical pelvic inflammatory disease, with no current evidence of tubo-ovarian abscess or sepsis. Discussed examination findings, sexually transmitted infection testing, partner notification and abstinence until treatment is complete and partners have been assessed. Offered analgesia with paracetamol; avoid intercourse while symptomatic.

Commence ceftriaxone as a stat dose, followed by doxycycline and metronidazole according to local antimicrobial guidance. Check allergy status and provide written medicines advice, including avoiding alcohol with metronidazole. She is suitable for ambulatory management, provided observations remain stable.

Discharge safety-net: return to A&E for increasing pain, fever, vomiting, faintness, heavy bleeding or inability to take tablets. GP or sexual health review within 72 hours; urgent gynaecology review if not improving after 48–72 hours.

Date: 02/03/2023

Dear Colleague,

Re: Abdulrazaq, MRN 001416410

I am referring Abdulrazaq from Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh for specialist assessment and advice regarding suspected generalised anxiety disorder. The specific question is whether the current presentation would benefit from psychological therapy, medication adjustment, or both, and whether any further assessment is required to exclude a physical contributor to the symptoms.

Abdulrazaq describes persistent, difficult-to-control worry across several areas of life, accompanied by muscle tension, irritability and poor sleep. They report lying awake for prolonged periods with repetitive thoughts and waking unrefreshed. Sleep is disturbed, but they are still managing basic daily activities. There is no history of panic-related collapse, mania, psychosis or previous psychiatric admission. They deny thoughts of harming themselves or anyone else, and identified supportive family contact as a protective factor.

They have also noticed intermittent pressure-type headaches for 3 days, without visual loss, focal weakness, facial asymmetry, fever or neck stiffness. Examination in the surgery was reassuring: alert and appropriately engaged, with normal speech and gait. Blood pressure was 128/78 mmHg, pulse 76 beats per minute and oxygen saturation 98% on air. There was mild trapezius muscle tenderness, but no focal neurological deficit. Recent blood tests, including full blood count, thyroid function, ferritin, vitamin B12 and renal profile, were within the laboratory reference ranges.

Sertraline has been taken regularly at the current prescribed dose, with partial improvement in the intensity of the worry but continuing sleep disturbance and tension. There have been no troublesome adverse effects. We discussed taking it consistently, avoiding abrupt discontinuation, limiting caffeine in the afternoon and keeping a regular sleep routine. I have advised against using alcohol as a sleep aid. A brief safety plan was agreed: if suicidal thoughts emerge or become difficult to resist, Abdulrazaq should contact the GP surgery urgently, NHS 111, or attend A&E in an emergency.

Please could your service review the diagnosis and advise on an appropriate evidence-based talking therapy, such as cognitive behavioural therapy, together with recommendations about whether sertraline should be continued or altered. I would also welcome guidance on managing the current headaches if they persist or change character.

Yours faithfully,

zeenah french
General Practitioner

text:
NHS LABORATORY MEDICINE REPORT

Patient: RUIEN MOORE
Report/accession ID: LAB-08664712
Specimen: Serum, venous blood
Clinical information: Acute monoarthritis with joint pain, swelling and erythema affecting the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Request states suspected gout flare; current treatment includes naproxen and colchicine.

Results

Analyte                         Result             Reference interpretation
Urate                           510 µmol/L         Raised; typical adult reference interval 210–420 µmol/L
Creatinine                      118 µmol/L         Mildly increased; interpret with eGFR and baseline
eGFR (CKD-EPI)                  59 mL/min/1.73 m²   Reduced
C-reactive protein              46 mg/L             Raised
Full blood count:
  Haemoglobin                   138 g/L             Within expected range
  White cell count              10.8 × 10⁹/L        Upper end of reference interval
  Neutrophils                   8.2 × 10⁹/L         Mild neutrophilia
  Platelets                     328 × 10⁹/L         Within expected range

Interpretive comment

The serum urate concentration is substantially elevated at 510 µmol/L and supports hyperuricaemia in the stated clinical context. The raised C-reactive protein and neutrophil count are compatible with an acute inflammatory episode but are not specific for gout. Serum urate may fall during an acute attack; a result within the reference interval would therefore not exclude gout.

The renal impairment is relevant to prescribing. Please review renal function, hydration and concomitant medicines before continuing or escalating naproxen or colchicine. Avoid additional non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. If the diagnosis remains uncertain, joint aspiration for crystal analysis and microscopy should be considered, particularly if there is fever, systemic illness or concern about septic arthritis.

A repeat serum urate measurement is best obtained after the flare has settled, with subsequent assessment against the agreed treat-to-target strategy if urate-lowering therapy is initiated. The result should be interpreted alongside previous renal function and cardiovascular risk.

Specimen quality: No significant haemolysis or lipaemia detected. The reported creatinine and eGFR should be correlated with the patient’s usual baseline; eGFR is an estimate and may be less reliable during acute illness.

Planned review: 8 Dec 2024

Report validated by: Dr Suheib Childs, MBBS, laboratory physician
GMC professional identifier: 0165150

Nursing progress note
NHS number: 000 714 4904

Patient: SASKA SIMS  
Address: 161 ASHLEIGH MANOR, BANBRIDGE  
Gestation: 9+4 weeks' gestation  
Contact detail: 07700 900208

SASKA SIMS remains admitted under the early pregnancy team at Ulster Hospital with first-trimester hyperemesis. She reports persistent vomiting since yesterday evening, with four further episodes during this shift, mainly small amounts of clear fluid and bile. She describes ongoing nausea but no abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, dysuria or diarrhoea. Her relative, SIFN LANGLEY, was updated by telephone with the patient’s consent.

On review, she was alert and appropriately orientated but looked tired and mildly pale. Oral mucosa remains dry. Pulse 104 bpm, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturations 98% on air and temperature 36.7°C. Weight recorded as 61.8 kg, with a reported loss of approximately 2.5 kg over the past two weeks. Capillary blood glucose was 4.8 mmol/L. Urine remains concentrated; she has passed approximately 250 mL since the start of the shift and reports light-headedness when standing, although there has been no fall. Abdomen soft and non-tender. No calf pain or swelling noted.

A peripheral cannula remains patent in the left forearm. Intravenous sodium chloride was commenced as prescribed and infused without swelling, redness or discomfort at the site. Cyclizine was administered as prescribed, with partial improvement in nausea after approximately 40 minutes. She subsequently managed a few sips of oral rehydration solution and half a slice of toast, but vomited after attempting more fluid. Mouth care provided and emesis documented. She was encouraged to take frequent small sips rather than larger volumes and to avoid strong smells. Dietary advice leaflet offered.

Mobilising only with supervision because of postural dizziness. Falls precautions maintained, with the call bell within reach and advice to seek assistance before getting out of bed. Fluid balance chart updated. No signs of acute abdominal complication or haemodynamic instability at present.

Assessment

Ongoing vomiting with clinical dehydration and poor oral intake, with only partial response to cyclizine. Tachycardia persists but blood pressure is maintained. Urine output remains low and requires close monitoring.

Plan for next shift

Continue prescribed intravenous sodium chloride and cyclizine, reassessing effect and cannula site. Maintain strict fluid balance, including further urine measurements, and repeat observations after fluids. Encourage small, frequent sips and gradual oral intake as tolerated. Review blood results when available, including electrolytes and ketones, and escalate promptly to the medical or early pregnancy team if vomiting continues, urine output falls, ketones rise, observations deteriorate or she is unable to maintain any oral intake. Confirm ongoing support and discharge contact arrangements with SIFN LANGLEY before discharge planning.

NHS outpatient clinic note
NHS number: 0007109548

Patient: Prabh
MRN: 06606132
Seen at Sittingbourne Hospital
Occupation: Baker

Prabh was reviewed today with a three-week history of intermittent dizziness. The episodes are brought on by turning in bed, looking upwards, or bending down, and usually last less than a minute. There is a clear sensation that the room is moving rather than light-headedness or impending faint. Nausea accompanies the more severe episodes, although there has been no vomiting. The patient reports mild unsteadiness immediately afterwards but is walking independently.

There is no hearing loss, tinnitus, ear pain, diplopia, dysarthria, limb weakness, facial numbness, collapse or new headache. No recent head injury was reported. The patient has also had a separate mild sore throat for 3 days, without fever, cough or swallowing difficulty. This has not been associated with the dizziness.

On examination, observations were within the expected range. The patient was alert and communicated normally. Cranial nerves were intact, with no spontaneous nystagmus. Limb power, sensation and coordination were normal. Gait was steady in the room, although the patient felt briefly unsteady after lying down and sitting up. Dix–Hallpike testing reproduced the typical brief vertigo, with torsional nystagmus on head positioning to the right. Symptoms settled within approximately 30 seconds. There were no focal neurological findings.

The presentation is most consistent with right-sided benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. The short, position-related attacks and positive positional test are reassuring against a central neurological cause. The sore throat appears clinically mild and unrelated.

Assessment

Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, right-sided, with associated nausea and transient unsteadiness. Mild acute sore throat without concerning features.

Plan

The diagnosis and expected course were discussed. A right-sided Epley manoeuvre was demonstrated and completed in clinic, with written instructions provided for careful repetition at home if symptoms recur. The patient was advised to rise slowly, use the handrail on stairs and avoid driving, cycling or working at height while actively dizzy. Prochlorperazine may be taken as required for troublesome nausea, in accordance with the existing prescription; regular use was discouraged as it can cause drowsiness and may slow vestibular compensation.

Fluids, rest and simple analgesia were advised for the sore throat if required. The patient will contact the GP surgery if this is not improving. Urgent assessment via A&E is advised for persistent severe headache, new hearing loss, inability to walk, fainting, chest pain, double vision, speech disturbance or weakness/numbness. If the vertigo has not substantially improved after two to four weeks, or if episodes become spontaneous rather than positional, the GP should reassess and consider vestibular physiotherapy or ENT referral.

Seen and documented by Nylah-Mae Sanderson.

Discharge summary

Patient: honie hunt
Age: 40 y/o
Home address: 158 Merchants Road, Crossapol, PA77 6AB
Contact detail: honie.hunt19@outlook.com

honie hunt was admitted under the early pregnancy team after several days of persistent vomiting, with difficulty keeping down fluids and a noticeable loss of weight. At admission she was 9+4 weeks' gestation. Clinical assessment was consistent with first-trimester hyperemesis complicated by dehydration. There was no history to suggest abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding or urinary infection.

Initial blood tests showed a mild rise in urea and ketones, in keeping with reduced intake. Electrolytes were satisfactory apart from a small reduction in bicarbonate. Liver tests and full blood count were reassuring. Urinalysis confirmed ketones. A pregnancy ultrasound demonstrated a single intrauterine pregnancy with cardiac activity, measuring appropriately for the gestational age. No procedure was required.

She was treated with intravenous sodium chloride and monitored on the assessment ward. Thiamine was given before any glucose-containing fluid. Antiemetic treatment with cyclizine led to a clear reduction in vomiting, and she was gradually able to tolerate oral rehydration solution, soup and small meals. Her urine output improved, observations remained stable and repeat blood tests showed correction of the dehydration markers. Her weight was documented before discharge so that this can be reviewed at follow-up.

Please continue cyclizine as prescribed on the discharge medicines list, taking it regularly for the next few days and then reducing it as your symptoms settle. Take frequent small sips of fluid and eat little and often; bland or cold foods may be easier to manage. Avoid becoming completely without food for prolonged periods. If you cannot keep fluids or medicines down for 12 hours, pass very little urine, feel faint, develop severe abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding or fever, attend A&E urgently or contact your maternity assessment service.

The early pregnancy team will arrange review to reassess symptoms, hydration and weight. Your GP surgery should be informed of this admission and can continue prescribing anti-sickness medication if needed. Please bring this summary to any maternity or GP appointment.

At discharge, honie hunt was alert, haemodynamically stable and managing oral fluids without further vomiting. The plan and safety-netting advice were discussed, and contact details were confirmed as honie.hunt19@outlook.com.

Prepared by the admitting consultant obstetrician, GMC professional identifier GMC 0815888.

Emergency Department Assessment
NHS number: 000 936 1112

Patient: Nyomi WILKINS
Home address: 43 City Road, Llanfair-ym-Muallt / Builth Wells, LD2 3AA
36-year-old African-American female patient, attended A&E with an abrupt episode of racing heartbeat, central chest tightness and intense fear that she was dying. Symptoms began while on a crowded bus and peaked within approximately 10 minutes. She reported tingling around the mouth, tremulousness and rapid breathing. No syncope, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, unilateral leg swelling or recent infective symptoms. Similar, less severe episode six months ago. No known cardiac history.

At 08:15 she remained anxious but was speaking in full sentences. T 36.7°C, HR 112 initially, BP 148/86, RR 26, SpO₂ 99% on air. After coached slow breathing, HR reduced to 86 and chest tightness resolved. Heart sounds normal with no murmur; chest clear bilaterally. No calf tenderness or swelling. Neurology grossly normal. There was no suicidal ideation or psychotic symptomatology.

Investigations
12-lead ECG: sinus tachycardia, no ST-segment change or conduction abnormality. Chest radiograph clear. FBC, U&E, magnesium and glucose within reference range. High-sensitivity troponin below the reporting threshold; repeat sample not indicated given symptom resolution, non-ischaemic ECG and very low clinical risk.

Assessment and plan
Presentation is most consistent with an acute panic attack with hyperventilation. No current evidence of acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax or significant arrhythmia. No sedative medication required in the department. Breathing retraining practised at the bedside, with written advice to continue this during future episodes and to reduce caffeine.

Safety-netting given: return immediately for persistent or exertional chest pain, collapse, breathlessness, sustained palpitations or new neurological symptoms. Advised to contact GP for assessment of recurrent panic symptoms and consideration of talking therapy. Follow-up review arranged for 13 September 2035.

Discharged home in a stable condition with her usual breathing retraining plan. Assessment and discharge advice discussed with Dr Chahat Cook, MBBS, Emergency Medicine clinician.

Dear Colleague,

Re: Fia

Address: 71 ST. JOHNS PLACE EAST, ROSTREVOR
Occupation: Taxi driver
Employer: MAGHERAMASON Sports Club

Thank you for assessing this patient with established Parkinson disease. I am referring them for a specialist review of increasing motor symptoms, medication response and functional decline, with advice regarding optimisation of treatment and multidisciplinary support.

History and current concerns

The diagnosis of Parkinson disease was previously assessed and confirmed by neurology. Co-beneldopa was initiated following specialist assessment, and prescribing has subsequently been continued in primary care. The current regimen is co-beneldopa 25/100 mg three times daily, taken before meals. There have been no recent medication changes.

Over the past several months, the patient has noticed a gradually more prominent resting tremor, initially affecting the right hand and now intermittently present on the left. They describe slowness when dressing, preparing meals and rising from a chair, together with muscular rigidity on waking. They have not reported a definite fall, syncope or loss of consciousness. There is occasional start hesitation when turning in confined spaces, although no clear freezing episode has been documented. Speech is quieter than previously, but swallowing remains satisfactory and there is no choking history.

They remain employed by MAGHERAMASON Sports Club as Taxi driver. Increasing time is required for routine tasks, and they are concerned about maintaining work and household activities. Mood is variable in relation to reduced mobility, without suicidal thoughts. There are no reported hallucinations, marked daytime somnolence or impulse-control symptoms.

Examination in primary care

There is a low-amplitude resting tremor of the right hand, with re-emergence on maintaining posture. Bradykinesia is evident on finger tapping and rapid alternating movements, more marked on the right. Tone is increased at both wrists, again with right-sided predominance. Gait is slow with reduced right arm swing; stride length is mildly shortened, but balance on the pull test is preserved. No focal limb weakness was identified. Blood pressure was 132/78 mmHg seated, with no clinically significant postural symptoms.

Recent blood tests showed normal full blood count, thyroid function, liver profile and vitamin B12. Renal function was adequate for current prescribing. Medication adherence is reported to be good, although the patient is unsure whether the benefit consistently lasts until the next dose.

Reason for referral and requested action

I would be grateful for review by the movement-disorders team to confirm the current treatment response and advise whether co-beneldopa timing or dose requires adjustment. Please also consider physiotherapy, occupational therapy and assessment of gait, balance and work-related function. Advice regarding screening for non-motor symptoms and future advance care planning would be appreciated.

Yours sincerely,

R. WATSON

NHS LABORATORY MEDICINE REPORT

Patient: ATTA MARSH
MRN: 070967/77
Home address: 9 Geesh Road, Fareham, PO14 1AA
Specimen: Serum
Clinical indication: Acute joint pain with swelling and erythema, clinically consistent with a gout flare. Current treatment recorded as naproxen and colchicine. Ordering clinician not stated.

Investigations

Serum urate: 510 µmol/L
Reference interval: 200–430 µmol/L
Interpretation: Increased

C-reactive protein: 34 mg/L
Reference interval: <5 mg/L
Interpretation: Increased

Creatinine: 92 µmol/L
Reference interval: 60–110 µmol/L
Interpretation: Within reference interval

Estimated glomerular filtration rate (CKD-EPI): 78 mL/min/1.73 m²
Interpretation: Mildly reduced; interpret alongside age, previous results and clinical context

Alanine aminotransferase: 27 U/L
Reference interval: 0–40 U/L
Interpretation: Within reference interval

Full blood count:
Haemoglobin 146 g/L (130–170 g/L)
White cell count 9.8 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L)
Platelets 318 ×10⁹/L (150–400 ×10⁹/L)

Specimen comment

The sample was received as serum and was suitable for analysis. No significant haemolysis, icterus or lipaemia was identified. The reported urate concentration of 510 µmol/L is above the usual adult reference interval and supports hyperuricaemia in the context of the described acute monoarticular inflammatory symptoms.

Clinical interpretation

The biochemical findings are compatible with a current inflammatory episode and provide supportive evidence for gout, although serum urate alone cannot establish the diagnosis. Urate may fall during an acute attack; a normal result would therefore not exclude gout. Where diagnostic uncertainty persists, aspiration of the affected joint for polarised microscopy and culture should be considered, particularly if septic arthritis is a possibility.

Renal function is adequate for the present laboratory assessment, with mild reduction in estimated filtration. Continued review is appropriate if naproxen or colchicine is prescribed beyond the acute period. Please correlate with gastrointestinal, renal and cardiovascular risk factors, concomitant medicines and response to treatment. Escalating pain, fever, systemic illness or inability to move the joint should prompt urgent clinical assessment.

If urate-lowering therapy is being considered, treatment is generally reviewed after the acute inflammation has settled, with serial urate monitoring against the agreed clinical target. A repeat biochemical assessment may be useful during follow-up.

Planned clinical review: 24th February 1989

Validated and reported by sholah perkins
Laboratory medicine clinician
Interpretive comment: This report should be read with the clinical assessment and any joint-fluid microbiology or crystal analysis available.

Nursing Progress Note
NHS number: 000 002 4237

Patient: Nikoletta PERRY
Home address: 137 Drumlaken Path, West Linton, EH46 7AA
Clinical report/accession ID: 0833150296

Current assessment
36-year-old Black male patient admitted with confirmed pulmonary embolism. Reports sudden breathlessness has eased at rest but remains short of breath on mobilisation. Pleuritic right-sided chest pain persists, currently rated 5/10. Denies haemoptysis, dizziness or new calf pain. Alert and orientated, speaking in full sentences.

Observations
Respiratory rate 22/min, oxygen saturation 95% on 2 L/min via nasal cannula, pulse 104 bpm and regular, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, temperature 37.1°C. Chest expansion equal with mild bibasal reduction in air entry; no audible wheeze. Skin warm and dry. No signs of acute deterioration at time of review.

Mobility and intake
Mobilises short distances to the ensuite with one staff member and oxygen in place. Becomes visibly breathless after approximately 10 metres and requires a seated recovery period. Falls precautions maintained; call bell left within reach. Ate around half of lunch and tolerated oral fluids. Encouraged small, frequent drinks. Passing urine independently; no bowel movement reported this shift.

Treatment and response
Apixaban administered as prescribed; no bleeding, melaena, haematuria or new bruising observed. Supplemental oxygen continued at 2 L/min, maintaining target saturations. Repositioned upright for comfort and pacing of activity discussed. Following rest and analgesia prescribed for pleuritic discomfort, pain reduced from 5/10 to 3/10 and respiratory effort settled. No nausea.

Risk and escalation
Bleeding risk reviewed in view of anticoagulation. Advised to report worsening chest pain, increased breathlessness, coughing blood, faintness or bleeding. Medical team contacted earlier regarding persistent tachycardia on mobilisation; plan remains observation and oxygen therapy. GMC professional identifier for the reviewing doctor: 0099402. Escalate immediately to the nurse in charge and medical team if oxygen requirement rises, systolic blood pressure falls, respiratory rate exceeds 30/min, or conscious level changes.

Plan for next shift
- Repeat full observations, including oxygen saturation and response to mobilisation.
- Continue apixaban and prescribed oxygen; check administration record and monitor for adverse effects.
- Maintain falls precautions and supervised mobilisation.
- Reassess pleuritic pain and response to analgesia.
- Encourage oral intake and document urine output.
- Confirm ongoing medical review and update the patient regarding discharge planning when clinically appropriate.

Nursing handover: currently stable at rest, with exertional breathlessness requiring close observation.

Respiratory Outpatient Assessment

Patient: Abraar C.
Occupation: software developer
Employer: Sarn Mellteyrn Housing Association
Home address: 10 Mountford Close, Llangower, LL23 7AA
Preferred contact: abraar.clayton86@hotmail.com

Reason for review

Assessment of asthma control following several months of intermittent wheeze, night-time cough and episodic shortness of breath. The patient reports symptoms predominantly with cold air, brisk walking and exposure to household dust. There have been no emergency department attendances, hospital admissions or courses of oral corticosteroids since the previous review. No haemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, fever or unexplained weight loss is described.

Current treatment and adherence

The patient is prescribed a salbutamol inhaler as required and a beclometasone inhaler regularly. Salbutamol has been used on approximately three days per week, usually one or two puffs at a time, with good short-term relief. The beclometasone inhaler is taken most mornings, although evening doses are occasionally missed. Inhaler technique was observed: the patient initially actuated the inhaler before sealing the lips around the mouthpiece, but technique improved following demonstration and teach-back. A spacer was recommended for use with both inhalers if compatible with the prescribed devices.

Clinical findings

The patient was comfortable at rest and able to speak in full sentences. Respiratory rate was 16/min, oxygen saturation 98% on air, pulse 74 bpm and temperature 36.7°C. There was no cyanosis or peripheral oedema. Chest examination demonstrated mild bilateral polyphonic expiratory wheeze, without focal crackles. Heart sounds were normal. Peak expiratory flow was 410 L/min, compared with a reported personal best of approximately 470 L/min.

Spirometry performed in clinic showed FEV1 2.86 L (86% predicted), FVC 3.74 L (94% predicted) and FEV1/FVC 0.76. Following bronchodilator administration, FEV1 increased by 14% and 420 mL, supporting variable airflow obstruction. FeNO was 42 ppb, consistent with ongoing type 2 airway inflammation in the appropriate clinical context. The findings were reviewed with the patient by the consultant respiratory physician.

Impression

Asthma with currently suboptimal symptom control, most likely related to inconsistent preventer use and imperfect inhaler technique. There is no clinical evidence today of an acute exacerbation or infection.

Plan

Continue beclometasone inhaler at the prescribed dose, with emphasis on twice-daily regular use and mouth rinsing afterwards. Continue salbutamol inhaler as required, whilst monitoring frequency of use. The patient was given a written asthma action plan and advised to seek urgent medical attention if reliever treatment is required more frequently than every four hours, symptoms rapidly worsen, or speech becomes limited by breathlessness.

Avoidance of identified dust triggers and annual influenza vaccination were discussed. The patient will record morning and evening peak flow readings for two weeks. Review in respiratory clinic is planned after this period to reassess control and consider adjustment of preventer therapy.

Discharge summary for NOEMI MCMILLAN
NHS number: 0003486606

Encounter date: 02/05/2012
Age: 65 y/o

You were admitted after two days of frequent watery diarrhoea, vomiting and cramping abdominal pain. On arrival you were mildly dehydrated, with a dry mouth and a faster-than-usual pulse, but your blood pressure remained stable. There was no blood in the stool, persistent fever or concerning abdominal tenderness. Your current pain score is 5/10.

Blood tests showed a mild rise in urea consistent with dehydration. Kidney function and inflammatory markers improved after treatment. A stool sample was sent because of the frequency of the diarrhoea; no significant bacterial pathogen was identified. There was no clinical evidence of appendicitis, bowel obstruction or another condition requiring surgery. Your symptoms were felt to be due to infectious gastroenteritis, most likely viral.

During your stay you were given small, frequent amounts of oral rehydration solution and anti-sickness treatment with ondansetron when needed. You gradually tolerated fluids and then light meals. Vomiting stopped, urine output returned to normal and the diarrhoea became less frequent. Intravenous fluids were not required. You are now medically fit for discharge and can continue your recovery at home.

Discharge medicines

• Oral rehydration solution: prepare and take according to the packet instructions, particularly after each loose stool. Continue until you are eating and drinking normally.
• Ondansetron: take as required for nausea, in line with the labelled instructions supplied by the hospital. Do not take more frequently than advised.
• No antibiotics are required at present.

At home, take frequent sips of water or oral rehydration fluid and eat small, plain meals as tolerated. Avoid alcohol, very fatty food and large amounts of fruit juice until your bowel habit has settled. Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water after using the toilet and before preparing food. Do not prepare food for other people while you have diarrhoea or vomiting and for 48 hours after these symptoms stop.

Please contact your GP surgery if diarrhoea is not clearly improving within five days, if vomiting prevents you keeping fluids down, or if you develop ongoing abdominal pain, fever or reduced urine output. Attend A&E urgently if you become faint or confused, pass blood or black stool, develop severe abdominal pain, or cannot drink.

Your relative, Syona Sanders, who is based in LAURELVALE, was updated with your agreement. A discharge letter will be sent to your GP. No routine hospital follow-up is needed unless symptoms fail to settle or the stool result is subsequently amended.

Re: Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk assessment
NHS number: 0000507831

Patient: samar richards

Dear Genetics Team,

I am referring samar richards for assessment of a substantial family history of breast and ovarian cancer. The specific question is whether the pattern is consistent with a hereditary cancer syndrome and whether predictive germline testing is appropriate for the patient.

samar richards reports that their mother was diagnosed with breast cancer at 42 and subsequently developed ovarian cancer. A maternal aunt had breast cancer before the age of 50, and a maternal grandfather had pancreatic cancer. The family has not previously had a confirmed genetic diagnosis, although a relative’s paperwork refers to the variant BRCA1 c.68_69delAG. It is not currently clear whether this result has been independently verified or whether it relates to an affected family member.

The patient is currently well, with no breast lump, nipple discharge, unexplained weight loss or persistent abdominal symptoms. They are understandably worried about their own future cancer risk and are requesting predictive testing. There is no current treatment and they take no regular medicines. They have not had previous breast or ovarian surgery. They report no previous genetic counselling and have not received mammographic or MRI surveillance outside the routine screening programme.

At review, the patient was well appearing. There was no palpable cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy. Breast and abdominal examination were unremarkable, with no focal mass, skin change, organomegaly or ascites. These findings do not exclude an inherited predisposition, and I have explained that genetic testing is most informative when an affected relative is tested first, where this is possible.

Please review the available family history, clarify the significance of the reported BRCA1 variant, and advise on the most appropriate testing pathway. I would be grateful for pre-test counselling covering possible results, implications for screening and risk-reducing treatment, and the potential relevance to adult relatives. Jem Aston, the patient’s adult sibling, is aware of the referral and may be able to help obtain further family records.

Please correspond with the patient and copy me into the outcome. I am the referring clinician based in Braeswick.

Yours sincerely,

SABIRAH AKRAM
GMC: 0695920

GLANGWILI GENERAL HOSPITAL
NHS number: 0001152638
Clinical Microbiology and Biochemistry Laboratory Report

Patient: Lana-Rae Hamid
Report/accession ID: LAB-00121407
Specimen: Midstream urine
Clinical details: Acute febrile urinary tract infection with flank pain, dysuria and rigors. Current treatment recorded as cefuroxime and paracetamol.

Specimen quality and processing
Urine received in a sterile container and processed promptly. The sample was suitable for culture. Microscopy demonstrated numerous polymorphs and significant bacteriuria. No epithelial-cell excess was identified to suggest substantial contamination.

Urine microscopy
White cells: >100 × 10^6/L
Red cells: 18 × 10^6/L
Bacteria: Numerous
Squamous epithelial cells: <10 × 10^6/L

Culture
Significant growth of Escherichia coli, >10^5 colony-forming units/mL, in a predominantly pure growth.

Antimicrobial susceptibility
Cefuroxime: Susceptible
Co-amoxiclav: Susceptible
Trimethoprim: Resistant
Ciprofloxacin: Susceptible
Nitrofurantoin: Susceptible for lower urinary tract infection only; this result should not be used to guide treatment of pyelonephritis.

Interpretive comment
The findings support a clinically significant E. coli urinary tract infection and are compatible with acute pyelonephritis in the context of flank pain and rigors. The isolate is susceptible to cefuroxime, so the current prescription is microbiologically appropriate provided the patient is clinically improving and renal function permits standard dosing. Nitrofurantoin should not be substituted for cefuroxime in suspected renal parenchymal infection, despite in-vitro susceptibility.

If fever, rigors, vomiting, hypotension or worsening flank pain persists, urgent clinical reassessment is advised, with consideration of blood cultures, repeat renal function testing and imaging to exclude obstruction or a renal abscess. Patients who become systemically unwell should be directed to the emergency department. Antibiotic duration should follow local NHS antimicrobial guidance and the treating clinician’s assessment.

Additional laboratory findings
Serum creatinine: 89 µmol/L (reference interval 45–90 µmol/L)
Estimated glomerular filtration rate: 78 mL/min/1.73 m²
C-reactive protein: 146 mg/L (reference interval <5 mg/L)
White cell count: 14.8 × 10^9/L (reference interval 4.0–11.0 × 10^9/L)
Neutrophils: 12.6 × 10^9/L (reference interval 2.0–7.5 × 10^9/L)

These inflammatory markers are consistent with an acute bacterial infection. Renal function is currently adequate for usual cefuroxime dosing, subject to clinical review and any subsequent change in results. The urine culture result should be interpreted alongside temperature, blood pressure, hydration status and response to treatment.

A clinical review is recommended in 10 days, with follow-up appointment recorded for 2020-08-25.

Validated and reported by: emmaleigh garner
Laboratory clinician
GLANGWILI GENERAL HOSPITAL

Nursing progress note
Date: 2021-02-24
Patient: Roksana, a 50-year-old Black woman
Diagnosis: Infectious gastroenteritis

Assessment
Reviewed on the ward this morning. Ongoing watery diarrhoea and intermittent vomiting for 3 days, with cramping central abdominal pain before opening her bowels. No reported blood or mucus. She feels generally weak but denies chest pain, breathlessness or dysuria. Nausea reduced following ondansetron.

Observations at 09:20: temperature 37.8°C, pulse 96 bpm regular, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturations 98% on air. Alert and orientated, mildly dry oral mucosa. Abdomen soft, with mild diffuse tenderness and no guarding or rebound. Peripheral perfusion satisfactory.

Fluid balance
Two loose stools and one small vomit recorded since midnight. Took approximately 450 mL oral fluids, including oral rehydration solution, and managed half a bowl of soup and a banana at breakfast. Urine passed this morning; dark yellow but not offensive. Encouraged frequent small sips and ongoing intake recording.

Care delivered
Ondansetron administered as required at 08:40 for nausea, with good effect and no further vomiting during review. Oral rehydration solution offered regularly. Assisted to the bathroom with one staff member; mobilises slowly but safely, reporting light-headedness on standing. Falls advice reinforced and call bell left within reach. Contact precautions maintained, with dedicated toilet facilities and hand hygiene support. Stool sample remains awaited if further loose stool is passed.

Risk and escalation
At risk of dehydration and falls due to gastrointestinal losses and postural symptoms. No evidence of acute abdomen at present. Escalate to nurse in charge and medical team if persistent vomiting, reduced urine output, worsening pain, fever, blood in stool, confusion or observations deteriorate. Relative Teague updated by the patient and aware of the current plan.

Plan for next shift
- Continue four-hourly observations and fluid balance chart.
- Repeat lying and standing blood pressure if dizziness persists.
- Offer oral rehydration solution little and often; monitor tolerance of diet.
- Administer ondansetron as prescribed when required and document response.
- Obtain and label stool specimen if diarrhoea recurs.
- Review hydration status and need for medical assessment during the next safety huddle.

Nurse: Aiva-Rose Hope

text:
Neurology Headache Clinic Specialist Report

Patient: isra ratcliffe
Age: 47 y/o
Date of assessment: 22/02/2022
Report/accession ID: 098460977
Patient contact: isra.ratcliffe25@btinternet.com

Reason for review

Assessment of recurrent unilateral headaches with associated nausea and photophobia, and review of current acute treatment with sumatriptan and naproxen.

History

The patient describes a longstanding episodic headache syndrome, currently occurring approximately twice monthly. Attacks are predominantly right-sided and pulsatile, with gradual escalation over 30–60 minutes before reaching peak intensity. Headache duration is usually 8–12 hours if untreated. Nausea and marked photophobia are present during attacks; there is no consistent vomiting, phonophobia, osmophobia or cranial autonomic feature. There is no preceding visual, sensory or speech disturbance to suggest aura.

There has been no sudden “thunderclap” onset, progressive change in headache pattern, headache precipitated by exertion or Valsalva, or persistent headache on waking. The patient denies transient loss of consciousness, seizure, limb weakness, sensory loss or sustained visual impairment. Sleep is occasionally disrupted by headache, but there are no constitutional symptoms.

Sumatriptan is taken at the onset of a typical attack, with naproxen when required. This combination is generally effective, although treatment is sometimes delayed because of nausea. Use of acute medication is limited to fewer than 10 days per month. No regular preventive migraine medication is currently being taken.

Examination

The patient appeared well and was fully orientated. Current pain score was 5/10. Speech and cognition were normal. Visual fields were full to confrontation, pupils were equal and reactive, and ocular movements were intact without nystagmus. Facial sensation and power were symmetrical. There was no pronator drift. Tone, power, coordination and sensation were normal in all four limbs. Gait, including tandem gait, was normal. No neck stiffness was demonstrated.

Interpretation

The clinical phenotype is consistent with migraine without aura. The recurrent stereotyped unilateral headache, nausea and photophobia, together with a normal neurological examination and absence of red-flag features, are reassuring. There is no current indication for neuroimaging solely on the information available today.

Plan

1. Continue sumatriptan at the onset of headache, with naproxen taken with food if required and clinically tolerated. The patient was advised not to combine naproxen with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
2. Avoid acute migraine medicines on more than 10 days in any calendar month to reduce the risk of medication-overuse headache.
3. Maintain regular meals, hydration, sleep and caffeine intake. A headache diary should record frequency, duration, triggers, menstrual association where relevant, medication timing and response.
4. If attacks become more frequent, prolonged or disabling, discuss preventive treatment with the GP or headache service.
5. Seek urgent assessment through A&E for a sudden maximal headache, new neurological deficit, persistent visual symptoms, fever with neck stiffness, or a substantial change in the established pattern.

Follow-up will be arranged if control deteriorates or the diagnosis becomes clinically uncertain.

Discharge summary

Patient: Johnjames Jama
Discharging service: Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh
Report/accession ID: 045755516

Reason for admission
Admitted via the emergency department with a two-day history of increasing redness, warmth and tenderness affecting the left lower leg. The erythema had extended proximally despite initial oral treatment in the community. There was no reported injury, animal bite or recent travel. She felt generally tired but denied rigors, vomiting, chest pain or breathlessness.

Assessment and key findings
On admission, there was a well-demarcated area of erythema and local warmth over the left shin, with mild swelling and tenderness on palpation. The skin was intact, without fluctuance, crepitus or clinical evidence of an abscess. Peripheral pulses and sensation were preserved. There was no calf asymmetry to suggest deep vein thrombosis. She remained haemodynamically stable and afebrile throughout the admission.

Initial blood tests showed a mildly raised white cell count and C-reactive protein, with preserved renal function and normal lactate. Blood cultures were not suggestive of bacteraemia. An ultrasound scan was considered because of the leg swelling, but was not required following serial examinations and a low clinical suspicion of venous thrombosis. The affected margin was marked to monitor progression.

Hospital course
The patient received intravenous flucloxacillin with regular analgesia. The erythema stopped spreading during the first 24 hours, and the local warmth and tenderness subsequently reduced. She remained able to mobilise independently and maintained oral intake. There was no collection requiring incision and drainage, and no surgical intervention was indicated.

After clinical improvement, treatment was stepped down to oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily to complete the prescribed course. Paracetamol was advised for discomfort, subject to the maximum daily dose. No adverse drug reaction was observed during the admission.

Problem list
1. Cellulitis of the lower leg, improving with antibiotics.
2. Local pain and swelling, improving.
3. No evidence of abscess, sepsis or deep vein thrombosis.

Discharge medicines
• Flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily, continuing until the course is complete.
• Paracetamol when required for pain, according to the packet instructions. Do not combine with other paracetamol-containing medicines.

Condition on discharge
Discharged home clinically well, with stable observations, improving erythema and a clear plan for community follow-up. The patient was able to walk safely and understood the medication instructions. A copy of this summary has been sent to the GP surgery for continuity of care. The admission and discharge plan were reviewed with Dr Aureya Oakley, MBBS.

Follow-up and safety-netting
The patient should arrange a GP review if the redness or swelling has not continued to improve after 48 hours, or sooner if there is concern. She should seek urgent help through NHS 111 or attend A&E if the redness spreads rapidly, pain becomes severe, the skin becomes blistered or dusky, or she develops fever, shaking chills, confusion, dizziness, vomiting or difficulty breathing. She was advised to elevate the leg when resting, keep the skin clean and dry, and avoid applying creams or dressings unless advised by a clinician.

Emergency contact information was confirmed as being available through a relative in Fanagmore.

Discharging clinician: Dr Aureya Oakley, MBBS

Emergency Department Assessment – 7 Apr 2024
NHS number: 0009146238

Patient: STANISLAW KIRK

STANISLAW KIRK was brought to the emergency department by Keaon IRVING with approximately two hours of central chest pressure. The discomfort began while he was sitting at home, was persistent, and was associated with marked diaphoresis and nausea. He described no pleuritic component and no preceding infective symptoms. There was no syncope, haemoptysis or unilateral calf swelling. Keaon IRVING reported that he appeared pale and clammy before arrival. No medication allergies were reported in the information available at triage.

On arrival he was alert and able to give a clear history. He appeared uncomfortable and mildly sweaty. Pulse was regular at 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 148/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturations 97% on air, and temperature 36.5°C. Heart sounds were normal with no murmur, and the chest was clear bilaterally. There was no clinical evidence of heart failure, and peripheral perfusion was satisfactory. The abdomen was soft and non-tender. Calves were symmetrical and non-tender.

A 12-lead ECG performed shortly after arrival showed sinus rhythm with approximately 1 mm horizontal ST depression in the lateral leads and T-wave inversion in leads V4–V6. There was no ST elevation. The patient was placed on continuous monitoring using the Model X3 cardiac monitor. Initial high-sensitivity troponin I was raised at 86 ng/L, with a repeat value of 214 ng/L after two hours. FBC, renal profile and clotting results were acceptable for treatment; potassium was 4.2 mmol/L and creatinine 91 micromol/L. Chest radiograph showed no focal consolidation, pleural effusion or widened mediastinum.

Assessment

The history, dynamic troponin rise and ischaemic ECG changes are consistent with a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. There was no evidence of cardiogenic shock, pulmonary oedema or an alternative acute thoracic diagnosis. The case was discussed with the cardiology team at BRONGLAIS GENERAL HOSPITAL.

Treatment and plan

Aspirin 300 mg was given orally after confirmation that there was no allergy or active bleeding. Fondaparinux was administered subcutaneously, and atorvastatin 80 mg was given. Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate relieved the pressure, with repeat blood pressure remaining stable. Analgesia and antiemetic treatment were offered, although the nausea settled promptly. He is to remain nil by mouth apart from medication pending cardiology review and possible early angiography. Further serial ECGs and troponin testing are planned, with repeat observations and escalation for recurrent pain or haemodynamic change.

Disposition

Admitted under cardiology from the emergency department for ongoing monitoring and management of NSTEMI. Rivan Cassidy, emergency clinician at BRONGLAIS GENERAL HOSPITAL, completed the assessment and discussed the plan with the patient and Keaon IRVING.

Date: 17th December 2025
NHS number: 0009496364

To: Movement Disorders Service

Re: Nash Black
Report/accession ID: 021828246
Referring organisation: ULSTER HOSPITAL

Reason for referral
Please review this patient with established Parkinson disease for assessment of current motor control, medication timing and multidisciplinary support. I would also value advice regarding optimisation of co-beneldopa and management of functional difficulties.

Clinical history
The diagnosis was previously assessed and confirmed by neurology. Co-beneldopa was initiated following specialist assessment and prescribing has subsequently been continued in primary care. The patient reports a gradually increasing resting tremor, predominantly affecting the right hand, with associated bradykinesia and muscular rigidity. Symptoms are more troublesome before the next dose and on waking. There have been no reported hallucinations, syncope or recent falls. Sleep is fragmented, with occasional difficulty turning in bed. Mood is generally stable, although the patient describes reduced confidence outdoors.

Current treatment
Co-beneldopa as prescribed, with doses taken at consistent times. No recent changes to dopaminergic medication. The patient understands the importance of avoiding unsupervised dose adjustments and reports no adverse effects such as dyskinesia or nausea.

Assessment today
There is a mild resting tremor, reduced facial expression and slowed finger tapping, with increased tone at both elbows, worse on the right. Gait is cautious with reduced arm swing; there is no postural instability on brief examination. Speech is slightly quiet. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations are unremarkable. The patient remains independent with personal care but is slower with dressing and meal preparation.

Requested action
Please undertake a medication and multidisciplinary review, including consideration of physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy. Advice on wearing-off symptoms and whether the current co-beneldopa regimen requires adjustment would be appreciated. Please also advise on follow-up arrangements and any monitoring required in primary care.

Yours faithfully,

H. Gill
GP, ULSTER HOSPITAL

Nursing progress and handover note

Patient: Tulise  
Current address: 149 Provost Ferguson Drive, Aberdeen, AB11 5AA  
Contact email: tulise.paterson84@yahoo.co.uk  
Named relative/emergency contact: Moeed Bell

Admitted with acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Increased breathlessness, audible wheeze and thick yellow-green sputum for 3 days. Alert and orientated, speaking in short sentences on exertion. Chest sounds reduced bilaterally with widespread expiratory wheeze. No chest pain reported. Temperature 37.4°C, pulse 96 bpm, respiratory rate 24/min, BP 138/76 mmHg.

At start of shift SpO₂ 94% on room air, above prescribed COPD target range of 88–92%; oxygen was not commenced. Following medical review and rest, repeat SpO₂ 91% on room air, respiratory rate 20/min. Continue to monitor closely and commence/titrate oxygen only if clinically indicated to maintain 88–92%. Escalate promptly if increasing work of breathing, drowsiness, cyanosis or inability to maintain target.

Nebulised bronchodilator administered as prescribed with good initial effect; wheeze less prominent and patient reports easier breathing afterwards. Regular salbutamol inhaler available, technique reinforced. Prednisolone and doxycycline given; no adverse reaction observed. Encourage oral fluids and sputum clearance. Intake adequate with prompting; ate approximately half of evening meal and drank 650 mL during shift. Sputum container at bedside.

Mobilising short distances to the toilet with one staff member and frame; becomes breathless on exertion but recovers after sitting. Falls risk due to dyspnoea and reduced exercise tolerance. Call bell within reach, non-slip footwear worn. Rest periods advised.

Plan for next shift: repeat respiratory observations and SpO₂ at least four-hourly and after mobilisation; document oxygen requirement if commenced. Continue prescribed steroids, antibiotic and bronchodilator therapy. Encourage deep breathing, supported coughing and fluids. Review sputum colour/volume, temperature and response to treatment. Contact medical team if deterioration, rising oxygen requirement, SpO₂ persistently outside target, worsening purulence or concerns regarding possible infection. Treating team: QUEEN ELIZABETH UNIVERSITY HOSPITAL.

Patient: saphia knight
Occupation: Cleaner
Clinic review

History
Acute right first metatarsophalangeal joint pain, swelling and erythema for 3 days. Pain began overnight and is worse with weight-bearing. No preceding injury. No fever, rigors, skin break or other joint involvement. Previous similar episode approximately 18 months ago, treated as gout. Diet and alcohol intake discussed. No recent antibiotic treatment.

Examination
Afebrile and clinically well. Right first MTP markedly tender with soft-tissue swelling and erythema; skin intact. Ankle and other peripheral joints non-tender. Calf soft and non-tender. No lymphangitis.

Assessment
Likely acute gout flare. Septic arthritis considered less likely in the absence of systemic upset or wound, but advised to seek urgent assessment if fever develops or redness spreads.

Plan
Naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food for five days, then stop when settled; avoid ibuprofen and other NSAIDs. Continue lansoprazole while taking naproxen. Colchicine 500 micrograms (0.5 mg) orally twice daily for three days, maximum 1 mg in 24 hours and maximum total course 3 mg. Do not repeat a course within three days. Stop and seek advice if diarrhoea, vomiting, abdominal pain, muscle weakness or unusual bruising occurs. Avoid colchicine with clarithromycin, erythromycin, ciclosporin or other potent CYP3A4/P-glycoprotein inhibitors. Renal and liver function to be checked before any further course; do not use this regimen in severe renal or hepatic impairment without specialist advice. Patient reports no known renal or liver disease and is not taking a statin or macrolide.

Rest, elevate and use a wrapped ice pack. Blood tests requested: FBC, U&E/eGFR, LFTs, CRP and serum urate; urate may be normal during an acute attack. Consider urate-lowering treatment after recovery if recurrent attacks.

Report/accession ID: 0948065450
Reviewed and plan agreed with V. Sidhu, Crickhowell Medical Centre.

Patient: N. Russell
Home address: 152 LISTOODER PARK, KILLADEAS
Patient contact: 07700 900297
Admission: Acute pelvic pain, abnormal vaginal discharge and dyspareunia.
Responsible clinician: S. Bishop

Clinical problems
• Pelvic inflammatory disease.
• Lower abdominal pain with cervical motion tenderness.
• Abnormal discharge; sexually transmitted infection screen pending at discharge.

Key results
Urine pregnancy test negative. FBC and renal profile satisfactory. CRP mildly raised. Pelvic ultrasound: no tubo-ovarian abscess or significant free fluid. Vaginal and cervical swabs taken. HIV and syphilis blood tests sent following consent.

Results to be reviewed by the sexual health service; patient will be contacted if treatment requires alteration. Sexual intercourse avoided until treatment completed, symptoms resolved and partners assessed. GP review within one week; return to A&E for worsening pain, fever, vomiting or collapse.
