Emergency Department Assessment
NHS number: 000 271 4834

Patient: Ismaaeel MCGRATH
DOB: 5 Apr 1934
Address: 129 Wychbury Close, Middlewich, CW10 0AA
Contact: 07700 900006

Presenting complaint
Three-day history of markedly reduced urine output with increasing tiredness and poor oral intake. Reports drinking very little because of nausea, without vomiting or diarrhoea. No dysuria, visible haematuria, flank pain, chest pain or breathlessness. No recent contrast exposure. Has taken usual medicines but has been eating and drinking poorly.

Background and medicines
Known hypertension and osteoarthritis. No documented chronic kidney disease in the available GP summary. Regular medicines reviewed; nephrotoxic and blood-pressure-lowering medicines to be withheld temporarily while renal function and hydration are reassessed. No known drug allergies recorded.

Examination
Alert and appropriately responsive, speaking in full sentences. Temperature 36.4°C, pulse 96 bpm regular, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturations 98% on air. Dry tongue and mildly reduced skin turgor. Heart sounds normal, chest clear bilaterally. Abdomen soft and non-tender, with no palpable bladder and no renal angle tenderness. No peripheral oedema. Urine passed only a small amount since arrival.

Investigations
Blood tests show urea 18.2 mmol/L, creatinine 186 µmol/L, estimated GFR reduced from the previous documented result, with mild hyperkalaemia at 5.5 mmol/L. Sodium 136 mmol/L, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L, venous lactate 1.4 mmol/L. Full blood count without significant anaemia or leukocytosis. Urinalysis: concentrated urine, trace protein, no blood or nitrites. ECG shows sinus rhythm with no acute T-wave or QRS changes.

Management and decision-making
Clinical picture is most consistent with acute kidney injury, probably related to volume depletion and poor intake. A 500 mL bolus of intravenous sodium chloride was given, followed by slower replacement with close monitoring because of the reduced renal function. Repeat observations remained stable. Bladder scan showed 74 mL after voiding; renal tract ultrasound requested to exclude obstruction.

The case was reviewed with the on-call medical registrar, who advised admission for continued intravenous fluids, strict fluid balance, repeat U&E and review of withheld medicines. The patient understands the rationale and agrees to admission.

Disposition
Admit to the acute medical unit. Nursing staff asked to record urine output and escalate oliguria, hypotension, breathlessness or worsening confusion. Repeat potassium and renal profile arranged for four hours after treatment.

Documented by: MERCI CONWAY

LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: fatema clay
Report/accession ID: L25Q12952
Clinical details: Plantar ulceration with reduced sensation and local discharge. Diabetic foot ulcer. Wound care and co-amoxiclav reported on request form. Specimen from ulcer swab; superficial sample, received in charcoal transport medium. Ordering clinician not stated.

Results
HbA1c (IFCC): 74 mmol/mol
CRP: 38 mg/L
White cell count: 12.6 × 10⁹/L
Wound swab: Heavy growth of Staphylococcus aureus. No Group A streptococcus isolated.
Susceptibility: Sensitive to flucloxacillin and co-amoxiclav; resistant to penicillin. No MRSA detected.

Interpretation
HbA1c is above the usual treatment target and indicates suboptimal glycaemic control. Raised CRP and leucocytosis support active local inflammation/infection in the clinical context. The isolate is susceptible to the currently documented co-amoxiclav; correlate with wound depth, perfusion and systemic features. A superficial swab may not represent deeper infection.

Comment
Please assess urgently if spreading erythema, increasing pain, fever, tissue necrosis, exposed bone or systemic deterioration. Continue specialist wound care and pressure off-loading. Review antimicrobial choice and duration against local diabetic-foot guidance and clinical response. Consider deep tissue sampling if debridement is undertaken. Check renal function before antimicrobial adjustment. Podiatry/diabetic foot team follow-up recommended.

Patient contact detail: fatema.clay37@outlook.com
Planned clinical review: 19 October 2004

Validated and reported by: Dr Lamara BROOKES, MBBS

Endocrinology Outpatient Review

Patient: Mallie
Occupation: Administrative assistant
Home address: 18 Teasdale Road, Fleet, GU52 0AB
Contact telephone: 07700 900509
Employer: Moorend Public Library

Reason for review

Assessment of persistent symptoms in the context of established primary hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine.

Clinical history

Mallie describes gradually worsening fatigue, particularly in the late afternoon, with reduced exercise tolerance but no exertional chest pain or breathlessness. They report increased sensitivity to cold and constipation for 3 days, although bowel frequency has generally been reduced over recent months. There has been no dysphagia, neck pain, change in voice or subjective thyroid swelling. Weight has increased by approximately 3 kg since the previous review. Appetite is unchanged.

Levothyroxine is currently taken every morning with water. On detailed questioning, breakfast is sometimes taken within 20 minutes of the dose, and a calcium-containing supplement is taken later in the morning. There are no other regular prescribed medicines. No recent A&E attendance or intercurrent infection was reported. Sleep is adequate, although the patient feels unrefreshed on waking. Mood is mildly low in relation to reduced energy, without suicidal thoughts or other features suggestive of a major depressive episode.

Examination

The patient was comfortable at rest and communicated appropriately. Pulse 62 beats per minute and regular; blood pressure 118/72 mmHg; temperature 36.4 °C. There was no tremor, lid lag or conjunctival injection. The thyroid was not enlarged or tender, with no palpable nodules or cervical lymphadenopathy. Heart sounds were normal, with no murmur. Chest examination was clear. There was dry skin over the forearms but no peripheral oedema. Neurological examination showed normal power and reflexes, with a mildly delayed relaxation phase at the ankles.

Investigations

Recent thyroid function testing showed TSH 8.6 mIU/L (reference range 0.4–4.0 mIU/L) and free T4 11.2 pmol/L (reference range 10–22 pmol/L). Full blood count was satisfactory, with haemoglobin 128 g/L. Ferritin was 42 micrograms/L, vitamin B12 318 ng/L and HbA1c 35 mmol/mol. Renal and liver profiles were unremarkable. These results are consistent with biochemical under-replacement rather than a new structural thyroid disorder.

Impression and plan

The symptoms and raised TSH most likely reflect suboptimal levothyroxine absorption or administration timing. Levothyroxine will be increased to 75 micrograms once daily. It should be taken with water on an empty stomach, ideally 30–60 minutes before breakfast; calcium supplements should be separated by at least 4 hours. No indication for thyroid imaging is identified today.

Repeat TSH and free T4 are requested in 8 weeks, with review arranged thereafter. Earlier clinical assessment is advised if palpitations, tremor, marked anxiety or chest pain develop. Discharge summary
NHS number: 000 867 7078

Patient: Afsheen F.
Date of discharge: 28th March 2019
Contact detail: afsheen.fitzgerald72@gmail.com

A 77-year-old White male patient admitted via A&E with new central chest pressure associated with diaphoresis and nausea. Initial ECG showed sinus rhythm without ST elevation. Serial high-sensitivity troponin demonstrated a significant rise and fall, consistent with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). There was no clinical evidence of acute heart failure or cardiogenic shock.

Key results
Chest radiograph showed no focal consolidation or pulmonary oedema. Renal function remained satisfactory during admission. Cholesterol was above target and HbA1c was in the non-diabetic range. Echocardiography demonstrated mildly impaired left ventricular systolic function with regional hypokinesia; no important valve abnormality was identified.

Hospital course
The patient was treated with aspirin, fondaparinux and high-intensity atorvastatin. Symptoms settled promptly and there was no further chest pain or documented arrhythmia. Cardiology reviewed the case. In view of the clinical stability and overall risk assessment, an invasive strategy was not pursued during this admission. The patient mobilised independently and remained haemodynamically stable.

Discharge medicines
• aspirin 75 mg once daily, to continue indefinitely
• clopidogrel 75 mg once daily, planned for 12 months following cardiology review
• atorvastatin 80 mg at night
• bisoprolol 1.25 mg once daily, provided pulse and blood pressure remain acceptable
• glyceryl trinitrate spray as required for recurrent angina

Fondaparinux was stopped before discharge. The cardiology antiplatelet plan is aspirin plus clopidogrel; clopidogrel should not be stopped early without discussion with cardiology or the GP, unless significant bleeding or another urgent contraindication develops.

Condition and follow-up
Discharged home clinically euvolaemic, pain-free and tolerating oral medication. A cardiology follow-up appointment and cardiac rehabilitation referral have been requested. The GP is asked to review blood pressure, pulse, adherence and tolerance of medication, and arrange a repeat lipid profile after treatment has been established.

Safety-net advice
Use glyceryl trinitrate as instructed for chest discomfort. If pain is severe, lasts more than a few minutes, recurs despite the spray, or is accompanied by breathlessness, collapse or sweating, call 999 and do not drive. Seek urgent advice for black stools, vomiting blood or other significant bleeding.

The patient’s adult child, Kyen Uddin, was involved in discharge discussions. The patient confirmed understanding and can be contacted using the recorded contact detail.

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT ASSESSMENT

Patient: Y. Ratcliffe
Contact number: 07700 900714
Accompanied by: C. Firth, relative

Presenting complaint
Pain, redness and discharge from a recent operative wound. The patient reports increasing tenderness over the last two days, followed by yellow purulent fluid staining the dressing this morning. No chest pain, breathlessness, vomiting or urinary symptoms. They have felt intermittently shivery but have not measured a temperature at home.

Relevant history
Recent surgery with an abdominal wound. No known immunosuppression reported. Medication history reviewed; no regular antimicrobial treatment before attendance. Allergy status checked and no antibiotic allergy was disclosed.

Examination
Alert, coherent and haemodynamically stable. Temperature 37.8°C, pulse 96 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturations 98% on air. Blood pressure 120/80 mmHg.

The operative wound has surrounding erythema extending approximately 2 cm from the margins, with local warmth and moderate tenderness. A small superficial area has separated, producing thick yellow discharge. No crepitus, bullae, skin anaesthesia or disproportionate pain. No palpable fluctuance suggestive of a deep collection. Abdomen otherwise soft, with no guarding or rebound tenderness. Peripheral perfusion is normal.

Investigations
Blood tests: white cell count 12.4 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 9.8 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 86 mg/L. Haemoglobin and renal function are satisfactory. Venous lactate 1.2 mmol/L. Wound swab obtained after removal of the old dressing and sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivities.

The laboratory result has been logged under report/accession ID: 079064513.

Clinical impression and management
Findings are consistent with a superficial postoperative wound infection. There is no current clinical evidence of necrotising infection, peritonitis, septic shock or a drainable deep abscess. The wound was irrigated with sterile saline, gently dried and covered with a non-adherent dressing. Flucloxacillin commenced in the department, with oral dosing supplied for continuation in the community in accordance with local antimicrobial guidance. Analgesia advised with paracetamol; dosing instructions discussed.

The case was discussed with the on-call surgical team at University Hospital Llandough. They advised outpatient review provided the patient remains clinically stable, with reassessment of the wound and culture results.

Disposition
Suitable for discharge with clear safety-netting. Return immediately to A&E for spreading redness, escalating pain, fever, recurrent vomiting, confusion, faintness, wound breakdown or increasing discharge. Wound review arranged through the surgical service/GP within 48 hours. Patient and C. Firth understood the plan and had the opportunity to ask questions.

I reviewed the patient today following referral from the GP for persistent, painless swelling in the left side of the neck. There have been drenching night sweats on several occasions and an unintentional loss of approximately 6 kg over the past two months. Appetite is reduced but the patient is still managing ordinary meals. There is no reported fever, pruritus, cough or breathlessness.

They have been using paracetamol occasionally for discomfort, with reasonable effect. No drug allergies were discussed today. The patient’s preferred contact detail is primo.rice20@yahoo.co.uk.

Persistent painless cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy with night sweats and weight loss. Hodgkin lymphoma is suspected; tissue diagnosis remains outstanding.

Discharge summary for Arthur-James R.
Patient identifier (MRN): 091922804
Treating organisation: ULSTER HOSPITAL

Arthur-James R. was admitted with a severe painful sickle cell crisis affecting both limbs and the lower back. They also reported reduced oral intake and symptoms of dehydration. There was no history of chest pain, breathlessness or fever. Examination on arrival showed marked tenderness in the limbs and lumbar region, with no focal neurological deficit. Oxygen saturations remained satisfactory on room air.

Initial blood tests were consistent with the patient’s known sickle cell disorder, including anaemia and a raised reticulocyte count. Kidney function was preserved. Inflammatory markers were not significantly raised, and chest imaging did not show an acute chest complication. Blood cultures were taken because of the risk of infection in sickle cell disease; these remained negative. The admission was managed as an uncomplicated vaso-occlusive painful crisis.

Pain relief was started with regular paracetamol and subcutaneous morphine, followed by a patient-controlled intravenous morphine infusion under the acute pain team’s guidance. The dose was reduced as the pain settled, and morphine was stopped before discharge. Intravenous fluids were given for dehydration, with careful monitoring of fluid balance and urine output. They were encouraged to drink regularly once able. There was no indication for red-cell transfusion during this admission.

The pain improved steadily, although the current score is 5/10 with movement. Arthur-James R. is now mobilising independently, eating and drinking, and has no fever, chest symptoms or new neurological symptoms. Observations and renal function are stable.

Discharge medicines are:
• Paracetamol regularly as advised on the label.
• Oral morphine solution only for severe breakthrough pain, using the dose supplied by the ward; avoid driving or alcohol while taking it.
• Continue the usual sickle cell medicines and folic acid as previously prescribed.
• Maintain good oral hydration and avoid becoming overheated or chilled.

Please seek urgent help through NHS 111 or A&E if there is worsening or uncontrolled pain, fever, chest pain, shortness of breath, persistent vomiting, severe headache, weakness, confusion or reduced urine output. Do not delay assessment because infection can become serious quickly in sickle cell disease.

A discharge letter and medication plan will be sent to the GP surgery. Follow-up should be arranged with the usual haematology team at ULSTER HOSPITAL. Cora-Mae Calvert, who lives in Clare, has been updated about the discharge plan with the patient’s agreement and can support them at home. The patient should contact the sickle cell service if the pain is not continuing to improve or if further crises occur.

Emergency department handover – suspected acute appendicitis

Patient: tudur rafiq
The patient, aged 20, was reviewed in the emergency department with 18 hours of worsening abdominal pain. Initially central/periumbilical, now localised to the right lower quadrant. Associated nausea and marked loss of appetite; no diarrhoea. One episode of vomiting. No urinary symptoms or testicular symptoms reported.

Observations at 08:15: temperature 37.8°C, pulse 102 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, SpO₂ 98% on air. Alert, mildly uncomfortable but not toxic. Abdomen soft with focal right lower-quadrant tenderness, guarding and percussion tenderness; no generalised rigidity. Bowel sounds present. Chest clear, heart sounds normal. No calf tenderness.

Investigations: FBC shows WCC 14.6 ×10⁹/L with neutrophilia. CRP 68 mg/L. Urea and electrolytes and liver profile within acceptable limits. Urinalysis negative for nitrites and blood. Pregnancy testing not clinically indicated. Ultrasound demonstrates a non-compressible blind-ending tubular structure in the right iliac fossa, measuring 8 mm, with surrounding inflammatory change; appearances support acute appendicitis. No collection seen.

Treatment given: oral paracetamol initially, followed by intravenous analgesia with improvement. Intravenous fluids commenced. Intravenous co-amoxiclav administered after allergy check; no documented drug allergies.

Priority 1 – surgical review and admission under the acute general surgical team for laparoscopic appendicectomy assessment. Keep nil by mouth, continue maintenance fluids, repeat observations and provide antiemetic as required. Escalate promptly for fever, hypotension, increasing pain or peritonism. Thromboprophylaxis to be considered on admission.

Discussed working diagnosis, likely operative management and risks of perforation with the patient, who understands and agrees to admission. Referral made to Newham General Hospital.

Follow-up/review arranged for 23 September 2026 if operative management is deferred or symptoms persist. Safety-net: return immediately for collapse, worsening abdominal pain, repeated vomiting or inability to drink.

Reviewed and handed over by Dr Caileb Slade, MBBS.

text:
NHS Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report

Patient: Miyana Hawkins
Age: 23 y/o
MRN: 090509935
Request: Predictive germline testing for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk

Specimen and referral context

Peripheral blood was received in an EDTA tube for constitutional genetic analysis. The request was made because of a significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer and the patient’s concern regarding inherited cancer risk. The patient reports no current treatment and is clinically well at the time of testing. This analysis is intended as predictive testing in an unaffected individual; appropriate pre- and post-test counselling is required.

Laboratory findings

Targeted analysis of the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes was undertaken using next-generation sequencing with confirmatory assessment by an orthogonal method where indicated. Sequence coverage and quality metrics were satisfactory across the reportable coding regions and relevant splice junctions.

No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant was identified in BRCA1 or BRCA2.

The familial variant specified for review, BRCA1 c.68_69delAG, was not detected in the submitted specimen.

Interpretation

This is a negative predictive result for BRCA1 c.68_69delAG, assuming that this is the confirmed familial variant and that the submitted sample is correctly attributed to the patient. The result substantially reduces the likelihood that the patient carries this particular familial BRCA1 variant. It does not exclude the possibility of a different pathogenic variant in BRCA1 or BRCA2, a pathogenic variant in another cancer-predisposition gene, or a non-genetic explanation for the reported family history.

Risk assessment should therefore take account of the complete pedigree, the ages and tumour types of affected relatives, and any relevant pathology findings. If the familial variant has not previously been confirmed in an affected relative, the clinical significance of a negative predictive result is more limited. Testing an affected relative, where feasible, remains the most informative approach for unresolved familial cancer syndromes.

Clinical comment

This result should be discussed with the referring genetics team or GP in conjunction with the formal risk assessment. A negative result does not by itself determine breast or ovarian surveillance requirements; these should follow the final risk calculation and national guidance. No alteration to medication is indicated on the basis of this laboratory result alone.

Please ensure that the patient understands the scope and limitations of the test. Any discrepancy in family history, sample identity, or the reported familial variant should be referred to the laboratory before clinical decisions are made. A genetics review is planned for 1st May 2035.

Report validated by:
thisbe mcmahon
Laboratory reporting clinician

Follow-up and advice
The early pregnancy/maternity team will review ongoing symptoms and nutritional status. GP review is advised if vomiting recurs or medication is ineffective. She should seek urgent assessment through the emergency department or maternity service if unable to keep fluids down for 12 hours, passing very little urine, fainting, developing severe abdominal pain, fever, blood in vomit, or any vaginal bleeding.

Dear Diabetic Foot Service,

Re: KISA STEVENSON, home address 140 TAVNAGHMORE ROAD, CLOGH

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient with a persistent plantar ulcer beneath the right first metatarsal head. The specific question is whether there is underlying osteomyelitis or clinically significant peripheral arterial disease, and whether specialist off-loading or surgical management is required.

The ulcer has been present for approximately three weeks following a small area of callus breakdown. There has been intermittent local discharge but no rigors, vomiting or other systemic symptoms. The patient describes reduced sensation in both feet and has not noticed much pain from the wound. They remain able to mobilise indoors, although walking is limited by discomfort and the dressing. There is no reported calf pain at rest.

On review today, the ulcer measures approximately 14 x 9 mm, with a shallow granulating base and a small amount of serous discharge. The surrounding skin is mildly macerated without spreading erythema or lymphangitis. The wound does not visibly probe to bone. The right foot is warm, with capillary refill of approximately three seconds; dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are difficult to palpate. There is reduced protective sensation to 10 g monofilament testing at several plantar sites bilaterally. No crepitus or fluctuance is present. Temperature is 37.1°C and observations are otherwise stable.

A wound swab was taken because of the discharge. The associated laboratory report/accession identifier is 0553952501. The initial inflammatory markers were only mildly raised, with CRP 18 mg/L and a normal white cell count. Plain radiographs have been requested, although I appreciate that cross-sectional imaging may be needed if concern about bone involvement persists.

The wound has been cleansed with saline and covered with a non-adherent dressing. The patient has been advised to avoid barefoot walking and to reduce weight-bearing through the affected forefoot. A temporary felt aperture pad was supplied, pending formal off-loading advice. Please note that the current medication instruction is co-amoxiclav 625 mg three times daily; this was started for the local discharge and will be reviewed in light of the culture result and clinical response. The patient has been asked to seek urgent assessment through A&E if fever, rapidly spreading redness, increasing swelling or marked deterioration develops.

Assessment

Diabetic foot ulcer with peripheral sensory neuropathy and possible vascular insufficiency. At present there is no convincing evidence of systemic infection, but the duration, discharge and difficult-to-palpate pulses warrant specialist review.

Requested action

Please assess promptly, including vascular assessment and advice regarding definitive off-loading, wound care and the need for further imaging or debridement. A follow-up appointment has been arranged for 5th October 2012, but I would appreciate earlier review if feasible.

Yours sincerely,

Dr Renaiyah Anwar, MBBS

Patient: JAEGO PLANT  
Age: 40 y/o  
MRN: 082003369  
Home address: 76 Culduie Circle, Brig o'Turk, FK17 8AA

Admitted with first-trimester hyperemesis at 9+4 weeks' gestation. She reports ongoing nausea with four episodes of vomiting since the previous shift, although the volume has reduced this morning. No haematemesis, abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding or dysuria reported. She feels weak when standing but denies dizziness at rest. Bowels opened yesterday. She remains alert and orientated, engaging appropriately with care.

At review, temperature was 36.7°C, pulse 96 bpm, blood pressure 104/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 and oxygen saturations 99% on air. Mucous membranes remain dry and urine is concentrated; she passed approximately 250 mL during the shift. Weight is down from her reported pre-pregnancy baseline, consistent with the documented weight loss. Capillary blood glucose was 4.8 mmol/L. No peripheral oedema noted. Abdomen soft and non-tender. Peripheral cannula remains patent with no redness, swelling or discomfort.

Intravenous sodium chloride has continued as prescribed. Cannula site checked before and after administration, with good flow and no signs of infiltration. Cyclizine administered for nausea; she reported partial relief after around 40 minutes and was able to retain sips of water and two crackers. Oral intake remains limited, with approximately 450 mL taken so far. She was encouraged to take small, frequent sips of fluid and bland food rather than larger amounts. A fluid balance chart is in use, and urine output will continue to be monitored closely.

She mobilises independently to the bathroom but was advised to call for assistance if light-headed, particularly after vomiting or when getting out of bed. Falls risk remains increased because of weakness and dehydration. Vomit bowl and call bell left within reach. Mouth care offered and accepted. Emotional support provided; she is worried about the effect of vomiting on the pregnancy and was reassured that the team is monitoring hydration and symptoms, with further review available if she deteriorates.

Assessment

Persistent vomiting with clinical features of dehydration, but currently haemodynamically stable and showing some response to cyclizine and intravenous fluids. No acute abdominal or obstetric red flags reported this shift.

Plan for next shift

Continue prescribed sodium chloride and cyclizine, strict fluid balance and regular observations. Reassess nausea, oral tolerance, urine output and postural symptoms. Escalate to the medical team if vomiting becomes more frequent, oral intake remains negligible, urine output falls, observations deteriorate or abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding develops. Discharge summary
NHS number: 000 213 8779

Patient: maksimilian day
Home address: 73 SOUTH PROMENADE, CREGGAN
Contact email: maksimilian.day53@gmail.com

22-year-old White female patient admitted with a two-day history of increasing redness, warmth and tenderness affecting the left lower leg. The erythema had spread from the ankle towards the calf despite elevation at home. There was no preceding injury, ulcer or animal bite, and no systemic symptoms apart from feeling generally tired. The patient was assessed in the emergency department on 2 May 2021 and admitted for intravenous treatment and observation.

On arrival, the patient was alert and haemodynamically stable. The affected leg had sharply tender, warm erythema extending to the mid-calf, without crepitus, fluctuance or pain out of proportion to examination. Distal pulses and sensation were preserved. Temperature was 37.8°C. At 08:15, blood tests showed a white cell count of 13.2 × 10⁹/L and C-reactive protein of 96 mg/L; renal function was satisfactory. Blood cultures were taken before antibiotics and remained negative. Venous Doppler ultrasound showed no evidence of deep-vein thrombosis.

The patient received intravenous flucloxacillin, leg elevation and regular analgesia with paracetamol. The margins of erythema were marked on admission. Over the following 48 hours, the redness ceased to extend, pain and warmth reduced, and inflammatory markers began to fall. There was no abscess requiring drainage and no clinical evidence of necrotising infection. Following this improvement, treatment was changed to oral flucloxacillin to complete the course.

Assessment at discharge: improving uncomplicated cellulitis of the lower leg, with no evidence of bacteraemia or venous thrombosis. The patient is mobilising independently, eating and drinking, and remains apyrexial. The skin changes have substantially receded from the marked border, although mild residual erythema and tenderness remain.

Discharge medicines:
• Flucloxacillin 500 mg orally four times daily, to complete a total 7-day course.
• Paracetamol 1 g orally up to four times daily when required for pain, leaving at least four hours between doses and not exceeding 4 g in 24 hours.

Please keep the leg elevated when resting, maintain good fluid intake and continue gentle mobilisation. Keep the skin clean and dry, and do not apply creams or dressings unless advised. The patient should seek urgent medical attention through NHS 111 or A&E if the redness spreads again, pain worsens, fever or rigors develop, the leg becomes numb or discoloured, or they feel acutely unwell. A routine review with the GP surgery is recommended within 48–72 hours of discharge to confirm continued improvement. Contact details have been checked and the patient can be reached via maksimilian.day53@gmail.com.

Emergency Department Assessment

Date: 23 Feb 2022
Patient: janice morrison
Report/accession ID: 0425781922

Presenting complaint
Two-day history of dysuria, urinary frequency and intermittent suprapubic discomfort. Passing small volumes frequently. No visible haematuria, flank pain, rigors, vomiting or vaginal symptoms. Background
No significant renal history documented. Medication reconciliation completed. No known drug allergies recorded. Established regular medication includes nitrofurantoin 100 mg modified-release twice daily, commenced before attendance for presumed lower urinary tract infection; symptoms have not yet fully settled.

Alert, comfortable at rest and clinically euvolaemic. Temperature 37.1°C, pulse 84 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 98% on air. Abdomen soft with mild suprapubic tenderness only. No guarding or rebound. No costovertebral angle tenderness. No evidence of sepsis.

Findings are consistent with uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection. No clinical evidence of pyelonephritis, obstructed infection or acute kidney injury.

Discussed with the emergency clinician at Queen Elizabeth Hospital. Continue nitrofurantoin 100 mg modified-release twice daily with food and complete the prescribed course; the medication instruction was checked against the current prescription. Encourage oral fluids and regular bladder emptying. Paracetamol may be used as needed if normally safe to take.

Safety-net advice given to return to A&E urgently for fever, rigors, flank pain, persistent vomiting, worsening abdominal pain, confusion or inability to pass urine. GP review advised if symptoms are not improving within 48 hours or if cultures indicate resistance. GP review – hypothyroidism

Date: 4 January 2026
Patient: Levison
Contact detail: levison.reeves22@hotmail.com
Report/accession ID: LAB-03056593

History
Levison is a 35-year-old Caucasian female patient reviewed regarding persistent tiredness. Fatigue has been present for approximately three months, with reduced stamina by late afternoon but no exertional chest pain or breathlessness. Reports feeling unusually cold compared with others and opening bowels every three to four days. No rectal bleeding, abdominal pain or unintentional weight loss. Appetite is unchanged.

Taking levothyroxine regularly, usually first thing with water, although on some mornings breakfast follows within 20 minutes. No recent dose changes. Does not take iron or calcium supplements. No new prescribed medicines. Sleep is generally adequate, though not always refreshing. Mood described as “flat” at times; denies persistent low mood, suicidal thoughts or loss of interest in usual activities.

Examination
Alert and appropriately engaged. Pulse regular at 68 bpm; blood pressure 118/72 mmHg. Weight stable by history. Skin mildly dry, with no obvious facial puffiness. No tremor. Thyroid not enlarged or tender; no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Chest clear and heart sounds normal. Abdomen soft and non-tender. No ankle oedema. Reflexes present and symmetrical.

Investigations
Recent thyroid blood tests reviewed under report/accession ID LAB-03056593: TSH mildly raised with free T4 within the laboratory reference range, consistent with suboptimal replacement rather than overt hypothyroidism. Full blood count and ferritin were satisfactory. Renal profile and liver tests unremarkable. No biochemical evidence of anaemia to account for the fatigue.

Assessment
Symptoms remain compatible with mild under-replacement of levothyroxine, with possible reduced absorption from taking breakfast soon afterwards. Constipation is likely contributing to discomfort but there are no alarm features. The presentation is not suggestive of acute thyroid dysfunction.

Plan
• Continue current levothyroxine dose for now and take it with water on an empty stomach, ideally at least 30 minutes before breakfast. Keep any calcium, iron or antacid preparation four hours apart.
• Increase fluids and dietary fibre gradually; maintain regular activity. Consider an over-the-counter bulk-forming laxative if dietary measures are insufficient.
• Repeat TSH and free T4 in eight weeks, with dose adjustment if TSH remains elevated.
• Safety-netted to seek review sooner for marked deterioration, palpitations, chest pain, persistent vomiting, rectal bleeding or unexplained weight loss.
• Follow-up with the GP surgery after repeat blood tests. If control remains difficult despite confirmed adherence, consider discussion with a consultant endocrinologist.

Reason for admission

Admitted with a three-day history of worsening lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge and deep dyspareunia. She was afebrile but uncomfortable on arrival. Pregnancy test was negative. The working diagnosis was pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), with no clinical evidence of sepsis or tubo-ovarian abscess.

At 08:15, observations were stable: temperature 37.4°C, pulse 92 bpm, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation 99% on air. Abdominal examination showed suprapubic and bilateral iliac fossa tenderness without guarding or rebound. Following review by the gynaecology team, treatment was commenced with ceftriaxone, doxycycline and metronidazole. Analgesia was provided with paracetamol and, when required, oral ibuprofen. She remained haemodynamically stable throughout the admission and tolerated oral medication. Pain and discharge had improved by the following morning, with no new abdominal signs. There was no indication for operative intervention.

• Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily to complete 14 days.
• Metronidazole 400 mg twice daily to complete 14 days.
• Ceftriaxone was given as a single dose in hospital.
• Paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily when required, maximum 4 g in 24 hours.

She was advised to avoid alcohol during metronidazole treatment and for 48 hours afterwards. Abstinence from sexual intercourse was advised until treatment is completed, symptoms have resolved and sexual partners have been assessed and treated. Sabriin Gordon, from Achfrish, was recorded as her emergency contact with the patient’s consent.

The sexual health service will review pending results and arrange partner notification where required. She should return to A&E urgently for fever, vomiting, fainting, escalating pain or inability to take antibiotics.

Past medical history reviewed in the electronic record; no active immunosuppression recorded. Regular medicines checked with the patient. No drug allergies reported. Amoxicillin and paracetamol were not previously prescribed for this episode.

Examination
Alert, speaking in full sentences but appears tired. Temperature 38.4°C, pulse 104 bpm, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, oxygen saturations 95% on air. Capillary refill under two seconds. No peripheral oedema or calf tenderness.

Chest examination showed reduced air entry with coarse inspiratory crackles at the right base and focal bronchial breathing. No wheeze. Heart sounds normal with no murmur. Abdomen soft and non-tender. No meningism or focal neurological deficit.

Investigations
Chest radiograph demonstrates patchy right lower-zone air-space opacity, consistent with infective consolidation, without pleural effusion or pneumothorax. ECG: sinus tachycardia, no acute ischaemic changes. Blood tests show mild neutrophilia and raised CRP; renal function and electrolytes are satisfactory. Venous lactate normal. Respiratory viral swab negative for influenza A/B and SARS-CoV-2.

Assessment
Clinical and radiological findings support community-acquired pneumonia. Coding recorded as SNOMED CT 233604007. CURB-65 assessment does not identify a requirement for admission, and the patient remains haemodynamically stable with acceptable oxygenation.

Treatment and plan
First dose of oral amoxicillin given in the department and tolerated. Continue the prescribed antibiotic course as supplied on the discharge prescription. Continue paracetamol for fever or pleuritic discomfort, observing the maximum stated daily dose. Encourage oral fluids and rest.

Safety-netting provided: return urgently for worsening breathlessness, persistent vomiting, confusion, blue lips, chest pain unrelated to breathing, or inability to maintain fluids. GP review advised if not clearly improving within 48–72 hours, with consideration of repeat chest imaging if symptoms persist.

Disposition
Discharged home from the emergency department with written advice and discharge medicines. Patient understands the plan and has no immediate safeguarding concerns.

Clinician: O. FITZPATRICK

Dear Colleague,
NHS number: 000 889 0324

Re: Min – referral for specialist assessment of major depressive episode

I am referring Min to Ulster Hospital for assessment and advice regarding persistent depressive symptoms despite an adequate primary-care trial of sertraline. The specific clinical question is whether further psychological or pharmacological intervention is indicated, and whether there are features requiring more intensive mental health support.

The current episode has been characterised by pervasive low mood, loss of interest and enjoyment, reduced motivation and early-morning waking. Min describes diminished concentration and increasing difficulty managing ordinary daily tasks. Appetite is variable, with no reported significant weight change. They deny symptoms suggestive of mania, psychosis or an acute confusional state. There is no reported use of illicit substances and alcohol intake is described as low.

At review, Min appeared tired and subdued but was appropriately dressed and engaged throughout the consultation. Speech was quiet, of normal rate, and coherent. Affect was constricted and congruent with the reported mood. There was no evidence of thought disorder or perceptual disturbance. They were orientated, with fair insight into the change in their mental health. Sleep remains fragmented by waking in the early hours, after which they often remain awake ruminating.

A structured risk discussion was completed. Min has experienced intermittent thoughts that life is not worth living but denies current intent, preparation or access to a specific means. They identify family responsibilities as protective and agreed to seek urgent help via the emergency department or 111 if risk escalates. A brief safety plan has been discussed, including contacting the GP surgery, involving a trusted relative and avoiding isolation during periods of marked deterioration.

There is no history provided of previous manic episodes or psychiatric admission. Physical symptoms are not currently suggestive of an acute medical cause. Recent primary-care blood tests, including full blood count, renal profile, liver function, thyroid function and ferritin, were not clinically concerning.

Current treatment is sertraline 50 mg once daily. Min reports taking this consistently, with no significant adverse effects, although the improvement to date has been limited. We have reinforced regular dosing, sleep routine, gentle activity and avoidance of abrupt discontinuation. No dose change has been made pending specialist advice.

I would be grateful for a comprehensive psychiatric assessment, including review of diagnostic formulation, suicide risk and suitability for psychological therapy. Please advise whether optimisation or augmentation of antidepressant treatment should be considered and whether follow-up through secondary care is required.

Yours faithfully,

F. Sharpe

Known decompensated heart failure. Reports worsening breathlessness on minimal exertion and orthopnoea, requiring three pillows overnight. Bilateral ankle swelling has been present for 3 days. Ongoing fluid overload and falls risk. No new oxygen requirement. Continue strict fluid balance, daily weight and four-hourly observations. Maintain upright positioning, assist with all transfers and review response to further prescribed diuretic doses. Patient: Yvi
Occupation: Postal worker
Seen with ongoing CPAP treatment for previously confirmed obstructive sleep apnoea. Reports loud snoring and witnessed apnoeas before starting treatment, with marked daytime somnolence. Since using continuous positive airway pressure, partner reports no further pauses in breathing and snoring is substantially quieter. Daytime sleepiness has improved; no unintentional dozing while driving or at work. Epworth Sleepiness Scale today 6/24.

CPAP use is generally consistent, averaging 6–7 hours per night. Occasionally removes the mask during the early morning because of nasal dryness. No significant leak reported. Device review: acceptable residual apnoea-hypopnoea index on current settings, with intermittent mask leak. Discussed humidification, regular mask cleaning and replacing consumables through the supplier. Advised to use CPAP for every sleep period, including naps, and not to drive if sleepy.

1. Obstructive sleep apnoea – symptomatic and objective improvement with treatment.

Plan
Continue continuous positive airway pressure at current settings. Trial heated humidifier and review mask fit; respiratory sleep service to arrange replacement interface if leak persists. text:
Discharge summary
National Insurance number: NT 87 66 30 B

Patient: Seth R.
MRN: 086393/79
Responsible consultant: C. Hubbard, GMC number 0186728
Discharging organisation: Royal Victoria Hospital

Reason for admission
Admitted with a three-day history of markedly reduced urine output, fatigue and poor oral intake. There was no reported dysuria, visible haematuria, chest pain or diarrhoea. On arrival she was clinically dry, with a postural fall in blood pressure and mild tachycardia. Initial blood tests demonstrated acute kidney injury, with creatinine 238 micromol/L and eGFR 19 mL/min/1.73 m²; previous renal function had been within the normal range.

Key findings and hospital course
Urinalysis showed concentrated urine without significant blood or protein. Renal ultrasound demonstrated normal-sized kidneys with no hydronephrosis or other evidence of obstruction. The clinical impression was pre-renal acute kidney injury related to poor intake and dehydration, with a possible contribution from regular medicines affecting renal perfusion. There was no evidence of sepsis, and inflammatory markers remained low.

She received intravenous sodium chloride with careful fluid balance monitoring. Her usual blood-pressure-lowering medication and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medicine were held during the admission. Urine output improved over the first 24 hours and remained satisfactory thereafter. Renal function progressively recovered: creatinine fell to 164 micromol/L, then to 112 micromol/L on the day of discharge. Potassium was 4.5 mmol/L and bicarbonate 24 mmol/L. She was eating and drinking independently and mobilising safely.

During review, she reported a mild headache for 3 days, which settled with improved hydration and did not require investigation beyond routine clinical assessment. There were no focal neurological signs. A medication review found no other nephrotoxic agents.

Problem list
1. Acute kidney injury, likely pre-renal, substantially improved with rehydration.
2. Reduced oral intake and dehydration.
3. Temporary cessation of medicines that may worsen renal function.
4. Mild anaemia, stable and suitable for outpatient review.

Discharge medicines and changes
• Continue regular prescribed medicines except those listed below.
• Do not restart the held blood-pressure medication until reviewed by the GP, with home blood-pressure readings if available.
• Avoid ibuprofen, naproxen and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medicines unless specifically advised by a clinician.
• Maintain regular oral fluids, aiming for pale urine unless a clinician has advised fluid restriction.
• Paracetamol may be used for simple pain, in accordance with the packet instructions.

Follow-up and safety-netting
The GP surgery should arrange repeat urea and electrolytes and creatinine within one week, together with blood-pressure review and assessment of whether the held medication can be restarted. A copy of this summary has been provided for continuity of care. The patient was advised to seek urgent medical help via NHS 111 or A&E if urine output falls again, she cannot keep fluids down, develops increasing drowsiness, breathlessness, chest pain, fever or severe abdominal pain.

Condition at discharge
Clinically euvolaemic, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Passing urine normally, tolerating diet and fluids, and discharged home with the above plan.

Prepared and authorised by C. Hubbard, GMC number 0186728, on behalf of Royal Victoria Hospital.

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT HANDOVER

Patient: meira butcher  
MRN: 0789363  
Home address: 83 Mill Park Avenue, Kennington, OX14 1AA  
Contact: meira.butcher23@hotmail.com  
Emergency contact: arihaan lambert

Presenting problem
Severe limb and lower back pain, typical of previous sickle cell painful episodes, with reduced oral intake and dizziness on standing. Pain began overnight and has progressed despite usual oral analgesia. No preceding injury. Denies chest pain, breathlessness, cough, fever, abdominal pain or focal weakness.

Initial assessment
Alert, distressed by pain but engaging appropriately. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Airway patent; respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturations 98% on air. Pulse 108, blood pressure 112/68, temperature 37.1°C. Clinically dry mucous membranes and delayed capillary refill at approximately 3 seconds. No jaundice noted. Chest clear bilaterally with no increased work of breathing. Heart sounds normal apart from tachycardia. Abdomen soft and non-tender. Diffuse tenderness through both thighs and lumbar paraspinal region; no focal joint swelling, erythema or neurological deficit. Mobilising slowly.

Investigations
Venous blood gas: no significant acidosis, lactate 1.4 mmol/L. FBC, reticulocytes, U&E, LFTs, CRP and group-and-save sent; results pending. Urinalysis concentrated, no nitrites or blood. Blood cultures to be taken if febrile. Chest radiograph not currently indicated in the absence of respiratory symptoms, but low threshold if chest pain, hypoxia or fever develops.

Management and decision-making
Cannula inserted. Intravenous crystalloid commenced for dehydration. Morphine given in titrated doses with improvement from 9/10 to 6/10; sedation and respiratory rate monitored. Antiemetic prescribed as required. Avoid NSAIDs pending renal results. No current clinical evidence of acute chest syndrome, sepsis or stroke.

Priority is reassessment of pain, observations and blood results, with early discussion with the haematology team. Continue prescribed analgesia pathway and fluids; consider admission if pain remains uncontrolled or oral intake is inadequate. Discharge only when stable, drinking and managing with oral medication, with clear return advice for fever, chest symptoms, breathlessness, increasing drowsiness, weakness or uncontrolled pain.

Patient: N. Uddin
MRN: H7300661
Requesting service: Rheumatology, Skewen Medical Centre
Specimen collection/report date: 29 February 2020
Specimen: EDTA whole blood and serum
Clinical details: Established rheumatoid arthritis with increased morning stiffness, swollen hand joints and fatigue. Current treatment includes methotrexate 15 mg once weekly, folic acid and naproxen.

HAEMATOLOGY

• Haemoglobin: 126 g/L (115–160)
• White cell count: 7.8 × 10⁹/L (4.0–11.0)
• Neutrophils: 5.1 × 10⁹/L (2.0–7.5)
• Platelets: 392 × 10⁹/L (150–400)
• Mean cell volume: 89 fL (80–100)

No anaemia, leucopenia or clinically significant neutropenia identified. Platelet count is at the upper end of the reference interval.

INFLAMMATORY MARKERS

• C-reactive protein: 28 mg/L (<5) — raised
• Plasma viscosity: 2.05 mPa·s (1.50–1.72) — raised

BIOCHEMISTRY

• Alanine aminotransferase: 31 U/L (5–35)
• Alkaline phosphatase: 82 U/L (30–130)
• Bilirubin: 9 µmol/L (<21)
• Albumin: 39 g/L (35–50)
• Creatinine: 68 µmol/L (45–90)

Liver enzymes, albumin and renal function are within the stated laboratory intervals. Results are suitable for interpretation alongside the patient’s clinical assessment and treatment history.

Laboratory comment

The raised C-reactive protein and plasma viscosity support active systemic inflammation and are compatible with the reported rheumatoid arthritis flare, although these markers are non-specific. Full blood count, hepatic indices and renal function show no current laboratory evidence of methotrexate toxicity.

Please confirm adherence to the prescribed dosing schedule. The medication record states methotrexate 15 mg once weekly; accidental daily administration requires urgent clinical review. Continue routine disease-modifying antirheumatic drug monitoring in accordance with local rheumatology protocol. Patient: radiance partridge
Occupation: Police officer
Home address: 170 Walled Garden Close, Beckenham, BR3 1AB
Preferred contact: radiance.partridge23@outlook.com
Community correspondence/support affiliation: Norwood Green Community Centre

Presenting complaint
Several months of painless swelling in the left side of the neck, with drenching night sweats and reduced appetite. Reports unintentional weight loss over the same period; no deliberate dietary change. No fever recorded at home. Denies sore throat, dental symptoms, dysphagia, stridor or recent infection. No cough, chest pain or haemoptysis. No abdominal pain or change in bowel habit.

Background
Hodgkin lymphoma is the working clinical diagnosis following assessment of persistent lymphadenopathy. Tissue diagnosis remains pending. No regular prescribed medication apart from supportive care pending tissue diagnosis. No known recent exposure to tuberculosis documented. Smoking and alcohol history not recorded during the acute assessment.

Alert and appropriately concerned. Haemodynamically stable and afebrile in the department. Multiple firm, non-tender cervical lymph nodes, greatest in the left lower cervical chain; no overlying erythema or fluctuance. Initial blood tests requested: full blood count, renal profile, liver function, calcium, lactate dehydrogenase, C-reactive protein and blood film. Chest radiograph arranged. Painless progressive cervical lymphadenopathy with constitutional symptoms, clinically concerning for Hodgkin lymphoma. No current airway compromise, sepsis or other indication for admission identified.

Discharge summary for rushawn adam

DOB: 13th September 1973

You were admitted after developing sudden breathlessness, sharp pain worse when breathing in, and a fast heart rate. You also reported a dry cough for 3 days. Your oxygen level was low on arrival, and an electrocardiogram showed tachycardia.

A CT pulmonary angiogram confirmed blood clots in branches of both lungs, consistent with a pulmonary embolism. There was no evidence of strain on the right side of your heart. An ultrasound scan of your legs did not show a deep-vein thrombosis. Blood tests showed a raised D-dimer, as expected in this situation, but your kidney function and full blood count remained satisfactory. A chest X-ray did not show pneumonia.

You were initially given supplemental oxygen and anticoagulation treatment. Your breathing and chest pain improved steadily, and the oxygen was stopped before discharge. You remained mobile on the ward without a fall or fainting episode. There was no bleeding during your admission.

Discharge medicines

• Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for the first 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily thereafter. Take each dose regularly and do not stop it unless advised by a healthcare professional. The intended duration of treatment will be reviewed by your GP and the anticoagulation team; at present, treatment is planned for at least 3 months.
• Do not take ibuprofen, naproxen or aspirin unless a doctor specifically tells you to do so, as these medicines can increase bleeding risk. Paracetamol may be used for pain within the recommended dose.
• Supplemental oxygen is no longer required at home.

Please arrange a medication review with your GP surgery within one week. Kidney function and a full blood count should be checked at that review, with further anticoagulation follow-up as arranged. Your GP should also review possible provoking factors and whether longer-term anticoagulation is needed.

Seek urgent medical help through A&E or 999 if you develop severe or worsening breathlessness, new severe chest pain, cough up blood, collapse, or have signs of a serious bleed such as vomiting blood, black stools or bleeding that will not stop. Contact your GP promptly for heavy bruising, persistent nosebleeds or any other bleeding concern. Avoid contact sports while taking apixaban and tell dentists, pharmacists and other clinicians that you are anticoagulated.

Please keep this summary with your medicines. Your recorded home address is 169 Richardson Road, Insch, AB52 6AB, and your contact detail is 07700 900609.

Emergency Department Assessment – 05/11/2024

Patient: ALIDIA WILLIS
Seen at Royal Alexandra Hospital by della-rae ayres

The patient attended A&E with lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge and pain during intercourse. The abdominal pain began gradually and has been present for 3 days, initially central but now more marked bilaterally in the lower abdomen. She describes the discharge as increased in volume and yellowish, without offensive odour. There has been dyspareunia but no post-coital bleeding. She denies dysuria, urinary frequency, diarrhoea or constipation. She reports no measured fever, rigors or vomiting. Last menstrual period was approximately two weeks ago; pregnancy is not suspected. N. Bryant accompanied her and provided additional history with the patient’s consent.

Past medical history is unremarkable. No previous pelvic inflammatory disease is documented. She takes no regular medicines and reports no known drug allergies. She is sexually active with one recent partner and does not routinely use condoms. Safeguarding concerns were not identified during the private part of the consultation.

On assessment she was alert and uncomfortable when mobilising. Temperature was 37.8°C, pulse 96 bpm, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturations 99% on air. The abdomen was soft, with moderate suprapubic and bilateral iliac fossa tenderness, but no guarding or rebound. There was no palpable mass. Speculum examination showed mucopurulent discharge from the cervical os. Bimanual examination elicited cervical excitation and bilateral adnexal tenderness, without a discrete adnexal mass.

Urine pregnancy test was negative. Urinalysis showed trace blood and 1+ leucocytes, with nitrites negative. Blood tests demonstrated a mildly raised CRP of 38 mg/L and white cell count of 11.2 × 10⁹/L; renal and liver profiles were within normal limits. Vaginal and endocervical swabs were taken for chlamydia, gonorrhoea and other microbiology. Pelvic ultrasound was requested because of the adnexal tenderness; this showed no tubo-ovarian abscess, ovarian torsion or significant free fluid.

Assessment

The clinical picture is most consistent with uncomplicated pelvic inflammatory disease. There is currently no evidence of pregnancy, sepsis, torsion or tubo-ovarian abscess. The diagnosis and the importance of completing treatment were discussed. Partner notification and testing were advised, with sexual intercourse avoided until treatment is complete and partners have been assessed.

Plan

Ceftriaxone was administered in the department, followed by doxycycline and metronidazole as discharge treatment in accordance with local sexual health guidance. Analgesia with paracetamol and ibuprofen was advised if tolerated. The patient was given written safety-netting advice to return urgently for worsening pain, persistent vomiting, faintness, high fever or new heavy bleeding. Sexual health follow-up was arranged, and results will be communicated when available.

Discharged home in a stable condition with N. Bryant accompanying her. Review by the GP or sexual health service is recommended within 48–72 hours if symptoms are not clearly improving. Signed by della-rae ayres.

NHS LABORATORY REPORT
NHS number: 0007468530

Patient: Salvatore
Patient identifier (MRN): MRN-05960339
Specimen type: EDTA blood and serum
Clinical information: Painless lymphadenopathy with night sweats and unintentional weight loss. Clinical diagnosis under investigation: Hodgkin lymphoma. Supportive care only pending tissue diagnosis.

Haematology
• Haemoglobin: 108 g/L (115–160) — low
• Mean cell volume: 82 fL (80–100)
• White cell count: 12.8 × 10⁹/L (4.0–11.0) — high
• Neutrophils: 9.6 × 10⁹/L (2.0–7.5) — high
• Lymphocytes: 1.7 × 10⁹/L (1.0–4.0)
• Platelets: 468 × 10⁹/L (150–400) — high
• Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 74 mm/hour (0–20) — high

Clinical chemistry
• C-reactive protein: 68 mg/L (<5) — high
• Lactate dehydrogenase: 312 U/L (120–250) — high
• Albumin: 31 g/L (35–50) — low
• Alanine aminotransferase: 24 U/L (0–40)
• Alkaline phosphatase: 126 U/L (30–130)
• Bilirubin: 9 µmol/L (0–21)
• Creatinine: 71 µmol/L (45–90)
• Estimated GFR: >90 mL/min/1.73 m²

Specimen comment
The sample is suitable for the tests performed. The full blood count shows a mild normocytic anaemia with neutrophilic leucocytosis and thrombocytosis. Raised C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and lactate dehydrogenase, together with low albumin, indicate a significant inflammatory process but are not specific for malignancy.

Interpretive note
This pattern is compatible with the reported systemic symptoms and may be seen in Hodgkin lymphoma, although blood results cannot establish the diagnosis or stage disease. There is no biochemical evidence of renal or hepatic impairment in this specimen. Correlate with examination findings and cross-sectional imaging.

Recommended next steps
• Expedite image-guided or excision lymph-node biopsy for histological assessment, including appropriate immunohistochemistry.
• Consider baseline viral serology and fertility, pregnancy or contraception assessment where clinically relevant before systemic treatment.
• Repeat FBC, renal profile, liver profile, LDH and inflammatory markers if symptoms progress or before treatment.
• Review in the haematology pathway on 6th March 2026.

Current treatment: supportive care pending tissue diagnosis; no cytotoxic treatment recorded.

Validated and authorised by:
Z. Mellor, Consultant Clinical Haematologist
GMC professional identifier: 0302604

Discharge summary

Patient: Ela'Nur
Encounter date: 12/07/2045

Reason for admission
The patient, aged 31, presented with a 36-hour history of profuse watery diarrhoea, repeated vomiting and cramping central abdominal pain. There was no blood in the stool and no recent antibiotic exposure. A relative, Muaz, was updated during the admission; the family’s locality is BALLYMARTIN.

Assessment and investigations
On arrival, the patient was clinically dehydrated with dry mucous membranes and mild postural dizziness. Abdomen was soft, with generalised mild tenderness but no guarding or rebound. Blood tests showed a mild pre-renal biochemical pattern; creatinine 97 µmol/L. CRP was not significantly raised and the white cell count was within the local reference range. Stool culture was requested, with no result available before discharge. There were no features to suggest an acute surgical abdomen.

Hospital course
Managed with intravenous crystalloid initially, followed by oral rehydration solution as tolerated. Ondansetron was given intermittently for nausea, with good effect. Vomiting settled within 12 hours and diarrhoea reduced in frequency. The patient remained apyrexial, maintained oral fluids and passed urine normally. Repeat examination was reassuring, with no focal abdominal tenderness.

Discharge medicines
• Oral rehydration solution: prepare and take according to the packet instructions, with additional clear fluids.
• Ondansetron as required for nausea, for short-term use only, in accordance with the supplied directions.

No pre-admission regular medicines were stopped. Ondansetron was supplied for short-term use as required; it is not intended as a continuing regular medicine.

Follow-up and advice
Continue frequent fluids and light meals, advancing diet as tolerated. Observe strict hand hygiene and avoid preparing food for others until 48 hours after the last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting. Do not attend work or school during this period. Seek urgent medical advice via NHS 111 or A&E if unable to keep fluids down, passing very little urine, developing blood in the stool, severe or localised abdominal pain, confusion, or persistent fever. GP review is advised if symptoms have not substantially improved within 72 hours. The pending stool result will be reviewed if clinically significant.

Condition at discharge: clinically improved and haemodynamically stable.

Emergency Department Assessment

Patient: Ilhan Duggan
Age: 60 y/o
Home address: 37 Bengarth Road, Barnetby le Wold, DN38 6AA
Contact detail: ilhan.duggan71@gmail.com

Ilhan Duggan attended A&E with a four-day history of cough, initially dry but now productive of yellow-green sputum. They have felt feverish with rigors overnight and report sharp right-sided chest pain on inspiration and when coughing. There has been reduced appetite but they have managed fluids. No haemoptysis, unilateral calf swelling, recent surgery or prolonged travel. They deny palpitations, syncope and urinary symptoms. The patient has been taking paracetamol at home, with partial relief, and has not yet started any prescribed antibiotic.

Past medical history is notable for no known chronic respiratory disease. No regular medication other than intermittent paracetamol was reported. There are no known drug allergies. The patient does not smoke. Their email contact detail is recorded as ilhan.duggan71@gmail.com for follow-up communication.

On arrival, temperature was 38.4°C, pulse 104 bpm, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min and oxygen saturation 95% on air. They appeared tired but were alert, conversing in full sentences and clinically euvolaemic. There was reduced air entry with coarse inspiratory crackles at the right base, with mild focal tenderness over the lower right lateral chest wall. No wheeze was heard. Heart sounds were normal, with no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Abdomen was soft and non-tender. There was no neck stiffness or rash.

A chest radiograph demonstrated patchy right lower-zone air-space opacity consistent with infection, without pleural effusion or pneumothorax. Blood tests showed a mildly raised white cell count of 12.8 × 10⁹/L and C-reactive protein 86 mg/L. Urea, electrolytes and renal function were within the expected range. Venous lactate was 1.2 mmol/L. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A/B and SARS-CoV-2. The presentation and investigations support community-acquired pneumonia; the diagnostic coding entry is SNOMED CT 233604007.

Assessment

This is a clinically stable, uncomplicated right lower-lobe community-acquired pneumonia. There is no current evidence of sepsis, respiratory failure or a complication requiring inpatient management. CURB-65 is 0, and the patient is suitable for treatment at home with clear safety-netting.

Plan

The patient was given the first dose of oral amoxicillin in the department and advised to complete the prescribed course. Paracetamol may be continued as directed for fever and pleuritic discomfort, with attention to the maximum daily dose. Regular oral fluids and rest were encouraged. They were advised to seek urgent medical help for increasing breathlessness, confusion, persistent vomiting, blue lips, worsening chest pain or inability to maintain hydration, and to contact their GP if not improving within 48–72 hours.

Discharged home in a stable condition. Treating clinician: Dr Murron MISTRY, MBBS.

text:
Patient: zohaa sewell
NHS number: 0006774912
Occupation: Librarian
Department: Accident and emergency
Report/accession ID: LAB-09100621
Reviewing clinician: Dr Yakoub Ratcliffe, MBBS
Healthcare organisation: Ealing Hospital

Today you were assessed in the emergency department because of short episodes of spinning, particularly when turning in bed, looking upwards or changing position. You also described nausea and some unsteadiness, but no continuous loss of balance.

Your symptoms and examination are most consistent with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). This is caused by tiny calcium particles moving within the balance canals of the inner ear. Although the spinning can feel alarming, BPPV is not usually due to a problem in the brain and it commonly improves with the correct repositioning manoeuvre.

Your observations were reassuring. There was no new weakness, facial droop, speech disturbance, double vision or severe headache. Limb coordination and sensation were intact. The positional assessment reproduced brief vertigo without persistent neurological abnormality. There was no history to suggest fainting, chest pain or an acute hearing loss. These findings support BPPV rather than a central neurological cause.

Please take prochlorperazine as required for troublesome nausea, following the directions on the dispensing label. It may make you sleepy, so do not drive, cycle on the road, operate machinery or drink alcohol if affected. Avoid driving until the vertigo has settled and you can turn your head safely.

A canalith repositioning exercise, such as the Epley manoeuvre, was discussed. This can be performed at home if you feel safe, ideally with someone nearby the first time. Move slowly when getting out of bed, keep fluids up, and avoid sudden head movements for the next few days. A referral for vestibular physiotherapy can be arranged through your GP if symptoms persist or recur.

Please seek urgent medical help through A&E or 999 if the dizziness becomes continuous, or if it occurs with new weakness, numbness, difficulty speaking, collapse, severe headache, chest pain, inability to walk, or persistent vomiting. Arrange a GP review if there is no clear improvement in about 8 weeks, if episodes are becoming more frequent, or if hearing symptoms develop.

This assessment and plan have been explained in plain language, and questions were answered before discharge.

Signed by Dr Yakoub Ratcliffe, MBBS
Accident and emergency, Ealing Hospital

Please maintain good fluid intake unless another clinician has advised you to restrict fluids.

Seek urgent medical help through NHS 111, an urgent treatment centre or A&E if you develop recurrent rigors, a high or persistent fever, worsening flank or abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, confusion, fainting, difficulty passing urine or feel markedly more unwell. Call 999 for severe breathing difficulty, collapse or new chest pain. If symptoms have not clearly continued to improve after completing antibiotics, contact your GP surgery promptly.

Discharge summary
NHS number: 000 459 9854

Patient: RILWAN WATSON
Age: 21 y/o
Admission date: 20th June 1996
Discharge: day 4 of admission
Contact detail: rilwan.watson84@yahoo.co.uk

Reason for admission

RILWAN WATSON was admitted via the emergency department with a severe vaso-occlusive painful crisis related to sickle cell disease. The pain had developed over approximately 24 hours and was predominantly in both lower limbs and the lower back. This was associated with reduced oral intake, dark urine and clinical dehydration. There was no preceding chest pain, breathlessness, fever or infective symptomatology. Mette Chen, the patient’s relative, was updated during the admission with the patient’s consent.

Initial assessment and results

On arrival, the patient was alert but distressed by pain and had dry mucous membranes. Observations remained stable, with no oxygen requirement. Initial pain score was 9/10. There was tenderness through the thighs and lumbar paraspinal region without focal neurological deficit, joint swelling or features of cauda equina syndrome. Chest examination was clear.

Blood tests showed the patient’s expected chronic anaemia, with no marked fall from their usual baseline. Reticulocytes were raised in keeping with haemolysis. Renal function was preserved, bilirubin was mildly elevated and inflammatory markers were not significantly raised. Chest radiograph showed no acute infiltrate. Blood cultures were not indicated clinically and there was no evidence of acute chest syndrome.

Hospital course

Treatment followed the established sickle cell pain pathway. Intravenous fluids were given initially for dehydration, with careful monitoring of fluid balance and urine output. Analgesia comprised regular paracetamol and oral morphine, with intermittent intravenous morphine for breakthrough pain during the first night. Antiemetic treatment was available as required. The patient was encouraged to mobilise and maintain oral hydration once nausea had settled. Thromboprophylaxis was prescribed while mobility was reduced.

Pain gradually improved over the following days, and intravenous opioid treatment was stopped without withdrawal symptoms. There was no fever, hypoxia, neurological change or clinical evidence of infection. Renal function remained stable and repeat haemoglobin was satisfactory for the patient’s baseline. At the time of discharge, pain was controlled with oral medication, oral intake was adequate and the patient was mobilising independently. Current pain score was 5/10.

Problem list

1. Sickle cell painful crisis affecting the limbs and back.
2. Dehydration, resolved with intravenous and oral fluids.
3. Chronic haemolytic anaemia, stable compared with baseline.
4. No evidence of acute chest syndrome or bacterial infection during this admission.

Discharge medicines and advice

Continue regular paracetamol as previously prescribed. Morphine oral solution may be used for severe breakthrough pain strictly according to the supplied dosing instructions; avoid driving, alcohol and operating machinery while taking it. Continue usual sickle cell medicines and ensure good oral hydration. Do not take additional sedating medicines unless discussed with a clinician.

The patient should contact their GP surgery or sickle cell clinical team promptly if pain is not controlled, oral intake falls or vomiting develops. Attend A&E urgently for fever, chest pain, shortness of breath, new weakness, confusion or worsening pain despite the agreed rescue analgesia plan.

Follow-up

The GP is asked to review recovery and analgesic requirements within one week. The existing haematology follow-up should continue, with routine monitoring of full blood count, reticulocytes, renal function and bilirubin as clinically indicated. A written crisis plan was discussed before discharge, including early presentation for future severe pain or symptoms suggestive of acute chest syndrome.

Comparison with previous renal function and assessment of fluid status are advised; laboratory findings alone cannot distinguish pre-renal, intrinsic or post-renal disease.

Clinical comment
Continue close monitoring of urine output, fluid balance, creatinine, potassium and bicarbonate. Review medicines for renal dosing and avoid further nephrotoxic exposure where possible. Consider urinary tract imaging if obstruction is clinically plausible. Urgent senior review is appropriate if potassium rises, urine output remains poor, or there are symptoms or ECG changes suggestive of hyperkalaemia.

Planned renal function review: 21 Feb 2019

Validated and authorised by Iyla-Rose Murphy

Nursing progress note

Karsyn B. remains on contact precautions in a side room with suspected infectious gastroenteritis. The patient reports that diarrhoea has continued overnight but is less frequent than on admission. Two loose, watery stools were recorded during this shift, with one episode of vomiting shortly after breakfast. They describe intermittent cramping around the lower abdomen, rated 4/10 at its worst, without focal tenderness or blood in the stool. No chest pain, breathlessness or dizziness reported.

At 08:15 the patient was alert and orientated, with a temperature of 37.4°C, pulse 92 bpm, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 and oxygen saturations 98% on air. Mucous membranes are slightly dry, although capillary refill remains under two seconds. The patient passed urine independently; urine was concentrated in appearance, and output will continue to be monitored. No new rash noted.

Oral rehydration solution was offered regularly and tolerated in small, frequent amounts. The patient has taken approximately 650 ml of fluid this shift and a small portion of toast and banana. Ondansetron was administered as required before the midday intake, with good effect and no further vomiting for three hours afterwards. Abdominal discomfort improved following the episode of vomiting and has not required additional analgesia. Hand hygiene with soap and water was reinforced, and the patient was reminded not to use the communal bathroom. Equipment remains dedicated to the side room and enhanced environmental cleaning has been requested through Queen Elizabeth University Hospital.

The patient mobilises independently to the bathroom but was advised to call for assistance if light-headed, particularly after opening their bowels. Falls risk is currently low; the call bell is within reach and the floor is dry. Fluid balance documentation is in progress. Stool sample collection has been discussed, and the patient understands the need to notify staff before flushing if another sample is required.

Assessment: Ongoing diarrhoea with reduced frequency, one further vomiting episode and mild clinical dehydration. Haemodynamically stable at present, with a satisfactory response to oral rehydration and ondansetron. No evidence of acute abdomen or sepsis on this review.

Plan for the next shift is to continue contact precautions, four-hourly observations, strict fluid balance and regular offers of oral rehydration solution. Encourage bland food as tolerated and administer ondansetron according to the prescription if nausea recurs. Escalate promptly to the nurse in charge and medical team for persistent vomiting, inability to maintain fluids, reduced urine output, worsening abdominal pain, blood in stool, fever or deteriorating observations. Confirm the discharge contact details recorded as 07700 900318 and home address 123 Morrison Lane, Alford, AB33 8AA before any discharge planning; the patient states that Lexsie Watts can assist with transport and support at home.
