text:
Discharge summary

Patient: Lilia Haque
Discharging service: Gynaecology, Ulster Hospital
Report/accession ID: 0815228527

Reason for admission
Lilia Haque was admitted via the emergency department with a three-day history of worsening lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge and deep dyspareunia. She reported nausea without vomiting and no urinary frequency or dysuria. Pregnancy testing was negative. There was no history suggestive of acute bowel obstruction or urinary sepsis.

Assessment and investigations
On arrival she was haemodynamically stable and afebrile. Abdominal examination demonstrated suprapubic and bilateral iliac fossa tenderness without guarding or rebound. Speculum examination showed mucopurulent discharge from the cervical os. Bimanual examination was uncomfortable, with cervical excitation and bilateral adnexal tenderness, but no palpable mass.

Initial blood tests showed a mildly raised C-reactive protein and white cell count, with normal renal and liver function. Urinalysis did not support a urinary tract infection. Pelvic ultrasound demonstrated a small volume of free fluid but no tubo-ovarian abscess, adnexal torsion or other surgical pathology. Vaginal and endocervical samples were sent for microscopy, culture and sexually transmitted infection testing; results were pending at discharge. The current pain score is 5/10.

Hospital course
The clinical findings were consistent with pelvic inflammatory disease. Treatment was commenced promptly with intramuscular ceftriaxone, followed by oral doxycycline and metronidazole. Analgesia with paracetamol and, when required, ibuprofen provided reasonable relief. She remained clinically stable throughout admission, with improving abdominal tenderness and a marked reduction in discharge. She tolerated oral fluids and medication, and was independently mobile before discharge.

There was no indication for operative intervention. The possibility of sexually transmitted infection was discussed sensitively, including the need for partner notification and testing. She was advised to avoid sexual intercourse until treatment has been completed, symptoms have settled and any partners have been assessed and treated as appropriate.

Medication on discharge
• Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily to complete a 14-day course.
• Metronidazole 400 mg orally twice daily to complete a 14-day course.
• Paracetamol 1 g orally up to four times daily when required, maximum 4 g in 24 hours.
• Ceftriaxone has been administered in hospital and does not require continuation at home.

She was advised not to drink alcohol while taking metronidazole and for 48 hours after the final dose. She should take doxycycline with plenty of water, remain upright after taking it, and protect her skin from excessive sunlight. The potential for nausea, diarrhoea and thrush was explained, with advice to seek help if severe or persistent.

Follow-up and safety-netting
The sexual health service will review outstanding microbiology results and arrange contact tracing where indicated. A follow-up appointment has been requested within one week, with repeat assessment in primary care if symptoms have not fully resolved. She should attend A&E urgently for increasing pain, fever, vomiting, fainting, heavy vaginal bleeding or inability to take antibiotics.

Her nominated relative, erys imran, lives in DRUMBEG and was updated with the patient’s consent. At discharge, Lilia Haque was comfortable at rest, able to mobilise and understood the treatment plan and safety-netting advice.

Emergency Department Assessment and Handover
National Insurance number: NK 28 53 21 C

Patient: Zalayah ROPER
MRN: 099 508 763
Referring service: Queen Victoria Hospital
History from patient and relative, A. Said.

Presenting problem
Sudden episode of pounding heartbeat, central chest tightness and intense fear of dying while at rest. Symptoms began abruptly and peaked within several minutes. Associated trembling, tingling around the mouth and feeling unable to get a satisfying breath. No collapse, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, unilateral leg swelling or recent febrile illness. No exertional chest pain reported. Similar, shorter episode several months ago; no previous formal treatment.

Assessment
Alert, distressed initially but able to engage and speak in full sentences. Symptoms easing during review. Airway patent; chest clear bilaterally with no increased work of breathing. Heart sounds normal, regular pulse by examination, no peripheral oedema. Neurology grossly intact. Skin warm and dry. No features of intoxication or acute psychosis.

Observations: pulse 102 initially, settling to 86; respiratory rate 18; oxygen saturations 99% on air; temperature normal; blood pressure 120/80 mmHg.

Investigations
12-lead ECG: sinus rhythm, no acute ischaemic changes or arrhythmia. Capillary glucose within normal range. Pregnancy status discussed and not clinically indicated for the immediate investigations undertaken. No red flags to suggest pulmonary embolism, acute coronary syndrome or significant metabolic disturbance; further blood tests not felt necessary following senior review.

Management and decision
Reassurance and coached breathing retraining undertaken in the department, with clear reduction in hyperventilation and chest tightness. No sedative medication required. Presentation is most consistent with a panic attack, but recurrent palpitations require GP review if episodes continue.

Disposition
Safe for discharge with A. Said aware of the plan. Advised to avoid excess caffeine and alcohol, practise slow diaphragmatic breathing, and seek urgent help via 999 for persistent chest pain, syncope, severe breathlessness or new neurological symptoms. GP follow-up arranged for 21 January 2023 to review anxiety symptoms, triggers and consideration of talking therapy. Written advice supplied.

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient with persistent essential hypertension, despite treatment with amlodipine and ramipril. The specific question is whether further investigation or modification of antihypertensive therapy is indicated, particularly in view of intermittent headache and light-headedness.

The patient reports episodic, non-focal headaches and a sensation of light-headedness without syncope. The current episode of headache has been present for 3 days. There is no associated visual loss, diplopia, facial weakness, dysphasia, limb weakness, chest pain, palpitations or breathlessness. They have not described features suggestive of temporal arteritis, including scalp tenderness or jaw claudication. There is no history of episodic sweating, tremor or panic associated with the blood pressure readings.

Home monitoring has shown repeated elevated readings, generally in the 150–165/85–95 mmHg range, although occasional lower readings have been recorded when symptomatic. In clinic today, blood pressure was 158/92 mmHg in the right arm and 154/90 mmHg in the left arm, with a regular pulse of 76 beats per minute. After sitting quietly for five minutes, the repeat reading was 152/88 mmHg. There was no significant postural fall. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated normal heart sounds without murmur, and the chest was clear. Neurological examination was non-focal, with normal gait, power, sensation and coordination.

The patient is currently taking amlodipine 5 mg once daily and ramipril 5 mg once daily. Adherence was discussed and appears reliable, with no regular use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or decongestants. They do not report ankle swelling, persistent cough or other clear adverse effects. I have advised continuation of the current medicines pending specialist review and encouraged twice-daily home blood pressure recording, including the time of measurement and any associated symptoms.

Recent blood tests showed normal sodium, potassium and renal function. Urinalysis was negative for blood and protein. An ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm without evidence of left ventricular strain. Report/accession ID: LAB-02643395.

I would appreciate your opinion on optimal blood pressure targets and whether titration of either current agent, addition of a further class, or ambulatory blood pressure monitoring would be appropriate. Please also advise whether any secondary hypertension screen is warranted based on the clinical pattern.

C. Short

text:
LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: Carter P.
MRN: H3453567
Specimen/report date: 29 Sep 2024
Clinical indication: Flank pain, dysuria and rigors for 3 days. Provisional diagnosis: acute pyelonephritis. Current medication includes cefuroxime and paracetamol.

Specimen details

Midstream urine submitted in a sterile container for microscopy, culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Specimen received in a suitable condition; no significant delay or leakage noted.

Urinalysis

Appearance: Turbid
pH: 6.0
Protein: 2+
Blood: 2+
Nitrite: Positive
Leucocyte esterase: 3+

Microscopy

White cells: >100 × 10^6/L
Red cells: 25 × 10^6/L
Squamous epithelial cells: <10 × 10^6/L

Culture

Significant growth of Escherichia coli, estimated at >10^7 colony-forming units/L. The isolate is consistent with a urinary pathogen and is reported as a pure growth.

Antimicrobial susceptibility

Cefuroxime: Susceptible
Co-amoxiclav: Susceptible
Trimethoprim: Resistant
Ciprofloxacin: Susceptible
Nitrofurantoin: Susceptible for lower urinary tract infection only
Gentamicin: Susceptible

Interpretation

The findings support significant E. coli urinary infection. In the context of flank pain and rigors, the result is compatible with acute pyelonephritis rather than uncomplicated cystitis. Cefuroxime is active in vitro against the isolate and may be continued if the patient is demonstrating an appropriate clinical response and renal function permits.

Nitrofurantoin should not be selected for treatment of suspected upper urinary tract infection despite the reported susceptibility, as tissue penetration is inadequate. Trimethoprim resistance is present. Antimicrobial choice, dose and duration should be reviewed against local NHS guidance, renal function, allergy status and the severity of illness.

Clinical comment

Please correlate with temperature, blood pressure, renal function and inflammatory markers. Escalation for same-day medical assessment is advised if there is persistent rigoring, vomiting, hypotension, worsening pain, acute kidney injury or inability to tolerate oral treatment. Blood cultures should be considered if the patient is systemically unwell or febrile at the time of review. Repeat urine culture is not routinely required after clinical resolution, but should be discussed if symptoms persist or recur.

Paracetamol may be used for symptomatic relief within the prescribed maximum daily dose. The laboratory result should be interpreted alongside the clinical response rather than in isolation.

Validated and authorised by TAMAYA MACKENZIE
Professional identifier: 0069945
Laboratory medicine report issued 29 Sep 2024

Patient: Oluwafolabomi, 65-year-old Hispanic female patient
Home address: 31 Seaforth Avenue, MONEYMORE
Report/accession ID: 03790971

Current assessment
Reviewed on the morning shift following admission with decompensated heart failure. Reports breathlessness when lying flat and is sleeping propped upright on three pillows. Orthopnoea persists but is less marked than overnight. Bilateral ankle oedema remains present, with reduced exercise tolerance; patient becomes short of breath walking to the bathroom.

At 08:15 observations were: respiratory rate 22/min, oxygen saturations 94% on room air, pulse 86 bpm and regular, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, temperature 36.7°C. Alert and orientated, speaking in full sentences. Fine bibasal crackles on auscultation. No chest pain reported. Skin warm, with mild pitting oedema to both ankles. No pressure damage noted.

Fluid balance and mobility
Oral intake modest this morning: tea, toast and approximately 250 mL water. Fluid restriction reinforced as prescribed. Passing urine independently; urine output increased after diuretic administration. Mobilising short distances with a wheeled frame and one staff member. Call bell left within reach and advised to request assistance before standing. Falls precautions maintained.

Interventions and response
Furosemide administered as prescribed; response evident with increased urinary frequency and some subjective easing of chest heaviness. Bisoprolol given after confirming pulse and blood pressure. Supported into a high sitting position and encouraged paced breathing. Oxygen not required at present. Daily weight completed and documented on the fluid balance chart. Leg elevation provided while seated.

Risk and escalation
Continues to be at risk of fluid overload, falls and worsening breathlessness. Escalate urgently for increasing work of breathing, oxygen saturation below the prescribed threshold, new chest pain, confusion, marked reduction in urine output or systolic blood pressure below the escalation parameter. Medical review noted under GMC professional identifier GMC 0003083; no additional concerns raised during the review.

Plan for next shift
Continue four-hourly observations, strict fluid balance and daily weight. Maintain prescribed fluid and dietary restrictions. Reassess respiratory effort, crackles, oedema and mobility after the next dose of furosemide. Encourage rest between activities and assisted mobilisation only. Confirm ongoing medication tolerance and inform the medical team if orthopnoea or oxygen requirement increases.

Movement Disorders Clinic review

Patient: Aarez POWER
Address: 125 Lamlash Street, Royal Sutton Coldfield, B73 5AA
Telephone: 07700 900411
Occupation: Graphic designer
Employer: Norton Hawkfield Further Education College

Aarez POWER was seen in clinic today for review of Parkinson disease, accompanied by their partner. They report a gradual increase in slowness over the past three months, particularly when getting dressed and turning in bed. The resting tremor remains most noticeable in the right hand and is less troublesome after taking co-beneldopa. There has been some muscular rigidity in the shoulders and thighs, with occasional discomfort after sitting for prolonged periods. They have not noticed any new falls, fainting, hallucinations or significant change in memory.

They take co-beneldopa as prescribed, currently three times daily, and usually remember the doses. There is a mild wearing-off effect before the next tablet, described as reduced mobility and increased tremor for approximately 20–30 minutes. They deny dyskinesia. Sleep is generally settled, although turning in bed can be difficult. Appetite is reasonable and there is no choking or unexplained weight loss. They continue to manage personal care independently and remain in work, though tasks requiring prolonged standing are taking longer.

On examination, the patient was alert and engaged. Speech was slightly quiet but clear. There was a mild right-sided resting tremor, with increased tone at both wrists, more marked on the right. Finger tapping was slowed with decrement bilaterally, again worse on the right. Facial expression was mildly reduced. They rose from the chair without using their arms and walked with short steps and reduced right arm swing; there was no freezing observed in the room. Turning was performed safely. Postural reflexes were mildly impaired but there was no current evidence of a high falls risk. Blood pressure was 132/78 mmHg sitting and 128/76 mmHg standing, with no symptomatic postural drop.

Assessment

Parkinson disease with mild progression of bradykinesia and rigidity and a predictable, short wearing-off period before doses. No evidence today of troublesome dyskinesia, psychosis or significant autonomic instability.

Plan

The diagnosis and expected fluctuation of symptoms were discussed. Co-beneldopa will continue at the current dose for now; the patient will keep a simple diary of medication times, mobility and tremor for two weeks. If wearing-off becomes more frequent, the GP or movement disorders team can consider adjusting the dosing interval or adding an adjunctive treatment. I advised regular walking, stretching and balance exercises, with referral to physiotherapy if mobility deteriorates. They were reminded to rise slowly, maintain adequate fluids and report falls, hallucinations, swallowing difficulty or sudden functional decline.

A follow-up appointment will be arranged in approximately four months. The patient has been advised to contact the Parkinson’s nurse specialist sooner if symptoms worsen or medication effects become difficult to manage.

Discharge summary

Patient: Ruadh
Home address: 118 Helenslee Place, Halkirk, KW12 6AB
Report/accession ID: 04316696

You were admitted with several days of lower abdominal pain, an abnormal vaginal discharge and pain during intercourse (dyspareunia). Examination and pelvic ultrasound were consistent with pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), with no evidence of a tubo-ovarian abscess or an ectopic pregnancy. A pregnancy test was negative. Blood tests showed a mildly raised inflammatory marker, which improved during your admission. Swabs were taken before treatment; the results did not identify gonorrhoea or chlamydia, although this does not exclude PID caused by other organisms.

You were reviewed by the consultant obstetrician-gynaecologist and treated with antibiotics. Ceftriaxone was given by injection, followed by doxycycline and metronidazole. Your pain and discharge improved, and you remained without a fever. You were able to eat, drink and walk safely before leaving hospital. No operation was required.

Please continue:
• doxycycline 100 mg twice daily to complete the prescribed 14-day course;
• metronidazole 400 mg twice daily to complete the prescribed 14-day course.

Do not drink alcohol while taking metronidazole and for 48 hours after the final dose. Take doxycycline with plenty of water while sitting or standing, and avoid taking it immediately before bed. It can make your skin more sensitive to sunlight. If you develop a rash, swelling of the lips or face, severe diarrhoea, vomiting that prevents you taking the antibiotics, or worsening abdominal pain, seek urgent medical advice through NHS 111 or A&E.

PID can affect fertility if treatment is delayed or incomplete. Please avoid sexual intercourse until you and any current sexual partner(s) have completed treatment and your symptoms have settled. A sexual health clinic can arrange confidential partner notification, further testing and advice about contraception. Please attend the follow-up appointment arranged by the sexual health service in approximately two weeks, or sooner if symptoms are not improving.

Your GP surgery should review you if pain, discharge or fever returns. A repeat pregnancy test and further assessment may be needed if symptoms persist.

Discharged home today in a stable condition with the above medicines and written safety-netting advice.

NHS number: 000 686 1700

Patient: Vardhan D.

Requested investigation: Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk assessment

Clinical indication

Predictive testing has been requested because of a significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer and continuing concern regarding inherited cancer risk. The familial finding under review is BRCA1 c.68_69delAG. The patient is not receiving current treatment.

Specimen and methodology

Specimen type: Peripheral blood in EDTA
Test performed: Germline BRCA1 and BRCA2 sequence and copy-number analysis
Platform: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) with confirmation of reportable variants by an orthogonal method where indicated
Reporting framework: Analysis and interpretation undertaken in 2028 using the current laboratory pipeline and reference transcript set.

The assay examines coding exons and relevant splice junctions in BRCA1 and BRCA2. Large genomic rearrangements are assessed by read-depth analysis. This is a germline test and cannot determine whether an identified variant is present in a tumour.

Result

BRCA1 c.68_69delAG was not detected in the submitted specimen.

No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant was identified in the tested regions of BRCA1 or BRCA2. This result substantially reduces, but does not eliminate, the likelihood of a detectable inherited BRCA1- or BRCA2-associated predisposition. It does not exclude a pathogenic variant in another cancer-predisposition gene, a variant outside the regions covered by this assay, or a technical limitation affecting detection.

Interpretation

If BRCA1 c.68_69delAG is a confirmed familial variant, the negative result is potentially informative and is consistent with the patient not having inherited that specific familial alteration. Correlation with the original family laboratory report is essential before applying this interpretation. Where the familial variant has not been independently verified, the result should be regarded as non-diagnostic for the wider family history.

A negative molecular result does not remove the need for risk assessment based on the pedigree. Management should remain guided by the specialist genetics team, the documented family history and applicable national guidance. Predictive testing and disclosure of results should be undertaken with appropriate counselling, including discussion of possible implications for relatives and the limits of testing in an individual without a confirmed familial result.

Clinical comment

Please ensure that the requesting team has supplied the relevant family cancer diagnoses and ages at diagnosis, together with the laboratory report confirming the familial BRCA1 c.68_69delAG finding if available. Referral or ongoing review through the regional clinical genetics service is recommended. A genetics follow-up appointment is recorded for 2028-12-31.

Report validated and authorised by:
TALLINN GREAVES
Laboratory validating clinician

This report should be interpreted alongside the clinical referral information and is not, in isolation, a diagnosis of hereditary cancer syndrome.

Consultation – GP surgery

The patient, aged 74, was reviewed following an episode of sudden palpitations and central chest tightness yesterday evening. Symptoms began while watching television, with trembling, breathlessness and a marked fear of dying. Peak intensity lasted approximately 15 minutes, then settled gradually after a family member stayed with them. No collapse, exertional chest pain, haemoptysis or unilateral leg swelling. Similar, less severe episode around two months ago.

No current chest pain or breathlessness. Eating and drinking normally. Denies excess caffeine, recreational drugs or recent infective symptoms. Sleep disturbed by worry about recurrence.

Obs in clinic: BP 128/76, pulse 82 regular, SpO2 98% on air, RR 16, temperature 36.7°C. Alert and comfortable. Heart sounds dual, no murmur. Chest clear bilaterally. No calf tenderness or ankle oedema. ECG: sinus rhythm, no acute ST-T changes.

Assessment: panic attack with prominent autonomic symptoms. Current presentation and examination do not suggest acute cardiopulmonary disease. Discussed the benign but frightening nature of panic symptoms, and safety-netted regarding persistent chest pain, syncope, severe breathlessness or new neurological symptoms—call 999/A&E if these occur.

Plan: continue breathing retraining, practising twice daily when settled and at onset of symptoms. Reduce caffeine and keep a brief trigger/symptom record. Offered talking therapy referral; patient wishes to try self-management initially. Review in about 3 weeks, sooner if recurrent or worsening episodes. Consider further assessment and treatment options if frequent attacks continue.

Discharge summary

Patient: Y. Ball
Age: 27 y/o
Admission/discharge date: 6 February 2012

Reason for admission
Presented with a 4-day history of worsening lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge and deep dyspareunia. No vomiting or urinary symptoms. Pregnancy test was negative.

Assessment and key results
On admission she was haemodynamically stable and afebrile. There was bilateral lower abdominal tenderness without guarding. Speculum examination showed mucopurulent cervical discharge and cervical excitation. Current pain score was 5/10.

FBC and renal profile were unremarkable; CRP was mildly raised at 38 mg/L. Urinalysis did not suggest infection. Pelvic ultrasound demonstrated no tubo-ovarian abscess or free fluid. Vaginal and endocervical swabs were taken. Chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT were negative; other microbiology remains pending and will be reviewed by the sexual health service.

Hospital course
Managed as uncomplicated pelvic inflammatory disease. Received ceftriaxone 1 g IV on admission, followed by doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and metronidazole 400 mg twice daily. Analgesia with paracetamol and ibuprofen gave good symptomatic improvement. She remained apyrexial, tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently. No operative intervention was required.

Discharge medicines
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily to complete 14 days.
Metronidazole 400 mg twice daily to complete 14 days.
Paracetamol as required, within recommended dose limits.
Avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole and for 48 hours after the final dose. Doxycycline should be taken with water while upright; avoid pregnancy during treatment and use sun protection.

Follow-up and advice
Discharged home in stable condition. Sexual health clinic follow-up is advised within 1 week for results, partner notification and testing. Avoid sexual intercourse until treatment is complete, symptoms have settled and partners have been assessed. Seek urgent medical attention for fever, increasing pain, vomiting, faintness or new heavy bleeding.

Home address: 27 ASPENBURN, TEDD
Contact telephone: 07700 900114

Patient: NEDAS STANTON
NHS number: 000 518 4704
Occupation: Administrative assistant
Employer: Polinard Further Education College
Relevant family contact: L. Houghton

Dear Rheumatology Team,

I would be grateful for your assessment of NEDAS STANTON, who is experiencing a clinically significant flare of rheumatoid arthritis despite continuing disease-modifying treatment. The specific question is whether treatment escalation is now indicated and whether the current symptoms represent active inflammatory disease rather than a mechanical hand problem.

Over the past several weeks, the patient has developed worsening morning stiffness, lasting approximately two hours, with painful swelling affecting both hands. Fatigue has also become troublesome and is limiting usual activities at work. There has been no reported fever, recent infection, unexplained weight loss or night sweats. The patient describes no new psoriasis, inflammatory bowel symptoms or eye pain. L. Houghton has been helping with some household tasks because opening jars and fastening clothing have become difficult.

On examination in the surgery, there was visible soft-tissue swelling and tenderness of several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints bilaterally, with reduced grip strength owing to pain. There was no clear joint deformity, skin rash or dactylitis. The wrists were mildly tender, although range of movement was largely preserved. Observations were stable, and the chest and cardiovascular examination were unremarkable.

Current medicines are methotrexate 15 mg once weekly, folic acid as prescribed and naproxen with food when required. The patient reports good adherence and has not taken additional over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medicines. We have discussed the importance of taking methotrexate on one designated day each week and avoiding it during significant infection. Naproxen has provided only partial relief; I have advised using the lowest effective dose and stopping it if dyspepsia, melaena or other gastrointestinal symptoms occur.

Recent primary-care blood monitoring showed no anaemia or significant liver enzyme abnormality, with renal function satisfactory for current treatment. I will arrange repeat full blood count, liver profile, creatinine and inflammatory markers before the specialist appointment. Please review the need for a short corticosteroid bridge, ultrasound or radiographs of the hands, and adjustment of disease-modifying therapy. An expedited appointment would be appreciated because of persistent swelling and functional impairment.

Yours sincerely,

fatheha rigby

Patient: ramina collier
Collection/report date: 2020-12-24
Report/accession ID: L25Q47597
Reporting laboratory: AMMAN VALLEY HOSPITAL

Specimen
Venous blood collected into EDTA tube. Sample suitable for analysis.

Results
HbA1c (IFCC): 70 mmol/mol
Interpretation: Above the usual diagnostic threshold of 48 mmol/mol and above the general treatment target of 53 mmol/mol for many adults with type 2 diabetes. Individual targets should reflect frailty, hypoglycaemia risk, comorbidity and patient preference.

The HbA1c is consistent with suboptimal glycaemic control in the context of reported thirst, fatigue and frequent urination. It reflects glycaemia over approximately the preceding 8–12 weeks and does not indicate the current capillary glucose concentration. Correlate with home glucose readings and assess for intercurrent illness or osmotic symptoms requiring prompt review.

Consider renal profile including eGFR and urine albumin:creatinine ratio, lipid profile, liver enzymes and thyroid function where clinically indicated. Please ensure annual diabetic eye screening, foot assessment and blood pressure review are up to date.

Clinical information supplied
Known type 2 diabetes mellitus. Current medicines include metformin and atorvastatin. No medication changes have been made by the laboratory. If symptoms are worsening, oral intake is poor, or there is vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness or rapid breathing, same-day assessment via the GP surgery, NHS 111 or the emergency department is advised.

Clinic review note

Patient: anesa hogan
Occupation: civil engineer
Report/accession ID: LAB-07233662
Seen at: Groby Road Medical Centre
Clinician: nevaeha horner

The symptoms discussed today are in keeping with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. You described a burning sensation behind the breastbone, particularly after larger meals and when lying down, with acid coming back into the throat. A dry cough is also disturbing your sleep at night. There has been no difficulty swallowing, food sticking, vomiting blood, black stool, unexplained weight loss or persistent vomiting. You have not had exertional chest pain, breathlessness or fainting.

Your observations in clinic were reassuring. The abdomen was soft and non-tender, without guarding or a palpable mass. Your throat was not inflamed and there was no wheeze on chest examination. The pattern is more suggestive of reflux irritating the oesophagus and upper airway than of a primary chest infection. The absence of alarm symptoms is reassuring, although you should seek urgent advice if any of these develop.

Please continue omeprazole as currently prescribed, taking it regularly before food rather than only when symptoms are troublesome. Continue alginate suspension after meals and at bedtime when required, following the instructions on the bottle. We discussed practical measures that may reduce symptoms: smaller meals, avoiding food for three hours before going to bed, reducing alcohol and caffeine if these trigger symptoms, and raising the head end of the bed rather than relying on extra pillows. Stopping smoking, if relevant, would also be beneficial.

If symptoms remain frequent despite consistent treatment, please arrange a further GP review so that the dose and duration can be reconsidered and other causes assessed. Referral for gastroscopy may be appropriate if symptoms do not settle or if alarm features appear. Please contact the surgery sooner if swallowing becomes painful or difficult, or if you notice bleeding, persistent vomiting or unintentional weight loss. Sudden severe chest pain, particularly with sweating or breathlessness, should be treated as an emergency by calling 999.

A symptom check and medication review are planned in 8 days. At that point we will clarify whether the night-time cough has improved and whether alginate is still needed regularly.

Signed by nevaeha horner

Discharge summary

Patient: ella-rai hewitt
Discharge date: 27 Jun 2023
Responsible service: Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh

Reason for admission
Admitted with a vaso-occlusive sickle cell painful crisis causing severe bilateral limb pain and lumbar back pain, with reduced oral intake and clinical dehydration. No history of trauma or infective symptoms.

Hospital course
Pain was assessed using the hospital pain pathway. Initial treatment comprised intravenous crystalloid fluids, regular paracetamol and titrated intravenous morphine, with antiemetic cover as required. Hydration and urine output improved. Morphine was gradually reduced as the pain settled, and the patient was converted to oral analgesia.

Temperature remained normal and oxygen saturations were maintained on air. Chest radiograph showed no acute infiltrate; there was no clinical evidence of acute chest syndrome. No focal neurological deficit or evidence of sepsis developed. Renal function remained stable and haemoglobin was near the patient’s usual baseline. Mobilising independently and tolerating diet and fluids at discharge.

Discharge medicines
• Morphine sulfate oral solution 10 mg/5 mL: take 5 mL (10 mg) by mouth every 4 hours when required for severe pain, maximum six doses (60 mg) in 24 hours, for up to 3 days. Do not take with alcohol, drive, cycle or operate machinery if drowsy. Keep secured and return unused medicine to a pharmacy.
• Paracetamol 1 g by mouth four times daily regularly for 48 hours, then up to four times daily when required; maximum 4 g in 24 hours.
• Continue usual prescribed medicines.

Safety-netting and follow-up
Maintain regular oral fluids and use the agreed sickle-cell pain plan. Seek urgent help via A&E/999 for breathlessness, chest pain, fever, increasing drowsiness, confusion, inability to drink or uncontrolled pain. Contact the GP surgery if symptoms are worsening or morphine is needed beyond the prescribed course.

Haematology follow-up is arranged in about 3 weeks. The patient’s relative, Melchizedek Rowlands, from Whitefield, was updated with consent. Discharged home clinically improved and haemodynamically stable.

text:
Microbiology and Clinical Chemistry Report
NHS number: 0005279705

Patient: Emileigh Rahman
Report/accession ID: 0889107214
Specimen collection/report date: 03/03/2026
Requesting service: General Medicine
Specimen: Deep wound swab from plantar diabetic foot ulcer
Clinical details: Plantar ulceration with reduced sensation and local discharge. Current treatment includes wound care and co-amoxiclav.

Specimen receipt and quality

The specimen was received in a sterile wound transport container. Superficial swab contamination cannot be excluded; correlation with the clinical appearance and, where appropriate, a subsequently obtained tissue specimen is advised. During data-quality checking, the submitted specimen-date entry 31/04/2025 was rejected as an invalid calendar date. The report date and accession record have therefore been retained independently of that entry.

Microscopy

No epithelial cells seen.
Moderate polymorphonuclear leucocytes.
Mixed Gram-positive cocci and Gram-negative bacilli observed.

Culture

Heavy growth of Staphylococcus aureus.
Moderate growth of mixed enteric Gram-negative organisms.
Mixed skin flora also isolated.

Antimicrobial susceptibility

Staphylococcus aureus:
Flucloxacillin: susceptible
Clindamycin: susceptible
Doxycycline: susceptible
Trimethoprim: susceptible
Co-amoxiclav: susceptible
Linezolid: susceptible
Vancomycin: susceptible

No inducible clindamycin resistance detected. The isolate is not suggestive of meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus on the submitted testing.

Interpretive comment

The heavy growth of S. aureus, together with the reported leucocytes and local discharge, may represent clinically significant infection, although a wound swab does not distinguish colonisation from invasive infection. The mixed Gram-negative growth is compatible with a polymicrobial diabetic foot wound. Continue or modify antimicrobial treatment according to the clinical assessment, renal function, allergy history and local diabetic-foot antimicrobial guidance. If there is spreading erythema, increasing pain, systemic illness, tissue necrosis, crepitus or concern for osteomyelitis, urgent surgical and diabetic-foot review is required.

Please ensure pressure off-loading, regular wound assessment and vascular evaluation where indicated. A tissue or deep wound specimen obtained after cleansing and debridement is preferable if the wound fails to improve, deteriorates, or requires operative management. Antibiotic therapy should be reviewed against the clinical response rather than culture results alone.

This result has been validated and authorised by Malgorzata Ashby, Consultant Clinical Microbiologist, GMC reference 0879560.

Temporary medication hold remains in place pending review of renal function. No adverse effects observed from intravenous fluids. Blood samples have been obtained as requested for renal profile and electrolytes; results are awaited. Avoided non-essential nephrotoxic medicines and confirmed that the medical team is aware of ongoing oliguria. The supervising physician's GMC identifier is 0300563.

Risks and escalation
Falls risk remains increased because of fatigue and urgency when mobilising. Call bell left within reach; advised to ask for assistance before standing. Escalate promptly for worsening confusion, hypotension, breathlessness, vomiting, new pain or further fall in urine output. Medical review requested if urine output remains below the agreed monitoring threshold or if blood results deteriorate.

Plan for next shift
- Continue strict fluid balance, including all oral and intravenous intake.
- Record urine volume and appearance after each void.
- Continue intravenous sodium chloride and temporary medication hold as prescribed.
- Encourage small, frequent oral fluids and nutritional intake.
- Review renal profile when available and document medical plan.
- Maintain assisted mobilisation and falls precautions.

GP review – reflux symptoms
NHS number: 000 649 1434

Gena attended for review of ongoing reflux symptoms. She describes a burning discomfort behind the sternum, usually after meals and particularly when bending forwards. There is frequent acid regurgitation into the throat and a dry cough which is worse at night when lying flat. She has not experienced dysphagia, odynophagia, vomiting, haematemesis or melaena. There has been no unintentional weight loss and her appetite remains normal. She reports no exertional chest pain, breathlessness or palpitations.

She has been taking omeprazole once daily and alginate suspension after meals and at bedtime. This has helped during the day, although symptoms still break through overnight. She tends to eat her evening meal late because of work with Bettws Newydd Secondary School, and often goes to bed within two hours afterwards. She drinks several cups of tea daily and has noticed that spicy food and chocolate make the burning worse. She does not smoke. Alcohol intake is occasional.

Occupation: Receptionist. Home address: 119 Ffordd Glasgoed, Hendy-Gwyn / Whitland, SA34 0AA. Preferred contact telephone: 07700 900982.

On examination, she appeared well and was speaking in full sentences. Observations were within the expected range. There was no pallor or jaundice. Chest examination was clear bilaterally, with no wheeze. Heart sounds were normal and the rhythm was regular. The abdomen was soft and non-tender, without guarding or palpable masses. There was no epigastric tenderness today.

Assessment

Symptoms remain most consistent with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, with incomplete control on current treatment. The nocturnal cough is likely related to reflux. There are no current alarm features or findings to suggest an acute cardiopulmonary cause.

Plan

Increase omeprazole to twice daily for a short therapeutic trial, taken before breakfast and the evening meal. Continue alginate suspension after meals and at bedtime as required. We discussed measures to reduce reflux, including smaller meals, avoiding food for at least three hours before lying down, raising the head of the bed, and limiting identified triggers such as spicy food, chocolate, excess tea and alcohol.

She will seek urgent medical attention via A&E or the emergency department if she develops severe or exertional chest pain, vomiting blood, black stools, progressive difficulty swallowing or marked breathlessness. Otherwise, arrange GP review in about 5 weeks. If symptoms remain troublesome despite treatment, consider further investigation and referral for specialist assessment.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: kareemah newman
MRN: H8255832
Responsible organisation: Ulster Hospital
Consultant: Dr Imogine Rahman, MBBS, consultant physician
GMC number: 0331559

Reason for admission
Admitted via the emergency department with a 48-hour history of profuse watery diarrhoea, repeated vomiting and intermittent abdominal cramps. Oral intake had been poor, with dizziness on standing and reduced urine output. There was no reported rectal bleeding, recent travel or recent antibiotic exposure.

Assessment and key results
On arrival, the patient was clinically dehydrated but haemodynamically stable. Abdomen was soft, with mild diffuse tenderness and no guarding or peritonism. Initial pain score was 5/10. Blood tests showed a mild pre-renal acute kidney injury and borderline hypokalaemia; inflammatory markers were only mildly raised. Liver function and venous lactate were satisfactory. Stool microbiology, including testing for Clostridioides difficile, did not identify a bacterial or viral pathogen. Urinalysis was unremarkable.

Hospital course
The patient received intravenous crystalloid during the first day, followed by frequent oral rehydration solution as vomiting settled. Ondansetron was given as required, with good effect. Renal function and electrolytes normalised on repeat testing, and urine output improved. Diarrhoeal frequency reduced substantially and the patient tolerated a light diet without further vomiting. There was no indication for antimicrobial treatment.

At the time of discharge, the patient was afebrile, alert and mobilising independently. The abdomen remained soft and non-distended, with only minimal residual cramping. Hydration was clinically adequate.

Discharge medicines
• Oral rehydration solution: prepare and take according to the product instructions, with additional fluids after each loose stool.
• Ondansetron as required for nausea, according to the labelled dose. Do not exceed the prescribed daily maximum.

No regular medicines were stopped or newly commenced other than the above short-term treatment.

Follow-up and advice
Continue small, frequent meals and fluids, advancing diet as tolerated. Wash hands carefully with soap and water, avoid preparing food for others while symptomatic, and remain away from work or school until 48 hours after the last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting.

Seek urgent medical attention for inability to keep fluids down, worsening abdominal pain, blood in the stool, fainting, confusion, very reduced urine output or persistent symptoms. Contact the GP surgery if diarrhoea has not clearly improved over the next few days.

Discharge authorised by Dr Imogine Rahman, MBBS, consultant physician, on behalf of Ulster Hospital.

Nursing Progress Note

Date: 8 Nov 2012
Patient: R. Marks
DOB: 9 July 1956
Working diagnosis: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction

Situation
Patient remains on telemetry following admission with central chest pressure, diaphoresis and nausea. Reports that the pressure has settled at rest; currently describes mild residual tightness, 2/10, without radiation. No further vomiting. Skin warm and dry. Alert, orientated and communicating appropriately. His sister, Raqib Prince, visited and was updated with the patient’s consent.

Observations and assessment
At 14:20: temperature 36.7°C, pulse 78 bpm and regular, BP 132/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturations 97% on room air. No increased work of breathing. Chest clear bilaterally. Peripheral perfusion satisfactory; no new ankle oedema.

Continuous monitoring remains in place using the Model X3 cardiac monitor. No sustained arrhythmia noted during this shift. Occasional ventricular ectopics displayed; patient asymptomatic at the time. Twelve-lead ECG completed after the reported tightness and reviewed by the medical team. Repeat high-sensitivity troponin sample sent as requested; result awaited.

Care delivered
• Aspirin administered as prescribed and tolerated.
• Fondaparinux given subcutaneously; injection site clean with no bleeding or bruising.
• Atorvastatin administered with evening medicines.
• Encouraged small sips of fluid and a light diet. Ate approximately half of lunch and drank 600 mL during the shift; nausea improved following prescribed antiemetic.
• Mobilised from bed to chair with one nurse supervising. Steady on standing, although mildly fatigued. Call bell left within reach.

Response and risks
Chest discomfort reduced following rest and prescribed treatment. No hypotension, syncope or acute breathlessness. Falls precautions maintained because of fatigue and anticoagulant therapy. Advised to report any recurrent pressure, sweating, nausea, palpitations or shortness of breath immediately. Patient understood and repeated the advice.

Escalation
Nurse in charge informed of intermittent ectopics and residual discomfort. Medical team contacted; continue telemetry and obtain urgent ECG if symptoms recur. Escalate immediately for persistent or worsening chest pain, haemodynamic change, significant rhythm disturbance or bleeding.

Plan for next shift
Continue observations and cardiac monitoring as per NSTEMI pathway. Review repeat troponin and any further ECG findings. Maintain prescribed aspirin, fondaparinux and atorvastatin; check for bleeding. Encourage rest with assisted mobilisation, monitor oral intake and nausea, and support preparation for the planned cardiology review.

Completed by: Aksha Monk, registered nurse

43-year-old Latino female patient
Home address: 169 Admirals Way, Rannoch, PH17 2QA

Wound review is not routinely required unless there is concern; arrange assessment through the GP surgery or NHS 111 if increasing redness, swelling, discharge or wound separation develops. Seek urgent medical attention for persistent vomiting, worsening abdominal pain, fever, faintness or inability to eat and drink. Avoid heavy lifting and strenuous activity for two weeks, then increase activity as comfortable. Surgical outpatient follow-up will be arranged if clinically indicated, and histology will be reviewed when available.

Discharged home today in stable condition.

LABORATORY MEDICINE REPORT
National Insurance number: TN 57 04 73 A

Patient: Mickayla H.
MRN: 076107174
Requesting service: MILLOM HOSPITAL
Specimen: Serum and EDTA whole blood
Clinical details: Acute painful, swollen and erythematous first metatarsophalangeal joint for 3 days. Known or suspected gout flare. Current treatment includes naproxen and colchicine.

RESULTS

Biochemistry
Urate: 0.49 mmol/L (reference interval 0.20–0.42) — raised
Creatinine: 98 µmol/L (60–110)
eGFR (CKD-EPI): 72 mL/min/1.73 m²
CRP: 68 mg/L (<5) — raised
ALT: 31 U/L (0–41)
ALP: 88 U/L (30–130)
Albumin: 40 g/L (35–50)

Haematology
Haemoglobin: 145 g/L (130–170)
White cell count: 11.8 × 10⁹/L (4.0–11.0) — mildly raised
Neutrophils: 9.2 × 10⁹/L (2.0–7.5) — raised
Platelets: 328 × 10⁹/L (150–400)

Specimen quality and interpretation

Sample received as serum and EDTA blood, with no significant haemolysis or clotting identified. The raised urate and inflammatory markers support an acute inflammatory arthritis, and the clinical presentation is compatible with a gout flare. Serum urate may be normal during an attack; the current elevated result therefore supports, but does not independently establish, the diagnosis.

The mild neutrophil leucocytosis is consistent with acute inflammation. Renal function is currently adequate for usual prescribing considerations, although dosing and toxicity risk should be reviewed if renal function changes, particularly while taking colchicine and an NSAID. Liver enzymes are within the stated reference intervals.

CLINICAL COMMENT

If diagnostic uncertainty remains, aspiration of the affected joint for polarised microscopy is recommended where clinically appropriate, both to demonstrate monosodium urate crystals and to exclude septic arthritis. Urgent clinical assessment is indicated if fever, systemic illness, rapidly progressive erythema or inability to move the joint develops. Please interpret alongside examination findings and medication history.

Suggested follow-up: repeat serum urate after resolution of the acute episode and review of long-term urate-lowering management at the appointment on 21st September 2022. This laboratory result is not a substitute for clinical assessment.

Outpatient hypertension review
NHS number: 000 480 1980

Patient: Raydon HODGSON
Report/accession ID: LAB-04870325
Seen at Dolgellau & Barmouth District Hospital Site
Clinician: A. Banks

Reason for review
Follow-up of essential hypertension after intermittent headache and light-headedness. No recent emergency department attendance. The patient reports that headaches are generally mild, frontal and more noticeable after a busy working day. Light-headedness occurs briefly on standing, without collapse, chest pain, palpitations or focal neurological symptoms. No visual loss, speech disturbance or unilateral weakness. No symptoms suggestive of secondary hypertension.

Background
Occupation: Builder

Taking amlodipine and ramipril as prescribed. No missed doses reported apart from one evening dose while travelling. No over-the-counter decongestants or regular NSAID use. Alcohol intake discussed; no change required based on the history provided. The patient does not smoke.

Examination
Comfortable at rest and communicating normally. Clinic BP 148/86 mmHg, pulse 76 bpm and regular. Repeat seated BP after five minutes 142/82 mmHg. On standing, BP 136/78 mmHg with a transient sensation of light-headedness but no marked postural drop. Height and weight not recorded at this appointment. Heart sounds normal with no murmur. Chest clear. No peripheral oedema. Neurological screening examination normal.

Investigations
Previous renal function and electrolytes satisfactory for continued ramipril. Urine albumin:creatinine ratio not elevated. The patient has been asked to complete a home blood pressure record, taking two readings morning and evening for seven days, with a suitable rest period beforehand. Please bring the monitor to the next appointment if readings remain unexpectedly high, so that its accuracy can be checked.

Assessment
Essential hypertension, above individual clinic target but improved on repeat measurement. Headache is non-specific and there are no current red-flag features. Mild postural light-headedness may relate to blood-pressure treatment or hydration.

Plan
• Continue current doses of amlodipine and ramipril; no increase today because of postural symptoms.
• Maintain good fluid intake, rise slowly from sitting or lying, and avoid abrupt prolonged standing.
• Continue dietary measures, including reduced salt intake and regular activity as tolerated.
• Seek urgent assessment via A&E or 999 for sudden severe headache, new neurological deficit, fainting, severe chest pain or breathlessness.
• Review home readings and symptoms in about 4 weeks. Arrange earlier contact if readings are persistently above 160/100 mmHg or light-headedness worsens.

Signed: A. Banks
Organization: Dolgellau & Barmouth District Hospital Site

Discharge summary – Cardiology
NHS number: 000 270 6025

Patient: M. Ryder
The patient, aged 68, was admitted with a one-week history of worsening orthopnoea, bilateral ankle oedema and reduced exercise tolerance. There was no chest pain or infective prodrome. mariyambibi guest, who lives in NEWRY, was updated regarding the admission and discharge arrangements.

Assessment and key results

On arrival, examination showed raised JVP, bibasal inspiratory crackles and pitting oedema to the lower shins. Blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg. Chest radiograph demonstrated pulmonary vascular congestion with small bilateral pleural effusions. NT-proBNP was substantially raised. ECG showed sinus rhythm without acute ischaemic changes. Echocardiography confirmed moderate left ventricular systolic impairment with an ejection fraction of approximately 35–40%; no significant valvular lesion was identified. Renal function remained suitable for ongoing diuretic treatment.

Hospital course

The patient was treated with intravenous furosemide, subsequently converted to oral therapy, with good symptomatic and weight response. Oxygen was required briefly on admission but was not needed before discharge. Bisoprolol was continued at the pre-admission dose. A low-salt diet and fluid awareness were discussed. No significant arrhythmia was recorded on telemetry.

Discharge condition and medicines

Breathing is now comfortable at rest and on gentle mobilisation. Peripheral oedema has markedly improved, with residual mild ankle swelling. Discharge medicines are furosemide and bisoprolol as listed on the electronic medicines reconciliation; the GP should review renal function, electrolytes and blood pressure after discharge. Further optimisation of guideline-directed heart-failure therapy should be considered once clinically stable.

Follow-up and advice

Heart-failure nurse follow-up has been requested, with cardiology clinic review on 16 February 2026. The patient should monitor daily weight where possible and seek urgent medical attention for rapidly worsening breathlessness, inability to lie flat, fainting or rapidly increasing swelling. Continue usual activity gradually and avoid non-prescribed anti-inflammatory medicines unless advised by a clinician. A discharge letter has been sent to the GP surgery.

Patient: Agnes S.
MRN: 078780072
Clinical context: The patient, aged 30, was reviewed for painless lymphadenopathy with drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss. Hodgkin lymphoma is the working diagnosis. Supportive care pending tissue diagnosis.

Specimens: EDTA blood and serum. Adequate for analysis.

Full blood count
Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115–160) — low
White cell count 12.6 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0) — high
Neutrophils 9.8 ×10⁹/L (2.0–7.5) — high
Lymphocytes 1.6 ×10⁹/L (1.0–4.0)

ALP 146 U/L (30–130) — mildly high
Bilirubin 8 µmol/L (0–21)

Plan: Continue supportive care pending tissue diagnosis. Urgent haematology pathway and PET-CT staging as clinically indicated. Repeat FBC, CRP, renal and liver profiles at follow-up on 2035-10-24.

GP consultation note

Kyra-Rose A. attended the surgery to review blood pressure control. They report intermittent, dull headaches over the past three weeks, usually later in the day, together with brief episodes of light-headedness when standing up quickly. There has been no collapse, chest pain, palpitations, breathlessness, focal weakness, visual loss or speech disturbance. They have not described a sudden or severe headache. No recent intercurrent infection.

Kyra-Rose A. says that home blood pressure readings have generally been between 145–155/85–92 mmHg, although readings are sometimes taken shortly after walking or having coffee. They have been taking amlodipine 5 mg once daily and ramipril 5 mg once daily. No missed doses were reported, and there has been no ankle swelling, persistent cough or facial swelling. They use ibuprofen occasionally for headaches and were advised to avoid regular NSAID use where possible.

Occupation: software developer. They are currently under some work-related pressure at South Knighton Voluntary Service, with reduced sleep on several nights each week. They do not smoke and drink alcohol within recommended limits. Diet remains higher in salt than ideal, particularly with ready meals. They are managing their usual activities and have not needed to attend A&E.

On examination, Kyra-Rose A. was comfortable and conversational. Blood pressure was 148/88 mmHg in the right arm after several minutes seated, reducing to 142/84 mmHg on repeat. Pulse 76 bpm and regular. There was no postural drop of clinical significance. Heart sounds were normal, with no murmur; chest was clear. Neurological examination was grossly normal, with normal gait, power and speech. No peripheral oedema.

The patient mentioned that a consultant cardiologist had previously advised maintaining good blood pressure control during an assessment for a family history of cardiovascular disease. There is no known history of ischaemic heart disease, stroke or chronic kidney disease.

Assessment

Essential hypertension, currently above target in the surgery and at home. Headache and light-headedness are most consistent with suboptimal control and possible dehydration or rapid postural change; no red-flag neurological features today.

Plan

Increase amlodipine to 10 mg once daily and continue ramipril 5 mg once daily. Arrange U&Es, creatinine, eGFR and urine albumin:creatinine ratio. The patient will record morning and evening blood pressure readings for seven days, seated and rested, and bring the log to review. Encourage regular fluids, gradual position changes, reduced salt intake, continued activity and avoidance of frequent ibuprofen.

Safety-netting given: seek urgent assessment via NHS 111 or the emergency department for a sudden severe headache, new neurological symptoms, collapse, chest pain or significant breathlessness. Review in four weeks, sooner if symptoms worsen.

Home address: 145 Wylds Lane, Stockton-on-Tees, TS20 1AA
Contact telephone: 07700 900709

text:
Discharge summary
NHS number: 000 838 1969

Patient: Codie-Leigh M.
MRN: 071612427
Admitting organisation: ABERDEEN ROYAL INFIRMARY
Responsible consultant: oghenetejiri johns

Reason for admission
Admitted via the emergency department with worsening breathlessness, orthopnoea, bilateral ankle swelling and reduced exercise tolerance. The patient reported a gradual deterioration for 3 days, with difficulty sleeping flat and a noticeable increase in weight. There was no chest pain, fever or productive cough.

Admission findings and investigations
On arrival, the patient was breathless at rest with bibasal inspiratory crackles and pitting oedema to both lower legs. Oxygen saturations were 91% on air, improving with low-flow oxygen. Chest radiography showed pulmonary vascular congestion with small bilateral pleural effusions. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm without acute ischaemic changes. Blood tests showed a raised NT-proBNP and mild renal impairment compared with the documented baseline, with stable haemoglobin and no significant inflammatory response. Serial troponins were negative.

An echocardiogram confirmed impaired left ventricular systolic function, with an estimated ejection fraction of approximately 35%, alongside mild functional mitral regurgitation. There was no significant valvular stenosis. The findings were consistent with acute decompensated heart failure.

Hospital course
The patient was treated with intravenous furosemide, oxygen therapy and fluid and salt restriction. Urine output improved promptly, with progressive resolution of the pulmonary congestion and peripheral oedema. Oxygen was discontinued before discharge, and the patient was able to mobilise around the ward without significant breathlessness. Renal function initially worsened slightly during diuresis but subsequently stabilised; potassium remained within the acceptable range following replacement on one occasion.

Bisoprolol was continued at the pre-admission dose once the patient was clinically euvolaemic. Furosemide was converted from intravenous to oral treatment with a modest increase in the regular daily dose. An ACE inhibitor was discussed, but initiation was deferred because of renal function and blood pressure; this should be reconsidered in the outpatient heart failure clinic. The patient received advice from the heart failure specialist nurse regarding daily weights, fluid intake and recognition of deterioration.

Problem list
1. Acute decompensated heart failure with reduced left ventricular systolic function.
2. Peripheral oedema and pulmonary congestion, improved following diuresis.
3. Mild chronic kidney disease with transient acute deterioration during treatment, now stable.
4. Reduced exercise tolerance, improving.

Discharge condition and medicines
At discharge the patient was comfortable at rest, haemodynamically stable and maintaining oxygen saturations on air. There was only minimal residual ankle oedema and no significant postural dizziness.

Discharge medicines:
• Furosemide, increased to the agreed oral daily dose recorded on the accompanying medicines list.
• Bisoprolol, continue the usual prescribed dose.
• Other regular medicines, continue as listed on the reconciliation sheet.

Follow-up and safety-netting
The GP surgery should arrange a renal function and electrolyte blood test within one week and review the response to the increased diuretic dose. A referral has been made to the heart failure service for medication optimisation and education. The patient should weigh themselves each morning and seek medical advice if the weight rises rapidly, swelling returns, or breathlessness worsens. Urgent assessment is required for severe breathlessness at rest, fainting, new chest pain or bluish lips.

The patient’s relative lives in Cessford, and the discharge advice was discussed with the patient and family. Discharge documentation completed by oghenetejiri johns.

10th May 2012

Referral to Neurology

Dear Neurology Team,

Re: isla-belle page
Report/accession ID: 080820138

Clinical question
Please assess this patient with probable Parkinson disease, particularly to confirm the diagnosis, optimise dopaminergic treatment and advise on management of progressive motor symptoms.

History
There has been a gradual onset of right-sided resting tremor, accompanied by slowness with dressing, turning in bed and initiating gait. The patient also describes muscular rigidity affecting the shoulders and lower limbs. Symptoms are more troublesome in the morning and before the next dose of medication. There have been no reported falls, syncope or visual hallucinations. Speech is quieter than previously, but swallowing remains satisfactory. Mood is mildly low; cognition is subjectively intact.

Examination
At review, the patient was alert and engaged. There was a low-frequency resting tremor of the right hand, with bradykinesia on finger tapping and reduced right arm swing. Mild cogwheel rigidity was present at the wrists. Gait was slow, with a short-stepped pattern, although turns were completed independently. No focal limb weakness was identified. BP was 132/78 mmHg sitting and 126/74 mmHg standing.

Management to date
Co-beneldopa has been commenced and is currently taken three times daily. This has provided partial improvement in tremor and mobility, without reported dyskinesia or troublesome nausea. The patient has been advised to maintain regular activity and has accepted referral to community physiotherapy. Medication adherence is reported as good.

I would be grateful for a specialist opinion regarding diagnostic confirmation, dose titration and whether occupational therapy, speech and language therapy or falls-prevention input would be appropriate. Please also advise on monitoring for non-motor features and suitability for ongoing shared care with the GP.

Yours faithfully,

Dr Ezza Frost, MBBS
Ulster Hospital

Clinical review – 5 March 2020
NHS number: 000 184 4769

Patient: Naama P., Age 56 y/o

Naama P. was seen in the diabetic foot clinic for review of a plantar ulcer beneath the right first metatarsal head. They report that the wound has been present for approximately three weeks and has produced a small amount of yellow local discharge over the last four days. There has been no fever, rigors or vomiting. They describe reduced sensation in both feet and have not noticed significant pain from the ulcer. Their home blood glucose readings have been higher than usual, generally between 9 and 14 mmol/L.

They have been attending for wound care and have been taking co-amoxiclav as prescribed. They have continued to walk in ordinary shoes for essential activities but have tried to reduce weight-bearing at home. They were reminded to check both feet every day, as the reduced protective sensation increases the risk of unnoticed trauma. Preferred contact number is 07700 900579.

On examination, there is a 1.2 cm diameter ulcer on the plantar surface beneath the right first metatarsal head. The base contains mostly healthy granulation tissue with a small amount of slough. There is scant serous-purulent discharge and approximately 1 cm of surrounding erythema, without lymphangitic streaking. No foul odour, necrosis, fluctuance or exposed bone is seen. The wound does not probe to bone. The right foot is warm, with palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses. Capillary refill is approximately two seconds. Protective sensation is reduced to 10 g monofilament testing at several plantar sites bilaterally. There is no calf tenderness or ankle swelling.

The wound was cleansed and redressed with an appropriate absorbent dressing. A felted off-loading pad was applied, and the importance of avoiding pressure through the ulcer was discussed. They were advised to wear the provided off-loading footwear and to avoid barefoot walking. Continue co-amoxiclav to complete the prescribed course, unless an adverse reaction occurs. No further antibiotics were issued today.

Assessment

Diabetic plantar foot ulcer with reduced protective sensation, local discharge and mild surrounding cellulitis. There is no current clinical evidence of deep abscess or osteomyelitis, but close review is required because of the discharge and erythema.

Plan

Continue regular wound care through the podiatry service and maintain strict off-loading. The wound should be reviewed in five days, with earlier assessment if there is any deterioration. They were advised to attend A&E or contact their GP urgently if they develop a fever, increasing pain, spreading redness, worsening discharge, blackened skin or feel systemically unwell. They should seek same-day advice if the dressing becomes saturated or the foot becomes markedly swollen.

Report/accession ID: 28/504210. A routine diabetic foot review is also planned in about 11 weeks, provided the ulcer has healed and there are no interim concerns.

Reason for admission

You were admitted to hospital after several days of feeling unusually tired, eating and drinking very little, and passing less urine than normal. You were assessed by the medical team, including the consultant nephrologist, L. Douglas (GMC number 0419076).

Key findings and treatment

Your initial blood tests showed a raised creatinine and urea, with no evidence of a dangerous change in your potassium level. A urine sample did not suggest a significant infection. Ultrasound imaging showed kidneys of expected size without a blockage to the drainage system. Your blood pressure and observations remained stable.

You were treated with intravenous sodium chloride to replace fluid and support kidney recovery. Medicines that could worsen kidney function were placed on a temporary hold while your blood tests improved. You were encouraged to drink regularly once you were able to manage fluids by mouth. There was no indication for dialysis.

Your urine output increased during admission and repeat blood tests showed a clear improvement in kidney function, although they had not quite returned to your previous baseline at the time of discharge. You were eating and drinking more normally, walking safely, and felt less fatigued.

Medicines on discharge

Please restart only the medicines listed on your separate discharge medicines list. Do not restart any medicine marked as withheld until your GP or hospital team confirms that it is safe to do so. Avoid anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen unless a clinician specifically advises you to take them. Paracetamol may be used as directed on the packet, provided you have not been told otherwise.

Follow-up and safety-netting

Please arrange a blood test through your GP surgery within one week of discharge to check kidney function and electrolytes. The results should be reviewed by the GP, with further medication changes made if required. Maintain regular fluid intake, unless another clinician has advised you to restrict fluids.

Seek urgent medical help through NHS 111 or A&E if you become unable to keep fluids down, pass very little or no urine, develop increasing breathlessness, chest pain, confusion, severe weakness, or rapidly worsening swelling.

You have been discharged home in a stable condition with the above plan.

Emergency department handover – 10th January 2022

Patient: Eirinn  
Report/accession ID: 031756847  
Care provider: UNIVERSITY HOSPITAL

Presenting problem  
Dysuria, marked urinary frequency and low central abdominal discomfort since yesterday. No flank pain, rigors, vomiting or visible haematuria. Eating and drinking adequately. No vaginal symptoms reported. R. Murphy accompanied the patient and confirms no recent confusion or collapse.

Assessment  
Alert, comfortable at rest and communicating normally. Temperature 37.4°C, pulse 86 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturations 99% on air. Mucous membranes moist. Abdomen soft, with mild suprapubic tenderness only; no guarding or rebound. No renal angle tenderness. Clinically euvolaemic and not septic.

Blood tests not required at this stage given stable observations, uncomplicated symptoms and absence of systemic features. Urine report/accession reference is recorded above.

Working diagnosis and treatment  
Likely uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection. First dose of nitrofurantoin given in the department, with an oral course supplied in line with local antimicrobial guidance. Encourage fluids and regular bladder emptying. Paracetamol advised if required for discomfort, subject to the usual dosing instructions. Antibiotic choice to be reviewed if culture demonstrates resistance or symptoms fail to settle.

Disposition and priorities  
Suitable for discharge home today with R. Murphy. GP review if not clearly improving within 48 hours, or sooner for persistent symptoms. Urgent reassessment via A&E if fever, rigors, vomiting, new flank pain, reduced urine output, worsening abdominal pain or feeling faint develops. Culture result to be checked and treatment amended if necessary.

Routine clinical review arranged in 19 days if symptoms have not fully resolved; otherwise no planned hospital follow-up. Patient understands the plan and safety-net advice.

Dear Ryan-Junior M.,

I am writing to explain the reason for your referral to the respiratory service and what will happen next. You have had asthma symptoms despite using your prescribed inhalers, and we would like a specialist opinion on how best to improve your control.

You describe wheeze and shortness of breath on most days, particularly when walking briskly or in cold air. You are also waking with a cough on approximately three nights each week. There has been no coughing up blood, chest pain, fainting or unexplained weight loss. You have not needed admission to hospital, although you attended A&E once during the past year because your breathing became difficult. You recovered after nebulised treatment and a short course of steroid tablets.

At review, your oxygen level was 98% breathing room air. Your chest was clear at rest, but there was a mild expiratory wheeze after walking. Your peak flow readings have varied considerably, with the best home reading approximately 420 litres per minute and lower readings during symptomatic periods. This pattern is consistent with asthma that is not yet fully controlled. The main clinical question for the respiratory team is whether your diagnosis and inhaler treatment should be reassessed, including whether another cause is contributing to the persistent night-time cough.

You currently use a salbutamol inhaler when needed and a beclometasone inhaler every morning and evening. Please continue these medicines as prescribed. We discussed inhaler technique and the importance of using a spacer if one has been supplied. Try to record your morning and evening peak flow, symptoms, night waking and reliever use until the specialist appointment. Please bring the inhalers and any peak flow diary with you.

I have requested respiratory assessment, spirometry with bronchodilator response and consideration of FeNO testing. The specialist may also review possible triggers, nasal symptoms and reflux, and decide whether your preventer dose needs changing. We will arrange a follow-up appointment after their advice.

Please seek urgent help through 999 if you are unable to speak in full sentences, become exhausted, or your reliever is not helping. Contact NHS 111 or your GP sooner if symptoms are worsening.

LABORATORY REPORT
NHS number: 0009249312

Patient: S. Wyatt
MRN: 026944124
Specimen collection/report date: 29/10/2024
Request: Thyroid function assessment
Requesting clinician: Not stated
Specimen: Serum, venous blood
Clinical details: Established hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. Reports fatigue, increased sensitivity to cold and constipation for 3 days. No recent acute infection recorded.

Results

Analyte                         Result       Reference interval       Interpretation
TSH                             12.8 mIU/L   0.35–4.50 mIU/L           High
Free thyroxine (FT4)            8.9 pmol/L    9.0–19.0 pmol/L           Slightly low
Free triiodothyronine (FT3)     3.4 pmol/L    3.1–6.8 pmol/L            Within interval
Thyroid peroxidase antibody     286 IU/mL     <34 IU/mL                 Positive

Specimen quality

Sample received adequately labelled and suitable for analysis. No significant haemolysis, icterus or lipaemia detected. Results are based on the serum specimen received and should be interpreted alongside adherence, dose and timing of levothyroxine. If biotin-containing supplements are being taken, these should be recorded as they may interfere with some thyroid assays.

Interpretive comment

The raised TSH with borderline-low FT4 is consistent with biochemical under-replacement or recent interruption of levothyroxine in the context of known hypothyroidism. Positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies support autoimmune thyroiditis, although antibody concentration does not guide dose adjustment. Please confirm the prescribed dose, administration on an empty stomach, separation from calcium or iron preparations, and any missed doses.

If treatment has been taken consistently, clinical review and consideration of a modest levothyroxine dose adjustment are appropriate, subject to the patient’s age, weight, cardiac history and pregnancy status. Repeat TSH and FT4 no earlier than 6 weeks after a dose change; a sooner sample may not reflect the new steady state. Consider checking full blood count, ferritin, renal profile and liver profile if fatigue persists despite biochemical correction. Urgent assessment is not indicated from these results alone, unless there are severe symptoms or clinical concern.

Medication recorded: levothyroxine. Dose and adherence information were not supplied with the request.

Outpatient musculoskeletal review

Patient: ADHEEN SHARIF
MRN: MRN-09242879
Seen at WALTON HOSPITAL ACUTE BEDS by L. CURRY

ADHEEN SHARIF was reviewed today regarding persistent low back pain with right-sided shooting leg pain and intermittent paraesthesia into the lateral calf and dorsum of the foot. Symptoms began gradually and have been present for several weeks. The pain is worse after prolonged sitting and when bending forwards, although gentle walking is usually manageable. There has been no fall or other injury. The patient reports no change in bladder or bowel control, no saddle numbness and no constitutional symptoms.

Naproxen and paracetamol have provided partial relief. Naproxen is being taken with food, and there have been no reported problems with indigestion, melaena, wheeze or ankle swelling. Occupation: Cleaner. The patient is keen to remain active and has been avoiding heavier lifting but is still managing usual personal care and work duties.

On examination, the patient appeared comfortable at rest and mobilised independently. Lumbar flexion was reduced by pain, with less restriction on extension. There was right paraspinal tenderness but no focal spinal percussion tenderness. Straight-leg raise reproduced the familiar leg pain on the right at approximately 55 degrees. Power was 5/5 in hip flexion, knee extension, ankle dorsiflexion and great-toe extension bilaterally. Sensation was mildly altered over the right L5 distribution. Knee and ankle reflexes were symmetrical, and there was no foot drop.

Assessment

The presentation remains most consistent with uncomplicated lumbar radiculopathy, without evidence today of progressive neurological deficit or cauda equina syndrome.

Plan

Continue regular paracetamol within the labelled maximum dose. Continue naproxen only as prescribed and stop it if significant stomach pain, black stools, facial swelling or breathing difficulty develops. A referral has been made to the physiotherapy service at WALTON HOSPITAL ACUTE BEDS for graded exercise, lumbar strengthening, posture advice and a paced return to normal activity. The patient was advised to avoid bed rest and to change position regularly during sedentary work.

If symptoms are not clearly improving, a further clinical review is planned in about 11 weeks. Earlier assessment is required if weakness develops, walking deteriorates, numbness spreads, or there is new urinary retention, urinary or faecal incontinence, saddle anaesthesia, fever or unexplained weight loss. The patient understood and agreed with the plan.

Signed electronically by L. CURRY
