Discharge summary for merel bridges

DOB: 16 Mar 1972

Admission reason and diagnosis

You were admitted with a sickle cell painful crisis, causing severe pain in both limbs and the lower back, together with dehydration. On arrival your pain was rated 9/10. There was no history or examination evidence of acute chest syndrome, stroke or bacterial sepsis.

Key findings

Initial blood tests showed haemoglobin 86 g/L, in keeping with your known sickle cell disease, with a raised reticulocyte count. Kidney function and electrolytes were satisfactory apart from mild dehydration. A chest radiograph showed no focal consolidation. Oxygen saturations remained normal on air, and repeated observations did not suggest respiratory compromise.

Treatment in hospital

You received intravenous fluids and regular analgesia, including intravenous morphine with additional doses when required. Paracetamol was given regularly, and anti-sickness medication was available. A thrombosis risk assessment was completed and you received prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin while your mobility was reduced. Your pain gradually improved, allowing conversion from intravenous morphine to oral analgesia. You were encouraged to drink regularly and mobilise as tolerated.

At discharge, your limb and back pain had substantially settled. Your current pain score is 5/10, which you feel is manageable with tablets. You are eating and drinking, passing urine normally and walking independently. There has been no fever, chest pain or breathlessness during the final 24 hours of admission.

Discharge medicines

• Continue paracetamol as previously advised.
• Take the prescribed oral morphine only for severe breakthrough pain, following the label instructions. Do not drive, drink alcohol or take sedating medicines while affected by morphine.
• Complete the medication supplied at discharge and return unused controlled medication to a pharmacy.
• Continue your usual sickle cell medicines unless your haematology team has told you otherwise. No changes were made to disease-modifying treatment during this admission.

Follow-up and safety-netting

Your haematology review is arranged for 2028-10-21. Please contact your GP surgery if pain remains difficult to control or you are unable to maintain fluid intake. Seek urgent help through NHS 111 or attend A&E if you develop a temperature of 38°C or above, chest pain, difficulty breathing, new weakness, confusion, persistent vomiting or pain that is not responding to the prescribed treatment.

You asked that khira biggs be kept informed of the plan. A copy of this summary will be sent to your GP. Your preferred contact detail for discharge communication is merel.bridges36@outlook.com.

Please keep drinking little and often, dress warmly, avoid becoming overtired and follow your established sickle cell crisis plan.

Dear Colleague,

Re: THELONIOUS EATON

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient’s persistent lumbar radiculopathy, particularly whether spinal imaging and specialist management are now indicated. THELONIOUS EATON has had low back pain with shooting pain down the left leg and intermittent paraesthesia for approximately eight weeks. The pain is aggravated by prolonged sitting, lifting and walking on an incline, and is now affecting sleep and attendance at work with Belfast Voluntary Service. Dunya, the patient’s sister, reports that mobility has become noticeably slower over the past fortnight, although there has been no fall or acute injury.

There is no reported loss of bladder or bowel control, saddle numbness, fever, unexplained weight loss or previous history of malignancy. The patient has not described progressive leg weakness, but does occasionally feel that the left foot is less reliable on stairs. There is no history of intravenous drug use or recent significant infection.

On examination in the surgery, lumbar flexion and left-sided rotation were limited by pain. Straight-leg raising was positive on the left at approximately 45 degrees, reproducing the posterior thigh and calf pain. There was reduced sensation to light touch over the left lateral calf compared with the right. Knee reflexes were symmetrical; the left ankle jerk was slightly reduced. Power was 5/5 on formal hip, knee and ankle testing, including dorsiflexion and great-toe extension. Gait was antalgic but stable, and there was no foot drop. Abdominal examination was unremarkable.

Initial management has included advice to remain gently active, avoid heavy lifting and undertake a home exercise programme. The patient has been taking paracetamol as required and naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food, with only partial relief. A short course of physiotherapy has improved confidence with movement but has not substantially reduced the radicular pain. No imaging has yet been undertaken.

Assessment

The clinical picture is consistent with left lumbar radiculopathy, with sensory change and a mildly reduced ankle jerk but no established motor deficit or current cauda equina symptoms. Symptoms are limiting function despite conservative treatment.

Plan and request

Please assess whether MRI of the lumbar spine is appropriate and advise on further management, including whether an injection or spinal surgical opinion should be considered. The patient has been advised to seek urgent assessment in A&E if urinary retention or incontinence, saddle sensory loss, rapidly progressive weakness, or inability to walk develops. I would also welcome advice regarding ongoing analgesia and physiotherapy while awaiting review.

This referral is made from Bangor. Please direct correspondence to me via the usual professional route.

Yours sincerely,

ZEEVA VICKERS

Blood tests showed an increased inflammatory response, with a raised white cell count and C-reactive protein. Kidney function and liver tests were satisfactory. Blood cultures did not grow bacteria, and testing for common respiratory viruses was negative. There was no evidence of a blood clot on the clinical assessment, and your oxygen requirement settled with treatment.

You were treated with intravenous fluids, regular paracetamol and antibiotics, initially through a cannula and then by mouth. Your fever and pleuritic pain improved, and the cough became less troublesome. You remained clinically stable without the need for critical care or assisted ventilation. Before discharge you were walking independently, eating and drinking, and maintaining safe oxygen levels while breathing room air.

Discharge medicines:
• Amoxicillin, to complete the prescribed antibiotic course. Please follow the directions on the dispensing label and do not stop early unless advised by a clinician.
• Paracetamol when required for pain or fever, within the maximum dose stated on the packet. Do not take other medicines containing paracetamol at the same time.

Reduced urine output over approximately 36 hours, with marked fatigue and poor oral intake. No dysuria, visible haematuria or loin pain reported. One episode of vomiting yesterday; no ongoing diarrhoea. D. Bhatti accompanied the patient and provided collateral history.

Initial assessment
Alert but tired, speaking in full sentences. Dry mucous membranes. Pulse 104 bpm, BP 98/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% on air, temperature 36.7°C. Working impression
Acute kidney injury, clinically most consistent with reduced circulating volume from poor intake and vomiting. No current evidence of sepsis, urinary retention or fluid overload. Requires observation and repeat renal profile.

Intravenous sodium chloride commenced cautiously; strict fluid balance and urine output monitoring. Encourage oral fluids if tolerated. Regular medicines temporarily held pending senior review, particularly any potentially nephrotoxic or blood-pressure-lowering treatment. Repeat observations and U&E after fluid challenge. Escalate promptly for worsening hypotension, breathlessness, confusion, anuria or rising potassium.

Disposition
Discussed with the medical registrar. Admit under acute medicine for ongoing fluids, investigation and renal function monitoring. Do not discharge until clinically euvolaemic with improving urine output and a clear GP follow-up plan.

Patient: T. Garner
MRN: 06011943
Date: 2022-04-13
Contact: 07700 900314

Dear patient,

You were assessed in the emergency department today after an episode of sudden, forceful palpitations with chest tightness and a frightening feeling that you might die. I appreciate how alarming this was. In an 83-year-old Asian female patient, new chest symptoms and a racing heartbeat must be checked carefully before attributing them to anxiety or panic.

An ECG was performed and showed sinus rhythm without acute ischaemic changes or a significant arrhythmia. Cardiac blood tests, including serial high-sensitivity troponin measurements, were not suggestive of heart muscle injury. Your examination was reassuring, with no clinical evidence of heart failure, a significant breathing problem, or an acute neurological event. The overall assessment is therefore most consistent with a panic attack, following appropriate exclusion of an immediately dangerous cardiac cause today. This does not mean that the symptoms were imagined; panic can produce very real palpitations, chest pressure, shaking, breathlessness and a fear of dying.

We discussed breathing retraining. When symptoms begin, try to slow the breathing rather than taking large, rapid breaths: breathe in gently through the nose and out slowly through pursed lips, continuing for several minutes while keeping both feet supported. Practise this when you are well so that it is easier to use during an attack. Please avoid repeatedly checking your pulse, as this can maintain the cycle of fear and bodily awareness.

Your GP surgery should review this episode and consider whether further assessment, such as ambulatory ECG monitoring, is needed if palpitations recur, particularly if they occur independently of panic. Please arrange follow-up in 20 days, or sooner if symptoms are troublesome. At review, discuss triggers, sleep, caffeine, alcohol, mood and any ongoing anxiety; psychological support or talking therapy may be helpful if attacks continue.

Return to A&E or call 999 immediately if chest tightness is persistent or severe, occurs with exertion, or is accompanied by fainting, marked breathlessness, sweating, new weakness, or pain spreading to the arm, back or jaw. Seek urgent help as well if the heartbeat remains very fast or irregular and does not settle with rest.

This plan is based on the reassuring examination, ECG and cardiac blood-test results from today, while recognising that recurrent or changing symptoms require reassessment.

Reason for admission

Treated initially with aspirin, fondaparinux and high-intensity atorvastatin. Coronary angiography was reviewed by the cardiology team. In view of diffuse coronary disease, preserved haemodynamic status and the balance of procedural risk and benefit, the decision was for medical management rather than PCI. Renal function and haemoglobin remained stable. Blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg prior to discharge. Mobilising independently and tolerating oral intake.

• Aspirin 75 mg once daily, lifelong.

• Atorvastatin 80 mg at night.
• Bisoprolol 2.5 mg once daily.
• Ramipril 1.25 mg once daily, to be titrated if tolerated.
• Glyceryl trinitrate spray as needed for chest pain.
Fondaparinux has been stopped at discharge. The patient was advised not to discontinue aspirin or ticagrelor without discussing this with cardiology.

Follow-up and advice
GP review within one week for blood pressure, renal function and medication tolerance. Repeat U&E and liver blood tests should be arranged after medication titration. Cardiology follow-up and cardiac rehabilitation referral will be made. Smoking cessation, Mediterranean-style diet and gradual activity were discussed. If chest pain persists after glyceryl trinitrate, or is accompanied by severe breathlessness or collapse, call 999.

Clinically stable, pain-free and suitable for discharge home.

Patient: A. Garrett
Seen in A&E with a 36-hour history of pruritic erythematous rash and burning skin irritation, predominantly across both forearms and the upper chest. Started after using a new fragranced body lotion. No previous similar episode reported. Tulise, accompanying relative, confirms no facial swelling, wheeze, vomiting or collapse.

Assessment
Alert, comfortable at rest and speaking in full sentences. Airway patent; no lip, tongue or pharyngeal oedema. Chest clear bilaterally, with no wheeze or stridor. Cardiovascular observations stable: BP 120/80 mmHg, pulse 78, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 99% on air, temperature 36.7°C.

Working diagnosis: allergic contact dermatitis, likely triggered by the new cosmetic product. Differential includes irritant dermatitis; less likely urticaria, drug eruption or early bacterial infection.

Management
Advised immediate cessation of the fragranced lotion and avoidance of other new topical products until settled. Continue cetirizine as previously directed for itch. Hydrocortisone cream in a thin layer to affected areas, avoiding broken skin, face and genital region; use only for the advised short course. Emollient recommended regularly, with gentle unperfumed wash and avoidance of scratching.

No blood tests or imaging indicated today. Case discussed with T. RICE, Emergency Department clinician at ROYAL GWENT HOSPITAL. Safe for discharge with relative. Written advice provided, including return precautions for rapidly spreading rash, facial or oral swelling, breathing difficulty, fever, blistering or mucosal lesions.

GP review if not improving within several days, or sooner if worsening. Consider dermatology or patch-test referral for recurrent symptoms. Follow-up appointment planned for 2 Mar 2025.

Dear Colleague,

Home address: 98 LEASIDE GARDENS, ANNSBOROUGH

Thank you for assessing this patient, whom I am referring for specialist opinion regarding recurrent migraine with increasing functional impact. The specific question is whether the current pattern remains consistent with migraine without aura and whether preventive treatment should now be introduced, given the frequency of attacks and reliance on acute medication.

The headaches have been present for several years but have become more frequent over recent months. Episodes are typically unilateral and throbbing, lasting between 6 and 24 hours when untreated. They are accompanied by nausea and marked photophobia, with a preference for resting in a quiet, dark room. There is no reported visual, sensory or speech disturbance preceding the pain. The patient denies collapse, seizure, fever, neck stiffness, persistent vomiting or a recent head injury. There is no description of a sudden maximal-onset headache. Symptoms are aggravated by routine activity and improve with sleep.

At review, the patient was alert and communicating normally. Blood pressure and pulse were within the expected range, and temperature was 36.7 °C. Cranial nerves were grossly intact, with no diplopia, facial asymmetry or dysarthria. Limb power, sensation, coordination and gait were normal. Fundoscopy was not suggestive of papilloedema. There was no meningism. The clinical examination therefore provides no current evidence of a focal neurological deficit or raised intracranial pressure.

Current acute treatment is sumatriptan, used at the onset of severe attacks, with naproxen when required. This combination is generally helpful if taken promptly, although some attacks recur later the same day. The patient has been advised to take the medicines with food where possible and to avoid exceeding the prescribed frequency, in view of the risk of medication-overuse headache. A headache diary has been recommended to record frequency, duration, triggers, associated symptoms and treatment response. Sleep irregularity, missed meals, dehydration and prolonged screen exposure appear to be relevant potential triggers.

There is no indication from the history or examination for urgent imaging at this stage. I would nevertheless value your assessment as a consultant neurologist, particularly regarding diagnostic confirmation, the need for MRI or other investigation, and selection of an appropriate prophylactic agent if attacks remain frequent. Please also advise on optimisation of acute therapy and any further safety-netting or follow-up requirements.

The patient has been advised to seek urgent assessment through A&E for a thunderclap headache, new persistent neurological symptoms, confusion, fever with neck stiffness or a substantial change in the established pattern.

Yours sincerely,

IRUM THOMSON

Sleep Medicine Clinic Report

Patient: KALON DOWNES
Patient identifier (MRN): 076783/95
Referring clinician: Evander Potter
Healthcare organisation: Maesteg General Hospital
Occupation: Lawyer

Reason for review

KALON DOWNES was assessed in the sleep service because of persistent loud snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing during sleep and troublesome daytime somnolence. The history was provided by the patient, with corroborative observations from their bed partner. Symptoms have been present for several months and are reported to be worse when sleeping supine. There has been no history of cataplexy, sleep paralysis or recurrent sleep-related hallucinations. The patient reports no recent shift-pattern change and does not describe restless legs symptoms.

Current treatment

The patient has been using continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy. Usage has been inconsistent because of nasal obstruction and intermittent mask discomfort. On nights when the device is worn, the patient reports less morning headache and improved alertness. Download information showed residual respiratory events above the desired range, with reduced use on several nights. The humidifier had not been routinely filled, and the mask seal was suboptimal during parts of the recording.

Clinical findings

The patient was alert and appropriately engaged during the consultation. Speech was clear, with no observed evidence of excessive somnolence during the appointment. Examination of the upper airway demonstrated a crowded oropharynx with a relatively low soft palate and enlarged tonsillar tissue. There was no audible stridor. Chest examination was clear, with normal air entry bilaterally, and cardiovascular examination was unremarkable. No peripheral oedema was identified.

The patient also described nasal blockage for 3 days, without fever, facial pain or purulent discharge. This appears clinically consistent with a short-lived upper respiratory or allergic nasal problem rather than a new lower respiratory disorder. Advice was given regarding saline nasal irrigation and avoidance of sedating over-the-counter preparations.

Interpretation

The clinical history and available CPAP data remain consistent with obstructive sleep apnoea with incomplete treatment adherence and probable residual upper-airway obstruction. Daytime somnolence is likely to be contributed to by insufficiently treated sleep-disordered breathing. The patient was advised not to drive or undertake safety-critical work if sleepy, and to take regular breaks on prolonged journeys.

Plan

A mask refit and replacement interface will be arranged through the CPAP service. The patient was shown how to adjust the headgear without overtightening and was advised to use the humidifier each night. A trial of saline spray is appropriate for nasal symptoms; if blockage persists, the GP may consider a topical nasal corticosteroid, provided there are no contraindications. Weight, alcohol intake near bedtime and sleep position were discussed, with encouragement to maintain a regular sleep schedule.

Repeat CPAP download and symptom review are requested in approximately 8–12 weeks. Earlier contact with the sleep service is advised if there is marked deterioration in alertness, intolerance of therapy or new cardiopulmonary symptoms.

Report prepared and signed by Evander Potter, Maesteg General Hospital.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
NHS number: 0004859872

Patient: Fabio
DOB: 25/03/2009
Home address: 126 HILLMAN COURT, DUNDRUM
Contact telephone: 07700 900525
Admission and discharge date: 23 November 2045

Reason for admission
Presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge and deep dyspareunia. She reported no vomiting, urinary frequency or diarrhoea. Pregnancy testing was negative. There was no history of recent pelvic surgery or intrauterine device use documented.

Assessment and key results
At 08:15 she was haemodynamically stable and afebrile. Abdominal examination demonstrated suprapubic and bilateral iliac fossa tenderness without guarding or rebound. Speculum examination showed mucopurulent cervical discharge; cervical excitation was present.

Investigations showed:
• Urine pregnancy test negative.
• FBC and renal function within acceptable limits; CRP mildly raised.
• Urinalysis without convincing evidence of urinary tract infection.
• Pelvic ultrasound: no tubo-ovarian abscess, adnexal torsion or significant free fluid.
• Vaginal and endocervical swabs sent for chlamydia, gonorrhoea and other microbiology. Results were pending at discharge.

Hospital course
The presentation was assessed as clinically consistent with pelvic inflammatory disease without evidence of sepsis or an abscess requiring drainage. She received ceftriaxone intramuscularly in the emergency department, followed by the first oral doses of doxycycline and metronidazole. Analgesia with paracetamol was effective. Pain and nausea improved during observation on the same day, and she remained clinically stable with oral intake tolerated.

Discharge medicines
• Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily to complete a 14-day course.
• Metronidazole 400 mg orally twice daily to complete a 14-day course.
• Paracetamol as required, within the labelled maximum dose.
Ceftriaxone was given as a single supervised dose and is not required after discharge. She was advised to avoid alcohol during treatment with metronidazole and for 48 hours after the final dose.

Follow-up and advice
The GP surgery should review pending swab results and ensure treatment is adjusted if required. Sexual health follow-up has been advised for contact tracing, screening and review of symptom resolution. She should avoid sexual intercourse until treatment is complete, symptoms have settled and partners have been assessed and treated.

She was given clear safety-net advice to return to A&E for worsening pain, fever, vomiting, faintness, heavy bleeding or inability to take antibiotics. Discharged home in stable condition on 23 November 2045.

Laboratory medicine report
NHS number: 000 295 0422

Patient: A. Gill
MRN: 056132946
Specimen: Midstream urine, collected in emergency department during assessment of flank pain, dysuria and rigors for 3 days. Clinical details indicate acute pyelonephritis. Current treatment: cefuroxime and paracetamol.

Urine microscopy
White cells: >100 /µL (reference <10)
Red cells: 18 /µL (reference <10)
Bacteria: numerous
Squamous epithelial cells: few

Urine culture
Significant growth of Escherichia coli, >10^5 CFU/mL.

Antimicrobial susceptibility
Cefuroxime: susceptible
Co-amoxiclav: susceptible
Trimethoprim: resistant
Ciprofloxacin: susceptible
Nitrofurantoin: susceptible in vitro; not appropriate for treatment of pyelonephritis.

Findings support a urinary tract infection with significant E. coli growth. The isolate is susceptible to the prescribed cefuroxime. Correlate with temperature, renal function and clinical response. If persistent rigors, vomiting, hypotension or worsening flank pain, urgent reassessment is advised.

Laboratory comment
No mixed growth identified. Please review culture result alongside blood culture findings if obtained. Adjust antimicrobial therapy according to local antimicrobial guidance and clinical progress.

Patient contact detail: arla-mae.gill88@proton.me

Follow-up
GP review booked for 07/07/2004 to confirm symptom resolution and review renal function. Seek same-day medical advice if unable to retain oral medication or if symptoms worsen.

Validated and reported by G. Bennett, laboratory clinician.

Nursing progress note
NHS number: 000 673 0770

Patient: keelen morgan
MRN: 0324722
Home address: 78 Hillcrest Gardens, BALLYMONEY
Review: The patient, aged 81, was reviewed during the evening shift for cellulitis affecting the lower leg.

Clinical assessment:
Spreading erythema remains present from the ankle towards the mid-calf, with local warmth and leg tenderness. The borders were checked against the previous skin-marking line; erythema has not extended beyond the marked area this shift. Skin intact, with no blistering or visible discharge. Patient reports pain 5/10 on movement and when the leg is dependent, settling when elevated. No new shortness of breath, chest pain or dizziness reported.

Observations:
Temperature 37.4°C, pulse 92 bpm regular, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturation 97% on air. Alert and communicating appropriately. No acute deterioration observed.

Mobility and intake:
Mobilised to the bathroom with one staff member and a walking frame. Gait slow due to tenderness but steady with supervision. Left leg elevated in the chair for periods during the shift. Ate approximately three-quarters of the evening meal and drank 750 mL orally. Passed urine independently; no bowel movement reported this shift.

Treatment and response:
Flucloxacillin administered as prescribed; no nausea, rash or other immediate adverse effect noted. Paracetamol given for leg discomfort, with reported reduction in pain on reassessment. Warmth persists, although the patient states the leg feels less tight than earlier. Encouraged oral fluids and regular repositioning. Aseptic technique maintained for inspection and skin care.

Risk and escalation:
Falls precautions in place; call bell within reach and patient advised to request assistance before mobilising. Continue monitoring for extension of erythema, increasing pain, fever, hypotension, confusion or signs of systemic infection. The covering medical clinician’s professional identifier is 0793020; medical review to be requested promptly if observations worsen or the redness extends beyond the marked margin.

Plan for next shift:
Continue prescribed flucloxacillin and paracetamol, record response and adverse effects, repeat observations as scheduled, and reassess the skin margins. Maintain leg elevation when resting, support supervised mobilisation, monitor oral intake and document urine output. Escalate to the nurse in charge and covering medical team for any clinical deterioration. Review need for ongoing analgesia and confirm the next antibiotic dose is administered on time.

Accident and Emergency clinical note

Patient: Bivon
Occupation: Housing officer
Employer: Woodlands East Housing Association
Address: 20 Gibbon Walk, Eastleigh, SO50 0AB
Contact: 07700 900405

Presenting complaint: Retrosternal burning and acid taste.

History: Reports intermittent burning behind the sternum, worse after meals and when lying flat. Acid regurgitation into the mouth, particularly overnight, with associated night-time cough. Symptoms have been present for 3 days. No exertional chest pain, dyspnoea, haematemesis, melaena, dysphagia or unexplained weight loss. No fever or recent respiratory illness. Has used over-the-counter alginate suspension with partial relief. Previously prescribed omeprazole but taking inconsistently.

PMH: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. No known cardiac history recorded.

Examination: Comfortable at rest. Observations within normal limits. Heart sounds normal, no murmur. Chest clear bilaterally, no wheeze or crackles. Abdomen soft and non-tender, no guarding. No calf swelling.

Impression: Symptoms clinically consistent with reflux flare, with likely reflux-related nocturnal cough. No features currently suggesting acute coronary syndrome, pneumonia or upper gastrointestinal bleed.

Plan: Restart omeprazole as previously prescribed and take regularly before food. Continue alginate suspension after meals and at bedtime as needed. Reflux measures discussed: smaller meals, avoid eating late, raise head of bed, and reduce trigger foods, alcohol and smoking if applicable. Safety-netted to return to A&E urgently for persistent or exertional chest pain, breathlessness, collapse, vomiting blood, black stools or difficulty swallowing. GP review advised if not improving or if symptoms recur despite regular treatment. Patient verbalised understanding and is happy with plan.

text:
Discharge summary
National Insurance number: TN011679B

Patient: M. Dickson
Admission date: 11 Jan 2019
Responsible organisation: Aberdeen Royal Infirmary

Reason for admission
M. Dickson was admitted with a four-day history of worsening breathlessness, increased wheeze and purulent yellow sputum. Their usual salbutamol inhaler was providing only brief relief. There was no chest pain, haemoptysis or recent travel. A relative, XIANA HOWE from North Sandwick, provided additional collateral history and was updated during the admission.

Assessment and key results
On arrival the patient was tachypnoeic with widespread expiratory wheeze and reduced air entry bilaterally. Oxygen saturations were 89% on air and improved with controlled oxygen. At 08:15, observations were otherwise stable, with no clinical evidence of sepsis. Chest radiography showed hyperinflation but no focal consolidation or pleural effusion. Blood tests demonstrated a mildly raised white cell count and C-reactive protein, with stable renal function. Viral respiratory PCR was negative. The presentation was felt to represent an acute exacerbation of established chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, without radiographic pneumonia.

Hospital course
Treatment was commenced with nebulised bronchodilators, a five-day course of prednisolone and doxycycline, and oxygen titrated to a target saturation of 88–92%. The patient responded well, with less wheeze and improved exercise tolerance over the following 48 hours. Nebulisers were stepped down to the usual salbutamol inhaler, with a spacer supplied and technique checked by the respiratory nurse. They remained afebrile and were able to mobilise to the bathroom and along the ward corridor without significant desaturation.

The patient did not require non-invasive ventilation or intensive care review. Smoking cessation was discussed, and written advice was provided. Inhaler technique and recognition of future exacerbation symptoms were reviewed before discharge.

Discharge medicines
Continue salbutamol inhaler two puffs when required, using the spacer. Complete the prescribed courses of prednisolone and doxycycline as directed on the discharge medicines list. No other regular medicines were altered during this admission. The patient was advised not to take additional steroid or antibiotic doses unless prescribed.

Condition and follow-up
At discharge the patient was comfortable at rest, eating and drinking, and maintaining their usual oxygen saturations on air. There was mild residual wheeze but no respiratory distress. The GP should review recovery within one week and arrange ongoing COPD management, including vaccination status, inhaler review and consideration of pulmonary rehabilitation. A repeat chest radiograph is not currently required unless symptoms fail to settle.

Safety-net advice was given to seek urgent medical help for rapidly worsening breathlessness, inability to speak in full sentences, blue lips, confusion, chest pain or poor response to salbutamol. The patient and XIANA HOWE confirmed understanding of the plan.

Emergency department handover
NHS number: 0002766435

Patient: Odyn  
MRN: 089183850  
Known to Glangwili General Hospital. Emergency contact/relative: A. Hughes. Patient contact detail: odyn.phillips44@gmail.com

Presenting problem  
Sudden onset left arm weakness with left facial droop and slurred speech while at home. Symptoms began approximately 45 minutes before arrival and resolved completely after around 20 minutes. No persistent deficit on transfer to the emergency department. No loss of consciousness, seizure activity, severe headache, visual loss or chest pain. Relative confirms the episode and reports no previous similar event.

Assessment  
Alert, orientated and speaking fluently. Airway patent; respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturations 98% on air. Pulse regular at 76 bpm. Blood pressure 120/80 mmHg. Temperature 36.7°C. Capillary glucose 6.2 mmol/L.

Neurology: pupils equal and reactive, eye movements full. Face now symmetrical. Speech clear. Normal power and sensation in all four limbs, no pronator drift, coordination intact. Gait steady. NIHSS 0 at review. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations unremarkable. No carotid bruit.

Investigations  
ECG: sinus rhythm, no acute ischaemic changes. Blood tests sent: FBC, U&Es, glucose, LFTs, coagulation screen and lipid profile; no clinically significant abnormality identified on initial results. CT head requested urgently and shows no intracranial haemorrhage or established infarction. Arrange carotid imaging and outpatient/rapid-access neurovascular review as per local pathway.

Impression and plan  
Most consistent with transient ischaemic attack, with resolved unilateral weakness, facial droop and dysarthria. No indication for thrombolysis as symptoms have resolved and examination remains normal. Commence/continue aspirin in accordance with local TIA protocol and continue atorvastatin; confirm doses on the electronic prescription and provide discharge supply. Avoid driving until advised by the relevant authority.

Discharge home with urgent specialist follow-up. Safety-net clearly: call 999 immediately for recurrent facial asymmetry, arm or leg weakness, speech disturbance, visual symptoms, collapse or severe headache. GP review of vascular risk factors and medication adherence. Patient and A. Hughes verbalise understanding.

From: Altnagelvin Area Hospital
Referring clinician: Imojen FARROW, 0442181
Correspondence locality: Acton
Patient: Darci-Leigh Haines

Clinical question

Please assess this patient with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, particularly regarding non-operative pain management, physiotherapy and whether an orthopaedic opinion is indicated because of persistent functional limitation.

History

There is a several-month history of gradually worsening knee pain, worse on walking, stairs and prolonged standing. Morning stiffness lasts approximately 20 minutes and settles with movement, although mobility remains reduced. The patient reports difficulty rising from a chair and has recently limited usual outdoor activity. There has been no acute injury, locking, giving way, fever or unexplained weight loss.

Examination

The affected knee has a small effusion, medial joint-line tenderness and crepitus through flexion and extension. Flexion is mildly restricted by pain. There is no erythema or significant warmth. Collateral and cruciate stability is preserved, and distal neurovascular examination is normal. The contralateral knee is less symptomatic.

Investigations and treatment

Recent plain radiographs show medial compartment joint-space narrowing with marginal osteophytes, consistent with osteoarthritis; there is no fracture. The patient has tried activity modification, pacing and a home strengthening programme with limited benefit. Current analgesia is paracetamol as required and topical ibuprofen applied to the knee. There is no reported gastrointestinal bleeding, anticoagulant treatment or previous joint infection.

Plan requested

I would be grateful for review and advice on an appropriate multidisciplinary management plan, including supervised physiotherapy, exercise progression, weight-neutral activity advice and consideration of an intra-articular injection if clinically suitable. Please advise whether further imaging or orthopaedic referral is warranted. A primary-care review is planned in about 5 weeks to reassess pain control and mobility.

Specialist Mental Health Review

Patient: C. Davenport
DOB: 27 December 1997
Contact telephone: 07700 900880
Report/accession ID: 22/858787

Reason for review

C. Davenport was reviewed in the outpatient mental health clinic following referral from primary care for assessment of persistent depressive symptoms despite treatment with sertraline.

History

They describe a sustained lowering of mood, with markedly reduced enjoyment of previously valued activities and diminished motivation. Early-morning waking occurs on most nights, followed by prolonged rumination and difficulty returning to sleep. Energy and concentration are reduced, and routine tasks require considerable effort. Appetite has been mildly reduced, although there has been no reported significant weight change.

They have also experienced intermittent nausea for 3 days. This is not associated with vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, fever or dizziness. They report no recent change in prescribed medication and are maintaining oral fluids. The symptom is currently mild; advice was given to monitor it and seek GP assessment if it persists, worsens, or is accompanied by inability to eat or drink.

There is no history suggestive of mania, psychosis, obsessive-compulsive disorder or a current substance-use disorder. They deny thoughts of harming others. Passive thoughts that life is difficult have occurred, but there is no current suicidal intent, plan or preparatory behaviour. Protective factors include engagement with treatment, a supportive family network and willingness to seek help if risk increases.

Medication

Sertraline remains the only regular psychotropic medication. Adherence is described as good, with no troublesome adverse effects identified apart from the recent, mild nausea noted above. No over-the-counter or illicit drug use was disclosed.

Mental state examination

C. Davenport attended appropriately dressed and was cooperative throughout. Eye contact was intermittent. Speech was normal in volume and mildly reduced in spontaneity. Affect was constricted and congruent with the reported mood. Thoughts were coherent and goal-directed, without delusional content. No hallucinations were elicited. They were orientated and able to engage in a reasoned discussion of treatment options. Insight and judgement were intact.

Impression

The presentation remains consistent with a major depressive episode, currently of moderate severity, characterised by low mood, anhedonia, biological sleep disturbance and reduced functioning. There is no evidence of psychosis or bipolarity. Current suicide risk is assessed as low, though symptoms warrant active follow-up.

Plan

Continue sertraline as prescribed pending review by the prescribing clinician. A further medication review, including consideration of dose optimisation, should take place with the GP or responsible prescriber. Continue psychological therapy, with emphasis on behavioural activation, sleep regularity and graded re-engagement with usual activities. The nausea should be reviewed in primary care if it does not settle.

A follow-up appointment has been arranged for 7th June 2024. The patient was advised to contact their GP, NHS 111, or attend A&E if suicidal intent develops, mental state deteriorates rapidly, or they cannot maintain safety.

Discharge summary
National Insurance number: NK 59 26 72 B

Patient: Gurmeher Chambers
MRN: 0021710
Discharging organisation: ROYAL VICTORIA HOSPITAL

Reason for admission  
Admitted via the emergency department with a three-day history of profuse watery diarrhoea, repeated vomiting and intermittent abdominal cramps. The symptoms had led to reduced oral intake and dizziness on standing. There was no reported blood in the stool, persistent fever or recent antibiotic exposure.

Assessment and key results  
On arrival, the patient was clinically dehydrated, with dry mucous membranes and mild postural light-headedness. Abdominal examination demonstrated generalised, crampy discomfort without guarding, rebound tenderness or focal peritonism. Initial blood tests showed a mild pre-renal rise in urea with otherwise satisfactory renal function, electrolytes and inflammatory markers. A stool sample was sent for microbiological testing; no inpatient antimicrobial treatment was indicated, and the clinical picture remained most consistent with acute infectious gastroenteritis. There was no evidence of an acute surgical abdomen.

Hospital course  
The patient received intravenous crystalloid initially, followed by oral rehydration solution as vomiting settled. Ondansetron was given for symptomatic relief. Diarrhoea reduced substantially during admission, abdominal cramps resolved, and oral fluids and light meals were tolerated before discharge. Urine output was satisfactory and repeat clinical assessment confirmed improved hydration. No further vomiting was observed overnight.

Discharge medicines  
• Oral rehydration solution, prepared and taken according to the packet instructions, with additional clear fluids as tolerated.  
• ondansetron 4 mg every 8 hours as needed for nausea or vomiting. Use only for the short course supplied and seek advice if symptoms persist.

Assessment and plan  
This was an uncomplicated episode of presumed infectious gastroenteritis with dehydration, now clinically improved. Continue frequent small amounts of fluid and gradually return to a normal diet. Avoid alcohol and very fatty foods until fully recovered. Careful handwashing with soap and water is advised, and the patient should not prepare food for others while diarrhoea continues and for 48 hours after the last episode.

The GP surgery should review the patient if diarrhoea has not settled within several days, or sooner if there is recurrent vomiting, worsening abdominal pain, reduced urine output, marked dizziness or inability to maintain fluids. Attend A&E urgently for blood in the stool, severe or localised abdominal pain, confusion, collapse or breathing difficulty. Any outstanding stool result will be communicated through the usual clinical route.

Condition at discharge  
Clinically stable, drinking independently and mobilising safely. Discharge advice was discussed and understood.

Discharging clinician: caeran ellison
GMC professional identifier: 0084119

text:
Emergency Department Assessment

Patient: Najma R.
The patient, aged 36, was reviewed in the emergency department with sudden-onset breathlessness and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Symptoms began while walking upstairs and were associated with palpitations and marked anxiety. There was no syncope, haemoptysis or recent respiratory infection. They reported reduced mobility during an illness for 3 days, but no previous venous thromboembolism was known. Medication history confirmed apixaban, although the patient was unsure whether the morning dose had been taken. No drug allergies were reported.

On arrival, the patient was alert and speaking in short sentences. Respiratory rate was 26 breaths/minute, oxygen saturations 89% on air, improving to 95% with 2 litres of oxygen via nasal cannula. Heart rate was 124 beats/minute and regular, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, temperature 36.8°C. Chest examination demonstrated mildly reduced air entry at the right base without wheeze or focal crepitations. Heart sounds were normal apart from tachycardia. There was no unilateral calf swelling or tenderness, and the abdomen was soft and non-tender. No clinical evidence of shock was present.

Initial ECG showed sinus tachycardia without ST-segment elevation or convincing right-heart strain. Chest radiograph did not demonstrate consolidation, pulmonary oedema or pneumothorax. Blood tests showed haemoglobin 132 g/L, platelets 241 × 10⁹/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L and normal liver enzymes. D-dimer was not pursued because the clinical probability was high. A CTPA demonstrated bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli, greater on the right, with no saddle embolus or radiological evidence of right ventricular enlargement. High-sensitivity troponin was mildly raised at 34 ng/L; a repeat result was 31 ng/L.

Assessment

This is an acute bilateral pulmonary embolism causing hypoxaemia and tachycardia. The patient remains haemodynamically stable, with no indication for thrombolysis or emergency thrombectomy. The small troponin rise is considered secondary to right-heart pressure burden; there is no clinical or ECG evidence of acute coronary syndrome.

Treatment and plan

Oxygen was continued and titrated to maintain saturations between 94% and 98%. Apixaban was reconciled with the patient and the anticoagulation plan discussed, including bleeding precautions and the importance of not missing doses. Analgesia was provided with paracetamol, with avoidance of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. The case was discussed with the medical registrar at Burnley General Hospital, and admission was accepted for oxygen weaning, observation and anticoagulation review.

The patient was advised to seek immediate help for worsening breathlessness, collapse, significant bleeding or new chest pain. Follow-up has been arranged for 11/12/2026. Care transferred to the acute medical team under M. HANCOCK.

Laboratory report
NHS number: 000 529 4119

Patient: A. Qureshi
MRN: 0720275
Collection date: 8 July 2035
The patient, aged 53, was reviewed with acute pain, swelling and erythema affecting the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Current pain score: 5/10. Specimen: serum, received promptly and suitable for analysis. Clinical details supplied: suspected gout flare.

Results
Urate: 0.49 mmol/L (0.18–0.48) — marginally raised
C-reactive protein: 68 mg/L (<5) — raised
White cell count: 11.8 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0) — mildly raised
Neutrophils: 9.4 ×10⁹/L (2.0–7.5) — raised
Creatinine: 92 µmol/L (60–110) — within reference interval
eGFR: 78 mL/min/1.73 m² (>60) — preserved
Alanine transaminase: 31 U/L (0–41) — within reference interval

Interpretation
Hyperuricaemia with an inflammatory response. The findings support, but do not independently confirm, an acute gout flare. Serum urate may be normal during an attack; joint aspiration with crystal examination remains the diagnostic reference standard where infection is a concern or the presentation is atypical.

Clinical comment
Correlate with examination and temperature. If the joint is markedly hot, systemic symptoms develop, or there is diagnostic uncertainty, urgent assessment for septic arthritis is advised. Naproxen and colchicine are listed as current treatment; review gastrointestinal, renal and drug-interaction risks before continuation. Consider repeat urate after resolution and subsequent long-term management discussion with the GP.

Validated by: Dr Urja Williamson, MBBS
Laboratory clinician
Report date: 8 July 2035

Neurology outpatient review
NHS number: 0001542568

Patient: FABIA DENTON
Occupation: Pharmacist
Report/accession ID: 0916333040
Seen at: Witton Medical Centre
Clinician: latika iqbal

Reason for review
Follow-up of Parkinson disease, with increasing right-sided tremor and slowness over recent months.

History
The resting tremor remains most noticeable in the right hand and is less evident when the hand is being used. It has not been associated with loss of consciousness or episodes suggestive of seizure. FABIA DENTON describes gradually slower movement, particularly when turning in confined spaces, rising from a low chair and getting started after sitting. Muscular rigidity is worse on waking and improves after the morning dose of co-beneldopa.

There have been two near-falls but no actual falls. No freezing reported in open spaces. Handwriting has become smaller and fastening buttons takes longer. Speech is softer, without choking or aspiration. Sleep is interrupted by nocturia; no clear dream enactment. Mood is generally stable and there are no hallucinations or impulsive behaviours.

Medication
Co-beneldopa taken three times daily, with a clear but incomplete benefit. No recent missed doses. No dyskinesia, nausea or postural light-headedness reported.

Examination
Alert and appropriately conversant. Mild hypomimia and reduced volume of speech. Resting tremor of the right hand, with re-emergence on maintaining posture. Bradykinesia on finger tapping and hand opening, greater on the right. Mild cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist and elbow. Gait is slightly stooped with reduced right arm swing; stride length improves with prompting. Turns in four steps. Pull test mildly impaired. No focal weakness or cerebellar signs.

Assessment
Clinical features remain consistent with Parkinson disease. Motor symptoms are becoming more intrusive, but there is no current evidence of psychosis, significant autonomic instability or troublesome dyskinesia.

Plan
• Increase co-beneldopa cautiously to four doses daily, keeping doses evenly spaced and avoiding administration immediately with high-protein meals.
• Discussed possible nausea, dizziness, involuntary movements, confusion and hallucinations; seek advice if these occur.
• Physiotherapy referral for gait, balance and falls-prevention work.
• Encourage regular walking, stretching and activity within safe limits. Consider an occupational therapy assessment if dressing or kitchen tasks worsen.
• Blood pressure to be checked sitting and standing at the next review, or sooner if light-headedness develops.
• Review in approximately three months; contact the neurology team earlier for falls, marked wearing-off or new cognitive symptoms.

Report filed under 0916333040

Discharge summary
NHS number: 000 455 9216

Patient: C. Drew
DOB: 13th September 1909
Home address: 170 Lady Menzies Place, Aberdeen, AB23 8AA
Contact telephone: 07700 900884

Reason for admission
Admitted following sudden onset of left arm weakness, right facial droop and slurred speech while at home. Symptoms resolved before assessment in A&E, with no persistent neurological deficit.

Assessment and key results
Initial observations were stable; capillary glucose was normal. CT head showed no acute haemorrhage or established infarction. CT angiography demonstrated no large-vessel occlusion or significant carotid stenosis. MRI brain showed no acute infarct. ECG confirmed sinus rhythm. Routine blood tests were unremarkable, with satisfactory renal function and no significant anaemia. The presentation was considered most consistent with a transient ischaemic attack (TIA).

Hospital course
The patient was monitored on the stroke unit. There was no recurrence of weakness, facial asymmetry or dysphasia. Swallow assessment was passed and the patient mobilised independently. Following discussion with the stroke team, aspirin and high-intensity statin treatment were commenced for secondary prevention. No indication for anticoagulation was identified.

Discharge medicines
Aspirin 300 mg once daily for 14 days, then 75 mg once daily thereafter.
Atorvastatin 80 mg at night.
Continue other regular medicines as previously prescribed unless advised otherwise by the GP. Avoid over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medicines unless discussed with a clinician.

Follow-up and advice
Urgent TIA clinic follow-up has been requested, including vascular risk assessment and review of blood pressure, lipids and glycaemic status. Please arrange a GP review within one week. Seek emergency help immediately, using 999, if facial droop, arm weakness, speech disturbance, visual loss or sudden severe imbalance returns, even if symptoms settle.

The discharge discussion and medication changes were documented at 08:15. The patient was clinically well and suitable for discharge home with usual support.

Responsible consultant: stroke medicine consultant

Dear Gastroenterology Team,

Re: MCKENZIE-JOHN PATEL

Thank you for assessing this patient with persistent symptoms consistent with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. I would be grateful for your opinion regarding the ongoing retrosternal burning and acid regurgitation despite treatment, and specifically whether further investigation is indicated to exclude erosive oesophagitis, a motility disorder or another upper gastrointestinal cause.

Clinical background

The patient reports several months of troublesome retrosternal burning, usually after meals and when lying flat. Acid regurgitation occurs on most days, with an unpleasant acidic taste and occasional throat irritation. There is also a night-time cough, which is more prominent when symptoms have disturbed sleep. They deny dysphagia, odynophagia, haematemesis, melaena or persistent vomiting. There has been no reported unintentional weight loss. Appetite is broadly maintained.

There is no documented history of upper gastrointestinal surgery. The patient does not describe exertional chest pain, breathlessness or syncope. Symptoms have been considered clinically gastrointestinal in character, although the recurrent chest discomfort warrants specialist review if the pattern changes.

Occupation: Administrative assistant
Employer: NEWRY Housing Association
Home address: 46 Cotton Road, FINNIS

Current treatment and prior management

The patient has been taking omeprazole 20 mg once daily, with administration reviewed as before breakfast. They also use alginate suspension after meals and at bedtime when required. This has provided partial and short-lived relief, but breakthrough burning and regurgitation remain frequent. Advice has included avoiding meals close to bedtime, reducing dietary triggers, moderating caffeine and alcohol intake, elevating the head of the bed and maintaining a healthy weight. Adherence is reported to be reasonable, although symptoms are not fully controlled.

Examination in primary care has been reassuring. The patient appeared well, with no clinical evidence of dehydration or acute distress. The abdomen was soft and non-tender, without palpable masses or organomegaly. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable at the most recent review.

Request

Please assess whether upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is appropriate, and advise on optimisation of acid suppression or alternative therapy. If endoscopy is not currently indicated, guidance on the duration and method of treatment, including a suitable step-down plan once control is achieved, would be appreciated. Please also advise whether the nocturnal cough warrants respiratory assessment should it persist after adequate reflux treatment.

The patient has been advised to seek urgent assessment through A&E if they develop progressive swallowing difficulty, vomiting blood, black stools, severe or exertional chest pain, or unexplained weight loss.

Yours sincerely,

Aashiyana CARROLL

text:
LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: isaq o'hara
Report/accession ID: L24S92492
Report date: 19 Dec 2018
Reporting organisation: Wellington Medical Centre

Clinical indication
Germline hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk assessment. Referred for predictive testing because of a significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer and expressed concern regarding personal cancer risk. The request was submitted by the clinical team; the ordering clinician is not named on this report. No current treatment is recorded.

Specimen and methodology
Specimen received: peripheral blood in EDTA.
DNA extraction and quality assessment were satisfactory. Targeted analysis of BRCA1 and BRCA2 was undertaken using next-generation sequencing with confirmation of reportable findings by an independent method where required. Copy-number analysis was included. This assay is intended to identify constitutional pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants; it does not exclude all deep intronic, regulatory or low-level mosaic variants.

Result
BRCA1 c.68_69delAG detected in the heterozygous state. This is a pathogenic loss-of-function variant, consistent with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome.

No additional pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant was identified in the genes covered by the requested panel. Variants of uncertain significance are not reported routinely and should not be used to guide predictive testing or risk-reducing treatment.

Interpretation
The finding provides a molecular explanation for the reported family history and indicates substantially increased risks of breast, ovarian, fallopian tube and primary peritoneal cancer. The result is compatible with a germline finding, although formal familial segregation may be helpful where relatives are available. A positive result in an affected or unaffected relative should be interpreted alongside the full pedigree and specialist risk assessment.

Recommendations
• Refer to the regional clinical genetics service for post-test counselling and discussion of surveillance and risk-reducing options.
• Offer targeted familial testing for the identified BRCA1 variant to appropriate adult relatives following counselling.
• Management should follow current UK clinical genetics and breast/ovarian cancer guidance; this report is not, by itself, a treatment prescription.
• The patient should advise the GP and relevant hospital teams of this result before future cancer screening, surgery or reproductive planning.

Limitations
A negative result in another family member would not necessarily exclude familial risk if the tested relative is not the carrier of the familial variant. Interpretation may change if the clinical history or laboratory classification is revised.

Validated and authorised by:
LEILAH SIMMONS
Laboratory clinical scientist
Report status: Final

Accident and Emergency Specialist Assessment

Patient: Lyra M.
Occupation: Community development worker
Employer: Aberaman Community Centre
Address: 54 Talfan Road, Caerfyrddin / Carmarthen, SA31 1AD
Contact: lyra.mcleod46@gmail.com

Reason for attendance

Seen in the emergency department following several days of intermittent headache and light-headedness. The headache is described as a pressure-like discomfort across the forehead, without sudden onset, visual loss, neck stiffness, photophobia or vomiting. Current pain score is 5/10. Light-headedness is most noticeable on standing and has not been associated with collapse, palpitations, chest pain, breathlessness, focal weakness, facial droop, speech disturbance or altered awareness.

The patient reports taking amlodipine and ramipril as prescribed, although doses have occasionally been taken later than intended when working at Aberaman Community Centre. No recent medication changes are reported. There is no use of recreational drugs and no regular non-prescribed sympathomimetic medication. Fluid intake has been reduced recently. No infective symptoms were elicited.

Clinical findings

The patient was alert, appropriately conversant and clinically euvolaemic. Blood pressure was elevated on arrival and remained above target on repeat measurement after a period of rest; there was no evidence of hypertensive emergency. Pulse was regular, with normal heart sounds. Chest examination was clear bilaterally, with no respiratory distress. There was no peripheral oedema.

Neurological examination demonstrated normal speech, cognition, cranial nerve function, power, sensation and coordination. Gait was steady. There was no nystagmus or meningism. Fundoscopy did not show papilloedema on the examination possible in the department. Capillary glucose was within the expected range. An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm without acute ischaemic changes. Blood tests, including renal function and electrolytes, did not identify an acute complication of hypertension.

Impression

The presentation is most consistent with symptomatic suboptimally controlled essential hypertension, with headache and probable postural light-headedness contributed to by reduced oral intake. There are no current clinical features to suggest intracranial haemorrhage, acute coronary syndrome, stroke, sepsis or hypertensive encephalopathy. The absence of neurological deficit and the non-thunderclap character of the headache do not indicate an immediate need for neuroimaging.

Plan and follow-up

Amlodipine and ramipril should be continued as currently prescribed until reviewed by the GP; the patient was advised not to self-escalate either medicine. Improve hydration, rise slowly from sitting or lying, and avoid excessive dietary salt. Home blood pressure readings should be recorded twice daily for the next several days, with readings taken after five minutes seated and the arm supported.

The GP should review the home readings, adherence, postural symptoms and renal blood results, and consider adjustment of antihypertensive therapy if blood pressure remains persistently elevated. The patient was advised to seek urgent medical attention for sudden severe headache, new neurological symptoms, chest pain, breathlessness, collapse, confusion or persistent vomiting. Discharged from the emergency department in a stable condition.

Discharge summary

Patient: Ashbie  
Age: 46 y/o  
Admission and discharge date: 24/11/2021

Ashbie was admitted with increasing redness, purulent discharge and localised pain from a postoperative wound. They had noticed a small amount of drainage at home, followed by worsening tenderness over the subsequent 48 hours. There was no history of vomiting, chest pain or urinary symptoms.

On assessment, the patient was alert and haemodynamically stable. The wound edges were erythematous with a small area of superficial separation and purulent exudate. There was no crepitus, fluctuance or evidence of deep tissue involvement. Blood tests showed a mildly raised C-reactive protein with a normal white cell count and stable renal function. A wound swab was taken before antibiotics were commenced; the result was pending at discharge.

The wound was reviewed by the surgical team and irrigated thoroughly. A small amount of retained superficial suture material was removed, with subsequent improvement in drainage. There was no indication for return to theatre. Regular wound care was provided by the ward nursing team, and the patient was taught how to keep the area clean and covered. They remained afebrile throughout admission, with improving erythema and pain.

Assessment

This was a superficial postoperative wound infection without clinical evidence of systemic infection or fascial involvement. The patient responded to local treatment and oral antibiotics and is suitable for discharge with community follow-up.

Discharge plan

Continue flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily to complete the prescribed course. The patient should take each dose as directed and seek advice if they develop a rash, facial swelling or breathing difficulty. Analgesia may be taken as required in accordance with the discharge medicines list.

The dressing should remain clean and dry and be changed if soiled. The patient should attend their GP surgery or the practice nurse for wound review within 48–72 hours. The surgical team will review the wound as arranged, and the wound swab result will be checked with antibiotics amended if required.

Return to A&E urgently for fever, rapidly spreading redness, increasing swelling or pain, offensive discharge, wound breakdown, dizziness or feeling significantly unwell. Written wound-care advice was provided and the patient was able to repeat the key instructions before leaving hospital.

Ashbie’s relative, Nerissa, who is based in DUNSEVERICK, was informed of the discharge plan with the patient’s consent.

Emergency Department Assessment
NHS number: 0003675174
Date: 8 March 2022
Patient: Anaser Tanner
Report/accession ID: 055267913

Presenting complaint
Three-day history of worsening pain, swelling and erythema of the right first metatarsophalangeal joint. Pain is severe and aggravated by weight-bearing; no preceding injury. Reports similar attacks over the past two years. Took usual colchicine with limited benefit. His brother, R. Davison, accompanied him and reports no confusion or collapse.

Background
Known recurrent gout. Current medicines include colchicine and naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food. No known prosthetic joints or immunosuppression. No recent surgery, intravenous drug use or skin infection.

Examination
Alert, uncomfortable but not systemically unwell. Temperature 37.2°C, pulse 88 bpm, BP 138/82, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on air. Marked tenderness, warmth and erythema over the right first MTP joint, with pain on active and passive movement. No wound, fluctuance or lymphangitis. Calf soft and non-tender. Other joints unremarkable.

Investigations
FBC and renal profile within acceptable limits. CRP 34 mg/L. Uric acid 0.46 mmol/L; noted that this does not confirm or exclude an acute flare. Plain radiograph shows no fracture or dislocation, with mild chronic first MTP degenerative change. Accession recorded under 055267913.

Assessment and decision-making
Presentation is most consistent with an acute gout flare, given the typical recurrent pattern and localised podagra, without fever or other systemic illness. Septic arthritis is less likely but cannot be excluded solely by the absence of systemic features. There is no prosthetic joint or immunosuppression. Following discussion with the emergency medicine clinician at Bishop Auckland General Hospital, joint aspiration was not pursued today because symptoms and examination were typical, inflammatory markers were only mildly raised, and there was no clinical deterioration.

Treatment and disposition
Given oral analgesia in the department and advised rest, elevation, ice wrapped in a cloth and oral fluids. Continue colchicine as previously prescribed; avoid exceeding the labelled dose. Safety-netted to return immediately for fever, spreading redness, rapidly worsening pain, vomiting or inability to mobilise.

Discharged home. GP review within one week to review urate-lowering therapy and recurrence prevention.

Progressive symptomatic knee osteoarthritis with pain, morning stiffness and reduced functional mobility despite simple analgesia and topical anti-inflammatory treatment. There is no current clinical suggestion of acute trauma, septic arthritis or inflammatory arthropathy.

RENAL BIOCHEMISTRY REPORT
National Insurance number: GB663716B

Patient: E. BURGESS
Report/accession ID: L21M60788
Specimen: Serum, urgent inpatient sample
Clinical information: Reduced urine output, fatigue and poor oral intake for 3 days. Acute kidney injury under assessment. Intravenous sodium chloride commenced; potentially nephrotoxic and renally cleared medicines placed on temporary hold.

Results
Sodium: 136 mmol/L (133–146)
Potassium: 5.4 mmol/L (3.5–5.3)
Urea: 18.2 mmol/L (2.5–7.8)
Creatinine: 238 µmol/L (45–90)
eGFR: 24 mL/min/1.73 m² (interpret with caution in acute kidney injury)
Bicarbonate: 19 mmol/L (22–29)
Chloride: 103 mmol/L (95–108)
Albumin: 37 g/L (35–50)
Adjusted calcium: 2.28 mmol/L (2.20–2.60)
CRP: 18 mg/L (<5)

Interpretation
Marked creatinine and urea elevation with reduced estimated filtration, consistent with significant acute kidney injury in the stated clinical context. Mild hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis are present. The eGFR value should not be used for chronic kidney disease staging during changing renal function.

Clinical comment
Please correlate with previous renal results, fluid balance, blood pressure and examination for hypovolaemia or obstruction. Continue careful fluid assessment following intravenous sodium chloride, avoiding fluid overload. Repeat U&E and bicarbonate promptly, with earlier testing if urine output falls further or clinical condition deteriorates. Review all medicines for renal dosing and nephrotoxins. Escalate urgently if potassium rises, acidosis worsens, pulmonary oedema develops or there is persistent oliguria; seek renal advice if recovery is not evident.

A urine sample for dipstick testing, microscopy and culture should be considered, with renal tract imaging if obstruction is clinically suspected. Follow-up biochemical review is requested for 2024-04-12.

Ongoing tiredness, intermittent light-headedness and reduced exercise tolerance. Dizziness is most noticeable on standing or when climbing stairs. text:
Discharge Summary – Cardiology

Patient: A. Wells
Report/accession ID: 05912350
Discharging service: Cardiology, Queen Elizabeth University Hospital

Reason for admission
Admitted via the emergency department with sudden central chest pressure associated with diaphoresis and nausea. The discomfort began at rest and persisted despite stopping activity. There was no preceding febrile illness, pleuritic component or recent trauma. The patient reported intermittent milder chest discomfort for 3 days before presentation.

Initial assessment and key results
On arrival the patient was haemodynamically stable, with cool peripheries and ongoing chest discomfort. Heart sounds were normal, with no clinical evidence of pulmonary oedema. Initial electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with non-specific ST-segment and T-wave changes but no ST elevation. Serial high-sensitivity troponin demonstrated a significant rise and fall consistent with a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Chest radiograph showed no acute cardiopulmonary abnormality. Renal function and haemoglobin remained satisfactory during admission; lipid profile was elevated, and HbA1c was in the non-diabetic range.

Hospital course
The patient was treated promptly with aspirin, fondaparinux, sublingual glyceryl trinitrate as required and high-intensity atorvastatin. Symptoms settled following initial treatment, with no further sustained chest pain or arrhythmia. Telemetry showed sinus rhythm throughout the monitored period. Echocardiography demonstrated mild regional left ventricular systolic impairment, with preserved overall function and no significant valve disease.

The case was reviewed by the interventional cardiology team. In view of the clinical presentation, biochemical findings and overall risk assessment, a medically managed strategy was agreed rather than immediate invasive angiography. The patient remained clinically stable with mobilisation on the ward and was counselled regarding secondary prevention.

Medication changes at discharge
• Aspirin 75 mg once daily, to continue indefinitely.
• Clopidogrel 75 mg once daily, planned for 12 months following cardiology review of the medically managed NSTEMI.
• Atorvastatin 80 mg once daily.
• Bisoprolol 2.5 mg once daily, provided pulse and blood pressure remain acceptable.
• Glyceryl trinitrate 400 micrograms per spray, one or two sprays under the tongue as needed for chest pain.

Fondaparinux was stopped before discharge. The patient was advised not to stop aspirin or clopidogrel without first speaking to the cardiology or GP team. Potential bleeding symptoms and statin-related muscle symptoms were discussed.

Condition on discharge and follow-up
Discharged home clinically well, pain-free and independently mobile. A discharge medication list and written advice were provided. The GP is asked to review blood pressure, pulse, adherence and tolerance of treatment, and to repeat liver blood tests and lipid profile after initiation of high-dose atorvastatin. Cardiology follow-up will include review of left ventricular function, risk-factor modification and confirmation of the antiplatelet duration. Referral to a cardiac rehabilitation programme has been recommended.

The patient should seek emergency help immediately if chest pain recurs and does not settle promptly with rest and glyceryl trinitrate, or if associated with breathlessness, collapse or marked sweating. Smoking cessation, a Mediterranean-style diet and gradual return to activity were advised.

Emergency contact locality recorded as Wester Balgedie.

Prepared and electronically signed by Dr Efan Da Silva, MBBS, Cardiology clinician.

text:
Emergency Department Assessment
NHS number: 000 653 8976

Patient: Meadow-Rae Fatima
Date: 25 Jan 2035
Address: 134 Wig Lane, Felindre, SA5 4AA

Presenting complaint
Persistent vomiting in early pregnancy for 6 days, with inability to keep fluids down since yesterday. Reports approximately 3 kg weight loss over the past fortnight, light-headedness on standing and reduced urine output. No haematemesis, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, dysuria or vaginal bleeding. The patient, aged 44, was reviewed with her partner present. Current pregnancy is 9+4 weeks' gestation.

Relevant history
Previously well apart from nausea and vomiting of pregnancy. Cyclizine prescribed by GP, with limited benefit; has taken only occasional doses because of vomiting. No regular medication otherwise. No known drug allergies.

Examination
Alert but tired and mildly distressed. Dry mucous membranes and cracked lips. Pulse 108 bpm, BP 102/66 mmHg lying and 94/60 mmHg standing, temperature 36.7°C, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on air. Abdomen soft and non-tender, without guarding. No peripheral oedema. Capillary refill approximately 2 seconds.

Investigations
Urinalysis: 3+ ketones, 1+ protein, no nitrites or blood. Venous blood gas: pH 7.41, lactate 1.2 mmol/L. Blood tests show sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 3.6 mmol/L, urea 6.8 mmol/L and creatinine 68 micromol/L; FBC and CRP unremarkable. Serum beta-hCG not required today. Pregnancy assessment unit contacted; ultrasound confirms an intrauterine pregnancy with cardiac activity, in keeping with dates.

Management and decision
Treated with 1 litre intravenous sodium chloride 0.9% and intravenous cyclizine, with marked improvement in nausea. Tolerated oral water and crackers subsequently. Repeat pulse 92 bpm and blood pressure 108/70 mmHg. No indication for admission at present, provided oral intake remains adequate.

Disposition
Discharged with cyclizine as prescribed, frequent small sips and bland meals. Safety-netted to return for inability to retain fluids, fainting, abdominal pain, bleeding or reduced urine output. Same-day contact with early pregnancy assessment service arranged via her GP surgery.

Seen and signed by sharmake ellis

text:
LABORATORY REPORT – URINE CULTURE AND INFLAMMATORY MARKERS
NHS number: 000 350 5090

Patient: L. Howells
Home address: 105 Queen Mary's Close, Whitchurch, RG28 7AB
Report/accession ID: L24O54853
Clinical indication: Acute pyelonephritis with flank pain, dysuria and rigors. Current pain score 5/10.

Specimen details

Midstream urine submitted in a sterile container. Specimen received promptly and processed for microscopy, culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Blood samples were collected during the same episode for full blood count, renal profile and C-reactive protein.

Results

Urine microscopy:
• White blood cells: >100 × 10^6/L – markedly increased
• Red blood cells: 18 × 10^6/L – mildly increased
• Squamous epithelial cells: <10 × 10^6/L
• Nitrite: positive
• Leucocyte esterase: 3+

Culture:
Significant growth of a single organism, Escherichia coli, estimated at >10^8 colony-forming units/L. The growth pattern is consistent with a urinary pathogen rather than contamination.

Antimicrobial susceptibility:
• Cefuroxime: susceptible
• Co-amoxiclav: susceptible
• Nitrofurantoin: susceptible
• Trimethoprim: resistant
• Ciprofloxacin: susceptible, subject to clinical suitability and local prescribing policy

Blood results:
• Haemoglobin: 126 g/L
• White cell count: 15.8 × 10^9/L – raised
• Neutrophils: 13.4 × 10^9/L – raised
• Platelets: 286 × 10^9/L
• C-reactive protein: 168 mg/L – substantially raised
• Creatinine: 92 µmol/L
• Estimated GFR: 78 mL/min/1.73 m²

Interpretive comment

The urine findings and heavy growth of E. coli support a diagnosis of acute bacterial pyelonephritis in the stated clinical context. The isolate is susceptible to cefuroxime, which is compatible with the reported treatment. Correlate with temperature, haemodynamic status, renal function and response to therapy. Persistent rigors, vomiting, worsening flank pain or clinical deterioration should prompt urgent reassessment for obstruction, sepsis or an alternative source of infection.

The patient is currently taking cefuroxime and paracetamol. Ensure adequate hydration where clinically appropriate, review analgesia requirements and avoid relying on urine results alone if symptoms fail to improve. Repeat urine culture is not routinely required after clinical resolution, but should be considered if symptoms persist or recur.

Planned clinical review: 07/12/1988

Validated and reported by Dr Ottis Wade, MBBS.
This report should be interpreted alongside the examination findings and antimicrobial stewardship guidance.

text:
Nursing Progress Note
NHS number: 000 387 4231

Patient: E. Rigby
Ward: Medical inpatient area
Primary issue: Diabetic foot ulcer with reduced protective sensation and local discharge.

Current assessment
Patient awake, alert and orientated, reporting intermittent aching at the plantar aspect of the affected foot, rated 4/10 at rest and 6/10 when mobilising. States the dressing felt “wet” earlier this shift. Plantar ulcer inspected following removal of the outer dressing: moderate serous discharge with a small amount of yellow staining, no active bleeding. Surrounding skin warm with mild erythema at the wound margin; no obvious tracking or crepitus. Reduced sensation persists on monofilament assessment. Foot warm, dorsalis pedis pulse palpable and capillary refill under three seconds.

Observations
Temperature 37.4°C, pulse 92 bpm, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturations 97% on air, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg. Early Warning Score remains 0. Patient denies rigors, nausea or new malaise. Capillary blood glucose 12.8 mmol/L before lunch; encouraged to follow the diabetic meal plan and avoid additional snacks between meals.

Mobility and intake
Mobilising short distances with a frame and supervision. Kept weight-bearing to a minimum on the affected foot and reminded not to walk barefoot. Reviewed safe transfer technique with the patient. Eating and drinking adequately; approximately 900 ml oral fluids taken during the shift. Passing urine without reported difficulty.

Interventions and response
Wound cleansed with sterile saline and redressed using the prescribed non-adherent dressing and absorbent secondary layer. Patient tolerated the procedure, with pain reducing to 2/10 afterwards. Co-amoxiclav administered as prescribed; no rash, wheeze or gastrointestinal upset noted. Foot elevated intermittently in the recliner. Pressure-relieving footwear remains in use. Patient advised to report increasing pain, spreading redness, offensive odour, fever or feeling generally unwell.

Escalation and communication
Findings discussed with the nurse in charge and documented for review by the tissue viability/diabetic foot team at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary. No indication for emergency escalation at present, but medical review requested if erythema extends beyond the marked margin or observations deteriorate. Patient’s relative, ishah morley, is recorded as the named contact. Patient confirmed current contact details as eva-jane.rigby69@outlook.com and home address 78 Glenspean Place, Bellshill, ML4 1AB.

Plan for next shift
Continue four-hourly observations and blood-glucose monitoring as prescribed. Maintain dressing clean and intact, reassess wound drainage and erythema, administer co-amoxiclav on schedule, and reinforce off-loading and falls precautions. Confirm specialist review and document any change in neurovascular status, pain, discharge or systemic symptoms.
