Patient: Joselyn Head
MRN: 040098093
Clinic: Llandudno General Hospital Site

Occupation: accountant

History
Review of persistent low back pain with right-sided shooting pain extending through the buttock and posterior thigh to the calf. Paraesthesia is intermittent in the lateral calf and dorsum of the foot. Symptoms are worse after sitting for prolonged periods and on bending. Walking remains possible, although the right leg feels less reliable after approximately fifty minutes. Sleep is disturbed on some nights.

No urinary retention, faecal incontinence, saddle anaesthesia or progressive bilateral symptoms. No fever, unexplained weight loss or recent significant trauma. Has been taking paracetamol with partial benefit. Current anti-inflammatory instruction is naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food. No reported dyspepsia or melaena.

Examination
Mobilises independently with a mildly antalgic gait. Lumbar flexion restricted by pain; extension less affected. Straight-leg raise positive on the right at approximately fifty degrees, reproducing posterior leg pain. Power 5/5 at hip flexion, knee extension and ankle dorsiflexion/plantarflexion. Reflexes symmetrical. Reduced light-touch sensation over the right L5 distribution. Left leg neurological examination normal. No focal spinal tenderness.

Assessment
Clinical picture remains consistent with right lumbar radiculopathy, most likely L5 nerve-root irritation. No current red-flag features or objective motor deficit.

Plan
Continue regular paracetamol within recommended dose limits and naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food for the shortest effective period. Take naproxen after meals; stop and seek advice if gastrointestinal bleeding, severe indigestion or wheeze develops. Discussed remaining active, avoiding prolonged bed rest, pacing activities and use of heat. Refer for community physiotherapy and exercise-based rehabilitation. MRI lumbar spine to be considered if symptoms fail to improve, progress, or if intervention is being contemplated.

Safety-netted to attend A&E urgently for new bladder or bowel disturbance, saddle numbness, marked weakness or rapidly worsening pain. Review in four weeks, sooner if deterioration.

Seen and documented by Dr Nancy-Ann FOLEY, MBBS, clinician.

Discharge summary
NHS number: 0002741378

Patient: Ihtisham S.
Home address: 23 Manor Hill, BELCOO
Contact detail: ihtisham.spence29@sky.com

Reason for admission and assessment

Ihtisham S. was admitted with a severe sickle cell painful crisis affecting both limbs and the lower back. The pain had not settled with the usual medicines at home and was accompanied by poor oral intake and clinical dehydration. There was no history to suggest chest pain, breathlessness, focal neurological symptoms or infection during this admission.

On arrival, observations were stable and oxygen saturations remained satisfactory on air. Examination showed marked tenderness in the limbs and lumbar region without joint swelling or focal neurological deficit. Initial blood tests were consistent with the patient’s known sickle cell disorder, with no significant acute kidney injury. C-reactive protein was not raised, and chest examination remained clear. Blood cultures were not indicated clinically.

Treatment in hospital

A patient-controlled analgesia regimen was commenced using morphine, with regular review by the acute pain team. This was gradually reduced as the pain improved, and the patient was able to manage with oral analgesia before discharge. Intravenous fluids were given for dehydration, followed by a planned increase in oral fluids. Anti-sickness treatment was available and was not required after the first day. There was no indication for blood transfusion, antibiotics or oxygen therapy.

The patient remained mobile with encouragement and completed deep-breathing exercises. There were no complications such as acute chest syndrome, fever, worsening anaemia or renal impairment. Oral intake and urine output improved, and the cannula was removed before discharge.

Discharge plan

Please continue the discharge medicines supplied by the ward, including the agreed oral analgesia regimen. Use the lowest effective dose and do not take additional opioid-containing medicines unless specifically advised. Maintain good fluid intake and avoid becoming chilled or overheated. Continue the usual sickle cell medicines unless the haematology team has told you otherwise.

A review with the GP or haematology service is requested in 7 days, with earlier assessment if pain is not controlled. The patient should contact the sickle cell team or attend A&E urgently for fever, chest pain, difficulty breathing, new weakness, confusion, persistent vomiting, markedly reduced urine output or pain that is worsening despite the prescribed medicines.

At discharge, Ihtisham S. was comfortable at rest, drinking independently and walking safely. The discharge advice and medication changes were discussed, and understanding was confirmed.

Prepared and signed by Dr Kol Omar, MBBS, GMC identifier 0146399.

A&E emergency assessment
National Insurance number: GB 56 29 13 C

Patient: rosa-belle fernandes
MRN: 04990036
Home address: 50 Daphmoir Close, Wellington, TA21 0AA
Contact telephone: 07700 900936

Presenting complaint
36-hour history of left flank pain, dysuria and urinary frequency, with two episodes of shaking rigors overnight. Nauseated but no vomiting. Reports feeling feverish. No vaginal symptoms. No previous renal stones. Altina, her sister, accompanied her and provided collateral history.

Assessment
Alert, uncomfortable but not toxic. GCS 15. T 38.4°C, HR 108 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg, RR 18, SpO₂ 98% on air. Mucous membranes slightly dry. Heart sounds normal, chest clear. Marked left renal angle tenderness; mild left upper-quadrant abdominal discomfort without guarding or rebound. No rash. No focal neurological deficit.

Investigations
Urine dip: blood ++, leucocytes +++, nitrites positive, protein +. Urine sent for MC&S. FBC: WCC 15.8 ×10⁹/L, neutrophils 13.7. U&E: creatinine 92 micromol/L, eGFR 74. C-reactive protein 86 mg/L. Lactate 1.4 mmol/L. Pregnancy test negative. Blood cultures obtained before antibiotics.

Impression
Acute left-sided pyelonephritis with systemic inflammatory response. Currently haemodynamically stable; no clinical evidence of obstruction or peritonism.

Treatment and plan
Given IV fluids 1 litre Hartmann’s and IV cefuroxime 1.5 g, with oral paracetamol 1 g for pain/fever. Symptoms and observations improved after treatment; repeat HR 94 bpm and temperature 37.8°C. Discussed admission versus ambulatory management. Suitable for discharge with oral cefuroxime, completion course as prescribed, regular paracetamol, fluids and rest. Safety-netted to return immediately for persistent vomiting, worsening pain, confusion, reduced urine output or recurrent rigors. GP follow-up requested for culture review and clinical reassessment.

text:
Dear Gastroenterology Team,

Re: MEI EVANS

I am referring this adult patient for assessment of persistent gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, particularly to clarify whether further investigation is needed despite acid-suppression treatment. The main symptoms are retrosternal burning, acid regurgitation and a troublesome cough at night. The cough has been present for 3 days and is most noticeable after lying down. There is no reported difficulty swallowing, vomiting blood, black stool, unexplained weight loss or persistent vomiting.

The patient describes partial relief with omeprazole, although symptoms recur when doses are missed. Alginate suspension provides short-term benefit after meals and at bedtime. They have tried avoiding late meals and raising the head of the bed, with limited improvement. Caffeine and spicy foods appear to aggravate the burning. They do not report exertional chest pain, breathlessness or syncope.

At review, the patient was comfortable and able to speak in full sentences. Observations were stable. The abdomen was soft and non-tender, without guarding or a palpable mass. Oropharyngeal examination was unremarkable. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy. A recent full blood count, liver profile and renal function were within the local reference ranges; there was no evidence of anaemia.

Current medicines:
• Omeprazole, taken regularly as prescribed.
• Alginate suspension after meals and at bedtime when required.

Occupation: Architect
Home address: 27 Turpie Drive, Strome Ferry, IV53 8UG

I would be grateful for your opinion on optimisation of treatment and whether upper gastrointestinal endoscopy should be arranged. Please consider alternative causes of the nocturnal cough if the reflux burden does not fully account for it. In the meantime, I have advised continuing omeprazole as directed, using alginate after meals and before bed, avoiding food for at least three hours before sleep, and reducing identified dietary triggers. The patient has been advised to seek urgent medical attention through A&E or 999 if they develop severe or persistent chest pain, vomiting blood, black stools, or sudden difficulty swallowing.

A follow-up review has been arranged for 16/05/2019 to assess response and ensure that the specialist plan has been received. Please send your advice to the referring clinician.

Yours faithfully,

Nermin Knowles
Referring clinician

LABORATORY REPORT
NHS number: 000 900 6592

Patient: Sabaa
MRN: 09767853
Requesting service: Rheumatology
Reporting organisation: Llanidloes and District War Memorial Hospital
Specimen collected: 15/01/2020
Specimen: Blood, EDTA and serum
Clinical indication: Suspected rheumatoid arthritis flare with increased morning stiffness, swollen hand joints and fatigue. Current treatment recorded as methotrexate, folic acid and naproxen.

RESULTS

Full blood count
Haemoglobin: 118 g/L (115–160)
White cell count: 8.7 × 10⁹/L (4.0–11.0)
Platelets: 428 × 10⁹/L (150–400)
Mean cell volume: 86 fL (80–100)

Inflammatory markers
C-reactive protein: 34 mg/L (<5)
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 48 mm/hour (1–20)

Renal profile
Sodium: 139 mmol/L (133–146)
Potassium: 4.4 mmol/L (3.5–5.3)
Urea: 5.8 mmol/L (2.5–7.8)
Creatinine: 72 µmol/L (45–90)
Estimated GFR: >90 mL/min/1.73 m²

Liver profile
ALT: 46 U/L (0–40)
Alkaline phosphatase: 93 U/L (30–130)
Bilirubin: 9 µmol/L (0–21)
Albumin: 38 g/L (35–50)

Rheumatology serology
Rheumatoid factor: 186 IU/mL (<14)
Anti-CCP antibody: >250 U/mL (<7)

INTERPRETATION

Raised CRP and ESR, with mild thrombocytosis, support active systemic inflammation and are compatible with the reported rheumatoid arthritis flare. Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP remain strongly positive. Renal function is satisfactory for the current treatment. ALT is minimally above the laboratory reference interval; bilirubin, albumin and alkaline phosphatase are within range.

CLINICAL COMMENT

The results should be interpreted alongside joint examination and disease activity assessment. The mild transaminase elevation may be medication-related, including methotrexate or intermittent naproxen use, although other causes should be considered if persistent. Please review alcohol intake, concurrent medicines and recent illness. Repeat liver profile and full blood count according to the local DMARD monitoring schedule, or sooner if clinically indicated.

The patient should seek urgent assessment for fever, marked breathlessness, severe mucosal ulceration or other features of infection while taking immunomodulatory treatment. Rheumatology review is recommended in about 8 weeks, with earlier assessment if swelling or functional limitation progresses.

Validated and reported by:
Eusebiu Hogan
Laboratory clinician
Report date: 15/01/2020

Nursing Progress Note

Patient: M. KERR
Home address: 112 FOUNTAIN CLOSE, KILLEAD
The patient, aged 34, was reviewed on the evening shift following admission with a sickle cell painful crisis. She reported severe aching pain in both lower limbs, with additional thoracic and lumbar back pain. Pain was worse on movement and rated 8/10 at the start of the shift. She appeared tired and mildly dry, with cracked lips and reduced oral intake. No chest pain, cough or breathlessness was reported. She remained alert and orientated, speaking in full sentences.

Observations at 18:40 were: temperature 37.3°C, pulse 104 bpm, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% on air. Peripheral circulation was warm, with no new focal swelling or skin breakdown noted. Urine output had been low earlier in the day, although she passed a small amount of concentrated urine during this shift. The medical team was informed of the ongoing pain and reduced intake.

Morphine was administered as prescribed, with the dose checked against the drug chart and the patient monitored for sedation and respiratory depression. Intravenous fluids continued via the left forearm cannula; the site remained clean, dry and patent with no redness or discomfort. She was encouraged to take frequent small amounts of water, and a jug was left within reach. A heat pack was offered for her back, which she found helpful. She was assisted to reposition regularly and mobilised a short distance to the bathroom with one staff member and a walking frame. She was unsteady when first standing but did not fall.

On reassessment approximately 45 minutes after analgesia, pain had reduced to 5/10 and she was able to rest intermittently. Respiratory rate remained stable, and there was no vomiting or evidence of opioid-related confusion. She declined a full meal but tolerated soup and several sips of oral fluid. Falls precautions remain in place, including call bell access, non-slip footwear and assistance with transfers.

Assessment and plan: ongoing vaso-occlusive limb and back pain with clinical dehydration, showing partial response to morphine and fluids. Continue prescribed analgesia and intravenous hydration, record pain score and sedation level after each dose, and encourage oral intake as tolerated. Maintain regular observations and monitor temperature, oxygen saturation, urine output, cannula site and any respiratory symptoms. Escalate promptly to the nurse in charge and medical team if pain remains uncontrolled, oxygen saturation falls, fever develops, urine output decreases further or she becomes excessively drowsy.

Report/accession ID: 0136398791. Medical review was documented under GMC professional identifier 0085148. The next shift should reassess analgesic effectiveness, hydration status and mobility, and confirm that a further medical review has occurred if pain remains above the patient’s agreed comfort goal.

Outpatient consultation record

Patient: oba simmons
Address: 154 Overbrook Close, Lawford, CO11 1AA
Telephone: 07700 900525
Occupation: Sales assistant
Employer: Hemingbrough Further Education College

Reason for attendance
Review following an episode of acute anxiety with prominent physical symptoms.

History
Reports a sudden episode while travelling to work, beginning with forceful and rapid palpitations, central chest tightness and a marked fear of dying. Symptoms escalated quickly and settled gradually after approximately 20 minutes. No collapse, unilateral weakness, speech disturbance or seizure activity. She has had intermittent anticipatory anxiety since then and is avoiding crowded transport.

Also describes poor sleep and increased awareness of her heartbeat. No exertional chest pain, syncope, orthopnoea or ankle swelling. No recent infective symptoms. Has experienced similar, shorter episodes in the past but has not previously sought help. Current gastrointestinal upset has been present for 3 days, without vomiting or blood in the stool.

No thoughts of self-harm or suicide. Denies use of recreational drugs and reports only occasional alcohol. Caffeine intake increased recently because of tiredness.

Medication and allergies
No regular prescribed medication recorded. Breathing retraining discussed and commenced as the current treatment strategy. No known drug allergies reported.

Examination
Alert, appropriately dressed and engaged. Tearful when describing the episode but settles during consultation. Speech normal, with no evidence of thought disorder. Pulse regular at 78 bpm; blood pressure 128/76 mmHg; oxygen saturations 99% on air. Heart sounds normal, no murmur. Chest clear with good air entry bilaterally. No calf tenderness or peripheral oedema. Abdomen soft and non-tender. Neurological screening examination normal.

Assessment
Presentation is most consistent with a panic attack, with subsequent anticipatory anxiety. No current clinical features to suggest acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism or a neurological event. Physical symptoms and the fear of dying were explained as part of the sympathetic response, while acknowledging that the experience was frightening. Mild gastrointestinal symptoms appear self-limiting.

Plan
• Practise slow diaphragmatic breathing twice daily and at the first sign of escalating symptoms; written breathing-retraining advice provided.
• Reduce caffeine, maintain regular meals and sleep routine, and continue ordinary activities in small manageable steps rather than avoiding transport altogether.
• Offered referral for NHS talking therapies; patient wishes to consider this and will self-refer if symptoms persist.
• Safety-netted to contact 999 for prolonged or exertional chest pain, collapse, severe breathlessness or new neurological symptoms.
• GP review if recurrent attacks, persistent low mood, worsening avoidance or thoughts of self-harm. Encourage fluids and routine care for the gastrointestinal upset; seek advice if it persists or blood develops.

Discharge Summary

Patient: BOLAN GOULD
Age: 48 y/o
Admission date: 10th April 2023
Discharge destination: Home

Reason for admission

BOLAN GOULD was admitted with a two-day history of worsening left flank pain, dysuria and rigors, associated with nausea and reduced oral intake. There was no reported vaginal discharge or recent urinary instrumentation. On arrival the patient was febrile at 38.6°C, with left renal angle tenderness and mild tachycardia. Blood pressure remained stable and there were no features of septic shock.

Key findings and hospital course

Initial blood tests showed a raised white cell count of 15.2 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein of 164 mg/L. Creatinine was within the expected range, with no evidence of acute kidney injury. Urinalysis demonstrated leucocytes, nitrites and blood. A midstream urine sample subsequently grew Escherichia coli sensitive to cefuroxime. Blood cultures remained negative. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis or visible calculus.

The patient received intravenous fluids, analgesia and intravenous cefuroxime on admission. Paracetamol was given regularly for pain and fever, with good effect. Symptoms and inflammatory markers improved over the subsequent 48 hours, and the patient remained apyrexial with improving oral intake. The case was discussed with the consultant nephrologist, who agreed that there was no indication for urgent intervention or further inpatient imaging in the absence of obstruction or renal impairment.

Assessment at discharge

Acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis, clinically improved following intravenous treatment. The patient was mobilising independently, tolerating food and fluids, and passing urine without difficulty at the time of discharge. Mild residual flank discomfort was present but was controlled with oral medication.

Discharge medicines

Cefuroxime 500 mg orally twice daily to complete a 7-day course in total. Paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily when required for pain or fever, provided the daily maximum dose is not exceeded. No other medication changes were made.

Follow-up and advice

The patient should arrange a GP review within one week, or sooner if symptoms do not continue to settle. A repeat urine sample is not routinely required if fully recovered. Please seek urgent medical attention through NHS 111, A&E or emergency services if fever or rigors recur, flank pain worsens, vomiting prevents the antibiotics being taken, urine output falls, or there is new confusion or marked weakness.

Discharge information and correspondence can be sent to bolan.gould68@sky.com. The patient’s relative, Haniel Thomas, was updated with the patient’s consent and understands the safety-netting advice.

Emergency department handover – acute abdominal pain

Patient: aleeza wright
Seen with her sister, Maura Peters, who confirms the history.

Presenting problem
Approximately 18 hours of worsening abdominal pain, initially peri-umbilical and now localised to the right lower quadrant. Nausea and marked loss of appetite; no vomiting. Reports feeling feverish but no urinary symptoms or vaginal bleeding. No previous abdominal surgery.

Assessment
Alert, uncomfortable but conversant. Pulse 96, BP 124/76, temperature 37.8°C, respiratory rate 18, SpO₂ 99% on air. Abdomen soft overall, with focal right iliac fossa tenderness, guarding and percussion tenderness. No generalised peritonism. Negative renal angle tenderness. Bowel sounds present. Pregnancy test negative.

Investigations
FBC: WCC 14.8 × 10⁹/L, neutrophils 12.6 × 10⁹/L. CRP 48 mg/L. U&Es and LFTs within reference range; venous lactate 1.1 mmol/L. Urinalysis: trace blood, no nitrites or leucocytes. CT abdomen/pelvis demonstrates a dilated inflamed appendix with surrounding fat stranding, no abscess or perforation.

Treatment and decision
Paracetamol given for pain, with partial improvement. Intravenous co-amoxiclav commenced following discussion of the working diagnosis and need for surgical review. Nil by mouth apart from essential medication; intravenous fluids running. No evidence currently of septic shock or perforation.

Plan / priorities
1. Admit under the emergency general surgical team at The Grange University Hospital for review and management of acute appendicitis.
2. Repeat observations and abdominal examination; escalate for increasing pain, hypotension, tachycardia, fever or new generalised tenderness.
3. Surgical decision regarding laparoscopic appendicectomy versus continued antibiotic management. Confirm consent and antimicrobial plan on arrival to ward.
4. Analgesia and antiemetic as required. Ensure pregnancy result and CT findings are communicated at handover.

Discharge is not appropriate at present. If managed non-operatively, arrange surgical follow-up on 18/02/2025, in about 8 weeks, with clear return advice for recurrent pain, vomiting, fever or inability to tolerate fluids.

Dear Consultant,

Re: jorel church

Clinical question

I would be grateful for specialist assessment of recurrent migraine with unilateral headache, nausea and photophobia, particularly to confirm the diagnosis, advise on preventive treatment, and review the frequency of acute medication use. Please also advise whether any further investigation is indicated.

History

jorel church reports a longstanding pattern of episodic headaches, previously managed in general practice. Attacks are usually unilateral and throbbing, with associated nausea and marked photophobia. There is no reported fever, persistent visual loss, collapse, seizure, focal limb weakness, speech disturbance or loss of consciousness. The headaches are sufficiently disabling to interfere with usual activities, and the patient has recently required more frequent use of rescue treatment.

There is no history provided of recent head injury, anticoagulant use or known malignancy. The patient does not describe a new persistent morning headache or headache provoked by coughing or exertion. Family history is not fully documented; Samuil Delaney, the patient’s relative, has helped to clarify the chronology and impact of recent episodes.

Previous management

Acute treatment has consisted of sumatriptan and naproxen, with partial benefit when taken early in an attack. Advice has been given regarding hydration, regular meals, sleep, limiting screen exposure during attacks and maintaining a headache diary. The patient has been asked to avoid excessive reliance on acute medication, although the precise number of treatment days per month remains to be established.

Examination and available findings

At the most recent primary-care review, the patient was clinically well between attacks. There was no reported meningism, papilloedema or focal neurological deficit. Cardiovascular observations were unremarkable, and there were no symptoms to suggest an acute systemic illness. A medication and symptom review did not identify a clear precipitant, although stress and irregular sleep may contribute.

The patient works for DUNLOY Secondary School, where recurrent episodes are affecting attendance and concentration. A period of structured monitoring would be helpful in distinguishing episodic migraine from a developing chronic pattern and in identifying any medication-overuse component.

Request

Please assess the diagnosis and consider whether migraine prophylaxis is appropriate, taking account of attack frequency, functional impairment and current use of sumatriptan and naproxen. I would also welcome guidance on an individualised acute-treatment plan and indications for imaging or other investigation should the clinical pattern change.

I will arrange primary-care follow-up in about 3 weeks to review the headache diary and medication use. The referral is made from COLERAINE.

Yours sincerely,

davis rowley

Orthopaedic Outpatient Clinic Report
National Insurance number: BG 71 26 45 A

Patient: RAYN MONAGHAN
Contact: rayn.monaghan97@outlook.com
Report/accession ID: 0600309789

Reason for review

The patient, aged 54, was assessed regarding persistent mechanical knee pain, morning stiffness and reduced mobility consistent with osteoarthritis of the knee. Symptoms are predominantly activity-related, with discomfort on walking on uneven ground, rising from a chair and using stairs. There is no history of acute injury, locking, recurrent giving way or inflammatory morning stiffness lasting longer than approximately 30 minutes. No fevers or systemic symptoms were reported.

Current treatment

The patient is using paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily and topical ibuprofen applied to the affected knee as required. There have been no reported adverse effects from either treatment. The patient has not previously undertaken a structured physiotherapy programme and is not currently using a walking aid.

Examination

The patient mobilised independently, with a mildly antalgic gait. There was a small right knee effusion and medial joint-line tenderness. Flexion was limited by pain to approximately 110 degrees, with a small fixed flexion deformity. Crepitus was present through the range of movement. The knee was stable to varus and valgus stress, and there was no clinical evidence of an acute meniscal injury. The contralateral knee had less pronounced crepitus but preserved movement. Distal neurovascular examination was normal.

Interpretation

The clinical findings are in keeping with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, with a predominantly medial compartment pattern. There are no current features to suggest septic arthritis, inflammatory arthropathy or an acute ligamentous injury. Plain radiographs would be appropriate if not obtained previously, particularly to document the extent of joint-space narrowing and osteophyte formation; urgent imaging is not indicated in the absence of red-flag symptoms.

Plan

The importance of regular, graded exercise was discussed. I have recommended referral to physiotherapy for quadriceps and hip abductor strengthening, range-of-movement work and advice regarding pacing. Weight management should be addressed where relevant, as even modest reduction may improve pain and function. The patient may continue topical ibuprofen provided the skin remains intact and should continue paracetamol within the stated dose. Oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medication should not be commenced without review of renal, gastrointestinal and cardiovascular risks and any interacting medicines.

If symptoms remain limiting despite conservative management, an intra-articular corticosteroid injection could be considered for short-term relief. Knee replacement is not currently the first step, but referral for surgical opinion would be reasonable if pain and functional restriction become substantial despite an adequate non-operative programme.

A follow-up review has been arranged for 2036-01-18. Earlier assessment is advised via the GP or urgent care service if the knee becomes acutely hot, markedly swollen, persistently locked, or if weight-bearing becomes impossible.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
National Insurance number: ZZ 68 57 08 A

Patient: C. Hall
Gestation: 9+4 weeks' gestation
Discharging service: Early Pregnancy and Acute Gynaecology, ROYAL VICTORIA HOSPITAL
Report/accession ID: 0779293053

Reason for admission
Admitted with five days of persistent vomiting, inability to maintain oral fluids and reduced urine output. She reported a 3.5 kg weight loss since early pregnancy. There was no abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, fever or urinary symptoms.

Assessment and key results
On arrival she was clinically dehydrated, with dry mucous membranes and postural dizziness. Initial blood tests showed mild hypokalaemia (potassium 3.2 mmol/L), raised urea consistent with volume depletion and urinary ketones. Full blood count, liver profile, amylase and inflammatory markers were otherwise unremarkable. A urine culture showed no growth. Ultrasound confirmed a single live intrauterine pregnancy, appropriate for the stated gestation, with no evidence of ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage.

Hospital course
She received intravenous sodium chloride with potassium replacement and thiamine before any glucose-containing fluids. Antiemetic treatment with cyclizine was given intravenously initially, then changed to oral dosing once vomiting settled. Her nausea improved over the next 24 hours and she tolerated water, oral rehydration solution, toast and a light meal. Urine output normalised and repeat blood tests showed correction of the electrolyte abnormality.

The obstetric team reviewed her. There was no indication for surgical intervention or further inpatient investigation. Her relative, Kia-Louise BOULTON, was updated with the patient’s agreement and is based in SESKINORE.

Discharge medicines
• Cyclizine 50 mg orally up to three times daily when required for nausea.
• Continue prescribed antenatal vitamins once able to tolerate them.
• No further intravenous treatment is required following discharge.

Condition at discharge
Comfortable at rest, haemodynamically stable and mobilising independently. She is keeping down oral fluids and small meals, with no ongoing abdominal pain, bleeding or urinary symptoms.

Advice and follow-up
Take frequent small sips of fluid and eat little and often, choosing bland foods initially. Return to A&E or contact the early pregnancy service urgently if unable to keep fluids down for 12 hours, passing very little urine, feeling faint, developing severe abdominal pain, fever, vaginal bleeding or recurrent rapid weight loss.

The early pregnancy team will arrange outpatient review and repeat weight, urine and blood assessment. She should also contact her GP surgery if antiemetic treatment is insufficient or causes troublesome drowsiness. Discharge information was discussed with the patient before leaving hospital.

Outpatient dermatology review
NHS number: 000 775 1231

Patient: aqsa dale
MRN: 03092227
Seen at Crystal Peaks Medical Centre by N. Regan

Presenting problem
Persistent itchy rash affecting both wrists and the lower abdomen. Symptoms began after use of a new fragranced body wash and have continued despite stopping it. No facial swelling, wheeze, fever or mucosal involvement. Sleep mildly disturbed by itching. Reports occasional skin irritation beneath a watch strap.

Occupation: Warehouse operative

Examination
Well and comfortable. Symmetrical erythematous, slightly scaly plaques to the volar wrists and a smaller patch at the lower abdominal waistband. No weeping, crusting or cellulitis. Hands, face and oral mucosa clear. No lymphadenopathy.

Assessment
Appearance and distribution remain most consistent with allergic contact dermatitis, with likely contribution from fragrance and/or metal exposure. No evidence of secondary bacterial infection today.

Plan
Continue avoidance of the fragranced wash, scented moisturisers and the watch until symptoms have settled. Discussed checking labels for fragrance mix and nickel-containing fasteners. Apply hydrocortisone cream thinly to affected areas once or twice daily for up to 7 days, then stop; avoid use on broken skin or the face. Continue cetirizine if helpful for pruritus, according to the prescribed dose. Use a bland emollient frequently, including after washing, and keep nails short.

If the rash persists or recurs despite avoidance, consider referral for patch testing. Seek urgent help for rapidly spreading redness, facial or throat swelling, breathing difficulty, blistering or fever. Contact the GP surgery if there is increasing pain, discharge or crusting.

Review planned in about 10 weeks, sooner if required.

Discharge summary

Patient: NEVAEH-RAE DUFFY
Home address: 102 Dickie Drive, Boat of Garten, PH24 3AY
Reason for admission

Admitted under gynaecology with several days of worsening lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge and deep dyspareunia. She was haemodynamically stable on arrival but uncomfortable, with suprapubic and bilateral adnexal tenderness. There was no history of vomiting, urinary frequency or bowel disturbance. Pregnancy testing was negative.

Key findings and investigations

Initial observations remained within normal limits. Abdominal examination showed lower abdominal tenderness without guarding or rebound. Pelvic examination identified mucopurulent discharge and cervical motion tenderness. A vaginal and endocervical swab was taken before antibiotics; the report/accession identifier was 024700117. Urine dip was unremarkable. Blood tests showed a mild inflammatory response, with no significant anaemia or renal impairment. Pelvic ultrasound demonstrated a small volume of free fluid but no tubo-ovarian abscess or adnexal torsion.

The overall presentation was consistent with pelvic inflammatory disease. Gonorrhoea and chlamydia nucleic acid amplification testing was sent and was pending at discharge. She was advised that any positive result would require partner notification and treatment through the sexual health service.

Hospital course

Treatment was commenced with intravenous ceftriaxone, followed by oral doxycycline and metronidazole once oral intake was established. Analgesia was provided with regular paracetamol and intermittent ibuprofen, with good effect. There was no clinical deterioration, fever or evidence of sepsis. Pain improved steadily; at the point of discharge she reported a current pain score of 5/10 but was mobilising independently and managing food and fluids.

The case was reviewed with the on-call consultant, Minal Callaghan, GMC identifier 0088838. No operative intervention was required. The patient received counselling regarding abstinence from sexual intercourse until treatment was completed and symptoms had resolved. Condoms were recommended thereafter. She was also advised to avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole and for at least 48 hours after the final dose.

Discharge medicines

• Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily to complete a 14-day course.
• Metronidazole 400 mg orally twice daily to complete a 14-day course.
• Ceftriaxone course completed in hospital; no further dose required.
• Paracetamol as required for pain, according to the packet instructions.
• Ibuprofen as required if tolerated, avoiding it in the event of stomach ulcer symptoms, renal problems or asthma triggered by anti-inflammatory medicines.

Condition at discharge and follow-up

Discharged home clinically stable, afebrile and tolerating oral medication. She understands the diagnosis, treatment plan and safety-netting advice. A sexual health clinic appointment has been requested for review of swab results, partner notification and screening for other sexually transmitted infections. GP review is advised if symptoms have not substantially improved within 72 hours, or sooner if concerned.

She should attend A&E urgently for increasing or severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fever or rigors, fainting, heavy vaginal bleeding, rash or difficulty breathing. She should seek review if symptoms recur after completing treatment, as this may indicate treatment failure, reinfection or an alternative diagnosis.

Discharging clinician: Minal Callaghan

There has been nausea with reduced oral intake and loss of appetite, but no vomiting. No diarrhoea, constipation, dysuria or visible haematuria. The patient reports feeling feverish at home but has not recorded a temperature. No previous abdominal surgery is reported.

Medication history includes paracetamol taken at home, with only partial relief. No known drug allergies were disclosed. T. Bowen, an adult relative, accompanied the patient and assisted with the history. The patient consented to assessment and examination.

Examination

The patient appears uncomfortable but is alert and communicating appropriately. Temperature 37.8°C, pulse 96 bpm, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturations 98% on air. Abdomen is soft but tender in the right iliac fossa, with localised guarding and percussion tenderness. There is no generalised rigidity or palpable mass. Rovsing’s sign is equivocal. Bowel sounds are present. Chest is clear and heart sounds are normal. No calf swelling or other peripheral abnormality.

Investigations

Urine dipstick is negative for blood, nitrites and leukocytes. Blood tests show raised inflammatory markers and a mild neutrophil leucocytosis; haemoglobin, platelets, renal function and liver enzymes are satisfactory. Serum amylase is not raised. A pregnancy test was negative where clinically applicable. CT abdomen and pelvis demonstrates an enlarged inflamed appendix with surrounding inflammatory change, without perforation, abscess or bowel obstruction. The report was reviewed with the surgical team at The Royal Glamorgan Hospital.

Assessment and plan

The clinical picture and imaging are consistent with acute uncomplicated appendicitis. There is no current evidence of perforation, sepsis or another acute abdominal process. The patient was kept nil by mouth and cannulated. Intravenous fluids were commenced, analgesia given, and intravenous co-amoxiclav administered in accordance with the local antimicrobial guideline. Paracetamol may be continued as required, provided the recommended daily maximum is not exceeded.

The on-call general surgical team has accepted the patient for admission and operative management, subject to their final review. The patient and T. Bowen were advised about the diagnosis, likely laparoscopic appendicectomy, possible conversion to open surgery, and the risks of bleeding, infection and injury to adjacent structures. They understood the need to remain nil by mouth and to report any worsening pain, vomiting or dizziness. Transfer to the surgical ward is arranged with observations and repeat clinical review pending surgery.

Date: 18 Sep 2021
NHS number: 0009325400

Dear Colleague,

Re: Tzirel  
Home address: 171 BALLYMOTE ROAD, BERAGH  
Report/accession ID: L23Q20069

Thank you for reviewing this patient, whom I am referring for specialist assessment of persistent essential hypertension despite treatment with two antihypertensive agents. The specific question is whether her current blood pressure pattern and associated symptoms warrant alteration of therapy, ambulatory monitoring, or investigation for a secondary cause.

She reports intermittent frontal headache and episodes of light-headedness over the past several weeks. The light-headedness is most noticeable when standing after sitting for a prolonged period, although she has not experienced syncope, falls, chest pain, palpitations or focal neurological symptoms. There is no reported visual loss, dysarthria or unilateral weakness. She does not describe symptoms suggestive of acute hypertensive emergency.

Medication reconciliation confirmed that she is taking amlodipine 5 mg once daily and ramipril 10 mg once daily. She reports good adherence and has not recently used non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, decongestants or oral corticosteroids. She does not smoke. Alcohol intake is modest. Dietary review identified a tendency towards processed foods, and we have discussed reducing salt intake, maintaining regular activity and recording home blood pressure readings.

At review, she was comfortable at rest. Blood pressure was 168/96 mmHg in the right arm after five minutes seated, with a pulse of 78 beats per minute and regular rhythm. On repeat measurement after standing for two minutes, blood pressure was 158/90 mmHg, without a significant postural fall, although she described mild light-headedness. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. There was no peripheral oedema, radio-radial delay or clinically evident heart failure. Neurological examination was normal.

Recent blood tests showed normal full blood count, sodium, potassium and liver enzymes. Creatinine was 82 micromol/L with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 78 mL/min/1.73 m². Urinalysis was negative for blood and protein. A twelve-lead ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm without left ventricular strain or acute ischaemic change. Home readings supplied over seven days have generally remained above target, although the timing of measurements has not been entirely consistent.

I would be grateful for your assessment of the apparent suboptimal control and advice on further management, including whether ambulatory blood pressure monitoring would help distinguish sustained hypertension from variability related to symptoms. Please also advise whether echocardiography, renal imaging or endocrine investigations are indicated. I will continue current medication pending your review and have advised her to seek urgent assessment through A&E if severe headache, chest pain, breathlessness, neurological deficit or collapse develops.

Yours sincerely,

Ayeshia Molloy
GP and referring clinician

LABORATORY MEDICINE REPORT

Patient: RILEY-THOMAS NICHOLSON
Report/accession ID: 04094943
Requesting service: Keswick Hospital
Specimen: Serum, venous blood
Clinical details: Acute joint pain with swelling and erythema, clinically consistent with a gout flare. Current treatment reported as naproxen and colchicine.

Specimen context

The sample was received as serum for assessment of renal function and urate status during an acute inflammatory episode. The specimen was suitable for analysis, with no significant haemolysis or lipaemia identified. Results should be interpreted alongside the examination findings and medication history. A serum urate concentration obtained during an acute attack may be lower than the patient’s usual baseline and does not exclude gout.

Results

Analyte                         Result             Reference interval / interpretation

Urate                           510 µmol/L         Raised; target for established gout generally <360 µmol/L
Creatinine                      118 µmol/L         60–110 µmol/L
Estimated GFR (CKD-EPI)         58 mL/min/1.73 m²  Reduced; interpret in clinical context
Urea                            8.9 mmol/L         2.5–7.8 mmol/L
Sodium                          139 mmol/L         133–146 mmol/L
Potassium                       4.6 mmol/L         3.5–5.3 mmol/L
C-reactive protein              74 mg/L            <5 mg/L
Alanine aminotransferase        28 U/L             0–40 U/L
Full blood count: haemoglobin   141 g/L            130–180 g/L
Full blood count: white cells   11.8 × 10⁹/L       4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets                       326 × 10⁹/L        150–400 × 10⁹/L

Interpretation

The markedly raised serum urate, together with an inflammatory response, supports the reported diagnosis of an acute gout flare. The modest renal impairment is clinically relevant: both naproxen and colchicine require careful review in the context of renal function, particularly if symptoms persist or treatment is prolonged. These results do not distinguish gout from septic arthritis. If the joint is unusually painful, there is systemic upset, fever, rapid clinical deterioration or diagnostic uncertainty, urgent assessment is indicated and joint aspiration for microscopy, crystal analysis and culture should be considered.

Following resolution of the acute episode, repeat urate measurement may be useful to establish the baseline concentration. Long-term urate-lowering treatment should be considered according to the overall clinical history, number of attacks, renal function and presence of tophi or radiographic disease. The laboratory result alone should not be used to commence or adjust treatment without clinical review.

A repeat biochemical assessment and medication review are recommended at the planned follow-up appointment on 2022-09-16. Please correlate with hydration status and any intercurrent illness when reviewing the creatinine and eGFR.

Validated and authorised by:
G. Alam
Laboratory medicine clinician
Report issued for Keswick Hospital

Patient remains on the ward for management of a diabetic foot ulcer affecting the plantar surface of the right forefoot. At 08:15 the patient was awake, orientated and able to describe the current plan. They report intermittent throbbing discomfort around the wound, rated 4/10 before dressing care, with no new numbness; baseline reduced sensation remains present in both feet. No chest pain, shortness of breath, fever or rigors reported. Appetite is fair and the patient took approximately three-quarters of breakfast with good oral fluids. Capillary blood glucose was elevated before breakfast and was recorded and handed over to the medical team for review.

Observations are stable. Temperature is within normal range, pulse regular and blood pressure satisfactory for the patient. The plantar ulcer has a moist wound bed with a small amount of yellow local discharge and mild surrounding erythema. No spreading cellulitis, malodour, crepitus or visible tendon is noted. Distal foot is warm with palpable pulses. The patient tolerated cleansing and redressing, although discomfort increased briefly during removal of the old dressing and settled after the procedure. Wound care was completed using the prescribed technique, with a non-adherent dressing applied and the foot protected from pressure.

Co-amoxiclav administered as prescribed; no adverse reaction observed. The patient was reminded to complete the antibiotic course and to report rash, diarrhoea, increasing pain or feeling shivery. Pressure-relieving footwear remains in use, and the patient was assisted to transfer to the chair with supervision. Mobilises short distances using a frame but remains unsteady when turning. Falls precautions are in place, including call bell within reach, clear floor area and advice to seek assistance before standing. The affected foot is to remain elevated when resting, with weight-bearing limited in accordance with the current podiatry plan.

Assessment: diabetic plantar ulcer with reduced protective sensation and small-volume local discharge. At present there is no evidence of systemic infection or rapidly progressing tissue damage. Ongoing risks are deterioration of the wound, hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia, pressure injury and falls.

Plan for the next shift is to repeat observations and blood glucose monitoring as prescribed, assess pain and wound appearance, maintain pressure off-loading, encourage suitable oral intake and document stool and urine output. Escalate promptly to the nurse in charge and medical team if temperature rises, erythema extends, discharge increases, the foot becomes cold or pale, pain becomes disproportionate, or glucose remains persistently outside the prescribed range. Continue antibiotic administration and wound care as charted. The responsible doctor’s professional identifier is 0697542.

Re: Corley F. – referral for suspected Hodgkin lymphoma

Dear Haematology Team,

I am referring Corley F. for urgent assessment of persistent, painless lymphadenopathy with associated night sweats and unintentional weight loss. The clinical question is whether these findings represent Hodgkin lymphoma or another lymphoproliferative disorder, and whether tissue diagnosis and staging can now be arranged.

The patient first noticed a lump above the left collarbone approximately six weeks ago. It has gradually increased in size and remains non-tender. There are now smaller palpable nodes in the left axilla. They report drenching night sweats on most nights and an unintentional loss of approximately 6 kg over the same period, despite no deliberate change in diet. There is no reported fever, pruritus, recurrent infection, or recent vaccination. They have not described difficulty swallowing, chest pain or breathlessness.

Collateral history from shahroz sajid suggests reduced energy and appetite, but the patient remains independent with personal care. Occupation: Office manager. They have informed Drumligair Community Centre that they may need time away from work for investigations.

On examination today, there is a firm, mobile, non-tender left supraclavicular node measuring approximately 3 cm, with palpable left axillary nodes. No cervical skin changes are present. The chest is clear, heart sounds are normal and the abdomen is soft; I cannot clearly palpate the spleen. There is no peripheral oedema or focal neurological deficit. Observations are stable, including temperature 36.8°C and oxygen saturation 98% on air.

Initial blood tests show haemoglobin 118 g/L, white cell count 9.8 × 10⁹/L, platelets 462 × 10⁹/L, ESR 68 mm/hour and LDH 312 U/L. Renal and liver profiles are satisfactory. An urgent chest radiograph has not demonstrated focal consolidation, although cross-sectional imaging is still required. The working diagnosis is Hodgkin lymphoma, and I have explained that this cannot be confirmed without a biopsy.

The patient is currently receiving supportive care pending tissue diagnosis. This consists of regular fluids, nutritional encouragement and paracetamol as required; no anti-cancer treatment has been started. Please could you arrange urgent specialist review, PET-CT or suitable staging imaging, and image-guided core biopsy or excision of the most accessible node. I would also appreciate advice regarding interim monitoring and management of night sweats or further weight loss.

Yours sincerely,

Dr Pippa-Mae Hogg, MBBS

LABORATORY REPORT
National Insurance number: NK 72 54 22 A

Patient: MARLIE-MAE WHEATLEY
Age: 39 y/o
Collection/report date: 2035-12-15
Report/accession ID: 0913788222

Specimen context
Blood sample received for investigation of an acutely painful, swollen and erythematous first metatarsophalangeal joint. Clinical details state that symptoms have been present for 3 days. The patient is currently taking naproxen and colchicine. No information was supplied regarding recent trauma, fever or renal replacement therapy.

Results

Serum urate: 0.51 mmol/L
Reference interval: 0.18–0.48 mmol/L
Interpretation: Mildly increased.

C-reactive protein: 86 mg/L
Reference interval: <5 mg/L
Interpretation: Increased.

White cell count: 12.8 × 10^9/L
Reference interval: 4.0–11.0 × 10^9/L
Interpretation: Mild leucocytosis.

Neutrophils: 10.4 × 10^9/L
Reference interval: 2.0–7.5 × 10^9/L
Interpretation: Neutrophilia.

Creatinine: 118 µmol/L
Reference interval: 60–110 µmol/L
Interpretation: Slightly increased; calculate eGFR using the patient’s age and sex, and interpret alongside previous renal results.

Estimated GFR: 61 mL/min/1.73 m²
Interpretation: Reduced. A single result does not establish chronic kidney disease.

ALT: 29 U/L
Reference interval: 0–40 U/L
Interpretation: Within reference interval.

Laboratory comment
The raised serum urate, inflammatory markers and neutrophilia support an acute inflammatory arthritis, and the overall pattern is compatible with a gout flare in the stated clinical context. Serum urate may be normal during an acute attack; conversely, an increased result does not by itself confirm monosodium urate crystal disease. If diagnostic uncertainty remains, aspiration of the affected joint for crystal analysis and culture should be considered, particularly if there is fever, systemic illness or concern regarding septic arthritis.

The creatinine result is mildly above the stated reference interval. Naproxen may adversely affect renal function, especially during intercurrent illness or dehydration, and colchicine dosing requires consideration of renal function and interacting medicines. Please correlate with previous biochemistry, hydration status and the prescribed treatment plan. Repeat renal profile after the acute episode or sooner if clinically indicated.

Clinical authorisation
Result reviewed and electronically validated by ABINASH WARDLE, laboratory clinician.

This report should be interpreted with the examination findings and any joint aspirate results; it does not replace urgent clinical assessment where septic arthritis is suspected.

Discharge summary – Cardiology

Patient: diarmuid donnelly
Principal diagnosis: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI)

Reason for admission
Presented to the emergency department with central chest pressure, diaphoresis and nausea for 3 days. Initial ECG showed no ST-segment elevation. High-sensitivity troponin was elevated with a dynamic rise and fall, consistent with NSTEMI.

Inpatient course
Managed on the cardiology ward with telemetry, aspirin, fondaparinux and high-intensity atorvastatin. There was no recurrent chest pain or haemodynamic instability. Echocardiography demonstrated mildly impaired left ventricular systolic function with regional wall-motion abnormality. Renal function remained stable and there were no bleeding complications.

Following discussion with the patient and the cardiology team, a conservative strategy was agreed. Coronary angiography was not undertaken during this admission because symptoms settled, the patient remained clinically stable and the anticipated benefit was felt to be limited. The case was reviewed by Aberdeen Royal Infirmary cardiology services.

Discharge medicines
• Aspirin 75 mg once daily, lifelong.
• Clopidogrel 75 mg once daily for 12 months, unless stopped earlier by cardiology because of bleeding or another clinical indication.
• Atorvastatin 80 mg at night.
• Bisoprolol 1.25 mg once daily, if tolerated.
• Glyceryl trinitrate spray as needed for chest pain; use as directed on the accompanying instructions.

The patient has been counselled that aspirin and clopidogrel should not be stopped without speaking to the cardiology or GP team. Avoid non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs unless specifically advised.

Condition at discharge
Mobilising independently and pain-free, with stable observations. Discharge home with relative E. O'Sullivan, who is based in Parton, and with written medicines and safety-netting advice.

Follow-up and advice
Cardiology review is requested for 16th January 1997, with consideration of outpatient coronary assessment and optimisation of secondary prevention. Presenting complaint
Productive cough with fever and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Symptoms began several days ago and have worsened despite paracetamol. Sputum is yellow-green. No haemoptysis, unilateral leg swelling or recent travel. Denies vomiting and has been drinking adequately.

Past history and medicines
No significant respiratory history reported. Regular medicines: paracetamol as needed. No known drug allergies.

Alert and speaking in full sentences. Temperature 38.4°C, pulse 104 bpm, BP 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, oxygen saturations 95% on air. Mucous membranes moist. No calf tenderness or oedema. Clinical and radiographic findings are consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, SNOMED CT 233604007. No features currently suggesting sepsis or respiratory failure. Given oral amoxicillin in the department and advised to complete the prescribed course. Continue paracetamol for fever and pleuritic pain, maintain oral fluids and rest. Safety-netting provided regarding increasing breathlessness, confusion, persistent vomiting, blue lips, inability to maintain fluids or worsening chest pain.

Disposition
Suitable for discharge with GP follow-up if not clearly improving within the expected short interval, and earlier review if symptoms deteriorate. Written pneumonia advice supplied. Patient understands the treatment plan and return precautions.

Referral to Community Mental Health Team

Patient: Rozina P.
Referring organisation: Belfast City Hospital
Referring clinician: Leana Beck, GMC-TEST-0340295
Service locality: FINTONA

Dear Mental Health Assessment Team,

I would be grateful for an urgent assessment of Rozina P. for a major depressive episode. The specific questions are whether specialist psychological or psychiatric treatment is indicated, whether the current antidepressant should be adjusted, and how best to manage the patient’s recent deterioration and suicide risk.

Over recent weeks, the patient has described persistent low mood, loss of interest and pleasure in usual activities, marked reduction in motivation, poor concentration and early-morning waking. Appetite is reduced but fluids are maintained. There are no reported symptoms suggestive of mania, psychosis or a substance-related cause. The patient remains able to attend to basic personal care, although routine tasks are taking considerably longer than usual.

Current medication is sertraline 50 mg once daily, taken consistently for several weeks. There has been limited improvement so far and no troublesome adverse effect has been reported. We have discussed adherence, avoiding abrupt discontinuation and allowing time for treatment response. The patient is not taking other regular prescribed medication.

Suicide risk was explored directly today. The patient reports recurrent thoughts that life is not worth living and has considered taking an overdose, but denies current intent, has made no specific preparations and has not selected a date or quantity. There is no history of a recent attempt or self-injury disclosed today. The patient has access to prescribed medication at home; this was discussed as a potential means of harm. Protective factors include a supportive relative, willingness to accept help, future plans and a clear wish not to cause distress to family. The patient agreed to tell the relative and contact the surgery or emergency services if intent develops, thoughts become harder to control, or medication is gathered for this purpose.

An immediate safety plan has been agreed: medication will be kept by the relative and supplied in small quantities where practical; the patient will not remain alone if risk escalates; and urgent help will be sought through NHS 111, the local crisis service or A&E. If there is imminent danger, the patient understands that 999 should be called. The patient has consented to this referral and to appropriate information-sharing with the relative.

Please arrange an urgent clinical assessment and advise on medication and psychological treatment. I would also welcome guidance on ongoing risk monitoring and whether a formal crisis plan is required.

Yours faithfully,

Leana Beck

URINE MICROBIOLOGY REPORT

Patient: R. Jama
Report/accession ID: 06333779
Requesting service: Longmoor Lane Medical Centre
Specimen: Midstream urine
Clinical details: Flank pain, dysuria and rigors. Acute pyelonephritis suspected. Current treatment includes cefuroxime and paracetamol.

Specimen quality and data check
The container was received adequately labelled and suitable for processing. An initial electronic entry recorded the specimen date as 31/04/2025; this is not a valid calendar date and was rejected during data-quality checking. The report has been released against the verified laboratory receipt record.

Results
Urine microscopy:
Leucocytes: >100 × 10^6/L
Erythrocytes: 18 × 10^6/L
Squamous epithelial cells: few
Bacteria: numerous

Culture:
Escherichia coli: >10^7 colony-forming units/L
Mixed growth: not detected

Antimicrobial susceptibility:
Cefuroxime: susceptible
Co-amoxiclav: susceptible
Trimethoprim: resistant
Ciprofloxacin: susceptible
Nitrofurantoin: susceptible, but unsuitable for treatment of suspected upper urinary tract infection
Gentamicin: susceptible

Interpretive comment
Significant growth of E. coli with marked pyuria supports a urinary tract infection and is consistent with the supplied clinical diagnosis of acute pyelonephritis. The isolate is susceptible to cefuroxime; treatment should be reviewed against the patient’s clinical response, renal function, allergy history and local antimicrobial guidance. Nitrofurantoin should not be selected for pyelonephritis because renal tissue penetration is inadequate. If fever, rigors or flank pain persist despite treatment, assess urgently for obstruction, sepsis or an alternative source of infection.

Clinical action
Please correlate with observations and blood results, including renal function and inflammatory markers. Escalate to the emergency department if the patient becomes hypotensive, confused, unable to retain oral medicines or clinically deteriorates. A follow-up review is booked for 18 February 2018.

Dr Liviya JENNINGS, MBBS

Nursing progress note
NHS number: 000 153 0403

Patient: J. Adamson
Ward: Cardiology
Treating organisation: ABERDEEN ROYAL INFIRMARY

J. Adamson was reviewed during the morning shift following admission with decompensated heart failure. The patient remained short of breath when lying flat and reported sleeping propped upright with three pillows. Bilateral ankle swelling was still present, although the patient felt this was slightly improved compared with yesterday. Exercise tolerance remained poor; the patient became breathless walking from the bed to the bathroom and required a seated rest before returning.

At 08:00, the patient was alert and able to engage appropriately in conversation. Respiratory rate was 24 per minute, oxygen saturations 94% on air, pulse 86 beats per minute and blood pressure 120/80 mmHg. Temperature was 36.7°C. There were bibasal fine crackles on auscultation, with no wheeze. Both ankles had pitting oedema to the lower shins. The abdomen was soft and non-tender. No chest pain, dizziness or new confusion was reported.

The patient was supported into an upright chair and encouraged to pace activity. Furosemide was administered as prescribed, with an explanation given regarding the need to pass urine regularly and to call for assistance when mobilising. Bisoprolol was also given after the morning observations were reviewed. A fluid balance chart was commenced and reinforced; urine output was moderate during the first part of the shift. The patient drank tea and water with breakfast, taking approximately 60% of the meal. Intake was recorded and the patient was reminded to follow the prescribed fluid restriction.

Following treatment and rest in the chair, breathing appeared less laboured and the patient was able to speak in full sentences. Oxygen was not required. The patient mobilised to the bathroom with one staff member and a walking frame. Gait was steady but slow. There was no fall or near miss.

Assessment: Ongoing fluid overload with orthopnoea, bibasal crackles and peripheral oedema, with modest symptomatic improvement after diuretic therapy. The patient remains at risk of falls because of exertional breathlessness and at risk of worsening congestion. Continue close observation for increasing respiratory effort, falling oxygen saturations, chest pain, reduced urine output or acute confusion.

Plan for the next shift: repeat observations at least four-hourly and sooner if symptomatic; continue strict fluid balance, daily weight and prescribed fluid restriction; administer further medicines as charted; encourage upright positioning and supervised mobilisation; inspect skin around the swollen ankles and elevate the legs when resting. Escalate promptly to the nurse in charge and medical team if respiratory status deteriorates or urine output falls significantly. The patient’s relative, Ada-Lily Baines, is listed as the family contact. The patient’s home address is 116 Raith Road, Inverness / Inbhir Nis, IV99 1AA and preferred email contact is jedidah.adamson71@sky.com; these details were confirmed for discharge planning.

Outpatient Musculoskeletal Review
National Insurance number: ZZ 60 54 69 C

Patient: S. Raja
Report/accession ID: L29T03034
Seen at: Llandrindod Wells Hospital
Clinician: CALLA WILSON

Reason for review
Persistent left knee pain with morning stiffness and reduced walking tolerance. Symptoms are worse on stairs and after sitting for prolonged periods. No recent fall, locking episode or giving way. No fevers, night sweats or other hot, swollen joints.

Background
Occupation: software developer

Using paracetamol when required, with topical ibuprofen applied to the knee. Reports partial benefit and no adverse effects. No current oral anti-inflammatory medication. Sleep is occasionally disturbed by turning in bed, but pain is not consistently waking the patient.

Examination
Mobilising independently, mildly antalgic on the left. Small bony enlargement of the left knee with mild medial joint-line tenderness. Range of movement reduced at terminal flexion; discomfort on weight-bearing flexion. No appreciable effusion, erythema or increased warmth. Ligament testing stable. Calf soft and non-tender. Hip movement does not reproduce the knee pain. Distal sensation and circulation intact.

Investigations
Plain-film report reviewed under accession ID L29T03034. Findings are in keeping with degenerative change of the knee, with medial compartment joint-space narrowing and marginal osteophyte formation. No acute fracture or destructive lesion reported.

Assessment
Clinical and radiographic features consistent with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis. No evidence today of an acute inflammatory or septic process.

Plan
• Continue regular paracetamol within the labelled maximum dose, rather than waiting until pain is severe.
• Continue topical ibuprofen if helpful; avoid applying to broken skin and stop if local irritation develops.
• Discussed pacing, avoiding prolonged inactivity, supportive footwear and use of a stick in the opposite hand if required.
• Provided advice on low-impact exercise, including cycling, swimming and strengthening of the quadriceps. Physiotherapy referral offered for an individual exercise programme.
• Discussed weight management sensitively where relevant and the potential risks of oral NSAIDs; not commenced today.
• Seek urgent assessment via NHS 111 or A&E if the knee becomes acutely hot and swollen, if unable to bear weight, or if fever develops.

Follow-up
Review in about 4 weeks to assess pain control, mobility and response to exercise-based management. Consider injection or further musculoskeletal referral if function remains significantly limited despite conservative measures.

Signed: CALLA WILSON

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
NHS number: 0000744205

Patient: Kielan H.
MRN: 08248825
Responsible consultant: Dr Barlas Paul, MBBS, GMC identifier 0672990
Healthcare organisation: Ulster Hospital

Reason for admission
Presented via A&E with approximately 24 hours of worsening abdominal pain, initially periumbilical and subsequently localised to the right lower quadrant. This was associated with nausea and loss of appetite. No urinary symptoms or diarrhoea were reported.

Assessment and investigations
On arrival, the patient was haemodynamically stable. Blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg, with mild tachycardia and a low-grade temperature. Abdominal examination demonstrated focal right lower-quadrant tenderness with guarding but no generalised peritonism.

Initial blood tests showed a raised white cell count and C-reactive protein. Renal function and liver tests were satisfactory. Urinalysis did not suggest urinary infection. CT abdomen and pelvis demonstrated an enlarged, inflamed appendix with surrounding inflammatory change, in keeping with acute uncomplicated appendicitis. No collection or perforation was identified.

Hospital course
The patient was admitted under the general surgical team, kept nil by mouth initially and given intravenous fluids, analgesia and antiemetic treatment. Intravenous co-amoxiclav was commenced. Following discussion of operative and non-operative options, laparoscopic appendicectomy was performed. The appendix was inflamed but not perforated; there was no drain requirement and no operative complication. Histology was sent for routine examination.

Recovery was uncomplicated. Oral fluids and diet were reintroduced gradually and tolerated. Mobilisation was independent, and pain was controlled with oral paracetamol. There was no postoperative vomiting, fever or wound concern.

Discharge condition
Fit for discharge home. Port-site wounds are clean, dry and intact with dressings in place. Observations are stable and the abdomen is soft, with only expected mild postoperative tenderness.

Discharge medicines
• Paracetamol as required for pain, within the dosing instructions on the supplied label.
• No further antibiotic course is required unless advised following review of the operative or histology findings.

Advice and follow-up
Keep the wounds clean and dry and follow the dressing instructions provided. Avoid heavy lifting and strenuous activity until comfortable and reviewed according to local surgical guidance. Seek urgent medical advice via NHS 111 or A&E if increasing abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fever, spreading redness, wound discharge, abdominal swelling or inability to eat and drink develops.

The surgical team will review the histology result and arrange follow-up if clinically indicated. A discharge information sheet has been provided, and the GP should be informed through the electronic discharge communication.

Dear Hypertension Service,

Re: Meeya F., MRN 072234783

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient with essential hypertension, as blood pressure control has remained inconsistent despite treatment with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor and a calcium-channel blocker. The specific question is whether the current pattern represents resistant hypertension or an alternative cause of variable readings, and whether you would recommend changes to the medication regimen or further investigation.

The patient reports intermittent pressure-type headaches and episodes of light-headedness, particularly when standing quickly. There has been no collapse, chest pain, palpitations, breathlessness, focal neurological disturbance or visual loss. Home readings have generally been above target, although there is considerable variation between measurements. Recent surgery readings have also been elevated, with a clinic blood pressure of 168/94 mmHg and a pulse of 78 beats per minute. The patient has been asked to keep a twice-daily log, including seated and standing readings, and to bring the monitor to the next review so that its accuracy can be checked.

Current treatment is amlodipine 5 mg once daily and ramipril 10 mg once daily. The patient reports taking both medicines consistently and has not described ankle swelling, troublesome cough or other significant adverse effects. We have discussed limiting dietary salt, avoiding excessive alcohol, maintaining regular physical activity and taking readings after five minutes of quiet rest. There is no reported use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medication or decongestants.

Examination today was otherwise reassuring. Heart sounds were normal, the chest was clear and there was no peripheral oedema. Renal function and electrolytes remain suitable for continuation of ramipril, with no significant proteinuria on the most recent urine testing. Thyroid function and glucose were within the reference range. The headaches have not been accompanied by symptoms suggestive of hypertensive emergency, but I have advised attendance at A&E if severe sudden headache, neurological symptoms, chest pain or acute visual change develops.

Assessment

Essential hypertension with suboptimal and fluctuating control, associated with headache and light-headedness. Adherence appears reasonable, but confirmation with structured home or ambulatory monitoring would be helpful before further escalation.

Requested action

Please review the blood pressure diary and consider 24-hour ambulatory monitoring, assessment for secondary causes where clinically indicated, and advice on the next pharmacological step. I would also appreciate guidance on managing the postural light-headedness while achieving better daytime control.

A follow-up appointment has been arranged for 21 February 2024, when the home readings and repeat renal profile will be reviewed.

Yours faithfully,

SHER KENT
GP
QUEEN ELIZABETH UNIVERSITY HOSPITAL

Patient: N. Daniel

Source: Emergency department
Clinical details: Known type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin and atorvastatin. Presented with increased thirst, fatigue and frequent urination. History provided by the patient, with collateral information from a friend.

Presenting complaint
NHS number: 000 105 1645
Zylan attended A&E with dysuria, urinary frequency and central lower abdominal discomfort for 3 days. Reports passing small volumes of urine frequently, with burning at the end of micturition. No visible haematuria, loin pain, rigors, vomiting or vaginal symptoms. Eating and drinking adequately. No previous resistant urinary infection reported.

Patient details
Age: 68 y/o
Address: 129 Aragon Street, Cardiff / Caerdydd, CF10 1AA
Friend present with patient’s consent.

Assessment
Alert, comfortable at rest and clinically euvolaemic. Temperature 37.2°C, pulse 86 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturations 99% on air. Abdomen soft with mild suprapubic tenderness only. No guarding or rebound. No renal angle tenderness. Chest clear and cardiovascular examination normal.

Investigations
Urine dip: leucocytes 2+, nitrites positive, blood 1+, protein trace. Urine sample sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivities. Pregnancy test negative. No blood tests indicated at this stage given stable observations and absence of systemic features.

Impression and plan
Findings are consistent with uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection. No evidence currently of pyelonephritis, sepsis or obstructive pathology. Started nitrofurantoin, with advice to take with food and complete the prescribed course. Encourage oral fluids and regular voiding; simple analgesia if required. Safety-netted to return urgently for fever, flank pain, vomiting, worsening abdominal pain, confusion or inability to pass urine.

Discharge
Discharged home in stable condition. GP/surgery review advised if symptoms have not begun to improve within 48 hours, or sooner if deterioration. Urine culture result to be reviewed and antibiotic changed only if clinically required. Follow-up appointment: 24 March 2036.

Documented by kiara-leigh slater, emergency clinician.

Please assess persistent hypertension with intermittent headache and light-headedness, and advise on further investigation and optimisation of treatment.

Blood pressure was found to be repeatedly elevated during recent attendances to the accident and emergency department, although there was no evidence of acute end-organ injury. The patient reports several weeks of frontal headache and brief episodes of light-headedness, without syncope, focal neurological symptoms, chest pain, palpitations or visual loss. Amlodipine 10 mg once daily and ramipril 10 mg once daily. No recent medication changes. The patient does not report regular NSAID use and drinks alcohol within recommended limits.

Clinic BP today was 168/96 mmHg, repeated at 164/94 mmHg after rest. Pulse regular at 78 bpm. Neurological examination was normal, with no papilloedema clinically. There was no peripheral oedema. I would be grateful for specialist review to confirm resistant or uncontrolled essential hypertension, consider ambulatory blood pressure monitoring and assess for secondary causes if indicated. Please advise whether a third agent, such as indapamide, would be appropriate and provide a blood-pressure target. Safety-netting has been given regarding severe headache, neurological deficit, chest pain or collapse.

PAEDIATRIC LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: D. Stafford
Clinical context: 14-year-old Middle Eastern male patient assessed for several weeks of tiredness, intermittent dizziness and reduced exercise tolerance. Parent reports heavier menstrual bleeding and inconsistent tolerance of prescribed ferrous fumarate. Patient assented to blood sampling; parent present for the history.

Report/accession ID: 07542613
Collection/report date: 1 May 1988
Specimen: EDTA whole blood and serum

Full blood count
Haemoglobin: 92 g/L (115–155)
Red cell count: 3.86 ×10¹²/L (3.80–5.20)
Mean cell volume: 69 fL (78–98)
Mean cell haemoglobin: 23.8 pg (26–34)
White cell count: 6.7 ×10⁹/L (4.0–12.0)
Platelets: 468 ×10⁹/L (150–450)
Red cell distribution width: 18.9% (11.5–14.5)

Iron studies
Ferritin: 5 µg/L (15–150)
Serum iron: 4.1 µmol/L (5–25)
Transferrin: 3.9 g/L (2.0–3.6)
Transferrin saturation: 4% (15–45)
C-reactive protein: 2 mg/L (<5)

Test code: LOINC 718-7 — haemoglobin

Interpretation: Moderate microcytic, hypochromic anaemia with markedly depleted iron stores and a mild reactive thrombocytosis. Normal C-reactive protein does not suggest an inflammatory explanation. Findings are consistent with iron-deficiency anaemia.

Clinical comment: Please review adherence, gastrointestinal tolerance and the prescribed ferrous fumarate regimen with the family. Assess menstrual blood loss and dietary iron intake; consider coeliac screening if response is inadequate or the history warrants it. Repeat full blood count and ferritin after an appropriate treatment interval, with earlier clinical review if dizziness worsens, syncope develops or exercise tolerance declines.

Validated by: mohammed-ali bedford
Paediatric Laboratory Medicine

Nursing handover – Neonatal unit

Situation: Baby Nkemdilim remains under phototherapy for neonatal jaundice. The patient, aged 3 days, was reviewed in cot-side assessment; skin still visibly jaundiced, more settled between feeds.

Background: born at 39+2 weeks' gestation. Mother, eibhlinn mcgowan, present and participating in feeds. Sleepy at breast with reduced intake overnight; expressing support offered.

Encouraged three-hourly feeds and expressed breast milk top-ups by cup; took small but improved volume on last feed. Feeding support provided and tolerated.
