Patient: SANCHIA BYRNE
Contact: 07700 900090
Review type: General medicine genetics risk assessment

90-year-old Middle Eastern female patient seen regarding substantial family history of breast and ovarian cancer and concern about personal future risk. The patient requests predictive genetic testing. No current breast, ovarian or other cancer symptoms reported. No current treatment or regular medication.

Family history reviewed in detail. An adult child of the patient has recently raised concerns about a familial pathogenic variant, and records available for discussion include BRCA1 c.68_69delAG. The precise relationship of the affected relatives, ages at diagnosis and confirmation of the familial result require verification before any predictive test is arranged. Patient is understandably anxious but demonstrates good understanding of the difference between a familial result and an individual's own test result.

No abnormal examination findings identified today; patient declined breast examination as there are no symptoms and the consultation was focused on risk assessment. No palpable mass, nipple change or unexplained bleeding reported. We discussed that testing should ideally begin with an affected relative where possible, and that a negative result is only informative if the familial variant is confirmed.

Plan:
• Obtain copies of relevant pathology/genetic reports and construct a three-generation pedigree.
• Refer to the regional clinical genetics service for counselling and consideration of predictive testing.
• Advised to seek GP review promptly for any new breast lump, nipple change, persistent abdominal symptoms or abnormal vaginal bleeding.
• Patient consented to correspondence by telephone and understands that results may have implications for relatives.

Report/accession ID: 20/606686

Follow-up appointment booked for 16/05/2004 to review documentation and referral progress.

Discharge summary

Patient: aadhi mcmanus
Admission date: 06/02/2012
Discharging service: Respiratory Medicine

aadhi mcmanus was admitted with a painful, progressively spreading area of redness affecting the lower leg. The patient, aged 53 years, described increasing tenderness and local warmth, without preceding trauma or an obvious break in the skin. There was no breathlessness, chest pain or systemic infective symptom reported. Arthur-John Hogg, the patient’s adult child from Moy, was involved in discussions regarding the admission and discharge plan.

On assessment, the affected lower leg had well-demarcated erythema, increased skin temperature and tenderness to palpation. There was no fluctuance, crepitus or clinical evidence of compartment syndrome. Distal perfusion and sensation remained intact. Blood tests showed a modest inflammatory response, with preserved renal function. Blood cultures were not suggestive of bacteraemia, and there was no indication for surgical drainage or further imaging during this admission.

The patient was treated with intravenous flucloxacillin initially, with clear clinical improvement in the extent of erythema and discomfort. Treatment was changed to oral flucloxacillin once clinically stable and tolerated. Paracetamol was used for analgesia, with good effect. The leg was elevated when resting, and mobility was encouraged as tolerated. Nursing observations remained stable throughout the stay.

Assessment at discharge

Uncomplicated cellulitis of the lower leg, improving with antibiotic treatment. The patient is eating and drinking, mobilising safely and has no fever or new systemic symptoms. The erythematous area was marked before discharge, and the patient and relative were advised to seek urgent review if redness extends beyond the mark, pain worsens, fever develops, or the leg becomes increasingly swollen.

Plan

Complete the prescribed course of oral flucloxacillin and continue paracetamol as required, following the directions on the discharge prescription. Keep the leg elevated where possible and maintain adequate fluids. The GP surgery should review the leg if improvement is not sustained. A routine clinical review is planned in about 12 weeks, with earlier assessment if symptoms recur or fail to settle.

A&E handover – suspected NSTEMI
NHS number: 000 366 5802

Patient: Jaimee Clarke
MRN: 0985052
Address: 86 Black Bear Lane, Stokesley, TS9 5AA
Contact: 07700 900143

Arrival and history:
Presented with sudden central, heavy chest pressure while at rest, associated with marked diaphoresis and nausea. Pain initially persistent, with partial improvement after treatment in the department. No pleuritic component, haemoptysis or unilateral leg swelling. No previous coronary intervention reported. Friend Jamee present and assisting with history.

At 08:15, observations: BP 154/88, pulse 96 regular, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturations 97% on air, temperature 36.7°C. Alert and coherent. Pale and clammy initially. Heart sounds dual, no murmur; chest clear bilaterally. No peripheral oedema. Calves soft and symmetrical. Abdomen non-tender.

Investigations:
Initial ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with horizontal ST depression in the lateral leads; no ST elevation. Repeat tracing showed persistent lateral repolarisation abnormality without dynamic ST elevation. High-sensitivity troponin I raised above the laboratory reference range, with a significant rise on repeat sample. FBC, renal profile and glucose acceptable for treatment. Chest radiograph without acute pulmonary or mediastinal abnormality.

Impression and actions:
Clinical picture and serial ECG/troponin results consistent with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Given aspirin loading dose, fondaparinux and atorvastatin; analgesia and antiemetic as required. Cardiac monitoring ongoing. No current pulmonary oedema or haemodynamic instability.

Plan:
Discuss with on-call cardiology regarding invasive risk assessment and timing of angiography. Admit to the acute cardiac pathway; repeat ECG for recurrent pain and continue serial observations and troponin testing. Escalate immediately for worsening pain, arrhythmia, hypotension or breathlessness.

Dear Colleague,

Re: Diana-Rose P.

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient’s established Parkinson disease, particularly the recent increase in motor fluctuations and whether the current dopaminergic regimen remains appropriate. The patient was previously assessed by neurology, who confirmed the diagnosis; co-beneldopa has subsequently been continued in primary care. I am requesting specialist review rather than re-establishing the diagnosis in primary care.

The main difficulties are a persistent resting tremor, progressive bradykinesia and muscular rigidity, now affecting transfers, dressing and meal preparation. Symptoms are most troublesome before the next dose and in the early morning. There has been no reported loss of consciousness, focal limb weakness or acute confusion. The patient describes occasional light-headedness on standing, without a documented fall. Their sibling, Samer, has noticed reduced facial expression and quieter speech over recent months.

On examination in surgery, there was a low-amplitude resting tremor of the right hand, bilateral cogwheel rigidity and slowed finger tapping, more marked on the right. Gait initiation was delayed, with short steps and reduced arm swing. There was no dysarthria severe enough to impair conversation, and limb power was grossly preserved. Blood pressure was stable when seated; formal lying and standing measurements would be useful given the postural symptoms. No cerebellar signs were elicited.

Current treatment is co-beneldopa, taken as prescribed, with no recent dose change documented. The patient reports partial benefit but describes wearing-off before scheduled doses. There have been no reported dyskinesias, hallucinations or impulse-control symptoms. Medication adherence and timing in relation to meals should be reviewed in detail.

Please could the movement-disorders team undertake a medication and multidisciplinary review, advise whether dose timing or formulation should be adjusted, and assess the need for physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, and falls-prevention input. Advice regarding orthostatic symptom management would also be appreciated. I will continue the existing prescription pending specialist recommendations and monitor blood pressure, falls risk and functional decline.

Referring clinician: tahmid-ur clark, GP
Professional identifier: 0209865
Service locality: Gunnister

Yours sincerely,

tahmid-ur clark

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report

Patient: Pessy G.
MRN: 00652663
Requesting organisation: ROOKWOOD HOSPITAL
Specimen: EDTA whole blood
Collection/report date: 15th November 2020
Request: Investigation of diabetes mellitus in the context of thirst, fatigue and frequent urination. The patient is taking metformin and atorvastatin. Spouse provided supplementary clinical history.

Results
HbA1c: 70 mmol/mol
Interpretation: Above the usual treatment target for most adults with established type 2 diabetes mellitus, consistent with suboptimal glycaemic control. Clinical targets should be individualised by the treating team.

Diabetes genetic panel
No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant identified in the genes analysed. This result does not support a currently recognisable monogenic diabetes syndrome, but does not exclude genetic susceptibility to type 2 diabetes or variants outside the assay scope.

Specimen quality
Specimen received in suitable condition. Internal quality-control measures were satisfactory. This is a laboratory result and should be interpreted alongside the clinical history, examination and previous glycaemic measurements.

Clinical comment
The raised HbA1c is compatible with the reported polyuria and thirst and warrants clinical review of adherence, diet, renal function and the current diabetes management plan. Consider repeat HbA1c after an appropriate interval and assessment for dehydration or other causes of fatigue if symptoms persist. The genetic result should not alter established treatment without clinical review.

Validated by: Dr Wolfie YASIN, MBBS
Clinical Genetics Laboratory
Report status: Authorised

Respiratory Medicine Specialist Review

Patient: M. SIMMONS
MRN: H3089245
Occupation: Retail assistant
Referring organisation: Princess Grace Hospital
Reviewing clinician: Emira Hamid

Reason for review:
Assessment of persistent low mood and reduced engagement with respiratory self-management, in the context of a major depressive episode. The patient was seen in the respiratory medicine clinic with the account obtained directly and with appropriate opportunity for confidential discussion.

Clinical history:
The patient describes several weeks of low mood, loss of interest in previously enjoyable activities and early-morning waking. Energy and motivation are reduced, and this has made adherence to routine respiratory care less consistent. There is no reported acute deterioration in breathing, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis or infective symptoms. Appetite is broadly unchanged. The patient denies thoughts of ending their life, current intent or plans, and identifies family support as protective. No symptoms suggestive of mania or psychosis were elicited.

Medication reconciliation confirms current treatment with sertraline. No adverse effects were reported today. The patient understands that benefit may be gradual and has not stopped treatment. Alcohol and recreational drug use were not contributory on today’s history.

Examination and interpretation:
The patient was appropriately dressed and engaged, with reduced spontaneous speech but coherent, goal-directed responses. Affect was constricted and mood objectively low. There was no evidence of formal thought disorder. Respiratory effort was comfortable at rest, with no audible wheeze or cough during the consultation. The presentation is consistent with a major depressive episode, without current suicidal intent, and is likely contributing to reduced participation in respiratory care. There is no clinical evidence of an acute respiratory process requiring escalation today.

Plan:
Continue sertraline as currently prescribed and arrange review with the GP surgery to assess response, tolerability and the need for psychological therapy or other mental health support. A written safety-netting plan was discussed: urgent help should be sought through NHS 111 or the emergency department if suicidal thoughts, intent or inability to remain safe develops. Respiratory treatment and follow-up should continue unchanged unless new symptoms arise.

Review in about 9 weeks, or sooner if concerns develop.

Report prepared and signed by Emira Hamid, Princess Grace Hospital.

Discharge summary

Patient: Anaya-Grace E.
Clinical area: Paediatrics
Admission diagnosis: Acute asthma exacerbation

Anaya-Grace E., who is aged 15 years, was admitted following two days of worsening wheeze, night-time cough and increasing work of breathing. History was obtained from the patient, with additional information from their uncle, Chuni Bray, who lives in Gleann dail bho Tuath. The patient gave assent to assessment and treatment, and their uncle was involved in discharge planning.

On arrival, there was audible wheeze with prolonged expiration and moderate intercostal recession. Oxygen saturations were maintained in air. Salbutamol was given through a spacer, with repeated doses initially according to response. The respiratory examination improved over the following hours, and no oxygen or intravenous treatment was required. There was no fever, focal chest sign or clinical evidence of pneumonia. A consultant respiratory physician reviewed the treatment plan during the admission.

The patient received practical spacer teaching and was able to demonstrate correct technique before leaving hospital. They were observed overnight without further deterioration; the night-time cough had settled and work of breathing was normal at discharge. Eating and drinking were satisfactory.

Discharge medicines:
• Salbutamol inhaler: two puffs through the spacer when required for wheeze or breathlessness. If symptoms are more troublesome, use four puffs and seek advice if there is no clear improvement.
• Continue the patient’s usual prescribed asthma preventer, if applicable, and bring all inhalers to the GP review.
• A written asthma action plan was provided.

Please arrange a review with the GP or practice asthma nurse within one week to assess control, inhaler technique and whether preventer treatment needs adjustment. The paediatric team will request follow-up through Aberdeen Royal Infirmary if symptoms remain poorly controlled or there have been further acute attacks.

Seek urgent help through emergency services if the patient is too breathless to speak or drink, becomes drowsy, develops blue lips, or requires salbutamol more often than every four hours. Their uncle confirmed understanding of the plan and had the opportunity to ask questions.

Emergency Department Assessment – Paediatric Emergency Medicine
National Insurance number: GB 35 78 90 C

Patient: BRYNLEE CHARLES, a 3-year-old Native American male patient, attended with his father, A. Casey, who provided the history. He has had two days of passing urine more frequently than usual, with stinging on urination and intermittent discomfort low in the abdomen. His father reports a temperature at home but no rigors, vomiting, diarrhoea or flank pain. He has continued to drink and has passed urine normally. There is no previous urinary tract infection, known renal abnormality or recent antibiotic treatment.

He was alert, settled with his father and appropriately interactive. Temperature was 38.1°C, heart rate 118 bpm, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturations 99% in air. Mucous membranes were moist and capillary refill was under two seconds. The abdomen was soft, with mild suprapubic tenderness but no guarding, rebound tenderness or palpable mass. There was no costovertebral angle tenderness. External genital examination was unremarkable. No rash was seen.

Urine obtained for bedside testing showed leucocytes ++, nitrites positive and blood +. A clean-catch specimen has been sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivities. Blood glucose was normal. There were no clinical features of sepsis, pyelonephritis, dehydration or an obstructive uropathy.

Assessment

The presentation and urine findings are most consistent with an uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection. He is clinically stable for treatment at home while awaiting the culture result. His father was advised to seek immediate reassessment if he develops persistent fever, vomiting, lethargy, worsening abdominal or loin pain, reduced urine output or difficulty taking fluids.

Plan

Started on oral nitrofurantoin, prescribed according to the paediatric dosing guidance and local formulary. Encourage regular fluids and frequent toileting; paracetamol may be given for discomfort or fever as directed on the bottle. The family will be contacted if the culture requires a change in antibiotic. Follow-up with the GP at GLANGWILI GENERAL HOSPITAL is arranged for 25th July 2024, in 15 days, or sooner if symptoms do not settle. Discharged home with father after safety-netting and opportunity for questions.

Identifies sibling and GP as sources of support and is willing to seek help if risk increases. Engaged appropriately throughout assessment; tearful at times but with coherent speech and good insight. No evidence of formal thought disorder.

Assessment: Major depressive episode with passive thoughts of death, without current plan or intent. Immediate risk assessed as low, though requires active follow-up.

Plan: Discussed findings with the patient and sibling. Continue current sertraline pending GP review; arrange urgent appointment with the GP to assess response and consider treatment adjustment. Referral to NHS talking therapies discussed and accepted. Written crisis information provided, with advice to attend A&E or contact emergency services if unable to remain safe. Discharged home with sibling and agreed safety plan.

Discharge summary – Cardiology
National Insurance number: BG414108B

Patient: Jamal Reilly
Home address: 125 ASCOT PARK, HAMILTONSBAWN
Contact: 07700 900905

Reason for admission
Presented to the emergency department with sudden breathlessness, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and tachycardia. Symptoms had been present for 3 days. No preceding operation, prolonged travel or recent immobilisation was identified.

Key findings
Initial observations showed sinus tachycardia with oxygen saturation below the expected range on air. CT pulmonary angiography demonstrated bilateral pulmonary emboli, with a moderate clot burden and no definite radiological evidence of right ventricular strain. Troponin was mildly raised but remained stable on repeat testing. Echocardiography showed preserved left and right ventricular systolic function. Lower-limb Doppler did not demonstrate deep vein thrombosis.

Hospital course
Managed on the cardiology ward with supplemental oxygen and therapeutic anticoagulation. Oxygen requirement reduced steadily and was discontinued before discharge; saturations remained satisfactory on room air. Haemodynamically stable throughout, with improving pleuritic pain and breathlessness. There was no bleeding complication.

Discharge medicines
Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for the first 7 days from treatment initiation, then 5 mg twice daily thereafter. Avoid NSAIDs unless specifically advised. No regular oxygen is required at home. The anticoagulation duration will be reviewed after assessment for provoking factors and recurrence risk.

Follow-up and advice
Anticoagulation clinic referral has been made, with GP review requested within one week. Return immediately to A&E for worsening breathlessness, syncope, haemoptysis, new chest pain or significant bleeding. Discussed medication adherence, bleeding precautions and avoidance of contact sports. The patient’s spouse was present for the discharge discussion.

Discharging clinician: Dr Adeoluwa Fatima, MBBS, Consultant Physician
GMC: 0478790

Emergency Department Assessment
NHS number: 0000415813

Patient: Macey
Clinical age: 83 y/o
Home address: 121 Membris Way, Uttoxeter, ST14 5AA
Contact: 07700 900230

Macey was referred to the emergency department by their sibling because of gradually worsening breathlessness over the past week. They now become short of breath walking across the room and have been sleeping propped up on three pillows. Both ankles have become swollen. There is no chest pain, pleuritic pain, fever, productive cough or recent travel. They report taking furosemide and bisoprolol as prescribed, with no recent medication changes. The family have noticed reduced appetite but no confusion or collapse.

On assessment, the patient was alert and speaking in full sentences at rest. Respiratory rate was 24/min, oxygen saturations 94% on air, blood pressure 146/88 mmHg, pulse 92/min and regular, and temperature 36.7°C. There was raised jugular venous pressure, bibasal fine inspiratory crepitations and bilateral pitting ankle oedema to the mid-shins. Heart sounds were dual without an audible murmur. The abdomen was soft and non-tender, with no focal neurological deficit.

ECG showed sinus rhythm with non-specific ST-T changes and no acute ischaemic pattern. Chest radiograph demonstrated cardiomegaly with pulmonary vascular congestion and small bilateral pleural effusions. Blood tests showed mildly impaired renal function from the patient’s usual baseline, with no significant electrolyte disturbance; troponin was not dynamically elevated. BNP 2,840 pg/mL. Viral respiratory PCR was negative.

Assessment: Acute decompensated congestive heart failure, without evidence of acute coronary syndrome or infection. The patient was given intravenous furosemide with good urine output and reported easier breathing after observation. Oxygen was not required. A fluid and salt-restricted diet was discussed, together with daily weights and advice to seek urgent help for worsening breathlessness, chest pain or syncope.

The case was reviewed with the medical registrar. Following clinical improvement, the patient was discharged with continuation of bisoprolol and an agreed short increase in oral furosemide pending review by the GP within 48 hours. An urgent heart-failure team referral and repeat renal profile were requested. The patient and sibling understood the plan and return precautions.

Seen and discharged by Rafsan Lynch.

Date: 1996-06-13

Dear Colleague,

Re: KAIAH LEWIS
Address: 73 Auld Coal Drive, Glasgow, G14 0AA
Occupation: Baker

Thank you for assessing this patient regarding persistent symptoms consistent with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, particularly whether further investigation is indicated and whether treatment should be optimised through specialist review.

History and current symptoms

The patient describes recurrent retrosternal burning with acid regurgitation, most troublesome after meals and when lying flat. Night-time cough has disrupted sleep and is reported to be worse during episodes of regurgitation. The cough has been present for 3 days. A friend has provided collateral history and reports occasional throat clearing and a hoarse voice on waking, without witnessed choking or nocturnal apnoeas.

There is no reported dysphagia, odynophagia, haematemesis, melaena or unintentional weight loss. Appetite remains satisfactory. There is no exertional chest pain, breathlessness or syncope. The patient does not describe persistent vomiting. Symptoms have nevertheless become intrusive despite adherence to treatment and lifestyle measures.

Examination and investigations

The patient was comfortable at review, with normal observations and no acute distress. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. The abdomen was soft and non-tender, without guarding or palpable mass. There was no clinical evidence of anaemia or dehydration.

No recent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is recorded. Previous routine blood tests were reportedly reassuring, although the results are not available with this referral.

Management to date

Omeprazole has been taken regularly, with incomplete relief. Alginate suspension is used after meals and at bedtime when required. The patient has been advised to avoid late meals, reduce trigger foods, elevate the head of the bed and avoid lying down soon after eating. These measures have helped intermittently but have not resolved the nocturnal cough or regurgitation.

Request

I would be grateful for gastroenterology assessment, including consideration of upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to assess for oesophagitis, Barrett’s oesophagus or another cause of refractory symptoms. Please advise on acid-suppression optimisation and whether ambulatory reflux monitoring or other investigation is appropriate. The patient has been advised to seek urgent medical attention if dysphagia, gastrointestinal bleeding, persistent vomiting or severe chest pain develops.

Yours faithfully,

Dr Zaland Cole, MBBS

Dr Yianna Hatton, MBBS medically reviewed the patient; continue current analgesia and hydration plan, with urgent review for increasing pain, fever, respiratory change or reduced urine output. Oxygen and emergency equipment available at bedside.

Patient: TALLULAH-BLU SHARP
MRN: 0672656
Contact: tallulah-blu.sharp65@icloud.com

Seen in the cardiology clinic following referral for intermittent exertional breathlessness and awareness of a fast heartbeat. The patient reports several weeks of painless swelling in the left side of the neck and above the collarbone, with drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss. There has been no chest pain, syncope, orthopnoea or ankle swelling. Appetite is reduced but fluids are maintained. A friend accompanied the patient and helped with the history.

This 35-year-old Native American female patient appeared tired but was comfortable at rest. Pulse was regular at 96 bpm and blood pressure was satisfactory. Heart sounds were normal, with no murmur or added sounds. The chest was clear, and there was no peripheral oedema. Several firm, non-tender cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes were palpable. No immediate airway compromise was evident.

The presentation is concerning for Hodgkin lymphoma, with tissue diagnosis still pending. The palpitations and breathlessness may be related to anaemia, systemic illness or deconditioning; there is currently no clinical evidence of heart failure or acute coronary syndrome. Supportive care pending tissue diagnosis remains appropriate, with treatment decisions to be led by the haematology team once pathology and staging are available.

Plan:
An ECG was arranged today and an echocardiogram requested as a baseline assessment before any potentially cardiotoxic systemic treatment. Blood tests requested include full blood count, renal and liver profiles, inflammatory markers and thyroid function. The patient has been advised to attend the emergency department if breathlessness becomes severe, chest pain develops, there is collapse, or swallowing or breathing becomes difficult.

The urgent lymph-node biopsy pathway and cross-sectional imaging will be followed up with the referring team. Cardiology review is booked for 13th June 2018, or sooner if the ECG or echocardiogram is abnormal. The patient and accompanying friend understood the plan and had the opportunity to ask questions.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
National Insurance number: BG 90 05 00 C

Patient: SIOUXSIE DONOVAN
Clinical area: Clinical Genetics
Contact: siouxsie.donovan27@icloud.com
Clinical age recorded at review: 63 y/o

Reason for admission
Presented via the emergency department with a short history of frequent watery diarrhoea, repeated vomiting and cramping central abdominal pain. Symptoms followed a self-limiting gastrointestinal illness in a household contact. There was no history of recent antibiotic treatment, overseas travel, blood in the stool or persistent fever. M. Platt, a friend, provided additional history with the patient’s agreement.

Assessment and key results
On arrival the patient appeared mildly dehydrated, with dry mucous membranes and postural light-headedness, but remained alert and haemodynamically stable. Abdominal examination demonstrated mild, diffuse tenderness without guarding, rebound tenderness or distension. Initial blood tests showed a mild rise in urea consistent with reduced intake; electrolytes, inflammatory markers and liver function were otherwise satisfactory. A stool sample was sent for microbiological testing and did not identify a reportable bacterial pathogen. There was no clinical evidence of an acute surgical abdomen.

Hospital course
Management consisted of oral rehydration solution in small, frequent amounts, with temporary intravenous crystalloid when vomiting prevented adequate intake. Antiemetic treatment enabled a gradual return to oral fluids, followed by light meals. Diarrhoea reduced in frequency during observation, and abdominal cramps settled without analgesia beyond simple paracetamol if required. The patient remained afebrile and did not require antibiotics. The clinical genetics team was informed because of the admission pathway; no genetics-specific intervention was required during this episode.

Medication on discharge
• Oral rehydration solution: continue regularly while stools remain loose and replace additional losses.
• ondansetron 4 mg every 8 hours as needed
• Paracetamol, if required, in accordance with the label instructions.

The patient was tolerating fluids, passing urine normally and mobilising independently at discharge. Advice was given regarding handwashing, separate towels where possible, avoiding preparation of food for others, and remaining away from work or communal activities until 48 hours after the last episode of vomiting or diarrhoea.

Problem list
1. Acute infectious gastroenteritis, clinically improving.
2. Mild dehydration, resolved with rehydration.
3. Vomiting, controlled with ondansetron.

Follow-up and safety-netting
Please arrange a GP review on 2019-06-17 if diarrhoea has not substantially settled, or sooner if concerns arise. Attend A&E urgently for inability to keep fluids down, markedly reduced urine output, fainting, severe or localised abdominal pain, blood in the stool, confusion or persistent high temperature. The discharge plan was discussed with the patient, who understood the advice and had no further questions.

Emergency Department Assessment
National Insurance number: NK572653B

Patient: Nalini
Contact: 07700 900533
Accompanied by partner, K. COATES

Nalini presented with approximately 18 hours of abdominal pain, initially central and now localised to the right lower quadrant. The pain has become steadily more severe and is worse on walking and coughing. There has been nausea with loss of appetite, but no vomiting. No diarrhoea or urinary symptoms were reported. The partner confirms that the patient appeared increasingly uncomfortable overnight.

On assessment, the patient was alert and haemodynamically stable, although uncomfortable when mobilising. Abdomen was soft overall, with marked right lower-quadrant tenderness, localised guarding and percussion tenderness. There was no generalised rigidity. Bowel sounds were present. No palpable hernia was identified. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable.

Blood tests showed a raised inflammatory response with neutrophil predominance. Renal function and electrolytes were satisfactory, and venous lactate was not elevated. Urinalysis did not suggest a urinary infection. Pregnancy testing was not clinically indicated. The abdominal ultrasound was limited by bowel gas but demonstrated a non-compressible blind-ending tubular structure in the right iliac fossa with surrounding inflammatory change, in keeping with acute appendicitis. Report/accession ID: 06173699.

The working diagnosis is acute uncomplicated appendicitis. There are no current clinical features of perforation, diffuse peritonitis or sepsis. The findings and management options were discussed with the patient and partner, including operative treatment, the need to remain nil by mouth, and the possibility that further imaging or examination may be required.

Treatment and plan

Intravenous fluids were commenced, with intravenous co-amoxiclav given after blood samples were obtained. Analgesia included paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily, with additional prescribed analgesia available if required. The patient is to remain nil by mouth and has been referred to the on-call general surgical team at University Hospital of Wales for review and likely laparoscopic appendicectomy. Observations and pain scores will continue in the emergency department pending surgical assessment. No discharge is planned at this stage.

Clinical Genetics Outpatient Report
NHS number: 000 691 3858

Patient: Temiloluwa Daniel
Occupation: Journalist
Report/accession ID: 0161906855
Referring service: Chepstow Community Hospital

Reason for review:
Assessment of persistent hypothyroid symptoms and consideration of a familial thyroid disorder. The patient describes ongoing fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation despite established levothyroxine treatment. There is no reported neck discomfort, dysphagia, change in voice, tremor or episodic palpitation.

Clinical history:
Levothyroxine is taken regularly, although the timing in relation to breakfast and other medicines was reviewed. There has been no recent dose change. The patient reports generally stable appetite and no unintentional weight loss. Bowel symptoms are longstanding and improve somewhat with increased dietary fibre. There is no history suggestive of adrenal insufficiency or a recent systemic illness.

Family history is notable for a sibling with thyroid disease; the precise diagnosis and age at onset are not currently documented. No known family history of thyroid malignancy, congenital anomalies, intellectual disability or a recognised genetic syndrome was elicited. The patient was advised to obtain available records from affected relatives if possible.

Examination and investigations:
The patient appeared clinically well. No obvious thyroid enlargement or cervical lymphadenopathy was identified. There was no tremor, lid lag or proximal muscle weakness. Heart rhythm was regular and the extremities were warm, with no peripheral oedema.

Recent thyroid function testing has been requested through primary care, including TSH and free T4, with thyroid peroxidase antibodies if not previously recorded. Medication adherence and administration technique should be confirmed before interpreting a mildly abnormal result. If biochemical hypothyroidism persists despite an apparently adequate dose, malabsorption, interacting medicines and incorrect administration should be considered.

Impression:
The current presentation is compatible with under-replacement or variable absorption of levothyroxine. The available history does not establish a syndromic or monogenic thyroid disorder. A familial tendency to autoimmune thyroid disease remains plausible, but genetic testing is not indicated on the information presently available.

Plan:
Continue the prescribed levothyroxine pending results and take it consistently on an empty stomach, separated from calcium or iron preparations. Primary care should review the results and adjust treatment in accordance with local guidance. The patient may be re-referred if there is a markedly unusual thyroid phenotype, multiple affected relatives, congenital hypothyroidism in the family or additional syndromic features.

Report prepared by tasleema reeves, consultant endocrinologist, Chepstow Community Hospital.

GP review within one week for vascular risk-factor assessment and blood-pressure management. Stroke/TIA clinic follow-up will be arranged. Seek emergency help immediately for recurrent weakness, facial droop, speech disturbance, visual loss or severe sudden headache, even if symptoms settle.

Date: 27/08/2026
Patient: Izabella-Rose J., 6-year-old Pacific Islander male patient

Repeated vomiting and loose stools since yesterday, with markedly reduced urine output today. History provided by the legal guardian. No blood in stool, bilious vomit, rash or breathing difficulty. No recent travel reported. Oral rehydration solution attempted at home but not retained.

Alert but tired, responding appropriately and accepting examination. Dry lips and tongue, mildly sunken eyes and reduced tears. Capillary refill approximately 2 seconds; peripheries warm. Capillary glucose 5.4 mmol/L. Urinalysis: concentrated urine, ketones ++, no blood or nitrites. No indication for blood tests or imaging at present.

Clinical picture consistent with viral gastroenteritis causing mild-to-moderate dehydration. No focal abdominal signs to suggest appendicitis or obstruction. A supervised oral rehydration trial was completed in the department, with no further vomiting and improved oral intake.

Discharge home with fasiha manning once tolerating fluids. Continue oral rehydration solution and offer usual light meals as tolerated. Return immediately for bilious or bloody vomiting, severe abdominal pain, increasing drowsiness, inability to keep fluids down, or no urine over the next several hours. Dear Respiratory Team,

Re: A. LOCK

I am referring this patient for assessment of asthma which has become increasingly symptomatic despite regular inhaled treatment. The specific question is whether the current diagnosis and preventer regimen remain appropriate, and whether further investigation or an alternative explanation for the persistent symptoms should be considered.

Over recent weeks, there has been intermittent wheeze, shortness of breath on exertion and a troublesome night-time cough. The cough is now disturbing sleep on several nights each week. There has been no reported haemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain or syncope. The patient’s sibling has accompanied them and describes increased use of the reliever inhaler, although there has been no recent admission to hospital or attendance at A&E.

Current treatment is salbutamol inhaler as required and beclometasone inhaler, prescribed as beclometasone two puffs twice daily. Inhaler technique and adherence were reviewed in the emergency department, with some uncertainty about whether the preventer is being taken consistently. A spacer was recommended, and the patient was advised to rinse their mouth after the steroid inhaler. There is no known recent course of oral corticosteroids.

At review, the patient was alert and speaking in full sentences. There was mild bilateral expiratory wheeze, without focal crepitations. Oxygen saturations were satisfactory at rest, and there was no evidence of acute respiratory distress. A chest radiograph did not show focal consolidation or pneumothorax. Report/accession ID: 27/546338. The patient was discharged with safety-netting advice to seek urgent help for severe breathlessness, inability to speak in sentences or poor response to salbutamol.

Assessment

Asthma with suboptimal symptom control, particularly nocturnal cough and exertional breathlessness. Poor adherence or inhaler technique may be contributing, although the frequency of symptoms warrants specialist review.

Plan

Please assess objectively with spirometry and bronchodilator response when clinically appropriate, and advise on optimisation of inhaled therapy. I would also appreciate guidance regarding trigger assessment, an asthma action plan and whether allergy or other respiratory investigations are indicated.

Yours faithfully,

Titilope Goodman
0452192
Queen Elizabeth University Hospital

Laboratory Report
NHS number: 000 840 0742

Patient: K. LANG
Patient identifier (MRN): 0433043
Clinical details: Rheumatoid arthritis with increased morning stiffness, swollen hand joints and fatigue. Cardiology department request for assessment of inflammatory activity and treatment safety during a suspected flare. Current treatment includes methotrexate 15 mg once weekly, folic acid and naproxen. Patient cohort: 53 y/o

Specimen information
Specimen: Venous blood
Request: Full blood count, renal profile, liver profile and inflammatory markers
Specimen quality: Suitable for analysis; no significant haemolysis or clot detected.

Results

Haemoglobin: 118 g/L (115–160)
White cell count: 8.7 × 10⁹/L (4.0–11.0)
Platelet count: 428 × 10⁹/L (150–400)
Mean cell volume: 87 fL (80–100)

Creatinine: 74 µmol/L (45–90)
Estimated glomerular filtration rate: 86 mL/min/1.73 m² (>60)
Alanine aminotransferase: 29 U/L (5–35)
Alkaline phosphatase: 102 U/L (30–130)
Bilirubin: 11 µmol/L (0–21)
Albumin: 37 g/L (35–50)

C-reactive protein: 34 mg/L (<5)
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 46 mm/hour (1–20)

Interpretation

Moderately raised C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, with mild thrombocytosis, support active systemic inflammation in the stated clinical context. Haemoglobin is at the lower end of the reference interval. Renal and hepatic indices are currently satisfactory for continuation of disease-modifying treatment, subject to clinical review and local monitoring policy.

Clinical comment

The biochemical profile is compatible with an inflammatory rheumatoid arthritis flare but is not specific; infection should be excluded if clinically indicated, particularly before escalation of immunosuppression. Please correlate with joint examination, temperature and functional decline. Continue folic acid as prescribed and verify that methotrexate remains prescribed as methotrexate 15 mg once weekly, rather than a daily regimen. Review analgesic requirements and gastrointestinal or renal risk associated with naproxen.

Repeat full blood count, renal profile, liver profile and inflammatory markers should be considered after treatment adjustment or sooner if symptoms worsen. A clinical review is booked for 19th September 2035.

Validated and authorised by: Marci O'SHEA
Laboratory medicine service
Report status: Final

Patient: Kingson Hodges
Occupation: Police officer
Employer: Nuptown Public Library
Address: 145 Tadorne Road, Willenhall, WV12 4AA
Contact: kingson.hodges31@hotmail.com

Dear Kingson Hodges,

I reviewed your ongoing knee symptoms in general medicine clinic. You describe pain that is worse with walking, stairs and standing for longer periods, together with stiffness after resting and in the morning. The stiffness settles as you get moving, although your overall mobility has become more limited. You reported a current pain score of 5/10. There has been no recent injury, locking episode, fever or unexplained weight loss.

On examination, you walked with a slight limp but were able to mobilise independently. The affected knee was not hot or acutely swollen. There was mild tenderness along the joint line, crepitus through movement and some loss of full flexion. The knee was stable on ligament testing, and the leg was warm with intact sensation and circulation. These findings fit with osteoarthritis rather than an acute inflammatory or traumatic problem.

Please continue regular activity within your limits. Short, frequent walks and low-impact exercise such as cycling or swimming are preferable to prolonged rest. A physiotherapy referral will be arranged for a strengthening and mobility programme, with advice on pacing and exercises that can be continued at home. If relevant to you, gradual weight reduction can also lessen load through the knee.

For pain relief, continue paracetamol as directed on the packet, provided this remains safe for you. You may continue topical ibuprofen to the knee according to the product instructions, avoiding broken skin and stopping if you develop a rash. Please do not add oral anti-inflammatory tablets without discussing this with your GP, particularly if you have stomach, kidney, heart or blood-pressure problems, or take medicines that increase bleeding risk.

Your GP surgery can review progress after the physiotherapy assessment. Please seek urgent medical advice if the knee becomes suddenly hot, markedly swollen or impossible to bear weight on, or if you develop fever or severe calf swelling. We can consider an X-ray or specialist musculoskeletal review if symptoms continue to restrict daily activities despite these measures.

Discharge summary for C. Weston
NHS number: 000 985 4445

Home address: 74 Carlock Walk, Port Glasgow, PA14 5AA
Report/accession ID: 0334201362

You were admitted under the respiratory medicine team because persistent vomiting had led to dehydration and weight loss during early pregnancy. Your pregnancy was assessed as 9+4 weeks' gestation. The pattern of symptoms and blood tests were consistent with first-trimester hyperemesis. There was no evidence of infection, abdominal emergency or diabetic ketoacidosis.

On admission you were unable to keep fluids down and felt dizzy when standing. Blood tests showed mild ketones and a raised urea, which improved after intravenous sodium chloride. Your potassium and sodium remained satisfactory. Urine testing did not suggest a urinary infection. An ultrasound confirmed an intrauterine pregnancy with cardiac activity, in keeping with the dates provided.

You received intravenous fluids, anti-sickness treatment with cyclizine and thiamine supplementation. Vomiting settled gradually, and you were able to drink, eat small portions and walk safely before leaving hospital. There was no ongoing oxygen requirement or respiratory problem.

Discharge medicines:
• Cyclizine 50 mg up to three times daily when required for nausea or vomiting.
• Thiamine as prescribed on the accompanying medicines list.
• Continue any pregnancy vitamins only if tolerated; pause iron-containing supplements temporarily if these worsen sickness, and discuss this with your midwife or GP.

Please take frequent small sips of fluid and eat little and often, choosing plain foods initially. Return to A&E urgently if you cannot keep fluids or medicines down for 12 hours, pass very little or dark urine, faint, develop severe abdominal pain, fever, blood in the vomit or vaginal bleeding. Contact your maternity assessment service for concerns about the pregnancy.

Your GP should review hydration, weight and anti-sickness treatment within one week. Please also arrange ongoing care with your community midwife and early pregnancy service. A repeat blood test may be needed if vomiting returns.

Discharge authorised by E. Bruce, consultant physician (GMC reference 0935269). The emergency contact recorded in your hospital notes should be informed of the plan if you wish.

Dear Cardiology Team,
National Insurance number: GB 81 23 37 A

Re: R. Booth

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient with iron-deficiency anaemia and persistent exertional symptoms. The specific question is whether the degree of reduced exercise tolerance and episodic dizziness is fully attributable to anaemia, or whether there is an additional cardiovascular cause requiring investigation.

The history is of several months of tiredness, light-headedness on standing and becoming short of breath with activities that were previously well tolerated. There has been no reported syncope, chest pain, sustained palpitations or peripheral oedema. The patient’s adult child has provided collateral history and remains involved in supporting attendance and medication adherence. There is no reported history of ischaemic heart disease or heart failure.

Recent blood tests demonstrated microcytic anaemia with depleted iron stores, consistent with iron deficiency. Renal function, thyroid function and serum electrolytes were not contributory. Ferrous fumarate has been started and is being taken regularly, although symptomatic improvement has been limited to date. Dietary review and investigation for a source of iron loss are ongoing in primary care.

On review, the patient was alert and comfortable at rest. Pulse was regular, with normal heart sounds and no murmur. Chest examination was clear, and there was no clinical evidence of fluid overload. Blood pressure was stable between sitting and standing measurements. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus rhythm without acute ischaemic changes. Despite these reassuring findings, the exertional limitation remains functionally significant and has not resolved with initial treatment of the anaemia.

I would appreciate cardiology review, including advice on whether echocardiography, ambulatory rhythm monitoring or exercise assessment is indicated. Please also advise whether any activity modification is required while the investigation is completed. The patient has been advised to seek urgent assessment through A&E for syncope, new chest pain, severe breathlessness or sustained palpitations.

A primary-care review is planned in about 7 weeks, with follow-up appointment scheduled for 15th September 2012. Home correspondence address: 139 CARSONSTOWN ROAD, AGIVEY. The associated result/accession identifier is 0029301109.

Yours faithfully,

Tam Hawkes

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report
NHS number: 000 146 4672

Patient: Lyra-Grace
MRN: 01391097
Requesting service: Bodmin Hospital Utc
Specimen: EDTA whole blood and serum
Clinical indication: Tiredness, dizziness and reduced exercise tolerance in the context of iron-deficiency anaemia. Current treatment includes ferrous fumarate.

Haematology
Haemoglobin: 96 g/L (115–160)
MCV: 72 fL (80–100)
MCH: 22 pg (27–33)
RBC count: 4.35 × 10^12/L (3.8–5.2)
RDW: 18.9% (11.5–14.5)
Platelets: 418 × 10^9/L (150–400)

Iron studies
Ferritin: 6 µg/L (15–150)
Serum iron: 4 µmol/L (10–30)
Transferrin saturation: 6% (20–50)

Haemoglobinopathy screen
HbA: 97.8%
HbA2: 1.7% (2.0–3.5)
HbF: 0.5% (<2.0)
Variant haemoglobins: Not detected

Test metadata: Haemoglobin assay code LOINC 718-7. Results are interpreted with the reported clinical history and may be affected by recent iron replacement.

Interpretation
Results demonstrate a microcytic, hypochromic anaemia with depleted iron stores. The low HbA2 is compatible with iron deficiency; there is no analytical evidence of a clinically significant haemoglobin variant in this sample. Co-existing alpha-thalassaemia trait cannot be excluded by this screen, particularly if microcytosis persists after iron repletion.

Clinical comment
Continue iron replacement as prescribed and investigate the source of iron loss or inadequate intake in primary care, according to clinical context. Repeat full blood count and ferritin after treatment. Consider alpha-globin gene analysis only if indices remain abnormal despite correction of iron deficiency.

Follow-up review requested for 2018-12-19.

Patient: emer parkinson
NHS number: 000 764 1495
Clinical age group: adolescent; 15 y/o
Date: 2019-07-15
Ward: Paediatric inpatient unit

Nursing progress note

emer parkinson remained settled in bed at the start of the shift, alert and appropriately interactive. Aunt, Akshit, was present and contributed to the history. They reported a night-time cough and intermittent wheeze before admission, with increased work of breathing on arrival. No chest pain, vomiting or rash reported. The patient was able to speak in full sentences and took fluids orally without difficulty.

At 20:00, respiratory rate was 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturations 96% on air, pulse 102 beats per minute, temperature 36.8°C and capillary refill under two seconds. Mild intercostal recession and scattered expiratory wheeze were noted bilaterally. No cyanosis. Following salbutamol inhaler via spacer, air entry improved and the wheeze became less prominent. The patient reported that breathing felt easier and was able to walk to the bathroom with supervision. No dizziness or desaturation on mobilisation.

Assessment

Acute asthma exacerbation showing a good response to bronchodilator treatment. Ongoing mild wheeze and increased work of breathing require observation overnight. Hydration is adequate by oral intake, with supper and approximately 400 ml of fluids taken during the shift. Urine passed once; no bowel concerns reported.

Interventions included positioning upright, reassurance, encouragement of regular fluids and reinforcement of inhaler technique. Spacer teaching was completed with the patient, who demonstrated correct shaking, seal and slow inhalation after coaching. Aunt observed the teaching and agreed to support the treatment plan. No oxygen required during this shift.

Escalation advice was discussed: call bell to be used for worsening breathlessness, inability to speak comfortably, exhaustion, blue lips or poor response to inhaler. The covering paediatric clinician reviewed the patient after the persistent wheeze was noted and advised continuation of the prescribed inhaler pathway, with medical review if observations deteriorate.

Plan for next shift: repeat respiratory observations and assess work of breathing before and after inhaler doses, continue oral fluids, encourage rest, and reassess inhaler technique. Confirm discharge education and follow-up arrangements; respiratory review is planned in 20 days.

Signed by jericho johnston, staff nurse.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
NHS number: 0008761893

Patient: Tiffany-Marie W.
Home address: 136 Florida Street, ANTRIM
Contact email: tiffany-marie.webb17@talktalk.net
Encounter date: 9 November 2021

A 68-year-old Pacific Islander female patient was assessed in A&E following four days of worsening breathlessness, increased wheeze and purulent yellow sputum. Their spouse provided additional history. No chest pain, haemoptysis or recent travel was reported.

Initial assessment showed respiratory distress with widespread expiratory wheeze and reduced air entry bilaterally. Oxygen saturations improved with controlled oxygen, subsequently maintaining the agreed target range on room air. At 08:15, the patient remained alert, speaking in full sentences and haemodynamically stable.

Investigations
Chest radiograph showed hyperinflation without focal consolidation or pleural effusion. Blood tests demonstrated a mild neutrophil-predominant leucocytosis; renal function and inflammatory markers were satisfactory. Viral respiratory PCR was negative. There was no clinical or electrocardiographic evidence of acute coronary syndrome.

Hospital course
Treated as an acute exacerbation of established chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with nebulised bronchodilators, a short course of oral corticosteroid and antibiotic therapy. Breathlessness and wheeze improved over observation, with reduced sputum production. No ventilatory support was required. The case was reviewed with the respiratory team, who agreed discharge with community follow-up.

Discharge medicines
• Prednisolone 30 mg orally each morning to complete a five-day course.
• Doxycycline 200 mg on the first day, then 100 mg once daily to complete five days, subject to tolerance.
• Salbutamol inhaler: two puffs as needed for breathlessness, using the spacer supplied.
Usual long-term medicines should otherwise continue as listed on the reconciled prescription. Avoid smoking and seek advice before taking non-prescribed anti-inflammatory medicines while completing treatment.

Condition and plan
Discharged home clinically improved, independently mobile and able to manage inhalers. The GP should review symptoms and inhaler technique within one week and consider pulmonary rehabilitation and COPD action-plan review. Return to A&E urgently for rapidly worsening breathlessness, cyanosis, confusion, inability to speak in sentences or chest pain.

Emergency Department Cardiology Handover – acute pelvic pain

Patient: Dade
MRN: 07329400
Accompanied by spouse, Lavell TERRY, who provided collateral history with the patient’s consent.

Presenting problem: Lower abdominal pain for 3 days, gradually worsening and now bilateral, with abnormal vaginal discharge and deep dyspareunia. No collapse, vomiting, dysuria or rectal bleeding. No reported pregnancy risk disclosed; last menstrual period not recorded in the initial handover. No known drug allergies documented.

Assessment: Alert and haemodynamically stable. Temperature 37.8°C, pulse 96, BP 112/70, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 99% on air. Mild suprapubic and bilateral iliac fossa tenderness, without guarding or rebound. Speculum examination: mucopurulent discharge from the cervical os. Cervical motion tenderness and bilateral adnexal tenderness on bimanual examination; no palpable mass. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations unremarkable.

Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative. FBC with mild neutrophilia; CRP moderately raised. U&Es and liver profile satisfactory. Urinalysis without convincing urinary infection. Vaginal and endocervical swabs sent for gonorrhoea, chlamydia and microscopy. Pelvic ultrasound requested to exclude tubo-ovarian abscess; no acute surgical abdomen currently evident.

Impression: Pelvic inflammatory disease, with no current evidence of sepsis or abscess.

Treatment and plan: Ceftriaxone administered in the department, then doxycycline and metronidazole commenced as prescribed. Analgesia given with improvement. Discussed abstinence until treatment is completed and partner notification/testing through ROYAL ALBERT EDWARD HOSPITAL. Discharge appropriate if ultrasound reassuring and oral intake maintained. Sexual health review arranged for 23rd March 2022. Return urgently for fever, worsening pain, vomiting, syncope or heavy bleeding; GP review advised for outstanding results.

J. McLoughlin

LABORATORY REPORT – HAEMATOLOGY AND HISTOPATHOLOGY

Patient: Chimerika Flynn
Report/accession ID: 0199570165
Specimen collected: 2024-06-20
Request: Unnamed medical team; investigation of painless lymphadenopathy, night sweats and unintentional weight loss.

Specimens received
- Left cervical lymph-node excision, fresh tissue for flow cytometry and formalin-fixed tissue for histology.
- EDTA blood sample for full blood count.
- Serum sample for biochemistry and inflammatory markers.

Blood results
Haemoglobin: 108 g/L (115–160) – low
White cell count: 13.8 × 10⁹/L (4.0–11.0) – high
Neutrophils: 10.9 × 10⁹/L (2.0–7.5) – high
Platelets: 492 × 10⁹/L (150–400) – high
CRP: 86 mg/L (<5) – high
Albumin: 31 g/L (35–50) – low
LDH: 382 U/L (120–250) – high
Urea: 5.9 mmol/L (2.5–7.8)
Creatinine: 74 µmol/L (45–90)
ALT: 22 U/L (5–35)
Bilirubin: 9 µmol/L (0–21)

Histopathology
Lymph-node architecture is effaced by a mixed inflammatory infiltrate containing scattered large atypical cells with prominent nucleoli. The atypical cells express CD30 and CD15, with weak PAX5 staining; CD20 is negative. Findings are diagnostic of classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Flow cytometry does not identify a clonal B-cell population.

Interpretive comment
The anaemia, neutrophilia, thrombocytosis, raised CRP and LDH, together with hypoalbuminaemia, are compatible with active systemic disease. The reported night sweats and unintentional weight loss should be documented as constitutional symptoms for staging purposes. Hodgkin lymphoma is confirmed on the excised lymph node; this report does not determine stage.

Please refer urgently to the haematology multidisciplinary team for staging with cross-sectional imaging and PET-CT, baseline cardiac assessment where indicated, and treatment planning. Supportive care pending tissue diagnosis is superseded by the confirmed histological result.

Validated and authorised by:
MERIDITH REHMAN, Consultant Physician
GMC: GMC-TEST-0445278

Discharge summary

Patient: Caoilfhinn
Admission date: 23 May 2028
Discharging service: ROYAL INFIRMARY OF EDINBURGH

Dear Caoilfhinn,

You were admitted after a sudden episode of weakness in one arm, facial drooping and slurred speech. These symptoms had settled before your assessment in the emergency department, which is consistent with a transient ischaemic attack (TIA). You also reported a mild headache for 3 days, without persistent neurological symptoms.

Your examination after arrival was normal, including limb power, speech and facial movements. A CT head scan showed no bleeding or established stroke. An MRI brain scan did not show a recent infarct. Ultrasound assessment of the carotid arteries did not demonstrate a significant narrowing requiring intervention. Your ECG showed a regular rhythm, and blood tests were satisfactory apart from raised cholesterol. The findings were reviewed by the stroke and cardiology teams.

You have been started on aspirin 300 mg once daily for 14 days, followed by aspirin 75 mg once daily thereafter, and atorvastatin 80 mg at night. Please continue these medicines unless a doctor advises otherwise. Avoid stopping aspirin without discussing this with your GP or the stroke team. Your GP should review blood pressure, cholesterol and cardiovascular risk, and arrange repeat cholesterol and liver blood tests as clinically indicated.

A rapid-access TIA clinic appointment will be arranged through ROYAL INFIRMARY OF EDINBURGH. If you develop new facial drooping, arm or leg weakness, speech difficulty, sudden loss of vision, severe dizziness or collapse, call 999 immediately, even if the symptoms improve. Do not drive until you have checked the current DVLA guidance and discussed this with your GP.

You told us that your partner, nova-lee brook, lives in Causewayhead and can support you at home. At discharge you were walking independently, eating and drinking normally, and had no ongoing weakness or speech problem. Please take your discharge medicines with you to your GP appointment and seek urgent advice if any symptoms recur.

Cardiology and stroke team discharge plan completed on 23 May 2028.

Re: Pradyun W.

Thank you for reviewing this child, currently 4 y/o, whom I am referring to Community Paediatrics for advice on persistent atopic eczema. The specific question is whether the severity and distribution of the eczema warrant specialist input, particularly regarding optimisation of treatment, possible allergic triggers and support with sleep disruption.

The history is provided mainly by the child’s father, SEEDY GRAHAM. He reports several months of very itchy, dry and inflamed skin affecting the cheeks, neck, elbows, behind the knees and wrists. Itching is worse overnight, with frequent waking and scratching. There has been no fever, wheeze, facial swelling or reduced appetite. Nocturnal scratching has occasionally caused small areas of bleeding, but there has been no purulent discharge or spreading redness.

On examination today, there are poorly demarcated erythematous, dry plaques with excoriations in the flexures and on both wrists. The cheeks are mildly inflamed. There is no crusting, weeping, honey-coloured exudate or clinical evidence of bacterial infection. Growth and general development appear appropriate, and the child was comfortable apart from scratching during the consultation. Current measured weight: weight 14.2 kg.

The family is applying an emollient several times daily and after bathing. Topical hydrocortisone has been used intermittently to the more inflamed areas, with partial improvement, although the family remains concerned about using steroid treatment and is not always clear about the quantity or duration required. We discussed liberal emollient use, soap avoidance, short lukewarm baths, keeping fingernails short and applying hydrocortisone as previously directed during flares. Written skin-care advice was provided, and the father was able to explain the plan back to me.

I would be grateful for your assessment of management, including whether a stepped topical regimen, eczema education support or investigation for contact or food-related aggravating factors is indicated. Please also advise on strategies to reduce night-time itch and restore sleep. There are no current safeguarding concerns.

Yours sincerely,

sierra-mae taylor

Discharge Summary

Patient: alfie-ryan singh
Discharging service: Acute medical unit
Healthcare organisation: ROYAL VICTORIA HOSPITAL
Report/accession ID: 02159375

Reason for admission
Admitted with a four-day history of productive cough, fever and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. There was no haemoptysis or recent travel. A sibling accompanied the patient and provided collateral history.

Assessment and key results
On arrival, the patient was febrile and mildly tachycardic, with reduced air entry and coarse crackles at the right base. Oxygen saturations remained satisfactory on room air. Chest radiograph demonstrated right lower-zone air-space consolidation, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia. Blood tests showed a modest neutrophil leucocytosis and raised C-reactive protein; renal function was suitable for oral treatment. SARS-CoV-2 and influenza testing were negative.

Diagnosis
Community-acquired pneumonia, SNOMED CT 233604007.

Hospital course
Treatment was commenced with intravenous fluids and antibiotics, followed by oral amoxicillin once clinically stable. Fever settled, pleuritic pain improved and oral intake was maintained. There was no requirement for supplemental oxygen, non-invasive ventilation or escalation to critical care. Blood cultures showed no significant growth.

Discharge medicines
• Amoxicillin, to complete the prescribed course.
• Paracetamol as needed for fever or pleuritic discomfort.
The patient was advised not to exceed the stated dose on the dispensing label and to avoid taking additional cold remedies containing paracetamol.

Condition and plan at discharge
Mobilising independently, eating and drinking, and clinically improved at discharge. Continue rest, fluids and gradual return to usual activity. The GP should review recovery if cough or fatigue persists beyond the expected period; a follow-up chest radiograph may be arranged if symptoms or examination findings do not resolve.

Seek urgent medical attention for increasing breathlessness, confusion, blue lips, recurrent high fever, inability to keep fluids down or worsening chest pain.

Discharging clinician: Mariana Simpson, GMC identifier 0779694

Sudden onset of rapid, forceful heartbeat with central chest tightness and a marked fear of dying. Symptoms began at rest and were at their most intense shortly before arrival. The patient described tingling around the mouth and in both hands with a sense of not getting enough air. No collapse, unilateral weakness, haemoptysis or calf pain. No recent infective symptoms reported.

Background
No previous cardiac diagnosis disclosed. The patient reports intermittent episodes of excessive worry but no previous emergency attendance for similar symptoms. Current management includes breathing retraining. No recent medication change or recreational drug use reported. Spouse states the patient remained conscious throughout and symptoms eased whilst waiting to be assessed.

Presentation is most consistent with a panic attack with hyperventilation. Acute coronary syndrome, clinically significant arrhythmia and pulmonary embolism considered less likely following examination, ECG and investigations. No indication for emergency sedative medication. Breathing retraining practised in the department, with gradual symptomatic improvement.

Discharged home with spouse. Advised to continue breathing retraining, avoid excess caffeine, and arrange GP review for assessment of recurrent panic symptoms and psychological support. Clear safety-netting given: return to A&E for persistent or exertional chest pain, syncope, severe breathlessness or new neurological symptoms.

DOB: 23rd March 1970
Home address: 152 Duntreath Drive, Glasgow, G5 0AB

Reason for admission
Admitted under general medicine with a 24-hour history of worsening right lower-quadrant abdominal pain, nausea and loss of appetite. There was no previous abdominal surgery. On assessment, the abdomen was locally tender in the right iliac fossa, without generalised peritonism. Current pain was recorded as 5/10.

Investigations and treatment
Blood tests showed a raised white cell count and inflammatory markers, with stable renal function and electrolytes. Urinalysis did not suggest a urinary infection. CT abdomen and pelvis demonstrated an enlarged, inflamed appendix with surrounding inflammatory change, without perforation or drainable collection.

The patient was kept nil by mouth, given intravenous fluids, analgesia with paracetamol and intravenous co-amoxiclav, and reviewed by the on-call surgical team. Laparoscopic appendicectomy was performed during the admission. The appendix appeared inflamed but non-perforated. Recovery was uncomplicated, and oral intake was reintroduced gradually. The port sites remained clean and dry, with no fever or recurrent vomiting.

Assessment at discharge
Acute uncomplicated appendicitis, treated with laparoscopic appendicectomy. The patient is clinically well, mobilising independently and tolerating food and fluids. Abdominal discomfort is improving, and observations remain stable.

Discharge medicines
Paracetamol for pain in accordance with the labelled dose. Avoid exceeding the stated daily maximum or taking other preparations containing paracetamol. No further antibiotics are required following review of the operative findings and clinical progress.

Follow-up and advice
The surgical team will arrange routine outpatient follow-up if required, and the histology result will be reviewed through the usual surgical pathway. Please seek urgent medical attention via A&E or NHS 111 if there is increasing abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fever, spreading redness or discharge from a wound, abdominal swelling, or inability to eat and drink. Keep the wounds clean and dry and avoid strenuous lifting until comfortable.

Relevant history

Known sensitive skin. No previous anaphylaxis. Current treatment includes hydrocortisone cream and cetirizine, with incomplete relief. No recent antibiotic use or change in regular medication. The patient has not applied the new product since the rash appeared.

Examination

Alert, comfortable at rest and speaking in full sentences. Airway patent; no lip or tongue oedema. Chest clear bilaterally with no wheeze or stridor. Pulse regular, observations stable and temperature normal. Widespread sharply demarcated erythematous, dry, mildly excoriated plaques over the exposed upper chest, lateral neck and volar forearms. No purpura, target lesions, mucosal involvement, weeping or secondary cellulitis. No palpable lymphadenopathy.

Assessment and decision-making

Appearance and distribution are most consistent with allergic contact dermatitis, probably triggered by the fragranced product. There is no clinical evidence of anaphylaxis, Stevens–Johnson syndrome, systemic infection or significant respiratory involvement. No blood tests or imaging indicated.

Treatment and plan

Advised to avoid the suspected product and other fragranced preparations, wash gently with lukewarm water, and use regular emollient. Continue cetirizine as previously directed. Hydrocortisone cream may be used sparingly to affected areas for a short course, avoiding broken skin and the face unless specifically advised. A stronger topical steroid is not required today.

Safety-netting given: return urgently for facial or oral swelling, breathing difficulty, blistering, mucosal soreness, fever or rapidly spreading redness. GP review if not improving within several days. Dermatology or respiratory follow-up planned in about 9 weeks.

Discharge

Discharged home in stable condition with written advice. amalia-ioana sheikh, clinician

Appearance: Cloudy

Protein: 1+

Targeted analysis of the requested immune-deficiency and urinary-tract susceptibility panel did not identify a pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant. The urine findings support an active urinary infection and are clinically compatible with acute pyelonephritis in the context of flank pain and rigors. Renal function is currently preserved. Please correlate antibiotic choice with the separately issued culture and susceptibility report, local antimicrobial guidance, renal function and clinical response. Escalation for persistent fever, vomiting, worsening flank pain or systemic deterioration is advised. Continue routine methotrexate safety monitoring in accordance with the shared-care protocol, and review the need for treatment adjustment with the established rheumatology team. NSAID use should be assessed alongside gastrointestinal, renal and cardiovascular risk.

A repeat inflammatory marker and medication review are suggested at the planned follow-up appointment on 23/01/2023. This report has been electronically validated by Nihan Lord, laboratory clinician, on behalf of St Bartholomews Hospital.

Nursing progress note – respiratory medicine ward
NHS number: 000 178 9660

Patient: S. Sanders; 66 y/o

Reviewed during the morning round. Patient was alert and able to engage appropriately, with Jermayne Myers present and contributing to the history as partner. Reports increased discomfort from the plantar ulcer and a small amount of local discharge for 3 days. Describes reduced sensation over both feet, with no new calf pain. No chest pain or breathlessness reported.

Observations remained stable: respiratory rate 17/min, oxygen saturations 97% on room air, pulse 84 bpm, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg and temperature 37.1°C. The plantar ulcer was assessed with the dressing removed using aseptic technique. Wound bed remains shallow with a small area of slough and scant serous discharge. Surrounding skin is mildly erythematous but not spreading, with no malodour or visible necrosis. Reduced protective sensation persists. Patient reported discomfort during cleansing, settling after the procedure.

The wound was irrigated with normal saline, patted dry and redressed with the prescribed non-adherent dressing and absorbent secondary layer. Co-amoxiclav administered as prescribed; no immediate adverse reaction noted. Patient was reminded to avoid weight-bearing directly through the affected area and to use the advised off-loading footwear. Mobilised to the bathroom with supervision and a frame, maintaining balance. Oral intake was satisfactory at breakfast and fluids were encouraged. Capillary blood glucose monitoring continues as prescribed, with results documented on the observation chart.

Assessment: diabetic foot ulcer with ongoing local discharge and impaired sensation. Current findings do not suggest systemic infection, although the mild surrounding erythema requires close review. Falls risk and risk of wound deterioration remain present because of altered sensation and reduced mobility.

The covering medical team was informed of the discharge and erythema for review today, with consideration of podiatry or tissue viability input if the wound does not improve. Escalate promptly for spreading redness, increasing pain, purulent discharge, fever, offensive odour or clinical deterioration.

Plan for the next shift is to repeat observations, inspect the dressing and surrounding skin, maintain pressure relief, support safe mobilisation, monitor intake and glucose, and continue co-amoxiclav and wound care as prescribed. Follow-up wound review is booked for 8 June 2023.

Documented and signed by kena dalton, Staff Nurse.

Paediatric Outpatient Clinic
National Insurance number: NK780699C

Patient: Zebedee A.
Date: 15 July 2024
Contact: 07700 900914

Zebedee A., the patient, aged 16 years, was reviewed in the paediatric outpatient clinic with their uncle, ellyse mahmood. The patient was seen initially with their uncle present and was then offered part of the consultation privately, with agreement to share relevant information with the accompanying adult.

They describe a six-month history of recurrent unilateral headaches, usually pulsatile and occasionally preceded by a vague visual disturbance. Episodes occur approximately twice a month and last several hours if untreated. Headache is accompanied by nausea and marked photophobia, without vomiting, collapse, weakness, altered speech or persistent visual loss. There are no early-morning headaches or headaches waking them from sleep. They report missing occasional activities but are otherwise managing education and daily routines. Sleep is variable, and they sometimes skip breakfast. No regular caffeine or energy drink intake was reported.

They have used sumatriptan at the start of more severe attacks and naproxen with partial benefit. They are not taking either medicine on most days and deny taking over-the-counter analgesics frequently. No medication allergy was reported. Current weight 54.0 kg.

On examination, the patient appeared well and was comfortable at rest. Pupils were equal and reactive, eye movements and fundoscopy were unremarkable, and there was no facial asymmetry. Power, sensation, coordination and gait were normal. There was no neck stiffness. Blood pressure and other observations were within the expected range for clinic.

Assessment: The history is consistent with migraine without concerning features or focal neurological deficit today. No indication for urgent neuroimaging on the current assessment.

Plan: Continue sumatriptan early in the attack and naproxen with food, avoiding medication on more than two days each week where possible. Keep a headache diary recording triggers, duration, associated symptoms and treatment response. Regular meals, good hydration, consistent sleep and limiting prolonged screen use were discussed. The patient and uncle understand red flags requiring A&E assessment, including sudden maximal headache, persistent neurological symptoms or repeated vomiting. Review in the paediatric headache clinic will be arranged, with earlier GP review if the pattern changes.

Blood glucose within the expected range. No blood tests indicated clinically. Stool sampling not required, as there was no blood, recent travel or prolonged illness.

Condition at discharge  
Alert, settling with parent, tolerating feeds and passing urine. Discharged home with parent following review by the paediatric team.

Plan and advice  
Continue fluids and usual feeds. Seek urgent medical help via A&E if the child becomes difficult to rouse, has persistent vomiting, blood in the stool, breathing difficulty or markedly fewer wet nappies. Contact the GP if diarrhoea is not improving over the next few days.
