Doctor’s professional identifier: 0115797.

Next shift plan
Continue prescribed IV fluids and analgesia, reassess pain and sedation score within one hour of further morphine, record fluid balance, encourage gentle mobilisation, and escalate promptly if respiratory observations change or pain remains uncontrolled.

Discharge Summary – Cardiology

Patient: Lysette K.
Responsible service: Queen Elizabeth University Hospital

The patient was admitted with increasing redness and tenderness around the lower aspect of the postoperative chest wound, associated with purulent discharge for 3 days. There was no reported chest pain, breathlessness or syncope. Their adult child, EMMIE-LOUISE ARIF, was present during the assessment and assisted with the history. They have been kept informed and will support the patient at home in Saval.

On examination, there was a small area of wound erythema with local pain and a limited amount of purulent material. The wound edges remained approximated, with no clinical evidence of sternal instability or deep wound involvement. The patient was haemodynamically stable and remained afebrile. Blood tests showed a mild inflammatory response without significant organ dysfunction. A wound swab was obtained before antibiotics; the result will be reviewed by the treating team and communicated to the GP if treatment needs to change.

Assessment

This was assessed as a superficial postoperative wound infection. There was no evidence during admission of mediastinitis, bacteraemia or recurrent cardiac ischaemia.

Hospital course and treatment

The wound was irrigated and dressed by the cardiothoracic nursing team. Flucloxacillin was commenced, with clinical improvement in the erythema, discharge and discomfort over the following period of observation. The patient remained mobilising independently and was able to manage oral medication and wound care with support.

Discharge plan

Continue flucloxacillin as prescribed and complete the course unless advised otherwise. Keep the dressing clean and dry, and do not apply creams or antiseptic preparations unless specifically instructed. The GP should inspect the wound promptly after discharge, with further review arranged through Queen Elizabeth University Hospital. A cardiology and surgical wound review is booked for 25th October 2028.

The patient has been advised to seek urgent medical attention through A&E if they develop fever, rapidly spreading redness, worsening pain, increasing discharge, wound separation, chest pain or breathlessness. They and EMMIE-LOUISE ARIF verbalised understanding of the plan and were provided with written discharge advice.

Dear Community Paediatrics Team,

Re: Daizy L. — referral for multidisciplinary review of type 1 diabetes mellitus

Daizy L. is an adolescent referred from primary care for assessment of recently recognised type 1 diabetes mellitus and support with ongoing management. This adolescent, 15 y/o, attended with their mother, Rahela Hutchings, who provided much of the collateral history. The specific question is whether current glycaemic control and insulin education are adequate, and whether additional psychological, dietary or school-based support is required.

Over the preceding weeks there had been marked thirst, frequent urination and unintentional weight loss. There has been no reported collapse, persistent vomiting or altered consciousness. Capillary glucose testing in primary care was substantially elevated, with subsequent blood tests supporting diabetes. Ketones were not persistently raised and there was no clinical evidence of diabetic ketoacidosis at the time of assessment.

Insulin therapy has been commenced with a basal-bolus regimen, alongside glucose monitoring before meals, at bedtime and when symptomatic. Rahela Hutchings reports that the family are becoming more confident with injection technique, correction doses and recognition of hypoglycaemia, although meal-related dosing remains a source of uncertainty. There have been no severe hypoglycaemic episodes. Dietary advice has been received, but the family would welcome review by a paediatric dietitian and structured education regarding carbohydrate estimation.

On review, Daizy L. was alert and clinically euvolaemic. There was no respiratory distress, abdominal tenderness or focal neurological abnormality. Injection sites were free of significant induration or lipohypertrophy. Current glucose records show variability, particularly after the evening meal, without a consistent pattern of overnight hypoglycaemia.

I would be grateful for community paediatric input regarding adjustment of the education plan, coordination with the diabetes multidisciplinary team and assessment of the emotional impact of the diagnosis. Please also advise on reasonable arrangements for glucose monitoring and insulin administration during education and extracurricular activities.

A review in about 4 weeks would be helpful, with earlier assessment if recurrent ketones, vomiting, marked drowsiness or inability to maintain oral fluids develops.

Yours sincerely,

rubyann wilcox

Patient: athalie hilton
MRN: MRN-07278594
DOB: 15 December 1976
Contact: athalie.hilton91@outlook.com

Cardiology outpatient clinic note

Reason for review
Referred with low back pain and intermittent shooting pain into the left leg. Also reports tingling over the lateral calf and dorsum of the foot. Symptoms have been present for 3 days and are worse when standing, coughing or climbing stairs. No chest pain, breathlessness, palpitations or exertional limitation.

History
The pain began after lifting a heavy box at home. No fall or direct trauma. Paracetamol has provided limited relief; naproxen was started recently and is being taken with food. No previous spinal surgery. Denies saddle numbness, urinary retention, faecal incontinence or progressive leg weakness. No fever, unexplained weight loss or history suggestive of malignancy.

Examination
Comfortable at rest, mobilising independently with a mildly antalgic gait. Lumbar flexion reduced by pain. Left straight-leg raise reproduces radiating pain. Mild altered sensation reported over the left L5 distribution. Power, reflexes and peripheral pulses are preserved bilaterally. No focal calf tenderness or swelling. Cardiovascular examination: regular pulse, normal heart sounds and no clinical evidence of fluid overload.

Assessment
Features are most consistent with acute lumbar radiculopathy, without current red-flag findings. The leg symptoms are not suggestive of a cardiac cause.

Plan
• Continue paracetamol as directed and naproxen for the shortest effective period, provided there is no dyspepsia, renal impairment, anticoagulant use or other contraindication.
• Avoid prolonged bed rest; maintain gentle activity and change position regularly.
• Arrange physiotherapy or musculoskeletal assessment if symptoms do not settle.
• Seek urgent assessment through A&E for new bladder or bowel disturbance, saddle anaesthesia, marked or worsening weakness, or inability to mobilise.
• No cardiac investigation is indicated on today’s findings.

Follow-up
GP review if not improving, with planned reassessment on 13th April 2004. Consider imaging or specialist spinal referral if persistent or progressive symptoms.

Presenting complaint: Four-day history of productive cough, fever and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. The sputum has been yellow-green, with no haemoptysis. Breathlessness is present on walking but there is no resting dyspnoea. No recent travel or known sick contacts. The patient’s sibling, Solin, accompanied them and provided additional history.

Past medical history is otherwise unremarkable. No known drug allergies. The patient has taken paracetamol with temporary improvement in temperature and has not yet started antibiotics. Oral intake is reduced but still adequate, with normal urine output.

Chest radiograph showed patchy right lower-zone air-space consolidation without pleural effusion or pneumothorax. Blood tests demonstrated a raised inflammatory response; renal function and venous lactate were satisfactory. A respiratory viral swab was negative for influenza and SARS-CoV-2. The presentation and imaging are consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, coded as SNOMED CT 233604007.

Assessment: Stable community-acquired pneumonia without current evidence of sepsis or respiratory failure. The patient was observed following oral fluids and antipyretic treatment, with improvement in heart rate and fever. Admission was considered, but there is reliable support at home and no significant comorbidity requiring inpatient monitoring.

Plan: Commence oral amoxicillin as prescribed and continue paracetamol as needed for pain or fever. Encourage fluids and rest. Written safety-netting advice given to return immediately for increasing breathlessness, confusion, inability to maintain hydration, persistent chest pain or deterioration. text:
Laboratory Report – Urine Culture and Acute Pyelonephritis

Patient: P. O'Sullivan
MRN: 060607774
Requesting location: Accident and Emergency
Healthcare organisation: Glangwili General Hospital
Specimen/report date: 6 June 2020
Specimen: Midstream urine

Clinical details:
Flank pain, dysuria and rigors. Clinical diagnosis of acute pyelonephritis. Current treatment includes cefuroxime and paracetamol. The patient’s spouse reports persistent urinary discomfort but no documented vomiting. Specimen collected before the first cefuroxime dose, according to the request form.

Macroscopic examination:
Appearance: Cloudy
Blood: 2+
Protein: 1+
Leucocyte esterase: 3+
Nitrite: Positive

Microscopy:
White blood cells: >100 × 10^6/L
Red blood cells: 24 × 10^6/L
Squamous epithelial cells: Few
Bacteria: Numerous

Culture:
Significant growth of a single organism: Escherichia coli, >10^5 CFU/mL.

Antimicrobial susceptibility:
Amoxicillin: Resistant
Co-amoxiclav: Susceptible
Cefalexin: Susceptible
Cefuroxime: Susceptible
Ciprofloxacin: Susceptible
Gentamicin: Susceptible
Nitrofurantoin: Susceptible
Trimethoprim: Resistant

Interpretation:
The findings support a significant Escherichia coli urinary tract infection. In the context of flank pain and rigors, the result is consistent with acute pyelonephritis rather than uncomplicated cystitis. The isolate is susceptible to cefuroxime, so the current prescription is microbiologically appropriate provided the patient is clinically improving and able to tolerate oral treatment. Nitrofurantoin should not be selected for treatment of pyelonephritis because it does not achieve adequate renal tissue concentrations.

Clinical comment:
Please review renal function, allergy status and clinical response when confirming treatment duration. Escalation to hospital-based assessment is advised if there is haemodynamic instability, ongoing rigors, inability to retain oral medication, worsening pain or concern regarding obstruction or sepsis. If symptoms have not substantially improved, repeat clinical assessment and consideration of renal imaging are appropriate. A treatment response review is recommended in about 4 weeks, or sooner if symptoms recur.

Validated and authorised by:
Dr Keron Riley, MBBS
Laboratory clinician
Report status: Final

Patient: duwa preece
Occupation: bus driver
Employer: Clwt Public Library
Address: 92 Davis Street, Cardiff / Caerdydd, CF15 5BF
Contact: 07700 900350

Thank you for attending the general medicine clinic. Your description of short bursts of the room spinning, particularly when turning in bed or looking upwards, together with nausea and some unsteadiness, is typical of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). This is caused by tiny calcium particles moving into one of the balance canals in the inner ear. It is unpleasant but usually settles, and it is not usually a sign of a stroke.

Your examination was reassuring. Eye movements were normal at rest, there was no new hearing loss, limb weakness, speech disturbance or persistent severe headache, and your walking was safe in the clinic. Positional testing brought on vertigo with characteristic eye movements, supporting the diagnosis of BPPV. There was no indication today for brain imaging or blood tests.

A repositioning manoeuvre was performed to guide the loose particles back into place. Please continue the home exercises demonstrated today, once or twice daily for the next several days, stopping if you develop severe symptoms. Move slowly when getting out of bed and use a handrail on stairs until your balance has returned. Avoid driving, cycling at traffic speed or working at height while an attack could occur.

You may use prochlorperazine as required for troublesome nausea or vertigo, following the directions on the dispensing label. It can cause drowsiness, so do not drive or drink alcohol after taking it. It should not be used routinely for prolonged periods, as it may slow recovery of balance.

Please seek urgent help through A&E or 999 if dizziness becomes continuous, or if it occurs with weakness, facial drooping, difficulty speaking, collapse, severe headache, chest pain or new double vision. Contact your GP surgery if symptoms are not improving, hearing symptoms develop, or the exercises are difficult to manage.

We will arrange a review in about 4 weeks, sooner if needed.

Patient: Ahona Craig
Clinical profile: 27 y/o
Admission date: 11/03/2045
Discharging service: Respiratory Medicine

Ahona Craig was admitted with a four-day history of productive cough, fever and right-sided pleuritic chest pain, with reduced appetite and increasing breathlessness on exertion. History was provided by the patient, with additional information from their sibling, M. Ahmad of WARINGSFORD. There was no history of haemoptysis, recent travel or aspiration. The admission diagnosis was community-acquired pneumonia (SNOMED CT 233604007).

On arrival, the patient was febrile at 38.4°C with a respiratory rate of 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation of 93% on air. Chest examination demonstrated coarse crackles and bronchial breathing at the right base. Chest radiography showed right lower-zone air-space consolidation without pleural effusion. Blood tests showed a raised white cell count and C-reactive protein, with preserved renal function. Blood cultures remained negative, and respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A, influenza B and SARS-CoV-2.

Treatment was commenced with intravenous antibiotics and fluids, followed by oral amoxicillin once the patient was clinically improved and tolerating food. Paracetamol was given for fever and pleuritic discomfort. Oxygen was required briefly during the first night but was discontinued the following morning, with stable saturations on room air thereafter. There was no clinical evidence of sepsis or respiratory failure, and escalation to critical care was not required.

At discharge the patient was afebrile, haemodynamically stable and mobilising independently. Cough and chest pain had improved, although some fatigue is expected during recovery.

Assessment and plan

Complete the prescribed course of amoxicillin and use paracetamol as directed for pain or fever. Maintain oral fluids and increase activity gradually. The patient should contact their GP surgery if symptoms worsen, fever returns, breathing becomes more difficult or oral intake falls. A follow-up chest radiograph should be arranged through primary care in approximately six weeks, particularly if cough or breathlessness persists. Discharge advice was discussed with the patient and M. Ahmad.

Mild reduction in right ankle dorsiflexion compared with the left; power otherwise preserved. Sensation slightly reduced over the right L5 distribution. Plantar responses flexor. No perineal sensory loss. Abdomen soft and non-tender.

Assessment: acute lumbar radiculopathy, likely disc-related. No current features of cauda equina syndrome or systemic spinal pathology.

Plan: continue paracetamol as directed and naproxen for a short course with food, provided no adverse effects. Encourage gentle activity and avoid prolonged bed rest. Safety-netted to return immediately for worsening weakness, new bladder/bowel disturbance, saddle numbness, fever or uncontrolled pain. GP review within one week; consider physiotherapy and MRI if symptoms persist or neurological deficit progresses.

Emergency Department Assessment – Clinical Genetics

Patient: Lavana Brooks
Date: 23rd November 2026
Referring healthcare organisation: Southport & Formby District General Hospital

The patient, aged 46 years, was reviewed in the emergency department with their partner present. They reported approximately two days of markedly reduced urine output, increasing fatigue and poor oral intake following several episodes of vomiting. No chest pain, breathlessness, dysuria or visible haematuria. The partner felt the patient was more tired than usual but remained coherent and mobilising independently.

On examination, the patient was alert and orientated, with dry mucous membranes and cool peripheries. Blood pressure was 102/64 mmHg, pulse 96 bpm, respiratory rate 18, temperature 36.7°C and oxygen saturations 98% on air. Heart sounds were normal, chest clear and abdomen soft without focal tenderness or palpable bladder. No peripheral oedema or rash. No features to suggest acute neurological deterioration.

Initial blood tests showed urea 18.2 mmol/L, creatinine 286 micromol/L and eGFR 18 mL/min/1.73 m². Previous renal function was not immediately available. Sodium was 134 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L and CRP 12 mg/L. FBC showed mild haemoconcentration without anaemia or leukocytosis. Urinalysis showed concentrated urine with trace protein and no blood or nitrites. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm without acute ST-T changes. Bladder scan showed 110 mL post-void residual. Renal tract ultrasound was requested to exclude obstruction.

Impression is acute kidney injury, most consistent clinically with volume depletion in the context of poor intake and vomiting; obstruction and medication-related renal injury remain to be excluded. Intravenous sodium chloride was commenced, with strict fluid balance and repeat renal profile planned. Potentially nephrotoxic and blood-pressure-lowering medicines were placed on temporary medication hold pending reconciliation and senior review. The patient was advised that urine output may improve with hydration, but deterioration would require urgent escalation.

Discussed with the medical registrar, who accepted the patient for admission for ongoing fluids, monitoring and investigation. Partner updated and aware of the plan.

Reviewed and documented by ibran preece.

Dear Rheumatology Team,

Re: mmachi salter
Address: 78 Fernlea Drive, Hamilton, ML3 0AA
Occupation: Barista

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient, who has developed a probable rheumatoid arthritis flare despite ongoing disease-modifying treatment. The specific question is whether the current symptoms represent active inflammatory disease requiring adjustment of therapy, and whether a short course of corticosteroid treatment or other bridging treatment would be appropriate.

Over recent weeks there has been increasing morning stiffness, with difficulty opening jars and managing buttons, together with swelling and tenderness affecting both hands. Fatigue has also become prominent and is limiting usual activities. Their partner reports that the patient is slower to get going in the morning and has needed more help at home, although there has been no fever, weight loss, rash, ocular symptoms or recent infection. There is no reported chest pain or breathlessness.

Current medicines are methotrexate, folic acid and naproxen. The patient reports taking these as prescribed, with naproxen providing only partial relief. There have been no recent medication changes. I have advised taking naproxen with food and avoiding additional over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medicines. We have discussed the importance of continuing folic acid and arranging routine monitoring blood tests if these are due.

On examination in the surgery, there was visible swelling and tenderness at several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, with reduced grip because of pain. The wrists were mildly tender. There was no obvious large-joint effusion, nodular rash or clinical evidence of an acute infection. Recent blood tests showed raised inflammatory markers, with stable renal and liver results; the full blood count was satisfactory.

Assessment and plan: probable rheumatoid arthritis flare with functional deterioration despite methotrexate. Please review disease activity, confirm whether methotrexate optimisation or an alternative disease-modifying strategy is indicated, and advise on interim symptom control. I have arranged follow-up in about 5 weeks, on 28/02/2028, but would welcome earlier advice if symptoms worsen.

Yours faithfully,

NICHA RAI

Discharge summary

Patient: OLUWADUNSIN WALL
Date of admission and discharge: 6th July 1996
Clinical age group: 82 y/o

You were admitted after a sudden episode of weakness in one arm, facial drooping and slurred speech. These symptoms had completely settled by the time you were assessed, which is consistent with a transient ischaemic attack (TIA). There was no ongoing weakness or speech difficulty during your stay.

CT brain imaging showed no acute bleed or established infarct. Subsequent vascular imaging did not identify a significant carotid narrowing. Heart rhythm monitoring remained in sinus rhythm, and the ECG did not show atrial fibrillation. Blood tests, including glucose and cholesterol assessment, were reviewed. Your examination was normal before discharge.

You have been started on secondary prevention treatment. Please take aspirin 75 mg once daily and atorvastatin as prescribed on your discharge medicines list. Do not stop either medicine without discussing this with your GP or the stroke team. If you develop unusual bruising, black stools, severe muscle pain or dark urine, seek medical advice promptly.

Your GP should review your blood pressure, cholesterol and vascular risk factors, and arrange repeat blood tests to assess the effect and tolerance of atorvastatin. A rapid-access TIA/stroke clinic referral has been requested for further review. Please attend any appointment offered, even though you are now feeling well.

If you experience new facial drooping, arm or leg weakness, difficulty speaking, sudden loss of vision or severe imbalance, call 999 immediately and say that you may be having a stroke. Do not drive yourself to A&E.

Your emergency contact, Kalifa, was recorded during the admission. Please ensure the hospital and your GP surgery have an up-to-date contact detail: oluwadunsin.wall43@outlook.com.

At discharge you were independently mobile, eating and drinking normally, and able to manage your medicines. This summary should be shared with your GP at your next appointment.

Date: 28th May 2020
Patient: L. Whittaker
MRN: 032677223
Contact: 07700 900856

Dear L. Whittaker,

Thank you for attending the clinical genetics clinic. You, the patient, aged 83 years, were reviewed regarding recurrent headaches which are most consistent with migraine. The attacks are usually one-sided and accompanied by nausea and discomfort with bright light. There is no history today of weakness, altered speech, collapse, persistent visual loss or headache waking you from sleep. Your neurological examination was reassuring, with normal eye movements, facial symmetry, limb power, sensation, coordination and gait.

The pattern does not currently suggest a progressive inherited neurological disorder, and genetic testing is not indicated for the migraine symptoms described. We discussed that migraine can nevertheless run in families because of a combination of genetic susceptibility and environmental factors. Keeping a headache diary may help identify triggers such as missed meals, dehydration, disrupted sleep, hormonal changes, stress or prolonged screen use. Please record the timing, duration, associated symptoms and medicines taken.

Continue sumatriptan at the start of a typical migraine, following the directions on your prescription. Naproxen may be taken with food if required and if you have no history of stomach ulceration, significant kidney disease, NSAID-sensitive asthma or an allergy to it. Avoid using acute headache medicines on more than two days in a week where possible, as frequent use can perpetuate headaches. Maintain regular meals, fluids and sleep.

We agreed that you should seek urgent assessment through A&E if a headache reaches maximum intensity suddenly, follows a significant injury, is associated with fever and neck stiffness, new weakness, confusion, seizure or persistent visual symptoms. Please contact your GP if the attacks become more frequent, change character, or the current treatment stops working; preventive treatment can then be considered.

I have not arranged genetic testing or routine genetics follow-up at present. A review of your headache pattern can be arranged in 11 days if symptoms remain troublesome, otherwise please continue care with your GP and bring the diary to your next appointment.

Reason for admission
Presented with sudden breathlessness, pleuritic right-sided chest pain and tachycardia. Initial oxygen saturations were reduced on air. Managed initially with supplemental oxygen and therapeutic anticoagulation. Oxygen requirement decreased steadily and was discontinued; saturations remained satisfactory on air, including mobilisation. Troponin was negative and ECG showed sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic change. Renal function and haemoglobin remained stable. No bleeding complications were observed. Supplemental oxygen is not required at discharge.

Condition and follow-up
Fit for discharge, independently mobile and haemodynamically stable. GP review is requested to assess ongoing anticoagulation, bleeding risk and duration of treatment, and to arrange appropriate investigation for unprovoked venous thromboembolism. Anticoagulation clinic follow-up will be arranged through Ulster Hospital.

Safety-net advice
Seek urgent medical attention for worsening breathlessness, syncope, haemoptysis, new chest pain, significant bleeding or black stools. Avoid contact sports and inform healthcare professionals that apixaban is being taken.

Given oral rehydration solution in the department with improvement in dizziness. Ondansetron as required prescribed for nausea, with advice to use oral rehydration solution after each loose stool. Disposition
Discharged home with C. Saunders. Safety-net advice given to return for inability to keep fluids down, worsening or localised abdominal pain, blood in stool, confusion, fainting or reduced urine output. GP review advised if not improving within 48 hours.

NHS number: 000 949 5569

Patient: mariel may
Referring organisation: Queen Elizabeth University Hospital

Clinical question
Please assess for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome and advise whether germline predictive testing is appropriate.

History
The patient attended the emergency department with marked concern about cancer risk after reviewing a significant family history. A first-degree relative has had breast cancer at a young age, and there is additional ovarian cancer in the wider maternal family. The patient reports no personal history of malignancy and no current breast, ovarian or constitutional symptoms. A friend accompanied the patient and provided emotional support.

The family history has not yet been verified against pathology or genetics records. The patient is specifically asking whether testing for the familial BRCA1 c.68_69delAG variant is indicated, and what surveillance or risk-reducing options would follow a positive result. They understand that testing may have implications for relatives and may not provide a definitive explanation if the familial variant is absent.

Assessment today
Observations were stable. Examination was non-contributory, with no breast or axillary abnormality identified on the limited assessment undertaken in A&E. No acute treatment was required. The patient is not taking regular medication.

Management to date
Reassurance was provided, and the patient was advised not to pursue private testing before specialist counselling. Written information regarding family-history documentation and the potential outcomes of genetic testing was supplied. The patient is keen to proceed and appears able to engage with pre-test counselling.

Request
Please review the pedigree, confirm the appropriate testing pathway, and advise on interim screening and referral to breast or gynaecology services if indicated. Consent can be revisited directly at appointment.

M. Oliver

Patient: Flynt Mackenzie
NHS number: 0007288078
Report/accession ID: 087290289
Clinic: Harleston Medical Centre
Occupation: Taxi driver

History
Reviewed in general medicine clinic with partner present. Ongoing tiredness for several months, worse towards the end of the day, with increased sensitivity to cold and constipation. No weight change, tremor, palpitations, neck swelling or dysphagia. Mood generally stable. Sleep is adequate. No recent intercurrent illness. Partner reports that concentration is sometimes reduced, although there has been no functional deterioration.

Medication
levothyroxine 75 micrograms once daily. Takes this before breakfast, usually with water, and reports good adherence. No recent dose changes. No other regular medicines reported. No known drug allergies documented.

Examination
Comfortable at rest. No obvious thyroid enlargement or cervical lymphadenopathy. Pulse regular. Hands warm, with no tremor. Reflexes and proximal limb power appear normal. Abdomen soft and non-tender; bowel sounds present. No peripheral oedema.

Assessment
Persistent symptoms may reflect suboptimal thyroid replacement, although examination is reassuring. Constipation may also be contributing to fatigue. No clinical features suggesting thyrotoxicosis or an acute systemic process.

Plan
Arrange thyroid function tests, FBC, ferritin, vitamin B12 and renal profile. Continue current levothyroxine dose pending results; reinforce administration separately from iron, calcium and antacids. Encourage fluids, dietary fibre and regular activity for constipation. Consider a short course of macrogol if symptoms do not settle with these measures.

Safety-netted to seek urgent review for chest pain, marked breathlessness, collapse or rapidly worsening symptoms. Results will be reviewed by Pavneet MEHMOOD at Harleston Medical Centre, with dose adjustment and follow-up arranged if indicated.

Discharge summary

Patient: EESHA ASIF
Clinical description: 17-year-old White male patient admitted under paediatrics with 24 hours of repeated vomiting, watery diarrhoea and noticeably reduced urine output. History was provided by the patient and their legal guardian, F. WATSON. There was no blood in the stool, persistent abdominal pain, rash or recent travel.

On arrival the patient was tired but alert, with dry lips and mildly delayed capillary refill. Observations at 08:15 showed a low-grade temperature, normal blood pressure and mild tachycardia. The abdomen was soft, with no focal tenderness or guarding. Urine output improved during the admission. Blood tests showed mild dehydration without significant electrolyte disturbance, and inflammatory markers were not raised. A stool sample was not required as symptoms settled and there were no red-flag features. The laboratory report was filed under report/accession ID 0356562383.

The patient was treated with small, frequent amounts of oral rehydration solution, initially supervised by nursing staff and then taken independently. Vomiting stopped after admission, and diarrhoea became less frequent. No antibiotics or anti-diarrhoeal medicines were indicated. Fluids and light food were reintroduced gradually and were tolerated. There was no need for intravenous fluids.

At discharge, the patient is bright, drinking well and passing urine normally. They may continue oral rehydration solution after loose stools, following the instructions on the packet, and should take regular small drinks. Normal food can be resumed as tolerated. Please avoid fizzy drinks and fruit juice until the diarrhoea has settled.

Seek urgent medical advice through NHS 111, the GP or the emergency department if there is persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down, no urine for a prolonged period, blood in the stool, severe or localised abdominal pain, increasing drowsiness, breathing difficulty or concern about deterioration. Good handwashing is important, and the patient should remain away from school or college until 48 hours after the last episode of vomiting or diarrhoea.

Follow-up with the GP is advised if symptoms have not substantially improved over the next few days. Discharge plan reviewed with the patient and legal guardian, with assent and questions addressed.

martyn bradbury
Paediatric clinician

History from father, Shain Croft. The patient, aged 2 years, was brought in with a barking cough for 3 days, hoarse voice and noisy breathing overnight. Father reports reduced sleep but normal fluid intake and urine output. No choking episode, drooling, rash, vomiting or known foreign-body exposure. Treatment and plan: Oral dexamethasone given in the department. Kept calm with father and observed after treatment; stridor resolved at rest and work of breathing remained normal. Supportive care discussed, including fluids and avoiding steam. Safety-net advice given to return immediately for stridor at rest, recession, cyanosis, drooling, exhaustion or inability to drink.

Disposition: Suitable for discharge home with father. Written croup advice provided. GP review if symptoms fail to improve; planned follow-up on 2 Mar 2035 if still symptomatic. Discharge assessment completed by Oreoluwa Choudhury.

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report

Patient: Ianna Kemp
MRN: 0458603
Home address: 65 Cardigan Walk, Darlaston, WS10 0AA
Specimen/report date: 3rd October 1988
Specimen: EDTA blood and serum
Request: Investigation of primary hypothyroidism in the context of persistent symptoms despite levothyroxine.

Clinical details:
Fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation reported. Levothyroxine is currently prescribed. No acute intercurrent illness recorded on the request form. Ordering clinician not stated.

Results:
TSH: 8.6 mIU/L (reference interval 0.27–4.20) – high
Free T4: 11.2 pmol/L (reference interval 12–22) – slightly low
Thyroid peroxidase antibody: 486 kU/L (reference interval <34) – positive
Thyroglobulin antibody: 178 kU/L (reference interval <115) – positive

Interpretation:
The biochemical pattern is consistent with under-replacement or inadequate absorption of levothyroxine in established primary hypothyroidism. Strongly positive thyroid autoantibodies support autoimmune thyroiditis. These findings do not indicate a primary genetic disorder; routine genetic testing is not recommended on the basis of this result alone.

Clinical comment:
Please confirm adherence, timing in relation to food, calcium, iron and antacid preparations, and whether any recent formulation change has occurred. If doses are being taken correctly, the treating clinician may consider a cautious levothyroxine adjustment according to local guidance. Repeat TSH and free T4 after a suitable interval, with review in about 5 weeks. Seek earlier assessment if marked deterioration, chest pain or palpitations develop.

Validated and reported by: Dr Hunaiza Walker, MBBS

Discharge summary
NHS number: 000 220 6561

Patient: Rajpal
Home address: 79 CASTLE MEADOW AVENUE, NEWTOWNSTEWART
Contact telephone: 07700 900392

Reason for admission
The patient, aged 82 years, was assessed in the emergency department following a sudden episode of left arm weakness, facial droop and slurred speech. Symptoms resolved before arrival and there was no persistent visual disturbance, headache or loss of consciousness. The history was provided by the patient and their partner.

Assessment and key results
On examination, speech was clear, facial movements were symmetrical and power was normal in all four limbs. There was no limb ataxia or sensory deficit. Capillary glucose was within the normal range, and routine blood tests did not show a significant electrolyte, inflammatory or haematological abnormality. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm. CT head showed no acute intracranial haemorrhage or established infarction. The clinical presentation was felt to be most consistent with a transient ischaemic attack.

Hospital course
The patient remained neurologically well during observation, with no recurrence of weakness, facial asymmetry or dysarthria. Swallowing was assessed safely and the patient mobilised independently. The case was discussed with the stroke team, who advised secondary prevention and rapid outpatient assessment. There was no indication for thrombolysis or thrombectomy because the symptoms had completely resolved and there was no disabling deficit at review.

Medication changes
Start aspirin 300 mg once daily for 14 days, then reduce to aspirin 75 mg once daily. Atorvastatin 80 mg at night has been commenced for vascular risk reduction. The patient was advised to continue their usual prescribed medicines unless instructed otherwise and to avoid non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs unless agreed with a clinician.

Condition and plan at discharge
Discharged home clinically stable with their partner. A rapid-access TIA clinic appointment has been requested for 16 Jun 2012, in about 6 weeks. The GP should review blood pressure, diabetes and lipid management and ensure completion of vascular risk assessment.

The patient was advised to dial 999 immediately for recurrent facial droop, arm weakness, speech disturbance or other sudden neurological symptoms, even if these resolve. They should not drive until they have checked the current DVLA advice.

Dear Clinical Genetics Team,

Re: thanujan nguyen

I would be grateful for your advice regarding whether clinical genetics assessment is appropriate for this patient, who has generalised anxiety disorder with persistent worry, poor sleep and prominent muscle tension. The specific question is whether the reported clustering of anxiety and related difficulties in the family warrants genetic counselling or any further investigation, rather than whether genetic testing should be arranged routinely for an isolated anxiety disorder.

thanujan nguyen describes excessive worry across work, health and family matters, with difficulty controlling the thoughts and a tendency to anticipate adverse outcomes. Sleep is fragmented, and there is sustained neck and shoulder tension without focal neurological symptoms. There is no history of mania, psychosis, substance misuse or self-harm. The patient remains engaged with daily activities and is able to work as a Pharmacist at Aird-dhubh Secondary School, although concentration is reduced during periods of increased worry. Jassem Rashid is recorded as the emergency contact.

The anxiety has been managed in primary care with psychoeducation, sleep-hygiene advice and referral for talking therapy. Sertraline is currently prescribed and has been tolerated without significant adverse effects; there has been partial improvement in the physical symptoms but ongoing worry and sleep disturbance. The patient understands that a genetics appointment may not lead to testing and is seeking clarification about whether the family history is clinically relevant.

On review, the patient was appropriately dressed and cooperative, with normal speech and good rapport. Affect was anxious but reactive. Thought form was coherent, with no delusional content or suicidal ideation. There was mild bilateral trapezius tension, but no weakness or sensory deficit. Recent primary-care blood tests, including thyroid function and full blood count, were reportedly unremarkable.

Assessment: generalised anxiety disorder with incomplete response to current treatment. A genetic contribution to common anxiety disorders is possible but is not, by itself, an indication for testing. I would appreciate your assessment of the family history and advice on whether counselling, targeted testing or no genetics input is most appropriate.

I will arrange a clinical review in about 12 weeks and continue sertraline and psychological support in the interim.

Yours faithfully,

Dr Tonichia Bedford, MBBS

Chloride                        101 mmol/L         95–108 mmol/L
Adjusted calcium                2.28 mmol/L        2.20–2.60 mmol/L
C-reactive protein              18 mg/L            <5 mg/L

Interpretation
The creatinine is elevated at 186 µmol/L, with a corresponding reduction in estimated glomerular filtration. In the reported clinical setting this is consistent with acute kidney injury, most likely contributed to by reduced oral intake and possible intravascular volume depletion. The eGFR should not be used to stage chronic kidney disease during an evolving acute illness. Mildly raised urea and C-reactive protein are also present. Potassium and bicarbonate are currently within the stated laboratory ranges.

Clinical comment
Please correlate with the patient’s known baseline creatinine, fluid balance, blood pressure and examination findings. Continue assessment of urine output and response to intravenous sodium chloride, avoiding fluid overload. Review recently held medicines before reintroduction, particularly nephrotoxic or renally cleared treatment, and ensure appropriate dose adjustment. Repeat renal profile after clinical reassessment, or sooner if urine output falls further, potassium rises, or the patient develops worsening nausea, breathlessness or confusion. Consider renal ultrasound if the cause remains uncertain or obstruction is clinically suspected.

This result should be interpreted alongside the clinical picture; urgent medical review is advised if deterioration is observed.

Nursing progress note

Patient: amaanah hassan
Clinical age: 8 y/o
Date: 18/12/2021
Ward: Paediatric inpatient unit

Presentation and observations:
Admitted with a painful sickle cell crisis. Mother, A. Logan, reports increasing pain in both legs and lower back since overnight, with reduced oral intake. Child alert but subdued, pale, and intermittently tearful. Pain reported as severe on the age-appropriate scale, initially 9/10. No chest pain, cough or increased work of breathing. Peripheral oxygen saturation maintained on air; respiratory rate and temperature within the prescribed observation parameters. Capillary refill approximately two seconds. Lips and mucous membranes dry.

Care delivered:
At 08:15, intravenous access was checked and remained patent. Prescribed intravenous fluids continued via pump; fluid balance commenced with regular urine monitoring. Morphine administered as prescribed following assessment, with observations repeated in accordance with the paediatric analgesia policy. Encouraged small, frequent sips of fluid and offered a preferred drink. Warm packs applied to the lower limbs and back; repositioned for comfort. Child and mother given clear explanation of the plan and advised to report increasing pain, breathlessness, fever, drowsiness or reduced urine output.

Response:
Thirty minutes after morphine, pain reduced to 5/10 and child was able to settle intermittently. Subsequently accepted several small drinks and passed a small volume of dark urine. No vomiting. Remains haemodynamically stable, with no new respiratory symptoms or focal neurological change. Cannula site clean, dry and without swelling.

Mobility and safety:
Mobilising only short distances with one nurse and close supervision because of pain and dizziness on standing. Falls precautions maintained; call bell and drink placed within reach. Safeguarding concerns not identified. Mother remains involved with consent and comfort measures; child assented to interventions where appropriate.

Escalation and next shift plan:
Continue prescribed analgesia, intravenous hydration, strict fluid balance and four-hourly observations, with earlier review if pain remains above the agreed target. Monitor for acute chest symptoms, fever, increasing sedation, worsening dehydration or reduced urine output. Covering clinician to review analgesic response and hydration status on the next round; seek urgent medical review for any deterioration.

Documented by A. Nguyen, Staff Nurse

Accident and Emergency Clinical Review
National Insurance number: ZZ 06 90 60 B

Patient: Alfin McIntosh
MRN: 055145238
Date: 20 December 2022
Contact: 07700 900163
Clinical age form: 21 y/o

Presenting complaint

Seen in the emergency department with an itchy erythematous rash affecting both forearms and the upper chest, associated with local skin irritation for 3 days. History was obtained from the patient, with additional details provided by their partner. There was no reported fever, facial swelling, wheeze, throat tightness, dizziness or vomiting. No mucosal ulceration, eye involvement or genital symptoms were described.

The eruption developed after recent use of a new fragranced body product. The patient has not started any other new prescribed medicines and reports no recent antibiotics. They have used hydrocortisone cream intermittently with partial reduction in itch and have taken cetirizine, also with some benefit. There was no history of blistering, skin peeling or similar widespread reaction.

Examination

The patient appeared comfortable and was not systemically unwell. Observations were within the expected range, with no respiratory distress. There was a sharply erythematous, mildly excoriated papular eruption over the volar forearms and scattered upper anterior chest. The involved skin was dry, without vesicles, pustules, weeping, crusting or palpable purpura. No facial or lip oedema was present. Oral mucosa was clear. There was no lymphadenopathy or clinical evidence of cellulitis. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Impression

The distribution, morphology and temporal relationship to a newly introduced fragranced product are most consistent with allergic contact dermatitis. There are no features at this assessment to suggest anaphylaxis, severe cutaneous adverse drug reaction, bacterial superinfection or a vesiculobullous disorder.

Management and follow-up

Advised immediate discontinuation of the suspected fragranced product and avoidance of other perfumed emollients until the eruption has settled. Continue cetirizine as previously directed and apply hydrocortisone cream sparingly to affected areas for a short course, avoiding the face, broken skin and skin folds. Regular bland emollient use was recommended, applied after washing and not shared with other household members.

Safety-net advice given to attend A&E urgently if facial or tongue swelling, breathing difficulty, rapidly progressive rash, blistering, skin pain, mucosal involvement or systemic symptoms develop. GP review is advised if the rash has not substantially improved within one week or if recurrent episodes occur, with consideration of dermatology referral and patch testing.

NHS number: 000 011 9149

Patient: Nahida
Admission date: 18 Oct 2023
Discharging service: Cardiology, Aberdeen Royal Infirmary

Nahida was admitted with increasing redness, pain and purulent discharge from a postoperative wound. The symptoms had developed over the preceding few days, with no reported rigors, chest pain, palpitations or breathlessness. The emergency contact, L. Waite from Gord, was updated during the admission with the patient’s agreement.

On assessment, the wound was tender with surrounding erythema and a small amount of purulent material. There was no clinical evidence of wound dehiscence, spreading cellulitis or systemic sepsis. Observations remained stable throughout the admission. Blood tests showed a mild inflammatory response, with no significant renal or hepatic abnormality. A wound swab was collected before antibiotics; the result was pending at discharge and will be reviewed by the treating team.

The wound was irrigated and dressed by the ward team. Following discussion with the surgical and microbiology services, oral flucloxacillin was commenced. The patient remained clinically well, with reducing pain and no further purulent discharge after treatment. There was no indication for operative washout during this admission.

Medication on discharge: flucloxacillin, to complete the prescribed course as detailed on the accompanying medicines list. Continue usual regular medicines unless otherwise advised. Analgesia may be taken as directed on the discharge prescription.

Condition at discharge: haemodynamically stable, mobilising independently and managing oral intake. The wound should remain covered with a clean dressing. Keep the area dry except when following the dressing-care instructions, and seek urgent medical advice if redness spreads, pain worsens, discharge increases, the wound opens, or fever or systemic unwellness develops.

The practice nurse or district nursing team should review the wound and dressing within 48–72 hours. A follow-up appointment with the postoperative team has been requested in 19 days. The pending swab result will be communicated to the GP surgery and patient if treatment needs to change. Fresh dressing supplies and written wound-care advice were provided before discharge.

Emergency Assessment – Clinical Genetics

Date: 6th February 2024
Patient: PEBBLES CARR
Emergency contact: modou pitt
Referring healthcare organisation: WITHYBUSH GENERAL HOSPITAL

Presenting complaint:
Sudden onset of marked palpitations while at rest, associated with central chest tightness, trembling and an intense fear of dying. Symptoms reached maximum severity within several minutes before gradually easing. No syncope, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, unilateral leg swelling or recent febrile illness. The patient reports similar, shorter episodes over recent weeks, usually during periods of heightened stress. No recreational drug use disclosed. Breathing retraining has been attempted, with partial benefit.

Assessment:
Alert, distressed but engaging appropriately. Speaking in full sentences. No cyanosis or increased work of breathing. Pulse regular on examination; heart sounds normal with no murmur. Chest clear bilaterally. No calf tenderness or oedema. Neurological screening examination normal. Current blood pressure 120/80 mmHg. Temperature and oxygen saturations within the expected range.

Investigations:
12-lead ECG showed sinus rhythm without acute ischaemic changes or pre-excitation. Capillary glucose was normal. Blood samples were taken for FBC, U&E, magnesium and thyroid function; no immediate biochemical abnormality was identified. Clinical assessment did not suggest pulmonary embolism, acute coronary syndrome or a significant arrhythmia.

Clinical impression:
Presentation most consistent with a panic attack, with autonomic symptoms and catastrophic fear during the episode. The patient was advised that the symptoms were real but that today’s assessment did not identify an acute cardiac or respiratory cause.

Management and disposition:
Supported in a quiet area and coached through slow diaphragmatic breathing. Symptoms settled during observation without medication. Discussed avoidance of excess caffeine and the importance of regular meals and sleep. Advised to arrange prompt review with the GP surgery for assessment of recurrent panic symptoms and consideration of talking therapy; continue breathing retraining.

Safety-net advice given to seek urgent help for persistent or exertional chest pain, collapse, severe breathlessness or sustained palpitations. Discharged home with modou pitt as emergency contact, subject to feeling back to baseline.

Seen and documented by melak kirby.

Occupation: Builder
Seen at: Dewi Sant Hospital

Reason for review
Assessment of recurrent unilateral headaches and suitability of ongoing migraine treatment in the context of intermittent awareness of a fast heartbeat.

History
Reports several months of episodic left-sided headache, usually accompanied by nausea and marked photophobia. Episodes last for several hours and improve with rest in a dark room. Sumatriptan is used at the onset of severe attacks, with naproxen if pain persists. No syncope, exertional chest pain or sustained breathlessness. Comfortable at rest. Pulse regular on examination; heart sounds normal with no murmur. Blood pressure acceptable in clinic. Chest clear. Neurological screening examination normal, including gait, speech and gross visual fields. No peripheral oedema.

Assessment
Migraine with unilateral headache, nausea and photophobia. Palpitations are brief and currently low risk from the history, but an arrhythmia should be excluded before assuming they are solely migraine-related. No clinical evidence of acute coronary syndrome or heart failure today.

Plan
• Arrange 12-lead ECG and seven-day ambulatory recording through Dewi Sant Hospital.
• Continue sumatriptan and naproxen as previously advised, avoiding excess frequency and taking naproxen with food.
• Keep a combined headache/palpitations diary, including triggers and medication use.
• Seek urgent assessment via A&E for prolonged palpitations, collapse, new neurological deficit or sudden maximal headache.
• GP review after monitoring; consider discussion with neurology if attacks become more frequent or treatment response worsens.

Clinical Genetics and Inherited Arrhythmia Review

Patient: Meredith Greaves
Occupation: Warehouse operative
Employer: Well Street Public Library
Address: 143 Stansfeld Road, St Albans, AL4 0AA
Contact: meredith.greaves74@gmail.com

Reason for review

Assessment requested following atrial fibrillation with symptomatic palpitations, fatigue and exertional breathlessness. The patient reports intermittent episodes of a rapid, irregular heartbeat, initially lasting several minutes and now occasionally persisting for longer periods. There has been no syncope, seizure-like activity or exertional chest pain. Breathlessness settles with rest. No recent infection or excess alcohol intake was identified.

Family history

The patient describes a family history of atrial arrhythmia affecting an adult child, although the available information is limited and no prior genetic result is known. There is no reported sudden unexplained death, cardiomyopathy, or implantable defibrillator in the wider family. A three-generation pedigree was commenced today; further clarification of diagnoses and ages at onset within the family would be useful.

Clinical findings and investigations

The patient was comfortable at rest, with no clinical evidence of fluid overload. Heart rhythm was irregularly irregular on examination, with satisfactory peripheral perfusion. There was no ankle oedema. Recent cardiac investigations demonstrate atrial fibrillation without documented ventricular pre-excitation. Echocardiographic information available for review does not suggest a major structural abnormality. Thyroid function and routine blood tests have reportedly been checked; the underlying results should be confirmed in the primary-care record.

Interpretation

The presentation is compatible with common atrial fibrillation, but the family history raises the possibility of familial susceptibility. At present there is insufficient evidence to attribute the arrhythmia to a defined monogenic syndrome, and genetic testing is unlikely to alter immediate management. Testing may be reconsidered if a relative is found to have cardiomyopathy, conduction disease, ventricular arrhythmia or a clearly pathogenic genetic result.

Plan

Continue apixaban and bisoprolol as currently prescribed, with adherence and bleeding risk reviewed by the usual treating team. The patient should seek urgent assessment for sustained chest pain, syncope, severe breathlessness or a persistent rapid rate. A consultant cardiologist should review rate-control adequacy and discuss rhythm-control options if symptoms remain troublesome. Family members with palpitations, unexplained collapse or documented arrhythmia should seek clinical assessment. The patient will provide any available family cardiology letters for review.

Emergency Department Assessment
National Insurance number: TN626338D

Patient: Mohammed-Musa D.
Location: Respiratory assessment area
Report/accession ID: 0732776021

Presenting complaint
Central chest pressure beginning at rest, associated with marked diaphoresis and nausea. Symptoms persisted for approximately 40 minutes before arrival and had eased but not fully resolved after initial treatment. No pleuritic component, haemoptysis, syncope or unilateral leg swelling. Layanne, the patient’s sibling, accompanied them and provided collateral history.

Assessment
Airway patent. Respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 97% on air, pulse 88/min regular, blood pressure 146/84 mmHg, temperature 36.7°C. Patient pale and clammy initially, with ongoing mild central pressure. Heart sounds dual without murmur; chest clear bilaterally. No calf tenderness or peripheral oedema. Abdomen soft and non-tender. Alert, orientated and mobilising independently.

Investigations
ECG at 08:15 demonstrated sinus rhythm with horizontal ST depression in the anterolateral leads and no ST elevation. Repeat ECG showed persistent changes without dynamic elevation. Initial high-sensitivity troponin was raised at 86 ng/L, increasing to 214 ng/L on repeat testing. Chest radiograph showed no focal consolidation, pulmonary oedema or pneumothorax. FBC, renal profile and coagulation screen were suitable for anticoagulation.

Management and clinical decision-making
Presentation, ECG findings and rising troponin are consistent with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction rather than primary respiratory pathology. Aspirin administered, followed by fondaparinux after review of renal function. Atorvastatin commenced. Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate was given with partial improvement in pressure; further doses withheld pending blood pressure and symptom review. No clinical evidence of heart failure or cardiogenic shock.

Discussed with the on-call cardiology team at ROYAL ALEXANDRA HOSPITAL. Patient requires admission to a monitored bed for telemetry, serial ECGs and cardiology review. Coronary angiography and ongoing antiplatelet strategy to be determined by cardiology. Patient and sibling informed of findings and plan. Contact detail recorded: 07700 900234.

Disposition
Admitted under cardiology/acute medical team in stable condition. Handover completed, with advice to report recurrent pain, arrhythmia or haemodynamic change immediately.

Referral from Accident and Emergency
National Insurance number: NK 11 58 04 D

Patient: Qiao Charlton
Address: 28 WESTWAY GARDENS, Newcastle
Occupation: University lecturer
Employer: KILLOUGH Housing Association

Dear Colleagues,

I am referring Qiao Charlton for urgent assessment of a diabetic foot ulcer affecting the plantar surface of the left forefoot. The specific question is whether there is underlying deep infection or osteomyelitis, and whether surgical or specialist podiatry intervention is required to achieve healing and prevent deterioration.

The patient reports approximately one week of increasing pain on weight-bearing, despite reduced sensation in both feet. There has been local discharge from the ulcer, without reported rigors or vomiting. They remain systemically well and have been managing the wound with dressings at home. Diabetes control has reportedly been variable. A friend accompanied the patient to the department and assisted with the history.

On examination, there is a plantar ulcer beneath the first metatarsal head, measuring approximately 1.5 cm across, with a shallow sloughy base and a small amount of purulent discharge. The surrounding skin is mildly erythematous and warm, extending less than 1 cm from the wound edge. There is reduced protective sensation to monofilament testing in both feet. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable, and the foot is warm. There is no crepitus, lymphangitis, or visible tendon or bone. Observations were reassuring, with no clinical evidence of sepsis.

Blood tests showed a mildly raised inflammatory response; renal function was suitable for the prescribed antibiotic. Plain radiographs did not demonstrate gas or a definite bony abnormality, although early osteomyelitis cannot be excluded clinically. A wound swab was obtained before treatment. The patient has commenced co-amoxiclav and has been advised to avoid weight-bearing on the affected foot, keep the dressing clean and dry, and attend promptly if fever, spreading redness or increasing pain develops. Ongoing wound care has been arranged through the surgery.

I would be grateful for same-day diabetic foot service review, including assessment of perfusion, debridement and off-loading requirements, with consideration of advanced imaging if the ulcer fails to improve. Please also review diabetes management with the consultant endocrinologist and advise on prevention of recurrence.

Yours faithfully,

Dr Nasar Bruce, MBBS

MOLECULAR GENETICS REPORT

Patient: N. Chamberlain
Report/accession ID: L26S36093
Report date: 1 Jun 2022
Reporting laboratory: Bupa Hospital Clare Park
Request: Predictive testing for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk. Ordering clinician: not stated.

Specimen
Peripheral blood in EDTA, received for germline DNA analysis. Specimen identity and quality were satisfactory for testing.

Result
Pathogenic familial variant detected: BRCA1 c.68_69delAG.

Interpretation
The identified BRCA1 variant is associated with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome. This result is consistent with a significantly increased lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer, with additional risks that should be considered during specialist counselling. The finding is germline in origin on the submitted blood specimen and is not, by itself, evidence of malignancy.

Clinical comment
The result should be discussed in a regional clinical genetics service, including review of the family pedigree, cancer surveillance, risk-reducing options and reproductive implications. Management should follow current UK clinical genetics guidance and be individualised after counselling. First-degree relatives may be offered targeted testing where clinically appropriate; relatives should be referred through their own healthcare team rather than tested without counselling.

No current treatment is recorded. The patient reports significant family history, ongoing cancer-risk concern and a request for predictive testing. This report should be interpreted alongside the documented familial result and the genetic counselling assessment. A negative result in another relative would not be inferred from this report.

Authorisation
Validated and released by Dr Kial Clay, MBBS, laboratory reporting clinician, Bupa Hospital Clare Park.

Paediatric Outpatient Clinic Review

Patient: Skyler-Grace
Age group: 4-month-old White female patient
Accompanied by: Father, Leeloo
Contact: 07700 900583

Reason for review
Review of neonatal jaundice following recent community bilirubin monitoring and a course of phototherapy. Father reports that the yellow colour of the skin is less marked, although feeding remains slow and the baby is sleepier than usual around feeds. This has been present for 3 days. No fever, vomiting, abdominal distension, pale stools or dark urine reported. Wet nappies continue, though fewer than the family would usually expect.

History
Father describes breastfeeding with supplementary expressed milk when the baby tires. Feeds are being offered regularly, with feeding support from the community midwifery team. No choking, sweating or colour change during feeds. No concerns regarding responsiveness between feeds. Pregnancy and delivery history reviewed in the referral; no additional risk factor identified today.

Examination
Settled in father’s arms, rousable to handling and briefly alert. Mild facial and upper chest jaundice remains. No bruising or rash. Anterior fontanelle soft. Mucous membranes slightly dry. Heart sounds normal with good peripheral perfusion; chest clear with no increased work of breathing. Abdomen soft and non-distended, no palpable liver or spleen enlargement. Tone and spontaneous movements appropriate on today’s assessment.

Impression
Improving neonatal jaundice after phototherapy, with ongoing sleepy feeding and mildly reduced intake. No clinical evidence of acute sepsis or biliary obstruction at present, but hydration and feeding adequacy require close observation.

Plan
• Continue feeding support; offer frequent feeds and wake gently for feeds if needed.
• Record feeds and wet nappies. Seek same-day medical advice if intake falls further, the baby is difficult to rouse, develops fever, has markedly fewer wet nappies, worsening jaundice, pale stools or dark urine.
• Repeat bilirubin and assess weight through the usual neonatal pathway if symptoms do not continue to improve.
• Follow-up appointment arranged for 09/03/2024; father understands the safety-netting advice.

Discharge summary

Rudhran was admitted under the acute gynaecology team with a several-day history of lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge and dyspareunia. The patient, aged 45 years, was reviewed with an emergency contact, L. Farmer, from HELEN'S BAY, kept informed with the patient’s consent.

On admission there was bilateral lower abdominal tenderness without guarding or rebound. Observations remained stable and there was no clinical evidence of sepsis. A pregnancy test was negative. Blood tests showed a mild inflammatory response, with otherwise satisfactory full blood count, renal function and liver enzymes. Urine testing did not suggest a urinary tract infection. Vaginal and endocervical swabs were taken; results were not available at discharge and will be reviewed by the treating team. A pelvic ultrasound showed no tubo-ovarian abscess or other acute pelvic collection.

The presentation was felt to be consistent with uncomplicated pelvic inflammatory disease. Treatment was commenced with ceftriaxone, followed by doxycycline and metronidazole. Pain improved with simple analgesia, and the patient was able to eat, drink and mobilise independently. There was no vomiting or worsening abdominal tenderness during observation.

Discharge plan

Complete the prescribed course of doxycycline and metronidazole exactly as directed. Avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole and for 48 hours after the final dose. Doxycycline can cause photosensitivity and should be taken with plenty of water while sitting or standing upright. Sexual intercourse should be avoided until treatment is complete, symptoms have settled and recent partners have been assessed and treated. Partner notification and sexual-health screening were discussed.

The patient was clinically well for discharge and understood the safety-net advice. Return to A&E urgently if pain becomes severe, fever develops, vomiting prevents medication being taken, faintness occurs or there is heavy vaginal bleeding. Please contact the sexual health service if symptoms persist or recur.

A follow-up review has been arranged for 7 May 2025, in about 3 weeks. The pending swab results will be checked at that review, with earlier contact if they require a change in treatment. A copy of this summary should be shared with the GP surgery.

Patient: DEYA CURRY
MRN: 021180122
Occupation: Taxi driver
Seen in the respiratory medicine clinic at Stroud General Hospital for review of recurrent headaches, with the history provided by the patient and their spouse.

They describe a longstanding pattern of left-sided throbbing headache, usually building over several hours and associated with nausea and marked photophobia. There has been no recent change in frequency or character. They deny fever, neck stiffness, head injury, visual loss, diplopia, weakness, facial droop, altered speech or collapse. The spouse has not noticed any episodes of unresponsiveness or abnormal movements. Headaches are more likely after poor sleep and may be aggravated by bright light. There are no current respiratory symptoms, including cough, wheeze or exertional breathlessness.

On examination, the patient was comfortable and able to give a clear account. Speech and gait were normal. Pupils were equal and reactive, with full eye movements and no reported visual field deficit. Facial movements and limb power were symmetrical. There was no neck stiffness. Chest examination was clear with normal air entry bilaterally.

Assessment

The presentation remains consistent with migraine without new focal neurological features. There is no clinical suggestion today of an acute secondary headache or active respiratory disease.

Plan

Continue the current migraine strategy and keep a headache diary recording timing, possible triggers, associated symptoms and use of analgesia. Take sumatriptan 50 mg at onset of migraine, following the prescribed directions, and avoid using it on more than the advised number of days each month. Naproxen may be taken with food when required, provided there is no history of gastrointestinal bleeding, significant kidney disease or intolerance. The importance of limiting frequent analgesic use was discussed.

The patient and spouse understand the red-flag symptoms requiring urgent assessment through A&E, including a sudden maximal headache, persistent vomiting, new weakness, confusion, seizure, fever with neck stiffness or a sustained visual disturbance. Routine follow-up with the GP will be arranged, with referral for further headache review if control deteriorates.

Signed by Zenil HANSON, clinician at Stroud General Hospital

Interpretation
Normocytic anaemia with neutrophilic leucocytosis, thrombocytosis and raised inflammatory markers. Mild hypoalbuminaemia and increased LDH. Findings are non-specific but compatible with an active inflammatory or lymphoproliferative process.

Emergency department follow-up note
National Insurance number: BG247636D

Patient: GHENA FLETCHER
Occupation: Carpenter
Employer: Hasguard Voluntary Service
Address: 142 Dare Road, Southgate, SA3 1AA
Contact: 07700 900010

You were assessed in the accident and emergency department because of several weeks of tiredness, intermittent dizziness and becoming short of breath more easily when walking or climbing stairs. You did not describe chest pain, black stools, vomiting blood or fainting. A friend accompanied you and helped provide the history.

Your examination was reassuring: blood pressure and pulse were stable, oxygen saturations were normal, and there was no evidence of heart failure or an acute neurological problem. The blood tests showed a low haemoglobin with small, pale red cells and reduced ferritin, which is consistent with iron-deficiency anaemia. Kidney function and the initial blood glucose were satisfactory. There was no indication for admission today.

Please continue ferrous fumarate as prescribed. Take it regularly; it may cause constipation, abdominal discomfort or darker stools. Taking it with water or a source of vitamin C can help absorption, whereas tea, coffee and calcium supplements should not be taken at the same time. Seek urgent medical attention through A&E if you develop chest pain, breathlessness at rest, collapse, heavy bleeding or rapidly worsening symptoms.

The cause of the iron deficiency still needs to be established. Your GP should review menstrual or other blood loss, dietary intake and any bowel symptoms, and arrange repeat full blood count and ferritin. Further investigation, including gastrointestinal assessment, may be considered depending on the history and response to treatment. Continue the tablets until the blood count and iron stores have recovered, unless side effects require an earlier review.

Please arrange a GP review in about 4 weeks, or sooner if symptoms are worsening. Bring an up-to-date list of medicines and any concerns about tolerating ferrous fumarate to that appointment.

Emergency Department Assessment

Patient: Maisey-Rose Coles
Report/accession ID: LAB-02104996
Referring healthcare organisation: Southampton General Hospital
Relative/emergency contact: Cullum HOLMES

Presenting problem
Three-day history of markedly reduced urine output with increasing fatigue and poor oral intake. Reports nausea but no vomiting, diarrhoea, dysuria, flank pain or visible haematuria. No recent contrast exposure. Medication history reviewed; no recent NSAID use reported. The patient has been advised by the referring clinical genetics team to attend for assessment following an abnormal renal blood result.

Assessment
Alert and able to give a coherent history. Dry oral mucosa and mild postural light-headedness. Heart sounds normal, regular pulse; chest clear bilaterally. Abdomen soft and non-tender, without palpable bladder or renal angle tenderness. No peripheral oedema or rash. Observations remained stable during assessment. Bladder scan showed no significant retention.

Investigations
Blood tests demonstrated acute deterioration in renal function, including creatinine 186 µmol/L, with mild urea elevation. Potassium was within the reference range and bicarbonate was preserved. Full blood count showed no significant anaemia or leucocytosis. Urinalysis: concentrated urine, trace protein, no blood or nitrites. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis or obstructing calculus.

Clinical impression
Acute kidney injury, most consistent with reduced circulating volume in the context of poor intake. No evidence currently of urinary obstruction, sepsis or significant electrolyte disturbance. The genetics history was noted, and the result was discussed with the on-call medical team at Southampton General Hospital.

Management and disposition
- Intravenous sodium chloride commenced with careful reassessment of urine output and fluid balance.
- Potentially nephrotoxic and blood-pressure-lowering medicines placed on temporary medication hold pending repeat renal blood tests.
- Oral fluids encouraged as tolerated; written advice given regarding symptoms requiring urgent return.
- Repeat U&Es arranged through the GP surgery within 24–48 hours, with same-day review if urine output does not improve.

Discharged home after clinical improvement and a further period of observation. Follow-up renal review booked for 2022-11-08.

The patient, aged 41 years, was reviewed in the assessment area following referral for reduced urine output, increasing fatigue and poor oral intake. Ruth, the patient’s adult child, is present and reports that fluid intake has been noticeably less than usual since yesterday, with no vomiting or diarrhoea. The patient denies chest pain, breathlessness or dysuria. They remain alert and able to answer questions appropriately.

At review, airway was clear and breathing unlaboured. Respiratory rate was 18, oxygen saturations 97% on air, pulse 92 regular, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg and temperature 36.7°C. Skin appeared slightly dry; mucous membranes were dry. No peripheral oedema noted. The patient has passed only a small amount of dark urine since arrival; urine output is being measured in a calibrated container. No urine sample obtained yet.

Blood results were reviewed by the covering clinician and are consistent with acute kidney injury. A peripheral cannula remains patent in the left forearm. Intravenous sodium chloride is infusing as prescribed, with the patient tolerating this without discomfort or signs of fluid overload. Temporary medication hold has been implemented pending review of the regular medicines and renal function. Oral fluids were offered in small, frequent amounts, and the patient managed approximately half a cup of water without nausea.

The patient mobilised from the trolley to the commode with one member of staff supporting and remained steady, although they reported fatigue afterwards. Falls precautions are in place: call bell within reach, trolley lowered and non-slip footwear provided. The patient and Ruth were advised to request assistance before standing. Escalation advice was given regarding worsening drowsiness, breathlessness, chest discomfort or inability to pass urine.

Assessment: clinically mildly dehydrated with ongoing oliguria, currently haemodynamically stable. Continue strict fluid balance, repeat observations and monitor response to intravenous fluids. Reassess urine output and oral intake during the next shift, maintain the medication hold until reviewed, and escalate promptly to the covering medical team if output remains poor or observations deteriorate. GP follow-up is planned in about 3 weeks.

Documented by M. Allen, registered nurse.

Clinical Genetics / diabetic foot review

Patient: havva wainwright
Occupation: bus driver
Report/accession ID: 063646819
Seen at: HOLYWELL COMMUNITY HOSPITAL
Clinician: S. Dickson, consultant endocrinologist

Reason for review: plantar ulceration beneath the right first metatarsal head, with reduced sensation and local discharge. Friend attended with the patient and assisted with the history.

History: Ulcer noticed approximately 10 days ago after a small area of broken skin. No reported fever, rigors or vomiting. Discharge remains scant and pale. Blood glucose readings have been variable. No previous lower-limb amputation reported. Footwear reviewed; advised not to walk barefoot.

Examination: Alert, systemically well. Plantar ulcer approximately 1.2 cm diameter, shallow, with a clean base and surrounding callus. Small amount of serous discharge. No malodour, fluctuance or exposed tendon. Mild local erythema, not extending beyond the forefoot. Dorsalis pedis pulse present. Reduced protective sensation to monofilament testing. Calf soft and non-tender.

Assessment: Neuropathic diabetic foot ulcer with mild local infection. No clinical evidence of osteomyelitis or critical ischaemia today.

Plan: Wound cleansed and redressed; continue district nursing wound care and pressure off-loading. Co-amoxiclav prescribed as documented on the medicines list. Safety-netted to attend A&E for spreading redness, increasing pain, fever, blackening skin or systemic upset. Urgent diabetic foot team follow-up arranged through HOLYWELL COMMUNITY HOSPITAL. Relevant family history and medication history to be clarified at the next genetics review. Consultant endocrinologist input requested regarding glycaemic optimisation.
