text:
Discharge summary

Patient: koby-jai hadley
Responsible consultant: General Medicine
Treating organisation: Royal Victoria Hospital
Report/accession ID: 0660977023

Reason for admission
koby-jai hadley presented via the emergency department with approximately 24 hours of worsening right lower-quadrant abdominal pain, nausea and loss of appetite. There was no reported diarrhoea or urinary symptom. bobby-john brennan, the patient’s spouse, provided collateral history and lives in CRANAGH.

Initial assessment and results
On examination, the abdomen was tender in the right iliac fossa with localised guarding but no generalised peritonism. Blood tests showed a raised white cell count and C-reactive protein. Renal function and liver enzymes were satisfactory. Urinalysis did not suggest urinary infection. CT abdomen and pelvis demonstrated an enlarged, inflamed appendix with surrounding inflammatory change, without abscess or perforation. The report was filed under the above report/accession ID.

Hospital course
The patient was admitted under the general surgical team, kept nil by mouth initially and treated with intravenous fluids, analgesia and intravenous co-amoxiclav. Symptoms and inflammatory markers improved following treatment. Laparoscopic appendicectomy was undertaken during the admission. The appendix was inflamed but not perforated; there was no drain requirement and no operative complication. Histology was consistent with acute appendicitis.

Post-operatively, oral intake was reintroduced gradually and tolerated. The patient mobilised independently, passed urine normally and remained afebrile. Port-site wounds were clean and dry with no evidence of bleeding or infection. Pain was controlled with oral paracetamol, and no further intravenous antibiotics were required.

Problem list
• Acute uncomplicated appendicitis, treated with laparoscopic appendicectomy.
• Post-operative abdominal discomfort, improving.
• No evidence of intra-abdominal collection or sepsis.

Discharge medicines
Paracetamol as required for pain, following the instructions on the dispensing label. Avoid taking other preparations containing paracetamol at the same time. No antibiotic course is required on discharge.

Follow-up and advice
The surgical team will review the patient in about 10 weeks, with routine wound and histology follow-up as indicated. The GP should be contacted if pain is not settling or if there are concerns about the wounds.

Please seek urgent medical attention for fever, increasing abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, abdominal swelling, redness or discharge from a wound, inability to keep fluids down, or feeling faint. Keep the wounds clean and dry, avoid strenuous lifting until comfortable, and gradually return to normal activity. Discharge advice was discussed with koby-jai hadley and bobby-john brennan, who confirmed understanding.

Emergency Department Assessment

Patient: Maneli S.
Home address: 47 Jubilee Place, Appleby-in-Westmorland, CA16 6AA
Contact: 07700 900706
Emergency contact: Evon FITZPATRICK

Presenting complaint:
Pruritic erythematous rash affecting both forearms, upper chest and neck, with burning skin irritation. Symptoms have been present for 3 days. The patient reports recent use of a new fragranced body wash and laundry product but no new prescribed medicines, food exposure or insect bite. No facial swelling, wheeze, throat tightness, dizziness or vomiting.

Past history and medication:
No previous episode requiring hospital treatment reported. Current treatment is hydrocortisone cream applied thinly to affected areas and cetirizine once daily, with limited relief. No known drug allergy documented.

Examination:
Alert, comfortable at rest and speaking in full sentences. Airway patent; no lip, tongue or facial oedema. Chest clear with equal air entry and no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination unremarkable. Widespread sharply erythematous, mildly raised plaques with superficial excoriations over the exposed forearms and upper chest, extending to the lateral neck. No vesicles, purulent discharge, fluctuance, mucosal involvement or skin sloughing. No fever or clinical evidence of cellulitis. Observations remained within acceptable range during assessment.

Investigations:
No blood tests or imaging indicated. A clinical photograph was obtained with consent for the record. Report/accession ID: 039430467.

Assessment and plan:
Findings are most consistent with allergic contact dermatitis, probably related to a newly introduced fragranced product. There is no evidence of anaphylaxis, Stevens–Johnson syndrome or secondary bacterial infection. Advised to stop the suspected products, wash clothing and bedding with non-biological detergent, and avoid scratching. Continue cetirizine once daily and use hydrocortisone cream sparingly for a short course, avoiding broken skin and the face unless specifically advised.

Discharged home with written safety-netting. Return urgently for breathing difficulty, mouth or eye involvement, rapidly spreading rash, blistering, fever or marked pain. GP review recommended if not improving within several days; consider dermatology or patch-test referral for recurrent symptoms.

Dear Community Paediatrics Team,

Re: Waris

I would be grateful for your assessment of this school-age child with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes mellitus. The specific question is whether there are additional psychosocial, educational or developmental needs requiring community paediatric input, and whether the family would benefit from coordinated support in managing diabetes outside the hospital setting.

The history was provided by the patient’s father, River-Blue, who reports several weeks of increasing thirst, frequent urination and noticeable weight loss. There has been no reported abdominal pain, vomiting, altered consciousness or nocturnal enuresis. The patient, aged 11 years, was reviewed urgently following detection of marked hyperglycaemia and commenced on a basal-bolus insulin regimen under paediatric diabetes team supervision. Glucose monitoring is being undertaken with capillary checks and recording of results; the family have also received advice regarding hypoglycaemia, sick-day rules and ketone testing.

At review, the child was alert and engaging, with no clinical evidence of dehydration or acute metabolic decompensation. Respiratory effort was normal, the abdomen was soft and non-tender, and there was no focal neurological abnormality. The father describes good initial engagement with treatment, although the family are understandably anxious about injections, fluctuating glucose readings and the practical implications for school attendance and activities. No safeguarding concerns have been identified. Parental understanding of insulin administration and hypoglycaemia management was checked, with further reinforcement provided.

The diabetes team has arranged ongoing specialist follow-up and has supplied a written management plan for the family and school. The family are due for review in about 7 weeks. In the interim, they have been advised to seek urgent medical attention for persistent vomiting, rising ketones, difficulty keeping fluids down, drowsiness or suspected diabetic ketoacidosis.

I would appreciate your assessment of the child’s adjustment to the diagnosis, functional needs within school and home, and whether further family support or liaison with education services is indicated. Please also advise whether any broader developmental or emotional assessment would be appropriate at this stage.

Yours faithfully,

safina abdullah
0783393

Nursing progress and handover note

Patient: Mylie-Mai
DOB: 5 Apr 1994
MRN: 018 484 422
Home address: 161 RED FORT PARK, BOHO

Reason for review: Rheumatoid arthritis flare with increased morning stiffness, painful swollen hand joints and marked fatigue. Patient reports difficulty making a fist and reduced ability to complete usual personal care. Sibling present and contributing to history with patient’s agreement.

Observations at 08:15: Alert and orientated, speaking in full sentences. Pain reported as 6/10 in both hands, worse on waking. Bilateral MCP and PIP joint swelling with reduced active movement; skin intact, no obvious erythema or focal heat. Afebrile. No chest pain, breathlessness or new rash reported. Oral intake adequate; encouraged regular fluids. Mobilising independently but slowly, with care taken during transfers.

Regular medicines confirmed: methotrexate, folic acid and naproxen. No missed methotrexate doses disclosed. Medication list checked and safety advice given regarding taking naproxen with food and avoiding additional over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medicines unless advised. Warm packs offered to hands, with partial improvement in stiffness. Rest periods encouraged while maintaining gentle range-of-motion exercises.

Priority risks: worsening joint inflammation, reduced function, gastrointestinal effects from naproxen and infection risk while taking methotrexate. Advised to report fever, acute deterioration, black stools, severe abdominal pain or rapidly increasing joint redness/swelling. Escalation required if unable to manage essential activities or if systemic symptoms develop.

Plan for next shift: reassess pain, hand swelling, mobility and oral intake; confirm blood monitoring is up to date and flag flare to the covering rheumatology clinician/GP for treatment review. Document response to supportive measures. Professional identifier for the reviewing doctor: 0453979.

General Medicine Clinic Note

Patient: ANESTIS DAVENPORT
Occupation: Warehouse operative
Employer: Grenofen Town Council
Address: 131 Wren View, Horam, TN21 0AA
Contact: anestis.davenport40@gmail.com

Reason for review
Assessment of suspected obstructive sleep apnoea following referral for loud snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing and persistent daytime sleepiness.

History
The patient attended with their adult child, who describes loud, disruptive snoring and repeated episodes of apparent breath-holding during sleep, followed by a snort or gasp. The patient reports unrefreshing sleep, morning headache on waking and difficulty remaining alert during quiet activities and whilst watching television. No history of cataplexy, sleep paralysis or vivid dream enactment. There have been no recent falls or driving incidents, although the patient has been advised not to drive if excessively sleepy.

Sleep pattern is otherwise regular. No night sweats, orthopnoea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. No recent sedative use. Alcohol intake is modest. The patient is keen to proceed with treatment and understands the importance of regular equipment use.

Examination
Alert and appropriately engaged in clinic. Speech clear. No respiratory distress at rest. Oropharyngeal examination shows a crowded upper airway. Chest clear with equal air entry. Heart sounds normal and there is no peripheral oedema. Blood pressure reviewed from the referral documentation and not repeated today.

Assessment
Clinical picture is strongly consistent with obstructive sleep apnoea, with significant daytime somnolence. No features today to suggest an alternative central hypersomnolence disorder or decompensated cardiorespiratory disease.

Plan
• Arrange/confirm overnight sleep study and respiratory sleep service assessment.
• Continue continuous positive airway pressure once issued, with mask-fit support and adherence monitoring through the sleep service.
• Discussed avoiding alcohol and sedating medicines near bedtime, maintaining a regular sleep routine, and weight management where appropriate.
• Safety-netted regarding drowsiness whilst driving or operating machinery; patient will stop and seek advice if this develops.
• Review in about 4 weeks to discuss sleep-study findings, symptom response and CPAP tolerance.

The patient and accompanying adult child were able to ask questions and agreed with the plan.

Discharge summary
National Insurance number: NT 12 03 21 B

Patient: Yva Ratcliffe
MRN: 0921821
Address: 24 Crichton's Close, Gateside, KY14 6AA
Responsible consultant: Dr Sascha Blair, MBBS, GMC reference GMC 0854065
Admission area: Respiratory medicine

Reason for admission

Admitted with worsening lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge and deep dyspareunia for 3 days. There was no reported vomiting, urinary retention or gastrointestinal bleeding. Initial assessment identified bilateral lower abdominal tenderness with cervical motion tenderness, in keeping with pelvic inflammatory disease. The patient was haemodynamically stable and did not require respiratory support despite admission under the respiratory medicine service.

Investigations and hospital course

Urine pregnancy testing was negative. Blood tests showed a mild inflammatory response without significant renal or hepatic abnormality. Urinalysis did not suggest a urinary tract infection. Vaginal and cervical swabs were collected for gonorrhoea, chlamydia and other sexually transmitted infections; results were pending at discharge and will be followed up by the appropriate clinical team. Pelvic ultrasound did not demonstrate a tubo-ovarian abscess or free pelvic fluid.

Treatment was commenced with intramuscular ceftriaxone, followed by doxycycline and metronidazole. Abdominal pain and discharge improved during observation, and the patient remained afebrile with stable observations. There was no indication for operative intervention or inpatient drainage.

Medication on discharge

Continue doxycycline to complete the prescribed course and metronidazole as directed on the discharge prescription. Ceftriaxone has been given as a single inpatient dose and does not require further administration unless advised following review. Avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole and for the period advised by the pharmacist after the final dose. Simple analgesia may be used if required, provided the packet instructions are followed.

Assessment and plan

This presentation is most consistent with uncomplicated pelvic inflammatory disease, clinically improved with treatment. Sexual intercourse should be avoided until treatment is complete, symptoms have resolved and recent sexual partners have been assessed and treated where indicated. Please attend the GP surgery or sexual health service for review of outstanding swab results and partner notification. Seek urgent help via A&E if severe or increasing pain, fever, fainting, persistent vomiting or heavy vaginal bleeding develops.

Discharged home in stable condition with the above advice.Dr Sascha Blair, MBBS
Consultant physician

Emergency Department Assessment
NHS number: 000 085 3632

Patient: Iov
Department: Accident and Emergency
Presenting complaint: Central chest pressure with sweating and nausea.

History of presenting complaint:
Sudden central, heavy chest pressure began at rest and persisted for approximately 45 minutes before arrival. Associated diaphoresis and nausea, without vomiting. No pleuritic component, haemoptysis, syncope or recent febrile illness. A friend, S. Maynard, accompanied the patient and confirms marked pallor during the episode. No previous similar pain reported. Medication history reviewed; no known drug allergy documented.

Examination:
Alert and appropriately responsive. Cool, clammy peripheries initially. Pulse regular, blood pressure stable, respiratory rate normal and oxygen saturation maintained on air. Heart sounds dual with no murmur. Chest clear bilaterally. No calf tenderness or unilateral leg swelling. Abdomen soft and non-tender. Peripheral perfusion satisfactory on reassessment.

Investigations:
Initial ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with horizontal ST-segment depression in the lateral leads and no ST elevation. Repeat tracing showed persistent changes without dynamic ST elevation. High-sensitivity troponin was elevated on the admission sample and increased on repeat testing, supporting non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Chest radiograph showed no acute abnormality. Routine blood tests showed no major electrolyte disturbance and renal function suitable for prescribed treatment.

Treatment and decision-making:
Given aspirin following ECG review, with fondaparinux and high-intensity atorvastatin commenced. Analgesia and antiemetic treatment provided, with improvement in pressure and nausea. Findings are consistent with NSTEMI rather than pulmonary embolism, aortic syndrome or gastrointestinal pain. Discussed urgently with cardiology at Royal Gwent Hospital; accepted for monitored admission and early invasive-risk assessment. Continue telemetry and serial ECG/troponin testing. Escalate immediately for recurrent pain, haemodynamic instability or arrhythmia.

Disposition:
Admit to the acute cardiac pathway under cardiology. The patient and S. Maynard understand the diagnosis, treatment and need for monitoring. Cardiology review arranged for 12 May 2024, in about 5 weeks, after the acute admission.

Documented and signed by: SASSI NICHOLLS

Date: 28th June 2025
NHS number: 000 820 3068

Dear Cardiology Team,

Re: ESMAE POLLARD  
MRN: 08713688  
Home address: 38 DRUMAKNOCKAN LANE, BAILEYSMILL

I would be grateful for your assessment of recurrent palpitations occurring in the context of generalised anxiety disorder, and advice on whether any cardiac investigation is indicated. The patient describes a persistent sense of worry, difficulty settling to sleep and associated muscle tension. Over the past few weeks there have also been intermittent episodes of a rapid, forceful heartbeat, usually at rest and without a clear exertional trigger. One episode was accompanied by light-headedness but there has been no syncope, chest pain, breathlessness or ankle swelling.

The patient attended A&E after palpitations had been present for 3 days. Initial observations were reassuring, and an ECG reportedly showed sinus rhythm, although I do not have the tracing available for review. There is no known structural heart disease. The patient does not report stimulant use and has reduced caffeine intake. There is no reported family history of sudden cardiac death.

Sertraline is currently prescribed for anxiety. It has helped somewhat with the persistent worry, although sleep remains poor. We have discussed regular meals, limiting caffeine, sleep hygiene and breathing exercises. The patient remains concerned that the palpitations represent a heart problem, and this health anxiety is contributing to ongoing distress.

On review in the surgery, the patient was comfortable at rest. Pulse was regular and blood pressure was within the usual range. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable, with no peripheral oedema. I have requested routine blood tests, including full blood count, renal function, thyroid function and magnesium, and will forward the results when available.

Assessment and plan: palpitations without documented arrhythmia, occurring alongside generalised anxiety disorder. Please consider ambulatory ECG monitoring and advise whether echocardiography or further cardiology review is required. The patient has been advised to seek urgent medical attention for sustained palpitations, syncope, chest pain or significant breathlessness. A primary care review is arranged for 28th June 2025.

Yours sincerely,

ijaaz boyd

Nursing progress / handover

Reports ongoing productive cough with yellow sputum and right-sided pleuritic pain on deep inspiration or coughing. No chest pain at rest. Felt hot earlier but now says feverishness has eased.

SNOMED CT 233604007 recorded for community-acquired pneumonia. Continue observations, oxygen saturation monitoring and prescribed antibiotics. Handover completed to incoming nurse. Documented by Tawanda Wallis.

text:
Paediatric Neurology Outpatient Clinic

Patient: Mashud P.
Contact: 07700 900269
Accompanied by: amadea hughes, uncle

Thank you for attending clinic today with your uncle. As a 12-year-old Caucasian female patient, you were able to describe the headaches clearly, and your uncle added useful information about their frequency and effect on your routine.

You report recurrent left-sided headaches, usually building over several hours and lasting until sleep. These are associated with nausea and marked sensitivity to light. There has been no collapse, persistent vomiting, weakness, altered speech, visual loss between attacks or headache waking you regularly at night. Examination today was reassuring: you were alert, communicating normally, and had full eye movements, normal pupils, symmetrical facial movements, normal limb power and coordination, and a steady gait. There was no neck stiffness.

The pattern is most consistent with migraine without a concerning neurological feature at present. We discussed that keeping a headache diary can identify triggers such as missed meals, dehydration, poor sleep, prolonged screen use and stress. Please aim for regular meals, sufficient fluids, a consistent sleep routine and breaks from screens.

At the start of a typical attack, take sumatriptan as previously prescribed, together with naproxen if needed and if you have eaten. Avoid using acute medication on more than two days each week, as frequent use can itself maintain headaches. Do not take naproxen if you have been advised to avoid anti-inflammatory medicines, and seek advice if you develop stomach pain, wheeze or an allergic reaction.

Please seek urgent assessment through NHS 111, the emergency department or A&E for a sudden maximal headache, new weakness, confusion, seizure, persistent vomiting, fever with neck stiffness, or a significant change in the usual pattern.

We will review your progress in about 5 weeks, on 17 June 2035. Please bring the headache diary and a list of any doses taken. Confidential time without family members was offered, and you were happy for your uncle to remain involved today.

Discharge summary
NHS number: 0008846368

Patient: Tahiry
Clinical context: The patient, aged 10 months, was admitted to paediatrics with 24 hours of frequent vomiting, watery diarrhoea and reduced urine output. History was provided by his father, Olivia-Rey, who reported fewer wet nappies and difficulty retaining feeds. No blood was seen in the stool and there was no reported rash or seizure.

On arrival, heart rate 128 beats/minute, with mildly dry mucous membranes and reduced tears. Capillary refill was 2 seconds; peripheral perfusion remained satisfactory. Abdomen was soft and non-distended, with no focal tenderness. Blood glucose was normal. Clinical assessment was consistent with viral gastroenteritis causing mild-to-moderate dehydration. No features suggested an acute surgical abdomen or serious bacterial infection.

Management and progress: Oral rehydration solution was given in small, frequent volumes with a period of observation. Vomiting settled and urine output improved. Feeds were gradually restarted and tolerated. There was no requirement for intravenous fluids or antibiotics. The infant remained clinically stable overnight and was reviewed with his father before discharge.

Discharge treatment:
• Oral rehydration solution, offered frequently after each loose stool or vomit.
• Continue usual milk feeds, offering smaller amounts more often.
• Supportive care only; no new prescription medicines.

Safety-netting: Return to the emergency department if unable to keep fluids down, markedly drowsy, persistently vomiting, passing blood in the stool, developing breathing difficulty, or producing substantially fewer wet nappies. Seek urgent advice if concerned.

Follow-up: Arrange review with the GP surgery if symptoms are not clearly improving. Father understands the plan and has been given written hydration advice.

Home address: 81 BALLYCAIRN DRIVE, MAGHERALIN
Contact: 07700 900186

National Insurance number: TN 52 50 18 B

Patient: Muqadaas
Home address: 98 Harbour View Road, Lighthorne Heath, CV33 8AA
Contact: 07700 900864
The patient, aged 84 years, was reviewed with their sibling present.

Presenting complaint
Watery diarrhoea for 3 days with four episodes of vomiting and intermittent, cramping central abdominal pain. No blood or mucus reported. Sibling reports reduced oral intake but ongoing urine output. No recent antibiotics, travel or known sick contacts.

Examination
Alert, conversing normally. Dry lips, warm peripheries, capillary refill 2 seconds. Pulse 104 bpm, BP 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on air, temperature 37.8°C. Abdomen soft, mild diffuse tenderness, no guarding or rebound. Bowel sounds present. No rash.

Investigations
Urinalysis: concentrated, otherwise negative. Capillary glucose 5.6 mmol/L. FBC and U&Es sent; no immediate biochemical evidence of significant dehydration. ECG obtained because of location in cardiology area: sinus tachycardia, no acute ST-T changes.

Impression
Likely viral infectious gastroenteritis with mild volume depletion. No clinical features of acute abdomen or sepsis.

Treatment and plan
Oral rehydration solution given in small, frequent volumes; tolerated 250 mL during observation. Ondansetron as required advised. Continue oral rehydration solution at home, avoid fruit juice, and take light food as tolerated. Safety-netting given regarding persistent vomiting, reduced urine, blood in stool, worsening pain, lethargy or breathing difficulty. Return to A&E if these occur; GP review if not improving.

Discharge
Discharged home with sibling. Daniah Bourne, clinician.

Dear Clinical Genetics Team,
NHS number: 000 995 4664

Re: Mariyam Donnelly

I would be grateful for your assessment of Mariyam Donnelly in relation to obstructive sleep apnoea and the possibility of an inherited predisposition. They report several years of very loud snoring, with Maab Ayres regularly witnessing pauses in breathing during sleep followed by choking or gasping. There is also troublesome daytime somnolence, including a tendency to nod off during quiet activities. The symptoms have affected concentration and general functioning at work.

Occupation: software developer
Employer: Coldrain Housing Association

A sleep assessment has supported obstructive sleep apnoea, and continuous positive airway pressure has been prescribed. The machine is used on most nights, although adherence has been inconsistent because of mask discomfort and nasal blockage. When it is worn throughout the night, Mariyam Donnelly notices less morning headache and improved alertness. There has been no reported episode of collapse, seizure-like activity or unexplained nocturnal injury. Maab Ayres has not observed unusual movements suggestive of parasomnia.

On review today, the patient remains clinically stable. They describe persistent tiredness despite treatment, but no exertional chest pain or unexplained breathlessness. We discussed avoiding driving when sleepy, maintaining regular sleep hours and taking the CPAP equipment to any sleep-related appointment. The patient understands that untreated sleep apnoea can contribute to cardiovascular and occupational risk.

Assessment

Obstructive sleep apnoea with witnessed apnoeas and residual daytime somnolence despite continuous positive airway pressure. The family history is not fully documented, and I would appreciate advice on whether the presentation warrants genetic assessment, testing or broader family screening.

Plan

Please review the clinical history and advise whether a genetics consultation is appropriate, including any features that would suggest a syndromic sleep-disordered breathing condition. I will arrange review of CPAP usage data and mask fit in parallel. If no genetic investigation is indicated, advice on the most appropriate sleep-medicine pathway would be helpful. Follow-up with the GP is planned in 14 days.

Yours sincerely,

Akwasi Sharif

LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: Razika ARIF
MRN: 06567257
Contact detail: razika.arif65@hotmail.com
Specimen: Serum, collected during assessment of acute painful swollen joint
Requesting clinician: Not stated
Clinical indication: Suspected gout flare with acute joint pain, swelling and erythema.

Results
Urate: 510 µmol/L (reference interval 210–420) – high
Creatinine: 96 µmol/L (reference interval 45–90) – mildly high
eGFR: 68 mL/min/1.73 m²
CRP: 38 mg/L (reference interval <5) – high
White cell count: 10.8 × 10⁹/L (reference interval 4.0–11.0)
Neutrophils: 8.2 × 10⁹/L (reference interval 2.0–7.5) – mildly high
ALT: 24 U/L (reference interval 10–50)
ALP: 81 U/L (reference interval 30–130)

Interpretation
Hyperuricaemia with a modest inflammatory response. The findings support, but do not independently establish, an acute gout flare. Serum urate may be normal during an attack; joint aspiration for crystal analysis should be considered if the diagnosis remains uncertain or infection is a concern.

Clinical comment
Please correlate with examination, particularly fever, skin breaks and the presence of an effusion. Septic arthritis requires urgent exclusion if clinically suspected. Renal function is adequate for cautious short-course treatment but should be reviewed before further NSAID use. The reported naproxen and colchicine should be reconciled with the GP record, including duration and response; avoid duplicate NSAIDs and review gastrointestinal and renal risk.

Follow-up review: 11/05/2004

Patient: G. Dyer
Home address: 84 RUSHCROFT AVENUE, THE TEMPLE
Contact email: gwilym.dyer28@outlook.com
Relative present: Sibling, SALEHA BUTCHER

Nursing progress note – respiratory medicine

Assessment:
Reports increased morning stiffness with painful swelling of both hands, worse around the MCP and PIP joints. Describes fatigue and reduced grip, making dressing and opening containers difficult. No chest pain or new breathlessness. Alert, orientated and communicating appropriately. Temperature 36.8°C, pulse 84 bpm, BP 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, SpO₂ 97% on air. Chest clear bilaterally. Hands warm with symmetrical joint swelling and tenderness; no skin breakdown noted.

Mobility and intake:
Mobilising independently to the bathroom, though slowly on rising. No falls reported. Eating approximately half of meals owing to fatigue; taking fluids well. Passed urine normally. Encouraged to request assistance if pain or dizziness develops.

Interventions:
Regular methotrexate and folic acid confirmed on medicines chart. Naproxen administered with food as prescribed; patient advised to report dyspepsia or melaena. Warm packs applied to both hands with partial relief. Supported with washing and dressing. Rest periods planned between activities.

Response and risks:
Pain reduced from 7/10 to 4/10 after intervention. No fever or clinical evidence of infection at present. Monitor closely for infection, gastrointestinal intolerance, reduced function and falls risk. At 08:15, patient remained comfortable and was resting in chair.

Escalation and plan:
Discussed ongoing swelling and functional limitation with the covering medical team; review requested, including consideration of inflammatory markers and rheumatology input via Royal Victoria Hospital. Continue observations, prescribed medicines and gentle mobilisation. Handover to next shift to reassess pain, hand swelling, oral intake and mobility.

text:
Accident and Emergency Clinical Note

Patient: A. Farooq
Occupation: software developer
Date: Today
Report/accession ID: 0542420737

Presenting complaint
Itchy erythematous rash affecting both forearms and the upper chest for 3 days. The patient reports increasing skin irritation after using a new fragranced body wash. No previous reaction to this product is known. No facial swelling, wheeze, throat tightness, dizziness, fever or vomiting. Emergency contact recorded in the demographic record.

Assessment
Alert and comfortable at rest. Airway patent; speaking in full sentences. No lip, tongue or facial oedema. Chest clear with no wheeze. Skin shows patchy erythema with fine papules over the volar forearms and upper chest, with excoriation but no blistering, weeping or mucosal involvement. No features of cellulitis. Observations stable during assessment.

Impression
Allergic contact dermatitis, likely triggered by a fragranced topical product. There is no clinical evidence of anaphylaxis, Stevens–Johnson syndrome or secondary bacterial infection at present.

Plan
- Stop the new body wash and avoid fragranced soaps, creams and detergents until resolved. Use lukewarm water and an unperfumed emollient.
- Continue hydrocortisone cream as a thin layer to affected areas twice daily for up to 7 days; avoid the face, broken skin and skin folds.
- Cetirizine may be taken once daily for itch, following the packet instructions.
- Discussed gentle skin care and avoidance of scratching; keep nails short.
- Return to A&E urgently if swelling of the lips or tongue, breathing difficulty, widespread blistering, skin peeling, fever or rapid progression develops.
- Arrange GP review if not clearly improving within one week, or sooner if the rash becomes painful, hot, oozy or increasingly swollen.

The patient understood the advice and was discharged home in a stable condition.

Treating clinician: Nikolay Lamb
Healthcare organisation: Photopheresis Service, Royal Hallamshire Hospital

Emergency Department Assessment

Patient: abdur-rahman leigh
Contact: 07700 900928
Report/accession ID: 07887335
Accompanied by spouse, K. Hodge
Referring healthcare organisation: University Hospital of Wales

Presentation
Sudden onset of forceful, rapid heartbeat while waiting in the clinical genetics department, with central chest tightness, trembling, shortness of breath and an intense fear of dying. Symptoms began at approximately 08:15 and reached maximum intensity within several minutes. No syncope, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, unilateral leg swelling or recent febrile illness. Reports previous brief episodes of similar symptoms but no established cardiac diagnosis. No alcohol or recreational drug use disclosed.

Examination
Alert, distressed initially but able to engage appropriately. Speaking in full sentences. Peripheral perfusion normal; chest clear bilaterally with no wheeze or crepitations. Heart sounds normal, regular rhythm at assessment, no murmur. No calf tenderness or oedema. Abdomen soft and non-tender. Neurological examination grossly normal. No features of psychosis or immediate safeguarding concern.

Observations
Temperature 36.7°C; pulse 96 bpm and regular; BP 132/78 mmHg; respiratory rate 18/min; oxygen saturations 99% on air.

Investigations
12-lead ECG: sinus rhythm, no acute ST-segment or T-wave changes. Capillary glucose 5.4 mmol/L. High-sensitivity troponin not indicated following clinical review and reassuring ECG, with no ongoing chest pain or cardiac risk features. Pregnancy status discussed where clinically applicable.

Clinical impression
Presentation is most consistent with a panic attack with prominent autonomic symptoms. Acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism and significant arrhythmia considered less likely on examination and initial assessment.

Management and disposition
Provided reassurance, calm surroundings and coached breathing retraining, with gradual reduction in palpitations and chest tightness. Discussed the physiology of panic and avoidance of over-breathing. No medication required in the department.

Discharged home with advice to contact the GP surgery for review of recurrent episodes and consideration of psychological support. Return immediately for persistent or exertional chest pain, collapse, sustained irregular palpitations, severe breathlessness or new neurological symptoms.

Community Paediatrics referral

Patient: Ottilie-Mae Brooks
Clinical age: 14 y/o
Accompanied by: aunt, K. BUCKLEY

Dear Community Paediatrics Team,

I am referring Ottilie-Mae Brooks for assessment of persistent atopic eczema, particularly because itching and poor sleep are continuing despite regular treatment. The specific question is whether the diagnosis and current management remain appropriate, and whether specialist advice on steroid-sparing treatment or wider support would be helpful.

The history was discussed with Ottilie-Mae Brooks and their aunt. There is dry, inflamed skin affecting the flexures of both arms, the backs of the knees and the neck. Scratching is most troublesome overnight, with frequent waking and tiredness the following day. There has been no fever, weeping, crusting or rapidly spreading redness to suggest a significant secondary bacterial infection. No breathing or swallowing symptoms have been reported. Ottilie-Mae Brooks is comfortable discussing the impact on sleep and daily activities privately, with their aunt involved in the consultation as agreed.

Current treatment is an emollient applied generously several times daily and topical hydrocortisone to active areas during flares. The family report that this settles the inflammation temporarily, but symptoms recur when treatment is stopped. We reviewed using emollient as a soap substitute, applying it in the direction of hair growth, and continuing it between flares. They understand that topical steroid should be applied as a thin layer to active eczema only, according to the prescribed course, rather than avoided altogether because of concern about skin thinning.

On examination, the skin is generally dry, with erythematous eczematous patches and excoriations in the areas described. There is no purulent discharge, honey-coloured crusting or mucosal involvement. Sleep disruption is the main functional consequence at present. Mood is understandably affected when symptoms are severe, but there are no immediate safeguarding concerns identified today.

Please assess severity, triggers and adherence, and advise whether a stepped-up topical regimen, steroid-sparing agent, infection plan or dermatology input is indicated. A review with the family is planned in about 7 weeks, or sooner if the eczema becomes painful, infected or rapidly worsens.

Yours sincerely,

Paniz Ward
Community clinician, MONKSTOWN

PAEDIATRIC MICROBIOLOGY REPORT

Patient: HIYABEL BRADBURY
Clinical context: The patient, aged 4 years, was reviewed following a two-day history reported by the mother of dysuria, urinary frequency and lower abdominal discomfort. No loin pain, vomiting or documented fever. Nitrofurantoin has been commenced pending culture.

Report/accession ID: 084439865
Specimen: Midstream urine, received in a sterile universal container
Collection/report date: 09/11/2022
Request: Urinalysis and culture; ordering clinician not stated

SPECIMEN QUALITY

The accompanying specimen-date entry of 31/04/2025 was rejected during data-quality checking as an invalid calendar date. The result below relates to the accepted urine specimen associated with this report.

RESULTS

Urinalysis:
• Appearance: slightly hazy
• Leucocyte esterase: 2+
• Nitrite: positive
• Blood: trace
• Protein: 1+
• Glucose: negative
• Ketones: negative

Microscopy:
• White blood cells: 180 × 10⁶/L
• Red blood cells: 12 × 10⁶/L
• Squamous epithelial cells: few
• Bacteria: numerous

Culture:
Significant growth of Escherichia coli, greater than 10⁵ colony-forming units/mL, in a predominantly pure culture.

Antimicrobial susceptibility:
• Nitrofurantoin: susceptible
• Trimethoprim: susceptible
• Cefalexin: susceptible
• Amoxicillin: resistant

INTERPRETATION

Findings are consistent with an uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection caused by E. coli. The positive nitrite, pyuria and significant predominantly pure growth support the clinical diagnosis. There is no laboratory evidence here to suggest contamination.

CLINICAL COMMENT

Please correlate with temperature, hydration and examination findings. Nitrofurantoin is microbiologically appropriate if the child remains systemically well and is able to take oral treatment. Review the prescribed course and local paediatric dosing guidance; amend treatment only if clinically indicated. If fever, flank pain, vomiting or deterioration develops, urgent same-day clinical assessment is advised to exclude upper urinary tract involvement.

Validated and reported by arwin wakefield, laboratory clinician.

Cardiology outpatient clinic note
NHS number: 0000147193

Patient: Poppy-Lee
Occupation: Warehouse operative
Employer: Llanfechain Secondary School
Address: 139 Bishton Street, Llantwit Major / Llanilltud Fawr, CF61 1AB
Contact: 07700 900589

Poppy-Lee attended the cardiology clinic following several weeks of intermittent awareness of a rapid heartbeat, particularly when trying to settle at night. The episodes are not associated with exertional chest pain, syncope, ankle swelling or breathlessness. They describe persistent worry about their health, difficulty switching off, and poor sleep, with prolonged sleep onset and occasional waking during the night. Muscle tension is most noticeable across the shoulders and jaw. Their adult child has commented that they appear increasingly anxious and has encouraged attendance.

There is no reported stimulant or recreational drug use. Caffeine intake is modest. They do not describe symptoms suggestive of mania, psychosis or significant depressive illness, and they deny thoughts of self-harm. The palpitations have not caused collapse and are less noticeable when distracted or engaged in conversation.

On examination, they were comfortable at rest and engaged appropriately. Pulse was regular during assessment, with normal heart sounds and no murmur. Chest was clear, and there was no peripheral oedema. An ECG performed in clinic showed sinus rhythm without acute ST-T wave changes. The presentation and examination do not currently suggest a significant structural or rhythm disorder. The episodic palpitations appear closely linked to heightened anxiety and poor sleep.

Assessment:
Generalised anxiety disorder with persistent worry, insomnia and muscle tension. Intermittent palpitations, likely anxiety-related, with reassuring examination and ECG.

Plan:
Continue sertraline 50 mg once daily. Discussed taking it consistently and allowing several weeks for full benefit; advised not to stop suddenly. We reviewed sleep hygiene, reducing reassurance-seeking, paced breathing and a gradual return to regular activity. A talking-therapy referral will be offered through the usual NHS route, with particular focus on cognitive behavioural strategies.

A short period of symptom monitoring was advised, including triggers and duration of palpitations. They should seek urgent assessment for sustained palpitations with collapse, severe chest pain or marked breathlessness. Routine GP follow-up is recommended to review response and tolerability, with cardiology review if symptoms become exertional, prolonged or otherwise change.

Discharge summary

Patient: Zobiya Reynolds
Responsible service: Ulster Hospital
Report/accession ID: 045374445

Reason for admission
Admitted with a four-day worsening of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, characterised by increased breathlessness, wheeze and purulent sputum. A friend accompanied the patient and provided collateral history.

Assessment and inpatient course
On arrival, oxygen saturations were reduced on air with widespread expiratory wheeze. Chest radiograph showed hyperinflation without focal consolidation. Blood tests demonstrated a raised inflammatory marker, with no significant renal or hepatic abnormality. Viral respiratory PCR was negative.

Treated as an infective exacerbation with controlled oxygen, nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and doxycycline. Oxygen was weaned successfully to air. Breathlessness and sputum production improved, and the patient remained haemodynamically stable without evidence of pneumonia or acute cardiac pathology. No invasive procedure was required.

Discharge medication
Prednisolone course to be completed as prescribed.
Doxycycline course to be completed as prescribed.
Salbutamol inhaler: two puffs when required, with spacer technique reviewed. Continue usual inhalers unless advised otherwise.

Condition and follow-up
Mobilising independently and managing oral intake at discharge. Safety-netting discussed with the patient and friend: seek urgent medical attention for increasing breathlessness, cyanosis, confusion, chest pain or inability to use the inhaler. GP review is requested in 17 days to reassess symptoms, inhaler adherence and need for pulmonary rehabilitation or smoking cessation support. Consider spirometry when clinically stable if not recently completed.

Discharging clinician: K. CHADWICK, GMC identifier 0859183

Date: 11/02/2028
NHS number: 000 183 8297
Patient: Anelis Lake
MRN: 027400387

Dear Spinal or Musculoskeletal Service,

I am referring Anelis Lake for assessment of persistent low back pain with shooting pain into the leg and intermittent paraesthesia. The main clinical question is whether this represents lumbar radiculopathy requiring imaging, specialist intervention, or physiotherapy-led rehabilitation, and whether there are features that would warrant more urgent spinal review.

Symptoms have continued despite initial conservative treatment. The pain is centred across the lower lumbar region and travels down the affected leg, with altered sensation described as tingling rather than complete numbness. Current pain is 5/10. There is no reported loss of bladder or bowel control, saddle numbness, or progressive difficulty walking. There has been no recent significant trauma or systemic illness.

On examination, lumbar movement is restricted by pain, particularly flexion and straight-leg raising on the symptomatic side reproduces the radiating discomfort. Lower-limb power is functionally preserved, with no clear foot drop. Sensation is slightly reduced in the patient’s reported distribution, although this is not consistently demonstrable on bedside testing. Peripheral pulses are present and there is no calf swelling.

Treatment so far has included naproxen and paracetamol, with only partial relief. Advice has been given regarding pacing, avoiding prolonged bed rest, and maintaining gentle activity within tolerance. There is no current record of spinal imaging or formal physiotherapy assessment.

I would be grateful for your review and recommendations regarding the need for MRI or other investigations, structured physiotherapy, and any suitable neuropathic pain treatment. Please also advise on safety-netting and the threshold for urgent reassessment should weakness, sphincter disturbance, or saddle sensory change develop.

This referral is made by mirab gardner on behalf of Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh.

ACCIDENT AND EMERGENCY LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: I. Barrow
Clinical context: 30-year-old Hispanic male patient attending A&E with headache and intermittent light-headedness. Known essential hypertension. Current medicines reported as amlodipine and ramipril. Headache severity at assessment: 5/10. No chest pain, focal neurological deficit or visual loss documented.

Report/accession ID: LAB-04488340
Specimen collection/report date: 19 June 2035
Ordering clinician: Not recorded on the laboratory request

Specimen details
Serum, lithium heparin plasma and EDTA whole blood received in suitable containers. Samples were not visibly haemolysed or lipaemic.

Results

Full blood count
Haemoglobin 142 g/L (115–160)
White cell count 7.8 × 10^9/L (4.0–11.0)
Platelet count 268 × 10^9/L (150–400)

Renal profile
Sodium 139 mmol/L (133–146)
Potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5–5.3)
Urea 5.8 mmol/L (2.5–7.8)
Creatinine 76 µmol/L (45–90)
Estimated GFR >90 mL/min/1.73 m²

Liver profile
Alanine transaminase 22 U/L (0–40)
Alkaline phosphatase 79 U/L (30–130)
Bilirubin 9 µmol/L (0–21)
Albumin 44 g/L (35–50)

Glucose and cardiac marker
Random glucose 5.7 mmol/L (3.5–7.8)
High-sensitivity troponin I 3 ng/L (reference interval <16 ng/L)

Interpretation
No significant haematological, renal or hepatic abnormality is identified. Electrolytes and creatinine are within the stated reference intervals, with no biochemical evidence of an acute complication of ramipril therapy. Troponin I is not elevated in this sample; interpret alongside symptom onset, examination and any serial measurement required by the local acute coronary syndrome pathway.

Clinical comment
The laboratory findings do not provide a biochemical explanation for the reported headache or light-headedness. Correlate with repeated blood-pressure measurements, postural observations, medication adherence and recent dose changes. If symptoms persist or blood pressure remains markedly elevated, assess for secondary causes and acute end-organ involvement according to the A&E protocol. Consider urine albumin:creatinine ratio and longer-term cardiovascular risk review through the GP surgery if not recently completed.

Validated and authorised electronically by DARCY-LEE CHAMBERLAIN
Laboratory medicine

Increase in breathlessness and persistent tachycardia discussed with Dr Taaha Parkin, MBBS, physician, who advised continued oxygen, observations and urgent review if hypoxia, syncope, haemodynamic change or worsening chest pain. Sibling RIYAAZ MOON updated at bedside with patient’s consent.

Four-hourly observations, reassess pain and oxygen requirement, supervise all mobilisation, maintain hydration, check for bleeding, and escalate promptly for deterioration. Confirm anticoagulation plan and discharge education when clinically stable.

Patient: rhosyn rafiq
National Insurance number: BG606970D
MRN: 08881187
DOB: 24 May 1938
Contact: rhosyn.rafiq51@gmail.com
Date: 1st May 1988
Clinic: Clinical Genetics

Reason for review
Seen with a flare of established rheumatoid arthritis and to discuss the possibility of an inherited predisposition, given a family history of inflammatory joint disease. The patient reports increasing pain and swelling affecting both wrists and several proximal interphalangeal joints, with morning stiffness lasting around two hours. Fatigue has been prominent for 3 days. No fever, rash, oral ulceration, eye symptoms or bowel disturbance. No recent infection.

Medication
Methotrexate as prescribed with folic acid supplementation; naproxen as needed. Reports good adherence and no recent dose changes. No adverse effects, although naproxen has caused occasional dyspepsia. Alcohol intake reviewed and kept low.

Examination
Alert and not systemically unwell. Bilateral wrist tenderness with synovial thickening and reduced grip. Tender, mildly swollen MCP and PIP joints, without deformity. No nodules or rash. Chest clear; heart sounds normal. No cervical lymphadenopathy.

Impression
Likely rheumatoid arthritis flare. There is no clinical evidence today of septic arthritis or an extra-articular complication. The reported family history may justify review of the wider pedigree, but does not establish a single-gene disorder.

Plan
Arrange urgent blood tests including FBC, U&E, LFTs, CRP and ESR; obtain updated rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP results if not available. Continue methotrexate and folic acid pending results. Use naproxen with food only if tolerated. Discussed contacting the rheumatology team for treatment escalation and arranging an assessment rather than increasing medication independently. Safety-netted to attend A&E for fever, rapidly worsening swelling, a hot single joint or marked functional deterioration.

Discharge summary – Paediatrics

Patient: L. Ibrahim
DOB: 22nd October 1985
Home address: 158 Forres Road, Cornhill, AB45 1AA
Accompanied by: mother, T. Mcleod

Reason for admission
Admitted from the emergency department with two days of frequent vomiting and watery diarrhoea, associated with poor oral intake and reduced urine output. Mother reported no blood in the stool, bilious vomiting, rash or breathing difficulty. There was a history of contact with a gastrointestinal illness at home. No significant previous medical history was identified.

Assessment and key results
On arrival, the child was tired but responsive, with dry lips and mildly reduced peripheral perfusion. There was no meningism, respiratory distress or focal abdominal tenderness. At 08:15, observations showed a temperature of 37.4°C, heart rate 122 bpm and capillary refill of approximately two seconds. Urine output improved during the admission. Blood glucose was normal; venous blood testing did not suggest significant acidosis or a clinically important electrolyte disturbance. Stool sampling was not indicated as symptoms settled and there was no blood, recent travel or prolonged course.

Hospital course
Initial oral fluids were poorly tolerated, so oral rehydration solution was given in small, frequent amounts with nursing support. A short period of intravenous fluid replacement was required because of ongoing losses and reduced urine output. Vomiting stopped thereafter, and diarrhoea became less frequent. The child subsequently managed oral rehydration solution and light food without further vomiting. No antibiotics or anti-diarrhoeal medication were required. Regular clinical review confirmed improving hydration, normal interaction and satisfactory urine output.

Problem list
• Acute gastroenteritis, clinically improving
• Mild to moderate dehydration, resolved following fluid replacement
• Reduced oral intake, now improved

Discharge plan
Discharge home today with mother, who understands the plan and has been given verbal and written advice. Continue oral rehydration solution, offering small frequent sips after each loose stool or vomit, alongside usual fluids and a gradual return to normal diet. Continue supportive care only. Avoid fruit juice and fizzy drinks while diarrhoea persists.

Return to A&E urgently if the child becomes unusually drowsy, cannot keep fluids down, passes very little urine, develops blood or green vomit, severe abdominal pain, breathing difficulty or a persistent high fever. Contact the GP surgery if symptoms are not clearly improving over the next few days or diarrhoea continues beyond one week.

No routine paediatric follow-up is required. The discharge advice and hydration plan were reviewed with T. Mcleod. Summary completed by the paediatric medical team; supervising doctor’s professional identifier: 0199011.

Differentials include cervicitis, urinary infection and ectopic pregnancy, although the negative pregnancy test and examination make ectopic pregnancy unlikely.

No indication for urgent imaging currently; arrange pelvic ultrasound if pain fails to settle or a tubo-ovarian abscess is suspected.

Treatment and plan: Ceftriaxone administered in A&E, with doxycycline and metronidazole prescribed as directed on the discharge medicines list. Abstain from sex until treatment is completed, symptoms resolved and partner management addressed. Sexual health clinic follow-up for results and partner notification.

Disposition: Suitable for discharge if observations remain stable and oral intake is tolerated. Return urgently for fever, collapse, worsening pain, vomiting or new bleeding; GP/sexual health review if not improving within 48–72 hours.

Patient: Heeva A.
Address: 110 LOUGH SWILLY PARK, MAGHERAFELT
Occupation: Hairdresser
Employer: KILRAGHTS Housing Association

Dear Colleague,

I would be grateful for your assessment of Heeva A., who attended the accident and emergency department with increasing fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation. The principal clinical question is whether these symptoms represent inadequate thyroid hormone replacement, and whether further endocrine investigation or adjustment of levothyroxine is required.

The patient reports a gradual reduction in energy and describes feeling unusually cold despite an otherwise comfortable environment. Constipation has been present for 3 days. Their partner has noticed that the patient is slower with usual activities but has not observed confusion, collapse, breathlessness or chest pain. There is no reported fever, vomiting or significant abdominal pain. Appetite is broadly maintained.

Current medication is levothyroxine; the prescribed strength and adherence should be confirmed with the GP surgery and dispensing record. The patient reports taking it regularly, although the timing in relation to breakfast and other medicines is uncertain. No other regular medicines were declared during the emergency assessment.

On examination, the patient was alert and communicating appropriately. Observations were stable, with no clinical evidence of acute cardiorespiratory compromise. The skin appeared mildly dry. There was no obvious neck swelling or focal thyroid tenderness. Neurological examination was non-focal, and there was no marked peripheral oedema. Abdominal examination was soft, without guarding or palpable mass.

Initial blood tests showed a pattern requiring correlation with thyroid function testing; repeat TSH and free T4 are requested if not already obtained, together with full blood count, renal profile, liver function and ferritin to assess other contributors to fatigue. Please also review the medication history for interacting supplements, particularly iron or calcium preparations.

I would appreciate specialist advice on interpretation of the thyroid results, the appropriate levothyroxine dose and administration schedule, and whether further endocrine follow-up is indicated. In the interim, the patient has been advised to maintain fluids, increase dietary fibre gradually and seek urgent review for confusion, marked drowsiness, syncope, chest pain or worsening abdominal symptoms.

Yours sincerely,

Gurnaaz Nadeem

Laboratory report – thyroid function

Patient: ALSTON RASHID
Report/accession ID: L20D98854
Collection/report date: 30 Aug 2018
Reporting laboratory: Irlam Medical Centre
Requesting clinician: Unnamed

Specimen
Serum, received for thyroid function testing. Sample quality acceptable; no visible haemolysis or lipaemia reported.

Results
TSH: 12.8 mIU/L (reference interval 0.27–4.20) – high
Free T4: 10.1 pmol/L (reference interval 12–22) – low
Free T3: 3.4 pmol/L (reference interval 3.1–6.8) – within interval
Thyroid peroxidase antibody: 286 IU/mL (reference <34) – positive

Clinical information
Fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation for 3 days. Current medication recorded as levothyroxine. The patient’s adult child provided collateral history and reports no recent admission, diarrhoeal illness or change in prescribed treatment.

Interpretation
Results are consistent with overt primary hypothyroidism, with positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies supporting autoimmune thyroiditis. The raised TSH and low free T4 suggest inadequate replacement, although adherence, administration with food or interacting medicines should be reviewed before dose escalation.

Comment
Please correlate with the prescribed levothyroxine dose, timing and missed doses. Repeat TSH and free T4 in approximately 6–8 weeks after any confirmed dose adjustment, or sooner if clinically indicated. In view of the cardiology setting, avoid rapid replacement without consideration of ischaemic symptoms, pulse and ECG history. If symptoms include chest pain, syncope or marked bradycardia, seek urgent clinical assessment.

Validated by: Piper ENGLISH
Laboratory clinician

General Medicine Outpatient Report

Patient: Oona
Occupation: Lawyer
Report/accession ID: 04928780
Referring healthcare organisation: University Hospital Llandough
Consultant: ROSALITA WEBBER

Reason for review:
Assessment of recurrent episodes of abrupt autonomic and emotional distress, characterised by sudden palpitations, chest tightness and an intense fear of dying.

History:
Oona describes several discrete attacks, usually reaching maximum intensity within minutes. The most recent cluster has occurred for 3 days, with episodes arising both at rest and during periods of work-related stress. There is associated trembling, subjective breathlessness, sweating and light-headedness, but no collapse, exertional syncope, pleuritic pain or haemoptysis. The patient has not reported unilateral leg swelling, persistent fever or recent immobilisation. Between episodes, symptoms settle substantially, although anticipatory anxiety has led to avoidance of busy environments.

There is no reported history of cardiac disease, stimulant use or recreational drug use. The patient denies thoughts of self-harm. A sibling has been involved in providing support and accompanied the patient to the appointment.

Examination and investigations:
The patient appeared anxious but engaged appropriately. Speech was coherent, with normal thought content and no evidence of psychosis. Pulse was regular on examination, with normal heart sounds and no murmur. Respiratory examination was clear bilaterally, without wheeze or crackles. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Peripheral perfusion was satisfactory.

A 12-lead ECG performed in clinic showed sinus rhythm without acute ischaemic change or pre-excitation. Basic blood tests, including full blood count, thyroid function and serum electrolytes, have been requested to exclude common physiological contributors to palpitations.

Impression:
The episodic, rapidly escalating symptoms and subsequent resolution are most consistent with panic attacks, with emerging anticipatory anxiety. There are currently no examination or ECG findings suggesting an acute cardiopulmonary cause. The differential diagnosis remains open pending blood results, particularly for thyroid dysfunction or anaemia.

Plan:
Breathing retraining was demonstrated and the patient was advised to practise this twice daily and at the earliest onset of symptoms. Written information on panic symptoms and graded reduction of avoidance behaviours was provided. Referral for NHS talking therapies, with cognitive behavioural therapy focus, is recommended via the GP surgery. No sedative medication was initiated. The patient was advised to seek urgent assessment through A&E if chest pain becomes persistent, occurs with exertion, or is accompanied by collapse or severe breathlessness.

Signed: ROSALITA WEBBER

Occupation: Shop manager

There has been some tiredness, but no persistent cough, breathlessness, chest pain, haemoptysis or recurrent infections. No recent dental infection or other clear infective trigger was identified.

There is no known history of tuberculosis exposure. The patient has not noticed enlarged nodes elsewhere and has no abdominal swelling or persistent bone pain. Assessment

The presentation is concerning for Hodgkin lymphoma, although metastatic malignancy and less likely granulomatous or infective lymphadenopathy remain possible. The constitutional symptoms and progressive supraclavicular node warrant expedited tissue diagnosis.

Plan

An urgent ultrasound-guided core biopsy has been requested, with arrangements for histopathological and flow-cytometry assessment. CT of the neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis will be arranged for staging once the initial pathology pathway is confirmed. Blood tests requested include full blood count, renal and liver profiles, inflammatory markers, LDH and viral screening before any potential treatment. The patient was advised to contact the respiratory team or attend the emergency department if there is rapidly increasing swelling, difficulty breathing, difficulty swallowing, fever or marked deterioration. Follow-up will be arranged after biopsy results are available.

Discharge summary
NHS number: 000 695 5003

Patient: Witold
Discharging service: Queen Elizabeth University Hospital
Report/accession ID: 0379459478

Witold was assessed in the emergency department with a two-day history of right-sided flank pain, painful urination and episodes of shaking chills (rigors). They felt nauseated but were able to drink fluids. Examination showed flank tenderness and a temperature consistent with infection; blood pressure and heart rate remained satisfactory after initial treatment.

Urine testing supported a urinary infection, with blood tests showing an inflammatory response. Kidney function was satisfactory. A urine sample was sent for culture; the result should be reviewed by the GP or the treating team, with antibiotics changed if the organism is resistant. There was no clinical evidence of urinary obstruction or sepsis requiring admission. The report/accession ID for the sample is 0379459478.

Treatment in the department included intravenous fluids, analgesia and an initial dose of antibiotic. Symptoms improved, oral fluids were tolerated and the pain was manageable before discharge. The working diagnosis is acute pyelonephritis (infection involving the kidney).

Please take cefuroxime 500 mg twice daily and complete the prescribed course, even if you begin to feel better. Paracetamol may be taken for pain or fever, following the dose instructions on the dispensing label and avoiding other medicines that also contain paracetamol. Drink regularly, rest, and avoid alcohol if it makes you feel unwell.

Arrange a review with your GP surgery within 48 hours, or sooner if symptoms are not clearly improving. The urine culture should be checked at this review. Return to A&E urgently if you develop worsening flank pain, persistent vomiting, confusion, faintness, difficulty passing urine, a marked reduction in urine, or fever and rigors despite antibiotics.

Date: 5th January 2045
Patient: Fitz Raza
MRN: 048449794
From: A. Howe, BELFAST CITY HOSPITAL

Dear Clinical Genetics Team,

I am referring Fitz Raza for specialist advice regarding a longstanding pattern of generalised anxiety disorder, with persistent worry, poor sleep and prominent muscle tension. The specific question is whether the clinical presentation, together with a reported family pattern of significant anxiety symptoms, warrants genetic counselling or any further assessment within your service. I would also be grateful for advice on whether an alternative inherited neuropsychiatric condition should be considered.

The patient describes excessive and difficult-to-control worry across several domains, including health, family matters and routine responsibilities. Symptoms are present on most days and are associated with difficulty initiating sleep, early waking and sustained shoulder and jaw tension. There have been no reported episodes of mania, psychosis or loss of consciousness. The patient denies current suicidal intent or plans, and there is no history provided of self-harm. Concentration is reduced during periods of heightened anxiety, although day-to-day functioning is being maintained.

Sertraline is currently prescribed and has been tolerated without significant adverse effects. Previous management has included discussion of sleep hygiene, reduction of caffeine, breathing exercises and referral for structured psychological therapy. Benefit has been partial, with ongoing symptoms despite adherence. There is no reported use of illicit substances, and alcohol intake is not felt to be contributing. Examination in primary care was reassuring: the patient was appropriately engaged, speech was normal in rate and form, and there was no focal neurological deficit. Observations were stable.

The family history is notable for anxiety-related difficulties affecting more than one relative, although formal diagnoses, treatment records and any previous genetic investigations are not available. I have explained that most anxiety disorders are multifactorial and that genetic testing may not provide a clinically useful result.

Please review the referral and advise whether genetic counselling, targeted testing or onward assessment is indicated. If genetics input is not appropriate, guidance on the most suitable specialist pathway would be appreciated. Ongoing sertraline and psychological management will continue in the interim, with follow-up planned in about 4 weeks.

Yours faithfully,

A. Howe

Accident and Emergency follow-up clinic note
National Insurance number: KN 15 13 85 A

Patient: NIVEN TURNBULL
Date: 4 October 2004
Report/accession ID: 23/061172
Contact: 07700 900148

The patient, aged 90 years, was reviewed following attendance in A&E with concern about worsening daytime sleepiness. Their adult child accompanied them and described several months of very loud snoring, with repeated pauses in breathing during sleep followed by gasping. The patient reports falling asleep unintentionally while reading and feeling unrefreshed on waking. There has been no recent collapse, chest pain, breathlessness when awake or witnessed seizure. They have had a sore throat for 3 days, without fever or difficulty swallowing.

The patient has a known diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnoea and uses continuous positive airway pressure overnight. They report using the mask on most nights, although it has recently become uncomfortable and they sometimes remove it after waking. The adult child has noticed the snoring is worse when the mask is not worn. No sedating medicines or alcohol excess were reported.

On examination, the patient was alert and engaging, with clear speech and no respiratory distress. Oropharyngeal examination showed mild erythema without exudate. Heart sounds were normal and the chest was clear. There was no focal neurological deficit. The presentation is most consistent with suboptimally treated obstructive sleep apnoea, probably related to mask fit or reduced tolerance. The sore throat appears uncomplicated and is not suggestive of a lower respiratory infection.

Plan

Advised to continue continuous positive airway pressure every night and during daytime naps, and not to drive or operate machinery when sleepy. A referral will be made to the established sleep service for mask review, device-download assessment and consideration of pressure adjustment. The adult child was asked to support adherence and to report any witnessed prolonged apnoeas or concerning deterioration.

Fluids and simple analgesia were advised for the sore throat. Safety-netting given regarding increasing breathlessness, inability to swallow, severe drowsiness or collapse, with instructions to seek urgent medical attention if these occur. Follow-up with the GP surgery was recommended after sleep-service review.

Review by GP if symptoms are not clearly improving, or sooner if unable to keep fluids down. Attend A&E urgently for marked drowsiness, persistent vomiting, blood in stool, severe abdominal pain, or no urine for an unusually prolonged period.

I have requested renal function, inflammatory markers and urate testing, with the results linked to report/accession ID 064742539. A joint aspiration should be considered if the diagnosis becomes uncertain or infection is suspected. Once this attack has settled, the GP can review whether urate-lowering treatment is indicated and check blood pressure and cardiovascular medicines before further anti-inflammatory treatment.

The appendix appeared inflamed but not perforated. The operation was uncomplicated, and the specimen was sent for histology. There was no postoperative vomiting or fever, and oral intake was reintroduced without difficulty.

Pain was controlled with regular paracetamol and occasional additional analgesia. At the time of final review, current pain was 5/10, improving with medication, and the patient was mobilising independently. Wounds were clean, dry and intact, with no clinical evidence of infection.

Discharge medicines
• Paracetamol as required for pain, following the instructions on the supplied packaging.
• No further antibiotics are required unless advised following review of the histology or because of a new clinical concern.

Condition and follow-up
The patient is clinically suitable for discharge home today. Histology will be reviewed when available and communicated through the usual hospital or GP pathway. A routine postoperative review will be arranged by the surgical team. The clinical genetics service has no additional inpatient intervention required for this episode.

Advice given
Keep the wound sites clean and dry and avoid strenuous activity until comfortable. Seek urgent medical advice via NHS 111, the emergency department or emergency services if abdominal pain worsens, persistent vomiting develops, fever occurs, the wound becomes increasingly red or discharges, or the patient feels faint or acutely unwell. Dear Respiratory Medicine Team,

Re: KLEON LLOYD

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient, who has recently developed recurrent palpitations, persistent fatigue and breathlessness on exertion in the context of atrial fibrillation. The specific clinical question is whether there is an additional respiratory cause for the exertional limitation, and whether respiratory optimisation might improve functional capacity alongside ongoing cardiac management.

The patient describes intermittent episodes of a rapid, irregular heartbeat, sometimes occurring at rest and sometimes after modest activity. Breathlessness is most noticeable when walking uphill or climbing stairs. There is no reported pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, fever or nocturnal wheeze. The partner, C. Waller, reports that the patient has appeared more tired over recent weeks but has not noticed cyanosis, syncope or witnessed apnoeas.

Current treatment is apixaban and bisoprolol. Adherence is reported to be good, with no recent bleeding, dizziness or missed doses. The patient has not previously used inhalers and has no established respiratory diagnosis recorded. There is no known recent infective illness. Nursing progress note

Patient: Jahidul Atherton
DOB: 5 June 2027
Home address: 157 Midtown, Alva, FK12 5AA
Parent present: JAAP DAVIES
Report/accession ID: 02266311

Situation
Admitted with viral croup following worsening barking cough, hoarse voice and noisy breathing overnight. Parent reports reduced oral intake but continued wet nappies. Child remains alert and settles when held by parent.

Observations and assessment
Airway patent. Mild inspiratory stridor heard when unsettled, absent at rest after treatment. No chest recession or nasal flaring observed. Skin warm and pink; capillary refill under two seconds. Temperature within normal range. Current heart rate 108 beats/minute, respiratory rate mildly raised for age, oxygen saturations maintained on air. Voice remains hoarse. No drooling or difficulty managing secretions.

Intake, output and mobility
Took small amounts of water and diluted juice during the shift, with encouragement. Ate a few spoonfuls of yoghurt. One wet nappy documented; parent will continue to report urine output. Mobilising safely with supervision, though activity limited by cough and tiredness.

Interventions and response
Dexamethasone administered as prescribed. Calm handling, upright positioning and reassurance provided; unnecessary observations and procedures minimised. Stridor and work of breathing improved after the child settled. No supplemental oxygen required. Parent advised not to use steam and to call staff promptly if breathing becomes noisier or the child appears exhausted.

Risks and escalation
Ongoing risk of recurrent upper-airway obstruction, particularly when distressed. Nurse in charge aware of admission status. Escalate immediately to the paediatric medical team if stridor occurs at rest, recession develops, oxygen saturations fall, oral intake deteriorates, urine output reduces or the child becomes drowsy. Emergency response if severe respiratory distress or cyanosis occurs.

Plan for next shift
Continue respiratory observations and comfort measures, with review after sleep and following any episode of agitation. Encourage frequent small fluids and document intake and wet nappies. Maintain parent involvement, check response to dexamethasone, and confirm medical review before considering discharge.

Laboratory genetics report
NHS number: 000 602 6193

Patient: Muhammad-Hamza
Report/accession ID: 073869519
Specimen collected: 3 Apr 2004
Patient contact: muhammad-hamza.foster12@talktalk.net

Clinical indication:
Predictive testing requested because of a significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer. Patient reports ongoing cancer-risk concern. Partner aware of referral; consent discussion completed before sampling. Ordering clinician not recorded on this report.

Specimen:
Peripheral blood in EDTA. Sample received suitable for analysis. DNA extraction and quality control satisfactory.

Molecular analysis:
Targeted analysis of BRCA1 and BRCA2 performed by next-generation sequencing with copy-number assessment. Variant review included BRCA1 c.68_69delAG, a well-established pathogenic founder variant.

Result:
BRCA1 c.68_69delAG not detected.
No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant identified in the genes tested.

Interpretation:
This is a negative predictive result for the specific familial BRCA1 variant assessed, provided the familial variant is correctly documented and the assay has adequate coverage. The result does not exclude an alternative hereditary cancer predisposition or alter risk based on family history alone. If the affected relative’s molecular result is unavailable, testing that relative should be considered where clinically feasible.

Clinical comment:
Recommend review in the regional clinical genetics service to confirm the familial variant and agree surveillance and risk-reduction advice. Routine population screening should continue unless genetics advises otherwise. Genetic counselling is recommended before any further predictive testing.

Validated and authorised by:
PAKHI THOMAS
Laboratory genetics clinician

Report date: 3 Apr 2004

Patient: erinn rutherford
MRN: 047487092
Clinical age: 60 y/o
Contact: erinn.rutherford61@icloud.com

General medicine outpatient review

erinn rutherford was seen with their spouse because of increasing hand pain and stiffness over the past fortnight. They describe prolonged morning stiffness, difficulty making a fist and swelling affecting both hands, particularly the knuckles and wrists. Fatigue has also become more troublesome, although there has been no reported fever, night sweats, weight loss, rash, mouth ulceration or new breathlessness. They have continued methotrexate, folic acid and naproxen as prescribed. There has been no recent infection or antibiotic course.

On examination, erinn rutherford looked tired but was not acutely unwell. There was synovial thickening and tenderness of several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, with reduced grip because of pain. The wrists were mildly swollen and warm. There was no overlying cellulitis, nodular rash or evidence of a large-joint effusion. Chest was clear and cardiovascular examination was unremarkable.

Assessment

This is clinically consistent with a rheumatoid arthritis flare, without features today to suggest septic arthritis or another systemic inflammatory complication. The current symptoms warrant confirmation of inflammatory activity and review of disease-modifying treatment rather than relying on regular analgesia alone.

Plan

Blood tests requested: full blood count, renal profile, liver function, CRP, ESR and rheumatoid arthritis monitoring bloods. A urine sample will be arranged if clinically indicated. Continue methotrexate and folic acid pending results, and continue naproxen with food if tolerated. They were advised not to take naproxen if unwell with vomiting, dehydration or significant indigestion, and to seek advice regarding any black stools or reduced urine output.

I will discuss the results with the rheumatology team and seek an expedited medication review. The patient will contact the surgery urgently if a joint becomes markedly hot and acutely painful, or if fever develops. Routine review is booked for 13/03/2018, in about 4 weeks, with earlier assessment if symptoms worsen.
