Patient: Dumitru Wood
NHS number: 000 452 2894
MRN: H4382260
Occupation: Architect
Clinic: Llandudno General Hospital Site
Clinician: Junayd Sims

Today we reviewed your ongoing knee pain, stiffness and difficulty walking. You explained that the discomfort is most noticeable when standing for longer periods, using stairs or getting up after sitting. Morning stiffness settles after moving around, without prolonged stiffness or symptoms in other joints. There has been no recent injury, locking, giving way, fever or unexplained weight loss. You also mentioned a separate cough for 3 days, with no breathlessness, chest pain or coughing blood; this should be monitored and is not typical of the knee problem.

On examination, you walked with a mildly reduced stride. The affected knee was slightly stiff through flexion and extension, with bony enlargement and tenderness along the joint line. There was no significant warmth, redness or effusion. Ligaments felt stable and the calf was soft and non-tender. Your chest was clear, with normal breathing at rest.

The findings are consistent with osteoarthritis of the knee. This is a wearing and irritation process within the joint rather than an infection. Symptoms often fluctuate, and keeping the joint moving usually helps more than prolonged rest. Please continue paracetamol as currently advised, staying within the dose on the packet or your prescription. You may also continue topical ibuprofen if your skin remains well, avoiding broken skin and washing your hands after application. Do not add oral ibuprofen without checking with a pharmacist or GP, particularly if you have stomach, kidney, heart or asthma problems.

I have recommended a gradual strengthening and mobility programme through physiotherapy, concentrating on the thigh and hip muscles. Short, regular walks are preferable to pushing through a long painful session. A supportive walking aid may be useful temporarily. We will arrange weight-bearing knee radiographs if symptoms do not improve with these measures, and consider an injection or further specialist assessment depending on the result and your progress.

Seek urgent help if the knee becomes hot and markedly swollen, you develop fever, or you cannot bear weight. For worsening breathlessness, chest pain or coughing blood, attend A&E.

Patient: Laura-Jane Latif
Address: 107 DRUMNAGREAGH ROAD, GARRISON
Contact: 07700 900970

Reason for admission
This 33-year-old South Asian male patient attended the emergency department with several days of lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge and pain during intercourse. There was no collapse, heavy bleeding or urinary retention. A friend accompanied her and provided support.

Assessment and key results
Examination showed lower abdominal tenderness and cervical motion tenderness, with abnormal discharge. She was haemodynamically stable and did not require admission for surgery. Pregnancy testing was negative. Blood tests showed a mild inflammatory response; renal and liver function were satisfactory. Urine testing did not suggest a urinary infection. Vaginal and cervical swabs were taken for chlamydia, gonorrhoea and other organisms. Results were not available before discharge and will be reviewed by the sexual health service.

Treatment and progress
The clinical findings were consistent with pelvic inflammatory disease. She received ceftriaxone in the department and was started on oral doxycycline and metronidazole. Please take doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and metronidazole as prescribed, completing the full course even if symptoms improve. Avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole and for 48 hours after the final dose. Doxycycline can cause sensitivity to sunlight; use suitable protection and take it with plenty of water while sitting or standing.

Pain improved during observation, and she was able to eat, drink and walk independently. There was no evidence of an acute surgical abdomen. She is safe for discharge with clear advice to return to A&E if pain becomes severe or localised, vomiting prevents medication, fever develops, she feels faint, or there is heavy vaginal bleeding.

Follow-up and advice
Please avoid sexual intercourse until treatment is complete, symptoms have settled and any partners have been assessed and treated. Recent sexual partners should be informed through the sexual health service; do not attempt to manage partner treatment without advice. A follow-up appointment has been arranged for 29 Aug 2025. The swab results and symptom response will be reviewed then.

Please contact the emergency department sooner if you are worried or deteriorating. A copy of this summary should be shared with your GP surgery.

Increasing redness, tenderness and discharge from a postoperative wound. The patient reports worsening local pain for 3 days, with purulent fluid noticed on the dressing today. Accompanied by a friend, who assisted with the history. No chest pain, dyspnoea, rigors, vomiting or syncope reported.

Initial assessment
Alert and conversing normally. Airway patent; breathing unlaboured with clear breath sounds bilaterally. Heart sounds normal, peripheral perfusion maintained. Abdomen soft, with discomfort confined to the wound area and no generalised tenderness. No calf swelling. Temperature mildly elevated; blood pressure and pulse acceptable for the clinical context.

Wound examination
Postoperative wound with surrounding erythema, warmth and localised tenderness. Small amount of thick purulent discharge expressed from the lower aspect. No wound dehiscence, crepitus, bullae or disproportionate pain. Erythema marked for monitoring. No clinical evidence of necrotising soft-tissue infection at present.

Investigations
Blood tests requested: full blood count, C-reactive protein, urea and electrolytes, liver function and venous lactate. Blood cultures to be taken if febrile. Wound swab obtained before antibiotics. ECG showed sinus rhythm without acute ischaemic change. Results to be reviewed by the receiving surgical team.

Management and decision-making
Wound irrigated with sterile saline and covered with a clean dressing. Flucloxacillin commenced in the emergency department following allergy check. Analgesia offered, with advice to keep the wound clean and avoid soaking it. Given purulent discharge and spreading erythema after surgery, outpatient treatment is not considered sufficiently safe without specialist review.

Disposition
Discussed with the on-call surgical team at University Hospital of North Durham. Patient accepted for surgical assessment and likely intravenous antibiotics, with consideration of drainage or further wound exploration depending on examination and inflammatory markers. Safety-net advice given regarding fever, rapidly extending redness, increasing pain, confusion or collapse.

Signed: kali-ann paul

MOLECULAR GENETICS LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: Razvan Fitzgerald
Clinical descriptor: 40 y/o
Report/accession ID: LAB-08184546
Request: Predictive germline testing for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk
Specimen: Peripheral blood, EDTA; DNA extracted for constitutional variant analysis
Ordering clinician: Unnamed clinician

Clinical information

The patient was referred because of a significant family history of breast and ovarian malignancy and expressed concern regarding their own future cancer risk. Predictive testing was requested following pre-test counselling. No current treatment is reported. The patient attended with a friend, who provided emotional support; consent and the implications of testing were reviewed with the patient directly.

Laboratory findings

Targeted analysis of BRCA1 and BRCA2 was performed using next-generation sequencing with supplementary copy-number assessment. The assay covered coding exons and flanking splice regions; analytical sensitivity is expected to exceed 99% for single-nucleotide variants and small insertions/deletions within the regions assessed.

BRCA1 c.68_69delAG: not detected.
No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant was identified in the regions examined. No variant of uncertain significance is reported.

Interpretation

This is a negative result for the familial variant or gene changes detectable by the assay, but it does not exclude a hereditary predisposition caused by a variant outside the regions tested, a gene not included in this panel, or a mechanism not detectable by the methodology. If a specific familial pathogenic variant has previously been identified, the result should be correlated with the original family report to confirm that the appropriate variant was analysed.

The result does not remove the need for risk assessment based on the documented pedigree. Screening and risk-reducing options should be determined by the specialist genetics or breast service according to the family history and any additional clinical information. The patient should be advised to report new relevant family diagnoses, as this may alter risk estimation and indicate broader testing.

A post-test genetics review is recommended to explain the residual familial risk and implications for relatives. Follow-up appointment: 29/06/2035.

Validated and reported by:
Sherridan Deakin
Laboratory validating clinician

Accident and Emergency clinical letter

You were assessed in A&E because your breathing had become more difficult, with increased wheeze and purulent sputum. Your examination was consistent with an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Your oxygen level remained satisfactory on room air, and there was no clinical evidence of pneumonia or another immediate cause requiring admission. A chest radiograph was reassuring. Please seek urgent help if your breathing deteriorates, you develop chest pain, feel faint or confused, or cannot speak in full sentences.

Treatment plan:
• Prednisolone has been prescribed as a short course. Take it exactly as directed on the discharge label and take it with food.
• Doxycycline has been prescribed because of the change in sputum colour. Complete the course unless a clinician advises you to stop. Avoid taking it at the same time as indigestion remedies containing calcium, magnesium or aluminium.
• Use your salbutamol inhaler for episodes of wheeze or breathlessness as instructed. A spacer should be used if one has been supplied.

Please arrange a review with your GP surgery within the next few days, particularly if symptoms are not steadily improving. Your GP can check inhaler technique, confirm that your regular COPD inhalers remain appropriate and consider referral to pulmonary rehabilitation. If you smoke, stopping will substantially reduce future flare-ups; support is available through NHS stop-smoking services.

The respiratory opinion recorded during your assessment was from a consultant respiratory physician. This episode does not replace your usual COPD follow-up. Continue your regular medicines unless specifically told otherwise, and bring all inhalers to your next appointment so that they can be checked.

Discharge Summary
NHS number: 000 712 0738

Patient: Aryana Whitfield
Admission date: 13 Nov 1996
Discharging service: Cardiology, Queen Elizabeth University Hospital

Reason for admission
Admitted with a four-day deterioration in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, with increased breathlessness, audible wheeze and purulent sputum. There was no history of chest pain or syncope. Initial oxygen saturation was 88% on air, improving with controlled oxygen.

Key findings
Chest examination demonstrated widespread expiratory wheeze and reduced air entry at both bases. Chest radiograph showed hyperinflation without focal consolidation or pulmonary oedema. ECG showed sinus rhythm with no acute ischaemic changes. Blood tests showed a raised C-reactive protein, with no significant renal or electrolyte abnormality. Viral respiratory PCR was negative.

Hospital course
Treated for infective COPD exacerbation with oral prednisolone, doxycycline, regular nebulised bronchodilators and supplemental oxygen. Sputum became less purulent and breathlessness returned to baseline. Oxygen was weaned successfully; the patient maintained satisfactory saturations on air, including during mobilisation. No evidence of acute heart failure was identified.

Medication changes at discharge
• Prednisolone to complete the prescribed short course.
• Doxycycline to complete the antibiotic course.
• Salbutamol inhaler, two puffs as needed for wheeze or breathlessness, using a spacer.
• Continue usual maintenance inhalers as previously prescribed.

The inhaler technique was reviewed by the respiratory nurse, and smoking cessation advice was provided. The patient was advised to seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E for severe breathlessness, cyanosis, confusion or inability to speak in sentences.

Follow-up
GP review is requested within one week to reassess respiratory symptoms, oxygenation and inhaler use. A respiratory clinic appointment has been requested in about 12 weeks. The patient’s adult child, Murrin ROONEY, from Gannochy, was present for the discharge discussion and will assist with transport and medicines.

Condition on discharge
Alert, haemodynamically stable and mobilising independently. Discharged home with written advice and discharge medicines.

Presenting complaint
Severe limb and lower back pain since yesterday, with reduced oral intake and dark urine. Patient reports this feels similar to previous sickle cell painful crises. Sibling present and confirms increasing lethargy overnight. No chest pain, breathlessness, fever, cough, vomiting or focal neurological symptoms.

Assessment
Alert and orientated, distressed by movement. Airway patent; respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturations 98% on air. Pulse 104/min, blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, temperature 37.1°C. Mucous membranes dry. No jaundice noted. Heart sounds normal and chest clear bilaterally. Abdomen soft and non-tender. Diffuse tenderness of both thighs and lumbar paraspinal region without swelling, erythema or focal bony tenderness. Peripheral perfusion maintained; no calf asymmetry. Current pain score 5/10 after initial analgesia.

Investigations
Venous blood sample sent for full blood count, reticulocytes, U&Es, liver profile, bilirubin, CRP and group and save. Haemoglobin is reduced in keeping with known haemoglobinopathy; reticulocytosis present. Creatinine is not elevated from baseline and CRP is not significantly raised. Urinalysis shows concentrated urine without nitrites or blood. ECG demonstrates sinus tachycardia with no acute ischaemic changes. Chest radiograph requested owing to the risk of acute chest syndrome; no focal consolidation reported.

Treatment and decision-making
Oral fluids encouraged, followed by intravenous crystalloid for clinical dehydration. Morphine administered in titrated doses with antiemetic available; pain and mobility improved, with no respiratory depression. No infective or acute chest features currently. Acute pain team contacted for ongoing analgesia advice. Haematology review arranged, and the patient will be observed in the ambulatory assessment area for repeat observations and reassessment of pain, hydration and urine output.

Plan
Continue prescribed analgesia, maintain oral intake and avoid further discharge until pain is controlled on oral medication. Admit under haematology if symptoms remain severe or observations deteriorate; otherwise discharge with clear return advice for fever, chest symptoms, increasing breathlessness or uncontrolled pain.

Emergency Department Assessment – Paediatric Emergency Medicine

Patient: Jaego Lawson
Patient identifier/MRN: MRN-00307423
Accompanied by her father, allena woolley
Referring healthcare organisation: SKIPTON GENERAL HOSPITAL

14-year-old South Asian female patient attended with a two-day history of burning on passing urine, increased urinary frequency and intermittent discomfort low in the abdomen. She has passed small amounts of urine frequently but has not been incontinent. There has been no visible haematuria, loin pain, vomiting or diarrhoea. She reports feeling shivery at times but has not measured a fever. No vaginal discharge or genital rash was described. Her father provided collateral history, with the patient also speaking privately for part of the assessment; she was comfortable with this arrangement and gave assent to examination and treatment.

She appeared alert and mildly uncomfortable, but not toxic. Temperature was 37.4°C, heart rate 92 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg and oxygen saturations 99% on air. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Hydration was satisfactory, with moist mucous membranes and normal peripheral perfusion. Abdomen was soft, with mild suprapubic tenderness and no guarding or rebound. There was no costovertebral angle tenderness. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Urine dipstick showed positive leukocytes and nitrites, with trace blood. A midstream urine sample was sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivities. There was no clinical evidence of pyelonephritis, sepsis, acute abdomen or pregnancy-related complication. The working diagnosis is an uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection.

Following discussion with the patient and her father, nitrofurantoin was prescribed in accordance with the local paediatric formulary. She was advised to take the full course with food, maintain oral fluids and use paracetamol if required according to the label. The importance of reviewing the culture result was explained, including possible antibiotic adjustment if resistance is identified.

She was discharged home with her father and advised to seek urgent review for fever, flank pain, repeated vomiting, worsening abdominal pain, reduced urine output or marked deterioration. Routine follow-up with the GP surgery was recommended if symptoms had not clearly improved within 48 hours. The patient was given an opportunity to ask questions confidentially before discharge.

Patient: Lleyton S.
Location: Cardiology ward
Healthcare organisation: Royal Victoria Hospital
Home address: 70 Longlands Drive, LIMAVADY
Contact telephone: 07700 900319
Relative: H. O'Hara (adult child)

Assessment
Reviewed following admission with transient ischaemic attack. At 08:15 patient reported sudden heaviness and weakness of the right arm, associated facial droop and slurred speech, which had resolved before assessment. No recurrent focal deficit during this shift. Alert and orientated, speech clear, equal hand grips, no facial asymmetry. Denies headache, chest pain or visual disturbance. Pupils equal and reactive. NEWS observations stable; afebrile.

Mobility and intake
Mobilising independently to the bathroom with supervision initially; gait steady. Falls advice given and call bell left within reach. Eating and drinking without difficulty. Swallow screen completed and passed; no coughing with fluids. Fluid intake encouraged.

Interventions
Aspirin and atorvastatin administered as prescribed. Neurological observations continued. Patient reminded to report any new weakness, facial change, speech difficulty, loss of vision or severe headache immediately. Emotional reassurance provided; patient understands the reason for monitoring. Adult child updated with the patient’s agreement.

Risk and escalation
Falls risk low with current mobility, but supervision advised overnight. No pressure damage noted. Any recurrent neurological symptoms to be treated as urgent: call emergency team, record time of onset and inform the covering medical team. Maintain nil delay for urgent brain imaging pathway if symptoms recur.

Plan for next shift
Continue neurological observations and routine vital signs as charted. Confirm pending investigations and medical review, including secondary prevention plan and discharge arrangements. Reinforce medication adherence and provide written safety-netting before discharge.

Patient: Adeoluwa D.
Occupation: Paralegal
Department: Clinical Genetics
Healthcare organisation: Park Edge Medical Centre
Report/accession ID: 013709594

Clinical review

Thank you for attending the clinical genetics appointment. We discussed your recent low mood, loss of interest in usual activities and early-morning waking. You described feeling particularly flat and withdrawn, with reduced concentration and motivation. You have been taking sertraline as prescribed. You reported a new physical symptom, present for 3 days, but no associated chest pain, breathlessness or fainting.

Your adult child was included in the discussion with your agreement. We reviewed the family history available today, including mental health difficulties in relatives. Depression is common and usually has several contributing factors; a family history can increase susceptibility but does not, by itself, establish a single inherited genetic cause. On the information currently available, there is no indication for a predictive genetic test for major depressive episode.

Please continue sertraline at the prescribed dose and arrange a medication review with your GP surgery, particularly if there has been little improvement or if side effects are troublesome. Do not stop it suddenly. We also discussed practical measures including a regular sleep routine, gentle daily activity, maintaining contact with supportive people and considering talking therapy. Your GP can refer you to NHS Talking Therapies where appropriate.

We agreed that you should seek urgent help through the emergency department or NHS 111 if you develop thoughts of harming yourself, feel unable to remain safe, or become severely distressed. If there is immediate danger, call 999. Please let your adult child or another trusted person know if your mood worsens.

The genetics team will review the family information provided and will write to you and your GP if any further assessment is indicated. Otherwise, no routine genetics follow-up has been arranged at present.

SHALEIGH VERNON
Clinical Genetics clinician
Park Edge Medical Centre

Discharge summary – General Medicine

Patient: Aarani Baines
DOB: 8th November 1984
Home address: 24 Park Way, Fochabers, IV32 7AA
Contact detail: aarani.baines65@gmail.com
Current gestation: 9+4 weeks' gestation

Reason for admission

Admitted with five days of persistent vomiting in early pregnancy, with inability to retain fluids or prescribed tablets. She reported reduced urine output, dizziness on standing and unintentional weight loss. There was no abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, fever or urinary symptomatology. A friend accompanied her and assisted with the history.

Assessment and hospital course

On arrival she appeared clinically dehydrated, with dry mucous membranes and postural symptoms. Blood tests showed a mild ketonaemia and hypokalaemia, with preserved renal function and no evidence of infection. Urinalysis was otherwise unremarkable. An obstetric ultrasound confirmed an intrauterine pregnancy with cardiac activity, consistent with the stated gestation.

She was treated with intravenous sodium chloride and antiemetic therapy with cyclizine. Thiamine was given before any dextrose-containing fluid. Her nausea and vomiting settled over the following 24 hours, and she was subsequently able to tolerate oral fluids, soup and small meals. Repeat electrolytes normalised and urine output improved. There was no clinical evidence of a surgical or infective cause for her symptoms.

Medication changes

Cyclizine 50 mg orally up to three times daily as needed for nausea has been supplied. She should take this only as directed and avoid driving if it causes drowsiness. No other regular medicines were changed. She has been advised to continue pregnancy vitamins when able to tolerate them.

Condition and plan at discharge

She is haemodynamically stable, mobilising independently and managing oral intake at the time of discharge. The early pregnancy team will review her, with the appointment to be arranged through the usual maternity pathway. She should contact her GP or maternity assessment service promptly if vomiting recurs, she cannot keep fluids down, urine becomes markedly reduced, she develops abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding, or feels faint.

Discharge advice was discussed with the patient and her friend, including frequent small sips of fluid and small, carbohydrate-containing meals. A copy of this summary will be sent to her GP.

Discharging doctor: Consultant physician, professional identifier 0632039

Emergency Department Assessment
NHS number: 000 812 8619

Patient: Oluwayanmife REED
Home address: 174 Bradford Place, Porthcawl, CF36 3AA
The patient, aged 34 years, was reviewed with a sibling present. Presented with a 36-hour history of marked itching and burning erythematous rash over both forearms and the upper chest. Symptoms began after using a new fragranced body product. No facial swelling, wheeze, throat tightness, fever, vomiting or mucosal ulceration. No recent antibiotics or other new medicines.

Past history otherwise unremarkable. Current treatment includes hydrocortisone cream and cetirizine, with partial relief. No known drug allergy reported.

Examination: alert and comfortable at rest. Airway patent; no lip or tongue oedema. Chest clear with equal air entry and no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination normal. Blanching, sharply demarcated erythematous papular plaques with excoriation on the exposed forearms and upper chest. No vesicles, purpura, cellulitis, discharge or skin loss. Observations within normal range. No blood tests or imaging indicated.

Impression: allergic contact dermatitis, without evidence of anaphylaxis, bacterial infection or systemic involvement.

Management discussed with the patient and sibling. Advised to stop the fragranced product, wash affected areas with lukewarm water, avoid scratching and use an unperfumed emollient frequently. Continue cetirizine and apply hydrocortisone cream sparingly for a short course, avoiding broken skin and the face. Safety-netted to return urgently for breathing difficulty, facial swelling, rapidly spreading rash, fever or mucosal involvement.

Discharged home in stable condition. GP review arranged in 18 days, on 22 November 2035, if symptoms have not settled or recur.

Treating clinician: FREDERIC LAKE

Patient: RONIE NICHOLSON
NHS number: 000 689 6406
Address: 71 BALLYHOLLAND PARK, PORTBALLINTRAE
Occupation: Warehouse operative
Employer: AGHALEE Further Education College

Dear Adult Mental Health Team,

I am referring RONIE NICHOLSON for assessment and treatment of probable generalised anxiety disorder. The specific question is whether specialist psychological therapy, medication optimisation, or both would be most appropriate, as persistent symptoms are now affecting sleep, concentration and day-to-day functioning.

RONIE NICHOLSON describes excessive worry across several areas of life, with difficulty controlling the thoughts even when there is no immediate problem to address. They report poor sleep, waking with a tense feeling, and sustained muscle tension in the neck and shoulders. There has also been intermittent nausea and reduced appetite, with a marked increase in physical anxiety for 3 days. Their adult child has noticed that they are increasingly withdrawn and seek repeated reassurance, although there is no reported confusion or change in personality.

There are no current thoughts of self-harm, suicidal intent or harm to others. They deny hallucinations, elevated mood or periods of unusually reduced need for sleep. At review in the accident and emergency department, they were appropriately dressed and engaged well. Speech was normal in rate and volume; mood was anxious, with congruent affect. They were orientated, with coherent thought processes and no evidence of psychosis. Observations were stable, and there was no acute medical explanation identified.

Sertraline has been started by the GP and is being taken regularly, with no significant adverse effects reported so far. We discussed that benefit can take several weeks and advised against stopping it suddenly. Sleep hygiene, reducing caffeine and paced breathing have been tried, but these measures have not adequately controlled the anxiety. The adult child is supportive and is aware of the referral, with the patient’s consent.

Please assess for a structured psychological intervention, particularly cognitive behavioural therapy, and advise whether the current sertraline treatment should be adjusted. We will continue primary-care follow-up and review risk while awaiting your assessment.

Yours faithfully,

Dr Mathew Godfrey, MBBS

LABORATORY REPORT – URINE MICROBIOLOGY AND INFLAMMATORY MARKERS

Patient: FREYAH PLANT
Home address: 177 Blows Road, Sittingbourne, ME10 1AA
Report/accession ID: 097076409
Requesting clinician: Unnamed clinical team
Reporting clinician: T. DONOVAN

Specimen and clinical context

Midstream urine and venous blood received for investigation of flank pain, dysuria and rigors. The patient reports a current pain score of 5/10. Cefuroxime and paracetamol are documented on the medication list; antibiotic exposure may reduce urine culture yield.

Results

Urine microscopy:
• Leukocytes: >100 × 10⁶/L (raised)
• Erythrocytes: 18 × 10⁶/L (mildly raised)
• Squamous epithelial cells: few
• Bacteria: numerous

Urine culture:
Significant growth of Escherichia coli, >10⁵ CFU/mL. Phenotypic susceptibility testing:
• Cefuroxime: susceptible
• Co-amoxiclav: susceptible
• Trimethoprim: resistant
• Ciprofloxacin: susceptible
• Nitrofurantoin: susceptible in vitro; not appropriate for suspected upper urinary tract infection

Blood results:
• C-reactive protein: 146 mg/L (reference <5 mg/L) – markedly raised
• White cell count: 15.8 × 10⁹/L (reference 4.0–11.0) – raised
• Neutrophils: 13.9 × 10⁹/L (reference 2.0–7.5) – raised
• Creatinine: 89 µmol/L (reference 45–90) – within stated interval
• Estimated GFR: >90 mL/min/1.73 m²

Interpretive comment

The urine findings and inflammatory response support an acute bacterial upper urinary tract infection, consistent with acute pyelonephritis. The isolate is susceptible to cefuroxime, although clinical response, renal function and ability to tolerate oral treatment should be reviewed. Assess for systemic infection, hypotension or obstruction; urgent emergency department assessment is indicated if rigors persist, vomiting prevents medication, or the patient becomes clinically unwell. Antibiotic choice and duration remain the responsibility of the treating team.

Follow-up

Clinical and microbiology review requested on 18th August 1988, with repeat assessment sooner if symptoms fail to improve.

Validated and electronically reported by: T. DONOVAN

Patient: T. Cameron
NHS number: 000 013 5845
DOB: 28 Dec 1979
MRN: 0278876
Home address: 156 Fifty Pitches Place, Sgonnsair / Sconser, IV48 8AA
Legal guardian: J. Dobson

Nursing progress – paediatric inpatient

Assessment: Admitted with acute asthma exacerbation. Awake and appropriately responsive; assent obtained for observations and treatment, with J. Dobson involved in care discussion. Audible expiratory wheeze, prolonged expiration and increased work of breathing. Reports night-time cough affecting sleep. Speaking in full sentences. No cyanosis or chest pain.

Observations: RR 28/min, HR 112 bpm, SpO₂ 94% on air, T 36.8°C. Weight recorded as 54.0 kg. Air entry reduced bilaterally, more marked at bases. No exhaustion noted.

Interventions: Salbutamol inhaler administered via spacer as prescribed; spacer technique demonstrated and then returned correctly by patient. Encouraged upright positioning, paced breathing and oral fluids. Trigger avoidance and importance of completing the prescribed inhaler regimen discussed with patient and legal guardian. Bedside inhaler and spacer available.

Response: After treatment, work of breathing eased and wheeze less prominent. SpO₂ improved to 96% on air. Tolerated oral intake; passed urine, no vomiting. Mobilising independently to bathroom but advised to call for assistance if dizzy or more breathless.

Risks/escalation: Continue close respiratory observations. Escalate urgently to medical team if unable to speak, increasing recession, drowsiness, silent chest, falling saturations or poor response to salbutamol. Oxygen and emergency equipment checked at bedside.

Plan next shift: Repeat observations and respiratory assessment, including response to inhaler. Reinforce spacer teaching, monitor sleep and intake, and confirm inhaler/discharge education before discharge planning.

Patient: ruqayah lacey
Address: 127 Maple Tree Close, Porthaethwy / Menai Bridge, LL59 5AA
The patient, aged 5 years, was reviewed in the paediatric outpatient clinic with his father, E. Ashley. His father reports increased thirst and frequent urination for 3 days, with noticeable weight loss over the recent period. No vomiting, abdominal pain, fever or reduced level of consciousness. He remains active and is attending activities through Griffithstown Town Council.

History
No previous diagnosis of diabetes. Appetite is reasonable. No polyuria overnight reported, although he has woken to drink. No intercurrent infection. Family understand the need for urgent assessment and have brought him directly to clinic.

Examination
Bright and interactive, mildly dry mucous membranes. Heart sounds normal, chest clear, abdomen soft and non-tender. Peripheral perfusion satisfactory. No Kussmaul breathing or altered behaviour.

Assessment
Symptoms and examination are concerning for new-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus, with possible early dehydration. Discussed with the paediatric medical team. Capillary glucose and blood ketones checked urgently; venous bloods arranged for glucose, electrolytes, bicarbonate and HbA1c. Urine requested for glucose and ketones.

Plan
Admit via the emergency department today for confirmation, fluid assessment and commencement of insulin under paediatric diabetes team supervision. His father understands not to delay if drowsiness, vomiting, abdominal pain or deep breathing develops. Diabetes specialist nurse referral and education regarding insulin administration, hypoglycaemia management and glucose monitoring to follow diagnosis. The family were advised to bring all usual medicines and monitoring equipment.

Discharge summary

Patient: kinvara metcalfe
Admission/document date: 29/03/2012
Clinical area: Respiratory medicine

Reason for admission
The patient, aged 82 years, presented with 48 hours of worsening right flank pain, dysuria, feverishness and recurrent rigors. There was no reported vomiting or vaginal bleeding. Initial assessment was consistent with an upper urinary tract infection, with concern for acute pyelonephritis.

Key findings
On arrival, the patient was alert and clinically perfused. Blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg, with mild tachycardia and a raised temperature. Right renal angle tenderness was present. There was no peritonism. Urinalysis showed leucocytes, nitrites and blood. Blood tests demonstrated an inflammatory response with preserved renal function. Blood cultures remained negative. Urine culture grew a cefuroxime-sensitive Gram-negative organism, and the result was reviewed before discharge.

Hospital course
Intravenous fluids and analgesia were given, followed by intravenous cefuroxime. Rigors settled during observation, flank pain improved and oral intake was maintained. There was no clinical evidence of obstruction or sepsis requiring escalation. Renal tract imaging was not felt necessary after the uncomplicated response to treatment. The case was discussed with the medical registrar, who agreed that oral step-down treatment was appropriate.

Discharge medicines
• Cefuroxime orally, to complete the prescribed antibiotic course.
• Paracetamol as required for pain or fever.
No regular medicines were stopped.

Condition and follow-up
Discharged home clinically improved and haemodynamically stable. The patient was advised to complete all antibiotics, drink regularly and seek urgent medical attention for recurrent rigors, persistent fever, worsening flank pain, vomiting, confusion or reduced urine output. The urine culture result and antibiotic sensitivities should be reviewed by the GP surgery if symptoms do not continue to improve.

Emergency contact: DEION REEVES, based in GARRISON. Contact details were confirmed with the patient before discharge.

Emergency Department Assessment
NHS number: 000 241 2904

Patient: Artyom M.
MRN: 017923810
Home address: 154 Camborne Place, City of Westminster, W1U 1AT
Contact: artyom.muhammad61@outlook.com
History from patient and partner, J. Barnard

Presenting complaint:
Two-day history of left flank pain with dysuria and urinary frequency. Reports shaking rigors overnight and reduced appetite. No vomiting, visible haematuria, vaginal symptoms or recent travel. Partner confirms intermittent fever at home. No known previous renal disease or recurrent urinary infections documented.

Assessment:
Alert and communicating appropriately. Temperature 38.4°C, pulse 104 bpm, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturations 98% on air. Mucous membranes slightly dry. Left costovertebral angle tenderness and mild left upper abdominal tenderness without guarding or rebound. No rash. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations unremarkable. No clinical features of septic shock.

Investigations:
Urine dip positive for leucocytes, nitrites and blood. Blood tests show raised inflammatory markers with white cell count 14.2 × 10⁹/L and CRP 128 mg/L. Renal function preserved; venous lactate 1.4 mmol/L. Blood cultures obtained before antibiotics. Midstream urine sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivities. Pregnancy testing not clinically indicated.

Management and decision-making:
Presentation is consistent with acute left-sided pyelonephritis. There is no current evidence of obstruction, peritonism or organ dysfunction. Given stable blood pressure, preserved renal function and ability to tolerate oral treatment, admission is not required at this stage. Discussed return precautions and the possibility of admission if cultures show resistance or symptoms worsen.

Received oral paracetamol in the department with improvement in pain and temperature. Commenced cefuroxime, with the first dose given before discharge; prescription supplied to complete the planned course. Encouraged regular fluids and advised against driving if feverish or dizzy.

Disposition:
Discharged home with partner. GP review arranged within 48 hours to assess response and review cultures. Safety-netting given: return to A&E for persistent rigors, vomiting, worsening flank pain, confusion, faintness or reduced urine output. Renal tract review is planned in about 10 weeks.

Dear zedan henry,
National Insurance number: NT 44 38 60 D

I am referring you to the movement disorders service for review of your established Parkinson disease and, in particular, to clarify whether your current treatment remains appropriate as your tremor and slowness have become more troublesome.

You describe a resting tremor, bradykinesia and muscular rigidity, with increasing difficulty initiating movement after sitting for a while. Your partner, MANVEEN MAXWELL, has also noticed that you are taking longer with dressing and meal preparation. There has been no recent fall, fainting episode or swallowing difficulty. You remain able to manage at home, although you are understandably concerned about losing independence.

Parkinson disease was previously assessed by neurology. Co-beneldopa has been continued in primary care, and you report taking it regularly. There is no clear wearing-off pattern from the history today, but the timing of symptoms in relation to each dose needs documenting before any adjustment is made. Please do not increase, stop or miss doses without medical advice.

On examination in clinic, there was a fine resting tremor affecting one hand, reduced facial expression, slowed finger tapping and mild bilateral rigidity. Your gait was slow with a short stride, but there was no postural instability on today’s assessment. Speech was understandable and there was no obvious cognitive or mood change during the consultation.

I would be grateful for specialist review of the diagnosis and medication schedule, including consideration of dose timing, physiotherapy and occupational therapy input, and assessment for non-motor symptoms such as constipation, sleep disturbance, urinary symptoms and low mood. Please also advise whether falls prevention or speech and language therapy would be helpful. A medication and multidisciplinary review would be particularly useful before further prescribing changes are made.

This referral is sent from Glenmavis. If you need to discuss symptoms while waiting, please contact your GP surgery. I have explained the reason for referral and the expected next steps to you and MANVEEN MAXWELL.

Yours sincerely,

naksh booth
Referring clinician
Professional identifier: 0729845

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report
NHS number: 000 496 4927

Patient: Keifer
MRN: 01448759
Requesting service: DEESIDE COMMUNITY HOSPITAL
Specimen: EDTA blood, received for thyroid-related molecular assessment
Collection date: 12th April 2020

Clinical details
Known hypothyroidism on replacement therapy. Reports fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation. Family history and indication for testing supplied on the request form; ordering clinician not stated here.

Biochemistry available for interpretation
TSH: 6.82 mIU/L (reference interval 0.27–4.20)
Free T4: 13.1 pmol/L (12.0–22.0)
Thyroid peroxidase antibody: 286 IU/mL (negative <34)

Interpretation
Raised TSH with free T4 at the lower end of the reference interval is compatible with suboptimally replaced primary hypothyroidism. Positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies support autoimmune thyroid disease. Results do not indicate overt thyrotoxicosis.

Medication recorded
levothyroxine 75 micrograms once daily

Comment
Please correlate with adherence, administration timing and any recent dose changes. If treatment has been stable, repeat TSH and free T4 in approximately 6–8 weeks following any adjustment, in line with local endocrine practice. Molecular testing is unlikely to alter immediate management in the presence of this biochemical and antibody pattern; laboratory review of the genetic request is available if a specific familial phenotype is documented.

Reported and authorised by: edie-may ritchie
DEESIDE COMMUNITY HOSPITAL
Report date: 12th April 2020

Respiratory Medicine Outpatient Review

Patient: Aanchal P.
MRN: 0073939
Contact: 07700 900869
Clinical age: 50 y/o

Reason for review

Assessment of worsening respiratory symptoms in the context of established chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

Clinical history

The patient reports a five-day increase in breathlessness above usual exertional limitation, with more frequent wheeze and a change in sputum colour to yellow-green. There has been no pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope or new peripheral oedema. The patient denies rigors and has not required attendance at A&E. Salbutamol inhaler use has increased to several times daily, with only transient benefit. There is no reported difficulty taking oral medication.

Treatment and response

A short course of prednisolone 40 mg once daily for 5 days has been commenced, together with doxycycline for suspected infective exacerbation. Salbutamol inhaler is to continue as required, with a reminder regarding spacer technique. The patient understands the importance of completing the antibiotic course and was advised to seek urgent assessment if breathlessness becomes severe, oral intake is poor, confusion develops or symptoms fail to improve.

Examination and interpretation

The patient was able to speak in full sentences but appeared mildly tachypnoeic on arrival. Chest examination demonstrated widespread expiratory polyphonic wheeze with reduced air entry bilaterally; no focal bronchial breathing or pleural rub was identified. There was no clinical evidence of fluid overload. The presentation is most consistent with a moderate acute exacerbation of COPD, with purulent sputum supporting a bacterial component. There are currently no features strongly suggestive of pneumonia or pulmonary embolism, although reassessment will be required if the clinical trajectory is atypical.

Plan

Continue the prescribed prednisolone and doxycycline, maintain regular inhaled maintenance treatment, and use salbutamol for breakthrough symptoms. Smoking cessation and vaccination status should be revisited at the next clinical contact. If recovery is incomplete, arrange chest radiography and spirometry once clinically stable; spirometry should not be interpreted during the acute episode. The patient has been given clear safety-netting advice and will be reviewed at the respiratory clinic on 10 January 2023.

Discharge summary

Patient: SHAHISTA MCLOUGHLIN
Discharging service: Aberdeen Royal Infirmary
Report/accession ID: 0537521170

Reason for admission
Presented via A&E with five days of worsening breathlessness, orthopnoea, bilateral ankle swelling and reduced exercise tolerance. No chest pain or infective symptoms reported. Examination was consistent with fluid overload, with bibasal crackles and raised JVP.

Key findings
Chest radiograph showed pulmonary vascular congestion with small bilateral pleural effusions. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm without acute ischaemic change. NT-proBNP was elevated. Troponin was negative on serial testing. Renal function remained stable during admission; potassium was satisfactory following diuresis.

Hospital course
Treated with intravenous loop diuretic therapy, fluid and salt advice, and daily weights. Symptoms and peripheral oedema improved, with no further orthopnoea. Oxygen was not required after initial assessment. Echocardiography confirmed impaired left ventricular systolic function, with no significant valve lesion. Heart failure specialist nurse reviewed the patient and provided self-management advice.

Medication changes
• Furosemide increased and to continue as furosemide 40 mg once daily.
• Bisoprolol continued at the pre-admission dose.
• No ACE inhibitor was commenced during this admission because of borderline blood pressure; this should be reconsidered when reviewed in the community.
The discharge medicines list supplied to the patient should be followed.

Follow-up and advice
GP surgery to arrange blood pressure, U&E and weight review within one week, with medication optimisation thereafter. Cardiology/heart failure clinic referral has been made. Seek urgent help for breathlessness at rest, chest pain, syncope or rapidly increasing swelling. The patient’s sibling, who lives in Stirling Village, was updated with the patient’s agreement.

Discharged home clinically improved and mobilising independently.

Signed: K. Aslam

Emergency Department Cardiology Handover
NHS number: 000 852 1329

Patient: Akasya
Accompanied by adult child, Emmalia. Referred from GLANGWILI GENERAL HOSPITAL following sudden-onset left arm weakness, right facial droop and slurred speech at home. Symptoms resolved before arrival; total duration approximately 20 minutes. No loss of consciousness, seizure activity, headache, chest pain or persistent visual disturbance. Adult child reports normal speech and walking since the episode.

Assessment: Alert and coherent. Speech now clear, facial symmetry restored. Power 5/5 in all limbs, normal sensation and coordination, no pronator drift. Pupils equal and reactive. Cardiovascular examination regular, no audible murmur. Chest clear. Blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, pulse regular, oxygen saturation satisfactory on air, afebrile. Capillary glucose within normal range.

Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm without acute ischaemic change. Blood tests sent, including FBC, U&Es, glucose, lipids and clotting screen; no immediately significant abnormality reported. CT head shows no acute haemorrhage or established infarction. Discussed with the on-call stroke team; presentation consistent with transient ischaemic attack, with symptoms fully resolved and no indication for thrombolysis.

Treatment and plan: Commenced aspirin after excluding haemorrhage and continue atorvastatin. Avoid driving until reviewed in line with DVLA guidance. Urgent specialist TIA clinic assessment arranged for 28th December 2024, including consideration of carotid imaging and ambulatory rhythm monitoring. GP medication reconciliation and vascular risk-factor review requested.

Safety-netting given to patient and Emmalia: call 999 immediately for recurrent weakness, facial droop, speech disturbance, visual loss or collapse, even if symptoms settle. Discharge appropriate with reliable supervision and written advice.

Handover completed by Kalesha Riley.

Dear Community Paediatrics Team,

Re: L. Whitehead

I am referring this 5-year-old East Asian male patient from Belfast City Hospital for specialist assessment of persistent iron-deficiency anaemia, with particular advice regarding investigation of the underlying cause and optimisation of treatment.

The history has been provided predominantly by the patient’s mother, ADERYN KEENAN, with the patient contributing appropriately during the consultation. There has been progressive tiredness, intermittent dizziness and reduced exercise tolerance. The dizziness is most noticeable on standing or during physical activity. There has been no reported syncope, chest pain, palpitations, melaena, rectal bleeding or persistent abdominal pain. Appetite is variable, with no reported dietary exclusion apart from a limited intake of iron-rich foods. The patient has experienced increased tiredness for 3 days, although the broader reduction in stamina has been developing over a longer period.

Examination in primary care showed a pale conjunctival appearance but no jaundice, lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were otherwise unremarkable, with warm peripheries and no clinical evidence of heart failure. There were no focal neurological findings. Growth and development have been reviewed as appropriate for the clinical setting, without an acute safeguarding concern identified.

Recent blood tests demonstrated low haemoglobin with microcytosis and hypochromia, reduced ferritin and an elevated red-cell distribution width, supporting iron deficiency. Inflammatory markers were not raised, and renal and liver profiles were within the laboratory reference ranges. Coeliac screening has been requested; results are awaited. The family has been advised to increase dietary iron where feasible and to avoid taking iron with milk.

Ferrous fumarate has been commenced and is being taken as prescribed. Tolerance has been reasonable, with mild constipation but no vomiting or rash. The GP surgery is monitoring adherence and response, with repeat full blood count and ferritin planned after an appropriate treatment interval.

I would be grateful for your assessment of the anaemia, including consideration of dietary, menstrual if relevant to development, gastrointestinal or absorption-related contributors, and advice on the duration and monitoring of iron replacement. Please also advise whether further paediatric investigations or dietetic input are indicated.

Yours sincerely,

Fredrick Ashley

A&E assessment

Patient: A. IRELAND
Occupation: Builder
Report/accession ID: LAB-05748957
Seen at: HOMEWARD BOUND UNIT ROYAL GWENT HOSPITAL
Accompanied by: friend

Presenting complaint:
Unilateral headache since this morning, predominantly left-sided and throbbing. Associated nausea and photophobia. Gradual onset, similar in character to previous migraine episodes but more persistent today. No preceding head injury. No fever, neck stiffness, rash, visual loss, diplopia, limb weakness, facial droop, speech disturbance or collapse. Friend reports patient has been resting in a dark room and taking fluids poorly.

Medication history:
Sumatriptan used at home with limited benefit. Naproxen also taken, timing uncertain. No anticoagulants reported. No known drug allergy documented in the available record.

Observations and examination:
Alert, orientated and appropriately communicative. Appears uncomfortable, shielding eyes from light. Pain score 5/10. Pupils equal and reactive; visual fields grossly full. Cranial nerves grossly intact. No facial asymmetry or dysarthria. Upper and lower limb power equal, sensation intact, coordination normal. No meningism. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations unremarkable. Afebrile clinically.

Assessment:
Migraine with nausea and photophobia. No focal neurological deficit or clinical features currently suggestive of subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis or acute intracranial event.

Plan:
Treated in department with oral antiemetic and analgesia; encouraged oral fluids and rest in a quiet, dark environment. Reassess response before discharge. Avoid further triptan or NSAID dosing until medication timings confirmed. Safety-net advice given: return immediately to A&E for sudden maximal headache, persistent vomiting, fever with neck stiffness, new weakness/numbness, confusion, seizure or visual change.

Discharge dependent on symptom improvement and safe accompaniment home. GP follow-up for review of migraine frequency and consideration of a preventative strategy if recurrent. Documented by miley-rae english.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY – CARDIOLOGY

Patient: KIRSTINA KAY
Home address: 11 PORTROSSE PARK, CORKEY
Contact: 07700 900168

Reason for admission
Presented with new central chest pressure associated with diaphoresis and nausea. Initial ECG showed no ST-segment elevation. Serial high-sensitivity troponin demonstrated a dynamic rise, consistent with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI).

Key results
Chest radiograph without acute cardiopulmonary abnormality. Echocardiogram: mildly impaired left ventricular systolic function with regional hypokinesia; no significant valve disease. Coronary angiography demonstrated moderate coronary artery disease without a target lesion requiring PCI. Renal function remained stable. Telemetry using the Model X3 cardiac monitor showed sinus rhythm, with no sustained arrhythmia.

Hospital course
Managed on the cardiology ward with aspirin, fondaparinux and high-intensity atorvastatin. Chest discomfort settled and there was no recurrent diaphoresis or nausea. Haemodynamically stable throughout admission; mobilising independently and tolerating diet. Cardiology discussed the angiography findings and secondary prevention measures with the patient and partner.

Discharge medicines
• Aspirin 75 mg once daily, lifelong
• Clopidogrel 75 mg once daily, to continue for 12 months unless reviewed sooner by cardiology
• Atorvastatin 80 mg at night
• GTN spray as needed for chest pain
Fondaparinux stopped at discharge. Medication changes explained; GP to review adherence and adverse effects.

Follow-up and advice
Cardiology follow-up to be arranged, with cardiac rehabilitation referral. GP review within one week for blood pressure, lipid profile and general recovery. Seek emergency help immediately for chest pain lasting more than a few minutes, breathlessness, collapse or recurrent sweating; use GTN as instructed and do not drive yourself to A&E.

Discharging clinician: Dr Abida Wallis, MBBS, GMC professional identifier 0105230

A&E clinical assessment – handover

Patient: L. Brennan  41 y/o
Home address: 71 Test Rise, Welland, WR13 5AA
Contact detail: letia.brennan90@virginmedia.com

Presenting problem
Lower abdominal pain for several days, worsening overnight. Purulent vaginal discharge and deep dyspareunia. No collapse, vomiting or urinary symptoms. Reports feeling feverish but no rigors. Menstrual history reviewed; pregnancy possibility discussed.

Assessment
Alert, uncomfortable but not toxic. Haemodynamically stable. Abdomen soft, tenderness across the lower abdomen, no guarding or rebound. No palpable mass. Pelvic examination with consent and chaperone: mucopurulent cervical discharge, cervical motion tenderness and bilateral adnexal tenderness. No active bleeding. STI and safeguarding questions asked privately; no immediate concerns disclosed.

Investigations
Urine pregnancy test negative. Urinalysis without convincing evidence of UTI. FBC, CRP, renal profile and LFTs sent. Vaginal/cervical NAAT swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea; microscopy/culture requested. Blood cultures not indicated currently. Results to be reviewed by the sexual health service.

Impression / action
Clinical pelvic inflammatory disease. No peritonism or sepsis to mandate admission. Given ceftriaxone in ED, then commenced doxycycline and metronidazole; first doses tolerated. Analgesia advised. Avoid alcohol with metronidazole, avoid sex until treatment completed and partners assessed.

Plan
Discharge with written advice and sexual health follow-up in about 8 weeks. Partner notification and testing discussed. Return urgently for worsening pain, persistent fever, vomiting, fainting or inability to take medication. Safety-net documented.

Handover to Ryan-James Kelly, Clinical Genetics, for result awareness and continuity.

Address: 69 Playfair Steps, Bishopbriggs, G64 1AA

Dear Respiratory Team,

There has been intermittent wheeze, night-time cough and shortness of breath over recent months. Symptoms are worse with cold air and during viral illnesses, with occasional limitation of usual activity. No admission or previous ventilation has been reported. Advice regarding an appropriate written asthma action plan would also be appreciated. Follow-up in general practice is arranged for 11/12/1996.

Yours faithfully,

HANADI SHEPHERD

MOLECULAR GENETICS REPORT

Patient: M. Powell
MRN: 09456529
Report date: 04/09/2004
Patient contact: 07700 900528

Clinical indication
Significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer. Predictive testing requested following discussion of inherited cancer risk. Spouse involved in consultation with patient’s agreement. No current treatment.

Specimen
Peripheral blood, EDTA. Germline DNA extracted for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer panel. Sample suitable for analysis.

Test performed
BRCA1 and BRCA2 sequencing with deletion/duplication analysis. Variant classification undertaken against current laboratory and clinical databases.

Result
BRCA1 c.68_69delAG: detected, heterozygous.

Interpretation
Pathogenic BRCA1 variant identified. This result is consistent with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer susceptibility and is clinically significant in the context of the reported family history. The finding is not diagnostic of malignancy and does not indicate that cancer is currently present.

Clinical comment
Recommend referral to the regional clinical genetics service for formal counselling, discussion of breast and ovarian cancer surveillance and risk-reducing options, and cascade testing of appropriate relatives. Management should be guided by genetics and relevant specialist teams. The patient should be advised to seek prompt assessment of any concerning symptoms through the GP or usual NHS pathway.

Limitations
This assay does not exclude pathogenic variants in genes not included in the panel, deep intronic or regulatory variants, or alterations below the assay’s detection threshold. Variant interpretation may change as evidence develops.

Ordering clinician: not stated.
Validated and reported by: Gulshan Wright
Laboratory genetics service
Additional clinical information can be provided through the requesting team.

Home address: 30 MAYOGALL ROAD, LARNE
Clinical age: 32 y/o

Productive cough, fever and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Adult child present and contributing to history. Patient reports increased breathlessness on mobilising but comfortable at rest. No haemoptysis reported.

Airway patent. Respiratory rate 24/min, oxygen saturations 94% on room air, pulse 102 bpm, BP 118/64 mmHg, temperature 38.2°C. Alert and orientated. NEWS2 calculated as 4; observations increased to 1-hourly. Coarse crackles at right base with reduced air entry. Skin warm, mildly clammy.

Mobilises short distance to toilet with standby assistance; dizziness denied. Oral intake reduced today but tolerating sips of water. Passed urine. Falls risk discussed; call bell within reach.

Medical team informed of persistent tachycardia and exertional breathlessness. Escalate promptly for increasing work of breathing, saturation below target, confusion, hypotension or inability to maintain oral intake. Adult child updated at bedside.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: Abi-Mae Sanders
Clinical age: day 3 of life
Legal guardian: Raiqa Nixon
Contact: 07700 900167
Date of discharge: 6th October 2019

Reason for admission
Admitted to the neonatal unit with visible jaundice, sleepy feeding and reduced oral intake. Bilirubin was above the local treatment threshold for gestation and postnatal age.

Key results
Serum bilirubin monitored during admission, with a satisfactory fall following treatment. Blood group and direct antiglobulin testing not suggestive of immune haemolysis. Glucose remained stable. Examination otherwise reassuring: no temperature instability, respiratory distress or focal infection. Current observations include heart rate 142 beats/minute.

Hospital course
Received intensive phototherapy with eye protection. Feeds supported with frequent breastfeeds and expressed milk; supplemental feeds given as required under the neonatal feeding plan. Intake improved and urine and stool output remained appropriate. Lactation support provided to Raiqa Nixon, who is the legal guardian and participated in cares. Phototherapy stopped after bilirubin fell below the treatment threshold; rebound measurement remained satisfactory.

Discharge condition
Alerter at feeds, maintaining temperature in an open cot, and clinically well. Jaundice visibly reduced. Feeding orally with improved volumes. No intravenous treatment required at discharge.

Discharge plan
• Continue feeding at least 8–10 times in 24 hours, waking for feeds if sleepy.
• Continue expressed milk supplementation as advised by the neonatal feeding plan.
• Observe for increasing jaundice, poor feeding, fewer wet nappies, fever, unusual sleepiness or breathing difficulty.
• Seek urgent medical assessment via A&E if difficult to rouse, persistently refusing feeds or breathing abnormally.
• Community midwife/health visitor to review feeding and jaundice, with bilirubin reassessment if clinically indicated.
• GP follow-up arranged through routine newborn care.

Discharge medicines: none. Phototherapy completed in hospital.

Dear Respiratory Medicine Team,

Re: sujith hutchinson

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient’s probable obstructive sleep apnoea, particularly whether formal sleep studies and continuous positive airway pressure are indicated.

There is a longstanding history of loud snoring, with recurrent witnessed apnoeas reported overnight by the patient’s adult child, Emiliia. They describe pauses in breathing followed by noisy gasping and restless sleep. During the day, sujith hutchinson is increasingly sleepy, including occasional difficulty maintaining concentration at work with SCARVA Secondary School. There have been no reported episodes of collapse or driving-related incident.

The patient has attempted to improve sleep routine and reduce evening alcohol, without meaningful change. Examination in the surgery showed a crowded oropharynx and a raised blood pressure compared with previous readings; chest examination was clear and there was no peripheral oedema. Epworth Sleepiness Scale screening is suggestive of clinically significant daytime somnolence. No current nocturnal treatment has been started.

Assessment: probable obstructive sleep apnoea with symptomatic daytime sleepiness and witnessed apnoeas. Please note that a consultant respiratory physician is involved in the wider respiratory service, but specialist sleep assessment is not currently available in primary care.

I would appreciate review, consideration of overnight oximetry or polysomnography as appropriate, and advice regarding initiation and monitoring of continuous positive airway pressure. The patient understands the reason for referral and has been advised not to drive if excessively sleepy.

Yours sincerely,

E. HOLLOWAY
GP
Dundonald

Laboratory report – Emergency Department

Patient: Malaikha S.
Report/accession ID: LAB-07427983
Requesting location: Bft Southmead Melksham Hospital
Specimen: Venous blood, fluoride oxalate tube
Clinical details: Thirst, fatigue and frequent urination. Known/suspected type 2 diabetes mellitus. Current medication: metformin, atorvastatin. Sample taken in A&E; fasting status not confirmed.

Glucose                         16.8 mmol/L  3.9–7.8 mmol/L (random)
HbA1c (IFCC)                    78 mmol/mol  20–42 mmol/mol

Clinical Genetics Specialist Report

Patient: Cleo Craig
MRN: 03188418
Contact: 07700 900141
Referral reason: Review of hypothyroidism and consideration of a hereditary contribution.

Clinical history
Cleo Craig is a 44-year-old Middle Eastern male patient referred for assessment of longstanding hypothyroidism. The reported symptoms of fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation have been more noticeable recently, without a clear precipitant. No history of thyroid surgery, neck irradiation or exposure to iodine-containing medication was reported. Family history was reviewed with the patient and their partner; there is no documented pattern of early-onset thyroid disease, congenital anomalies or a recognised endocrine syndrome.

Current treatment includes levothyroxine 75 micrograms once daily. Adherence appears consistent, although administration alongside breakfast was discussed as a possible cause of variable absorption. No other regular medicines were disclosed.

Examination and investigations
The patient was clinically stable during the consultation. No dysmorphic features, goitre or palpable cervical lymphadenopathy were identified. Neurological examination was grossly normal. Recent thyroid function results were not available for review in this clinic record; repeat thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine testing is therefore recommended through the GP surgery.

Interpretation and plan
The presentation is most consistent with common acquired hypothyroidism. At present there are insufficient clinical or family-history features to support a specific monogenic thyroid disorder, and genetic testing is not indicated. The GP should review thyroid function and prescription timing, with dose adjustment guided by results rather than symptoms alone. Consider coeliac screening if biochemical control remains unstable or if gastrointestinal symptoms develop.

The patient and partner were counselled that fatigue and constipation are non-specific and may have causes unrelated to thyroid status. They understand the assessment and are content with the proposed plan. Genetics follow-up is not routinely required, but reassessment can be arranged if additional affected relatives, unusual thyroid findings or syndromic features emerge.

Planned review appointment: 2024-09-02

Discharge summary – General Medicine

Patient: Anwit M.
Report/accession ID: 0710557783
Discharging service: Royal Victoria Hospital

Reason for admission
Presented via A&E with profuse watery diarrhoea, repeated vomiting and crampy central abdominal pain for 3 days. Reduced oral intake and dizziness on standing. No blood in stool, chest pain or urinary symptoms. Adult child Luna-Blu, from GARRISON, provided collateral history.

Initial assessment
Clinically dehydrated with dry mucous membranes and mild postural tachycardia. Abdomen soft, diffusely uncomfortable but without guarding or rebound. Afebrile during admission.

Key results
U&Es initially showed mild pre-renal AKI, improving following IV fluids. CRP minimally raised; FBC without significant leucocytosis. Stool culture and norovirus PCR negative. Blood cultures no growth. Report reviewed before discharge.

Hospital course
Managed as likely self-limiting infectious gastroenteritis. Received IV crystalloid, then oral rehydration solution as tolerated. Ondansetron given as required with good effect. Vomiting settled within 24 hours; diarrhoea markedly reduced and oral intake restored. No indication for antibiotics. Renal function returned to baseline.

Discharge condition
Mobilising independently. Haemodynamically stable, passing urine, tolerating fluids and light diet. Abdomen soft and non-tender at discharge.

Discharge medicines
• Oral rehydration solution: frequent small amounts until adequately hydrated.
• Ondansetron as required for nausea, in accordance with the supplied prescription.
No regular medicines started or stopped.

Follow-up / advice
Continue fluids and gradual return to normal diet. Hand hygiene; avoid preparing food for others until 48 hours after symptoms have ceased. Seek urgent medical review for inability to keep fluids down, worsening abdominal pain, blood in stool, confusion, reduced urine output or recurrent dizziness. GP review if diarrhoea persists beyond one week.

PAEDIATRIC LABORATORY MEDICINE REPORT

Patient: R. Waller
MRN: 0587846
Clinical context: The patient, aged 3 years, was reviewed with a parent’s account of dysuria, urinary frequency and suprapubic discomfort for 3 days. Nitrofurantoin has been commenced in primary care. Urine specimen submitted for microscopy, culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Ordering clinician not stated on the laboratory request.

Specimen: Midstream urine
Specimen quality: Adequate volume; no significant epithelial cell contamination.
Specimen type: Urine
Laboratory accession: Urine culture accession recorded on the laboratory information system.

Microscopy
White blood cells: 270 ×10^6/L
Red blood cells: 18 ×10^6/L
Squamous epithelial cells: Few
Bacteria: Moderate

Culture
Significant growth of Escherichia coli, >10^5 CFU/mL, pure growth.

Antimicrobial susceptibility
Nitrofurantoin: Susceptible
Trimethoprim: Susceptible
Cefalexin: Susceptible
Amoxicillin: Resistant

Interpretation: Findings support a lower urinary tract infection due to E. coli. The isolate is susceptible to nitrofurantoin, consistent with the treatment documented on the request. No mixed growth to suggest contamination.

Clinical comment: Please correlate with clinical response and ensure an appropriate paediatric dose and course have been prescribed. If symptoms are not improving, recur promptly, or there is fever, loin pain, vomiting or reduced fluid intake, urgent clinical reassessment is advised to exclude upper urinary tract involvement. Consider repeat urine testing if symptoms persist or the specimen was collected after antimicrobial treatment had started. Nitrofurantoin is not appropriate for suspected pyelonephritis.

Result authorised by: ELANAH DRAPER
Laboratory validation: Paediatric laboratory medicine
Report status: Final

Follow-up: Clinical review planned for 17th August 2035, or sooner if deterioration occurs.

Patient: Arlyn Perkins
MRN: 090070256
Occupation: Retail assistant
Seen in general medicine clinic with partner present.

Presenting problem:
Three recent episodes of abrupt palpitations, chest tightness and intense fear of dying. Episodes reached maximum severity within several minutes and settled over approximately 20–30 minutes. First episode occurred at rest; subsequent attacks associated with crowded environments and worry about recurrence. No exertional chest pain, syncope, sustained breathlessness or calf swelling. No alcohol or recreational drug trigger reported. Sleep reduced since the first event. Appetite maintained.

Background:
No previous cardiac diagnosis documented. No regular prescribed medicines. Using breathing retraining during attacks, with partial benefit. Partner reports patient remains well between episodes but avoids travelling alone. No suicidal thoughts, psychotic symptoms or manic features disclosed.

Examination:
Comfortable at rest, speaking in full sentences. Pulse regular, heart sounds normal, no murmur. Chest clear bilaterally. No peripheral oedema. Anxious affect but coherent, good insight and appropriately engaged.

Assessment:
Recurrent panic attacks with anticipatory anxiety. Current history and examination do not suggest acute coronary syndrome, arrhythmia or pulmonary embolism. Discussed that palpitations can feel alarming but the pattern is consistent with panic. Safety-netted regarding persistent chest pain, collapse, marked breathlessness or palpitations that do not settle.

Plan:
Continue breathing retraining, practising when calm as well as during symptoms. Discussed grounding techniques, reducing caffeine and maintaining regular meals and sleep. Patient agreeable to NHS talking therapies referral via Bft Southmead Cheltenham General Hospital; advised to self-refer or contact the surgery if unable to access this. No medication started today. Review with GP if attacks increase, functioning deteriorates or symptoms remain troublesome.

Follow-up:
Routine review in about 9 weeks, sooner if required.

Clinician: Dr Leejay Blake, MBBS

A&E Assessment

Patient: Ronik Lucas
Clinical age: 88 y/o
MRN: 0093865
Address: 151 Heol Gadlys, Merthyr Tydfil / Merthyr Tudful, CF47 0AA
Contact: ronik.lucas55@btinternet.com

Presenting complaint:
Central chest pressure commenced at rest approximately 90 minutes before arrival, radiating to left arm. Associated diaphoresis and nausea. No syncope. Friend present; history obtained directly, with collateral from friend.

Background:
No previous documented myocardial infarction. No recent surgery or bleeding reported. Medication history checked; no anticoagulant use disclosed. Allergies not recorded at triage.

Alert, clammy, speaking full sentences.
BP 158/92 mmHg, pulse 96 regular, RR 18, SpO2 98% on air, temperature 36.7°C.

CXR: no acute cardiopulmonary abnormality.

Ongoing ischaemic-sounding pain with dynamic ECG changes and raised troponin — NSTEMI. Differential includes reflux and musculoskeletal pain, less likely given objective findings. No clinical evidence of pulmonary embolism or dissection.

Treatment/plan:
Aspirin given on arrival. Fondaparinux commenced following review of bleeding risk. Atorvastatin administered. GTN spray improved pressure. Analgesia and antiemetic as required. Continuous cardiac monitoring; repeat ECG and troponin arranged. Cardiology registrar contacted; admit to monitored bed for cardiology assessment and angiography decision. Safety-netted regarding recurrent pain.

Patient: Dahab S.
MRN: 07548229
Address: 80 KNOCKSALLAGH PARK, UPPERLANDS

Dear Colleague,

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient with treated hypothyroidism and persistent fatigue, particularly in relation to marked resting bradycardia and reduced exercise tolerance. The specific question is whether the current cardiac findings require further investigation, and whether the symptoms are adequately explained by thyroid dysfunction alone.

The patient reports several months of tiredness, increased sensitivity to cold and constipation. There has been no syncope, exertional chest pain, orthopnoea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. Occasional light-headedness is reported on standing, without collapse. No previous cardiac diagnosis is documented.

Current treatment is levothyroxine, taken regularly. Recent thyroid blood tests showed TSH 8.6 mIU/L with free T4 10.2 pmol/L. Repeat testing and review of adherence have been arranged in primary care. Examination today: pulse 48 bpm, regular; blood pressure 118/72 mmHg sitting and 110/68 mmHg standing. Heart sounds normal, with no murmur or clinical evidence of fluid overload. The patient appeared clinically euthyroid apart from the reported cold intolerance and fatigue.

A 12-lead ECG demonstrated sinus bradycardia without atrioventricular block or acute ST-segment changes. There is no current medication known to reduce the heart rate. I have advised gradual positional change and to seek urgent review for syncope, chest pain or breathlessness.

The patient has already been reviewed regarding thyroid management by a consultant endocrinologist, with levothyroxine adjustment to be guided by repeat thyroid function tests. I would appreciate cardiology review, consideration of ambulatory ECG monitoring and echocardiography if indicated, and advice regarding the significance of the bradycardia and any further management.

Yours sincerely,

Dr JORDAN Ritchie, MBBS

Seen in clinic regarding recurrent skin irritation and itching, reported to have started for 3 days after using a new fragranced laundry product. Advised to stop the fragranced product and avoid other newly introduced cosmetics or detergents until settled. Emollient recommended regularly, particularly after washing.

Discussed seeking urgent help via 999 if breathing difficulty, throat tightness or rapidly progressive swelling develops. GP review if the rash spreads, becomes painful or fails to improve; consider dermatology or allergy assessment if recurrent.

Patient: PRANAVAN BRUCE
DOB: 27/12/2014

Admitted with 24-hour history of worsening right lower-quadrant pain, nausea and loss of appetite. History obtained from patient and legal guardian. No diarrhoea or urinary symptoms reported.

Tenderness and guarding in the right iliac fossa. Bloods supportive of acute inflammation. Ultrasound abdomen consistent with acute appendicitis; no collection identified. Surgical team reviewed.

Kept nil by mouth initially. IV fluids, analgesia with paracetamol and intravenous co-amoxiclav commenced. Underwent laparoscopic appendicectomy under general anaesthesia. Appendix inflamed, not perforated. No operative complications. Histology pending at discharge.

Paracetamol orally as directed on the dispensing label for pain. No further antibiotic required unless advised following clinical review.

Clinically well, pain controlled, afebrile, suitable for discharge home with R. Saunders today.

Advice and follow-up
Keep wounds clean and dry; do not pick at skin glue. Avoid strenuous activity until reviewed. Return to A&E urgently for increasing abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fever, abdominal swelling, wound redness/discharge or inability to drink.

GP/surgical follow-up arranged as per local pathway; histology result to be reviewed by the surgical team. Guardian advised to contact the ward via the usual hospital number if concerns arise.
