Clinical Genetics Referral

Patient: Eldar ALLAN
Occupation: bus driver
Employer: Mansfield Town Council
Relative accompanying patient: Cherish Bradbury

Dear Clinical Genetics Team,

I would be grateful for your assessment of Eldar ALLAN regarding a diabetic foot ulcer with clinically significant peripheral sensory loss. The specific question is whether the extent and distribution of neuropathy warrant investigation for an underlying inherited neuropathy or other genetic predisposition, in addition to established diabetic complications.

There is a plantar ulcer beneath the forefoot, with reduced protective sensation on examination and local discharge. The surrounding skin is mildly erythematous, without lymphangitis or systemic upset. Foot pulses are palpable and the limb is warm. There is no reported rest pain. The patient describes altered sensation in both feet, most marked distally, and reports that the current area of discharge has been present for 3 days. No previous ulcer has been documented in the available primary-care record.

Initial management has comprised community wound care, pressure reduction advice and co-amoxiclav. The wound has been dressed regularly, and a tissue viability review has been requested. There is no current evidence of acute spreading infection, although the ulcer will require ongoing surveillance and consideration of imaging if it fails to improve. Glycaemic control and routine diabetic foot-risk management are being reviewed in parallel.

The history provided by Cherish Bradbury raises concern that other relatives may have had unexplained distal sensory symptoms, although the available family history is incomplete. There is no confirmed family diagnosis of hereditary neuropathy recorded. Please consider whether nerve conduction studies, targeted genetic testing or broader investigation would be clinically appropriate, and advise on any implications for relatives.

I would also appreciate guidance on whether the pattern of neuropathy is disproportionate to the documented diabetes and whether specialist neurological review should be arranged alongside genetics assessment.

Yours sincerely,

Zaiyah Mitchell

Patient: J. Allison
Clinical area: Respiratory medicine
Document type: Nursing progress note

Situation
A 67-year-old Middle Eastern female patient admitted with acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Ongoing increased breathlessness, audible expiratory wheeze and purulent sputum. Reports chest tightness on mobilisation, no pleuritic pain. Alert and communicating appropriately. Rayyan Burke listed as emergency contact.

Observations
Breathing laboured after washing and dressing. Oxygen saturations maintained on prescribed low-flow oxygen; target range reiterated. Respiratory rate elevated but settled with rest. Temperature within normal limits. Pulse regular. Chest: widespread wheeze with reduced air entry bibasally. Sputum thick, yellow-green; specimen sent as requested.

Mobility and intake
Mobilising short distances with frame and one staff member. Becomes breathless on exertion, requires seated recovery. Call bell in reach and advised to request assistance before getting out of bed. Eating small portions; taking fluids adequately. Urine passed this shift.

Interventions and response
Nebulised bronchodilator administered as prescribed with partial improvement in wheeze and reported breathing. Salbutamol inhaler technique reviewed; spacer available. Commenced doxycycline and prednisolone. Medication instruction: prednisolone 40 mg once daily for 5 days. Encouraged upright positioning, paced breathing and regular sputum clearance. Response satisfactory at rest.

Risks / escalation
Falls risk due to exertional dyspnoea and unsteady recovery after mobilisation. Pressure areas intact. No acute confusion. Safety-net advice given. Escalate promptly for increasing work of breathing, falling saturations, drowsiness, inability to speak in sentences or reduced response to treatment. Covering medical team aware of persistent exertional symptoms; review requested if deterioration.

Plan for next shift
Continue observations and oxygen target as prescribed; reassess after nebulisers. Monitor sputum, oral intake and mobility tolerance. Encourage breathing exercises and assisted mobilisation. Confirm discharge planning and inhaler supply when clinically stable. Follow-up respiratory review booked for 1 November 2025.

Documented by: H. Kavanagh, registered nurse

DISCHARGE SUMMARY – Cardiology
NHS number: 0000352552

Patient: Zenah
Admission date: 21 Jun 2028
Responsible service: Cardiology, ABERDEEN ROYAL INFIRMARY
Discharge destination: Home

Reason for admission
Presented with several days of increasing breathlessness, orthopnoea, bilateral ankle swelling and reduced exercise tolerance. No reported chest pain or infective symptoms. Emergency contact Jorden Rodgers (locality: Logie Coldstone) updated during the admission with the patient’s consent.

Key findings
On arrival, clinically fluid overloaded with raised JVP, bibasal inspiratory crackles and pitting oedema to the lower legs. Oxygen saturations improved with low-flow oxygen. Chest radiograph showed pulmonary vascular congestion and small bilateral pleural effusions. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm without acute ischaemic changes. Blood tests showed an elevated NT-proBNP; renal function remained suitable for continued diuretic treatment, with mild transient worsening during active diuresis. Echocardiogram demonstrated impaired left ventricular systolic function with no significant valvular lesion.

Hospital course
Treated for acute decompensated heart failure with intravenous loop diuretic therapy, fluid and salt restriction, and daily weights. Respiratory symptoms and peripheral oedema improved substantially, with weaning to room air. Converted to oral treatment once euvolaemic. Existing beta-blocker therapy was continued; no evidence of cardiogenic shock or sustained arrhythmia. Medicines reconciled with the patient before discharge.

Discharge medicines
• furosemide 40 mg once daily
• bisoprolol – continue at the established dose
• Commence/continue other heart failure disease-modifying treatment as listed on the accompanying electronic prescription, subject to GP review of renal function and blood pressure.
Do not stop bisoprolol or furosemide without medical advice. Avoid over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medicines unless specifically advised.

Condition at discharge
Comfortable at rest, mobilising independently and able to lie flat. Minimal residual ankle oedema. No supplemental oxygen requirement. Discharge weight and fluid balance recorded in the ward documentation.

Follow-up and advice
GP review within one week, including blood pressure, weight, urea and electrolytes, and renal function. Cardiology heart failure nurse follow-up and outpatient echocardiographic/medication review to be arranged by ABERDEEN ROYAL INFIRMARY. Continue daily weights at home and seek urgent medical help via NHS 111 or A&E for rapidly worsening breathlessness, chest pain, fainting, confusion, or marked reduction in urine output. Return sooner if unable to sleep lying flat or if swelling increases quickly.

Discharge date: 21 Jun 2028

Emergency Department / Neonatal Assessment  
National Insurance number: TN 35 19 10 C
Date: 04/06/2024  
Patient: M. Mcleod  
Accompanied by legal guardian: Alexas Bennett

The patient, aged 2 weeks, was brought to the emergency department by the legal guardian because of increasing yellow discolouration and reduced breast and bottle intake. Guardian reports that the baby has been sleepier during feeds today, requiring repeated prompting to continue. Wet nappies remain present, with no reported fever, vomiting, abnormal movements or breathing difficulty. No safeguarding concerns disclosed.

On examination, jaundice was visible to the chest and upper limbs. Baby sleepy but rousable, settled with handling. AVPU response: alert. Good air entry bilaterally with no recession; heart sounds normal and peripheral perfusion satisfactory. Abdomen soft and non-distended. No bruising, rash or hepatosplenomegaly appreciated. Fontanelle soft. Feeding observed with weak initial suck and early fatigue.

Capillary blood glucose was within the neonatal reference range. Blood was taken for serum bilirubin, full blood count, reticulocytes, blood group and direct antiglobulin test. Bilirubin was above the treatment threshold for the gestational-age and postnatal-age line on the local neonatal guideline. Haemoglobin was satisfactory, with no immediate evidence of significant haemolysis. Results and treatment requirement were discussed with the guardian, who understood and agreed to admission.

Assessment: neonatal unconjugated jaundice with suboptimal intake and sleepiness, requiring inpatient monitoring and treatment. No current clinical features of sepsis or respiratory compromise, but low threshold for reassessment if condition changes.

Plan: commence intensive phototherapy in the neonatal unit, with eye protection and temperature monitoring. Provide feeding support, including assisted breastfeeds and expressed milk or prescribed supplementary feeds as required. Record intake and urine output; repeat bilirubin according to the neonatal protocol and monitor glucose. Senior neonatal clinician at The Royal Glamorgan Hospital accepted the referral. Admitted to the neonatal unit for ongoing observation and management. Guardian accompanied the baby and was given return precautions and an explanation of the likely course.

I would be grateful for your assessment of Nalisha, who attended the emergency department with several weeks of increasing thirst, fatigue and frequent urination. They have been drinking freely and are managing oral intake.

Capillary glucose in the department was elevated, with no clinical evidence of dehydration or ketosis. Urinalysis showed glycosuria but no ketones. Venous blood gas was reassuring, and renal function was acceptable. HbA1c 8.6%. The presentation is consistent with suboptimally controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus rather than an acute hyperglycaemic emergency.

They report taking metformin regularly, although the dosing history was initially unclear and adherence has been less consistent during recent work pressures. Current medication also includes atorvastatin. No insulin or other glucose-lowering treatment is being taken. They deny hypoglycaemic episodes. Examination was otherwise unremarkable: clinically euvolaemic, abdomen soft and non-tender, and observations stable.

Symptomatic hyperglycaemia in established type 2 diabetes mellitus, without evidence of ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar emergency. Glycaemic control requires review, and the recurrent thirst and polyuria warrant timely follow-up.

Plan and request

Please review medication adherence, metformin dosing and suitability for additional glucose-lowering therapy. I would also appreciate assessment of cardiovascular risk, renal function and urine albumin:creatinine ratio, together with retinal and foot surveillance if these are not up to date. The patient has been advised to maintain hydration, avoid sugary drinks and seek urgent medical attention for vomiting, drowsiness, worsening weakness or inability to maintain fluids. They understand the plan and will arrange follow-up with their GP pending your appointment.

Yours sincerely,

I. Horner

Discharge summary – Respiratory Medicine
NHS number: 000 852 3771

Patient: Filippa M.
Admission/discharge date: 22/02/2045

Reason for admission
Presented via the emergency department with several days of worsening lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge and deep dyspareunia. No vomiting or urinary symptoms. Pregnancy test negative. The patient, aged 44 years, reported no previous similar admission.

Initial assessment and key results
Haemodynamically stable on arrival, with suprapubic and bilateral lower abdominal tenderness, without guarding or peritonism. Pelvic examination demonstrated mucopurulent cervical discharge and cervical motion tenderness. Urinalysis without evidence of urinary tract infection. FBC showed a mild neutrophil leucocytosis; CRP modestly raised. Renal and liver profiles satisfactory. Vaginal/cervical swabs were taken for gonorrhoea, chlamydia and other organisms; results were pending at discharge. Pelvic ultrasound showed no tubo-ovarian abscess or significant free fluid.

Hospital course
Treated as pelvic inflammatory disease following discussion with gynaecology and the sexual health team. Received ceftriaxone intravenously on admission, then commenced oral doxycycline and metronidazole. Analgesia with paracetamol and ibuprofen was effective. Pain and discharge improved over the admission, with no fever, haemodynamic instability or clinical evidence of an abscess. Tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently.

Problem list
• Pelvic inflammatory disease, clinically improving
• Lower abdominal pain and dyspareunia, improved
• Cervical/vaginal swabs pending

Discharge medicines
Doxycycline to complete the prescribed course.
Metronidazole to complete the prescribed course.
Paracetamol as required for pain, within the labelled maximum dose.
Avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole and for the period advised by the pharmacy.

Advice and follow-up
No sexual intercourse until treatment is completed, symptoms have settled and sexual contacts have been assessed and treated. Partner notification and testing arranged through sexual health services; advised to attend promptly if contacted regarding the pending swab results. Return to A&E for increasing abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fever, collapse or heavy vaginal bleeding.

Review with the GP or sexual health clinic in about 4 weeks, with repeat assessment to confirm clinical resolution. Amimah, the patient’s adult child, was updated with the patient’s consent and is available locally in Hilltown.

Discharged home in stable condition, with written medicines and safety-netting advice provided.

Disposition: Suitable for ambulatory PE pathway with same-day anticoagulation. VTE nurse follow-up arranged; GP to review provoking factors, duration of treatment and thrombophilia assessment where appropriate. Respiratory clinic review in about 10 weeks.

• Maintain regular oral fluids unless otherwise advised.
• Continue temporary medication hold until reviewed by GP; restart only following blood-test review.

• Avoid over-the-counter NSAIDs.

Dear Colleague,

I would be grateful for your assessment of Denziel Joyce regarding whether the clinical presentation and reported family pattern of anxiety and related mental health difficulties warrant genetic counselling or any targeted genomic investigation. The patient understands that most generalised anxiety disorder is multifactorial and that a genetics appointment may instead provide reassurance and appropriate discussion of limitations.

There has been persistent, excessive worry across several areas of daily life, with associated poor sleep and prominent muscle tension. Symptoms have been present on most days and are affecting concentration and routine activities. No episodes suggestive of mania, psychosis or seizure disorder have been described. There is no reported intellectual disability, developmental regression or unusual physical phenotype. The patient reports a family history of significant anxiety symptoms in more than one relative, although detailed diagnoses and previous genetic testing are not currently available.

Examination in primary care was unremarkable apart from observable tension and a mildly anxious affect. There were no focal neurological findings and no dysmorphic features noted. Risk assessment has not identified current suicidal intent or thoughts of harming others.

Sertraline has been prescribed and is being tolerated without significant adverse effects. Sleep hygiene, reduction of caffeine, breathing exercises and talking therapy have been discussed; referral for psychological treatment is in progress. Symptoms remain clinically significant despite these measures.

The specific questions are whether the reported family history meets criteria for a clinical genetics review, whether any recognised syndromic features should be sought, and whether testing would be informative or likely to create uncertainty. Please advise on the appropriate family-history information and records required before appointment.

I will review progress in about 8 weeks and would be grateful for your recommendations regarding further management.

Yours sincerely,

Dr Bright Blackburn, MBBS

A&E Emergency Assessment
NHS number: 0000819698

Patient: WAFI TUCKER
Patient identifier/MRN: 0254916
Home address: 146 Brocastle Avenue, Borth, SY24 5AA
Contact: 07700 900736
The patient, aged 47 years, was reviewed in the emergency department with worsening pain and discharge from a postoperative abdominal wound. Adult child present and contributing to history.

History
Increasing redness around the wound with purulent discharge since yesterday. Local tenderness, reduced appetite and felt feverish at home. No vomiting, diarrhoea, chest pain or breathlessness. Passing urine normally. No known drug allergy reported. Postoperative dressing changed at home; no wound dehiscence noted by family.

Examination
Alert, communicating appropriately. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Peripheral observations stable; afebrile in department. Abdomen soft, non-distended, with local tenderness around incision only. Erythema extending approximately 2 cm from wound margins, warmth and small-volume purulent drainage. No fluctuance, crepitus or exposed bowel. Rest of examination unremarkable.

Investigations
FBC and CRP sent; results pending at time of review. U&E requested. Wound swab obtained for microscopy, culture and sensitivities. No indication for immediate imaging clinically.

Impression
Likely superficial postoperative wound infection. No current evidence of fascial disruption, abscess or systemic sepsis.

Treatment/Plan
Wound irrigated with sterile saline and redressed. Oral flucloxacillin commenced; first dose given in department. Safety-net advice provided regarding spreading erythema, rigors, worsening pain, vomiting or feeling faint. Surgical team referral arranged for wound review and consideration of drainage if collection develops. GP follow-up within 48 hours; return to A&E sooner if deterioration. Discharged with adult child, condition stable.

Interventions: IV access patent. Intravenous fluids running as prescribed. Morphine administered for breakthrough pain following prescription; regular analgesia maintained. Encouraged small, frequent oral fluids. Warm pack applied to lower back, with consent. Repositioned for comfort and clustered care.

Response: Pain reduced to 5/10 30 minutes after morphine. More settled, tolerating sips of water and juice. No adverse effect observed; respiratory rate and sedation level monitored post-dose. IV site clean and dry.

Risk/escalation: Risk of worsening vaso-occlusive pain, dehydration and acute chest syndrome. Escalate immediately for fever, oxygen desaturation, chest symptoms, increasing drowsiness, reduced urine output or uncontrolled pain. ABERDEEN ROYAL INFIRMARY sickle cell pathway available on ward.

Plan for next shift: Continue prescribed IV fluids, analgesia and regular observations; reassess pain before and after medication. Maintain strict fluid balance and encourage oral intake. Review hydration and analgesic requirements with covering clinician. Patient contact detail recorded as shivanya.daniels44@gmail.com.

Clinical Genetics Specialist Report
NHS number: 000 009 5053

Patient: S. Mann
MRN: 044750852
Referring service: GLANRHYD HOSPITAL
Occupation: Paralegal

Reason for review:
Assessment of possible inherited susceptibility to type 2 diabetes mellitus in the context of symptomatic hyperglycaemia and a reported family history. History obtained from the patient, with additional information from their partner.

Clinical history:
The patient describes increased thirst, fatigue and frequent urination for 3 days. No reported weight change, vomiting, abdominal pain or altered consciousness. There is no known history of diabetic ketoacidosis. Current treatment is metformin and atorvastatin; adherence is described as consistent, although the timing of recent doses was not confirmed at this consultation. The partner reports increased overnight drinking and disrupted sleep.

The family history was reviewed in detail. Several relatives are reported to have diabetes, although the precise ages at diagnosis and treatment requirements remain to be verified from primary-care records. No clear history of renal cystic disease, deafness, pancreatic insufficiency or syndromic features was elicited. No consanguinity reported.

Examination and investigations:
The patient appeared clinically well during review. No dysmorphic features or obvious syndromic findings were noted on limited examination. Capillary glucose and HbA1c results were not available in the referral documentation. Renal function, urine albumin:creatinine ratio and fasting lipid profile should be checked or updated through the GP surgery.

Impression:
The current presentation is compatible with type 2 diabetes mellitus. A monogenic diabetes syndrome cannot be assessed reliably without a three-generation pedigree, documented biochemical phenotype and clarification of diabetes treatment in affected relatives. The short symptomatic duration warrants prompt routine diabetic review to exclude marked hyperglycaemia.

Plan:
Continue metformin and atorvastatin pending medication reconciliation. Arrange HbA1c, venous glucose, renal profile, urine albumin:creatinine ratio and ketones if clinically indicated. Provide sick-day advice and advise urgent assessment via A&E if vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness or inability to maintain oral intake develops. Obtain family records before considering genetic testing. Follow-up in clinical genetics after results and pedigree information are available.

Signed: Dr Juber SLATER, MBBS

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: liyaan carr
Discharging service: General Medicine, Royal Victoria Hospital
Report/accession ID: 01443535

Reason for admission
Acute exacerbation of COPD with 3 days of increased breathlessness, audible wheeze and purulent sputum. No chest pain or haemoptysis.

Key findings
On arrival tachypnoeic with widespread expiratory wheeze and reduced air entry bilaterally. Chest radiograph: hyperinflation, no focal consolidation. Viral respiratory PCR negative. Blood tests without significant leukocytosis; renal function satisfactory. Initial oxygen requirement 1–2 L/min via nasal cannula, subsequently weaned.

Hospital course
Treated with nebulised salbutamol/ipratropium, oral prednisolone and doxycycline. Responded well over 48 hours; sputum colour and exercise tolerance improved. No evidence of pneumonia or cardiac decompensation. Oxygen saturations maintained within usual target range on room air prior to discharge. Observations before discharge included BP 120/80 mmHg.

Medication changes
Prednisolone 30 mg once daily for a further 3 days, then stop.
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily to complete a 5-day course.
Salbutamol inhaler, 2 puffs as needed, with spacer. Continue regular maintenance inhalers as previously prescribed. Inhaler technique checked.

Condition at discharge
Clinically stable, mobilising independently, eating and drinking. Safety-netting discussed with patient and friend umayma patterson, who lives in DONAGHADEE.

Follow-up / advice
GP review within 1–2 weeks for COPD management and consideration of pulmonary rehabilitation. Smoking cessation advice given. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E for worsening breathlessness, inability to speak in sentences, cyanosis, confusion or poor response to salbutamol.

Dear Cardiology Team,

Re: Om

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient with recently documented atrial fibrillation, particularly regarding rate-control strategy and longer-term rhythm management. They attended the emergency department with intermittent palpitations, fatigue and exertional breathlessness, reported by their partner to have been more noticeable for 3 days.

An ECG in the department showed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 118 beats per minute. There was no chest pain, syncope or focal neurological symptom. Blood pressure was stable and oxygen saturations were satisfactory on air. Chest examination was clear, with no clinical evidence of peripheral oedema. Blood tests showed no significant anaemia or electrolyte disturbance; thyroid function was requested and the result is pending. A chest radiograph did not show acute cardiopulmonary disease. Report/accession ID: 09104821.

The patient was discharged with apixaban and bisoprolol, with advice regarding bleeding symptoms, dizziness and worsening breathlessness. They report taking both medicines as prescribed, although fatigue has persisted and palpitations remain episodic, particularly on walking. There is no known history of stroke or transient ischaemic attack. Please review the indication and dosing of anticoagulation, confirm the appropriate rate target, and advise whether echocardiography, ambulatory monitoring or elective cardioversion should be arranged.

Assessment: Symptomatic atrial fibrillation with exertional breathlessness despite initial rate-control treatment. Haemodynamically stable at present, with no evidence of acute heart failure or acute coronary syndrome.

Plan: Continue apixaban and bisoprolol pending specialist review. The patient has been advised to seek urgent medical attention for persistent chest pain, collapse, severe breathlessness or new neurological symptoms. I would appreciate cardiology review and written recommendations for ongoing management.

Yours sincerely,

HEZEKIEL OWENS
Aberdeen Royal Infirmary
GMC number: GMC 0140275

General Medicine Clinic Note

Patient: Kirpal
Occupation: Barista
Employer: Blakelands Voluntary Service
Home address: 2 Merritts Brook Close, Endon, ST9 0AA
Contact: 07700 900212

Seen in clinic for review of recently identified atrial fibrillation. Kirpal describes intermittent awareness of a rapid, irregular heartbeat, particularly when climbing stairs or walking briskly. There has also been persistent tiredness and breathlessness on exertion, without breathlessness at rest. No chest pain, syncope, haemoptysis or unilateral leg swelling. The patient’s adult child attended and confirms that reduced exercise tolerance has been noticeable over recent weeks.

Taking bisoprolol as prescribed. Apixaban commenced following discussion of stroke prevention; no bleeding, melaena, haematuria or unusual bruising reported. Medication reconciliation confirms apixaban 5 mg twice daily. No missed doses disclosed. Alcohol intake and over-the-counter medicines reviewed.

Atrial fibrillation, currently rate controlled on bisoprolol. Ongoing exertional fatigue and breathlessness, with no features of acute heart failure or acute coronary syndrome today. Anticoagulation tolerated.

Plan

Continue bisoprolol at the current dose and continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily. Discussed the importance of regular dosing and seeking urgent help for significant bleeding, collapse, severe chest pain or breathlessness at rest. Arrange transthoracic echocardiogram and review the result in general medicine clinic. Consider cardiology discussion regarding rhythm-control options if symptoms persist despite adequate rate control. The patient and adult child understand the plan and will contact the surgery if symptoms worsen.

Accompanied by: uncle, Erin-Leigh RHODES

Wheeze and increased work of breathing for 3 days, with night-time cough. Used salbutamol inhaler at home with partial, short-lived relief. No fever, coryzal symptoms, chest pain or choking episode. Drinking normally; no vomiting. Uncle reports disturbed sleep but usual activity between episodes.

Known episodic asthma. No previous intensive care admission or intubation reported. Regular medicines reviewed. No known drug allergy recorded. Assent obtained from patient; history supplemented by uncle.

Acute asthma exacerbation, mild to moderate. No clinical evidence of pneumonia, pneumothorax or impending respiratory failure.

Observed after treatment with sustained improvement. Discharged home with salbutamol inhaler via spacer as required, written asthma advice and safety-netting. I would be grateful for same-day community paediatric review to confirm the likely cause of the jaundice, interpret the bilirubin against postnatal treatment thresholds, and advise whether continued phototherapy or admission is required. Please also assess hydration and feeding effectiveness, and arrange repeat bilirubin and weight monitoring. The guardian has been advised to seek urgent assessment via the emergency department if the infant becomes difficult to rouse, stops feeding, develops fever, has markedly fewer wet nappies or appears unwell.

Yours sincerely,

Nellie-Mai Wild

Targeted hypertension gene panel, including CYP11B2, CLCN2, HSD11B2, KCNJ5, NR3C2, SCNN1A, SCNN1B, SCNN1G and WNK1.

Discharge summary

Patient: Shante Fitzgerald
Home address: 4 GRIEVE PARK, BOLEA
Contact: shante.fitzgerald50@yahoo.co.uk
Admission/discharge date: 11 November 2012

Reason for admission
Presented via A&E with several days of productive cough, fever and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Breathlessness on exertion but no resting dyspnoea. Initial assessment consistent with community-acquired pneumonia; coded as SNOMED CT 233604007.

Key findings
On arrival febrile with mild tachycardia and oxygen saturations below the usual target on air. Chest examination demonstrated coarse crackles at the right base. Chest radiograph showed right lower-zone air-space opacity, without pleural effusion. Blood tests showed raised inflammatory markers; renal function and liver profile remained satisfactory. Blood cultures were negative. Viral respiratory screen negative.

Hospital course
The patient, aged 83 years, was admitted for intravenous antibiotics and observation. Oxygen was given initially and weaned within the admission as saturations improved. Treated with intravenous amoxicillin, subsequently changed to oral therapy once clinically stable. Paracetamol used for fever and pleuritic discomfort with good effect. Oral intake and mobility improved, and there was no clinical evidence of sepsis or respiratory failure.

The spouse was updated regarding progress and discharge arrangements. By review on 11 November 2012, the patient was afebrile, haemodynamically stable and maintaining satisfactory oxygen saturations on air. Cough persists but is less frequent; pleuritic pain substantially improved. Eating, drinking and mobilising independently.

Discharge diagnoses
1. Community-acquired pneumonia, right lower zone.
2. Pleuritic chest pain secondary to infection.
3. Fever, resolved.

Discharge medicines
Amoxicillin orally to complete the prescribed course; follow the dispensing label and do not stop early unless advised by a clinician.
Paracetamol for pain or fever as required, within the stated maximum daily dose. No other medication changes documented.

Follow-up and advice
GP review if symptoms are not continuing to improve, or sooner for recurrent fever, increasing breathlessness, confusion, haemoptysis, inability to maintain fluids or worsening chest pain. Return to A&E for severe breathing difficulty, blue lips or sudden deterioration. Gradual return to normal activity; maintain fluids and rest. Consider follow-up chest radiograph through the GP if cough or breathlessness persists, in line with local practice.

Discharged home in stable condition. Discharge information provided and understood.

Molecular Genetics Laboratory Report
NHS number: 0007984970

Patient: K. Hussain
MRN: 060439920
Requesting service: Flint Community Hospital
Specimen: Peripheral blood, EDTA
Collection/report date: 2020-06-29
Clinical indication: Predictive testing owing to significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer; patient expresses cancer-risk concern. No current treatment.

Test performed:
Targeted analysis of BRCA1 and BRCA2, including the familial variant BRCA1 c.68_69delAG. Sequence confirmation by orthogonal method where indicated.

Result:
BRCA1 c.68_69delAG detected in the heterozygous state.

Interpretation:
Pathogenic BRCA1 variant identified. This result is consistent with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer predisposition. It is not diagnostic of current malignancy. The finding may explain the reported family history and has implications for surveillance, risk-reducing management and blood-relative testing.

Recommendations:
Genetic counselling advised to review inheritance, reproductive implications and options for cascade testing. Refer to the regional familial cancer service for individualised breast and ovarian risk management. The patient should discuss appropriate surveillance with the specialist team; management should not be based on this laboratory result alone.

Analytical limitations:
This assay does not exclude deep intronic variants, balanced rearrangements, low-level mosaicism or pathogenic variants in genes outside the tested panel. A negative result in a relative requires interpretation in the context of the familial variant.

Authorisation:
Validated and electronically reported by Dr Jolin Bhatti, MBBS, Laboratory Clinician.
Report status: Final

Admission: Acute painful sickle cell crisis

Reason for admission
Presented to A&E with severe bilateral limb pain and lower back pain for 3 days, associated with reduced oral intake and clinical dehydration. No chest pain, breathlessness, focal neurological symptoms or urinary symptoms. Previous sickle cell disease documented; no recent transfusion reported.

Key findings
Initial assessment: distressed with marked limb and back tenderness, dry mucous membranes and tachycardia. Oxygen saturations maintained on room air. No focal chest signs or features of acute chest syndrome.

Blood tests showed raised inflammatory markers without significant neutrophilia, haemoglobin close to the patient’s usual baseline and no biochemical evidence of acute kidney injury. Reticulocytosis was consistent with haemolysis. Chest radiograph showed no focal consolidation. Blood cultures remained negative. Group and save completed; transfusion was not clinically indicated.

Hospital course
Managed on the acute medical ward with a personalised analgesia plan. Intravenous fluids were given for dehydration, with regular reassessment of fluid balance. Morphine was administered initially by the prescribed route, then reduced as pain improved; antiemetic and laxative cover provided. Paracetamol was continued regularly. No evidence of sepsis or acute chest syndrome developed. Mobilisation improved with physiotherapy advice, and oral intake returned to baseline.

Pain was controlled on oral medication for the final period of observation. Renal function and haemoglobin remained stable. No transfusion, oxygen therapy or procedure required.

Problem list
• Sickle cell painful crisis – improved
• Dehydration – resolved following intravenous fluids

A&E medical assessment

Patient: SHARAINE CONWAY
Home address: 172 Melcombe Avenue, Lidlington, MK43 0AA
Contact: sharaine.conway27@outlook.com
History from patient and sibling.

Presenting complaint: Reduced urine output for 2 days, marked fatigue and poor oral intake. Passing only small amounts of dark urine. No dysuria, loin pain, vomiting or diarrhoea. No chest pain or breathlessness. Sibling reports increasing lethargy but remains orientated.

Background: 74-year-old African American female patient. Hypertension. No known chronic kidney disease. Recent viral-type illness. Regular medicines reviewed; no NSAID use reported.

Examination: Alert, tired-looking, clinically dry. Obs stable: BP 104/68, HR 96, afebrile, SpO2 98% on air. Mucous membranes dry. JVP not elevated. Heart sounds normal, chest clear. Abdomen soft, non-tender; bladder not palpable. No peripheral oedema. Urine dip: concentrated urine, trace protein, no blood or nitrites.

Investigations: FBC without significant anaemia. Urea and electrolytes: creatinine 186 µmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L. Previous renal function requested from GP; not immediately available. Venous lactate normal. Renal tract ultrasound: no hydronephrosis or obstructive cause.

Impression: Likely pre-renal acute kidney injury secondary to dehydration and poor intake. No current indication for emergency renal replacement therapy.

Treatment/plan: Intravenous sodium chloride commenced, with strict fluid balance and repeat observations. Temporary medication hold agreed pending renal recovery; avoid NSAIDs and other nephrotoxins. Repeat U&E after fluids showed improving urine output and stable potassium. Discussed admission versus ambulatory review with patient and sibling. Suitable for short-stay medical observation, repeat bloods and senior review; admit if renal function worsens or oral intake remains inadequate.

Documented by Lilly-June REED, General Medicine.

Dear Community Paediatrics Team,

Re: AISLIN HALL, 8 y/o

I would be grateful for your assessment of this child with persistent atopic eczema, particularly to clarify whether there is an additional contact or food-related trigger and to advise on longer-term management. The referral is made with the agreement of the patient and parent, Nir Anwar.

There is a history of dry, inflamed and markedly itchy skin affecting the antecubital fossae, wrists, neck and popliteal areas. Symptoms are worse overnight, with frequent waking and scratching. The current flare has been present for 3 days. No fever, reduced oral intake, wheeze or facial swelling. Parent reports occasional yellow crusting over excoriated areas but no spreading erythema or systemic upset.

Examination today shows xerosis with erythematous eczematous plaques and excoriations over the flexures and wrists. Mild lichenification is present at the antecubital fossae. No vesicles, honey-coloured crusting, pustules or evidence of cellulitis. The child is alert and comfortable at review. Growth and general development appear satisfactory by history.

Management to date has included regular emollient application, although use is inconsistent during school days. Topical hydrocortisone has been applied to inflamed areas during flares, with partial improvement. The family would benefit from a written flare plan and reinforcement of fingertip-unit quantities, safe steroid use and avoidance of fragranced products. Sleep remains disrupted despite these measures. There is no reported immediate reaction to a specific food, and I have advised against dietary exclusion without specialist guidance.

Please assess severity, review treatment technique and consider whether patch testing, allergy assessment or escalation to a stronger topical anti-inflammatory regimen is indicated. Advice regarding school-based skin care and management of nocturnal itch would also be appreciated.

Referring organisation: Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh

Yours faithfully,

J. Wilson

Interpretation: Within reference interval

Discussed ongoing tachycardia and exertional symptoms with covering medical team; continue observation and escalate urgently for worsening chest pain, syncope, increased oxygen requirement, haemodynamic change or new confusion. Avoid unsupervised mobilisation.

Four-hourly observations, oxygen titration to prescribed target, reassess pain and breathlessness, encourage fluids and gradual mobilisation. Confirm anticoagulant education and discharge arrangements. Follow-up review booked for 5th June 2012.

Typical posterior-canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. No evidence of central cause or acute cardiopulmonary pathology.

Sickle cell team review arranged for 9 July 2025. GP to review ongoing analgesia and hydration plan. Friend Daanvi, based in Milltown, aware of the discharge arrangements.

Return to A&E urgently for new chest pain, breathlessness, fever, increasing drowsiness, inability to drink, reduced urine output, or pain not controlled by the prescribed medication. Avoid excess exertion while recovering and seek advice early during future painful episodes.

EDTA blood received for targeted analysis related to recurrent urinary infection. Sample suitable for processing. No family history supplied beyond sibling involvement.

Laboratory findings
Urine culture result supplied with referral: significant growth of Escherichia coli. Antimicrobial susceptibility not performed within Clinical Genetics.
Blood-derived genomic DNA: adequate concentration and integrity for analysis.
Targeted hereditary tubulointerstitial kidney disease panel: no pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant identified in the genes assessed.
Variants of uncertain significance: none reported.
Copy-number analysis: no clinically significant deletion or duplication detected.

Interpretation
The genetic findings do not identify an inherited molecular cause for the current episode of acute pyelonephritis. A negative panel does not exclude a genetic contribution outside the tested genes or variants below assay sensitivity. This result does not alter antimicrobial management; continue clinical assessment and microbiology-directed treatment.

Clinical comment
Correlate with urine culture, renal function and response to cefuroxime. Consider renal ultrasound or urology review if recurrent infection, obstruction, atypical organism or poor clinical response. Genetic review is not routinely required for a single uncomplicated episode. Re-refer if recurrent pyelonephritis, persistent haematuria, declining renal function or a stronger family history emerges.

Laboratory section: Clinical Genetics

Persistent vomiting with poor oral intake and dizziness. Reports weight loss over recent days and reduced urine output. Pregnancy confirmed; 9+4 weeks' gestation. Spouse present and corroborates history.

Unable to retain food or fluids since yesterday despite cyclizine prescribed by GP. No haematemesis, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, dysuria or vaginal bleeding. No chest pain, palpitations or breathlessness. No previous cardiac history. No known drug allergies documented.

First-trimester hyperemesis with dehydration and starvation ketosis. Weight loss reported. No abdominal or haemodynamic features requiring immediate obstetric intervention.

Cannula inserted. Intravenous sodium chloride commenced, with antiemetic treatment using cyclizine. Thiamine given before further carbohydrate-containing intake. Discharge home with spouse after clinical improvement. GP and early-pregnancy service follow-up advised for ongoing weight loss and review of antiemetic regimen. Return to A&E if worsening.

Dear Colleague,

Re: A. McLoughlin

Thank you for assessing this adolescent, aged 17 years, referred from ROYAL VICTORIA HOSPITAL for specialist advice regarding recurrent headaches consistent with migraine, and to consider whether further investigation or preventive treatment is indicated.

History

Headaches have occurred for approximately six months, initially every few weeks but now around twice weekly. The pain is predominantly unilateral, throbbing and moderate to severe, lasting several hours if untreated. Episodes are associated with nausea and photophobia; there has been occasional vomiting but no persistent visual loss, diplopia, weakness, sensory disturbance, collapse or alteration in consciousness. No early-morning vomiting or headache waking the patient from sleep has been reported. There is no history of head injury or seizure.

nethra ray, the patient’s mother, reports that attacks are more likely after missed meals, poor sleep or prolonged screen use. The patient describes anxiety about missing education and has agreed to referral; confidentiality and involvement of the family in management have been discussed appropriately.

Examination

Reviewed in the community clinic. Alert and communicating normally. Weight 54.0 kg. Neurological examination is reassuring: pupils equal and reactive, full ocular movements without nystagmus, normal fundoscopy, facial movements and speech; normal power, tone, coordination and gait. No meningism. Blood pressure was within the expected range for the clinical setting.

Management to date

A headache diary has been commenced, with advice on regular meals, hydration, sleep routine, exercise and limiting analgesic use. Sumatriptan has been prescribed for severe attacks, with naproxen taken with food when required. The family understand the risk of medication-overuse headache and have been advised not to use acute treatment on more than two days per week where possible. Despite these measures, attacks remain disruptive.

Clinical question and request

Please review the diagnosis and management plan, advise whether neuroimaging or other investigations are warranted, and consider migraine prophylaxis and/or a structured adolescent headache programme. A written plan for school and primary care would also be helpful.

Yours sincerely,

Dr Saariyah Sheikh, MBBS

Neonatal bilirubin report

4 m/o

Specimen: Serum, neonatal sample
Request: Unnamed clinician; assessment of visible jaundice and poor feeding

Conjugated bilirubin: 9 µmol/L
Unconjugated bilirubin: 277 µmol/L
Haemoglobin: 168 g/L
Reticulocytes: 4.1%

DAT: Negative
Sample quality: No haemolysis detected.

Predominantly unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Conjugated fraction is not raised. Correlate total bilirubin with postnatal age, gestational age and local treatment threshold chart. Continue observations, fluid balance and stool chart. Offer oral rehydration solution regularly, antiemetic as required, review intake and mobility. Maintain isolation precautions and update partner with patient consent.

I would be grateful for your assessment of Annisa N., who has developed persistent fatigue with intermittent light-headedness and reduced exercise tolerance. The specific question is whether there is a cardiac contribution, particularly in view of a low resting heart rate recorded in the surgery, or whether these symptoms are adequately explained by hypothyroidism.

There is a background diagnosis of primary hypothyroidism, treated with levothyroxine. The patient describes increased sensitivity to cold and constipation, with fatigue present for 3 days on the current acute episode, although reduced energy has been more persistent. No chest pain, syncope, orthopnoea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea has been reported. Occasional awareness of the heartbeat occurs at rest but there is no sustained tachycardia. No family history relevant to sudden cardiac death is known.

At review, the patient was haemodynamically stable. Pulse was regular at 52 beats per minute and blood pressure was 118/72 mmHg. Heart sounds were normal, with no murmur; chest was clear and there was no peripheral oedema. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus bradycardia without acute ST-T wave change or conduction block.

Recent thyroid function testing showed TSH 6.8 mU/L with free T4 12.1 pmol/L. Full blood count, ferritin, renal profile and glucose were unremarkable. Levothyroxine adherence and administration away from food were discussed, and repeat thyroid function tests have been arranged following review of the dose by the GP. The patient is not taking a beta-blocker or other rate-limiting medicine.

Please advise whether ambulatory ECG monitoring, echocardiography or further cardiac investigation is indicated. I would also welcome guidance on the significance of the bradycardia and any precautions while the thyroid replacement is being optimised.

Yours sincerely,

Serenah Knowles

Discharge summary – Paediatrics

Patient: Amara-Louise
Clinical age: 11 y/o
Home address: 9 ESSEX GROVE, BELLANALECK
Contact: amara-louise.radford27@outlook.com
Parent/carer: father, Daniaal Phillips

Reason for admission
Presented with an acute painful episode related to sickle cell disease, with severe bilateral limb and lower back pain and reduced oral intake. Father reported increasing lethargy and poor fluid intake before attendance. No preceding chest pain, cough, breathlessness or focal neurological symptoms.

Initial assessment
Alert but distressed by pain. Clinically dehydrated with dry mucous membranes; peripheries warm and capillary refill maintained. No respiratory distress, chest clear. Abdomen soft, non-tender. No focal joint swelling or evidence of acute infection. Initial pain score 9/10.

Investigations
FBC in keeping with known haemoglobinopathy, with anaemia at baseline and reticulocytosis. White cell count mildly raised. U&Es showed mild dehydration without significant renal impairment. CRP not significantly elevated. Blood cultures remained negative. Chest radiograph showed no consolidation or features of acute chest syndrome.

Hospital course
Managed on the paediatric ward with regular observations, oral fluids as tolerated and intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride until hydration improved. Received intravenous morphine with subsequent conversion to oral analgesia; antiemetic given once for nausea. Pain team and paediatric haematology advice obtained. Oxygen saturations remained normal in air, with no fever, respiratory compromise or new neurological deficit. Fluids were stopped once oral intake and urine output were satisfactory. Morphine requirement reduced steadily. At review before discharge, pain was 5/10, mobilising around the ward and comfortable at rest.

Problems during admission
• Sickle cell painful crisis
• Dehydration, resolved
• Acute severe pain, improving
• No evidence of acute chest syndrome or bacterial sepsis

Discharge treatment and advice
Continue prescribed oral analgesia as per the supplied discharge medicines list, using morphine only for breakthrough severe pain and keeping a written record of doses. Encourage frequent oral fluids and usual diet. Avoid overheating, chilling and strenuous activity until fully recovered. Seek urgent assessment via A&E for fever, breathing difficulty, chest pain, unusual drowsiness, weakness, persistent vomiting, increasing abdominal swelling or pain not controlled by the discharge plan.

Father was present for the discharge discussion and able to repeat the warning symptoms and medication instructions. Follow-up with the usual sickle cell/paediatric haematology team and GP surgery; family to contact the haematology service if pain recurs or oral intake falls. Discharged home clinically improved, afebrile and haemodynamically stable.

Sumatriptan at onset, with partial benefit. Naproxen used with food when required. Advice given regarding regular meals, hydration, sleep and headache diary. No medication-overuse pattern identified. MRI brain requested locally because of changing frequency; result not yet available.

Clinical question:
Please advise whether the phenotype and reported family history warrant genetic assessment or testing, and whether any further investigation is indicated. Guidance on counselling the patient and adult child would be appreciated.

Dr Jhanae Ferguson, MBBS

Discharge summary – Cardiology/Medical Assessment
NHS number: 0008624969

Patient: Natalia Davidson
Primary diagnosis: First-trimester hyperemesis gravidarum with dehydration and weight loss.
Gestation: 9+4 weeks' gestation.

Natalia Davidson was admitted following several days of persistent vomiting with inability to retain fluids or oral medication. Her spouse, ella-ray flanagan, from Hardmuir, provided collateral history and remained involved during the admission. Initial assessment demonstrated clinical dehydration, with dry mucous membranes and postural symptoms. Urinalysis showed ketones. Blood tests showed mild hypokalaemia, which corrected with replacement; renal function and liver enzymes remained satisfactory. There was no abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding.

She was treated with intravenous sodium chloride, intravenous thiamine and antiemetic therapy. Cyclizine was given regularly initially, then changed to oral treatment when vomiting settled. Oral fluids and a light diet were reintroduced gradually. No further vomiting was recorded during the final day of admission, and she passed urine normally. Weight loss was documented on admission and dietary advice was provided. The early pregnancy service at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary was contacted for ongoing review.

Assessment at discharge: clinically euvolaemic, alert and mobilising independently. Abdomen soft and non-tender. Able to tolerate fluids, oral medication and small meals. Electrolytes stable.

Discharge medicines:
• Cyclizine 50 mg orally up to three times daily when required for nausea.
• Folic acid to continue as previously advised.
Avoid taking anti-inflammatory medicines unless specifically instructed. Maintain frequent small meals and regular sips of fluid; oral rehydration solution may be used if intake is poor. Return to A&E urgently if unable to keep fluids down, passing very little urine, fainting, developing severe abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding or fever.

Follow-up: early pregnancy and hyperemesis review arranged for 24th October 2019. GP to monitor hydration, weight and repeat electrolytes if symptoms recur. The patient and her spouse understood the discharge advice and when to seek further help.

text:
Cardiology outpatient review

Patient: Barakah Baker
MRN: 040000/43
Date: 10 Oct 2024
Contact: 07700 900066

Reason for review:
Fatigue and intermittent awareness of heartbeat. Referred for assessment of possible cardiac contribution; known hypothyroidism on levothyroxine.

History:
This 27-year-old Caucasian female patient reports several months of reduced energy, feeling unusually cold and constipation. No exertional chest pain, syncope, orthopnoea or ankle swelling. Palpitations described as brief, occasional fluttering, without dizziness. No recent change in levothyroxine dose and reports taking it regularly, separate from breakfast. No stimulant or recreational drug use reported.

Examination:
Comfortable at rest. Pulse regular, normal volume. Heart sounds normal, no murmur. Chest clear. No peripheral oedema. Clinically euvolaemic.

Investigations:
Resting ECG today: sinus rhythm, no acute ST-T change. Previous blood tests noted, but thyroid function results not available in the cardiology record.

Assessment:
Symptoms are more suggestive of under-replacement or fluctuating thyroid status than primary structural heart disease. Brief palpitations, currently low risk by history. No clinical evidence of heart failure or ongoing arrhythmia.

Plan:
1. Request TSH and free T4 through GP surgery; review levothyroxine dose once results available.
2. Continue current levothyroxine pending biochemical results; avoid self-adjustment.
3. Seven-day ambulatory ECG if palpitations become more frequent, prolonged or associated with presyncope.
4. Safety-net: urgent assessment via A&E for sustained palpitations with collapse, chest pain or severe breathlessness.
5. Follow-up in cardiology only if abnormal monitoring or persistent concerning symptoms. Consider endocrine input; the patient has previously been seen by a consultant endocrinologist.

Discharge summary

Patient: Harlee-Rose E.
Discharging service: Clinical Genetics, Royal Victoria Hospital
Report/accession ID: L28O68289

You were admitted after a brief episode of right arm weakness, facial drooping and slurred speech. The symptoms had completely settled by the time of assessment. A friend accompanied you and provided additional history.

CT brain and CT angiography showed no acute haemorrhage or large-vessel occlusion. ECG was in sinus rhythm, and routine blood tests were satisfactory. The episode was assessed as a transient ischaemic attack (TIA). No thrombolysis or procedure was required. You remained neurologically well during observation; at 08:15 the neurological examination was normal.

Cardiology advice was that there was no indication for anticoagulation. The agreed antiplatelet plan is aspirin 300 mg once daily with clopidogrel 75 mg once daily for 21 days, followed by aspirin 75 mg once daily long term. Continue atorvastatin as prescribed. Please do not stop these medicines without speaking to your GP or the stroke team. Your GP should review blood pressure, cholesterol and vascular risk factors.

A rapid-access TIA clinic appointment will be arranged by Royal Victoria Hospital. Please attend even if you feel well. Seek emergency help immediately if weakness, facial drooping, speech difficulty or sudden visual loss returns, even if it resolves before assessment.

Discharged home in a stable condition, with a friend aware of the plan.

Discharging clinician: Sonah Nicholson
Professional identifier: 0227221

A&E EMERGENCY ASSESSMENT
NHS number: 0003045561

Patient: Ansharah RAI
Clinical area: General Medicine
Accompanied by: adult child

Presenting complaint:
Sudden onset racing heartbeat with central chest tightness and intense fear of dying whilst at home. Episode peaked within approximately 10 minutes, now largely settled. No syncope, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis or unilateral leg swelling. Reports increased work stress and poor sleep recently. No previous cardiac history disclosed.

Initial observations:
Alert, speaking full sentences. Pulse 104, regular; BP 148/86; respiratory rate 20; SpO2 99% on air; temperature 36.7°C.

Examination:
Anxious but engaging. No pallor or diaphoresis. Heart sounds normal, no murmur. Chest clear bilaterally. No calf tenderness or oedema. Neurology grossly intact. Glasgow Coma Scale 15.

Investigations:
ECG: sinus tachycardia, no acute ischaemic changes.
High-sensitivity troponin below reporting threshold. FBC, U&E and glucose unremarkable. Chest radiograph not indicated clinically.

Assessment:
Features most consistent with panic attack/hyperventilation. Low current suspicion for ACS, PE or arrhythmia following assessment and reassuring investigations. Discussed diagnostic uncertainty and safety-netting with patient and adult child.

Treatment/plan:
Supported breathing retraining performed in department, with improvement in pulse and chest tightness. No sedative prescribed. Advised GP review for anxiety management and consideration of talking therapy; avoid excess caffeine. Return immediately for persistent chest pain, collapse, severe breathlessness or sustained palpitations.

Discharge:
Clinically stable for discharge from MONMOUTH GENERAL HOSPITAL. Follow-up appointment/review: 28/03/2026.

Documented by H. Tomlinson. Patient left with adult child, understanding advice. 47 y/o

Date: 18/10/2028

To: Respiratory Medicine Service

Re: yvie steel
Report/accession ID: L24B95263

Dear Colleague,

I would be grateful for your assessment of yvie steel, who has an established diagnosis of Parkinson disease, previously assessed by neurology. The current question is whether recent cough and intermittent choking represent oropharyngeal dysphagia with aspiration, and whether there is an associated respiratory complication.

Over the past several months, their friend has noticed coughing during meals, particularly with thin fluids, together with a wet-sounding voice afterwards. There has been no reported haemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain or documented fever. Breathlessness is occasional on exertion but has not been clearly progressive. No recent A&E attendance or lower respiratory tract infection is recorded.

Neurological symptoms remain evident, with resting tremor, bradykinesia and muscular rigidity. Mobility is slower and transfers take longer, although there has been no reported acute change in cognition. Co-beneldopa is prescribed as established treatment, with prescribing continued in primary care following specialist assessment. A medication and multidisciplinary review would be helpful, including consideration of speech and language therapy and dietetic advice.

On examination today, the patient was alert and able to provide a relevant history. Speech was soft but understandable. There was a mild resting tremor and increased tone in the upper limbs. Respiratory rate was 18/min, oxygen saturation 97% on air, and chest auscultation revealed slightly reduced air entry at the right base without focal crackles or wheeze. No peripheral oedema.

A recent chest radiograph was reported as showing mild bibasal linear atelectatic change, without focal consolidation or pleural effusion. The swallowing history remains concerning despite the absence of overt infection.

Please could you assess for aspiration-related airway or parenchymal disease and advise on further respiratory investigation, including whether CT thorax or pulmonary function testing is indicated. Guidance regarding coordinated management with neurology and speech and language therapy would also be appreciated.

Yours sincerely,

S. Ayres
ROYAL INFIRMARY OF EDINBURGH

text:
Molecular Genetics Laboratory Report

Patient: L. Lake
MRN: 0633523
Clinical context: 30-year-old Hispanic male patient referred from A&E for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk assessment. Significant family history reported, with cancer-risk concern and request for predictive testing. History obtained with the patient’s partner present. No current treatment.

Specimen
Peripheral blood in EDTA. Germline DNA extracted for BRCA1 and BRCA2 sequencing with deletion/duplication analysis. Specimen suitable for testing.

Results
BRCA1: No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant detected.
BRCA2: No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant detected.

A previously documented familial variant, BRCA1 c.68_69delAG, was not identified in this specimen.

Interpretation
This result does not demonstrate a pathogenic BRCA1 or BRCA2 variant in the tested sample. If the familial variant is confirmed to be BRCA1 c.68_69delAG, the negative result is consistent with the patient not having inherited that specific familial variant. Residual hereditary risk is not excluded, particularly where the family history is extensive or the familial result has not been independently verified.

The assay does not assess all genetic causes of hereditary breast and ovarian cancer, and a negative result should not be interpreted as eliminating population or family-history-based cancer risk. Correlation with the affected relative’s report and formal genetics counselling is recommended before assigning a definitive familial-risk category.

Laboratory quality
Internal control performance acceptable. No evidence of significant specimen degradation. This is a clinical laboratory result and should be interpreted alongside the referral information and family pedigree.

Recommendation
Genetic counselling follow-up to review the family history, confirm the familial report where available, and consider broader hereditary cancer panel testing if clinically indicated. Screening and risk-reduction advice should be based on the final genetics assessment rather than this result alone. Review appointment: 29 Mar 2036.

Validated and reported by: O. Lord
Laboratory genetics clinician

Nursing progress note – Cardiology

Patient: Amra Calvert
Usual residence: 146 ROEVILLE TERRACE, FINTONA
Contact: 07700 900361
Collateral: adult child, michee piper

Assessment:
Alert and orientated, speaking in short sentences. Reports orthopnoea overnight, improved when propped upright; ongoing bilateral ankle oedema and reduced exercise tolerance. Denies chest pain. Chest with fine bibasal crackles. Peripheral oedema to lower shins, skin intact. Tired on mobilisation but steady with frame and one staff member.

Observations:
Early warning score elevated due to tachypnoea and oxygen requirement; observations recorded on NEWS chart. Oxygen via nasal cannula maintaining target saturations. BP acceptable, pulse regular. Fluid balance commenced; urine output adequate following diuretic.

Interventions/response:
Sat out in chair for breakfast, tolerated approximately 20 minutes before breathlessness. Assisted back to bed, legs elevated. Administered prescribed furosemide 40 mg once daily and bisoprolol; no immediate adverse effects. Fluid restriction reinforced. Reviewed call bell use and advised to report increased breathlessness, chest discomfort or dizziness.

Risks:
Falls risk related to weakness and exertional dyspnoea. Pressure areas checked, no redness. Monitoring for worsening pulmonary congestion, hypotension and reduced urine output. Fluid balance remains incomplete for previous shift; discussed with covering clinician.

Escalation:
Breathlessness settled at rest after repositioning. Covering cardiology clinician updated regarding persistent crackles, oedema and exertional symptoms. Continue close observations and escalate promptly for rising oxygen requirement, acute confusion, chest pain or haemodynamic change.

Plan for next shift:
Continue oxygen and NEWS observations as prescribed, strict fluid balance, daily weight when safe, leg elevation and assisted mobilisation. Review renal profile and electrolytes when resulted. Confirm discharge planning and medication reconciliation with Royal Victoria Hospital.

Clinical Genetics Clinic Note

Patient: Ciena  
MRN: 0818054  
Occupation: Sales assistant  
Seen at: The Gordon Hospital  
Accompanied by a friend.

Ciena was reviewed in the clinical genetics clinic following referral from primary care for persistent iron-deficiency anaemia despite oral replacement. They describe ongoing tiredness, intermittent dizziness on standing and reduced exercise tolerance, particularly when climbing stairs. No syncope, chest pain, rectal bleeding or change in bowel habit. Menstrual history was discussed and is not felt to account fully for the degree or persistence of the anaemia. Appetite remains good and there has been no unintentional weight loss.

They are taking ferrous fumarate once daily, with occasional nausea but no vomiting. Previous blood tests reportedly showed low haemoglobin and ferritin; the most recent results were not available to view during this consultation. There is no known family history of a diagnosed blood disorder, recurrent anaemia or transfusion dependence. No consanguinity reported. The friend contributed to the history with the patient’s agreement.

The clinical picture remains most consistent with iron-deficiency anaemia, although the persistent nature and incomplete response to treatment raise the possibility of an underlying inherited red-cell trait or an alternative cause of iron loss or malabsorption. Examination was limited in clinic; patient appeared well, with no jaundice or obvious pallor. No hepatosplenomegaly was appreciated.

Assessment  
Persistent iron-deficiency anaemia with tiredness, dizziness and reduced exercise tolerance. Further clarification of blood results is required before considering genetic testing.

Plan  
Request current full blood count, ferritin, transferrin saturation, reticulocyte count, blood film and haemoglobinopathy screen via The Gordon Hospital. Primary care to continue investigation of blood loss and malabsorption as clinically indicated. Continue ferrous fumarate as tolerated and review adherence and administration separately. Genetic testing will be considered if results suggest an inherited red-cell disorder; implications, consent and possible outcomes were discussed.

Follow-up arranged in 13 days to review results.  
Clinician: Dr Eily WILKINS, MBBS

Two-day history of profuse vomiting and diarrhoea with poor oral intake and reduced urine output. Admitted for clinical dehydration and observation.

Tachycardic, dry mucous membranes and delayed capillary refill. blood pressure 108/66 mmHg. Abdomen soft, non-distended, no focal tenderness. No safeguarding concerns identified; history provided jointly by the patient and legal guardian.

Urea and electrolytes consistent with mild dehydration; glucose normal. Urine output improved during admission. No indication for stool sampling or antibiotics.

Managed with oral rehydration solution in frequent small amounts and supportive care. One further vomit shortly after arrival, then tolerated fluids and light diet. Diarrhoea reduced. Passing urine normally before discharge. Intravenous fluids not required.

Medications: oral rehydration solution as directed; no regular new medicines.
Continue frequent fluids and gradual return to usual diet. Avoid anti-diarrhoeal medicines unless advised by the GP.

GP review if symptoms are not settling. Return to A&E urgently for inability to keep fluids down, increasing drowsiness, severe abdominal pain, blood in stool or markedly reduced urine output. Legal guardian given verbal and written advice; patient involved in discharge discussion and assent confirmed.

Patient: ifenna aston
DOB: 1999-08-13
Address: 123 Fitzwilliam Close, Bargod / Bargoed, CF81 8AA
Contact: ifenna.aston85@proton.me
Accompanied by legal guardian: D. Mann

Paediatric Emergency Department Assessment

Presenting complaint:
Brought in following a witnessed generalised convulsion at home during a febrile illness. Guardian reports stiffening followed by rhythmic jerking of all four limbs, lasting approximately 2 minutes. No focal onset, trauma, choking or preceding collapse. Drowsy afterwards, now returning to usual interaction. No previous seizures reported.

History:
Fever since yesterday with coryzal symptoms and reduced appetite. Drinking small amounts; wet nappies maintained. No vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, neck stiffness or known sick contacts. Immunisations reported up to date. No regular medicines or known drug allergies.

Examination:
Initially sleepy but rousable, subsequently alert and appropriately responsive to guardian. Airway patent, breathing unlaboured. Temperature 39.1°C, heart rate 148 bpm, respiratory rate 28/min, oxygen saturations 98% in air. Warm peripheries, capillary refill  under 2 seconds. Mild nasal congestion. Tympanic membranes not clearly visualised due to wax. No meningism, petechial rash or focal neurological deficit. Chest clear; abdomen soft and non-tender.

Investigations:
Capillary glucose 5.8 mmol/L. No blood tests or imaging indicated following uncomplicated, self-terminating generalised seizure with reassuring examination.

Assessment:
Simple febrile seizure associated with presumed viral upper respiratory infection. No current features suggest meningitis, encephalitis, hypoglycaemia or epilepsy.

Management and disposition:
Observed in department until fully back to baseline and tolerating oral fluids. Antipyretic comfort measures discussed; avoid alternating medicines routinely. Guardian given seizure first-aid advice: place on side, remove nearby hazards, do not restrain or put anything in the mouth, and call 999 if seizure lasts 5 minutes or more, breathing is impaired, seizure recurs without recovery, or recovery is atypical.

Discharged home with guardian. GP review if fever persists or symptoms worsen; paediatric follow-up in about 7 weeks. Safety-net advice understood.

Re: K. Khatun

Address: 15 Clos yr Helyg, Cardiff / Caerdydd, CF24 0AA
Telephone: 07700 900431
Occupation: Receptionist
Employer: Horseman's Green Secondary School

Thank you for attending with your adult child. You described several weeks of low back pain with a shooting pain down the affected leg and intermittent pins and needles. There has been no change in bladder or bowel control, saddle numbness, fever or recent significant injury.

On examination, you mobilised independently. Lumbar movement was limited by pain, with reduced sensation in the symptomatic leg but no clear motor weakness. Straight-leg raise reproduced the leg pain. Peripheral pulses were present.

This is most consistent with lumbar radiculopathy, usually caused by irritation of a nerve as it leaves the lower spine. At present there is no indication for emergency admission or urgent imaging. Please continue paracetamol as directed and take naproxen with food, provided you have no history of stomach ulcer, kidney disease, anticoagulant treatment or previous reaction to anti-inflammatory medicines. Do not take additional ibuprofen while using naproxen.

I have advised regular gentle walking and avoidance of prolonged bed rest. A physiotherapy referral will be made for graded exercises and advice on posture and lifting. If symptoms do not improve, or if weakness develops, we will review the need for MRI and specialist assessment; a consultant neurologist may be involved if the diagnosis remains uncertain or neurological signs progress.

Please attend A&E urgently for new bladder or bowel difficulty, numbness around the saddle area, rapidly worsening weakness, or inability to walk. GP review is planned after physiotherapy or sooner if concerned.

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient’s recently identified atrial fibrillation, with particular advice regarding rate control and whether rhythm-control intervention should be considered.

There is a several-week history of intermittent palpitations, reduced exercise tolerance and fatigue, with exertional breathlessness when walking uphill or climbing stairs. No syncope, pleuritic chest pain or unilateral leg swelling has been reported. The symptoms are more noticeable in the evenings. Their partner, Lohith Lewis, has also observed episodes of rapid, irregular pulse at rest.

An ECG performed in the surgery showed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate 118 beats/minute. Blood pressure was stable and oxygen saturations were normal on air. Cardiovascular examination confirmed an irregular rhythm without murmur or clinical evidence of heart failure; chest examination was clear, with no peripheral oedema. There were no focal neurological symptoms.

Apixaban has been commenced for stroke prevention and is being taken as prescribed. Bisoprolol has also been started for ventricular rate control. The patient reports partial improvement in the palpitations but remains fatigued and breathless on exertion. There has been no bleeding, melaena or significant dizziness since commencing treatment.

Initial blood tests showed satisfactory renal function, normal thyroid function and no significant anaemia. A transthoracic echocardiogram has been requested locally; the result is not yet available. The patient has been advised to seek urgent assessment through A&E if persistent chest pain, collapse, severe breathlessness or new neurological symptoms occur.

Could you please review the diagnosis and undertake echocardiographic and cardiovascular risk assessment as appropriate, advise on the target for rate control, and comment on suitability for elective cardioversion or an alternative rhythm-control strategy? Guidance on the duration of anticoagulation and ongoing monitoring of apixaban and bisoprolol would also be appreciated.

Referring clinician: Alroy MORTIMER

Patient: dean dickinson

Ward: Paediatric inpatient unit

Overnight admission with vaso-occlusive sickle cell painful crisis. Father, Alfie Clay, remained at the bedside and reports that pain was most severe in both legs and across the lower back, with poor oral intake before admission. No vomiting, chest pain or shortness of breath reported. Passing urine, though less frequently than usual.

Assessment: Alert and appropriately interactive, tearful during movement. Skin warm, lips slightly dry. Respiratory rate regular with good air entry bilaterally; no increased work of breathing. Abdomen soft and non-tender. Peripheral perfusion satisfactory. Pain scored 8/10 on the faces scale before analgesia, predominantly in the limbs and back. Plan: Continue prescribed analgesia and IV fluids, with regular pain, sedation and respiratory observations. Encourage oral fluids and gentle mobilisation as tolerated. Maintain a calm environment and involve father in comfort measures. Monitor temperature, oxygen saturations, chest symptoms, increasing drowsiness, worsening pain or reduced urine output. Escalate promptly to the paediatric medical team if pain remains uncontrolled, observations deteriorate or acute chest symptoms develop. No concerns regarding safeguarding identified during this shift.

Paediatric haematology review arranged for 14/04/2025. Handover given to the incoming nurse.

Discharge summary

Patient: Ceilidh G.
MRN: 000889101
Admitting service: Accident and Emergency
Discharging organisation: Aberdeen Royal Infirmary

Ceilidh G. was admitted with several hours of worsening right lower-quadrant abdominal pain, nausea and loss of appetite. At 08:15 the pain had become more localised and movement was uncomfortable. Examination was consistent with acute appendicitis, with guarding in the right lower abdomen but no evidence of generalised peritonitis.

Blood tests showed a raised white cell count and inflammatory markers. Ultrasound imaging supported acute appendicitis without an abscess. The case was discussed with the on-call surgical team. Initial treatment included intravenous fluids, analgesia with paracetamol and intravenous co-amoxiclav.

A laparoscopic appendicectomy was performed under general anaesthetic. The appendix was inflamed but not perforated. There were no operative complications and the specimen was sent for histology. Recovery from anaesthesia was uncomplicated. Ceilidh G. subsequently tolerated oral fluids and food, passed urine, and mobilised independently. Pain was controlled with oral medication.

Discharge medicines:
• Paracetamol as needed for pain, following the instructions on the packet.
• No further antibiotics are required unless advised by the surgical team.

The three small wounds are closed with dissolvable sutures and covered with dressings. Keep them clean and dry; showering is acceptable, but avoid soaking the wounds until healed. Avoid heavy lifting and strenuous exercise until comfortable. Seek urgent medical advice via NHS 111 or the emergency department if there is worsening abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fever, increasing redness or discharge from a wound, or difficulty eating and drinking.

The surgical team will arrange routine follow-up and review the histology result. Please contact the GP surgery if recovery is not progressing as expected. The listed emergency contact locality is Culcharry.

Condition on discharge: clinically stable, ambulant and suitable for home.

Signed by: Dr Draisy Wakefield, MBBS
