Emergency Department Cardiology Assessment
Date: 21 May 2035
Patient: Haima
Address: 53 Bartlet Close, Tywyn, LL36 0AA

Presenting complaint: Pruritic erythematous rash, skin irritation.

History: A 71-year-old Hispanic female patient presented with a 3-day itchy rash affecting the upper chest, neck and both forearms. Started after use of a new fragranced body wash. Friend accompanied patient and provided collateral history. No facial swelling, lip/tongue swelling, wheeze, dysphagia, fever or syncope. No chest pain or palpitations. Hydrocortisone cream used with limited effect; cetirizine taken this morning. No new prescribed medicines. No previous anaphylaxis reported.

Examination: Alert, comfortable, speaking full sentences. Airway patent. No stridor or angioedema. Chest clear bilaterally, no wheeze. Heart sounds normal, regular pulse. Widespread well-demarcated erythematous papular eruption over upper chest, lateral neck and flexor forearms, with excoriation. No vesicles, purpura, mucosal involvement or cellulitis. Observations stable; afebrile. No clinical evidence of systemic allergic reaction.

Investigations: No blood tests or imaging indicated. ECG performed owing to cardiology-area attendance: sinus rhythm, no acute ST-T change.

Impression: Allergic contact dermatitis, likely fragranced product. No evidence of anaphylaxis or infection.

Treatment/plan: Advised to stop the new body wash and avoid fragranced products. Continue cetirizine as previously directed; short course of hydrocortisone cream to affected areas, avoiding face and broken skin. Emollient recommended. Safety-netted regarding breathing difficulty, facial swelling, mucosal involvement, fever or rapid spread; return to A&E if these occur. GP review in about 4 weeks if persistent.

Discharged home. M. Stacey, clinician.

MOLECULAR GENETICS REPORT

Patient: H. Riaz
MRN: H1453611
Address: 41 Old's Approach, Cockermouth, CA13 0AA
Collection/report date: 1988-03-29
Request: Predictive testing for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk; significant family history. Ordering clinician: not stated.

Specimen
Peripheral blood, EDTA. DNA extracted for targeted analysis of the familial BRCA1 variant. Specimen suitable for testing.

Result
BRCA1 c.68_69delAG: DETECTED
Zygosity: Heterozygous
Assay: Targeted variant analysis by next-generation sequencing with orthogonal confirmation.

Interpretation
Pathogenic loss-of-function variant identified. Result is consistent with a hereditary predisposition to breast and ovarian cancer and is concordant with the familial variant under review. This is a predictive result and does not indicate the presence or absence of malignancy at the time of testing.

Clinical comment
Genetic counselling recommended to explain implications for the patient and biological relatives, including cascade testing where appropriate. Referral to the regional clinical genetics service advised for individualised surveillance and risk-reduction discussion. Management should follow current UK guidance and be coordinated with the patient’s GP and relevant specialist teams. No current treatment reported.

Limitations
Targeted analysis does not exclude other pathogenic variants in BRCA1, BRCA2 or additional cancer-predisposition genes. Variant interpretation may be revised if new evidence emerges. Results should not be used in isolation for clinical decision-making.

Validated/reporting clinician: L. Paul
Laboratory medicine/genetics service
Final status: authorised.

Risks

Plan for next shift
Repeat observations and assess postural symptoms. Record fluid balance, emesis episodes and oral intake. Continue prescribed IV fluids and cyclizine, reassessing effect. Patient: Hayley Price
Occupation: Care worker
Employer: Newton Ferrers Secondary School
Address: 85 Glenmount Path, Carshalton, SM5 1AA
Contact: hayley.price81@outlook.com

Cardiology outpatient review

The itchy, red area on your upper chest and the surrounding skin irritation are most consistent with allergic contact dermatitis, probably related to recent adhesive contact during monitoring or examination. You attended with a friend, who helped describe when the rash began. There is no history today of facial swelling, wheeze, throat tightness, dizziness or fever. The symptoms have been present for 3 days.

On examination, there is a sharply defined erythematous, mildly scaly patch over the area of contact, with excoriation but no spreading cellulitis, blistering or discharge. Heart sounds are normal and the chest is clear. No mucosal involvement.

Please continue hydrocortisone cream as a thin layer to the affected skin twice daily for up to seven days, avoiding broken skin and the eyes. Continue cetirizine once daily if itching is troublesome. Use an unperfumed emollient several times daily and avoid fragranced soaps, creams and adhesive dressings until the skin has settled. Do not scratch; keeping fingernails short may help.

Please inform the cardiology team before any further ECG, ambulatory monitor or dressing is applied, as a different adhesive or a skin barrier may be needed. This rash does not suggest a cardiac cause and there are no current features requiring emergency treatment.

Seek urgent help via A&E or 999 if you develop difficulty breathing, swelling of the lips or tongue, faintness, rapidly worsening rash or widespread blistering. Otherwise, contact your GP surgery if there is no clear improvement within one week, or sooner if pain, warmth, pus or fever develops.

Reason for admission

Initial neurological examination was normal, with clear speech, symmetrical facial movement and full power in all limbs. Blood pressure remained stable. ECG showed sinus rhythm. Carotid Doppler identified no haemodynamically significant stenosis. Routine blood tests were satisfactory; lipid profile was elevated. The episode was reviewed with the consultant neurologist and felt most consistent with a transient ischaemic attack.

Observed overnight without recurrence of weakness, facial asymmetry or dysphasia. Swallow assessment was satisfactory and mobilisation was independent. No oxygen requirement or respiratory deterioration during the admission.

Aspirin 300 mg once daily for 14 days, then reduce to aspirin 75 mg once daily thereafter.
Atorvastatin 80 mg at night.
Continue other regular medicines as listed on the electronic discharge prescription. Avoid non-prescribed anti-inflammatory medication unless discussed with the GP.

Follow-up and advice
GP review requested for blood pressure, diabetes screening, lipid monitoring and medication reconciliation. Outpatient TIA/neurology clinic follow-up to be arranged, with consideration of longer-term rhythm monitoring if clinically indicated. Smoking cessation, regular activity and a heart-healthy diet discussed.

If any further facial weakness, arm or leg weakness, speech disturbance, visual loss or sudden severe imbalance occurs, call 999 immediately, even if symptoms settle.

Discharged home in a stable condition with independent mobility and clear understanding of the medication plan and safety-net advice.

text:
Discharge summary
NHS number: 000 420 1249

Patient: Torben Cullen
Admitting service: Ulster Hospital
Report/accession ID: 07841503

Reason for admission
Admission with worsening decompensated heart failure. The patient reported increasing orthopnoea, bilateral ankle oedema and reduced exercise tolerance for 3 days, with difficulty managing usual activities at home. No infective symptoms or chest pain reported.

Key findings
On arrival, clinically fluid overloaded with raised JVP, bibasal inspiratory crackles and moderate dependent oedema. Oxygen saturation remained satisfactory on room air. Chest radiograph demonstrated pulmonary vascular congestion with small bilateral pleural effusions. ECG showed atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular response. Echocardiography confirmed severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction, in keeping with the established heart failure diagnosis. Renal function was monitored during diuresis; potassium replacement was given when required.

Hospital course
Treated with intravenous furosemide and fluid/salt restriction, with good symptomatic response and progressive reduction in peripheral oedema. Mobilised independently by discharge and able to lie substantially flatter at night. No evidence of acute coronary syndrome or pneumonia. The heart failure nurse reviewed self-monitoring, weight recording and when to seek urgent help.

Medication changes
• Furosemide increased to 80 mg each morning for the next few days, then review with the GP for ongoing dose adjustment according to weight, oedema and renal function.
• Bisoprolol continued at the pre-admission dose.
• Potassium supplementation to continue only as listed on the final prescription.
• No other regular medicines were stopped during this admission.

Please check U&Es with the GP within one week, or sooner if clinically indicated. The GP should review blood pressure, renal function, electrolytes and volume status and consider optimisation of guideline-directed heart failure therapy if tolerated. Cardiology follow-up requested; the community heart failure team will contact the patient regarding ongoing monitoring.

Condition at discharge
Breathing improved, oedema reduced and haemodynamically stable. Safety-net advice provided: seek same-day medical advice for rapidly increasing swelling, worsening breathlessness or marked dizziness; call 999 for severe breathlessness at rest, collapse or chest pain.

Discharging clinician
FRANKA WINTER, consultant physician
GMC: 0214876

Urine dip: leucocytes ++, nitrites positive, blood +. Urine culture grew a urinary pathogen sensitive to cefuroxime. Blood cultures negative. Initial inflammatory markers raised; renal function remained within baseline. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis or obstructing calculus.

GP review if symptoms have not fully resolved after antibiotics. Seek urgent medical assessment if unable to keep medication down or if symptoms recur. Encourage oral fluids unless otherwise advised. Ongoing atopic eczema, predominantly antecubital fossae, neck and peri-orbital skin. Itching most troublesome overnight, with interrupted sleep several nights per week. Arrival with friend, T. HODGSON.

Presenting problem
Sudden brief spinning episodes since this morning, triggered by turning in bed and looking upwards. Each lasts less than a minute, with nausea and unsteadiness afterwards. No continuous vertigo, collapse, headache, diplopia, dysarthria, limb weakness, hearing loss or chest pain. No recent head injury. Prochlorperazine as required at home with partial relief.

Observations
Alert, orientated, speaking normally. BP 120/80 mmHg, pulse regular, afebrile, SpO2 satisfactory on air. Mobilises with mild initial unsteadiness.

Focused examination
Pupils equal/reactive. No nystagmus at rest. Cranial nerves grossly intact; normal power, sensation and coordination. No dysmetria. Gait mildly cautious but independent. Right Dix–Hallpike reproduces brief vertigo with fatigable torsional nystagmus; left negative. No focal neurological deficit.

Impression / priorities
Findings consistent with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. Low suspicion for posterior circulation event or acute vestibular syndrome given short, reproducible positional episodes and normal neurological examination.

Treatment and plan
Prochlorperazine given in department with improvement. Canalith repositioning manoeuvre performed and tolerated. Encourage oral fluids, slow positional changes and avoidance of driving/cycling until symptoms settled. Dear Cardiology Team,

Re: D. Barrow

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient’s recurrent episodes of shortness of breath, to clarify whether there is any cardiac contribution alongside their established asthma. They report intermittent wheeze and a persistent night-time cough, with breathlessness now occurring on ordinary household activity. There is no reported syncope, sustained palpitations or pleuritic chest pain. They describe occasional central chest tightness during the episodes, which settles with rest and use of their inhaler.

Asthma treatment is currently salbutamol inhaler as required and beclometasone two puffs twice daily. Inhaler technique and adherence have been reviewed in primary care, and the patient reports using a spacer. Despite this, symptoms have continued over recent weeks. There has been no recent admission to hospital and no course of oral corticosteroids documented. Examination in the surgery showed mild expiratory wheeze, with otherwise clear breath sounds, normal heart sounds and no peripheral oedema. Oxygen saturations were satisfactory at rest. A recent ECG was reported as showing sinus rhythm without acute ST-T changes; routine blood tests, including full blood count and thyroid function, were unremarkable.

The patient’s partner, Aathiya, has noticed that the breathlessness is more troublesome at night and is concerned about the episodes of chest tightness. There is no known history of ischaemic heart disease recorded in the available notes.

Assessment

Asthma remains a likely explanation for the wheeze and cough, although the exertional dyspnoea and intermittent chest tightness warrant cardiovascular review.

Request

Please assess for cardiac causes of breathlessness and advise whether echocardiography, ambulatory monitoring or any further investigation is indicated. A concurrent respiratory review will be arranged if symptoms remain poorly controlled.

Referring clinician: Nuriya JOHN, Stockiemuir
Professional identifier: 0526277

Yours faithfully,

Nuriya JOHN

Discharge summary

Patient: CONNIE-MAE GURUNG
Discharging service: Aberdeen Royal Infirmary
Report/accession ID: 072783773
Responsible clinician: Dr Lawie Biggs, MBBS

Reason for admission
Presented to A&E with a two-day history of progressively spreading redness and warmth of the left lower leg, associated with local tenderness and reduced mobility due to discomfort. No history of trauma, ulceration or recent travel. No systemic symptoms reported.

Initial assessment
Haemodynamically stable and alert. Left lower leg with diffuse erythema and increased temperature from the ankle to mid-calf; tender to palpation, without fluctuance, crepitus or visible abscess. Distal pulses and sensation intact. No clinical features of compartment syndrome or deep vein thrombosis. Blood tests showed a mild inflammatory response; renal function remained satisfactory. Blood cultures were not indicated clinically. The affected area was outlined and photographed for comparison during admission.

Hospital course
Treated as uncomplicated cellulitis with intravenous flucloxacillin and regular oral analgesia. The erythema initially extended marginally beyond the marked border but subsequently settled, with improving warmth and tenderness. Remained apyrexial and maintained oral intake. No collection requiring drainage was identified. Mobilising independently before discharge.

Medication on discharge
• flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily, to complete the prescribed course.
• Paracetamol as needed for pain, within the maximum dose stated on the dispensing label.

No other regular medicines were changed. The importance of completing the antibiotic course was discussed.

Problem list
1. Cellulitis of the lower leg – clinically improving.
2. Leg pain and tenderness – improved with treatment.
3. No evidence of abscess or systemic infection during admission.

Condition at discharge
Fit for discharge home today. Afebrile, observations stable, leg appearance improving and able to walk safely. Emergency contact locality recorded as Brabstermire.

Follow-up and safety-netting
Review with the GP surgery if the redness, swelling or pain is not continuing to improve over the next 48 hours, or sooner if concerned. Return to A&E urgently for rapidly spreading redness, severe or escalating pain, fever or rigors, vomiting, confusion, faintness, new blistering or darkening of the skin, or difficulty walking. Keep the leg elevated when resting, continue gentle movement, and maintain good oral fluid intake.

Discharge information provided and understood. Dr Lawie Biggs, MBBS

Specimen: EDTA whole blood

Full blood count
Haemoglobin: 86 g/L (reference interval 115–155)
Haematocrit: 0.29 L/L (0.35–0.45)

Microcytosis and hypochromia with anisocytosis. Occasional elliptocytes. No blast cells identified.

Specialist outpatient report

Patient: AKIO CLEGG
DOB: 15 March 1959
Contact: akio.clegg80@icloud.com
Report/accession ID: LAB-01979180

Reason for review:
Persistent pruritic erythematous rash with skin irritation affecting the volar wrists and lower neck. Symptoms began after use of a newly purchased fragranced body product and have continued despite stopping this. No fever, facial swelling, wheeze, mucosal involvement or systemic upset. The patient reports intermittent scratching, particularly overnight. No similar rash in household contacts.

Examination:
Well appearing. Localised erythematous, mildly scaly plaques with excoriation over both volar wrists and the lower anterior neck. No vesicles, pustulation, crusting or dermatomal distribution. No clinical evidence of cellulitis. Palms, oral mucosa and visible flexures clear. No lymphadenopathy.

Impression:
The distribution, morphology and temporal association are most consistent with allergic contact dermatitis, likely triggered by a fragranced topical preparation. Irritant contact dermatitis remains a consideration, although the degree of itch and recurrence at exposed sites favour an allergic component. There is no evidence today of secondary bacterial infection or an immediate hypersensitivity reaction.

Management:
Continue hydrocortisone cream as a thin layer to affected areas twice daily for up to 7 days, avoiding broken skin and the face. Cetirizine may be continued once daily while symptomatic. Regular bland emollient advised, applied frequently and after washing. Avoid fragranced soaps, detergents, cosmetics and the suspected body product; use soap substitute and lukewarm water. Do not scratch where possible, with nails kept short.

If symptoms persist or recur despite avoidance, arrange patch testing through dermatology. Seek urgent medical attention for rapidly progressive swelling, breathing difficulty, mucosal lesions, fever or spreading pain/redness.

Follow-up:
Review in about 5 weeks, on 27th April 2018, or earlier via the GP surgery if deteriorating. At review, assess response to topical treatment and consider referral for formal contact allergen assessment.

Discharge Summary

Patient: Tayshia S.
DOB: 13 Nov 2013
Admission/discharge date: 21st August 2019
Parent: Livvi Goodall
Contact: 07700 900643

Reason for admission
Presented with a short history of frequent vomiting and watery diarrhoea, with reduced urine output and poor oral intake. History obtained from the patient and parent. No blood reported in stool, no bilious vomiting and no significant abdominal pain. No relevant recent travel or known sick contacts documented.

Initial assessment
Clinically mildly to moderately dehydrated on arrival, with dry mucous membranes and reduced tears. Abdomen soft, non-distended and non-tender, with active bowel sounds. No meningism or focal neurological deficit. Initial observations included heart rate 92 beats/minute. Remained haemodynamically stable and afebrile during observation.

Key results
Capillary glucose within the normal range. Urea and electrolytes showed mild dehydration-related change without significant electrolyte disturbance. No indication for stool sampling during admission. Urine output improved with rehydration. No imaging required.

Hospital course
Managed on the paediatric ward with oral rehydration solution in small, frequent amounts alongside continued breastfeeding/normal fluids as tolerated. Vomiting settled and diarrhoea became less frequent. A brief period of supervised oral intake was completed without further vomiting. No intravenous fluids or antibiotics were required. Supportive care only.

Problem list
1. Acute gastroenteritis.
2. Mild to moderate dehydration, clinically improved.
3. Reduced oral intake, now improving.

Condition at discharge
Alert and interactive, tolerating fluids and light meals. Passing urine normally for them. Mucous membranes moist, peripheral perfusion good and abdomen remains soft. Parent feels confident with the plan and was involved in discussions throughout. Patient was offered an age-appropriate explanation and participated in the discharge discussion.

Discharge medicines and advice
Continue oral rehydration solution after each loose stool or episode of vomiting, given little and often. Resume usual diet gradually; avoid fizzy drinks and undiluted fruit juice. No routine anti-diarrhoeal medication advised. Continue supportive care at home.

Safety-netting
Seek urgent medical advice via the GP, NHS 111 or the emergency department if unable to keep fluids down, markedly drowsy, developing persistent or severe abdominal pain, blood or green vomit, blood in the stool, breathing difficulty, or significantly reduced urine output. Parent advised to seek review if symptoms are not clearly improving over the next few days.

Follow-up
No routine hospital follow-up required. GP review if ongoing diarrhoea, recurrent vomiting or concerns about hydration.

text:
Emergency Department Assessment
NHS number: 000 888 5932

Patient: Christoforos
Address: 5 Bruton Lane, London, UB11 1AA
Email: christoforos.weaver72@icloud.com
Report/accession ID: 27/147017

Presented with sudden breathlessness and sharp right-sided chest pain, worse on inspiration, beginning earlier today. Spouse, Priscilla-Marie, accompanied the patient and reports no collapse or haemoptysis. Known venous thromboembolism, taking apixaban 5 mg twice daily; states no missed doses. No recent operation or prolonged travel reported.

Alert and speaking in short sentences. Pulse 118 bpm, BP 136/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, oxygen saturations 90% on air, temperature 37.2°C. Improved to 95% with 2 L oxygen via nasal cannula. Chest clear to auscultation with mild right basal discomfort on deep inspiration. No calf asymmetry or obvious peripheral oedema. Heart sounds normal apart from tachycardia. No focal neurological deficit.

ECG: sinus tachycardia, no acute ST-segment change. Chest radiograph without focal consolidation or pneumothorax. Blood tests show raised D-dimer and mild troponin elevation; haemoglobin and renal function satisfactory. CT pulmonary angiogram demonstrates bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli without radiological right-heart strain.

Assessment: haemodynamically stable pulmonary embolism, with hypoxia and pleuritic pain. Discussed with the medical registrar. No indication for thrombolysis or thrombectomy. Continue therapeutic anticoagulation and observe oxygen requirement; analgesia given with oral paracetamol.

After several hours, saturations remained 94–95% on air and heart rate fell to 96 bpm. Suitable for discharge with anticoagulation clinic follow-up and GP review. Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily. Return immediately for worsening breathlessness, syncope, chest pain or bleeding. Discharge advice understood by the patient and Priscilla-Marie.

Continued apixaban and bisoprolol. Safety-netted regarding worsening breathlessness, chest pain or syncope; advised emergency assessment if these occur.

Please review and consider spirometry, pulmonary function testing and any additional imaging. Cardiology follow-up remains arranged separately.

Kind regards,

Dr Kiarah Lambert, MBBS

Date: 29th May 2022
Patient: Kallam Sutcliffe
Contact: 07700 900389
Clinical age group: 27 y/o
Report/accession ID: 09071438

Reason for review:
Recurrent brief episodes of positional vertigo with nausea and unsteadiness. Referral prompted by similar dizziness reported in a sibling.

History:
Spinning sensation when turning in bed or looking upwards; episodes last seconds. Intermittent unsteadiness afterwards. No collapse, hearing loss, tinnitus, diplopia, limb weakness or speech disturbance. No relevant medication change.

Alert, ambulant. Cranial nerves grossly intact. Limb power and coordination normal. Gait mildly cautious. Dix–Hallpike provoked brief vertigo, without persistent neurological signs.

• Epley repositioning manoeuvre demonstrated; written advice provided.
• Prochlorperazine as required for troublesome nausea.
• GP/vestibular physiotherapy review if persistent or recurrent.
• Urgent A&E assessment for continuous vertigo, new neurological deficit, severe headache or inability to walk.
• Clinical genetics follow-up in about 7 weeks, sooner if new family history or additional neurological features emerge.

Discharge summary – General Medicine

Patient: Z. Rigby
Home address: 179 Maryholm Street, Bunessan, PA67 6DA
Patient contact: 07700 900989

The patient, aged 86 years, was admitted with a four-day increase in breathlessness, wheeze and purulent sputum. Also reported cough for 3 days. No chest pain or haemoptysis. Background of COPD; usual exercise tolerance reduced over the preceding week.

On admission, tachypnoeic with widespread expiratory wheeze and oxygen saturations below usual baseline on air. Chest radiograph showed hyperinflation without focal consolidation. Blood tests demonstrated a mild neutrophilia and raised CRP; renal function remained satisfactory. Viral respiratory PCR was negative. ECG showed sinus rhythm without acute ischaemic change.

Treated for infective COPD exacerbation with controlled oxygen, nebulised salbutamol/ipratropium, oral prednisolone and doxycycline. Oxygen was weaned over the following 48 hours. Sputum became less purulent and breathlessness returned close to baseline. No evidence of pneumonia or cardiac decompensation. Mobilising independently and eating and drinking normally at discharge.

Problem list:
1. Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
2. Tobacco exposure discussed; smoking cessation advice provided.
3. Inhaler technique reviewed.

Discharge medicines:
• Prednisolone 30 mg each morning to complete a 5-day course.
• Doxycycline 200 mg on day 1, then 100 mg once daily to complete 5 days.
• Salbutamol inhaler, two puffs as needed.
Continue regular respiratory medicines as previously prescribed. The patient was advised to seek urgent help for worsening breathlessness, confusion, cyanosis or inability to manage at home.

GP to review within one week, including oxygen requirement, inhaler technique and consideration of pulmonary rehabilitation. Routine COPD follow-up and vaccination status to be addressed in primary care.

Discharging doctor: Consultant physician
Professional identifier: 0572188
Condition at discharge: stable, breathing comfortably on usual oxygen requirement.

Past history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidaemia. Current medication is metformin and atorvastatin, although adherence to metformin has been inconsistent recently because of gastrointestinal upset. Assessment: symptomatic deterioration in glycaemic control, without current biochemical evidence of ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar emergency.

Please review promptly to confirm the diagnosis and degree of dysglycaemia, arrange HbA1c and diabetic complication screening, and advise on medication optimisation and structured education. The patient understands the need to seek urgent reassessment if vomiting, drowsiness, abdominal pain or inability to maintain fluids develops.

Yours sincerely,

Charleston Bevan

Rheumatology clinic review
NHS number: 000 475 6062

Patient: Heavenly-Joy Lawson
MRN: 0895301
Occupation: Police officer

Referring service: SINGLETON HOSPITAL

Reason for review: Increased inflammatory joint symptoms over the preceding six weeks, with morning stiffness, swollen hand joints and marked fatigue. No recent infection reported. Methotrexate and folic acid taken as prescribed; naproxen used for symptomatic relief.

Examination: Appears tired but not acutely unwell. Tenderness and soft-tissue swelling at bilateral MCP and PIP joints, greatest at the second and third MCPs. Reduced fist closure owing to pain. Wrists mildly tender. No large-joint effusion or nodules identified. No features of active extra-articular disease on today’s assessment.

Recent blood results show raised inflammatory markers with stable full blood count, liver enzymes and renal function. The clinical pattern is consistent with a rheumatoid arthritis flare rather than mechanical hand pain. Medication toxicity is not suggested by the available monitoring results.

Plan: Arrange repeat FBC, U&E, LFT and CRP before treatment escalation. Continue methotrexate and folic acid pending results. Continue naproxen with food if tolerated; review gastrointestinal and renal precautions with the GP. If inflammatory markers remain elevated, discuss a short steroid course and optimisation of disease-modifying therapy at the multidisciplinary meeting. Urgent assessment advised for fever, an acutely hot joint or significant functional deterioration.

Follow-up: telephone review in about 4 weeks, with earlier contact if symptoms worsen.

Report author: Ronas Prince

Discharge summary

Patient: Abou | 76 y/o
Admission/discharge date: 13/11/2045
Ward: Respiratory medicine

Presented with several days of poor oral intake, fatigue and markedly reduced urine output. Initial blood tests showed acute kidney injury with raised creatinine and urea compared with the available baseline. No clear infective focus. Chest examination and oxygen saturations remained stable; respiratory viral screen negative. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis or other evidence of obstruction.

Managed with cautious intravenous sodium chloride, fluid balance monitoring and regular renal blood tests. Ramipril and furosemide were withheld during the acute illness. Urine output improved over the following 48 hours and renal function began to recover. No dialysis indication. Reviewed by the medical team; oral intake now adequate and mobilising independently. Current observations stable, including BP 120/80 mmHg.

Problem list
1. Acute kidney injury, likely multifactorial dehydration and reduced intake.
2. Poor oral intake and oliguria — improved.
3. Temporary hold of antihypertensive/diuretic medication.

At discharge, clinically euvolaemic with improving creatinine, passing urine normally and tolerating diet and fluids. Intravenous sodium chloride stopped. Continue usual medicines apart from ramipril and furosemide until reviewed by the GP; avoid NSAIDs and maintain regular fluid intake unless otherwise advised.

GP to repeat U&Es and blood pressure promptly, with medication review and consideration of restarting held medicines once renal function has returned towards baseline. Patient advised to seek urgent medical attention for recurrent reduction in urine output, vomiting, worsening weakness, breathlessness or inability to maintain fluids.

Discharge discussion held with the patient and sibling Carly-Rose ALLAN, who is based in DUNNAMORE. Written advice provided.

A&E Emergency Assessment

Patient: J. Gray
DOB: 05/07/1943
Address: 162 Osprey Walk, Manchester, M8 0AA
Contact: 07700 900455
Presenting complaint: Central chest pressure with sweating and nausea.

History:
Sudden central pressure while at rest, persistent on arrival. Associated diaphoresis and nausea; no collapse. Background and regular medicines checked with patient and friend. No known drug allergy documented.

Examination:
Alert, pale and clammy initially. Airway patent, speaking full sentences. Heart sounds normal, no murmur. Chest clear bilaterally. No focal neurology; Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Peripheral perfusion maintained.

Observations:
Haemodynamically stable. No clinical pulmonary oedema.

Investigations:
ECG: sinus rhythm with horizontal ST depression in the lateral leads; no ST elevation.
High-sensitivity troponin: elevated on arrival, with significant rise on repeat sample.
Chest radiograph: no acute cardiopulmonary abnormality.
Blood tests: renal function and haemoglobin acceptable for anticoagulation.

Problem: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction.
Action: Aspirin administered; fondaparinux commenced. Atorvastatin given. Analgesia and antiemetic as required, with cardiac monitoring.
Decision: Discussed with on-call cardiology; admission for telemetry, serial ECG/troponin and consideration of early coronary angiography. Not suitable for discharge from A&E.

Plan:
Keep nil by mouth pending cardiology review. Repeat observations and ECG if pain recurs. Friend updated with patient’s agreement.

Documented by: sharanya carey, Emergency Department clinician

Dear Respiratory Medicine Team,

Re: KIZZIE OMAR

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient’s persistent breathlessness and chest tightness, with the specific question of whether there is an underlying respiratory disorder contributing to symptoms currently attributed predominantly to generalised anxiety disorder.

There is a background of persistent worry, poor sleep and marked muscle tension. Over recent months, episodes of shortness of breath have become more intrusive, particularly during periods of heightened anxiety, although the patient also reports intermittent chest tightness outside clear panic episodes. There has been no documented haemoptysis or unexplained weight loss. A dry cough has been present for 3 days. The patient works for GORTIN Public Library and reports no clear occupational trigger. Their sibling, safire hogg, has been supportive with appointments and symptom monitoring.

Examination in primary care showed the patient to be comfortable at rest, with normal work of breathing and clear breath sounds bilaterally. Oxygen saturations were normal on air. There was no wheeze, peripheral oedema or clinical evidence of infection. Previous chest examination and basic observations have been reassuring. No inhaler has yet been started.

Sertraline has been prescribed for anxiety, with partial improvement in intrusive worry but limited effect on the somatic symptoms. Sleep remains poor. The patient has been advised regarding regular medication adherence and has accepted referral for talking therapy; access is pending.

Please review whether spirometry, bronchodilator reversibility testing or other respiratory investigations are indicated, and advise on management. I would also appreciate guidance on distinguishing dysfunctional breathing or anxiety-related symptoms from asthma or another respiratory condition.

Referring clinician: Dr Luna-Ivy Christie, MBBS
Service locality: GULLADUFF

To the Diabetic Foot Service

Re: Yezen  
MRN: 053 003 681

I am referring Yezen for urgent assessment of a diabetic foot ulcer and advice on whether deeper infection or ischaemia is present.

They attended the accident and emergency department with a plantar ulcer beneath the forefoot. Local discharge has been present for 3 days, with increasing redness and tenderness around the wound. Sensation is reduced in both feet. There was no reported fever or rigors, and observations were stable at review. The ulcer has a sloughy base with surrounding cellulitis; pedal pulses were difficult to feel clinically, although the foot remained warm. A plain radiograph did not show gas or an obvious bony abnormality. Blood tests showed a raised inflammatory marker, with renal function suitable for the prescribed antibiotic.

Initial management has been cleansing and a non-adherent dressing, pressure relief, and co-amoxiclav. The patient has been advised to avoid weight-bearing through the affected area and to attend the emergency department promptly if systemic symptoms develop. Glycaemic control is being reviewed in primary care.

Please could your team assess the ulcer depth, circulation and need for debridement or imaging, and advise on ongoing antimicrobial and off-loading management. An urgent multidisciplinary diabetic foot review would be appreciated.

This referral is made on behalf of Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh. I am the referring clinician.

ANAHITA BOURNE  
0978004  
For Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh

Discharge summary – Paediatrics

Patient: P. Lord
DOB: 7 May 2023
Informant: father, Dany Grant, from Mirbister

Reason for admission
Admitted with 24 hours of frequent vomiting and watery diarrhoea, with fewer wet nappies and reduced oral intake. Father reported no blood in stool and no breathing difficulty. Assessed in the emergency department and admitted for observation and rehydration.

Hospital course
At 08:15 on admission the infant was alert but unsettled, with dry lips and reduced urine output. Peripheral perfusion remained satisfactory and there were no clinical features of sepsis. Given small, frequent volumes of oral rehydration solution with supportive nursing care. Vomiting settled during the first day and diarrhoea became less frequent. No intravenous fluids or antibiotics were required. Tolerated breast/formula feeds before discharge and subsequently passed urine normally.

Investigations
Capillary glucose satisfactory. No blood tests indicated clinically. Stool sample not sent as there was no blood, recent travel or prolonged course.

Problems addressed
• Acute gastroenteritis
• Mild dehydration, resolved with oral rehydration
• Reduced oral intake, improving

Discharge medicines and advice
Oral rehydration solution: offer frequent small amounts after each loose stool or vomit, alongside usual milk feeds. No anti-diarrhoeal medication. Continue supportive care at home. Father advised to seek urgent medical review via NHS 111 or A&E if the infant becomes difficult to rouse, cannot keep fluids down, has markedly fewer wet nappies, develops blood in the stool, breathing difficulty or other deterioration. Hand hygiene and separate towels recommended to reduce household spread.

Follow-up
GP review arranged for 24th August 2023 if intake, urine output or stools have not returned to usual sooner. Discharged home clinically hydrated and feeding, accompanied by father. Discharge instructions discussed and understood.

Dear Headache Service,

I am referring Madalyne for assessment of increasingly frequent migraine and advice on preventive treatment. The headaches are usually unilateral and throbbing, with nausea and marked photophobia. They now occur several times each month and are beginning to affect normal activities and work. There is no reported persistent neurological deficit, loss of consciousness or sudden “worst ever” onset.

Current treatment is naproxen when required and sumatriptan 50 mg at onset of migraine. Sumatriptan provides partial relief, but attacks may recur later the same day. We have discussed taking treatment early, maintaining regular meals and sleep, and keeping a headache diary. There is no current preventive migraine medicine.

I would be grateful for your assessment, including advice on an appropriate preventive option and whether any further investigation or headache education would be helpful. Please also review the frequency of acute medication use.

This referral is from Royal Victoria Hospital, HILLSBOROUGH. Please direct correspondence to the referring surgery. I remain available through the practice for further clinical information.

O. Biggs

I reviewed you in the cardiology clinic because of the episodes of retrosternal burning and acid regurgitation. You also described a cough that is worse at night. The symptoms are related to meals and lying down, without exertional chest pressure, fainting or unexplained breathlessness. Your examination today was reassuring, and the pattern is most consistent with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease rather than a heart-related cause.

Please continue omeprazole 20 mg once daily, taken before breakfast, and use the alginate suspension after meals and at bedtime when needed. Try to avoid eating shortly before going to bed, and raise the head of the bed if the night-time cough persists. Reducing foods that clearly trigger symptoms, particularly large or fatty meals, may also help.

No cardiology investigation is required at present. Please arrange a GP review if symptoms are not settling after several weeks of regular treatment, or sooner if swallowing becomes difficult, you are losing weight unintentionally, or there is persistent vomiting. Seek urgent assessment through A&E for severe or unfamiliar chest pain, especially if it occurs with sweating, nausea or breathlessness.

We will review the symptoms and treatment response at the follow-up appointment on 22nd January 2036. Please bring an up-to-date list of medicines to that appointment.

Clinical Genetics Review
NHS number: 0000129993

Patient: Clarice J.
Occupation: Barista
Report/accession ID: L21X53099
Clinic: BASILDON HOSPITAL

Thank you for attending the hereditary cancer risk assessment with your friend. We discussed your significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer and your understandable concern about your own future risk. No current treatment is required for you, and you have no cancer symptoms reported at this appointment.

The family history may be consistent with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer susceptibility. A BRCA1 c.68_69delAG variant has been reported in the family and will be checked against the available laboratory and family documentation before any result is interpreted for you. This is important because predictive testing is most informative when the familial variant has first been confirmed in an affected relative.

We agreed to obtain consent for testing and to review the family history, including which relatives have had cancer and whether genetic results are available. If the familial result is confirmed, targeted predictive testing can usually be offered. We discussed possible outcomes: a positive result, a negative result, or an uncertain result if the familial information cannot be verified. The implications for surveillance, risk-reducing options and relatives will be explained once the result is known.

Please contact the genetics team through BASILDON HOSPITAL if further family information becomes available. I will write to you after the records have been reviewed and arrange follow-up to discuss the result.

Kind regards,

A. Hope
Clinical Genetics Team
BASILDON HOSPITAL

mariam haywood

Discharge summary – Paediatrics

Patient: K. PRESTON
DOB: 2017-01-11
Legal guardian: J. Coulson, locality GREENCASTLE

Reason for admission
Presented with approximately 24 hours of worsening abdominal pain, initially central and subsequently localising to the right lower quadrant, with nausea and loss of appetite. Guardian provided the history and remained involved in decisions and discharge planning.

Assessment and treatment
On examination, focal right lower-quadrant tenderness with guarding. Blood tests showed raised inflammatory markers. Ultrasound was consistent with acute appendicitis, without a drainable collection. Commenced on intravenous fluids, analgesia with paracetamol and intravenous co-amoxiclav. Reviewed by the paediatric surgical team; guardian consented to operative management.

Laparoscopic appendicectomy was undertaken under general anaesthesia. Operative findings were an inflamed, non-perforated appendix. No drain required. Histology was sent and was pending at discharge.

Progress on ward
Post-operatively remained haemodynamically stable and afebrile. Tolerated oral fluids, then a light diet, with satisfactory urine output. Mobilising independently; abdominal wounds clean and dry with dressings intact. Pain controlled with oral paracetamol. No further nausea or vomiting.

Discharge plan
Discharged home with guardian in good condition. Continue paracetamol as directed on the dispensing label for pain; encourage regular fluids and gradual return to normal diet and activity. Keep wounds clean and dry and avoid swimming until healed.

Seek urgent medical advice via NHS 111 or the emergency department for recurrent or worsening abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fever, increasing wound redness or discharge, or inability to drink.

Paediatric surgical follow-up arranged for 25 March 2025, in about 7 weeks. GP to review sooner if concerns arise; histology result to be communicated when available.

Emergency assessment – Clinical Genetics

Patient: brunella hoque
Report/accession ID: L25P83140
Seen with spreading redness and tenderness of the left lower leg, first noticed yesterday and extending upwards this morning. Reports local warmth and discomfort when walking. No preceding injury, bite or recent travel. Eating and drinking normally. Emergency contact recorded as M. Hallam.

Left lower leg with ill-defined erythema from the ankle to mid-calf, warm and tender, without fluctuance, crepitus or skin breakdown. Calf soft; distal pulses and sensation intact. No lymphangitic streaking. Chest clear and abdomen soft. No features of sepsis.

Assessment

Clinical picture consistent with uncomplicated cellulitis of the lower leg. No abscess requiring drainage and no current indication for admission. Blood tests taken: FBC and CRP mildly raised; renal function satisfactory. Blood cultures not indicated in the absence of systemic toxicity.

Plan

Commenced oral flucloxacillin and advised regular paracetamol for pain, in accordance with local antimicrobial guidance. Erythematous margin marked and leg elevation encouraged. Discussed urgent return for rapidly extending redness, fever, vomiting, severe pain, confusion or inability to take medication. GP review arranged through University Hospital Southampton NHS Foundation Trust if not clearly improving within 48 hours. Follow-up review booked for 2022-10-30. Discharged home with written advice and return precautions.

Yours sincerely,

JAMA BRAY

Reason for review: plantar ulceration of the right forefoot with reduced sensation and local discharge for 3 days.

Plan: wound cleansed and dressed today; off-loading advised and urgent podiatry input requested. Commence co-amoxiclav as prescribed, subject to allergy and renal-dose checks. Continue regular glucose monitoring and avoid barefoot walking. Review in the diabetic foot service within 48–72 hours, sooner via the emergency department if spreading erythema, increasing pain, fever or systemic deterioration develops.

Discussed with the patient and spouse. Follow-up arrangements explained by S. Frost, clinician, at Capio Springfield Hospital.

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report

Patient: PRASHIV SUTCLIFFE
MRN: 078704316
Specimen: Peripheral blood in EDTA
Clinical indication: Diabetic foot ulcer with plantar ulceration, reduced sensation and local discharge. Currently receiving wound care and co-amoxiclav. Query inherited susceptibility to diabetes and impaired wound healing.

Test performed: Targeted next-generation sequencing panel comprising genes associated with monogenic diabetes, peripheral neuropathy and syndromic ulceration.

Laboratory findings:
Coverage: 99.2% of target bases at ≥30×
Pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants: None detected
Variants of uncertain significance: Heterozygous variant in a gene associated with neuropathy; currently insufficient evidence for clinical significance
Copy-number analysis: No reportable exon-level deletion or duplication identified
Sample quality: Satisfactory; no evidence of contamination

Interpretation:
No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant was identified on the panel. The finding reported as a variant of uncertain significance does not establish a diagnosis and should not be used to guide treatment or predictive testing in relatives. A negative panel does not exclude acquired diabetic neuropathy, multifactorial diabetes, or genetic causes not detectable by this assay.

Clinical comment:
The reported ulcer symptoms are not explained by a molecular diagnosis from this test. Continue standard diabetic foot management, including wound-care review, assessment for infection and vascular status, and optimisation of glycaemic control. Correlate with the patient’s clinical and family history; consider specialist review if atypical features emerge.

Genetics follow-up: in about 4 weeks, appointment date 2027-01-20.

Report validated and authorised by krasimir sumner, GMC identifier 0594148.

Presenting with 3 days of worsening breathlessness, orthopnoea and bilateral ankle swelling. Reduced exercise tolerance despite usual furosemide. No chest pain or syncope. Emergency contact: Priyaa. Patient email: azmi.sullivan92@outlook.com

Known decompensated heart failure; previously reviewed through Bronglais General Hospital clinical genetics service. Regular furosemide and bisoprolol. No documented drug allergy in referral information.

Alert, speaking in short sentences. RR 24, SpO2 93% on air, BP 148/92, pulse 96 irregular. Bibasal fine crackles to mid-zones, raised JVP and pitting oedema to knees. Peripheries warm. Likely acute-on-chronic congestive cardiac failure; assess for renal impairment, infection or arrhythmia-related deterioration.

Sit upright, cardiac monitoring and fluid balance. Oxygen only if saturations fall below target. IV furosemide administered; repeat observations and renal profile. From: Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh
Patient: J. BENSON

Dear Consultant,

I would be grateful for your assessment of J. BENSON, who has developed intermittent palpitations, persistent fatigue and breathlessness on exertion. The breathlessness is now limiting normal walking and has not settled despite treatment for recently documented atrial fibrillation. The specific question is whether there is an additional respiratory cause, and whether pulmonary function testing or further chest imaging would be helpful.

An ECG recorded in primary care showed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate 118 beats/minute. The rate has improved on bisoprolol, although the patient still notices episodes of racing heartbeat. Apixaban has been started for stroke prevention and is being taken regularly. There is no reported haemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain or infective sputum. Chest examination in the surgery was clear, with no peripheral oedema; oxygen saturation was satisfactory at rest.

A recent chest radiograph did not show focal consolidation or pleural effusion. Blood tests, including full blood count and thyroid function, were unremarkable. We are arranging ongoing cardiovascular review separately, including consideration of echocardiography.

Please review and advise on respiratory investigations and management. In the meantime, the patient has been advised to seek urgent assessment through A&E if breathlessness occurs at rest, chest pain develops, or there is syncope.

Yours sincerely,

raahul millington

Home address: 115 Simpson's Fold Court, Broad Ford, TN12 0AA
Contact: 07700 900004

Reason for review:
New diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma following assessment of painless cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Reports drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss over recent months. Family history:
No known first-degree relative with Hodgkin lymphoma or another haematological malignancy. Limited information regarding paternal relatives. Friend provided some collateral history; patient gave consent for discussion in their presence.

Hodgkin lymphoma is usually sporadic. A modest familial component is recognised, but routine germline testing is not indicated solely on the basis of this diagnosis. • Patient to contact the service if additional information becomes available.
• Continue follow-up with haematology; genetics review can be re-opened if clinically indicated.

General Medicine Clinic Report

Patient: kelly amin
MRN: 003419/31
Contact: 07700 900236

The patient, aged 44 years, was reviewed with their sibling present. The history is of approximately six weeks of progressive, painless cervical and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, associated with drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss. No local infective symptoms were reported. The sibling confirms reduced appetite and fatigue, with no recent travel or known tuberculosis exposure.

Examination demonstrated non-tender, firm cervical and left supraclavicular nodes. No overlying erythema or fluctuance. There was no clinically evident hepatosplenomegaly. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Performance status remains adequate for normal activities, although energy levels are reduced.

Recent blood tests show mild normocytic anaemia and raised inflammatory markers. Liver and renal profiles are satisfactory. Chest radiograph demonstrates mediastinal widening, requiring urgent cross-sectional assessment.

Overall findings are highly suspicious for Hodgkin lymphoma, with nodal and constitutional features warranting expedited diagnostic work-up. Differential considerations include other lymphoproliferative disease and less likely chronic infection. The patient has been counselled regarding the need for tissue diagnosis; an urgent ultrasound-guided core biopsy or excision biopsy will be arranged, alongside CT imaging of the neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis. Further management will depend on histology and staging.

Supportive care pending tissue diagnosis: maintain oral intake as tolerated, simple analgesia if required, and seek urgent assessment for fever, rapidly enlarging nodes, breathlessness or difficulty swallowing. No disease-specific treatment has been commenced.

Follow-up in the rapid-access pathway is booked for 26/12/2020, subject to earlier review once pathology is available.

Parent shown fingertip-unit application and advised not to stop anti-inflammatory treatment prematurely when the skin remains inflamed. Review if not improving, or sooner for spreading redness, increasing pain, discharge or fever.

The concern is the pattern of hypertension in the family, with several close relatives affected at a relatively young stage of life. Their partner has accompanied them to consultations and is supportive of the referral. We have discussed that most hypertension is multifactorial, but a monogenic cause may be considered where there is a strong family pattern or unusual biochemical findings.

Recent primary-care blood tests showed preserved renal function and no persistent electrolyte abnormality. Urine testing did not indicate significant protein loss. Home blood-pressure readings remain above the agreed target, although adherence has been reviewed and appears reliable. I have advised continuation of the current medicines pending specialist advice and asked the patient to bring a seven-day home BP record.

Please advise whether genetic testing is indicated, which panel would be appropriate, and whether screening of relatives should be considered. Please also review for secondary causes and recommend any further biochemical investigations.

A follow-up review has been arranged for 2045-04-14, when we will reassess symptoms and blood-pressure readings.

Yours sincerely,

asim woods

DISCHARGE SUMMARY – General Medicine

Patient: A. Kay
MRN: 086869003
Spouse/emergency contact: LOVAN GUY, based in KIRKISTOWN
Responsible organisation: Royal Victoria Hospital

Admission reason
Reduced urine output, fatigue and poor oral intake over several days. Admitted for assessment of acute kidney injury (AKI), likely related to dehydration.

Key results
• Admission creatinine elevated from documented baseline; improved with rehydration.
• Urinalysis: concentrated urine, no significant blood or protein.
• Renal ultrasound: no hydronephrosis or obstructive lesion.
• Blood pressure stable; remained afebrile.

Hospital course
Treated with intravenous sodium chloride with careful fluid balance monitoring. Urine output increased and renal function improved. No indication for renal replacement therapy. Reviewed by consultant nephrologist; advice was continued clinical monitoring and repeat renal blood tests after discharge.

Medication actions
• Ramipril and other potentially nephrotoxic medicines withheld during AKI.
• Avoid NSAIDs unless specifically advised.
• Restarting regular medicines to be confirmed by GP following repeat blood results.
• No new long-term medicine commenced.

Condition at discharge
Clinically euvolaemic, eating and drinking, mobilising independently. Passing urine adequately. Discharged home with spouse aware of the plan.

Follow-up / actions
GP review and U&Es within 3–5 days, with medication reconciliation. Maintain oral fluids unless otherwise instructed. Return to A&E if urine output falls again, vomiting prevents drinking, increasing breathlessness, confusion or marked weakness develops.

Discharge status: Home, self-care.

Early pregnancy team review arranged through the usual maternity pathway, with GP follow-up if symptoms recur or medication is ineffective. Discharge summary

Patient: Masuma
DOB: 27/04/1967
Home address: 109 BALLYVELTON ROAD, CLONFEACLE
Contact: 07700 900425

Reason for attendance
Admitted from A&E with a severe sickle cell painful crisis affecting both limbs and the lower back, with reduced oral intake and clinical dehydration. No chest pain, cough or breathlessness during the admission.

Assessment and treatment
Initial observations were stable. Blood tests showed the patient’s usual chronic anaemia, with no significant acute kidney injury. Chest radiograph showed no focal consolidation. Blood cultures were not suggestive of infection. Managed according to the sickle cell pathway with regular analgesia, including intravenous morphine, anti-sickness treatment and intravenous fluids. Oxygen was not required. Pain improved steadily and oral intake returned. No transfusion was indicated.

Discharge plan
Discharge home today once comfortable on oral analgesia and mobilising safely. Continue usual prescribed medicines. Use paracetamol regularly for the next 48 hours, then as required; avoid anti-inflammatory tablets unless specifically advised by the sickle cell team or GP. Maintain good fluid intake and rest.

Please seek urgent medical help for fever, chest pain, difficulty breathing, worsening pain despite treatment, marked drowsiness, or inability to drink. Contact the sickle cell team or GP if pain is not settling.

Follow-up
Routine haematology review booked for 25 Oct 2025, in about 9 weeks. Please bring an up-to-date list of medicines and mention any further crises or emergency attendances. The GP should review ongoing analgesia and ensure the discharge medicines are available.

Reassurance and coached breathing retraining in department; symptoms fully resolved. The patient has previously been reviewed by a consultant respiratory physician, who advised that the familial pattern should be discussed with genetics.

Assessment: Obstructive sleep apnoea treated with continuous airway pressure, with possible familial clustering and clinical features meriting specialist advice.

Plan: Please review and advise whether genetic assessment or testing is indicated, and whether any additional phenotypic assessment or screening of relatives should be arranged. Respiratory management will continue in parallel.

Yours sincerely,

Dr Jessie-James HIGGINS, MBBS

Cardiology to determine timing of angiography and the P2Y12 inhibitor plan; if managed medically, discharge should include dual antiplatelet therapy unless contraindicated. Repeat ECG for recurrent pain and escalate promptly if haemodynamic or rhythm changes occur. Patient understands the need for admission and agrees.

Re: S. PERRY – urgent haematology assessment

The working diagnosis is Hodgkin lymphoma, although alternative causes of persistent lymphadenopathy remain possible. Current treatment is supportive care pending tissue diagnosis; no anticancer therapy has been started. Please arrange urgent specialist review, staging investigations as appropriate, and image-guided or excisional biopsy according to your assessment. I would also welcome advice on interim symptom control and whether any further primary-care investigations are required.

Early pregnancy team follow-up arranged. GP review if symptoms persist or medication is ineffective. Return to A&E for inability to keep fluids down, fainting, reduced urine, severe abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding.

Dear Colleague,

Re: recurrent left knee pain and reduced mobility

I would be grateful for your assessment of aoife-grace carey, who attended the emergency department with worsening atraumatic left knee pain on a background of progressive symptoms. The principal clinical question is whether the presentation is consistent with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis requiring specialist management, and whether further imaging or an injection-based intervention would be appropriate.

The spouse accompanied the patient and reports a noticeable reduction in day-to-day mobility. No recent injury, fever or systemic symptoms. Examination in the department demonstrated an antalgic gait, medial joint-line tenderness and crepitus through flexion, with reduced active range of movement owing to pain. Plain radiographs showed medial compartment joint-space narrowing with marginal osteophyte formation, in keeping with osteoarthritis. There was no acute fracture or dislocation. Initial management has been advice regarding pacing and activity modification, together with simple analgesia. Current treatment includes paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily and topical ibuprofen, with only partial relief.

Please review for confirmation of the diagnosis, optimisation of conservative treatment and consideration of physiotherapy, bracing or intra-articular therapy. An orthopaedic opinion would also be appreciated if symptoms remain disabling despite non-operative measures.

Yours faithfully,

Daphney COLLIER

The patient, aged 13 years, was admitted with a 36-hour history of profuse vomiting and watery diarrhoea, with reduced urine output. History was obtained from the patient and legal guardian, Juanita Austin, who lives in BALLYRONAN. No blood was reported in the stool and there was no recent travel.

Managed with oral rehydration solution in frequent small amounts, with supportive care and a short period of intravenous fluids when oral intake was initially inadequate. Acute gastroenteritis with dehydration, now clinically improved. The patient and legal guardian were counselled regarding continued hydration, hand hygiene and gradual return to normal diet. They understood the plan and agreed to discharge home.

Continue oral rehydration solution after each loose stool and encourage regular fluids. Paracetamol may be used if required, following the instructions on the packaging. Avoid anti-diarrhoeal medication unless advised by a clinician.

GP review if symptoms do not continue to improve. Paediatric outpatient review arranged for 25 December 2012. Return to A&E urgently if unable to keep fluids down, markedly drowsy, develops blood in the stool, severe abdominal pain or significantly reduced urine output.

No pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis or recent travel reported. No documented fever.

Written asthma action-plan advice provided, including escalation to emergency services for increasing breathlessness, inability to speak comfortably or poor response to salbutamol.

Discharge home considered appropriate with GP follow-up for asthma control review and assessment of preventer dose. Return to A&E advised if symptoms recur or fail to settle.

Admission: Acute sickle cell painful crisis

Admission details
Presented with severe bilateral limb and lower back pain, reduced oral intake and clinical dehydration. No chest pain or respiratory symptoms. Initial observations recorded at 08:15; afebrile and haemodynamically stable.

Key results
FBC consistent with baseline sickle cell disease; haemoglobin below usual level but stable on repeat. Reticulocytosis present. U&Es showed mild pre-renal change, corrected with rehydration. Chest radiograph clear. No evidence of acute chest syndrome, sepsis or focal neurological deficit.

Hospital course
Treated on the haematology ward with intravenous fluids, regular paracetamol and opioid analgesia, including morphine with antiemetic and bowel regimen as required. Pain improved progressively over 48 hours; intravenous analgesia weaned and converted to oral medication. Eating and drinking adequately, mobilising independently. No transfusion required.

Discharge medicines / actions
• Continue regular analgesia as per supplied discharge prescription; morphine only for breakthrough pain.
• Maintain oral fluids and usual sickle cell medicines.
• Avoid NSAIDs unless specifically agreed with the sickle cell team.
• GP to review analgesic requirement and repeat blood tests if symptoms persist.

Follow-up
Sickle cell nurse specialist telephone review within one week; haematology outpatient follow-up as arranged. Return to A&E for uncontrolled pain, fever, breathlessness, chest pain or new weakness.

Signed: Rhyder Crowther, consultant physician

Occupation: Architect
Report/accession ID: 0442620604

Seen with spouse following referral from Chelsea and Westminster Hospital - Valneva Covid19 Trials for assessment of recurrent unilateral headaches and associated palpitations. The patient reports approximately three months of episodic right-sided headache, usually pulsatile, with nausea and photophobia. Episodes last several hours and are sometimes accompanied by awareness of a fast heartbeat, which settles as the headache improves. No exertional chest pain, syncope or sustained palpitations. No focal weakness or speech disturbance reported.

Taking sumatriptan 50 mg at onset of migraine and naproxen when required. The patient feels sumatriptan is generally effective, although it has been used on several occasions close together during a difficult week. No regular cardiac medication.

On examination, comfortable at rest. Pulse regular, heart sounds normal, and blood pressure acceptable in clinic. Neurological examination grossly normal, with no apparent focal deficit. ECG today shows sinus rhythm without acute ST-T change.

Recurrent migraine with nausea and photophobia. Brief palpitations appear temporally related to pain; no current evidence of arrhythmia or structural cardiac symptoms.

Discussed limiting acute migraine treatment to avoid medication-overuse headache. Continue sumatriptan 50 mg at onset of migraine, with naproxen if needed and tolerated; avoid combining anti-inflammatory medicines. Seven-day home pulse and symptom diary requested. Arrange ambulatory ECG if palpitations become more frequent, prolonged or occur independently of headache. Seek urgent assessment for sudden severe headache, neurological deficit, syncope or persistent chest pain.

Reviewed by saam rhodes
Cardiology clinic, Chelsea and Westminster Hospital - Valneva Covid19 Trials

Molecular Genetics Report

Patient: Kasi CLEGG
MRN: 09546632
Requesting location: Cobalt Hospital
Specimen: EDTA blood; peripheral blood sample
Clinical indication: Significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer; predictive testing requested. Cancer-risk concern noted.
Current treatment: None.

Test performed: BRCA1 and BRCA2 germline variant analysis
Result: BRCA1 c.68_69delAG detected.
Interpretation: Pathogenic BRCA1 variant, consistent with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome. This is a germline finding; implications for the patient and blood relatives require formal genetics counselling.

Limitations: A negative result would not exclude familial risk from an undetected variant or another susceptibility gene. Variant classification and management should be reviewed against the current laboratory database and family history.

Clinical comment: Result should not be interpreted in isolation. Refer to clinical genetics for discussion of breast, ovarian, prostate and pancreatic cancer risk, surveillance options, and cascade testing for adult relatives. No change to treatment indicated from this report alone.

Action: Genetics review requested. Patient advised to bring available family cancer diagnoses and pathology details.
Follow-up: appointment/review due 25 Oct 2022.

Validated and reported by: T. West

Patient: KELSIE-MAE GUY
MRN: 029 419 048
Responsible team: General Medicine, Royal Victoria Hospital

Reason for admission

Key findings
On arrival clinically fluid overloaded, with bibasal crackles and pitting oedema to the mid-shins. Chest radiograph showed pulmonary vascular congestion with small bilateral pleural effusions. ECG: sinus rhythm, no acute ischaemic change. Blood tests demonstrated elevated NT-proBNP (BNP 2,840 pg/mL), with mild congestive liver enzyme derangement. Treated with intravenous furosemide, fluid balance monitoring and daily weights, with good symptomatic and weight response. Oxygen was required briefly on admission but was discontinued before discharge. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed impaired left ventricular systolic function, with no significant valve lesion. Cardiology advice obtained regarding guideline-directed treatment and outpatient review.

Furosemide increased to 40 mg each morning.
Bisoprolol continued at the pre-admission dose.
New low-dose ramipril commenced following stable renal function and potassium.
No medication allergies documented in the inpatient record.

At discharge, breathing comfortably at rest and mobilising independently. Oedema much improved; residual mild ankle swelling. Clinically euvolaemic and suitable for home.

Follow-up and advice
GP surgery to repeat U&Es and blood pressure within one week and review diuretic response. Heart failure nurse referral made through Royal Victoria Hospital; outpatient echocardiography/cardiology follow-up arranged. Maintain a low-salt diet, monitor daily weight and seek urgent assessment for rapidly worsening breathlessness, syncope, chest pain or marked fluid retention. Discharge information discussed with the patient and Shri Drew; both confirmed understanding.

Date: 26 Jan 2012
Patient: JESSICA LIN
MRN: 04871592
Address: 94 GORRAN ROAD, DUNNAMANAGH

Dear Colleague,

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient’s persistent low back pain with right-sided shooting leg pain and intermittent paraesthesia, consistent clinically with lumbar radiculopathy. The specific question is whether further imaging, electrodiagnostic testing or specialist intervention is indicated, and whether there is evidence of a progressive nerve-root deficit.

Symptoms began several weeks ago after increasing activity. The pain radiates from the lower lumbar region into the buttock and posterior thigh, occasionally reaching the calf. Paraesthesia is intermittent and positional. There is no reported saddle sensory change, bladder or bowel disturbance, fever, unexplained weight loss or recent significant trauma.

On review today, gait was mildly antalgic. Lumbar flexion and extension were restricted by pain, with right straight-leg raise reproducing the leg symptoms. Lower-limb power was functionally preserved, and there was no clear dermatomal sensory loss on brief examination. Reflexes were symmetrical.

Management to date has been naproxen with food and paracetamol, together with advice to remain mobile and avoid prolonged bed rest. Benefit has been limited. Physiotherapy has been discussed, although attendance has not yet commenced. Please note that a consultant neurologist previously advised that urgent reassessment would be appropriate if weakness or sphincter symptoms developed.

Assessment: persistent lumbar radicular pain without current clinical red flags, but with inadequate response to initial primary-care management.

I would appreciate your review and advice regarding imaging, physiotherapy escalation and analgesic options.

Yours sincerely,

Shian Burrows

NHS number: 000 528 7201
Date: 23rd March 2035
Patient: Las, aged 75 years
Address: 167 Wisteria Walk, Abergele, LL22 7AA
Emergency contact: relative listed in electronic record.

Presenting complaint: Central chest pressure for approximately 90 minutes, associated with diaphoresis and nausea. No syncope. Symptoms partially improved at rest.

Initial observations: BP 120/80 mmHg. Pulse regular. SpO₂ satisfactory on air. Afebrile.
Examination: Alert, clammy initially. Heart sounds dual, no murmur. Chest clear bilaterally. No calf tenderness or peripheral oedema.

ECG: Sinus rhythm with lateral ST-segment depression; no ST elevation.
Bloods: Initial high-sensitivity troponin elevated, repeat rise confirmed. FBC and renal profile acceptable.
CXR: No acute cardiopulmonary abnormality.

Impression: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Haemodynamically stable; ongoing ischaemic symptoms absent after treatment.

Treatment: Aspirin administered. Fondaparinux commenced. Atorvastatin given. GTN relieved residual pressure. Continuous cardiac monitoring.

Discussed with on-call cardiology team. Admit to cardiology for telemetry and early invasive assessment; consent and risks discussed with patient. Avoid strenuous activity. Repeat ECG/troponin if recurrent pain.

Clinical genetics department entry noted in referral pathway; acute management remains under cardiology.

Reviewed and signed: LILLY-ROSE STUBBS

From: Dr Nana-Ama Gilbert, MBBS, DOLLINGSTOWN
Organisation: Royal Victoria Hospital
Professional ID: 0244488

Patient: Chukwuma W.
Reason for referral: persistent hypertension with intermittent headache and light-headedness despite dual therapy.

Background:
• Essential hypertension, previously managed in primary care.
• Current medicines: amlodipine and ramipril; adherence reported as good.
• Home readings remain above target, with variable systolic values. No chest pain, focal neurological symptoms or syncope.
• Emergency contact recorded in practice details.

BP elevated on repeat measurement in surgery; pulse regular. No postural drop documented. Cardiovascular and neurological examinations unremarkable. Renal function and potassium acceptable on latest blood tests. Urine ACR not recently repeated.

Management to date:
Lifestyle advice reviewed, including salt reduction and home BP diary. Amlodipine and ramipril continued pending specialist advice. Headaches partially improved but light-headedness persists intermittently.

Request:
Please assess for resistant or secondary hypertension, review treatment and advise on further investigations. Please consider ambulatory BP monitoring and medication optimisation. Follow-up with our practice is planned in about 5 weeks, or sooner if advised.

Kind regards,

Dr Nana-Ama Gilbert, MBBS

MOLECULAR GENETICS LABORATORY REPORT
NHS number: 000 272 3671

Patient: hrian barratt
MRN: 002570/94
Address: 90 Cockmoor Road, London, SW17 0AA
Specimen: Peripheral blood, EDTA; germline DNA
Request: Predictive testing following significant family history of breast/ovarian cancer. No current treatment.

DNA purity (A260/280): 1.87

Clinical comment: Result should be interpreted with the family history and any previous affected-relative testing. No treatment indicated on the basis of this report.

Follow-up genetics review: 14 September 1988

Discharge summary

Patient: A. Hadley
Admitting service: Royal Victoria Hospital
Report/accession ID: S24-0120919

Reason for admission:
Admitted with several days of lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge and deep dyspareunia. Pelvic inflammatory disease was treated empirically following gynaecology assessment.

Key findings:
Observations remained stable throughout admission; most recent blood pressure 120/80 mmHg. Pregnancy test negative. Initial inflammatory markers were mildly raised. Vaginal and cervical samples were sent for microscopy, culture and sexually transmitted infection testing; results were pending at discharge. Pelvic ultrasound showed no tubo-ovarian abscess.

Hospital course:
Received ceftriaxone at presentation, then commenced doxycycline and metronidazole. Pain and discharge improved, and she remained afebrile, eating and drinking normally. No operative intervention was required. The importance of completing treatment and avoiding sexual intercourse until treatment is complete, symptoms have settled and partners have been assessed was discussed. A friend accompanied her for part of the admission at the patient’s request.

Discharge medicines:
Doxycycline to complete the prescribed course.
Metronidazole to complete the prescribed course.
Simple analgesia as required, according to the discharge prescription.

Follow-up and safety net:
Please arrange review with your GP or the sexual health service within 72 hours if symptoms are not continuing to improve. Return to A&E urgently for worsening pain, fever, vomiting, faintness or heavy bleeding. Results will be reviewed by the clinical team and communicated if treatment needs changing. Partner notification and testing were advised.

Discharging clinician: HARPER-JEAN COLLINS, GMC number 0974919

text:
Laboratory report

Patient: I. Mitchell
MRN: H0252603
Requesting location: Accident and Emergency, LOUDOUN SQUARE MEDICAL CENTRE
Specimen collected: 6 December 2020
Specimen: Deep wound swab, plantar ulcer, left foot
Clinical details: Diabetic foot ulcer with reduced sensation and local discharge. Current treatment includes wound care and co-amoxiclav. Specimen obtained following cleansing and removal of superficial exudate.

Microbiology
Gram stain: Few polymorphs; mixed Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms observed.
Culture: Moderate growth of Staphylococcus aureus and mixed enteric Gram-negative bacilli. No significant anaerobic growth isolated.
Susceptibility: Staphylococcus aureus susceptible to flucloxacillin. Enteric Gram-negative isolate susceptible to co-amoxiclav. Interpret in conjunction with the clinical picture and antimicrobial history.

Biochemistry
HbA1c: 74 mmol/mol
Interpretation: Above the usual treatment target for most adults with diabetes, consistent with suboptimal longer-term glycaemic control.

Comment
The culture indicates mixed bacterial growth from the ulcer. Results may represent colonisation as well as infection; correlate with spreading erythema, warmth, increasing pain, systemic features and depth of ulceration. Continue local wound management and off-loading assessment. Review antimicrobial need and duration against clinical response and local diabetic foot guidance. Urgent specialist assessment is advised if there is suspected deep infection, osteomyelitis, critical ischaemia or systemic deterioration.

Validated and reported by: zonain street
Report date: 6 December 2020
