Clinical Genetics Outpatient Report
National Insurance number: NT 41 75 43 B

Patient: M. Fraser
MRN: 008091513
Occupation: Builder
Referring service: OPTEGRA MANCHESTER HOSPITAL

Reason for review: Assessment of persistent anxiety symptoms and discussion of whether a genetic explanation is indicated.

History: The patient describes longstanding excessive and difficult-to-control worry across several areas of daily life, with associated poor sleep and sustained muscle tension. Symptoms have been more intrusive recently; an intermittent frontal headache has been present for 3 days. No reported episodes of loss of consciousness, focal neurological deficit, or unusual movements. There is no clear history suggestive of a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder or a progressive inherited neurological condition. The emergency contact is recorded in the referral information.

Medication: Sertraline, continued as prescribed. Tolerability reported as acceptable; adherence appears consistent. No other regular medicines disclosed.

Examination: Alert and engaged during consultation. Speech normal in rate and content. Affect anxious but reactive. No thought disorder, perceptual disturbance or overt cognitive impairment identified. Neurological screening examination unremarkable. Mild bilateral trapezius tension noted.

Impression: Clinical presentation is most consistent with generalised anxiety disorder. At present, the history and examination do not provide an indication for diagnostic genetic testing. The symptoms are not, in isolation, suggestive of a defined inherited syndrome.

Plan: Continue sertraline under GP review, with monitoring of response and adverse effects. Recommend evidence-based psychological therapy, preferably CBT, and attention to sleep routine and graded activity. Return to genetics if new syndromic features, a significant three-generation family history, or objective neurological change emerges.

Report authored and signed by Dr Navkirat Martin, MBBS.

Reason for admission:
Admitted under General Medicine with a vaso-occlusive sickle cell painful crisis, causing severe bilateral limb pain and lower back pain, with reduced oral intake and clinical dehydration. History was obtained with support from the patient’s sibling.

Hospital course:
Initial assessment showed significant pain without focal neurological deficit or features of acute chest syndrome. At 08:15 the patient was reviewed by the medical team; observations remained stable and oxygen saturations were satisfactory on air. Blood tests were consistent with the known sickle cell disorder, with no convincing evidence of bacterial infection. Chest radiograph was clear.

Managed according to the local sickle cell analgesia pathway with regular and breakthrough morphine, antiemetic medication as required, and intravenous crystalloid fluids. Analgesia was reviewed regularly and converted to oral treatment as the pain settled. Oral intake and urine output improved. There were no transfusion requirements, and no acute renal, respiratory or neurological complication during this admission.

Assessment at discharge:
Pain now mild and controlled with oral analgesia. Mobilising independently, drinking adequately and clinically euvolaemic. Afebrile and suitable for discharge home with sibling support.

Plan:
Continue usual disease-modifying and community medicines as listed on the discharge prescription. Use prescribed analgesia only as directed and maintain good oral hydration. Seek urgent medical attention for chest pain, breathlessness, fever, worsening pain, confusion or inability to drink. GP and specialist haemoglobinopathy follow-up to continue through the usual services.

Laboratory Report – Thyroid Function

Patient: D. Mann
MRN: H5167365
Specimen: Serum
Request: Thyroid function tests; clinical details recorded as fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation. On levothyroxine. Ordering clinician not stated.

Results
TSH: 8.2 mIU/L
Free T4: 13.1 pmol/L
Free T3: Not indicated
Sample quality: Satisfactory

Reference interpretation
TSH raised above the usual adult reference interval (approximately 0.3–4.5 mIU/L). Free T4 within reference range. Pattern consistent with under-replacement or suboptimal adherence in treated primary hypothyroidism.

Clinical comment
Correlate with prescribed dose, administration timing and recent missed doses. Review interacting medicines and supplements, particularly iron or calcium preparations. If clinically appropriate, consider levothyroxine dose review; repeat thyroid function after a suitable interval following any change. No evidence of overt biochemical hypothyroidism on this sample.

Follow-up: GP medication review booked for 9th August 2026.

Discharge summary

Patient: ANNALENA LEA
Date of admission/discharge: 10/02/2045
Clinical area: Respiratory Medicine

Reason for admission:
Postoperative wound infection following recent thoracic procedure. Increasing wound erythema, purulent discharge and local pain.

Initial assessment:
Afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Wound tender with surrounding erythema; small amount of purulent exudate. Current pain 5/10. No respiratory distress.

Investigations:
Wound swab obtained. Blood tests: inflammatory markers mildly raised; renal function satisfactory. Chest radiograph without new focal consolidation.

Hospital course:
Reviewed by respiratory and surgical teams. Wound opened locally and irrigated with saline. No evidence of deep collection or systemic sepsis. Clinical improvement after regular dressings and oral flucloxacillin. Tolerating diet and mobilising independently.

Discharge treatment:
Flucloxacillin to complete prescribed course.
Continue wound irrigation and dressing changes as demonstrated.
Paracetamol as required for pain.

Condition at discharge:
A 51-year-old Hispanic female patient, alert and clinically stable. Wound less erythematous, minimal discharge.

Follow-up/actions:
District nursing dressing review arranged. Surgical outpatient review requested; wound swab result to be reviewed and antibiotics amended if indicated. GP to monitor healing.

Communication:
Discharge advice discussed with the patient and adult child Fatiha, who lives in Saul. Return to A&E for fever, spreading redness, worsening pain, increased discharge or breathlessness.

Paediatric Outpatient Clinic Report
National Insurance number: NK315082A

Patient: Prianna Mann
Date: 01/03/2018
Contact: prianna.mann16@yahoo.co.uk

The patient, aged 6 years, was reviewed in the paediatric outpatient clinic with his father, syrena preston, who provided the history. Atopic eczema has been present intermittently, with recent worsening of pruritus and dry, inflamed skin affecting the antecubital fossae, wrists and popliteal creases. Sleep has been disturbed by scratching. There has been no fever, weeping, crusting or reduced oral intake. The current flare has been present for 3 days.

On examination, the child was comfortable and systemically well. Xerosis was widespread, with erythematous eczematous plaques and excoriations over the flexural surfaces and wrists. No honey-coloured crusting, pustulation or significant tenderness to suggest secondary bacterial infection. No facial or peri-orbital involvement. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Impression: atopic eczema, currently moderately active, without clinical evidence of infection. The distribution and morphology are consistent with eczema rather than scabies or contact dermatitis.

Management was discussed with the family. Continue liberal application of emollient several times daily and use as a soap substitute. Apply topical hydrocortisone to inflamed areas as previously advised, avoiding broken or infected skin; treatment technique and fingertip-unit quantities were demonstrated. Keep nails short and consider cotton nightwear to reduce excoriation. No oral antibiotics indicated today.

Review if worsening, spreading redness, pain, fever or failure to settle. Routine follow-up in the eczema service will be arranged.

Aarthav was admitted with a barking cough, hoarse voice and noisy breathing consistent with viral croup. History was obtained from his mother, Callum-James STEPHENS, who reported that symptoms were worse overnight. She is based in MAGUIRESBRIDGE.

On arrival there was mild inspiratory stridor at rest, without cyanosis or significant chest recession. Initial observations included heart rate 108 beats/minute. Three-day history of markedly reduced urine output with fatigue and poor oral intake. Mild nausea, no vomiting. Denies chest pain or breathlessness. Emergency contact confirms reduced fluid intake at home.

Chronic cardiac disease under outpatient follow-up. Medication reconciliation completed; recent diuretic and renin–angiotensin system inhibitor use noted. No known recent contrast exposure recorded.

Intravenous sodium chloride commenced cautiously with repeat clinical review. Temporary medication hold: diuretic and renin–angiotensin system inhibitor withheld pending renal recovery. Strict fluid balance; urine sample sent. Repeat U&E after fluids and senior review.

Admit to medical ward for monitoring, renal function trend and medication review. Escalate for worsening hyperkalaemia, oliguria or fluid overload.

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient with persistent primary hypothyroidism and a family history suggestive of an inherited thyroid disorder. The specific question is whether genetic testing is indicated, and whether the pattern warrants broader assessment for a syndromic cause.

viera waite reports several months of troublesome fatigue, marked cold intolerance and constipation despite regular levothyroxine. They describe good adherence and take the medicine before breakfast. Examination in surgery found a clinically euthyroid appearance overall, with dry skin and a mildly slow pulse; no palpable thyroid enlargement or cervical lymphadenopathy.

The dose of levothyroxine has been adjusted on more than one occasion, with only partial biochemical improvement. We have reviewed administration, possible interactions and the importance of repeat testing. There is a reported history of thyroid disease in more than one family member, although the available details are incomplete. Their friend, Malachai, has helped them gather previous family information.

Occupation: Farmer
Employer: Glentirranmuir Secondary School

Assessment and plan: persistent biochemical hypothyroidism with possible familial clustering. I would appreciate advice on the appropriate genetic work-up, any relevant clinical screening, and whether relatives should be offered targeted assessment. Further thyroid function tests will be arranged locally while awaiting your opinion.

Yours sincerely,

Dr Rezwan Bennett, MBBS

Discharge summary – Paediatrics

Patient: Hanzlah
An 8-year-old South Asian female child admitted with a 24-hour history of worsening right lower-quadrant abdominal pain, nausea and loss of appetite. History obtained from the patient and mother, DONYA MCFARLANE, who travelled from Woodend.

On arrival, the patient was mildly dehydrated with localised right iliac fossa tenderness and guarding. Initial blood tests showed raised inflammatory markers; urine dip was negative. Ultrasound demonstrated a non-compressible appendix with surrounding inflammatory change, consistent with acute appendicitis. Paediatric surgical team reviewed and consent was obtained from the mother, with the patient involved in the discussion as appropriate.

Underwent uncomplicated laparoscopic appendicectomy. Operative findings were an inflamed, non-perforated appendix; no abscess or peritoneal contamination. Appendix sent for histology. Received intravenous fluids, analgesia and intravenous co-amoxiclav peri-operatively. Pain and oral intake improved steadily post-operatively. No vomiting or fever following surgery.

At discharge: alert, comfortable, mobilising independently and tolerating a light diet. Abdomen soft with expected mild port-site tenderness; wounds clean and dry. Current observations include heart rate 92 beats/minute. Passing urine normally.

Problem list:
• Acute uncomplicated appendicitis
• Status post laparoscopic appendicectomy
• Mild dehydration, resolved

Discharge medicines:
Paracetamol as required for pain, according to the labelled dose for the patient. No antibiotics required on discharge unless advised following histology or clinical review.

Wound care and activity advice discussed with DONYA MCFARLANE. Keep dressings clean and dry; avoid swimming until wounds are healed. Seek urgent medical advice for increasing abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fever, spreading redness or discharge from a wound.

Follow-up: surgical outpatient review on 14th March 2023; histology result to be reviewed by the surgical team. GP to continue routine care and check wounds if concerns arise.

RESPIRATORY MEDICINE
Laboratory report – lymph node tissue

Patient: Romaysa B.
Report/accession ID: 015431110
Specimen collected: 19/11/2026
Specimen: Left cervical lymph node core biopsy
Request: Painless lymphadenopathy, night sweats and unintentional weight loss. Supportive care pending tissue diagnosis.

Histology:
Multiple cores show effacement of nodal architecture by a mixed inflammatory infiltrate containing scattered large atypical cells with vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli and occasional binucleation. Immunohistochemistry: atypical cells positive for CD30 and CD15, weak PAX5, and negative for CD20 and CD45. EBER in-situ hybridisation is negative. Findings are consistent with classical Hodgkin lymphoma, in the appropriate clinical and radiological context.

Ancillary results:
CD30: positive in atypical cells
CD15: positive in atypical cells
PAX5: weak positive
CD20: negative
CD45: negative
EBER: negative

Interpretation:
Lymph node biopsy demonstrates classical Hodgkin lymphoma. No evidence of metastatic carcinoma in the material examined. Classification and staging require correlation with PET-CT and clinical assessment; additional tissue may be required for molecular or research studies if clinically indicated.

Clinical comment:
Please refer promptly to the haematology multidisciplinary team for staging and treatment planning. The reported symptoms are compatible with active lymphoma. Current medication recorded as supportive care pending tissue diagnosis; no disease-specific treatment is documented in the submitted clinical information.

Dear Respiratory Medicine Team,

Re: pera horton
MRN: 0122147

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient’s persistent night-time cough, with particular consideration of reflux-related laryngeal or airway irritation and whether any respiratory investigation is indicated.

They report several months of intermittent retrosternal burning and acid regurgitation, worse after evening meals and when lying flat. The cough is predominantly nocturnal and has recently become more troublesome, including for 3 days during the latest flare. There is no reported haemoptysis, wheeze or exertional breathlessness. They have never smoked. Examination in the surgery was reassuring: oxygen saturations were normal on air, chest clear to auscultation, and there was no stridor. Weight is stable.

Treatment has included omeprazole, taken regularly before breakfast, and alginate suspension after meals and at bedtime. This has reduced the heartburn but has not resolved the cough. They have also been advised to avoid late meals, elevate the head of the bed and reduce trigger foods. No previous chest imaging or spirometry is documented. Dear Haematology Team,

Re: TALLAN SHARMA

I would be grateful for your urgent assessment of this patient, seen in the emergency department with progressive, painless lymphadenopathy, drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss. The principal clinical question is whether this represents Hodgkin lymphoma and, if so, how best to expedite tissue diagnosis and staging.

Examination demonstrated firm, non-tender cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes, with the largest palpable node approximately 3 cm. No airway compromise or focal neurological deficit was present. The patient was haemodynamically stable and afebrile during assessment. Chest radiograph showed widening of the superior mediastinum; CT imaging has been requested and is pending formal reporting. Initial blood tests demonstrated anaemia and a raised ESR; renal and liver profiles were suitable for contrast imaging.

There is no current cytotoxic treatment. Management from the emergency department has been supportive care pending tissue diagnosis, with oral fluids and simple analgesia advised. The patient has been asked to avoid commencing corticosteroids unless discussed with haematology, to reduce the risk of obscuring biopsy findings.

Occupation: Cleaner
Employer: DRUMBEG Town Council
Address: 179 Oakland Way, NEWTOWNSTEWART

Please arrange prompt review, examination of the available imaging and consideration of an image-guided core or excision biopsy, with staging investigations as clinically indicated. I would also appreciate advice regarding interim symptom control and the appropriate pathway for multidisciplinary review.

Yours sincerely,

Luqa Marks

Fluids little and often; return to normal diet as tolerated. Urine output may improve with hydration. Avoid anti-diarrhoeal medication unless advised by a clinician. Infection-control advice given, including handwashing and remaining away from school until symptom-free for 48 hours.

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report
NHS number: 000 452 0344

Patient: KEZA MUSTAFA
Patient category: 24 y/o
Report/accession ID: 0369336496
Specimen: EDTA whole blood
Clinical indication: Rheumatoid arthritis with current morning stiffness, swollen hand joints and fatigue; receiving methotrexate, folic acid and naproxen. Assessment requested before medication review.

Pharmacogenetic findings
TPMT genotype: *1/*1
Interpretation: No reduced-function TPMT allele detected. Predicted normal TPMT activity. This result does not exclude toxicity related to methotrexate or other clinical factors.

NUDT15 genotype: *1/*1
Interpretation: No tested reduced-function NUDT15 allele detected. Predicted normal NUDT15 activity.

Quality metrics
DNA concentration: 38.6 ng/µL
DNA purity (A260/280): 1.86
Assay control: Pass
Variant coverage: 100% of targeted regions

Reference interpretation
Genotype-based prediction applies to the tested TPMT and NUDT15 variants only. It is not a substitute for routine full blood count, liver function and renal monitoring. Results should be interpreted alongside treatment dose, adherence, intercurrent illness and other medicines. The assay does not investigate the cause of the reported rheumatoid arthritis flare.

Clinical comment
No pharmacogenetic evidence of reduced TPMT or NUDT15 activity was identified. There is therefore no genotype-based indication for an empiric thiopurine dose reduction; this test does not provide a methotrexate dosing recommendation. Please correlate with current inflammatory markers and clinical review. Continue standard methotrexate safety monitoring and consider rheumatology or multidisciplinary medication review if symptoms persist.

Suggested review: in about 5 weeks, on 2035-02-07.

Continue regular observations, pain scoring and prescribed analgesia. Maintain IV fluids and strict fluid balance. Encourage frequent oral fluids, assisted mobilisation and rest. Reason for admission
Presented to A&E following sudden right arm weakness, left facial droop and slurred speech while at home. Symptoms resolved before arrival. No preceding seizure, headache or loss of consciousness. Friend, FADUMO BRADBURY, from MALLUSK, provided collateral history.

Hospital course
Reviewed promptly by the acute stroke team. At 08:15 neurological examination was normal, with no residual facial asymmetry, dysphasia or limb weakness. Swallow screen passed. CT head showed no acute haemorrhage or established infarction. CT angiography demonstrated no large-vessel occlusion or significant carotid stenosis. MRI brain showed no acute infarct. • Aspirin 300 mg once daily for 14 days, then reduce to aspirin 75 mg once daily
• Atorvastatin 80 mg at night

No other regular medicines were changed. Medication counselling completed and the importance of adherence discussed.

Follow-up and advice
Urgent TIA clinic follow-up requested through ROYAL VICTORIA HOSPITAL. GP review advised for blood pressure, diabetes screening and cardiovascular risk-factor management. Avoid driving until discussed with the GP and in accordance with DVLA guidance. Return immediately via 999 if facial weakness, arm weakness, speech disturbance or other sudden neurological symptoms recur, even if they settle.

Dear Colleague,

Re: Anneka

I am referring this patient from Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh for urgent haematology assessment and treatment planning following a new diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma.

Anneka presented to the emergency department with several weeks of painless cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss. Examination identified firm, non-tender cervical nodes; there was no airway compromise or haemodynamic instability. Initial blood tests showed a mild normocytic anaemia and raised inflammatory markers. Chest imaging demonstrated bulky mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

Reason for admission

Admission findings and results
Clinically dehydrated on arrival, with dry mucous membranes and mild tachycardia. Abdomen soft, diffusely uncomfortable but without guarding or peritonism. Admission bloods showed mild acute kidney injury and raised inflammatory markers; venous lactate normal. Stool sample negative for C. difficile toxin. No evidence of pneumonia or other respiratory cause for symptoms.

Hospital course
Managed with intravenous crystalloid initially, then oral rehydration solution as vomiting settled. Ondansetron given for nausea with good effect. Renal function and electrolytes normalised on repeat testing. Diarrhoea reduced in frequency and there has been no vomiting since yesterday. Abdominal discomfort now mild, pain score 5/10, with oral intake improving. No antibiotics indicated; presentation felt most consistent with self-limiting infectious gastroenteritis.

Problem list
• Infectious gastroenteritis with vomiting and diarrhoea
• Dehydration with resolved pre-renal acute kidney injury
• Abdominal cramps, improving

Discharge medicines
Oral rehydration solution – take regularly while diarrhoea continues.
Ondansetron as required for nausea, in accordance with the dispensing label.
Usual medication unchanged.

Condition at discharge
Alert, haemodynamically stable and mobilising independently. Tolerating fluids and light diet. Passing urine normally. Discharge home with advice to rest, maintain fluids and gradually return to usual diet. Infection-control advice provided, including handwashing and avoiding preparation of food for others until symptom-free.

Follow-up
GP review if not substantially better within 48 hours. Return to A&E for inability to keep fluids down, worsening abdominal pain, blood in stool, fainting or reduced urine output.

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report

Patient: Chani A.
Report/accession ID: 22/662778
Specimen: EDTA blood, received for genomic analysis
Collection/report date: 31st August 2026
Requesting clinician: unnamed
Reporting clinician: Dr Roqaya Andrews, MBBS

Clinical details:
Current acute pyelonephritis with flank pain, dysuria and rigors. Symptoms present for 3 days. Treatment documented as cefuroxime and paracetamol. Sibling history noted; further pedigree details were not supplied.

Test performed:
Targeted next-generation sequencing of a renal/urinary tract disease panel, including genes associated with congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract, tubulointerstitial disease and inherited susceptibility to recurrent infection. Mean sequencing coverage: 148×; 99.1% of reportable coding regions covered at ≥30×.

Results:
No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant identified in the genes analysed. A heterozygous variant of uncertain significance was detected in UMOD, c.####A>T (p.####), subject to confirmation of transcript and genomic coordinates in the full technical record. No copy-number change was detected by the assay.

Interpretation:
This is a negative result for the tested panel and does not provide a molecular explanation for the current episode of acute pyelonephritis. The UMOD variant is of uncertain significance and should not be used to guide treatment or predictive testing in relatives. Correlation with renal imaging, urine culture, renal function and the detailed family history is advised. If infections recur, review by the renal/urology team and genetics service may be appropriate.

Authorised by:
Dr Roqaya Andrews, MBBS

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT ASSESSMENT

Patient: C. Wheatley
MRN: H3257249
Contact: chelsi.wheatley91@outlook.com
Emergency contact: Elijah-Blake
Referring service: ROYAL ALEXANDRA HOSPITAL

Presenting complaint:
Two-day history of right flank pain with dysuria, urinary frequency and rigors. Nausea, reduced oral intake. No vomiting or visible haematuria. Emergency contact reports increased shivering overnight.

Relevant history:
Previous uncomplicated urinary infection; no known renal disease. No recorded drug allergies. Current medicines: paracetamol as needed; cefuroxime commenced before review.

Examination:
Alert, uncomfortable, mildly flushed. Temperature 38.7°C, pulse 108, BP 112/68, respiratory rate 18, SpO₂ 98% on air. Right costovertebral angle tenderness. Abdomen soft, suprapubic discomfort, no guarding or peritonism. Clinically euvolaemic.

Investigations:
Urine dip: nitrite positive, leukocytes 3+, blood 1+.
FBC: neutrophilia. Urea and electrolytes acceptable, creatinine at baseline. C-reactive protein 86 mg/L. Lactate 1.4 mmol/L. Blood cultures and midstream urine sent.

Assessment:
Acute pyelonephritis. Sepsis screen triggered by fever and tachycardia, but no shock or organ dysfunction. No clinical evidence of obstructed infected system at present.

Treatment/action:
IV fluids given; paracetamol administered with symptomatic improvement. First dose IV cefuroxime given after cultures, then oral step-down planned when tolerating fluids. Renal ultrasound requested if persistent pain, fever or deteriorating renal function.

Disposition:
Admit under acute medical team for IV antibiotics and observation. Safety-net documented; urgent urology review if obstruction suspected.

Referral to sleep service

Patient: Kiesha F.
Referring organisation: Ulster Hospital
Referring locality: BOHO

Dear Sleep Service,

I would be grateful for your assessment of Kiesha F. for suspected obstructive sleep apnoea, with advice on investigation and suitability for continuous positive airway pressure.

There is a longstanding history of loud snoring and episodes of witnessed apnoeas reported by a friend. Kiesha F. describes marked daytime somnolence, particularly when sitting quietly, and this is now affecting concentration and routine activities. There has been no collapse or reported seizure activity. Sleep is described as unrefreshing despite a reasonable opportunity for rest.

The patient has tried sleeping on their side and reducing evening alcohol, without meaningful improvement. No formal sleep study has yet been performed and continuous positive airway pressure has not been issued. They have also reported increased tiredness for 3 days, although this appears to be an acute worsening on the background of the chronic sleep symptoms.

On review today, the patient was alert and able to give a clear history. There was no acute respiratory distress. Blood pressure and chest examination were unremarkable. I have advised avoidance of driving or operating machinery if sleepy and discussed seeking urgent help if severe breathlessness or collapse occurs.

Please arrange appropriate sleep assessment, including overnight testing as indicated, and advise regarding treatment options. I would particularly appreciate guidance on whether continuous positive airway pressure is appropriate and whether further assessment for contributing upper-airway or cardiometabolic factors is required.

Yours faithfully,

Dr Suhana Hayes, MBBS
GMC reference: 0812350
Ulster Hospital

To: Musculoskeletal and Spinal Service

Re: Godiva CLEGG
Referring organisation: Queen Elizabeth University Hospital

Dear Colleague,

I would be grateful for your assessment of Godiva CLEGG, who has developed persistent low back pain with shooting pain down the right leg and intermittent paraesthesia into the foot. The symptoms have been present for several weeks and are now limiting walking, sleep and ordinary household activities. Current pain score is 5/10.

There is no reported history of significant trauma. On review, lumbar movement is restricted by pain, with right-sided straight-leg raise reproducing the leg symptoms. Lower-limb power is grossly preserved, although the patient describes altered sensation intermittently. No bowel or bladder disturbance or saddle sensory change has been reported.

Management to date has been conservative with naproxen and paracetamol, alongside advice to remain mobile and avoid prolonged bed rest. These measures have provided only partial relief. The GP record notes no previous spinal procedure, and imaging has not yet been arranged.

Assessment

Clinical picture is most consistent with lumbar radiculopathy. Given the ongoing radicular pain, paraesthesia and functional impact despite initial treatment, specialist review would be helpful to confirm the diagnosis and advise whether imaging, physiotherapy or other intervention is indicated.

Plan/request

Please assess and recommend further management. The patient has been advised to seek urgent medical attention if new weakness, urinary or faecal symptoms, or perineal numbness develops. Follow-up review is booked for 21 March 2028.

Yours sincerely,

I. Crowther

Pruritic erythematous rash affecting both wrists and lower abdomen, for 3 days. Skin irritation began after using a new fragranced body wash. No fever, facial swelling or breathing difficulty.

Previous intermittent hand eczema. No known drug allergy recorded. Uses rubber gloves at work; no recent change in brand. Spouse present and contributed to history.

Well, clinically stable.

Likely allergic contact dermatitis, possibly related to fragranced product or glove exposure. No features of cellulitis or systemic allergic reaction.

Stop suspected body wash and avoid fragranced emollients. Trial hydrocortisone cream thinly to affected areas for up to 7 days; avoid broken skin and face. Cetirizine once daily as required for itch. Regular bland emollient advised.

Patient: Rukayah A.
Clinical details: 27 y/o, G2P0, 9+4 weeks' gestation
Address: 124 Upper River Bank, Llangurig, SY18 6AA
Contact: 07700 900289
Report/accession ID: 031030647
Accompanied by: partner

Presenting problem:
Persistent vomiting for several days with poor oral intake, dizziness on standing and reported weight loss. No haematemesis, abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding. Passing urine less frequently. Known early pregnancy; community cyclizine with limited benefit.

Observations:
Alert, uncomfortable. Pulse 108, BP 102/68 lying, 94/60 standing. RR 18, SpO2 99% on air, temperature 36.7°C. Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 2 seconds. Chest clear bilaterally. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no guarding.

Urinalysis: ketones 3+, protein trace, no nitrites.
Bloods: mild hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia; renal function preserved, normal CRP. Serum beta-hCG consistent with early pregnancy. ECG sinus tachycardia, no acute changes.

Hyperemesis gravidarum with dehydration and starvation ketosis. No clinical evidence of sepsis or acute abdominal pathology.

Cannula inserted. Intravenous sodium chloride commenced, with antiemetic treatment using cyclizine. Thiamine given before further dextrose-containing fluid. Electrolyte replacement prescribed following repeat blood results. Oral fluids tolerated after observation; urine output improved.

Disposition:
Discussed with obstetric early pregnancy service. Suitable for discharge with cyclizine, oral rehydration advice and antiemetic review through GP/early pregnancy unit. Return urgently for inability to retain fluids, fainting, abdominal pain, bleeding or reduced urine output.

On examination, Karmani was uncomfortable but not systemically unwell. The right first MTP joint was visibly swollen, warm and erythematous, with marked tenderness and reduced movement. Skin intact, with no discharge or obvious wound. Calf soft and non-tender. Observations were reassuring. Recent medication history reviewed: naproxen has been taken with food, and colchicine was started as previously advised. No reported adverse effects.

Assessment: clinically consistent with an acute gout flare. Septic arthritis considered less likely given the absence of systemic features, although discussed because of the degree of inflammation.

Plan: continue naproxen with gastroprotection as prescribed and complete the current colchicine course; avoid taking additional over-the-counter anti-inflammatories. Rest, elevate the foot and use a cool pack intermittently. Blood tests requested, including inflammatory markers, renal function and urate, with results to be reviewed by the treating team at Crickhowell Medical Centre. Advised urgent assessment via A&E if fever, rapidly spreading redness, severe deterioration or inability to mobilise develops.

N. SHAHZAD, General Medicine

Pulmonary embolism — continue apixaban 10 mg twice daily for the first 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily. Anticoagulation duration to be reviewed by the thrombosis service; minimum planned course 3 months.

Apixaban as above.

Supplemental oxygen discontinued.

GP review within 1 week; anticoagulation monitoring and assessment for provoking factors. Respiratory/thrombosis clinic appointment booked for 9 September 2021.

Covering medical registrar reviewed; GMC identifier 0219333. No indication for IV fluids currently. Symptoms may improve with hydration.

Next shift:
Repeat observations, monitor urine output and stool frequency, reassess oral intake and escalate persistent vomiting, worsening pain, blood in stool or clinical deterioration.

Nasal saline drops as needed.

Continue frequent feeds and nasal saline. Seek urgent medical review via NHS 111/A&E if breathing becomes laboured, feeds markedly reduce, fewer wet nappies, blue colour, unusual drowsiness or apnoea.

GP review if symptoms are not continuing to improve. Community nursing follow-up arranged through Aberdeen Royal Infirmary.

A&E assessment – 1 April 2004

Patient: Reannon H.
MRN: 072054322
Contact: 07700 900482

The 65-year-old Native American female patient attended with their sibling following increased shaking of the right hand and slower movement over the past fortnight. The tremor is most noticeable at rest and settles when reaching for objects. They report more stiffness on getting out of a chair, but no fall, head injury, fever or new confusion. Co-beneldopa has been taken as prescribed, with no recent dose changes. The sibling feels the patient is managing at home but is taking longer with washing and dressing.

On examination, alert and conversational. Resting tremor of the right hand with mild bradykinesia and muscular rigidity, greater on the right. Power grossly preserved. Gait slow with reduced right arm swing; no postural instability observed. Observations stable and capillary glucose normal. No acute focal neurological deficit.

Assessment

Established Parkinson disease, previously assessed by neurology. Current symptoms suggest gradual motor fluctuation rather than an acute neurological event. No evidence of infection or significant injury today.

Plan

Continue co-beneldopa at the current prescribed dose; do not self-adjust timing or dose. Urgent advice sent to the Parkinson’s service/neurology team requesting medication and multidisciplinary review, including physiotherapy and occupational therapy input. GP to review falls risk, cognition and home support. Return to A&E for sudden weakness, inability to walk, repeated falls, marked confusion or rapidly worsening symptoms.

Discharged home with sibling after discussion and understanding confirmed.

PAEDIATRIC LABORATORY MEDICINE

Patient: Rafid S.
MRN: 052 754 264
Report date: 9th December 2022
Specimen: Midstream urine
Collection context: Outpatient urine culture requested for dysuria, urinary frequency and suprapubic discomfort. Aunt present; patient consented to specimen collection and discussion of result. Current weight recorded as 54.0 kg.

The patient, aged 12 years, was reviewed in the clinical information supplied with the specimen.

Urinalysis
Leucocytes: 3+
Nitrite: Positive
Blood: 1+
Protein: Trace

Microscopy
White cells: >100 × 10⁶/L
Red cells: 18 × 10⁶/L
Squamous epithelial cells: Few

Culture
Escherichia coli: >10⁵ CFU/mL
Mixed growth: Not detected

Antimicrobial susceptibility
Nitrofurantoin: Susceptible
Trimethoprim: Susceptible
Co-amoxiclav: Susceptible
Cefalexin: Susceptible

Interpretation: Significant growth of a single uropathogen, with accompanying pyuria, consistent with uncomplicated urinary tract infection in the stated clinical context.

Action: Correlate with symptoms and allergy history. Nitrofurantoin is an appropriate directed option where renal function is suitable; review treatment response with the prescribing clinician. If persistent fever, flank pain, vomiting or systemic deterioration, assess promptly for upper urinary tract infection.

Dante Sharif
Laboratory clinician

Discharge summary

Patient: RYDEN FINN
Home address: 79 CARNVUE COURT, FLURRYBRIDGE
Contact telephone: 07700 900626
Admission/discharge date: 24 March 2025

RYDEN FINN, the patient, aged 43 years, presented to A&E with 24 hours of worsening right lower-quadrant pain, nausea and loss of appetite. Examination showed localised right iliac fossa tenderness with guarding. Observations remained stable; most recent blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg. An adult child was present during the assessment and discharge discussion.

Blood tests demonstrated a raised white cell count and C-reactive protein. CT abdomen and pelvis confirmed acute uncomplicated appendicitis without collection or perforation.

The patient was reviewed by the on-call surgical team and underwent laparoscopic appendicectomy. Findings were consistent with acute inflamed appendix; there was no perforation. Intravenous fluids, analgesia and intravenous co-amoxiclav were given peri-operatively. Recovery was uncomplicated, with oral intake tolerated and mobilisation independent. Histology has been requested.

Assessment at discharge: clinically well following laparoscopic appendicectomy. Wounds clean and dry, abdomen soft, and pain controlled with oral paracetamol.

Plan:
Discharge home today with paracetamol as required, observing the labelled maximum dose. Keep the wound sites clean and dry; showering is permitted, but avoid soaking until healed. No heavy lifting until reviewed by the surgical team.

The patient was advised to seek urgent medical attention for fever, increasing abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, wound redness or discharge, or inability to tolerate fluids. Surgical follow-up will be arranged in the usual post-operative pathway, with histology reviewed when available.

Emergency Department Cardiology Assessment

Patient: IZHAAR KUMAR
A 70-year-old Pacific Islander female patient presenting with three days of productive cough, fever and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. Partner reports reduced appetite but adequate fluids. No syncope or sustained palpitations. Amoxicillin and paracetamol taken before arrival, with only partial relief.

On assessment, alert and speaking in full sentences. Temperature 38.1°C, pulse 104 bpm, BP 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, oxygen saturations 95% on air. Localised crackles at the left base with mildly reduced air entry; no wheeze. Heart sounds normal, no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Chest pain reproducible only with deep inspiration.

ECG: sinus tachycardia, no acute ischaemic changes. Chest radiograph demonstrates left lower-zone patchy air-space opacity consistent with community-acquired pneumonia. Blood tests show mild neutrophilia; troponin negative. Coding recorded as SNOMED CT 233604007.

Assessment: Community-acquired pneumonia, clinically stable for ambulatory treatment. No evidence of acute coronary syndrome or respiratory failure.

Plan: Discussed with miceal dyson at University Hospital Bristol and Weston Virtual Site. Continue oral amoxicillin as prescribed and use paracetamol for fever or pain, observing the stated dosing instructions. Encourage fluids and rest. Return to A&E urgently for increasing breathlessness, confusion, persistent vomiting, blue lips or worsening chest pain. GP review arranged for 18th April 2026, with earlier reassessment if symptoms are not improving within 48 hours.

Discharged home with partner. Patient understood the advice and agreed with the plan.

Dear Clinical Genetics Team,
National Insurance number: BG500132C

Re: JAHMEL HANIF

I would be grateful for your opinion regarding possible familial susceptibility to obstructive sleep apnoea and whether genetic assessment is indicated. JAHMEL HANIF reports loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas and marked daytime somnolence. Symptoms have been present for 3 days, although the snoring is longstanding according to the emergency contact, Garon.

Occupation: Carpenter
Employer: Cardonald Town Council

There is no documented craniofacial syndrome, neuromuscular disorder or learning difficulty. Examination in primary care showed a crowded oropharynx with enlarged tonsillar tissue; chest was clear and cardiovascular examination was unremarkable. No focal neurological deficit was identified. Epworth Sleepiness Scale was elevated. The patient has been advised not to drive when sleepy and has been referred for formal sleep assessment.

Continuous positive airway pressure has been discussed as the anticipated treatment following diagnostic testing and titration; it has not yet been issued. Weight, airway anatomy and sleep-study findings will be reviewed by the sleep service. There is no confirmed family history of a named genetic condition, but Garon describes similar loud snoring in another family member and is concerned about inherited risk.

Please advise whether the presentation warrants clinical genetics review, targeted assessment or onward referral to respiratory sleep medicine alone. A family history and examination for syndromic features can be expanded at your assessment.

Yours sincerely,

Dr Abbie-Jane Ali, MBBS

Dear Colleague,

Re: Evelyn A.

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient with recurrent migraine, particularly to confirm the diagnosis and advise on preventive treatment. Episodes have become more frequent over recent months, with approximately six disabling attacks per month. The headache is typically unilateral and pulsatile, associated with nausea and photophobia, and lasts several hours if untreated. There is no reported persistent focal neurological deficit, loss of consciousness or preceding head injury. Their partner has observed occasional withdrawal to a dark room during attacks but no confusion or seizure-like activity.

Current treatment is sumatriptan 50 mg at onset of migraine, with naproxen taken when required. The patient reports partial benefit but increasingly needs to repeat analgesia. They are trying to limit acute medication use and are keeping a headache diary. No preventive therapy has yet been trialled. Examination in surgery today was unremarkable, including cranial nerves, limb power, coordination and gait; blood pressure was 128/76 mmHg. No papilloedema was seen on fundoscopy.

Please review the diagnosis, consider whether neuroimaging or other investigation is indicated, and recommend an appropriate preventive strategy. Advice regarding optimisation of acute treatment and medication-overuse risk would also be appreciated.

Referring clinician: SAWYER LOCK

Patient: Eris M.

Reason for admission
Presented with approximately one day of worsening right lower-quadrant pain, nausea and loss of appetite. Examination and inflammatory markers were consistent with acute appendicitis. Ultrasound demonstrated an inflamed, non-compressible appendix with no collection.

Hospital course
Managed initially with intravenous fluids, analgesia and intravenous co-amoxiclav. Reviewed by the general surgical team and underwent laparoscopic appendicectomy. Problem list

• Status post laparoscopic appendicectomy
• Post-operative pain, improving

Discharge medication
paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily as required for pain. Do not exceed the stated dose. No further antibiotics required following source control and clinical improvement.

Follow-up and advice
Surgical follow-up as arranged by ULSTER HOSPITAL; pathology will be communicated if it alters management. Keep the wound areas clean and dry, and avoid strenuous lifting until comfortable and wounds healed. Seek urgent medical advice via NHS 111 or A&E for increasing abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fever, spreading redness or discharge from the wounds, abdominal distension, or inability to keep fluids down.

Discharged home in stable condition with adult child informed of the plan.

Clinical Genetics Clinic Note
NHS number: 000 600 8802

Patient: Paolo  
MRN: 09386754  
Occupation: Builder  
Referring service: Haslemere Hospital Minor Injuries Unit

Paolo attended to discuss hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk following a significant family history in a sibling. They are well today and report no current breast or ovarian symptoms. Their main concern is the possibility of an inherited cancer predisposition and whether predictive testing would be appropriate.

The available family history was reviewed. Affected relatives’ diagnoses and previous genetic results will need confirmation before testing is arranged. In particular, the reported familial BRCA1 c.68_69delAG variant requires verification from an original laboratory report where possible. The implications of a positive, negative or uninformative result were discussed, including potential effects on surveillance, risk-reducing options and relatives. It was explained that testing is most informative when an affected relative has undergone testing first, although this may not be feasible in every family.

Paolo was given time to consider the information and wishes to proceed with obtaining the relevant family reports before providing a sample. No treatment is indicated from today’s consultation. They understand that a result may take several weeks once testing is authorised and that a further appointment will be offered to discuss the outcome.

Plan:
- Obtain copies of the sibling’s genetic and oncology records, if available.
- Reconstruct the three-generation family history at follow-up.
- Confirm the BRCA1 finding with the laboratory before predictive testing.
- Written information on hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk provided.

Seen and documented by JOOLS DEAN, Clinical Genetics, Haslemere Hospital Minor Injuries Unit.

Discharge summary – Respiratory Medicine

Patient: afolarin lloyd
DOB: 1989-04-20
Admission/discharge date: 03/05/2012

Reason for admission
Presented with several days of worsening lower abdominal pain, offensive abnormal vaginal discharge and deep dyspareunia. Referred from A&E for assessment and treatment of suspected pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). Sibling, B. Knowles, from GRACEHILL, was listed as emergency contact with the patient’s consent.

Assessment and key results
Afebrile and haemodynamically stable on admission. Lower abdominal tenderness, with cervical motion and bilateral adnexal tenderness on pelvic examination. Pregnancy test negative. FBC showed mild neutrophilia; CRP moderately raised. Renal and liver profiles satisfactory. Urine NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea negative. Vaginal swabs sent; results to be reviewed by the sexual health service. Pelvic ultrasound showed no tubo-ovarian abscess or other acute pelvic collection.

Hospital course
Treated as uncomplicated PID with ceftriaxone administered in the department, followed by oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and metronidazole. Analgesia with paracetamol and intermittent ibuprofen, with good effect. Pain and discharge improved during observation; able to eat, drink and mobilise independently. No evidence of sepsis or need for operative intervention.

Problem list
• Pelvic inflammatory disease, clinically diagnosed
• Lower abdominal pain and dyspareunia, improving
• Abnormal vaginal discharge; microbiology pending

Discharge medicines
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily to complete the prescribed course.
Metronidazole to complete the prescribed course.
Paracetamol as required for pain, within packet directions.
Avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole. Do not have sexual intercourse until treatment is completed, symptoms have settled and partners have been assessed and treated.

Follow-up
Sexual health clinic follow-up arranged for review of swab results, symptom response and partner notification. GP review if symptoms persist. Return to A&E for increasing pain, fever, vomiting, collapse or inability to tolerate medication. Condition at discharge: clinically improved and suitable for home.

text:
Emergency Department Assessment
NHS number: 000 812 9453

Patient: MUNESU HUSSAIN  
Seen in cardiology assessment area with 3-day history of worsening lower abdominal pain, predominantly suprapubic and right-sided. Reports abnormal yellow vaginal discharge and deep dyspareunia. No syncope, vomiting or urinary frequency. M. Iqbal, listed as emergency contact, accompanied her and provided collateral history.

Observations: temperature 37.8°C, pulse 96 bpm, BP 120/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturations 99% on air. Alert and haemodynamically stable. Abdomen soft, with suprapubic and bilateral iliac fossa tenderness, without guarding or rebound. Pelvic examination, with consent and a chaperone, showed mucopurulent cervical discharge and cervical motion tenderness. No adnexal mass was palpable.

Urine pregnancy test negative. ECG sinus rhythm. Blood tests showed mild inflammatory marker rise; haemoglobin and renal function satisfactory. Vaginal and endocervical swabs sent. Urinalysis did not support urinary tract infection. Findings are clinically consistent with pelvic inflammatory disease; tubo-ovarian abscess and appendicitis considered less likely clinically, but ultrasound arranged through Royal Gwent Hospital if pain fails to settle or inflammatory markers increase.

Treatment and plan

Given ceftriaxone in the department, then commenced on doxycycline and metronidazole. Analgesia provided with paracetamol and ibuprofen. Advised to avoid intercourse until treatment is completed and partners have been assessed. Discussed importance of completing medication and returning urgently for fever, vomiting, worsening pain or collapse.

Discharged home with written advice. GP or sexual health review booked for 10th February 2025. Assessment and treatment plan documented by M. Pollard.

Dear Clinical Genetics Team,
National Insurance number: GB482182C

Re: Milda S.  
MRN: 061 389 495

I would be grateful for your advice regarding this patient with rheumatoid arthritis and a possible familial predisposition to inflammatory joint disease. They report increasing morning stiffness, painful swollen hand joints and fatigue, with the current flare present for 3 days. A close friend has raised concern about whether the pattern could represent an inherited condition, although there is no confirmed genetic diagnosis in the available history.

The patient is taking methotrexate with folic acid and naproxen. Methotrexate monitoring has been undertaken through primary care; the most recent blood tests were acceptable, but symptoms have progressed despite adherence. Examination in clinic found tenderness and swelling of several MCP and PIP joints bilaterally, without fever or rash. There was no recent infection or new medication. I have advised continuation of the existing treatment pending specialist review and arranged repeat FBC, renal function, liver profile, CRP and ESR.

Assessment: rheumatoid arthritis flare with persistent small-joint synovitis. The immediate question is whether there is any indication for genetic assessment or testing, particularly in view of the reported family concern, and whether an alternative inherited inflammatory arthropathy should be considered.

Plan: please review the history and advise whether referral to rheumatology should precede any genetics assessment. I would also welcome recommendations regarding further investigation and management of the current flare. A follow-up review is planned for 2025-04-16.

Yours faithfully,

Alayah-Mae Paul  
ROYAL VICTORIA HOSPITAL

Laboratory Haematology Report

Patient: Ezzah A.
Report/accession ID: 080887218
Specimen: Peripheral blood, EDTA; serum for biochemistry
Requesting clinician: Unnamed
Clinical details: Painless lymphadenopathy with night sweats and unintentional weight loss. Hodgkin lymphoma under investigation; tissue diagnosis pending.

Results
Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115–160)
MCV 82 fL (80–100)
White cell count 12.8 ×10^9/L (4.0–11.0)
Neutrophils 9.6 ×10^9/L (2.0–7.5)
Lymphocytes 1.7 ×10^9/L (1.0–4.0)
Platelets 468 ×10^9/L (150–400)
ESR 78 mm/hour (1–20)
CRP 64 mg/L (<5)
LDH 312 U/L (120–250)
Urate 0.39 mmol/L (0.15–0.42)
Creatinine 74 µmol/L (45–90)
ALT 26 U/L (5–35)
Albumin 32 g/L (35–50)

Interpretation
Mild normocytic anaemia with neutrophilic leucocytosis and thrombocytosis. Markedly raised inflammatory markers and LDH. The findings are non-specific but support an active inflammatory or lymphoproliferative process in the stated clinical context. They do not establish a diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma.

Please correlate with examination findings and imaging. Excisional lymph-node biopsy with histology and immunophenotyping remains required for definitive diagnosis. Consider interval FBC, renal profile, liver profile, urate and LDH if clinically indicated. Supportive care pending tissue diagnosis.

Follow-up review: 07/07/2026

Professional identifier: 0100942

Patient: A. MIRZA  
DOB: 2014-11-22  
Legal guardian: Reva | Contact: 07700 900070  
Ward: Queen Elizabeth University Hospital

Situation: Adolescent admitted with acute asthma exacerbation. Audible expiratory wheeze and increased work of breathing on arrival; night-time cough reported by legal guardian.

Current: Alert, speaking in full sentences. RR mildly raised, SpO₂ maintained on air. Mild intercostal recession, bilateral wheeze, no cyanosis. Eating small amounts and drinking adequately; urine passed. Mobilising to bathroom with supervision, tires easily.

Actions: Salbutamol inhaler administered via spacer as prescribed, with spacer teaching completed and technique practised. Encouraged fluids, upright positioning and rest. Observations repeated after treatment: work of breathing reduced and wheeze less prominent. No adverse response.

Risks/escalation: Continue close observation for increasing recession, inability to speak comfortably, reduced air entry, falling saturations or poor response to salbutamol. Escalate promptly to medical team/paediatric registrar if deterioration; emergency buzzer accessible. Guardian updated and involved in plan, with patient assent maintained.

Next shift: Four-hourly observations and respiratory assessment; document inhaler use and response. Reinforce trigger avoidance and inhaler technique before discharge. Confirm GP follow-up in about 7 weeks and provide written asthma plan.

text:
Accident and Emergency Clinical Assessment

Patient: PALVI KHANOM
Report/accession ID: 096849106
Referring healthcare organisation: Deeside Community Hospital
Occupation: Journalist

History
Presented with intermittent frontal headache and light-headedness for 3 days. Symptoms are non-positional, without syncope, chest pain, dyspnoea, focal weakness or visual loss. Partner reports no confusion or change in speech. Known essential hypertension, prescribed amlodipine and ramipril; states doses have been taken regularly. No recent medication changes. No features to suggest acute infective illness.

Examination
Alert and orientated, communicating appropriately. Pulse regular. Blood pressure elevated on arrival and remained above target on repeat measurement after seated rest. Neurological examination non-focal, with normal gait and coordination. No meningism. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations unremarkable. Capillary glucose within the local reference range. ECG shows sinus rhythm without acute ischaemic change.

Interpretation
Symptoms are most consistent with headache and light-headedness associated with suboptimally controlled essential hypertension. There is no clinical evidence of hypertensive emergency, stroke or acute coronary syndrome at assessment. No indication for emergency intravenous antihypertensive treatment.

Plan
Continue prescribed amlodipine and ramipril pending medication reconciliation. Avoid additional over-the-counter decongestants or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs unless advised. Home blood pressure readings requested twice daily for the next week, with review by the GP surgery for treatment adjustment. Discharged with advice to return to the emergency department for severe or sudden headache, neurological deficit, chest pain, breathlessness or collapse.

Report completed by A. Hogg.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
NHS number: 0003292372

Patient: Dmytro B.
Home address: 64 Smith Court, ATTICAL
Contact: dmytro.bowman84@btinternet.com
Emergency contact: relative recorded in admission documentation
Consultant: stefanut saeed, GMC number 0227070
Admission specialty: Acute medicine with haematology input

Reason for admission
Sickle cell painful crisis with severe bilateral limb and lower back pain, reduced oral intake and clinical dehydration. No history of chest pain or breathlessness during this admission.

Key results
• Initial observations: tachycardia with otherwise stable haemodynamics.
• Blood tests consistent with known sickle cell disease; haemoglobin below usual baseline, no significant renal impairment.
• Chest radiograph: no acute chest syndrome.
• Blood cultures negative. Urinalysis without evidence of urinary infection.

Hospital course
Admitted for analgesia, hydration and monitoring. Intravenous fluids commenced; morphine administered initially by prescribed protocol, then converted to oral analgesia as pain settled. Encouraged oral fluids and mobilisation. No oxygen requirement, fever or neurological complication. At 08:15 on review, pain was mild and controlled with oral medication; eating and drinking adequately.

Discharge plan
Problem: painful crisis — improved.
Action: continue regular paracetamol and prescribed breakthrough analgesia; avoid excess sedation and driving.
Action: maintain good oral hydration and usual sickle-cell medicines. No new long-term medication commenced.

Follow-up
GP review if pain remains troublesome or medication is running out. Haematology follow-up as previously arranged. Return to A&E for worsening pain not controlled at home, fever, chest symptoms, severe headache, weakness or reduced urine output.

Discharged home clinically stable. Summary authorised by stefanut saeed.

Patient: autumn owen
Address: 139 Spencer Way, Bolton, BL1 1AP

Emergency contact recorded. Patient understands admission plan.

Assessed by Traian Vickers, ED clinician.

Recurrent acute otitis media, currently with a right-sided episode. No clinical evidence of mastoiditis or systemic compromise today. Given the frequency of episodes and possible impact on hearing, community paediatric review would be helpful.

Requested action:
Please arrange assessment of hearing, speech and language progress, and advise on ongoing surveillance or referral to ENT if appropriate. We will review the current episode in primary care in about 8 weeks.

Referring clinician: Dr Aminta Wyatt, MBBS

Laboratory Report – Acute Joint Pain

Patient: Cleagh K.
MRN: 004283902
Requesting location: Accident and Emergency, SALFORD ROYAL HOSPITAL - PPDS - NOVAVAX COVID19 TRIAL
Specimen collected: 2 July 2022
Specimen: Serum, routine biochemistry
Clinical details: Acute joint pain with swelling and erythema, for 3 days. Query gout flare. Current treatment recorded as naproxen and colchicine.

Results
Urate: 0.39 mmol/L (0.18–0.48) – within reference interval
Creatinine: 82 µmol/L (60–110) – within reference interval
eGFR (CKD-EPI): >90 mL/min/1.73 m²
CRP: 68 mg/L (<5) – raised
White cell count: 11.8 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0) – mildly raised

Interpretation
Raised CRP and mild leucocytosis support an acute inflammatory process. Serum urate is not elevated; this does not exclude gout during an acute attack. Correlate with joint examination and, if diagnostic uncertainty persists, consider aspiration for crystal analysis. Exclude septic arthritis promptly if fever, systemic upset or marked restriction of movement.

Medication / safety note
Naproxen and colchicine documented. Check renal function, gastrointestinal risk and concurrent medicines before further NSAID dosing. Review response and arrange GP follow-up after the acute episode; repeat urate when clinically settled if gout remains likely.

Date: 27 Sep 2023
National Insurance number: KN790881D
Patient: Vagmi | DOB: 28 October 1941
Ward: Cardiology

Situation: Admitted with cellulitis of the left lower leg. Erythema remains within marked border but still warm and tender; patient reports aching on movement. No chest pain or breathlessness overnight.

Background: IV flucloxacillin continued as prescribed. Paracetamol given once daily for pain with partial relief; avoid further doses until medication chart reviewed. Eating small amounts, drinking adequately. Passed urine; bowels opened yesterday.

Assessment: Alert and conversing appropriately. NEWS2 1 for temperature 37.8°C. Respirations even, SpO₂ 97% on air. Left calf moderately swollen, skin intact, no drainage. Mobilising short distances with frame and one staff member; discomfort increases on weight-bearing. Falls risk discussed. momena gregory, adult child, updated by telephone and aware of plan.

Actions/plan: Leg elevated when in bed or chair; encourage fluids and gentle mobilisation. Recheck observations and erythema at least four-hourly, document any spread beyond marker, increasing pain, new blistering or systemic symptoms. Escalate promptly to the covering medical team if fever, hypotension or rapid progression develops. Review IV access and antibiotic response on next round. GP follow-up planned in about 10 weeks.

Handover completed by Maisie-Louise Hussein, staff nurse.

Clinical Genetics Clinic Note

Patient: Morocco Underwood
DOB: 1 Nov 1937
Contact: 07700 900490
Report/accession ID: 0560439393

Reason for review:
Obstructive sleep apnoea; query familial contribution. Partner reports loud snoring and witnessed apnoeas. Marked daytime somnolence, particularly when sedentary. Throat irritation for 3 days.

History:
Previously assessed in sleep clinic. Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) prescribed; using most nights, though mask leak reported. No recent A&E attendances. No known neuromuscular diagnosis. Family history reviewed; no clear pattern of sleep-disordered breathing or sudden unexplained death.

Examination:
Alert, conversational. No dysmorphic features noted. Oral cavity without acute abnormality. Chest clear. No focal neurological deficit.

Assessment:
Established obstructive sleep apnoea, partially controlled on CPAP. Current symptoms do not suggest a syndromic disorder. Genetic testing not indicated on today’s information.

Plan:
Continue CPAP and liaise with sleep service regarding mask fit and residual symptoms. Avoid driving if sleepy. Partner to continue observing for nocturnal apnoeas. Sleep-clinic data download requested; report to be reviewed when available.

Follow-up appointment: 2024-04-22

Clinician: genetics team

text:
Discharge summary
National Insurance number: KN 58 42 93 D

Patient: olivia-jane stafford
Emergency contact: Heera Goddard, locality KILREA
Report/accession ID: 0270257665
Discharging service: Royal Victoria Hospital

Reason for admission:
Presented to A&E with approximately 24 hours of worsening right lower-quadrant abdominal pain, nausea and loss of appetite. No previous similar episode. Examination showed focal right iliac fossa tenderness with mild guarding.

Investigations:
Initial blood tests demonstrated raised inflammatory markers and a mild neutrophil leucocytosis. Urinalysis unremarkable. CT abdomen/pelvis confirmed acute uncomplicated appendicitis, without perforation, abscess or obstruction.

Hospital course:
Admitted under the general surgical team. Kept nil by mouth initially and treated with intravenous fluids, analgesia and intravenous co-amoxiclav. Reviewed by the on-call surgeon and underwent laparoscopic appendicectomy. Operative findings were an inflamed, non-perforated appendix. Recovery was uncomplicated; tolerating diet, mobilising independently and passing urine. Pain controlled with oral medication. Wounds clean and dry with dressings intact.

Discharge diagnosis:
• Acute uncomplicated appendicitis
• Status post laparoscopic appendicectomy

Discharge medicines:
• paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily when required for pain
• Ibuprofen with food if needed, provided no history of gastric ulcer, renal disease or NSAID intolerance
No further antibiotics required following source control.

Follow-up and advice:
Discharged home in stable condition with emergency contact information recorded above. Keep dressings clean and dry; showering permitted as advised by the surgical team. Avoid heavy lifting until wounds are comfortable. The GP should review histology if reported and assess wound recovery as clinically indicated. Surgical follow-up will be arranged by Royal Victoria Hospital if required.

Return to A&E urgently for increasing abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fever, spreading redness or discharge from a wound, abdominal distension, or inability to keep fluids down.

A&E respiratory assessment
National Insurance number: ZZ 14 04 58 A

Patient: S. Martin  67 y/o
Seen with partner. 3-day productive cough, fevers and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Reduced appetite, no haemoptysis. Took paracetamol with partial relief.

Obs: T 38.4°C, HR 104, BP 118/72, RR 22, SpO₂ 95% on air.
Chest: coarse crackles and bronchial breathing at right base; no wheeze. Mild tachycardia, otherwise clinically euvolaemic. Alert, speaking full sentences.

CXR: patchy right lower-zone air-space opacity, no effusion.
Bloods: WCC 13.2, neutrophils 10.8, CRP 86, creatinine 74. Lactate 1.3.

Impression: community-acquired pneumonia, low-risk physiology; suitable for ambulatory treatment. SNOMED CT 233604007 recorded.

Treatment: first dose amoxicillin given in department. Continue amoxicillin as prescribed and paracetamol as needed. Fluids, rest. Return if worsening breathlessness, confusion, persistent vomiting or unable to maintain intake.

Discharge home with partner. GP review via ROYAL LIVERPOOL HOSPITAL on 10 March 2026.
Documented by knightly brookes.

Dear Hypertension Service,
NHS number: 000 950 8563

Re: Romain BENSON

I am referring this patient from Queen Elizabeth University Hospital following attendance in the emergency department with a persistent headache and intermittent light-headedness. Blood pressure was repeatedly elevated during assessment, without chest pain, breathlessness, focal neurological symptoms or visual loss. The current pain score was 5/10. There was no clinical evidence of acute end-organ injury, and the patient was considered safe for outpatient follow-up.

The patient reports taking amlodipine and ramipril regularly, although home blood pressure readings have not been recorded consistently. Treatment adherence, timing of doses and use of over-the-counter medicines were discussed. Examination was otherwise reassuring, with no focal neurological deficit and normal heart sounds. Basic blood tests and an ECG were completed in the department; the report/accession ID is 01853482. Results did not identify an acute cause for the symptoms.

Assessment

Likely suboptimally controlled essential hypertension with associated headache and light-headedness. Please also consider postural blood pressure variation or medication-related dizziness. There is no current indication of hypertensive emergency.

Plan and request

I would be grateful for specialist review of the blood pressure pattern and cardiovascular risk, including confirmation of home or ambulatory readings and advice on optimisation of amlodipine and ramipril. Please advise whether further investigation is required. The patient has been advised to continue the prescribed medicines and seek urgent assessment for severe headache, new neurological symptoms, chest pain or breathlessness.

Yours faithfully,

rozy brett
0838839
Emergency clinician

Report/accession ID: L26K78399
Collection date: 23 Nov 2035
Request: hypertension monitoring; headaches and intermittent light-headedness.

Action: continue routine BP review with GP surgery; repeat U&E after any ACE-inhibitor dose change. Consider lifestyle and lipid-risk assessment.

Patient: hella hawkes
NHS number: 000 250 0460
Admitted as 16 y/o. Accompanied by uncle, AURIE NEWMAN.
Contact: 07700 900747

Situation: Acute appendicitis under paediatric surgical team, Ulster Hospital. Awaiting review for operative management.

Observations: Alert, orientated, haemodynamically stable. Afebrile. Respiratory rate and saturations within target range. Peripheral cannula patent, IV fluids running as prescribed.

Symptoms: R lower-quadrant abdominal pain, nausea and poor appetite. Pain 5/10 on assessment. Abdomen guarded locally; no vomiting reported this shift.

Intake/output: Nil by mouth maintained pending theatre decision. Small sips for essential medication only. Passing urine; no bowel action documented this shift.

Interventions: Regular paracetamol administered with good partial effect. IV co-amoxiclav given as prescribed. Antiemetic available PRN; not required. Repositioned for comfort, oral care provided.

Response: Pain reduced on reassessment, nausea settled. Resting intermittently.

Risk/escalation: Falls risk low but advised to call before mobilising due to IV line and abdominal discomfort. Surgical team updated regarding ongoing tenderness and nil-by-mouth status; continue observations.

Next shift: Repeat pain and abdominal assessment, monitor temperature, urine output and cannula site. Maintain fasting, IV therapy and prescribed antibiotics. Confirm theatre plan and support patient and uncle with updates; seek consent/assent discussion through surgical team.

Paediatric Respiratory Clinic

Patient: L. Richmond
MRN: 012 201 304
Seen with parent, oluwafikayomi ball
Clinician: Janeeta O'Sullivan

Reason for review: acute asthma exacerbation.

History:
Wheeze and increased work of breathing for 3 days. Night-time cough, waking twice overnight. No fever or vomiting. Salbutamol inhaler used frequently with home spacer; technique uncertain. Parent reports reduced exercise tolerance but drinking normally.

The patient, aged 5 years, was reviewed with parent present. Alert and interactive. No safeguarding concerns identified. Consent for assessment obtained from parent.

Observations:
RR mildly raised. Mild subcostal recession. Speaking in short phrases.
Chest: widespread expiratory wheeze, reduced air entry at both bases. No focal crackles.
Oxygen saturations satisfactory in room air.

Assessment:
Acute asthma exacerbation, currently mild–moderate. No clinical evidence of pneumonia or impending respiratory failure.

Plan:
Salbutamol via spacer administered in clinic with clinical improvement. Spacer teaching completed; parent able to demonstrate back.
Continue salbutamol inhaler via spacer as directed on asthma plan. Encourage regular fluids and rest.
Written inhaler action plan issued. Review with GP/surgery if not clearly improving; emergency department/A&E if increasing recession, exhaustion, cyanosis or poor response to salbutamol.

Follow-up: paediatric respiratory nurse review arranged.  
Signed: Janeeta O'Sullivan

Patient: nandita saunders
Home address: 41 Souter Head Road, Kinloch Rannoch, PH16 5AA

Central chest pressure with diaphoresis and nausea. Treated as non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI); no ST elevation on ECG.

Clinically stable, pain-free, understands the medication plan and when to seek urgent medical attention. Consultant: C. Ward

A&E handover – priority 2

Patient: milou blackburn  DOB: 09/08/1973
MRN: 0983175
Address: 47 Parc Waen, Saundersfoot, SA69 9AB  Contact: milou.blackburn31@hotmail.com

Situation: Acute left flank pain with dysuria and rigors for 3 days. Partner reports worsening overnight, reduced oral intake and feeling faint on standing. No vomiting.

Background: No known drug allergies documented. Took paracetamol at home with limited effect. Not currently on antibiotics.

Assessment:
Alert, clammy and uncomfortable. T 38.7°C, HR 116, BP 102/64, RR 20, SpO₂ 98% on air. Left renal angle tenderness; abdomen soft, no guarding. No focal neurological deficit.
Urine dip: nitrite positive, 3+ leucocytes, 2+ blood. Bloods sent including FBC, U&E, CRP and lactate; blood cultures obtained before antibiotics. Lactate 1.8 mmol/L. eGFR satisfactory. Renal ultrasound requested to exclude obstruction.

Actions:
IV access established. IV fluids commenced, paracetamol administered and IV cefuroxime given as prescribed. Analgesia and antiemetic PRN. NEWS2 monitoring; repeat observations after fluids. Discussed with medical registrar—admit to acute medical unit for IV antibiotics and review of imaging/cultures.

Safety: Escalate promptly for hypotension, increasing pain, reduced urine output or altered mental state. Partner updated and remains with patient.

Date: 15 Feb 2012
Report/accession ID: 083193213

Patient: V. Donaldson
Address: 25 CONNOR PARK, CREGGAN

Dear Movement Disorders Team,

I would be grateful for your review of this patient, who has an established diagnosis of Parkinson disease previously assessed by neurology. The specific question is whether the current tremor, slowness and stiffness represent inadequate symptom control, and whether the medication regimen or wider multidisciplinary support should be adjusted.

There has been a gradual increase in resting tremor, bradykinesia and muscular rigidity over recent months. The patient describes more difficulty turning in bed and managing buttons, although there have been no reported falls or episodes of loss of consciousness. Examination in clinic showed a resting tremor affecting the right hand, reduced finger tapping and increased tone, without focal weakness. Speech was quieter than previously. The cardiovascular examination was unremarkable.

Co-beneldopa is being prescribed in primary care following the established specialist diagnosis. There has been no recent medication change, and adherence is reported as consistent. I have advised the patient not to alter the dose independently and to bring an up-to-date medicines list to the appointment.

Please review motor control, timing and tolerability of treatment, and advise on physiotherapy, occupational therapy and any speech and language input. A medication and multidisciplinary review would be particularly helpful. The patient understands that this is a specialist assessment rather than an emergency referral.

Yours sincerely,

S. Ferguson

LABORATORY REPORT – URINE MICROBIOLOGY
NHS number: 000 000 4996

Patient: theertha roberts
MRN: 037249464
Requesting clinician: unnamed GP
Reporting laboratory: ST HELIER HOSPITAL
Specimen: Midstream urine
Clinical details: Dysuria, flank pain and rigors. Acute pyelonephritis suspected. Cefuroxime and paracetamol commenced.

Specimen received: Urine, adequate volume; microscopy and culture performed.

RESULTS
Leukocytes: >100 ×10⁶/L (reference: <10 ×10⁶/L) – raised
Erythrocytes: 18 ×10⁶/L (reference: <10 ×10⁶/L) – mildly raised
Nitrite: positive
Culture: Significant growth of Escherichia coli, >10⁵ CFU/mL
Antimicrobial susceptibility:
- Cefuroxime: susceptible
- Trimethoprim: susceptible
- Ciprofloxacin: susceptible
- Gentamicin: susceptible
- Nitrofurantoin: susceptible; not suitable for pyelonephritis

Blood results supplied with request:
C-reactive protein 86 mg/L
Creatinine 102 µmol/L (reference: 45–90 µmol/L) – mildly raised
eGFR: 58 mL/min/1.73 m²

Significant Escherichia coli bacteriuria with pyuria, consistent with an upper urinary tract infection in the stated clinical context. Cefuroxime is active in vitro.

ACTION
Continue treatment in accordance with local antimicrobial guidance and clinical response. Review hydration, renal function and fever trajectory; seek urgent assessment if haemodynamic instability, persistent rigors or vomiting.

Follow-up review: 2018-08-09

Validated by: ANAYLA HULL
Report status: Authorised

- Maintain falls precautions and supervised mobilisation.
- Monitor oral intake and report any recurrent symptoms promptly.
- Await ongoing TIA work-up and documented secondary-prevention plan.

Patient: NADIN HAYWARD
Occupation: Farmer
Employer: Llyn Penmaen Town Council
Address: 124 Lydstep Road, Llangefni, LL77 7AA
Contact: 07700 900817

Reason for review:
Breathlessness and reduced cough strength in the context of established Parkinson disease. Referred for assessment of possible respiratory muscle and aspiration-related symptoms.

History:
Parkinson disease previously assessed and diagnosed by Neurology; co-beneldopa continued in primary care. Increasingly slow movements, resting tremor and muscular rigidity. • Chest radiograph and baseline oxygen assessment.

• Consider physiotherapy-led airway clearance advice.
• Continue co-beneldopa pending medication and multidisciplinary review; Neurology follow-up advised.
• Safety-net: urgent assessment if persistent choking, fever, marked deterioration or breathlessness at rest.

NHS number: 000 735 4780

Patient: feigy vickers
Home address: 42 CAVANAMARA VIEW, RICHHILL
Contact: feigy.vickers60@gmail.com
Clinical age: 34 y/o
Presenting problem: Increasing redness, tenderness and purulent discharge from the lower abdominal operative wound. No rigors or vomiting reported.

Assessment
• Postoperative superficial wound infection.
• Haemodynamically stable; current observations 120/80 mmHg, pulse 86, temperature 37.4°C.

Flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days, unless changed following microbiology advice. Continue usual medicines. Simple analgesia as required, observing packet instructions.

Keep dressing clean and dry; arrange dressing changes through the GP surgery or community nursing team. Seek urgent medical review for spreading redness, fever, worsening pain, increasing discharge, wound breakdown or feeling unwell.

Follow-up: Surgical wound review booked for 6 Sep 2021.

Discharged home ambulant and clinically stable. Written advice provided and understood.

Reason for admission: Fever, productive cough and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. Community-acquired pneumonia (SNOMED CT 233604007).
