GP review if not clearly improving within 48–72 hours. Repeat chest radiograph via the GP at approximately six weeks, particularly if cough or breathlessness persists. Return to A&E for worsening breathlessness, confusion, recurrent high fever, chest pain or inability to keep fluids down.

LABORATORY REPORT – HAEMATOLOGY

Patient: Urav H.

Report date: 03/12/1988
Requesting service: Respiratory medicine
Specimen: EDTA whole blood, collected for investigation of persistent painless lymphadenopathy, night sweats and unintentional weight loss.
Clinical information: Hodgkin lymphoma suspected. Supportive care pending tissue diagnosis.

RESULTS
Haemoglobin: 108 g/L (115–160) – low
MCV: 82 fL (80–100)
White cell count: 13.8 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0) – high
Neutrophils: 10.9 ×10⁹/L (2.0–7.5) – high
Lymphocytes: 1.4 ×10⁹/L (1.0–4.0)

CRP: 74 mg/L (<5) – high
ESR: 68 mm/hour (1–20) – high

Mild anaemia with neutrophilic leucocytosis, thrombocytosis and substantially raised inflammatory markers. Raised LDH is non-specific.

Pattern is compatible with an active inflammatory or malignant process, including Hodgkin lymphoma, but is not diagnostic. Correlate with examination and imaging. Urgent tissue diagnosis via the appropriate specialist pathway is advised; excision biopsy preferred where clinically feasible. Consider repeat FBC, CRP and LDH if treatment is delayed.

Patient: DEACON-JAMES DAVISON
Current: day 3 of life
MRN: MRN-04391902
Father: MAYARA KANE
Discharging service: Ulster Hospital

Reason for admission
Admitted from the postnatal ward with visible jaundice, increasing sleepiness during feeds and reduced intake. Birth history: born at 39+2 weeks' gestation. No respiratory or infective concerns during admission.

Hospital course
Serum bilirubin was above the treatment threshold for gestation and postnatal day. Phototherapy commenced promptly and was continued overnight with good response. Bilirubin fell below the treatment line on repeat testing and remained satisfactory after a period off lights. Blood glucose remained stable. Examination at discharge: alert when handled, well perfused, normal tone, no signs of sepsis, and jaundice significantly improved.

Feeding support was provided by the neonatal nursing team. Feeding improved with regular breastfeeds and expressed milk top-ups as required. Wet nappies established and weight monitored. MAYARA KANE, the baby’s father, was present for teaching and understands the feeding plan and signs requiring review.

Assessment
Uncomplicated neonatal unconjugated jaundice, treated successfully with phototherapy. Clinically well for discharge.

Discharge plan
Continue feeding at least 8–10 times in 24 hours, waking for feeds if sleepy. Offer expressed milk top-ups according to the written plan. Community midwife to review feeding, hydration and jaundice. GP or maternity triage review urgently if the baby is difficult to wake, feeds poorly, has fewer wet nappies, develops worsening jaundice or has a temperature of 38°C or above.

Discharged home with father once feeding was satisfactory and repeat bilirubin remained below threshold. No medication prescribed. Follow-up arrangements provided to the family.

D. Best

• Arrange GP review within the next few days for reassessment and consideration of an asthma management plan.

Patient: A. ARIF

Specimen: EDTA blood and serum
Clinical details: Acute painful, swollen and erythematous first metatarsophalangeal joint for 3 days. Query gout flare. Current treatment: naproxen and colchicine.

Specimens received: blood samples, quality acceptable.

Haemoglobin 142 g/L (130–170)
White cell count 10.8 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0)

Urate: 0.48 mmol/L (0.18–0.48) – upper reference limit

Mild inflammatory response with urate at the upper reference limit. Serum urate may be normal or borderline during an acute attack; result does not exclude gout. Renal function suitable for usual prescribed anti-inflammatory treatment, subject to clinical review.

Correlate with joint examination and response to treatment. If diagnostic uncertainty, consider joint aspiration for crystal analysis; do not use serum urate alone to confirm or exclude gout. Dr Kendric Ahmed, MBBS

Dear Haematology Team,

Re: Sumeet Millar
Report/accession ID: 0901721321

Thank you for reviewing this patient, seen in the accident and emergency department with several weeks of tiredness, intermittent dizziness and reduced exercise tolerance. A friend accompanied the patient and provided additional history. There was no reported melaena, rectal bleeding or haematemesis. Menstrual history and dietary intake require further clarification in the outpatient setting.

Examination in A&E: haemodynamically stable, mildly pale conjunctivae, no jaundice, lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Chest clear; heart sounds normal. The patient mobilised independently but described light-headedness after walking across the department.

Blood tests showed microcytic, hypochromic anaemia with low ferritin and transferrin saturation, consistent with iron-deficiency anaemia. Renal and liver profiles were satisfactory. A pregnancy test was negative. No overt source of blood loss was identified during the attendance.

Treatment was commenced with ferrous fumarate 210 mg once daily, with advice to continue regularly and arrange repeat full blood count and ferritin through the GP surgery. Symptoms have improved slightly but reduced exercise tolerance persists. The patient has not previously undergone gastrointestinal investigation and there is no documented previous haematology assessment.

I would be grateful for specialist assessment to confirm the likely cause of the iron deficiency, advise on the need for gastrointestinal and/or gynaecological investigation, and recommend further replacement or intravenous iron if the response is inadequate. Please also advise on the appropriate interval for repeat blood tests.

At 08:15 alert but distressed, dry lips and reduced tears. Warm peripheries, capillary refill 2 seconds. HR 118, BP appropriate for age, SpO2 99% in air, afebrile. Marked tenderness of both thighs and lumbar region, no focal swelling or neurological deficit. Chest clear; abdomen soft.

Investigations
FBC, reticulocytes, U&E, LFT and group-and-save sent. Urinalysis concentrated, no nitrites. Bloods consistent with known haemolytic disease; no current features of sepsis or acute chest syndrome.

Actions / priorities
IV access obtained. IV 0.9% sodium chloride commenced; IV morphine given with monitoring, then reassess pain and sedation score. Encourage oral fluids when tolerated. Repeat observations and pain score 30 minutes post-analgesia. Discussed with paediatric haematology at Bronglais General Hospital; admit if pain remains uncontrolled or oral intake inadequate. Escalate urgently for fever, hypoxia, chest symptoms, increasing drowsiness or reduced urine output.

Discharge summary – Respiratory Medicine

Patient: RUTHRAN DA SILVA
DOB: 1954-02-08
Admission/discharge date: 06/12/2025

Reason for admission
Presented with a 48-hour history of profuse watery diarrhoea, repeated vomiting and intermittent abdominal cramps. Reduced oral intake with dizziness on standing. No recent antibiotics documented. kalaya marshall, the patient’s partner, provided collateral history and was updated during the admission; lives in ARMOY.

Key findings
On arrival mildly dehydrated with dry mucous membranes and postural symptoms. Abdomen soft, with mild diffuse cramping but no guarding or peritonism. Blood tests showed a mild pre-renal acute kidney injury and borderline hypokalaemia. Inflammatory markers not significantly raised. Stool culture and viral PCR subsequently negative; clinical picture felt most consistent with self-limiting infectious gastroenteritis.

Hospital course
Managed with intravenous crystalloid initially, followed by oral rehydration solution as tolerated. Vomiting settled after antiemetic treatment and diarrhoeal frequency reduced considerably over the next 24 hours. Renal function and electrolytes improved on repeat testing. No indication for antibiotics. Remained haemodynamically stable and afebrile. Eating small amounts and passing urine normally prior to discharge.

Problem list
• Infectious gastroenteritis, improving
• Dehydration with transient pre-renal kidney injury, resolved
• Mild hypokalaemia, corrected

Discharge medicines
Continue oral rehydration solution regularly today and after each loose stool.
ondansetron 4 mg every 8 hours as needed for nausea or vomiting. Stop once symptoms have settled.
No antibiotics prescribed.

Condition at discharge
Clinically euvolaemic, tolerating fluids, minimal abdominal discomfort and no vomiting since yesterday. Discharged home with partner on 06/12/2025.

Advice and follow-up
Gradually reintroduce light meals, avoid alcohol and rich foods until recovered, and maintain hand hygiene. Contact the GP surgery if diarrhoea persists beyond several days or recurs. Attend A&E urgently for inability to keep fluids down, increasing abdominal pain, fainting, blood in stool, or markedly reduced urine output. GP to review if not fully recovered within one week.

CLINICAL GENETICS LABORATORY REPORT
National Insurance number: NK 37 56 78 A

Patient: Caydon
Clinical age group: 71 y/o
Report/accession ID: LAB-04783706
Specimen: EDTA blood; germline DNA extracted for targeted familial variant analysis
Collection/report date: 14th October 2035
Request: Predictive testing following significant sibling history of hereditary breast and ovarian cancer; cancer-risk concern noted. Ordering clinician: not stated.

Test performed
Targeted analysis for BRCA1 c.68_69delAG, the familial variant supplied on the request form. No current treatment reported.

Result
BRCA1 c.68_69delAG: NOT DETECTED.

Interpretation
The familial BRCA1 variant was not identified in this sample. This substantially reduces, but does not entirely exclude, the possibility of a hereditary cancer predisposition. The result does not assess other BRCA1/BRCA2 variants or unrelated cancer susceptibility genes.

Problem: predictive testing requested on basis of affected sibling.
Result: familial variant absent in tested sample.
Action: genetic counselling recommended to review residual familial risk and confirm that the reported variant is the appropriate familial target. Management should remain guided by the wider family history unless a genetics specialist advises otherwise.

Quality and limitations
Internal controls satisfactory. Sample identity and request details concordant. This is a targeted familial-variant assay; it is not a comprehensive cancer predisposition panel.

Validated and reported by:
RITHIKA CLAY
Clinical genetics laboratory clinician
Report date: 14th October 2035

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: P. Payne
DOB: 24 Feb 1979
Contact: 07700 900191
Responsible service: Cardiology

Reason for admission
Central chest pressure with diaphoresis and nausea for 3 days. Initial ECG without ST elevation; serial troponin rise consistent with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI).

Key results
• Troponin I: dynamic rise and fall.
• Echocardiogram: mild left ventricular systolic impairment, no significant valve disease.
• Coronary angiography: moderate coronary artery disease; no target lesion requiring PCI.
• Renal function stable. Haemoglobin and potassium satisfactory before discharge.

Hospital course
Treated as medically managed NSTEMI with aspirin, fondaparinux and high-intensity atorvastatin. Chest discomfort settled and there was no further diaphoresis or arrhythmia on telemetry. Fondaparinux stopped after completion of inpatient course. Cardiology reviewed prior to discharge.

Medication changes
START clopidogrel 75 mg once daily, following cardiology advice, with aspirin 75 mg once daily for 12 months unless bleeding or other contraindication.
Continue atorvastatin 80 mg at night.
GTN spray supplied for recurrent angina.
Avoid non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs unless advised.

Condition at discharge
Mobilising independently, pain-free, haemodynamically stable. Discharge home with sibling KHALEN EATON aware of the plan.

Follow-up and advice
Cardiology follow-up arranged for 2028-12-24. GP medication and blood-test review within one week. Seek emergency help for chest pain lasting more than a few minutes, breathlessness, collapse or significant bleeding.

Three days of reduced urine output, fatigue and poor oral intake. No reported vomiting or diarrhoea. Friend concerned patient has been increasingly drowsy today. No chest pain or breathlessness.

Alert but tired. Airway patent; speaking in full sentences.
HR 96, BP 102/64, RR 18, SpO₂ 98% on air, temperature 36.7°C.

Repeat U&E after fluids. Medical registrar reviewed; admission to general medical ward for ongoing treatment and investigation.

Follow-up
GP renal blood test and medication review after discharge, appointment booked for 29/03/2035.

Documented by: S. Betts

Dear Community Paediatrics Team,

Re: nellie-rose sweeney, 8 y/o

I would be grateful for your assessment of this child following a recent episode of acute asthma exacerbation, particularly to clarify ongoing respiratory needs and advise on longer-term management.

S. Patterson, the child’s parent, reports wheeze and increased work of breathing for 3 days, with a night-time cough disrupting sleep. There has been no reported choking episode or preceding foreign-body event. Oral intake remains satisfactory and urine output is unchanged. The family have accessed support through NEWTOWNABBEY Voluntary Service.

At review, the child was alert and engaging. Mild intercostal recession was observed, with bilateral expiratory wheeze and prolonged expiration. Oxygen saturations were satisfactory in air. There was no stridor, focal crepitation or cyanosis. The child responded clinically to salbutamol delivered via spacer, although wheeze remained audible on reassessment.

The family have been issued a salbutamol inhaler and received spacer teaching, including demonstration and return demonstration. They have been advised to use the inhaler according to the acute plan and to attend the emergency department if breathing worsens, speech becomes limited or relief is not sustained. No preventer treatment has yet been commenced.

Could you please assess for confirmation of asthma phenotype, review inhaler technique and trigger history, and advise whether an inhaled corticosteroid or other preventer is indicated? A written personalised asthma action plan and follow-up arrangement would also be appreciated.

Yours sincerely,

Dr Kabishayan Rayner, MBBS

Symptoms are worse on sitting and forward flexion and are now limiting walking and sleep. The clinical picture is consistent with lumbar nerve-root irritation, most likely S1 radiculopathy. I would appreciate specialist review regarding the need for lumbar MRI, physiotherapy input, and consideration of an interventional pathway if symptoms persist. The patient has been advised to attend A&E urgently should weakness, saddle numbness, or sphincter disturbance develop.

Yours sincerely,

remirez love

Assessment and plan: admit to the cardiology ward under Royal Alexandra Hospital for serial troponins, telemetry and cardiology review. Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report

Patient: I. Khanom
MRN: 01192815
Specimen: EDTA blood; genomic DNA extracted
Clinical indication: Rheumatoid arthritis flare with morning stiffness, swollen hand joints and fatigue. Sibling with inflammatory arthritis. Current treatment includes methotrexate 15 mg once weekly, folic acid and naproxen.

Analysis: HLA-DRB1 rheumatoid arthritis susceptibility panel
Result: HLA-DRB1 shared-epitope alleles not detected.
Quality: Internal controls passed; adequate DNA yield.

Interpretation: This result does not support carriage of the tested HLA-DRB1 risk alleles. A negative result does not exclude rheumatoid arthritis or alter the clinical diagnosis; findings should be considered alongside examination, inflammatory markers and imaging. No pathogenic variant identified on the targeted assay.

Comment: Genetic testing is not diagnostic for an individual rheumatoid arthritis flare. Consider rheumatology review if synovitis persists or treatment response is inadequate.

Respiratory Medicine Clinic Report
NHS number: 000 677 6761

Patient: R. Bull
Occupation: Carpenter
Report/accession ID: 048980192
Referring and reporting organisation: St Cadocs Hospital

Reason for review: Persistent knee pain and reduced mobility noted during respiratory follow-up. The patient describes bilateral, predominantly mechanical knee pain with stiffness on first mobilising in the morning. Symptoms are aggravated by stairs and prolonged walking. No acute injury, locking or constitutional symptoms reported. Current treatment is paracetamol and topical ibuprofen, with partial benefit.

Examination: Antalgic gait, reduced flexion of both knees and palpable crepitus, greater on the symptomatic side. No erythema, effusion or focal calf tenderness. Peripheral oedema absent. Respiratory examination demonstrates symmetrical air entry with no wheeze or crackles; oxygen saturation remains satisfactory at rest.

Interpretation: Clinical findings are consistent with osteoarthritis of the knee causing activity limitation and reduced mobility. There is no examination evidence of an inflammatory arthritis or acute joint complication. The respiratory assessment is stable and does not account for the reported functional restriction.

Plan: Continue paracetamol as currently prescribed and topical ibuprofen, observing the product maximum and avoiding application to broken skin. Encourage pacing, low-impact exercise and consideration of physiotherapy-led strengthening. GP review is recommended if pain remains limiting despite conservative measures; plain radiographs and escalation of analgesia can then be considered. Respiratory follow-up in about 5 weeks.

Signed: M. Stuart

Discharge summary – Cardiology/Medical take
NHS number: 0001391004

Patient: M. Lees
Admitting service: Aberdeen Royal Infirmary
Reason for admission: Reduced urine output, fatigue and poor oral intake over several days. Admitted for assessment and treatment of acute kidney injury (AKI), felt most consistent with volume depletion in the context of inadequate intake.

Initial assessment showed clinical dehydration with stable blood pressure and no evidence of pulmonary oedema. At 08:15 urine output remained low. Blood tests demonstrated a raised creatinine and urea compared with the available baseline; potassium was not significantly deranged. Urinalysis without convincing evidence of infection. Renal tract ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis or other obstructive cause.

Managed with intravenous sodium chloride, fluid balance monitoring and encouragement of oral fluids. Potentially nephrotoxic and blood-pressure-lowering medicines were temporarily withheld. Urine output improved over the following day and renal function trended towards baseline. No requirement for renal replacement therapy. Mobilising independently and tolerating diet before discharge.

Problem list:
• Acute kidney injury secondary to poor intake/dehydration – improving
• Reduced oral intake – resolved
• Medication-associated risk during intercurrent illness

Discharge medicines:
Recommence usual long-term medicines only as listed on the accompanying medicines reconciliation. The temporarily withheld medicines should remain on hold until reviewed by the GP, with restart guided by repeat renal blood tests. Avoid over-the-counter NSAIDs. Maintain regular oral fluids unless otherwise advised.

Follow-up:
GP review and repeat U&Es/creatinine within one week. Renal function and medication restart to be reviewed at 20th March 2019 by the team at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary.

The discharge plan was discussed with the patient and spouse, ARZOO O'REILLY, who lives in Waterbeck. Return to A&E if urine output falls again, unable to keep fluids down, develops increasing breathlessness, chest pain or marked drowsiness.

Discharge summary – Paediatrics
NHS number: 000 053 3983

Patient: musfirah dutton
MRN: 0997142
Legal guardian: adeleine hull
Admitting service: Ulster Hospital

Reason for admission
Brought to the emergency department following a first generalised convulsion in the context of fever. The episode lasted approximately two minutes, with bilateral stiffening and rhythmic jerking, followed by drowsiness. adeleine hull witnessed the event and reported fever for 3 days with reduced appetite, but no preceding head injury or known ingestion.

At presentation, 3 y/o was febrile but cardiovascularly stable. Initial examination showed postictal drowsiness, improving during observation; no meningism, focal neurological deficit or respiratory distress. Capillary glucose was normal. No further seizure activity occurred.

Investigations and course
Blood tests were not felt necessary after senior paediatric review. Urinalysis was unremarkable. The child remained clinically well hydrated and returned to usual interaction and oral intake later that day. Fever settled with fluids, light clothing and paracetamol for comfort. No antibiotics or anticonvulsant treatment required. The presentation was considered consistent with a simple febrile seizure associated with a self-limiting viral illness. There were no features suggesting meningitis or a complex seizure.

Problem list
• First simple febrile seizure
• Acute febrile viral illness
• Recovered postictal drowsiness

Discharge condition and plan
Discharged home with adeleine hull after paediatric assessment. No regular discharge medicines. Continue antipyretic comfort measures if distressed or uncomfortable; avoid alternating preparations unless advised by the GP.

Seizure first-aid advice given: place on the side, protect from injury, do not restrain and do not put anything in the mouth. Call 999 if the seizure lasts five minutes or more, breathing is affected, recovery is not as expected, or another seizure occurs without recovery. GP review if fever persists or concerns arise. No routine paediatric follow-up arranged; referral to Ulster Hospital if recurrent, prolonged or atypical events.

MELONA CONNOR

Sudden left arm weakness, left facial droop and slurred speech at home, witnessed by spouse. Symptoms resolved before arrival, total duration approximately 20 minutes. Reports mild headache for 3 days. No collapse, seizure or chest pain.

Airway patent. Breathing unlaboured, SpO2 98% on air. Pulse regular; BP elevated on arrival. Alert and orientated, GCS 15. Speech now clear. No facial asymmetry. Power 5/5 in all limbs, normal sensation and coordination. No carotid bruit. Capillary glucose normal.

Bloods: FBC, U&E, glucose and coagulation screen without significant abnormality.
CT head: no acute haemorrhage or established infarct.

Discussed with stroke team. Aspirin administered after intracranial haemorrhage excluded; continue aspirin and existing atorvastatin pending specialist plan. Nil indication for thrombolysis as symptoms fully resolved and outside treatment pathway.

Disposition:
Admit to acute stroke unit for MRI brain, telemetry and TIA work-up. Spouse updated. Safety advice given regarding recurrent weakness, facial droop or speech disturbance.

A&E assessment

Patient: Hindy   MRN: 0334159
Arrival: ambulatory, accompanied by adult child LAUREL GARRETT

Presented with sudden onset pounding palpitations and central chest tightness while at home. Described marked fear of dying, tingling in both hands and rapid breathing. Symptoms peaked within approximately ten minutes and had substantially eased before assessment. No syncope, exertional chest pain, fever or recent stimulant use reported. Relative confirms no collapse or injury.

Alert and able to speak in full sentences, initially visibly anxious and hyperventilating. Pulse regular on examination, heart sounds normal, chest clear with good air entry bilaterally. No focal neurological deficit. Observations reassuring, including BP 120/80 mmHg. ECG: sinus rhythm, no acute ST-segment or T-wave changes. Capillary glucose within normal range. No clinical features to suggest acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism or arrhythmia requiring admission.

Assessment

Presentation most consistent with a panic attack, with autonomic symptoms and hyperventilation. Symptoms improved with reassurance and coached breathing. Discussed the benign nature of the current findings while acknowledging the distress caused.

Plan

Breathing retraining practised in the department; advised to continue this during future episodes. No emergency medication indicated. Discharged home with LAUREL GARRETT, who will remain available this evening. Advised to contact GP surgery for review of recurrent anxiety or panic symptoms and consideration of talking therapy. Return to A&E for persistent or exertional chest pain, collapse, severe breathlessness or new neurological symptoms.

Follow-up arranged with The Royal Marsden Hospital on 4 Mar 2022.

Severe vaso-occlusive pain affecting both limbs and lower back, with reduced oral intake and clinical dehydration. Known sickle cell disease.

Afebrile throughout admission. Initial examination: marked limb and lumbar tenderness, dry mucous membranes; no focal chest signs. Oxygen saturations maintained on air.

Usual sickle-cell medicines reconciled. Paracetamol and ibuprofen as required. Morphine stopped before discharge.

Discharge home with nyasia hughes. Continue good oral fluids and usual sickle-cell care plan. GP review within one week; haematology follow-up via QUEEN ELIZABETH UNIVERSITY HOSPITAL as arranged.

Condition on discharge
Clinically stable, pain controlled on oral medication, hydrated and tolerating diet. Guardian understands plan and safety-net advice.

Admitted with first-trimester hyperemesis at 9+4 weeks' gestation. Ongoing nausea with three episodes of vomiting since overnight; small sips only, unable to tolerate breakfast. Reports marked thirst, dizziness on standing and reduced urine output. Weight loss noted on admission.

High risk of worsening dehydration and electrolyte disturbance. Falls advice given; call bell within reach, assisted mobilisation to bathroom. Continue fluid balance chart, antiemetic review and observations. Reassess oral tolerance, urine output and dizziness. Weigh when safe; maintain assisted mobilisation. Handover outstanding blood results and escalation triggers.

Report/accession ID: L20D53866
Contact: 07700 900639

The patient, aged 49 years, was reviewed in the clinical genetics clinic regarding hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk. Their spouse attended with consent and contributed to the family history. The patient is not currently receiving treatment and reports no personal history of malignancy. The principal concern is the possibility of an inherited predisposition and the implications for relatives.

A three-generation family history was taken. There is a significant history of breast and ovarian cancer on the maternal side, although the available information is incomplete regarding tumour pathology and ages at diagnosis. We discussed that accurate confirmation of diagnoses and, where possible, obtaining relatives’ genetic test reports would improve risk assessment. The pedigree is sufficient to justify further evaluation for a hereditary cancer syndrome.

The family has previously been advised that a BRCA1 c.68_69delAG variant may be relevant; the original laboratory report was not available for review today. This variant should therefore not be assumed to be present in the patient without confirmation of the familial result and appropriate laboratory interpretation.

Predictive testing was discussed, including possible informative, negative and uncertain results, limitations of testing, confidentiality, and the potential relevance to cancer surveillance and reproductive planning. The patient wishes to proceed, subject to receipt and verification of the familial report. No sample was taken today. Written information was provided, and the patient will contact the service once the relative’s report is available. Risk-management recommendations will be finalised after variant confirmation and formal pedigree review.

Patient: Areef  
National Insurance number: BG353336C
MRN: 052 308 354  
Occupation: civil engineer  
Clinic: BENTHAM MEDICAL CENTRE  
Clinician: R. TALBOT

Thank you for attending the general medicine clinic to discuss your sleep symptoms. Your spouse’s account of loud snoring and pauses in your breathing during sleep, together with your daytime somnolence, is strongly suggestive of obstructive sleep apnoea. This occurs when the upper airway narrows repeatedly during sleep, briefly reducing airflow and disturbing normal rest.

We discussed the purpose of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). The machine provides a gentle flow of air through a mask to keep the airway open. Please use it whenever you sleep, including during naps, and bring the equipment to your review so that the mask fit, usage record and treatment pressures can be checked. If the mask is uncomfortable, or you develop troublesome dryness, contact the sleep service rather than stopping treatment without advice.

Until symptoms are improving, take particular care with driving and other activities requiring sustained alertness. Do not drive if you feel sleepy. Avoid alcohol close to bedtime, and aim for a regular sleep routine.

The diagnosis and treatment plan will be reviewed at follow-up in about 4 weeks. Please seek advice sooner if you are unable to tolerate CPAP, or if daytime sleepiness becomes markedly worse. A copy of this plan has been recorded in your clinical notes.

R. TALBOT  
General Medicine  
BENTHAM MEDICAL CENTRE

Discharge summary – Cardiology liaison / acute medical unit

Patient: Diyana R.
Discharging service: Queen Elizabeth University Hospital
Admission reason: Vaso-occlusive sickle cell painful crisis with severe bilateral limb pain, low back pain and reduced oral intake. Symptoms had been present for 3 days, with clinical dehydration on arrival.

Initial assessment showed tachycardia and dry mucous membranes. No focal neurological deficit, chest pain or hypoxia. Blood tests demonstrated anaemia consistent with the patient’s known sickle cell disorder, raised reticulocyte count and mild acute kidney injury, which improved with rehydration. Chest radiograph showed no acute chest syndrome. Blood cultures remained negative.

Hospital course: managed in accordance with the individual pain plan. Intravenous fluids commenced, with regular parenteral morphine and subsequent conversion to oral analgesia as pain settled. Antiemetic prescribed as required. Thromboprophylaxis given while mobility was reduced. Renal function and urine output normalised; inflammatory markers remained low. No transfusion required. Mobilising independently on the ward and tolerating diet and fluids at discharge.

Problem list
• Sickle cell disease with uncomplicated vaso-occlusive crisis
• Dehydration, resolved
• Mild acute kidney injury, resolved
• Opioid-related constipation risk

Discharge medicines:
Continue usual disease-modifying and prophylactic medicines as previously prescribed. Morphine oral solution for breakthrough pain only, according to the written pain plan; avoid driving or alcohol while taking it. Regular paracetamol permitted. Macrogol if constipation develops. Medication reconciliation completed with the patient.

Follow-up: GP review and haematology review at 2nd October 1996. The patient’s spouse, Frankie-Dean, was present for discharge counselling; emergency contact locality recorded as Knockglass. Written advice provided regarding oral hydration, pacing activity and early presentation with fever, breathlessness, chest pain, increasing pain or inability to drink. Return to the emergency department if symptoms recur or do not respond to the agreed plan.

Condition on discharge: haemodynamically stable, afebrile, pain controlled on oral medication, clinically euvolaemic.

Discharge summary – Respiratory Medicine

Patient: Ehsanul
Clinical age context: aged 35 years

Reason for admission
Admitted with a severe sickle cell painful crisis, affecting both limbs and the lower back, with reduced oral intake and clinical dehydration. T. Qureshi, the patient’s partner from DRAPERSTOWN, was present for part of the admission and updated with consent.

Hospital course
Pain was assessed regularly and treated initially with intravenous morphine, followed by a step-down to oral analgesia as symptoms improved. Intravenous fluids were given for dehydration. Oxygen saturations remained satisfactory on air and there was no clinical evidence of acute chest syndrome. Blood tests showed anaemia in keeping with the known sickle cell disorder; renal function remained stable. No transfusion was required.

At 08:15 on the day of discharge, pain was controlled on oral medication, oral fluids were tolerated and mobility had returned close to baseline. The cannula was removed without difficulty.

Discharge medicines
Continue regular medicines as listed on the accompanying medicines reconciliation. Use the prescribed oral analgesia for breakthrough pain and maintain good fluid intake. Do not take additional morphine or other sedating painkillers unless prescribed.

Follow-up and advice
Please contact your GP surgery if pain is not settling or medication is causing troublesome side effects. Attend A&E urgently for chest pain, breathlessness, fever, confusion, marked drowsiness or pain that cannot be controlled at home.

A haematology review has been arranged for 28 October 2012. The patient was advised to bring an up-to-date medicines list and to seek help early in any future crisis.

Discharging clinician: Respiratory Medicine team

Three-day history of worsening lower abdominal pain, predominantly suprapubic and bilateral. Abnormal yellow-green discharge and deep dyspareunia. No collapse or heavy vaginal bleeding. Nausea but tolerating fluids. Partner reports symptoms began after recent unprotected intercourse.

Stable for discharge with return precautions for fever, vomiting, worsening pain or collapse. Review arranged at 12th September 2024 with Dr Zameer Morley, MBBS.

Cardiology clinic review

Patient: CAIO LYNCH
DOB: 6 May 1933
MRN: 093136/64
Contact: 07700 900107

Seen for review of recently documented atrial fibrillation. Reports intermittent palpitations, mainly in the evenings, with reduced energy and breathlessness when walking uphill. No chest pain, syncope or ankle swelling. She has been taking apixaban and bisoprolol as prescribed, with no bleeding symptoms or problematic dizziness. Alcohol intake unchanged. Spouse accompanied her and helped with the medication history.

On examination, comfortable at rest. Pulse irregularly irregular, approximately 78 bpm. Blood pressure satisfactory. Heart sounds dual with no added murmur; chest clear and no peripheral oedema. ECG today confirms atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular response. Recent renal function and full blood count were acceptable for ongoing anticoagulation.

Assessment: Persistent atrial fibrillation, rate controlled on bisoprolol. Symptomatic with exertion but currently haemodynamically stable. Continue apixaban at the established dose and bisoprolol. Discussed adherence, avoiding NSAIDs unless advised, and seeking urgent assessment for significant bleeding, collapse, chest pain or marked breathlessness.

Arrange transthoracic echocardiogram and routine blood monitoring through the GP surgery. Rhythm-control options, including cardioversion, can be revisited after echocardiographic assessment and confirmation of uninterrupted anticoagulation. Review in about 9 weeks, booked for 15th May 2018.

Assessment: Clinical features remain consistent with migraine without aura. No red-flag features or examination findings to suggest secondary headache; imaging not indicated currently.

Plan: Continue sumatriptan and naproxen as previously advised, taken early in the attack. Keep a headache diary recording triggers, timing, medication and response. Discharge summary – Paediatrics
NHS number: 000 734 1491

Patient: Sheri B.
DOB: 1994-02-10
MRN: 07907101
Informant: father, Inaiya

Admission reason
First witnessed generalised convulsion during febrile illness. Fever with reduced oral intake. Postictal drowsiness, resolving before arrival.

Assessment
At 08:15: alert, consolable, maintaining airway. No focal neurological deficit. Mild coryzal symptoms. Hydration satisfactory. No meningism or ongoing seizure activity.

Investigations
Capillary glucose normal. Urinalysis unremarkable. No blood tests or imaging indicated following senior paediatric review. Clinical picture consistent with simple febrile seizure.

Hospital course
Observed on paediatric assessment unit. Temperature settled with fluids and antipyretic comfort measures. No recurrent seizure. Tolerated oral fluids and usual diet. Returned to baseline interaction, passing urine.

Discharge condition
Clinically well, afebrile, neurologically at baseline. Discharged home with father.

Medication / advice
No regular medicines commenced. Paracetamol or ibuprofen for distress associated with fever, according to the product instructions. Antipyretics do not reliably prevent further seizures.

Safety-net
Father advised to place child on side, protect from injury, remove nearby objects and time any seizure. Call 999 if seizure lasts 5 minutes or more, breathing is affected, seizures recur without recovery, or child remains unusually drowsy. Seek urgent review if worsening.

Follow-up
GP review if recurrent episodes or ongoing fever. Paediatric clinic follow-up not routinely required.

Discharging clinician: DOROTHY-ANN MCCABE

Dear Community Paediatrics Team,

I am referring Roshane Partridge, an adolescent with iron-deficiency anaemia, for assessment of persistent symptoms despite treatment and advice on ongoing management.

There has been no collapse, chest pain or breathlessness at rest. Their uncle, vrushti baxter, has helped provide the recent history and is concerned that the symptoms are affecting day-to-day activities.

Recent blood tests in primary care showed a low haemoglobin and reduced ferritin, consistent with iron deficiency. The remainder of the recorded blood count was not suggestive of an acute infection. Ferrous fumarate has been started and is being taken once daily, although adherence has been variable because of nausea and constipation. We have discussed taking it regularly and not with tea or milk. Please review response to treatment, consider whether further investigation is needed, and advise on an appropriate iron replacement regimen and duration. An assessment of nutrition, menstrual blood loss and any psychosocial factors would also be helpful.

The family is currently in contact with Beattock Town Council for practical support. Please share your findings and recommendations with the young person and family, with appropriate adolescent confidentiality and consent.

Yours faithfully,

ladon hogan
GP referring clinician

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report
NHS number: 000 985 0008

Patient: vada finn
MRN: 08841770
Specimen: EDTA blood
Request: Unnamed clinician; investigation of reduced plantar sensation and recurrent diabetic foot ulceration.
Clinical details: Plantar ulceration with reduced sensation and local discharge. Current management includes wound care and co-amoxiclav 625 mg three times daily.

Test performed: Targeted diabetic neuropathy gene panel, including copy-number analysis.
Result: No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant identified in the genes analysed. No reportable copy-number change detected.
Variant of uncertain significance: None.

Interpretation: This result does not provide molecular evidence for an inherited neuropathy within the scope of this assay. A negative panel does not exclude a genetic contribution, including variants outside the regions tested or conditions not represented on the panel. Clinical correlation required.

Laboratory comment: Findings should not be used to guide antimicrobial selection. Continue ulcer assessment, tissue sampling where clinically indicated, vascular review and routine diabetic foot surveillance. Consider broader genomic testing only if phenotype remains unexplained or there is a relevant family history.

Follow-up: Genetics review booked for 2004-11-20. Patient contact detail: 07700 900510.

Validated by: EMMY-ROSE SALEEM
Clinical Genetics Laboratory
Report status: Final

Respiratory Medicine Clinic Report

Patient: K. Wang
Occupation: software developer
Employer: North Wootton Sports Club
Address: 129 Barlow's Cottage Lane, Ruislip, HA4 0AA
Contact: 07700 900429

Reason for review: Persistent fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation in the context of recently identified biochemical hypothyroidism. Referred to exclude a respiratory contribution to reduced exercise tolerance.

History: Fatigue is present throughout the day, with slower recovery after routine activity. No exertional chest pain, wheeze, haemoptysis or nocturnal breathlessness. Cough absent. Sleep is reportedly restorative, although the patient’s spouse describes occasional loud breathing without witnessed apnoeas. Constipation and cold intolerance remain troublesome. Levothyroxine has been commenced and is being taken once daily; adherence is reported as good.

Examination: Comfortable at rest. Speech fluent, with no audible breathlessness. Chest expansion symmetrical; vesicular breath sounds bilaterally without crackles or wheeze. No peripheral oedema or clinical evidence of fluid overload. Oxygen saturation is maintained on room air.

Investigations reviewed: Chest radiograph unremarkable, with no focal consolidation, pleural abnormality or radiographic evidence of interstitial lung disease. Spirometry demonstrates preserved airflow and no significant obstructive ventilatory defect. The overall respiratory assessment is reassuring.

Impression: Symptoms are most consistent with under-treated or recently treated hypothyroidism rather than primary pulmonary disease. No current indication for further respiratory imaging or bronchoscopic assessment.

Plan: Continue levothyroxine under GP/endocrine supervision, with repeat thyroid function testing as arranged. Encourage graded activity as tolerated. Respiratory follow-up in about 7 weeks, or earlier via the GP if breathlessness, persistent cough or exercise limitation develops.

Discharge summary – Paediatric Respiratory Unit

Patient: Priscila
Clinical details: 15 y/o
Next of kin: mother, J. Harwood, Rhuvoult

Priscila was admitted with a two-day history of worsening wheeze, increased work of breathing and night-time cough. Mum reported reduced activity but continued oral intake. No fever or infective symptoms. This was managed as an acute asthma exacerbation at Queen Elizabeth University Hospital.

On arrival, there was widespread expiratory wheeze with mild subcostal recession. Oxygen saturations remained satisfactory in air. Chest radiograph was not indicated. The child responded promptly to repeated salbutamol via spacer, with improving air entry and work of breathing. A short course of oral steroid was given. No antibiotics were required.

By discharge, breathing was comfortable at rest and during mobilisation, with only occasional scattered wheeze. Eating and drinking normally. Salbutamol inhaler technique and spacer use were demonstrated and practised with Priscila and their mother. An asthma action plan was provided.

Discharge medicines:
- Salbutamol 100 micrograms: 2–10 puffs via spacer as required for wheeze or breathlessness. During the next 24 hours, give 4 puffs four-hourly, then reduce as symptoms settle.
- Complete the prescribed oral steroid course.

Assessment and plan:
Acute asthma exacerbation, clinically improved following bronchodilator treatment. Review with the GP or asthma nurse for inhaler and trigger assessment in about 12 weeks. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if salbutamol is needed more often than four-hourly, symptoms worsen, or speaking and drinking become difficult.

Date: 12th October 2021
NHS number: 0003792049

To: Clinical Genetics Service

Re: AMELIA-ANN RITCHIE
Report/accession ID: L27Q91308

Dear Colleague,

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient following presentation with persistent, painless cervical and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss. Examination identified several firm, non-tender nodes; there was no acute airway compromise. Initial blood tests showed an inflammatory response with mild normocytic anaemia. CT imaging demonstrated lymphadenopathy above and below the diaphragm. The working diagnosis is Hodgkin lymphoma, with tissue diagnosis and full staging in progress.

The clinical question is whether there is an indication for germline assessment for an inherited predisposition to haematological malignancy. The patient reports a family history of lymphoma in a first-degree relative, although the available details are incomplete. Please advise on the relevance of this history, appropriate genetic testing, and whether relatives require specific counselling or surveillance.

The patient is currently receiving supportive care pending tissue diagnosis, including antiemetic treatment, hydration advice and symptom monitoring. No systemic anti-cancer treatment has yet been commenced. A multidisciplinary review is planned once histology and PET-CT results are available.

I would appreciate review at the earliest appropriate opportunity, with advice on interim management and any additional family-history information required. The patient has consented to referral and understands that testing may have implications for relatives.

Yours sincerely,

Tilli Bowers
Referring clinician
ALTNAGELVIN AREA HOSPITAL

Accident and Emergency – clinical review

Patient: Omosede
Contact: 07700 900501
The patient, aged 29 years, was reviewed with a friend present.

Presenting complaint: Low back pain with shooting pain down the left leg and intermittent paraesthesia in the lateral calf and foot, for 3 days. No preceding significant trauma. Mobilising independently but painful. No reported bladder or bowel disturbance, saddle numbness or progressive leg weakness.

Examination: Alert, comfortable at rest. Lumbar flexion restricted by pain. Left straight-leg raise reproduces radicular pain. Mild altered sensation reported over the lateral calf; power grossly preserved, reflexes symmetrical. Abdomen soft and non-tender. No spinal step or focal vertebral tenderness.

Assessment: Lumbar radiculopathy, without current features of cauda equina syndrome.

Medication: Naproxen with food and paracetamol as needed. Patient reports partial benefit; advised not to combine naproxen with other NSAIDs. Consider gastroprotection if ongoing use or gastrointestinal risk.

Plan:
- Continue simple analgesia and gentle activity; avoid prolonged bed rest.
- GP review if not settling, for physiotherapy and consideration of further assessment.
- Return to A&E urgently for new urinary retention/incontinence, saddle sensory change, or worsening weakness.
- Follow-up appointment: 27 Oct 2024.
- Report/accession ID: 05372067.

Friend understood the advice; patient discharged home.

I would be grateful for your review of this patient with established Parkinson disease, previously assessed by neurology and currently managed in primary care. The specific question is whether the present motor symptoms warrant adjustment of co-beneldopa and renewed multidisciplinary input.

There has been a gradual increase in resting tremor, bradykinesia and muscular rigidity over recent months. The tremor is most troublesome in the right hand and is affecting dressing and meal preparation. There have been no reported falls, syncope or visual hallucinations. The patient has been advised to bring an up-to-date medication list and attend with their spouse if possible. A primary care review is arranged for 22/04/2028.

Yours sincerely,

Dr Lexi-Jay Joyce, MBBS

Patient: Frederick
Clinical area: Paediatric inpatient ward
Responsible parent: Milica
Contact: frederick.lees88@gmail.com
Referring/treating organisation: Ulster Hospital

Situation
A 6-year-old Black male patient admitted with acute appendicitis. Parent reports worsening right lower-quadrant pain overnight, nausea and no appetite. No vomiting reported since arrival.

Observations
Alert, anxious but engaging with staff. Temperature within normal limits; pulse mildly elevated with pain. Respirations unlaboured, saturations maintained on air. Abdomen tender in right lower quadrant with guarding on light palpation. Pain 5/10.

Intake / output
Nil by mouth maintained pending surgical review. Receiving prescribed IV fluids; urine passed this shift, satisfactory amount. No oral intake tolerated or requested.

Interventions and response
Paracetamol administered as prescribed, with partial reduction in pain and improved settling. IV co-amoxiclav given via patent cannula; site clean and dry, no reaction observed. Reassurance provided to patient and parent, explanation repeated in age-appropriate language. Parent remains at bedside and involved in care.

Mobility / safety
Mobilised to toilet with one nurse supporting; steady but uncomfortable. Falls precautions in place. Call bell and fluids for mouth care within reach.

Escalation
Ongoing abdominal tenderness and reduced comfort discussed with the covering surgical team; review requested before theatre list confirmation. Cannula observations continued.

Plan for next shift
Continue regular observations, pain assessment and prescribed IV therapy. Maintain nil by mouth, monitor urine output and nausea. Escalate increasing pain, fever, vomiting, abdominal distension or clinical deterioration promptly. Confirm consent and parent update following surgical review.

sophie-rose gee

Patient: Astyn ELLIOTT
Report/accession ID: 22/418665
Reporting organisation: ROYAL OLDHAM HOSPITAL
Specimen: ED admission bloods, serum; collected on presentation
Clinical details: Reduced urine output, fatigue and poor oral intake for 3 days. Suspected acute kidney injury.

Results
Sodium: 136 mmol/L (133–146)
Potassium: 5.4 mmol/L (3.5–5.3) – mildly increased
Urea: 18.2 mmol/L (2.5–7.8) – increased
Creatinine: 242 µmol/L (45–90) – increased
eGFR: 21 mL/min/1.73 m² – reduced
Bicarbonate: 19 mmol/L (22–29) – reduced
CRP: 18 mg/L (<5) – mildly increased
Haemoglobin: 128 g/L (115–160)
WCC: 10.8 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0)

Interpretation
Biochemistry consistent with significant renal impairment. In the stated clinical context, acute kidney injury is likely; correlate with previous renal function and urine output. Mild hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis noted.

Recommend repeat U&E after intravenous sodium chloride and review of fluid balance. Temporary medication hold documented; avoid nephrotoxic medicines pending reassessment. Escalate urgently if potassium rises, urine output remains low or clinical condition deteriorates.

Follow-up: GP/renal review booked for 6 Nov 2018.

Emergency Department Assessment

Patient: Isma H.   6 y/o
MRN: MRN-03672319
Accompanied by parent, THEODOR LAMB
Referred from: Royal Papworth Hospital

Presenting complaint:
Wheeze and increased work of breathing since this afternoon. Night-time cough for several nights. Salbutamol inhaler used at home with limited relief. No fever, vomiting or choking episode.

Airway patent. heart rate 92 beats/minute. RR 34/min, SpO₂ 94% in air, temp 37.1°C. Alert, speaking in short sentences. Intercostal recession with prolonged expiration. Bilateral widespread polyphonic wheeze, reduced air entry at bases. Peripheries warm, capillary refill <2 seconds.

Acute asthma exacerbation, moderate severity. No clinical evidence of pneumonia or foreign body aspiration. Parent present throughout; assent obtained for examination and treatment.

Salbutamol 10 puffs via spacer, administered with nursing supervision. Ipratropium given by nebuliser due to persistent work of breathing. Reassessed after 30 minutes: improved air entry, mild residual wheeze, RR 26/min, SpO₂ 97% in air.

Plan/disposition:
Observe further in department. Commence oral steroid course as prescribed. Spacer teaching completed with THEODOR LAMB, including inhaler technique and dose recording. Continue regular salbutamol initially, then reduce as symptoms settle. Paediatric asthma safety-net advice provided. Discharge home if stable after observation; GP review arranged.

To the spinal assessment service

Re: Eniola
Referring organisation: Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh
Report/accession ID: 05704511

I am referring Eniola for assessment of persistent left-sided lumbar radiculopathy. The clinical question is whether further imaging or specialist intervention is indicated, given ongoing shooting pain and paraesthesia despite initial treatment.

Symptoms began after lifting at home and have continued for several weeks. Pain starts in the lower back and travels through the left buttock into the lateral calf. There is intermittent tingling in the same distribution, worse with sitting and forward flexion. Walking remains possible, although limited by pain. No reported saddle numbness, urinary retention, faecal incontinence or progressive leg weakness. A sibling has been helping with day-to-day activities because movement is difficult.

In the emergency department, lumbar movement was restricted by pain. Left straight-leg raise reproduced the radiating symptoms. There was reduced sensation subjectively over the lateral calf, but power was preserved on examination and reflexes were symmetrical. No fever or systemic features. The report/accession ID above relates to the emergency department assessment.

Treatment to date has included paracetamol and naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food. Advice has been given regarding activity modification, avoiding prolonged bed rest and seeking urgent review if bladder or bowel disturbance, saddle sensory loss or new weakness develops.

I would be grateful for your review, including consideration of MRI and physiotherapy or pain-management input as appropriate.

Yours faithfully,

skanda daley

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report

Patient: Sunairah E.
MRN: 036418847
Patient address: 167 Eclipse Yard, Partington, M31 4AA
Specimen: Peripheral blood, EDTA
Request: Predictive testing for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk, submitted by the requesting clinician.

Testing performed:
Targeted analysis of the familial BRCA1 variant BRCA1 c.68_69delAG by validated molecular genetic methodology. Sequence alteration nomenclature follows current HGVS conventions.

Result:
BRCA1 c.68_69delAG: not detected in the submitted specimen.

Interpretation:
No evidence of the familial BRCA1 variant was identified. This result substantially reduces the likelihood that the patient has inherited the specific familial variant under investigation. It does not exclude other pathogenic variants in BRCA1, BRCA2 or additional cancer-predisposition genes, and does not remove risk attributable to the wider family history. The result should therefore be interpreted alongside the confirmed familial variant report and the patient’s pedigree.

Specimen and quality:
DNA yield and analytical quality were adequate. Internal assay controls passed. This is a predictive test performed on a blood specimen; identification of the familial variant in an affected relative should be confirmed before using a negative result for predictive purposes.

Clinical comment:
Genetic counselling is recommended to discuss residual breast and ovarian cancer risk, family communication and whether any further testing is indicated. No current treatment is required on the basis of this laboratory result. Please arrange genetics review on 1988-12-14 if the familial report or pedigree information requires clarification.

Report validated and authorised by:
V. Coles
Laboratory clinician, Clinical Genetics

Admission date: 5 Feb 2023
Discharging service: Cardiology, Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh

Reason for admission
Presented with four days of worsening breathlessness, increased wheeze and purulent yellow sputum. Required assessment in the emergency department for suspected infective exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. No chest pain or syncope reported.

Key findings
Initial examination: widespread expiratory wheeze with reduced air entry bilaterally. Oxygen saturations improved with controlled oxygen, subsequently maintaining target range on air. Chest radiograph showed hyperinflation without focal consolidation. ECG without acute ischaemic changes. Blood tests demonstrated a raised inflammatory marker; renal function remained satisfactory. Blood pressure on review was 120/80 mmHg.

Hospital course
Treated with nebulised bronchodilators, a five-day course of prednisolone and doxycycline. Respiratory symptoms and sputum volume improved, with no further oxygen requirement. No evidence of acute cardiac failure during admission. Salbutamol inhaler technique reviewed by the respiratory nurse; spacer supplied. Smoking cessation advice given.

Problem list
• Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, likely infective
• Wheeze and increased sputum production, improved
• No radiographic pneumonia or acute cardiac decompensation

Discharge medicines
Prednisolone to complete the prescribed five-day course.
Doxycycline to complete the prescribed course.
Salbutamol inhaler, two puffs as needed for breathlessness or wheeze, using spacer.
Continue regular inhalers as previously prescribed.

Condition at discharge
Mobilising independently and managing personal care. Afebrile, clinically euvolaemic and comfortable at rest. Discharged home with partner, who was updated at the bedside. Emergency contact recorded as ALVAR WILDE, living in Mambeg.

Follow-up and advice
GP review within one week for exacerbation follow-up and inhaler reconciliation. Consider spirometry and respiratory review once clinically stable if not already established. Seek urgent medical attention for rapidly worsening breathlessness, chest pain, confusion, haemoptysis or inability to maintain oral intake.

Dear Mental Health Liaison Team,

I would be grateful for an urgent assessment of Grant S., who attended the emergency department with their spouse following a marked deterioration in mood. They describe persistent low mood, loss of interest in previously enjoyable activities and early-morning waking. Their spouse reports reduced conversation and withdrawal at home. There has also been poor appetite, although no recent weight measurement is available.

At review, the patient was appropriately dressed but appeared tired and subdued. Speech was quiet but coherent, with no evidence of formal thought disorder or psychotic symptoms. They acknowledged feeling hopeless at times. They denied current suicidal intent or plans, although the spouse is concerned that the patient has become increasingly isolated. No previous psychiatric admission is reported. Sertraline is prescribed by the GP; adherence has been inconsistent over the past fortnight, with no other regular medication disclosed.

The patient also mentioned intermittent nausea for 3 days, without abdominal pain or vomiting. Physical observations in A&E were stable and no acute medical cause was identified. Alcohol and illicit drug use were denied.

Assessment: symptoms are consistent with a major depressive episode, with functional decline and a need for prompt review of risk and treatment.

Plan: please assess today if possible, including collateral history from the spouse, safety planning and consideration of medication optimisation or psychological support. The patient has been advised not to remain alone while awaiting assessment and to return to A&E if suicidal thoughts emerge.

Yours faithfully,

Dr Zeidan Sutcliffe, MBBS

Markedly raised urea and creatinine with reduced estimated GFR, consistent with significant renal impairment. Mild metabolic acidosis. Potassium currently within the laboratory reference interval. Correlate with fluid balance, urine output, blood pressure and examination findings. Review nephrotoxic medicines and other temporarily withheld treatment before restarting. Paediatric Haematology Outpatient Report
NHS number: 000 004 8691

Patient: passion javed
Age: 16 y/o
Accompanied by mother, Shada Doyle
Report/accession ID: 0388513132

Clinical history
Seen with her mother; history obtained jointly, with private time offered and accepted for part of the consultation. Several months of tiredness, intermittent light-headedness on standing and reduced exercise tolerance. No syncope, chest pain, melaena or overt bleeding. Menstrual history suggests heavy flow during the first two days of each cycle. Appetite reasonable. Ferrous fumarate taken regularly, although occasional nausea reported after dosing.

Examination
Weight 54.0 kg. Alert and appropriately interactive. Mild conjunctival pallor. No jaundice, lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Cardiovascular examination: regular pulse, soft flow murmur, no added sounds. Chest clear. Neurological examination grossly normal.

Investigations
Recent full blood count demonstrates microcytosis and hypochromia with haemoglobin below the laboratory reference range. Ferritin reduced, with normal inflammatory markers. Blood film consistent with iron deficiency; no features to suggest haemoglobinopathy on current results.

Impression
Iron-deficiency anaemia, most likely related to menstrual blood loss, with symptomatic tiredness and reduced exercise tolerance. Clinical response to oral replacement is present but incomplete.

Plan
Continue ferrous fumarate as prescribed, taken away from tea, coffee and calcium-containing products where practicable. Repeat full blood count and ferritin after a further treatment interval; blood tests to include reticulocyte response if clinically indicated. Discussed menstrual management with the patient and her mother, including GP review if heavy bleeding persists. Advised to seek urgent assessment for collapse, breathlessness at rest or significant bleeding.

yedidya pike
Paediatric Haematology Clinician

Discharge summary – Paediatrics

Presented with 24 hours of frequent vomiting and watery diarrhoea, with fewer wet nappies and reduced oral intake. Guardian reported no blood in stool and no bilious vomiting. Birth history: born at 39+2 weeks' gestation.

Clinically dehydrated but alert and responsive. Dry lips, mildly sunken eyes and reduced urine output; peripheral perfusion remained satisfactory. No respiratory distress. Abdomen soft, non-distended and non-tender.

Managed on the paediatric ward with oral rehydration solution in small, frequent amounts, alongside continued breast/formula feeds as tolerated. Guardian remained at the bedside and was involved in feeding and monitoring; consent obtained for treatment.

Key results
Capillary glucose normal. Urea and electrolytes reassuring, with no significant acidosis. Stool testing not indicated as symptoms were improving and there was no blood or travel history.

Problem list
1. Viral gastroenteritis.
2. Mild dehydration, resolved with oral rehydration.
3. Reduced urine output, resolved.

Discharge plan
Discharge home clinically well, alert and tolerating oral fluids. Continue oral rehydration solution after each loose stool and usual milk feeds; supportive care only. No regular discharge medicines.

Safety-net advice given to menisha munro: seek urgent medical review via NHS 111, A&E or emergency services if unable to keep fluids down, markedly fewer wet nappies, increasing drowsiness, blood or green vomit, breathing difficulty, or concern about deterioration. Discharge summary – General Medicine

Patient: Allistair T.
Admitting team: Royal Victoria Hospital
Report/accession ID: 0794666489

Reason for admission
Presented via A&E with 3 days of dysuria and urinary frequency, followed by worsening right flank pain, fever and rigors. No vomiting. Spouse Breindy, from AGIVEY, provided collateral history on arrival.

Initial temperature 38.7°C, pulse 108, BP 112/68. Right renal angle tenderness. Urine dip positive for leucocytes, nitrites and blood. Blood tests: WCC 15.2, CRP 186, creatinine 98 micromol/L. Treated initially with intravenous cefuroxime and fluids, with regular paracetamol for pain and fever. Rigors settled within 24 hours and inflammatory markers began to fall. Converted to oral cefuroxime once afebrile and tolerating diet. Renal function remained stable. No procedure required.

Cefuroxime 500 mg orally twice daily to complete a 7-day total course.

Usual regular medicines unchanged.

Condition at discharge
Clinically well, afebrile, haemodynamically stable and mobilising independently. Passing urine without difficulty.

Follow-up and advice
GP review if symptoms have not fully settled after antibiotics. Repeat urine testing only if symptoms recur. Seek urgent medical attention for recurrent rigors, persistent vomiting, worsening flank pain, confusion, or inability to keep fluids down. Urology referral if recurrent febrile urinary infections.

Laboratory report – urine culture
National Insurance number: NK 46 77 64 C

Patient: Kailyn
MRN: 007288193
Requesting clinician: unnamed
Reporting organisation: LLANGOLLEN COMMUNITY HOSPITAL

Specimen: Midstream urine
Clinical details: Dysuria, flank pain and rigors for 3 days. Suspected acute pyelonephritis. Current treatment: cefuroxime; paracetamol as required.

Macroscopy: Cloudy urine.
Leukocytes: >100 ×10^6/L
Erythrocytes: 24 ×10^6/L
Nitrite: Positive
Protein: 2+

Culture: Significant growth of Escherichia coli, >10^7 CFU/L.
Sensitivity: Cefuroxime – susceptible. Trimethoprim – resistant. Ciprofloxacin – susceptible; reserve for specialist-directed use.

Interpretation: Urine findings support a bacterial urinary tract infection. In the context of rigors and flank pain, results are consistent with acute pyelonephritis.

Clinical comment: Continue cefuroxime if improving and review antimicrobial choice against local guidance and susceptibility result. Check temperature, renal function and hydration status. Same-day clinical review if persistent rigors, vomiting, hypotension or deteriorating flank pain.

Follow-up: GP review on 16th September 2020; repeat specimen only if symptoms fail to resolve or recur.

Validated by: DELILAH-ANN LAWSON
Laboratory comment: Correlate with clinical findings. Culture result released to requesting team.

A&E assessment

Patient: Y. Gurung
Arrival with severe bilateral limb pain, predominantly thighs and lower back, beginning overnight and worsening despite usual oral analgesia. Reports reduced oral intake and dark urine. No chest pain, breathlessness, focal weakness or fever. Adult child, LUUK CROSSLEY, accompanied the patient and provided collateral history.

On assessment, alert and distressed with pain. Dry mucous membranes. Pulse regular, blood pressure maintained, afebrile and oxygenating normally on air. No respiratory distress. Diffuse tenderness through both thighs and lumbar paraspinal muscles without joint swelling or focal neurological deficit. Abdomen soft and non-tender. No clinical evidence of acute chest syndrome.

Blood tests: haemoglobin near the patient’s known baseline, reticulocytosis and mild leukocytosis. Urea mildly raised with concentrated urine; creatinine not significantly changed from previous results. CRP low. Group and save sent. Chest radiograph clear.

Assessment: uncomplicated vaso-occlusive sickle cell painful crisis with dehydration. No current features of sepsis, acute chest syndrome or stroke.

Given IV morphine in titrated doses with good reduction in pain, alongside IV crystalloid and antiemetic. Analgesia plan reviewed with the haematology team at Royal Alexandra Hospital. Pain score improved, oral fluids tolerated and observations remained stable. Admission was offered for ongoing analgesia, but the patient preferred discharge after shared decision-making.

Discharged with advice to continue the agreed analgesia regimen, maintain hydration and return immediately for fever, chest symptoms, increasing drowsiness or uncontrolled pain. Haematology review arranged for 6 Oct 2024, in about 6 weeks.

Senior review: Danyil Smyth, Emergency Medicine.

The patient has been given advice to attend A&E if fever, rapidly spreading redness, escalating pain or blackening of the foot develops.

Yours sincerely,

aksara reeves

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report
National Insurance number: KN027952C

Patient: Hadhirah Bedford
MRN: H7781807
Specimen: EDTA whole blood and serum
Collection/report date: 21st October 2026
Request: Investigation of diabetes phenotype; clinical details supplied include thirst, fatigue and frequent urination. Current medication: metformin and atorvastatin.

Results
HbA1c (IFCC): 70 mmol/mol
Reference interpretation: <42 mmol/mol non-diabetic range; 42–47 mmol/mol increased risk; ≥48 mmol/mol consistent with diabetes mellitus in the appropriate clinical context.

Fasting plasma glucose: 9.8 mmol/L
Total cholesterol: 4.6 mmol/L
eGFR: >90 mL/min/1.73 m²

Molecular analysis: No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant identified in the diabetes genes included in the requested panel. This result does not exclude multifactorial type 2 diabetes mellitus, regulatory variants, or genetic causes not represented by the assay.

Interpretation
The HbA1c is substantially above the diagnostic threshold and indicates suboptimal glycaemic control, consistent with the reported osmotic symptoms. Results support established type 2 diabetes mellitus rather than providing evidence for a recognised monogenic diabetes syndrome on the tested panel. Correlate with treatment adherence, diet, renal function and capillary glucose readings; consider review of metformin dose and diabetes management in primary care.

Please note that HbA1c may be misleading in the presence of altered red-cell survival or haemoglobin variants. Further testing should be guided by the clinical phenotype and family history.

Validated and authorised by: Dr Adaleine Bridges, MBBS, GMC: 0434015
Laboratory report date: 21st October 2026

Accident and Emergency Rheumatology Assessment
NHS number: 000 259 7234

Patient: Ousmane MAHMOOD
MRN: 03143289
Contact: 07700 900773

The patient, aged 34 years, was assessed in the emergency department with a 3-week increase in inflammatory hand symptoms. History was provided jointly with the patient’s spouse. Marked morning stiffness, progressive swelling of the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, and fatigue were reported. No recent infective illness, trauma or new rash. Current treatment: methotrexate with folic acid supplementation and naproxen; adherence reported as good.

Examination demonstrated bilateral tender, warm swelling of the second to fourth metacarpophalangeal joints and several proximal interphalangeal joints, with reduced grip secondary to pain. No focal neurological deficit, large-joint effusion or clinical evidence of septic arthritis. Afebrile and haemodynamically stable. There was no synovitis-related skin breakdown.

Blood tests showed raised inflammatory markers in keeping with active inflammatory disease; full blood count, renal function and liver enzymes were suitable for continuation of current disease-modifying treatment. The overall findings are most consistent with a rheumatoid arthritis flare rather than an acute infective or traumatic process.

Naproxen may continue with food, provided no gastrointestinal, renal or cardiovascular contraindication. Methotrexate and folic acid should continue unchanged pending specialist review. A short corticosteroid course was discussed, but deferred until infection screening and confirmation of the existing rheumatology plan. The patient was advised to return to A&E for fever, rapidly worsening swelling, marked functional loss or systemic deterioration.

Rheumatology follow-up requested in about 11 weeks, with appointment recorded for 17 May 2018. GP to monitor blood count, renal function and liver enzymes in accordance with the shared-care protocol.

No significant medical history disclosed. No fever, vomiting or urinary symptoms. Pregnancy possibility discussed; consented to examination and STI testing.

Haemodynamically stable, afebrile. Mild suprapubic and bilateral adnexal tenderness, no guarding or rebound. Speculum: mucopurulent cervical discharge; cervical excitation present. No active bleeding. PID clinically likely; torsion and ectopic pregnancy considered less likely.

Treat as outpatient with ceftriaxone administered in department, then doxycycline and metronidazole as prescribed; avoid alcohol with metronidazole and complete the course. No sex until treatment completed and partners reviewed. GP/sexual health follow-up for results and partner notification.

Return urgently for worsening or unilateral pain, fever, vomiting, collapse, heavy bleeding or inability to tolerate medication. Discharged ambulatory with friend; understanding confirmed.

Responds to father and staff, taking small amounts of water and diluted juice. Ate little at lunch. Wet nappy reported. No vomiting or rash noted. Neurological observations ongoing; pupils equal and reactive, moving all limbs.

Light clothing and oral fluids encouraged. Paracetamol given as prescribed for comfort; temperature reduced on recheck. Risks / escalation:
Falls and recurrent seizure precautions maintained; cot sides up, floor clear. Father advised to call immediately for altered responsiveness, breathing difficulty or another convulsion. Covering paediatric clinician updated regarding fever and intake; review completed, no further treatment requested currently.

Plan for next shift:
Continue four-hourly observations and neurological checks, monitor temperature, hydration and urine output. Encourage oral intake. Medical review and discharge readiness check in about 9 weeks at follow-up on 2019-05-05.

Dear Cardiology Team,

Re: albus sadler

Thank you for assessing this patient with recurrent episodes of palpitations and associated chest awareness. The principal working diagnosis in primary care has been generalised anxiety disorder, characterised by persistent worry, poor sleep and muscle tension; however, the episodic nature of the palpitations warrants cardiac review to exclude an arrhythmia.

Symptoms have been present intermittently for several months, occurring both at rest and during routine activity. There has been no documented syncope, exertional chest pain or sustained breathlessness. Examination in the surgery was unremarkable, with regular pulse and normal heart sounds. A recent resting ECG showed sinus rhythm without acute ST-segment or conduction abnormalities. Routine blood tests, including full blood count, renal profile and thyroid function, were within reference ranges.

The patient is taking sertraline, with partial improvement in anxiety but no clear reduction in palpitations. They have been advised to reduce caffeine and keep a symptom diary. Charlie-Mai Regan, the patient’s spouse, reports that several episodes have been noticed at home, although no pulse recording has been obtained.

I would be grateful for your assessment and advice regarding ambulatory rhythm monitoring, and confirmation that there is no cardiac explanation requiring specific treatment. Please also advise whether any further investigation is indicated before continuing management of the anxiety in primary care. Review of symptoms and treatment response is planned in about 8 weeks.

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report
National Insurance number: ZZ276339D

Patient: Alanood L.
Report/accession ID: 072160209
Report date: 18th June 2024
Requesting clinician: GP (not stated)

Specimen
Peripheral blood, EDTA. Clinical indication: fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation in the context of treated hypothyroidism with levothyroxine. Family history and detailed phenotype were not supplied.

Results
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH): 8.2 mIU/L
Free thyroxine (FT4): 11.6 pmol/L
Thyroid peroxidase antibody (TPOAb): 286 kU/L
Thyroglobulin antibody (TgAb): 74 kU/L

Targeted thyroid disease gene panel: No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant identified in the genes analysed, including TSHR, TPO, TG, DUOX2 and PAX8. No copy-number change was detected by the assay.

Interpretation
The raised TSH with low-normal FT4 and positive thyroid autoantibodies is consistent with suboptimally replaced autoimmune primary hypothyroidism. The negative genetic panel does not exclude a genetic contribution outside the regions or genes assessed, nor does it alter the biochemical diagnosis. Findings do not support a currently recognised monogenic thyroid dysgenesis or thyroid hormone synthesis disorder.

Clinical comment
Please correlate with adherence, timing of levothyroxine in relation to food and other medicines, and repeat thyroid function tests following any dose adjustment. Consider routine endocrine review if biochemical control remains suboptimal, symptoms progress, or there is a significant family history suggestive of inherited thyroid disease. Genetic counselling is not indicated on the present result unless additional clinical or family-history information becomes available.

Validated and reported by: shenaz shaw, Clinical Genetics Consultant
Professional registration: 0707366

Lasharn Oakes, Laboratory Clinical Geneticist

Clinically improved, mobilising independently and suitable for home with support from adult child. Advice given regarding fluids, light diet as tolerated and hand hygiene. Avoid preparing food for others until symptom-free for 48 hours.

General Medicine Clinic Note

Patient: amaray mansfield
MRN: 036110664
Occupation: Barista
Seen at Plas Y Bryn Medical Centre with a six-week history of an itchy erythematous rash affecting both wrists and the sides of the neck. The irritation began after changing to a fragranced washing product at home. No facial swelling, wheeze, fever or mucosal involvement. Cetirizine has reduced the itching slightly. She has also been using hydrocortisone 1% cream twice daily, with partial improvement.

On examination, well and not systemically unwell. Erythematous, mildly scaly plaques over the volar wrists and lower lateral neck, with a few excoriations. No weeping, crusting or features of secondary infection. The remainder of the exposed skin is clear.

Assessment

Distribution and timing are most consistent with allergic contact dermatitis, likely triggered by a fragranced product. No clinical evidence of cellulitis or severe drug reaction.

Plan

Advised to stop the new washing product and avoid fragranced soaps, detergents and creams. Continue regular emollient use, applied generously and frequently. Continue hydrocortisone 1% cream twice daily for up to seven days to the affected areas, avoiding broken skin and the face. Cetirizine may be continued as required for itch.

If symptoms have not settled after avoidance and topical treatment, GP review for consideration of patch testing or dermatology referral. Safety-netted to seek urgent assessment for rapidly spreading rash, facial or tongue swelling, breathing difficulty, blistering or fever.

Documented by zakiyyah pike, clinician, Plas Y Bryn Medical Centre.
