Paediatric Outpatient Clinic
Date: 15 April 2035
Patient: C. Barrow
Contact: 07700 900666
Attended with parent, gurraj moody

Currently 15 y/o, with a six-month history of intermittent left-sided headaches. Episodes occur approximately twice monthly, usually after a late night or missed meal, and last several hours. Headache is associated with nausea and marked photophobia; no vomiting, visual loss, weakness, collapse or waking from sleep reported. School attendance is occasionally affected. Parent has not noticed change in behaviour or coordination.

Examination today was reassuring: alert and comfortable, normal speech and gait, pupils equal and reactive, full eye movements, no papilloedema seen, and normal limb tone, power and coordination. Blood pressure and observations satisfactory.

The pattern remains most consistent with migraine without aura. There are no current features suggesting raised intracranial pressure or another secondary cause, so brain imaging is not indicated at present. We discussed regular meals, good hydration, consistent sleep and limiting screen use during an attack. A headache diary should record timing, possible triggers, symptoms, medicines taken and response.

Continue sumatriptan at the previously advised dose early in a significant attack, with naproxen if needed and tolerated; take naproxen with food and avoid combining it with other anti-inflammatory painkillers. Please limit acute medicines to avoid medication-overuse headache.

Review in paediatric clinic in three months, sooner if attacks become more frequent or treatment is ineffective. Seek urgent assessment for sudden maximal headache, persistent vomiting, new weakness, confusion, seizure or visual disturbance.

Relevant specialist input noted from the consultant neurologist.

Patient: NABHAAN ADAMSON
The patient, aged 18 months, was brought to the emergency department by his mother, Kamea, with a 24-hour history of barking cough, hoarse voice and noisy breathing, worse overnight. No choking episode or suspected foreign-body aspiration. Drinking less than usual but passing urine.

On assessment there was mild inspiratory stridor at rest with intermittent suprasternal recession. Oxygen saturations remained satisfactory in air; no cyanosis. Chest examination otherwise clear. The presentation was consistent with viral croup. No features to suggest bacterial tracheitis or epiglottitis.

Management and progress
- Single dose of dexamethasone given in the emergency department.
- Observed on the paediatric ward with supportive care, fluids encouraged and minimal handling.
- No nebulised adrenaline required.
- Stridor settled during observation and cough became less harsh. Remained afebrile, alert and interactive, with improving oral intake.
- No oxygen or intravenous treatment required.

Discharge condition
Clinically well for discharge home with mother. Breathing comfortable in air, no stridor at rest, tolerating fluids and passing urine. Diagnosis and expected course discussed with Kamea, who understood the advice.

Discharge medicines
No regular medicines. Supportive care only. Dexamethasone has been administered in hospital; do not repeat unless specifically advised by a clinician.

Advice given
Keep the child calm and upright if coughing. Offer frequent fluids. Return to A&E urgently if stridor occurs at rest, breathing becomes laboured, lips appear blue, the child is unusually drowsy, or unable to drink. Seek GP advice if symptoms are not continuing to improve.

Follow-up
GP review if ongoing cough or recurrent noisy breathing. Routine paediatric follow-up is not required; telephone review can be arranged in about 11 weeks if symptoms recur.

Emergency assessment – Clinical Genetics

Patient: D. McMahon
Home address: 103 Churchtown View, Esher, KT7 0AA
Contact: 07700 900257

The patient, aged 63 years, was brought to the emergency department by their partner with worsening breathlessness over the last several days. They now need three pillows to sleep and report orthopnoea, increasing bilateral ankle swelling and markedly reduced exercise tolerance. No chest pain, fever or productive cough. Known heart failure; taking furosemide and bisoprolol as prescribed.

On assessment, alert and speaking in short sentences. Respiratory rate elevated with oxygen saturations 94% on air. Bibasal fine crackles to mid-zones and bilateral pitting oedema to the shins. Heart sounds regular, peripheries cool but capillary refill maintained. No focal neurological deficit.

ECG showed sinus rhythm without acute ST-segment change. Chest radiograph demonstrated pulmonary vascular congestion and small bilateral pleural effusions. Blood tests showed raised NT-proBNP and mild renal impairment compared with previous results; troponin was not significantly dynamic. Findings consistent with acute decompensated heart failure rather than infection or acute coronary syndrome.

Treatment and plan:
Given intravenous furosemide with good urine output and symptomatic improvement. Oxygen was not required. Cardiology team advised admission for ongoing diuresis, fluid balance monitoring and review of heart-failure therapy, including renal function and beta-blocker dosing. Admitted to the acute medical unit.

Clinical genetics review remains planned in about 10 weeks, once medically stable. A. Riley documented the assessment and discussed the admission plan with the patient and partner.

Clinical Genetics Outpatient Report
NHS number: 0002403910

Patient: alarna-rae hull
Occupation: Police officer
Employer: Chancery Voluntary Service
Address: 101 Blaen Cefn, Crymych, SA41 3AA
Contact: alarna-rae.hull23@proton.me

Reason for referral: Persistent iron-deficiency anaemia with tiredness, intermittent dizziness and reduced exercise tolerance despite treatment with ferrous fumarate. The patient attended with their spouse, who contributed to the history.

Findings: Previous blood results reportedly showed low haemoglobin and ferritin, with a microcytic, hypochromic pattern. No reported congenital anomalies, disproportionate short stature, neurodevelopmental concerns or other features to suggest a syndromic disorder. There is no known family history of a defined inherited anaemia. The patient reports tolerating ferrous fumarate without significant gastrointestinal adverse effects. No current bleeding history was identified in the information available for this review.

Interpretation: The clinical picture is most consistent with acquired iron deficiency. At present there is no convincing indication of a monogenic anaemia or broader genetic syndrome, and genetic testing is not recommended. The response to oral iron and the cause of ongoing iron loss or reduced absorption require confirmation through routine clinical assessment.

Plan: Repeat full blood count, ferritin, transferrin saturation and inflammatory markers through the GP. Review adherence and haemoglobin response to ferrous fumarate; investigate menstrual or gastrointestinal blood loss as clinically appropriate, with gastroenterology referral if indicated. If anaemia persists despite documented repletion or the indices become atypical, reconsider haemoglobinopathy testing and re-refer to Genetics/Haematology.

Follow-up: Results review in about 5 weeks, with earlier reassessment if symptoms worsen.

Several-week history of painless cervical lymphadenopathy, with drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss. No infective symptoms reported. Appetite reduced.

Well but tired-appearing. Palpable, non-tender cervical and supraclavicular nodes; no overlying erythema. Chest clear. No peripheral oedema. Abdomen soft, possible splenic tip palpable.

FBC with mild normocytic anaemia; inflammatory markers raised. Chest radiograph reviewed. Ultrasound neck demonstrates abnormal nodal architecture. Report/accession ID: L24K03073.

Lymphadenopathy concerning for Hodgkin lymphoma. Tissue diagnosis required; differential includes other lymphoproliferative disorder and infection.

Urgent suspected cancer pathway referral for haematology review and image-guided/core or excision biopsy. CT neck/chest/abdomen/pelvis requested. Bloods: repeat FBC, U&E, LFT, LDH, ESR, HIV and hepatitis screen with consent.

Supportive care pending tissue diagnosis. Encourage oral fluids and regular nutrition. Paracetamol as required; avoid steroids before biopsy unless clinically essential. Safety-netted regarding fever, breathlessness, rapidly enlarging nodes or inability to maintain intake.

Respiratory Medicine, COLWYN BAY COMMUNITY HOSPITAL

Your recent review was for a persistent burning discomfort behind the breastbone, acid coming up into the throat and a cough which is worse at night. The pattern remains most consistent with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. There were no features in today’s history to suggest an acute chest problem, and your breathing was comfortable at rest. Your sibling’s observations about the night-time cough were also helpful.

Please continue omeprazole 20 mg once daily. Take this regularly, ideally before breakfast, rather than only when symptoms are troublesome. You can continue the alginate suspension after meals and at bedtime when required, following the instructions on the bottle. Avoid eating for two to three hours before lying down, and raise the head end of the bed if night symptoms continue. Reducing large evening meals, alcohol, caffeine and foods that clearly trigger symptoms may help.

If there is no clear improvement after the planned treatment period, your GP can review adherence and consider further assessment, including referral for upper gastrointestinal investigation if clinically indicated. Please seek urgent help through NHS 111 or A&E for severe or exertional chest pain, difficulty swallowing, vomiting blood, black stools or marked breathlessness.

Dr Faiyaz Healey, MBBS

Dear Clinical Genetics Team,
NHS number: 0008021598

Re: T. Corbett

I would be grateful for your advice regarding whether this patient’s persistent lumbar radiculopathy warrants genetic assessment. They have ongoing low back pain with shooting pain down the leg and intermittent paraesthesia. The pattern has been treated as a mechanical nerve-root problem, although the duration and reported family history have prompted discussion about whether an inherited neuropathy should be considered.

T. Corbett remains mobile but finds prolonged sitting and lifting difficult. There is no reported progressive limb weakness or sphincter disturbance. Examination in the surgery showed reduced straight-leg raise on the symptomatic side, with altered sensation in a dermatomal distribution; power was broadly preserved. Lumbar imaging has not demonstrated a clear surgical lesion. Current treatment is naproxen with food and paracetamol as needed, alongside physiotherapy and advice on pacing activity. Symptoms have improved only partially.

Their adult child, hewan rowley, is described as having recurrent back and leg symptoms, though I do not have access to that person’s records. The family would like to understand whether this represents more than coincidental spinal disease and whether testing or wider neurology review would be appropriate. The patient works as:

Occupation: Chef
Employer: Catlodge Housing Association

A consultant neurologist has previously reviewed the presentation and considered lumbar radiculopathy the leading diagnosis; no definite inherited disorder has been identified.

Please advise on the relevance of the family history, any examination or records you require, and whether referral for genetic counselling or testing is indicated.

Yours sincerely,

Dr Eli REES, MBBS

Patient: D. Long  
MRN: 024334/33  
Occupation: Farmer  
Clinic: Whipton Hospital

Seen in the clinical genetics clinic regarding obstructive sleep apnoea and the possibility of an inherited contribution. The patient reports longstanding loud snoring, with witnessed apnoeas described by a sibling, and troublesome daytime somnolence. There is no history of developmental concerns, unusual facial features or other syndromic features identified during today’s review.

Continuous positive airway pressure is being used overnight. The patient reports improved sleep quality when the mask is tolerated, although adherence has been inconsistent because of nasal congestion and discomfort with the headgear. No recent admissions or episodes of driving while excessively sleepy were reported.

Examination was unremarkable apart from a crowded oropharyngeal airway. No dysmorphic features or focal neurological abnormalities noted. We discussed that obstructive sleep apnoea is usually multifactorial; the reported family history may reflect shared risk factors rather than a single-gene condition. On the information available, there is no indication for broad genetic testing at present.

Assessment: Obstructive sleep apnoea, treated with CPAP; family history noted. Daytime somnolence persists when CPAP is not used.

Plan: Continue CPAP and liaise with the sleep service regarding mask fit, humidification and adherence data. Avoid driving if sleepy. The patient will seek review sooner if symptoms worsen. Clinical genetics follow-up in about 12 weeks, with reconsideration of testing if additional syndromic features or a stronger family pattern emerges.

Signed by areesh mclean

Discharge summary

Patient: MYAR LOCKWOOD
Encounter date: 19/06/2045
Clinical area: Respiratory medicine

Reason for admission
Admitted with a five-day increase in breathlessness, audible wheeze and purulent green sputum, with reduced exercise tolerance despite regular salbutamol inhaler use. 49-year-old Pacific Islander female patient. Adult child, D. Bush, from MAYOBRIDGE, updated during the admission with the patient’s agreement.

Key findings
On arrival, tachypnoeic with widespread expiratory wheeze and oxygen saturations below usual baseline on air. Chest radiograph showed hyperinflation without focal consolidation. Blood tests demonstrated a mild inflammatory response; renal function remained satisfactory. Viral respiratory screen negative. No clinical evidence of pulmonary embolism or acute cardiac failure.

Treated as an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with controlled oxygen therapy, nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and doxycycline. Oxygen was weaned over the following days, with improvement in work of breathing and sputum colour. No requirement for non-invasive ventilation. Prednisolone course completed as prescribed; doxycycline to complete the remaining doses. Continue salbutamol inhaler as required, with spacer. Usual long-acting inhalers continued unchanged. Medication reconciliation completed and inhaler technique checked.

Problem list
• Acute infective COPD exacerbation — improved
• Wheeze and increased sputum production — resolving
• Previous tobacco exposure

Follow-up and advice
GP review requested for assessment of recovery and inhaler regimen. Respiratory clinic follow-up arranged in about 3 weeks. Please seek urgent medical attention for worsening breathlessness, inability to speak in sentences, chest pain, confusion or blue lips. Smoking cessation support reiterated.

Condition at discharge: clinically stable, eating and drinking, ambulant, home with family support.

Discharge summary

Patient: Lexi-Lea
Report/accession ID: 041922401
Discharging service: Aberdeen Royal Infirmary

Lexi-Lea was admitted via the emergency department with sudden breathlessness, sharp pleuritic chest pain and a fast pulse. CT pulmonary angiography confirmed bilateral pulmonary emboli, without radiological evidence of right-heart strain. Troponin was not significantly raised and routine blood tests were satisfactory. Oxygen saturations improved with supplemental oxygen and were maintained on room air before discharge. Current observations included blood pressure 120/80 mmHg.

Treatment and progress
Anticoagulation was started with apixaban. There was no bleeding during admission and the chest pain and breathlessness settled. No procedure was required. Please take apixaban 10 mg twice daily for the first 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily thereafter, unless another clinician advises you differently. Do not stop it without speaking to your GP or the anticoagulation team. Avoid ibuprofen and other anti-inflammatory painkillers unless specifically advised.

At discharge, you were walking independently, eating and drinking, and clinically stable. Seek urgent help via 999 for severe or worsening breathlessness, fainting, coughing blood, new severe chest pain, or significant bleeding.

Follow-up
Your GP should review anticoagulation, renal function and bleeding risk within the next few weeks. The respiratory team at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary will arrange outpatient review and assess the duration of treatment. A discharge copy has been provided for your records. Your spouse, who is based in Limekilns, may support you at home if needed.

Signed: Dr Ce BURT, MBBS

Presented with a 10-day increase in bilateral hand pain and swelling, associated with prolonged morning stiffness and marked fatigue. Symptoms are limiting grip and usual activities. Partner reports no recent injury, fever, rash, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms. Established rheumatoid arthritis under rheumatology follow-up. Current treatment includes methotrexate 15 mg once weekly, folic acid and naproxen; reports adherence. No recent steroid course.

Examination
Alert and clinically stable. Bilateral tender synovitis affecting the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints and proximal interphalangeal joints, more pronounced on the right. Reduced fist closure owing to pain. No erythema, fluctuance or focal skin breach. Wrists mildly tender with preserved passive movement. No large-joint effusion. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations unremarkable. Afebrile on assessment.

Investigations
Blood tests demonstrate inflammatory response with preserved renal function and no significant cytopenia. Plain radiographs of both hands show established erosive changes without acute fracture or dislocation.

Impression
Findings are consistent with an inflammatory rheumatoid arthritis flare. There is no clinical evidence of septic arthritis or acute traumatic pathology at present.

Plan
Discussed with the medical team at BODNANT MEDICAL CENTRE. Continue methotrexate and folic acid as prescribed. Naproxen to continue with food, subject to usual gastrointestinal and renal precautions. Arrange expedited rheumatology review for disease-modifying treatment assessment; GP to repeat inflammatory markers and medication monitoring bloods. Return to A&E urgently for fever, rapidly progressive swelling, systemic deterioration or inability to use the hand.

Signed: lacey-maye corbett

Clinical Genetics outpatient review

Seen with partner for discussion of the genetic aspects of Parkinson disease. The diagnosis was made previously following assessment by neurology and remains clinically established. Current symptoms are predominantly a right-sided resting tremor, slowness of movement and muscular rigidity, with some fluctuation before the next dose. No reported cognitive decline, hallucinations or significant swallowing difficulty. Mobility remains independent, although turning in bed and getting started after sitting are slower than previously.

Medication reconciliation confirms co-beneldopa, prescribed and continued in primary care following specialist review. No recent changes or adverse effects reported. Examination today showed mild hypomimia and bradykinesia with a resting tremor, increased tone in both upper limbs and a short-stepped gait. Speech was clear. No dyskinesia observed during the consultation.

We discussed that most Parkinson disease is multifactorial, but that an inherited contribution can occasionally be identified, particularly where there is a strong or early family history. The available family history was reviewed with the patient and partner; further details from relatives may be useful before deciding on testing. Genetic testing, including the limitations of a negative result and possible implications for relatives, was explained. The patient wishes to consider this and will contact the service if they would like to proceed.

Assessment: Established Parkinson disease, currently managed with co-beneldopa; genetic counselling provided.

Plan: Continue current medication and neurology follow-up. Discuss medication and multidisciplinary review with the GP/neurology team. Review appointment arranged for 2021-02-28.

Dear Cardiology Colleague,

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus, referred to clarify whether recent exertional fatigue represents occult cardiovascular disease and to advise on further cardiac investigation and risk-factor management.

The patient reports increased thirst, frequent urination and fatigue for 3 days. There is no reported syncope or sustained chest pain. A friend has noticed reduced exercise tolerance over recent weeks. Examination in the surgery: clinically euvolaemic, pulse regular, blood pressure above usual surgery readings, heart sounds normal with no murmur, and chest clear. No peripheral oedema.

Recent blood tests showed raised HbA1c and fasting glucose, with preserved renal function and normal haemoglobin. An ECG recorded in the surgery demonstrated sinus rhythm without acute ST-segment change. The symptoms may be related to suboptimal glycaemic control, although the reduction in exercise tolerance warrants cardiovascular review given the diabetes-related risk profile.

Current medication is metformin and atorvastatin. Metformin adherence was discussed, and dietary measures and home glucose monitoring have been reinforced. The patient has been advised to seek urgent assessment via A&E if chest pain, breathlessness at rest, collapse or rapidly worsening symptoms develop.

Please assess cardiovascular risk, consider echocardiography and/or functional testing as clinically indicated, and advise whether optimisation of lipid and diabetes management is required from a cardiovascular perspective. A follow-up review is arranged for 18th December 2045.

Yours sincerely,

BAREERA JARVIS
Referral clinician

Dear Community Paediatrics Team,

Re: Llewellyn G., 15 y/o

I would be grateful for your assessment of this adolescent with iron-deficiency anaemia, particularly to clarify the cause of persistent symptoms and advise on further investigation and management. They describe ongoing tiredness, intermittent dizziness and reduced exercise tolerance, with a more noticeable episode of light-headedness for 3 days. There has been no collapse, chest pain or reported breathlessness at rest.

Recent primary-care blood tests showed microcytic anaemia with depleted iron stores. Ferrous fumarate has been started, but symptomatic improvement has been limited. Adherence and administration have been discussed, including avoiding concurrent tea or milk where possible. Menstrual history suggests regular bleeding, without reported flooding; dietary intake is variable. No gastrointestinal symptoms or weight loss have been reported.

The history was taken with the patient and their mother, CHELSEA-ROSE VERNON, present for part of the consultation. The patient was able to discuss their health privately and agreed to referral. Examination in surgery was reassuring apart from mild conjunctival pallor; observations were stable, with no clinical evidence of cardiac failure or acute neurological deficit.

Assessment:
Iron-deficiency anaemia with ongoing fatigue, dizziness and reduced exercise tolerance despite initial oral iron treatment. The underlying source of iron depletion remains uncertain.

Plan/request:
Please review the diagnosis, response to ferrous fumarate and need for repeat full blood count and ferritin. I would also appreciate advice regarding dietary assessment, menstrual management and whether coeliac screening or further paediatric investigation is indicated.

Yours faithfully,

S. Woolley
GP, DROMARA

Discharge summary

Patient: Sway
Discharging service: ROYAL VICTORIA HOSPITAL
Report/accession ID: 04462978

Reason for admission
Presented to A&E with sudden central chest pressure, diaphoresis and nausea. Initial ECG showed dynamic lateral ST-segment depression. Serial high-sensitivity troponin demonstrated a significant rise and fall, consistent with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). Monitored on Model X3 cardiac monitor; no sustained arrhythmia recorded.

Hospital course
Managed medically following cardiology review. Given aspirin and fondaparinux, with symptom resolution and no further chest pain. Coronary angiography was discussed; after assessment of the clinical picture and procedural risk, cardiology advised conservative management during this admission. Echocardiogram showed mildly impaired left ventricular systolic function with regional hypokinesia. Renal function remained stable and there was no clinical heart failure.

Problem list
• Medically managed NSTEMI
• Hypertension
• Hyperlipidaemia
• Mild left ventricular systolic impairment

Discharge medicines
Aspirin 75 mg once daily, lifelong.
Clopidogrel 75 mg once daily for 12 months, unless stopped earlier by cardiology.
Atorvastatin 80 mg at night.
Bisoprolol 2.5 mg once daily, commenced during admission.
GTN spray as needed for chest pain; use as instructed on the label.

Fondaparinux discontinued at discharge. Please do not take additional over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medicines without checking with the GP or pharmacist.

Condition and follow-up
Mobilising independently, haemodynamically stable and pain-free at discharge. Cardiology follow-up and cardiac rehabilitation referral arranged through ROYAL VICTORIA HOSPITAL. GP to repeat renal profile, liver function and lipid profile, and review blood pressure and tolerance of medication.

Return to A&E immediately for recurrent or prolonged chest pain, breathlessness, collapse or marked deterioration. Discharge plan explained and understood.

Signed: Dr Abdur-Rehman Godfrey, MBBS, Consultant Physician
GMC: 0638416

Dear Respiratory Medicine Team,
NHS number: 000 996 0385

Re: K. Fawcett
MRN: 00022266

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient’s persistent exertional breathlessness in the context of atrial fibrillation. The specific question is whether there is a co-existing respiratory disorder contributing to the reduced exercise tolerance, and whether further pulmonary investigation is indicated.

There are intermittent palpitations, fatigue and breathlessness on walking uphill or at a faster pace. No recent infective exacerbation has been reported. Examination in primary care showed an irregular pulse with acceptable rate control and clear breath sounds bilaterally. Oxygen saturations were satisfactory at rest; there was no peripheral oedema. A recent chest radiograph was reported as showing no focal consolidation or pleural effusion. Routine blood tests did not identify anaemia or a significant inflammatory response.

Atrial fibrillation has previously been assessed in the usual cardiology pathway. Current medication is apixaban 5 mg twice daily and bisoprolol, with no reported bleeding or postural symptoms. Despite rate control, the breathlessness remains troublesome and is limiting usual activities. There is no clear clinical evidence of decompensated heart failure at present, although cardiac contribution should remain under review.

Please advise regarding spirometry, full pulmonary function testing and any additional imaging or respiratory follow-up you consider appropriate. I will continue current treatment pending your opinion and ask the patient to seek urgent assessment if breathlessness becomes acute or occurs at rest.

Referring clinician: Badar ATKINS
Queen Elizabeth University Hospital

Planned primary care review: 24 May 1996

Accident and Emergency Laboratory Report

Patient: EBBA DALE
MRN: 043447/77
Contact: 07700 900094
Specimen: ED venous blood, serum
Clinical details: Acute painful, swollen and erythematous first metatarsophalangeal joint. Query gout flare. Naproxen and colchicine reported.

Results
Urate: 0.52 mmol/L (reference interval 0.21–0.42 mmol/L) — high
C-reactive protein: 68 mg/L (0–5 mg/L) — high
White cell count: 12.8 ×10^9/L (4.0–11.0 ×10^9/L) — high
Neutrophils: 10.4 ×10^9/L (2.0–7.5 ×10^9/L) — high
Creatinine: 96 µmol/L (45–90 µmol/L) — mildly high
eGFR: 78 mL/min/1.73 m²
Alanine transaminase: 24 U/L (0–40 U/L)
Aspartate transaminase: 22 U/L (0–40 U/L)

Interpretation
Hyperuricaemia with an inflammatory response, in keeping with the reported acute monoarthritis and clinically suspected gout flare. Serum urate may be normal during an acute attack; the raised result supports, but does not independently establish, the diagnosis. The neutrophilia and CRP elevation are non-specific. If fever, systemic deterioration or atypical joint features develop, urgent assessment for septic arthritis is indicated, with joint aspiration for microscopy, culture and crystal examination where clinically appropriate.

Renal function is mildly reduced; interpret colchicine and NSAID use alongside hydration status, comorbidity and concurrent medicines. Please review analgesic response and renal profile with the GP. Repeat urate when clinically settled and assess for longer-term urate-lowering treatment. Follow-up planned 29 Apr 2004, in about 11 weeks.

Validated and reported by: ADORA ARCHER

Paediatric Dermatology Outpatient Review

Patient: Xaiya M.
DOB/clinical details: 16 y/o
Home address: 143 White Farm Close, Clevedon, BS21 5AB
Education: Cringles Secondary School
Accompanied by aunt, R. Alam

Reviewed with the patient and her aunt regarding ongoing atopic eczema. Flares mainly affect the antecubital fossae, neck and hands, with itching worse overnight and some sleep disturbance. She reports dry, inflamed skin but no weeping, crusting or fever. Emollient is being applied most days; topical hydrocortisone is used during flares, although application has been inconsistent when symptoms improve. No new soaps or prescribed medicines.

Weight recorded as 54.0 kg. Well appearing. Dry eczematous plaques with mild erythema in both antecubital fossae and over the dorsal hands. Excoriations present, without fissuring, pustules or evidence of bacterial infection. No facial or periocular involvement.

Atopic eczema, currently mild to moderate, with nocturnal pruritus and sleep disruption. No clinical evidence of infection today.

Discussed regular liberal emollient use at least twice daily and after washing, including on clear skin. Continue topical hydrocortisone thinly to active areas for short flare treatment as previously advised, avoiding eyes and broken skin. Reviewed fingertip-unit application and the importance of continuing emollient between flares. Keep nails short and consider cotton clothing for sleep.

Aunt and patient advised to contact the GP if spreading redness, pain, weeping or fever develops. Review in paediatric dermatology if control remains poor despite consistent treatment; otherwise follow up with the GP. Patient involved in the discussion and agreed with the plan.

Clinical context: aged 4 years; early-childhood patient
Home address: 33 Kinneil Drive, Inbhir Aora / Inveraray, PA32 8AA

Admission reason:
Generalised convulsion with fever at home, followed by postictal drowsiness. First reported febrile seizure. No further events in hospital.

Assessment:
On arrival, heart rate 108 beats/minute. Febrile but maintaining airway; no focal neurological deficit after recovery. Hydration and feeding improved during observation.

Investigations:
Capillary glucose normal. Urinalysis unremarkable. No clinical focus of bacterial infection identified. Blood tests and imaging not indicated following senior review.

Observed on paediatric ward. Returned to usual interaction and oral intake. Temperature settled with comfort measures. No recurrent seizure activity. Parent Cybil updated and able to repeat seizure first-aid steps.

Antipyretic comfort measures as required for distress or fever; not prescribed to prevent further seizures. No regular anticonvulsant.

Place child on side, remove nearby hazards, note duration, and do not put anything in the mouth during a seizure. Call 999 if seizure lasts 5 minutes or more, breathing remains abnormal, or recovery is not occurring. Return to A&E if concerned.

Follow-up:
GP review if fever persists or further episodes occur. Paediatric follow-up not routinely required after this uncomplicated event.

Discharge summary

Patient: Shakirah Rodgers
MRN: 0222886
Discharging service: Queen Elizabeth University Hospital

Admitted via A&E with sudden breathlessness, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and palpitations. Initial observations showed tachycardia and mild hypoxia requiring low-flow supplemental oxygen. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia. CT pulmonary angiogram confirmed bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli, without right ventricular strain. Troponin was negative and routine blood tests were otherwise satisfactory, including an acceptable renal function for anticoagulation.

The patient remained haemodynamically stable throughout admission. Oxygen was weaned off before discharge, with satisfactory saturations on air at rest and after mobilisation. No bleeding was reported. The case was reviewed with the medical team and anticoagulation commenced with apixaban 5 mg twice daily. No thrombolysis or invasive procedure was indicated.

Assessment: Provoked pulmonary embolism, clinically improved. Suitable for ambulatory management with anticoagulation.

Plan on discharge:
Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily as prescribed; do not stop without advice. GP to review anticoagulation within one week and confirm intended duration, currently planned for at least three months subject to review. Please arrange repeat full blood count and renal profile through the surgery. A friend in Ballifeary has been advised of the discharge plan with the patient’s consent.

Return to A&E urgently for worsening breathlessness, fainting, haemoptysis, chest pain, or significant bleeding. Avoid NSAIDs unless specifically advised and seek advice before starting new medicines.

Discharged home in stable condition with written anticoagulation information.

Prepared and signed by ALBE HEWITT, on behalf of the discharging team.

Nurse: KALEAB BOWDEN

Cardiology clinic note

Patient: Zaihan G.  
Contact: zaihan.gibbs94@btinternet.com  
Clinical age: 35 y/o

Seen with their partner for cardiovascular assessment following referral from the haematology pathway. The current diagnosis is Hodgkin lymphoma, with supportive care pending tissue diagnosis. They report several weeks of painless lymphadenopathy, drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss. No exertional chest pain, syncope or sustained palpitations. Breathlessness only when climbing stairs, without orthopnoea or ankle swelling.

They have no known previous cardiac disease. Not taking regular medicines apart from supportive treatment advised by the oncology team. No drug allergies documented. Examination: comfortable at rest; pulse regular, heart sounds normal, no added sounds. Chest clear bilaterally and no peripheral oedema. Blood pressure was satisfactory in clinic.

A 12-lead ECG showed sinus rhythm with no acute ST-T change. Echocardiogram requested as a baseline assessment before any systemic treatment is commenced. The patient understands that treatment decisions remain with the haematology team and that tissue confirmation is awaited.

Assessment: No clinical evidence of heart failure or active ischaemia today. Baseline cardiac imaging appropriate in view of Hodgkin lymphoma management planning.

Plan: Arrange transthoracic echocardiogram and review the result electronically. Continue supportive care pending tissue diagnosis. Advised to attend A&E for new severe breathlessness, collapse or persistent chest pain. Cardiology follow-up appointment booked for 19th September 2026.

Report/accession ID: L27H72303

GP to review within 1 week. Anticoagulation clinic referral completed. Clinical Genetics outpatient review requested; bring relevant family history and any previous clotting results. Discharge medicines and written information provided.

Paediatric Laboratory Medicine – Interpretive Report

Patient: Fuzail
MRN: 061184475
Clinical context: The patient, aged 16 years, was reviewed following 24 hours of vomiting and diarrhoea with reduced urine output. History provided by the legal guardian. Oral rehydration solution and supportive care commenced.

Specimens: Venous blood and urine submitted for assessment of hydration status and renal function.

Results
Sodium: 136 mmol/L (reference interval 135–145)
Potassium: 4.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.0)
Chloride: 101 mmol/L (95–108)
Bicarbonate: 19 mmol/L (22–29)
Urea: 8.6 mmol/L (2.5–7.8)
Creatinine: 78 µmol/L (45–90)
Glucose: 5.2 mmol/L (3.5–7.8)
CRP: 12 mg/L (<5)
Haemoglobin: 143 g/L (120–160)
White cell count: 10.8 ×10^9/L (4.0–11.0)
Urine specific gravity: 1.030 (1.005–1.030)
Urine ketones: 1+
Urine blood, protein, nitrite and leucocytes: negative

Interpretation
Mildly reduced bicarbonate with borderline elevation of urea and concentrated urine, consistent with reduced intake and mild dehydration in the clinical context. Creatinine and glucose are within the stated reference intervals. Mild CRP elevation is non-specific and may accompany acute gastroenteritis. No laboratory evidence of significant renal impairment or urinary tract infection.

Clinical comment
Continue frequent oral rehydration in small volumes, with monitoring of urine output and tolerance of fluids. Emergency assessment is indicated if unable to retain fluids, becoming drowsy, developing bloody diarrhoea, or passing markedly less urine. Repeat U&E if symptoms persist or clinical status deteriorates. Laboratory review planned in about 7 weeks, on 12 Mar 1988, if clinically required.

Validated by: ABDISAMAD CRANE

Continue phototherapy and prescribed feeds; record intake/output and feeding tolerance. Check bilirubin result, repeat observations, support parent with feeds, and update neonatal team if not improving.

General Medicine – Hereditary Cancer Risk Assessment

Patient: Ingo D.
Occupation: Sales assistant
Employer: Bell Hill Town Council
Address: 113 St Gregory's Court, Birmingham, B19 1AA
Contact: 07700 900263

Reason for review: Significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer, with concern regarding personal future risk and request for predictive genetic testing.

History:
The patient reports a sibling previously investigated through the regional genetics service following breast cancer in the family. A familial pathogenic BRCA1 variant has been discussed, recorded as BRCA1 c.68_69delAG. The patient has not previously undergone germline testing and is currently receiving no treatment. No personal history of breast or ovarian malignancy is reported. The patient is seeking clarification of inherited risk and the implications of a positive result for surveillance and relatives.

Assessment:
The reported pedigree is potentially consistent with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome. The specific variant requires confirmation against the affected relative’s laboratory report before predictive testing is undertaken. Risk interpretation cannot be finalised from the verbal history alone.

Plan:
The patient will obtain consent for release of the affected relative’s genetic report, if available. Following confirmation of the familial variant and formal three-generation pedigree review, offer targeted predictive testing with pre- and post-test counselling. Discussion included possible positive, negative or uninformative results; implications for breast and ovarian cancer surveillance; and the potential relevance to biological relatives. No change to routine clinical management is advised pending genetics assessment. The patient was advised to contact the GP surgery if new breast or ovarian symptoms arise, rather than waiting for genetic testing.

Impression: Appropriate referral to the NHS clinical genetics service for verification of the familial result and predictive-testing pathway.

Keep wounds clean and dry; showering permitted as advised by the surgical team. Avoid strenuous activity until reviewed. Return to A&E for increasing abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fever, wound redness or discharge, or inability to tolerate fluids. GP review if concerns.

Follow-up
Paediatric surgical telephone review arranged according to local pathway; histology result to be reviewed by the surgical service. Guardian present for discharge discussion; adolescent involved in consent and instructions.

Discharging clinician: Dr Britnie Church, MBBS

Discharge summary – Cardiology assessment

Prabh was admitted with a 2-day history of right flank pain, dysuria and shaking rigors. Initial observations showed fever and tachycardia. Urine dipstick was positive for nitrites and leucocytes; subsequent culture grew a susceptible Gram-negative bacillus. Blood cultures remained negative. C-reactive protein 86 mg/L, with mild neutrophilia and preserved renal function. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis or obstructing calculus.

Treated with intravenous cefuroxime and fluids, with regular paracetamol for pain and fever. Symptoms and inflammatory markers improved over the following 48 hours, and she remained haemodynamically stable without further rigors. Antibiotics were changed to oral cefuroxime to complete the planned course. No operative intervention was required.

At discharge, afebrile, eating and drinking, passing urine normally and mobilising independently. Flank tenderness has largely resolved. Discharge medicines: cefuroxime as prescribed to complete the course; paracetamol as needed for pain or fever. No other medication changes were made.

Assessment: acute pyelonephritis, clinically improved with antimicrobial treatment. There was no evidence of sepsis or urinary tract obstruction during admission.

Plan: GP review arranged through ABERDEEN ROYAL INFIRMARY if symptoms do not continue to settle. Repeat urine testing is not required if fully asymptomatic, but should be considered for recurrent symptoms. Seek urgent medical attention for recurrent rigors, persistent vomiting, worsening flank pain, confusion or reduced urine output.

JANNATUN MOODY, her partner from Harpsdale, was updated regarding the discharge plan. Follow-up appointment: 21st June 2019.

Loud snoring and witnessed apnoeas reported by spouse. Wakes unrefreshed, with morning headache for 3 days. Daytime somnolence, including nodding off when watching television. No exertional chest pain, syncope or ankle swelling. Palpitations occasional, brief, non-sustained.

Treatment: Continuous positive airway pressure in use. Reports wearing mask most nights; occasional leak and dry mouth. Nocturnal symptoms improved when worn. Device download not available today.

Examination:
Alert, orientated. Pulse regular. BP acceptable in clinic. Heart sounds normal, no murmur. Chest clear. No peripheral oedema.

Assessment:
Obstructive sleep apnoea with residual daytime somnolence. Cardiovascular risk discussed in context of untreated or suboptimally treated disease.

Plan:
Continue continuous positive airway pressure every night and for naps. Contact sleep service regarding mask fit, humidification and download review. Avoid driving if sleepy; patient understands. Check CPAP adherence and symptom response at follow-up. GP to review blood pressure and cardiovascular risk factors. Return sooner for chest pain, syncope or sustained palpitations.

A&E Paediatric Assessment

Patient: Sajeev
DOB: 26th April 2016
Accompanied by legal guardian, kyarna coulson, who provides the history.

Presented with approximately 18 hours of abdominal pain, initially central and now localised to the right lower quadrant. Nausea and loss of appetite; no diarrhoea. One episode of vomiting at home. Passing urine normally. No previous abdominal surgery or significant medical history reported.

Alert but uncomfortable, prefers to lie still. Temperature 38.1°C, pulse 112, blood pressure 108/68, oxygen saturations 99% on air. Abdomen soft with focal right lower-quadrant tenderness, guarding and pain on movement. No generalised peritonism. Chest clear, heart sounds normal. Glasgow Coma Scale 15.

Bloods show raised inflammatory markers and neutrophilia. Urinalysis negative for blood and nitrites. Ultrasound demonstrates a non-compressible blind-ending tubular structure in the right iliac fossa, measuring 8 mm, with surrounding inflammatory change; appearances consistent with acute appendicitis.

Assessment: acute appendicitis, clinically stable. Discussed findings and likely need for laparoscopic appendicectomy with kyarna coulson, including anaesthetic and operative risks. Guardian understands and agrees to treatment. Paediatric surgical team at DORKING GENERAL HOSPITAL contacted and accepted the patient for admission.

Paracetamol given with partial improvement. Kept nil by mouth, intravenous fluids commenced and intravenous co-amoxiclav administered. Cannula patent; observations ongoing. No oral intake pending surgical review.

Transferred to the paediatric surgical ward with guardian accompanying. Surgical review arranged for 02/02/2027.

Thirst, fatigue and frequent urination at presentation. Type 2 diabetes mellitus currently managed in primary care. Taking metformin 500 mg twice daily with food and atorvastatin. Reports good adherence; no recent hypoglycaemia. Friend attended with patient and provided collateral history.

Well appearing, orientated. No acute distress. Weight trend reviewed in record. Feet warm with intact skin; no reported neuropathic symptoms.

1. Type 2 diabetes mellitus — suboptimal recent control.

Continue metformin and atorvastatin pending GP review. Arrange updated HbA1c, renal profile, urine ACR and lipid profile. Patient to obtain family diabetes diagnoses and treatment history. Discussed that genetic testing is not indicated until the pedigree and biochemical data are reviewed.

Dr Barez Shahid, MBBS

MOLECULAR GENETICS REPORT

Patient: Taras
Address: 159 Welcomb Street, London, SE10 0AA
Report/accession ID: L21O08674
Specimen: Peripheral blood in EDTA
Collection/report date: 1988-12-24
Test requested: Predictive germline testing for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk

Clinical information:
Significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer. Predictive testing requested following genetic counselling. No current treatment reported.

Analysis:
DNA extracted from the submitted blood specimen. Next-generation sequencing and copy-number analysis performed for BRCA1, BRCA2 and other genes associated with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer predisposition. Variant assessment undertaken against current laboratory and clinical databases.

Result:
No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant identified in the genes examined.

The familial BRCA1 c.68_69delAG variant was not detected in this specimen.

Interpretation:
This is a true negative result for the specified familial variant, assuming the reported family variant is accurately established and the tested individual is biologically related to the affected relative. The result substantially reduces the likelihood of inherited risk associated with that variant; it does not exclude cancer risk arising from other genetic or non-genetic factors.

Recommendation:
Result to be reviewed with the referring genetics service. Screening and risk management should be guided by the confirmed family history and national guidance. Further testing may be appropriate if the family variant has not previously been verified or if additional clinically significant cancers are reported in the pedigree. Genetic counselling is recommended before communicating the result to relatives.

Validated and authorised by:
jimmy-lee senior
Laboratory reporting clinician

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report
National Insurance number: GB802711D

Patient: Ella-Joy S.
MRN: H1706688
Requesting service: Royal Blackburn Hospital
Specimen: Peripheral blood, EDTA
Report date: 13th September 2022
Test: Predictive analysis for familial BRCA1 variant

Clinical indication:
Significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer. Predictive testing requested following identification of BRCA1 c.68_69delAG in a sibling. The patient reports concern regarding personal cancer risk. No current treatment.

Laboratory findings:
Targeted analysis identified the familial BRCA1 c.68_69delAG variant in the submitted specimen. The variant is present in the heterozygous state.

Interpretation:
This result is consistent with a pathogenic BRCA1 variant and confirms an increased inherited risk of breast, ovarian, fallopian tube and primary peritoneal cancer. The finding is not diagnostic of cancer. Management should be guided by the relevant NHS clinical genetics or specialist oncology service, including discussion of enhanced surveillance and risk-reducing options as appropriate.

This targeted result does not exclude other pathogenic variants in BRCA1 or in additional cancer-predisposition genes. It should be interpreted alongside the family history and, where relevant, confirmation of the familial variant in the affected relative.

Recommendation:
Genetic counselling is advised to discuss implications for the patient and biological relatives. Relatives should not use this report as a substitute for an individually requested laboratory test. Please ensure the family variant and nomenclature are reviewed at the next genetics appointment.

Validated and authorised by:
B. Kirby
Clinical Genetics Laboratory
Royal Blackburn Hospital

Department: Accident and Emergency
Encounter: Same-day assessment

Presenting complaint:
Sudden episode of pounding heartbeat with central chest tightness and intense fear of dying while at work. Onset at rest, peaked within minutes, settled before arrival. No collapse, pleuritic pain or unilateral leg swelling. Reports similar, shorter episodes over recent weeks.

Background:
No known cardiac history documented. No regular medication. Emergency contact details confirmed. Denies alcohol excess or recreational drug use on this occasion.

Observations/examination:
Alert, speaking full sentences, mildly anxious initially. Chest clear bilaterally. Heart sounds normal, regular pulse at review. No calf tenderness or focal neurological deficit. ECG: sinus rhythm, no acute ischaemic change. Troponin and routine blood tests reassuring. Chest radiograph not indicated clinically.

Assessment:
Panic attack with palpitations and chest tightness. Acute coronary syndrome and significant arrhythmia unlikely following assessment; symptoms resolved without medication.

Action:
Reassurance and explanation provided. Breathing retraining practised in department and written technique supplied. Advised to avoid excess caffeine and seek urgent review via A&E/999 for persistent chest pain, syncope or severe breathlessness.

Follow-up:
GP review in 14 days to assess recurrence, anxiety symptoms and need for talking-therapy referral. Patient agreeable; emergency contact aware of plan.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY – CARDIOLOGY

Patient: ayshah moon
Responsible service: ABERDEEN ROYAL INFIRMARY
Admission reason: Sudden breathlessness, pleuritic right-sided chest pain and tachycardia. CT pulmonary angiogram confirmed bilateral pulmonary emboli without CT evidence of right-heart strain.

Key results
• ECG: sinus tachycardia.
• Troponin mildly raised but falling; echocardiogram with preserved right and left ventricular systolic function.
• Lower-limb Doppler: no proximal DVT identified.
• Oxygen saturations improved on low-flow supplemental oxygen; weaned to room air before discharge.
• Pain score at review: 5/10.

Hospital course
Treated initially with therapeutic anticoagulation and supplemental oxygen. Haemodynamically stable throughout; no thrombolysis or thrombectomy required. Renal function remained suitable for direct oral anticoagulant therapy. Bleeding risk and anticoagulant precautions discussed with the patient and friend. Carver, who lives in Kyle of Lochalsh, was present for the discharge discussion with the patient’s agreement.

Discharge medicines
• Apixaban 10 mg twice daily to complete the initial treatment phase, then 5 mg twice daily as advised on the discharge prescription.
• Stop any over-the-counter NSAIDs unless specifically agreed with a clinician.
• No oxygen required at home.

Follow-up / actions
GP review requested for anticoagulation and assessment of provoking factors. Haematology/anticoagulation clinic appointment arranged for 10th September 1996. Return to A&E for worsening breathlessness, syncope, haemoptysis or significant bleeding. Stable and ambulant at discharge.

National Insurance number: TN496118B

Patient: Lexie-Jay
Report/accession ID: 05320206
Referring service: Bft Southmead Cheltenham General Hospital
Occupation: Chef

Reason for review: assessment of possible inherited thyroid disease in the context of treated hypothyroidism and a reported family history provided by the patient’s adult child.

Clinical findings: Persistent fatigue and cold intolerance despite levothyroxine. Constipation has been present for 3 days, without abdominal pain or vomiting. No reported neck swelling, dysphagia or change in voice. Medication reconciliation confirms levothyroxine; adherence and administration apart from food were discussed. Examination today shows a clinically euthyroid appearance, no palpable thyroid enlargement and no cervical lymphadenopathy. Skin is mildly dry. Neurological examination is non-focal.

Interpretation: The current symptoms are compatible with suboptimal thyroid replacement, although the short duration of constipation may be intercurrent. There are no syndromic physical features or examination findings to suggest a defined monogenic thyroid disorder at this assessment. A genetic contribution cannot be excluded without clarification of the family history and review of previous thyroid function results.

Plan: Obtain historical TSH and free T4 results from primary care and confirm the original indication for levothyroxine. Repeat thyroid function testing through the GP surgery before altering the dose. The patient will seek review if constipation persists or if compressive neck symptoms develop. Further genetic testing is not recommended at present; reconsider if multiple relatives have confirmed early-onset or congenital thyroid disease.

Report prepared and signed by N. Owens.

Address: 93 CARNRALLA PARK, CARRICKMORE

Employer: LURGAN Secondary School

Reason for referral:
Please assess recurrent migraine with recent change in pattern and advise on preventive management.

Unilateral throbbing headache, predominantly left-sided, for 3 days. Associated nausea and photophobia; no fever, neck stiffness, head injury or focal weakness. Similar episodes over the past year, increasing in frequency. No visual loss or collapse reported.

Current treatment:
Sumatriptan used at onset with partial relief. Naproxen also taken. No regular preventive medication. Occasional vomiting but tolerating small amounts of fluid.

Alert and orientated. Speech clear. Pupils equal and reactive; ocular movements full. No facial asymmetry or limb drift. Sensation grossly intact. No meningism. Observations stable. Pregnancy status checked and negative.

Capillary glucose normal. Treated with antiemetic and oral fluids, with improvement in nausea. Analgesia reviewed; advised not to exceed recommended triptan or NSAID use.

Neurology review of recurrent migraine, consideration of prophylaxis, and confirmation of need for outpatient imaging or further investigation. GP follow-up for interim medication review.

Referring clinician: EWAEN WHITAKER

Discharge summary – Respiratory Medicine

Patient: Aarjan
Clinical age group: 68 y/o
Admission/report date: 23/07/2012
Source of history: patient and partner, earnest thorpe of Strangford

Reason for admission
Presented to A&E with sudden breathlessness, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and palpitations. Initial ECG showed sinus tachycardia. Oxygen saturations were reduced on air and supplemental oxygen was commenced.

Key results
CT pulmonary angiogram demonstrated bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli, with no CT evidence of right heart strain. Lower-limb venous Doppler did not show deep-vein thrombosis. Troponin was negative and routine blood tests were satisfactory, including stable renal function. No provoking factor identified during admission; history reviewed for recent surgery, immobility, malignancy and hormone therapy.

Hospital course
Reviewed by the respiratory team, including the consultant respiratory physician. Remained haemodynamically stable throughout and did not require thrombolysis or ventilatory support. Pleuritic pain improved with simple analgesia. Oxygen was weaned before discharge; ambulatory saturations remained satisfactory on air. Apixaban started for treatment of pulmonary embolism following discussion of bleeding precautions and adherence.

Problem list
1. Bilateral segmental pulmonary embolism, currently stable.
2. Acute hypoxaemia, resolved.
3. Pleuritic chest pain, improved.

Discharge medicines
Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily. Continue as prescribed until reviewed; duration to be confirmed by the anticoagulation/respiratory team. Paracetamol as required for pain. No ongoing home oxygen required.

Follow-up and advice
Discharge home today in stable condition. GP to review within 1–2 weeks, including bleeding risk and medication reconciliation. Respiratory clinic follow-up requested at approximately three months to assess anticoagulation duration and consider investigation for an unprovoked event. Avoid NSAIDs unless specifically advised. Seek urgent medical attention for worsening breathlessness, syncope, haemoptysis, significant bleeding or recurrent severe chest pain.

A&E Emergency Assessment
NHS number: 0008762814

Patient: Aliki N.
MRN: 036424327
Address: 154 Glass's Rocks Lane, Wombwell, S73 0AA
Contact: 07700 900730
Accompanied by spouse, Chantel Blair

Presenting complaint:
Sudden severe pain and swelling of the right first metatarsophalangeal joint since overnight. Increasing erythema, difficulty weight-bearing. Similar episodes previously; no trauma. Spouse reports no fever, rigors or vomiting.

Background:
Known gout. Current treatment includes colchicine and naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food. No recent antibiotics or operative procedures reported.

Observations:
Alert, uncomfortable. Afebrile. Haemodynamically stable. NEWS2 0.

Examination:
Right great toe markedly swollen, erythematous and warm, with exquisite tenderness over the first MTP joint. Reduced movement secondary to pain. No wound, lymphangitis or skin break. Calf soft and non-tender. Peripheral pulses and sensation intact.

Investigations:
FBC and CRP requested; renal profile checked before further NSAID treatment. Results not suggestive of significant systemic infection. Uric acid not required during acute attack. Clinical picture most consistent with acute gout flare; septic arthritis considered less likely in absence of fever or systemic upset, but safety-netted.

Treatment/action:
Oral analgesia given in department with improvement. Continue colchicine as previously prescribed; avoid additional NSAIDs until renal results reviewed. Rest, elevate and apply wrapped ice pack. GP review for urate-lowering therapy assessment after flare settles.

Disposition:
Discharged home with spouse. Return urgently for fever, spreading redness, worsening pain or inability to mobilise.

Dear Cardiology Team,
National Insurance number: BG 14 13 70 C

Re: RAJEEV ULLAH

Clinical question: please assess recurrent palpitations and intermittent chest tightness, and advise whether cardiac investigation is indicated or whether symptoms are most consistent with anxiety.

RAJEEV ULLAH has established generalised anxiety disorder with persistent worry, poor sleep and marked muscle tension. Despite ongoing psychological symptoms, they have recently reported episodes of a rapid, forceful heartbeat with light-headedness and central chest tightness. The latest episode occurred for 3 days, without syncope or exertional collapse. Symptoms appear more prominent during periods of heightened worry, although the relationship is not sufficiently clear to exclude an arrhythmia.

Examination in the surgery: pulse regular at 84 bpm, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, oxygen saturation 98% on air. Heart sounds normal, no murmur or clinical heart failure. Chest clear. Resting ECG showed sinus rhythm with no acute ST-segment or T-wave abnormality. Recent blood tests, including full blood count, U&Es and thyroid function, were unremarkable.

Sertraline is taken regularly. No recent dose change. Sleep remains poor, and muscle tension is persistent. RODNEY MILNE, their sibling, reports that the patient has become increasingly preoccupied with the possibility of serious heart disease and is avoiding usual activities.

I would be grateful for cardiology review, consideration of ambulatory ECG monitoring and further assessment of the chest symptoms. Advice regarding reassurance and safe continuation of activity would also be helpful.

Referring clinician: Dr Cesar LAWRENCE, MBBS

Plan: Admit to cardiology under Mitchell Best at WITHYBUSH GENERAL HOSPITAL for IV diuresis, telemetry and echocardiogram. Reassess renal function and electrolytes tomorrow.

Clinical Genetics Referral
NHS number: 0005961672

Date: 5th December 2025
Report/accession ID: L25J87847

Patient: briony andrews
Referring organisation: Altnagelvin Area Hospital

Dear Clinical Genetics Service,

I would be grateful for your assessment of this adult patient with persistent worry, poor sleep and prominent muscle tension, currently managed in primary care as generalised anxiety disorder. The specific question is whether the reported familial pattern of longstanding anxiety and related functional difficulties warrants genetic counselling or any further inherited-condition assessment, rather than assuming a purely sporadic psychiatric presentation.

Symptoms have been present for approximately two years, with variable day-to-day severity but no documented manic or psychotic features. Sleep is fragmented by ruminative thoughts. Examination in surgery was unremarkable apart from observable muscular tension and a mildly anxious affect; speech, cognition and engagement were appropriate. There is no current concern regarding acute risk.

Current treatment is sertraline 50 mg once daily, commenced after discussion of psychological therapy and tolerated without significant adverse effects. The patient has also been offered structured talking therapy and advice regarding sleep routine. Response to medication has been partial, with ongoing worry affecting concentration and social functioning.

I would appreciate your view on the relevance of the family history, whether formal genetic counselling is indicated, and whether any targeted testing or onward neuropsychiatric assessment would be clinically appropriate. Please also advise on information that should be obtained from the patient’s adult child and other relatives before review.

Yours sincerely,

elenor connolly

DISCHARGE SUMMARY – Paediatrics

Patient: Priyana Burke
DOB: 26 April 2032
Next of kin: uncle, Simonas Amin
Admission reason: Acute asthma exacerbation with wheeze, increased work of breathing and night-time cough for 3 days.

Problems / key results
• Moderate respiratory distress on arrival; oxygen saturations maintained on air.
• Viral respiratory screen negative. Chest radiograph not indicated.
• Improved air entry following repeated salbutamol via spacer and a course of oral corticosteroid.
• No fever or focal chest signs. Eating and drinking adequately before discharge.

Hospital course
Admitted for observation and bronchodilator treatment. Salbutamol frequency reduced from 2-hourly to four-hourly without recurrent distress. Asthma education and spacer teaching completed with the patient and uncle; inhaler technique checked. Patient involved in discharge discussion and assented to the plan.

Discharge medicines
• Salbutamol inhaler: 2–10 puffs through spacer as needed for wheeze or breathlessness, in line with the asthma plan.
• Complete remaining prescribed oral steroid course.
Regular preventer therapy to be reviewed by GP; no other changes.

At discharge: comfortable at rest, speaking in full sentences, no recession, widespread wheeze much improved. Safety-net advice provided: seek urgent help if symptoms worsen or salbutamol is needed more often than advised.

Follow-up / actions
GP review within 1–2 weeks; asthma nurse or paediatric respiratory review if ongoing night symptoms. Written asthma action plan supplied.

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report

Patient: KIMARA PRATT
Report/accession ID: 054365678
Requesting service: Friarage Hospital Site
Specimen: EDTA whole blood
Collection date: 14th June 2018
Indication: Acute gout flare with joint pain, swelling and erythema. Current pain score 5/10. Naproxen and colchicine reported.

Test
HLA-B*58:01 genotyping by PCR-based assay

Result
HLA-B*58:01: Not detected
Genotype: HLA-B*58:01 negative

Interpretation
No HLA-B*58:01 allele identified in this specimen. The presence of HLA-B*58:01 is associated with increased risk of severe cutaneous adverse reactions to allopurinol, particularly in susceptible populations. A negative result does not exclude hypersensitivity; prescribe according to clinical indication and renal function.

Clinical comment
Result does not provide an explanation for the current flare. Continue acute management as clinically appropriate. If urate-lowering therapy is being considered, correlate with serum urate, renal profile and previous drug reactions. Avoid starting allopurinol during an uncontrolled acute flare unless specialist advice indicates otherwise.

Quality: Internal controls valid. No evidence of sample inhibition.
Authorised by: Dr Grishma Hamid, MBBS
Report status: Final

Discharge summary

Patient: Suad Thompson
Address: 149 BALLYMONTENAGH ROAD, MACOSQUIN
Contact: 07700 900504

A 73-year-old Middle Eastern female patient attended A&E with several hours of central chest pressure associated with diaphoresis and nausea. Initial ECG showed anterior ST-segment depression without ST elevation. High-sensitivity troponin was elevated with a dynamic rise, consistent with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). Chest radiograph showed no acute abnormality.

Admitted to the cardiology ward for monitoring and treatment. Received aspirin, fondaparinux and high-intensity atorvastatin. No recurrent chest pain or haemodynamic instability during admission. Renal function remained satisfactory and haemoglobin was stable. Echocardiogram demonstrated mildly impaired left ventricular systolic function with regional wall-motion abnormality. Coronary angiography was discussed; following review by the consultant cardiologist, the decision was for medical management with outpatient cardiology follow-up.

Problem list
• Medically managed NSTEMI
• Mild left ventricular systolic impairment
• Cardiovascular risk-factor optimisation required

Discharge medicines
Aspirin 75 mg once daily, lifelong.
Clopidogrel 75 mg once daily, planned for 12 months unless reviewed earlier by cardiology.
Atorvastatin 80 mg at night.
Bisoprolol and ramipril commenced at low dose, with GP review and titration as tolerated.
GTN spray supplied for recurrent angina.

Fondaparinux discontinued at discharge. Please seek urgent medical attention via 999 for persistent or severe chest pain, collapse, marked breathlessness or new neurological symptoms. Avoid driving until advised in line with DVLA guidance.

Cardiology clinic review arranged for 26 Feb 2021. GP to check blood pressure, renal function and electrolytes after medication initiation, and repeat lipid profile in due course. Patient advised regarding smoking cessation, graded activity and cardiac rehabilitation referral.

Condition on discharge: comfortable, ambulant and chest-pain free. Discharge information and medicines discussed; patient able to repeat the antiplatelet plan.

Clinical Genetics Review
NHS number: 0000858880

Patient: Akiva R.
Occupation: Builder
Employer: Alfrick Pound Sports Club
Address: 60 Calke Close, Tintagel, PL34 0AA
Contact: 07700 900877

Reason for review: Assessment of atrial fibrillation in the context of symptomatic episodes and discussion of possible inherited susceptibility.

History: The patient reports intermittent palpitations, associated fatigue and exertional breathlessness. Symptoms have not been accompanied by syncope or documented thromboembolism. A spouse provided additional history and confirms no known sudden cardiac death in first-degree relatives. The patient is taking apixaban and bisoprolol, with no reported difficulty adhering to treatment. There is no history supplied of a syndromic phenotype or a known familial pathogenic variant.

Findings: Clinical review today does not identify dysmorphic features, skeletal abnormalities or other extra-cardiac features suggestive of a recognised multisystem disorder. The phenotype is currently limited to atrial fibrillation and its associated symptoms. In the absence of a clear three-generation family history or a syndromic presentation, the likelihood of identifying a monogenic cause is considered low, although this cannot be excluded.

Interpretation and plan: Continue cardiology-directed management with apixaban and bisoprolol. Obtain further family history, including ages and circumstances of any sudden deaths, cardiomyopathy or early-onset arrhythmia. Genetic testing is not recommended routinely at this stage; reconsider if a relevant family history emerges or if structural heart disease is identified. Clinical review planned in about 12 weeks, with earlier reassessment if syncope, sustained chest pain or rapidly worsening breathlessness occurs.

A&E assessment

Patient: El-Roi  
History from patient and spouse, ROMAYNE KUMAR. Sudden central chest pressure while resting this afternoon, associated with marked diaphoresis and nausea. No pleuritic component or preceding infective symptoms. Symptoms improved after rest but not completely resolved on arrival. No previous myocardial infarction reported.

Observations: BP 120/80 mmHg, pulse 96 regular, respiratory rate 18, SpO₂ 97% on air, temperature 36.7°C. Alert and orientated. Warm peripheries, no signs of heart failure. Heart sounds normal; chest clear bilaterally. Abdomen soft and non-tender.

ECG shows sinus rhythm with horizontal ST depression in the lateral leads, without ST elevation. Initial high-sensitivity troponin I elevated at 86 ng/L, rising to 214 ng/L on repeat. Chest radiograph without focal consolidation or pulmonary oedema. Routine blood tests satisfactory; renal function suitable for anticoagulation.

Assessment: Clinical picture and dynamic troponin rise consistent with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. No ongoing haemodynamic instability or hypoxia. Discussed with the on-call cardiology team at WITHYBUSH GENERAL HOSPITAL, who advise admission for monitoring and early invasive assessment.

Given aspirin 300 mg orally, fondaparinux administered, and atorvastatin commenced. Further antiplatelet treatment to follow cardiology review; plan is dual antiplatelet therapy with a P2Y12 inhibitor unless contraindicated. GTN prescribed for recurrent pain, with repeat ECG if symptoms return.

Admit to the acute medical unit with telemetry. Cardiology review arranged for 23 January 2025. Patient and spouse understand the diagnosis and admission plan.

Documented by HARALAMBOS BRADBURY

Laboratory report – clinical genetics

Patient: A. Morris
MRN: 03748406
Specimen/report date: 10th February 2004
Patient contact detail: atara.morris95@outlook.com

Clinical information:
Flank pain, dysuria and rigors. Acute pyelonephritis suspected clinically. Current treatment includes cefuroxime 500 mg twice daily and paracetamol. Urine specimen submitted during the acute episode; specimen source recorded as midstream urine.

Laboratory findings:
Urine culture: significant growth of a single Gram-negative urinary pathogen.
Organism identification: Escherichia coli.
Quantitation: >10^5 CFU/mL.
Mixed growth: not detected.
Contamination indicators: no significant mixed flora.

Antimicrobial susceptibility:
Cefuroxime: susceptible.
Trimethoprim: susceptible.
Nitrofurantoin: susceptible; unsuitable for treatment of upper urinary tract infection.
Ciprofloxacin: susceptible, subject to local prescribing restrictions.
Extended-spectrum beta-lactamase phenotype: not detected.

Interpretation:
The culture supports a clinically significant E. coli urinary tract infection and is consistent with the reported symptoms of acute pyelonephritis. Cefuroxime is microbiologically appropriate on the result available. Review clinical response, renal function, allergy status and local antimicrobial guidance before confirming duration or changing treatment. Persistent rigors, vomiting, hypotension or failure to improve should prompt urgent reassessment.

This is a microbiological interpretation and does not replace clinical review. Ordering clinician not stated on the received request.

Validated and reported by:
I. Rawlings
Laboratory clinician
Clinical genetics laboratory
Report date: 10th February 2004

Referral to Community Paediatrics

From: Ulster Hospital
Re: Henderson, 5-year-old Pacific Islander male patient

I would be grateful for your assessment of Henderson following a recent acute asthma exacerbation, with particular advice on confirming the diagnosis and establishing an ongoing management plan.

He was brought to the surgery by his father, C. Giles, after several nights of cough and audible wheeze. His father also described increased work of breathing during the episode. There was no reported choking event or fever. Symptoms improved after salbutamol, although he continues to cough at night intermittently.

On review today he was alert and speaking comfortably. Mild expiratory wheeze was present with no marked recession or cyanosis. Oxygen saturations were satisfactory in the surgery. Current measured weight is 28.6 kg. I have not identified any safeguarding concerns.

He has been prescribed a salbutamol inhaler with a spacer. Spacer teaching was completed with C. Giles, including technique and the need to seek urgent help if the inhaler is not providing relief or breathing becomes difficult. We have not yet started a preventer, pending specialist advice and a clearer assessment of symptom frequency.

Please review whether this represents asthma or another cause of recurrent wheeze, and advise regarding inhaled corticosteroid treatment, an asthma action plan and follow-up. Consideration of spirometry when clinically appropriate would also be helpful.

Yours sincerely,

Dr Ozni Biggs, MBBS

Dear Respiratory Medicine Team,

Re: JENITA POLLARD

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient with persistent essential hypertension despite treatment with amlodipine and ramipril. The specific question is whether obstructive sleep-disordered breathing may be contributing to suboptimal blood pressure control and intermittent daytime symptoms.

MOLECULAR GENETICS REPORT
NHS number: 0007929367

Patient: zakariyya briggs
MRN: 05379775
Requesting service: General Medicine
Reporting laboratory: Cardigan and District Memorial Hospital
Specimen: Peripheral blood, EDTA
Clinical indication: Significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer; predictive testing requested. Affected sibling reported to have a pathogenic familial variant.

Test performed: Targeted analysis for familial BRCA1 c.68_69delAG variant
Result: Not detected in the specimen tested.

Interpretation:
No evidence of the familial BRCA1 c.68_69delAG variant was identified. Analytical result is negative for this specific familial variant. This does not exclude other pathogenic variants in BRCA1, BRCA2 or other cancer-predisposition genes, and interpretation depends on confirmation that the familial variant has been correctly identified.

Clinical comment:
If the familial result is documented and the tested variant is the relevant familial change, the patient is unlikely to have inherited this particular variant and may generally follow population-based screening advice, subject to the wider pedigree. Genetic counselling remains appropriate to review the family history and confirm variant details. No current treatment.

Action:
• Refer/return to clinical genetics for counselling and final risk assessment.
• Consider broader testing only if indicated by the pedigree or if the familial variant cannot be confirmed.
• Results to be discussed at follow-up on 08/03/2021.

Validated and authorised by:
AVA-JANE WARBURTON
Laboratory clinician

Clinical Genetics Specialist Report
NHS number: 000 007 7098

Patient: R. Woodhouse
Report/accession ID: 052397263
Referring service: Accident and Emergency, Purley Hospital
Occupation: Pharmacist

Reason for review:
Seen following an A&E presentation in which significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer was disclosed. The patient is concerned about inherited cancer risk and requests predictive testing. A sibling has a documented pathogenic BRCA1 c.68_69delAG variant; the original laboratory report is not currently available for verification.

Clinical findings:
No current breast or ovarian symptoms reported at this assessment. No current treatment. The patient understands that predictive testing is most informative when the familial variant has first been confirmed in an affected relative. Family history requires formal three-generation documentation, including ages at diagnosis and any male breast, pancreatic or prostate cancers. These details were not complete at review.

Interpretation and plan:
The history is compatible with possible hereditary breast and ovarian cancer susceptibility, but a definitive risk estimate cannot be issued until the sibling’s result and relevant family history have been obtained. Written consent and pre-test counselling are required before testing. The patient will be advised not to make screening or risk-reducing decisions on the basis of the unverified familial result alone.

Request the sibling’s original genetics report and arrange follow-up with the regional genetics service at Purley Hospital. Discussed confidentiality, possible test outcomes and implications for relatives. The patient agreed to seek further assessment rather than proceed with testing through A&E.

Report prepared and signed by C. Bashir, Clinical Genetics.

A&E medical assessment

Clinical age: 64 y/o
Home address: 125 Wike Ridge Close, Fairlands, GU3 1AA

Presented with 10 hours of severe bilateral limb pain, worst in the thighs and lower back. Pain is typical of previous sickle cell crises but has not settled with usual oral analgesia. Reports poor oral intake and dark urine today. No chest pain, breathlessness, fever or focal neurological symptoms. Spouse present and contributing to history.

On arrival alert but distressed by pain. Pulse 104, BP 132/78, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturations 98% on air, temperature 37.1°C. Mucous membranes dry. No jaundice noted. Heart sounds normal, chest clear with no increased work of breathing. Abdomen soft and non-tender.
