Chest radiograph not indicated clinically at present. No features to suggest acute chest syndrome, sepsis or stroke.

Assessment: uncomplicated vaso-occlusive painful crisis with dehydration. Cannula inserted and intravenous crystalloid commenced. Given titrated intravenous morphine with antiemetic; pain score improving but requires reassessment. Encourage oral fluids as tolerated and monitor urine output. Oxygen only if saturations fall.

Discussed with medical registrar AYKUT BYRNE. Admit to the medical ward for ongoing analgesia, hydration and observation. Haematology review requested. Patient contact and home address confirmed for admission records.

Date: 09/06/1996
Patient: Umit
MRN: 08191332
Referring organisation: Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh

Referral to Respiratory Medicine

I would be grateful for your assessment of Umit, who has developed persistent early-morning waking alongside a major depressive episode. The clinical question is whether an unrecognised sleep-related breathing disorder, particularly obstructive sleep apnoea, may be contributing to fragmented sleep and daytime symptoms, and whether respiratory investigation is indicated.

Umit describes several weeks of low mood, loss of interest in usual activities and waking earlier than intended, with difficulty returning to sleep. Their partner reports noisy breathing at night and occasional pauses followed by a gasp; the frequency is not yet clear. There has been no recent chest infection or exertional breathlessness. Daytime concentration is reduced, although there is no reported episode of falling asleep while driving.

The depression is being managed in primary care. Current treatment is sertraline 50 mg once daily, with tolerability reported as satisfactory. We have discussed sleep routine, avoidance of alcohol near bedtime and the importance of seeking urgent help if suicidal thoughts emerge. Current risk assessment identifies no immediate safeguarding concern.

I would appreciate review in your service, including consideration of overnight oximetry or a sleep study and advice on whether treatment of sleep-disordered breathing could improve sleep and mood. Please advise whether any further respiratory assessment is required before referral.

Yours faithfully,

ocean-grace barrett

MRN: 0249500
Date: 24th September 2018
Patient contact: ojay.aston30@icloud.com

Reason for review: Recurrent migraine with unilateral headache, nausea and photophobia. Referred for assessment of possible inherited susceptibility.

History and findings:
A 63 y/o patient attended with their partner, who assisted with the history. Headaches are episodic, predominantly unilateral, and associated with nausea and photophobia. No persistent neurological deficit, progressive change in pattern or features suggestive of raised intracranial pressure were described. There is no reported intellectual disability, developmental disorder or multisystem involvement. Examination in clinic was non-focal, with normal gait, speech and cranial nerve assessment.

Current treatment includes sumatriptan and naproxen. The patient has been advised to use sumatriptan 50 mg at onset of migraine, with naproxen as previously directed, and to avoid medication overuse. Headache frequency and triggers should continue to be recorded.

Interpretation:
The presentation is clinically consistent with migraine. In the absence of additional neurological or syndromic features, this does not currently suggest a defined monogenic migraine syndrome or provide a clear indication for diagnostic genetic testing. A multifactorial familial predisposition remains possible. Management should continue through the GP and headache service as appropriate.

Plan:
Continue current acute treatment and lifestyle measures. Review if attacks become more frequent, refractory, or associated with new neurological symptoms. Genetic clinic review can be reconsidered if a relevant family history or syndromic features emerge.

Discharge summary – Cardiology

Patient: Shanyce K.
Home address: 55 BURNET CLOSE, MULLAN
Patient contact: 07700 900305

Reason for admission
Presented to A&E following a brief episode of right arm weakness with facial droop and slurred speech. Symptoms resolved before hospital assessment. No persistent neurological deficit on arrival. Admitted for suspected transient ischaemic attack (TIA) and vascular risk assessment.

Investigations and hospital course
CT head showed no acute intracranial haemorrhage or established infarct. MRI brain demonstrated no acute diffusion restriction. Carotid Doppler without haemodynamically significant stenosis. ECG showed sinus rhythm; inpatient telemetry did not identify atrial fibrillation. Blood pressure during review 120/80 mmHg. Blood tests including glucose and renal function were satisfactory.

Seen by the stroke and cardiology teams. Clinical picture felt most consistent with TIA. No thrombolysis indicated as symptoms had fully resolved and the patient was outside the treatment window. Mobilising independently, eating and drinking normally, and neurologically at baseline at discharge. Spouse updated regarding the diagnosis and medication plan.

Problem list
• Transient ischaemic attack with resolved arm weakness, facial droop and dysarthria
• Vascular risk reduction
• No evidence of acute infarction or atrial fibrillation during admission

Discharge medicines
Aspirin 300 mg once daily for 14 days, then reduce to aspirin 75 mg once daily.
Atorvastatin 80 mg once daily.
Continue other regular medicines as listed on the electronic discharge prescription. Avoid stopping aspirin without advice from the GP or stroke team.

Follow-up and advice
Urgent TIA clinic review requested. GP to continue blood pressure, lipid and diabetes risk-factor management and review the need for longer-term rhythm monitoring. If facial weakness, arm weakness, speech disturbance or other sudden neurological symptoms recur, call 999 immediately, even if symptoms settle.

Discharging clinician: SADIE BLACKWELL
Professional identifier: 0262748
Consultant cardiologist sign-off.

Patient: Ayran
MRN: 0216952
Occupation: Office manager
Seen in: Milford Hospital

Today we reviewed your referral in the cardiology clinic, including the effect of Parkinson disease symptoms on your day-to-day activity. You describe a resting tremor, slowness of movement and muscular rigidity. There was no report of chest pain, syncope or sustained palpitations. Pulse was regular in clinic, and there was no clinical evidence of fluid overload. Blood pressure was acceptable, although we discussed standing slowly because Parkinson disease and its treatment can sometimes contribute to postural dizziness.

Your Parkinson disease is an established diagnosis previously assessed by neurology. You remain on co-beneldopa as prescribed, with no change made by us today. Please continue this regularly and do not stop it suddenly. We recommend a medication review with your GP and the neurology or movement-disorder team, particularly if tremor, stiffness, falls or light-headedness are worsening. The cardiology team will review any available ECG and ambulatory monitoring results alongside your symptoms; further testing will depend on those findings.

Please seek urgent medical help through A&E if you develop prolonged chest pain, collapse, severe breathlessness or a sustained rapid heartbeat. Otherwise, arrange follow-up with your GP and bring an up-to-date medicines list.

Signed electronically by
S. CURTIS
for Milford Hospital

Admission creatinine 286 micromol/L, urea 18.4 mmol/L; baseline renal function not previously documented. Urinalysis: concentrated urine, no significant blood or protein. Clinically stable, passing urine, tolerating diet and fluids. Discharged home with partner.

Follow-up/actions
GP: renal profile and blood pressure within 48–72 hours; review withheld medicines.
Renal clinic referral if renal function fails to return to baseline.
Return to A&E for worsening lethargy, vomiting, inability to drink or markedly reduced urine output.

Referral to Gastroenterology
NHS number: 000 250 9858

From: Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh
Report/accession ID: 06458739

Re: Kyu

Dear Gastroenterology team,

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient following recurrent episodes of retrosternal burning and acid regurgitation, associated with a troublesome night-time cough. Symptoms are worse after evening meals and when lying flat. The patient’s partner reports disturbed sleep and occasional nocturnal throat clearing. There has been no reported haematemesis, melaena, progressive dysphagia or unintentional weight loss.

In the emergency department, observations were stable and examination was non-contributory, with no respiratory distress and a soft, non-tender abdomen. ECG and chest radiograph did not identify an acute cardiopulmonary cause for the retrosternal symptoms. The presentation is clinically most consistent with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, although the persistent cough and incomplete response to initial treatment warrant specialist review.

Current treatment is omeprazole together with alginate suspension, with partial symptomatic benefit. Advice has been given regarding avoidance of late meals, remaining upright after eating and limiting individual dietary triggers. The patient has been asked to seek urgent review if dysphagia, gastrointestinal bleeding or severe chest pain develops.

Please assess the need for upper gastrointestinal investigation, optimisation of acid suppression and consideration of alternative explanations for the cough. Follow-up with the GP is planned in about 6 weeks, but earlier specialist advice would be appreciated if symptoms remain poorly controlled.

Yours sincerely,

ishan abbott
GMC 0943895
Referring clinician

Documented by HAJR PEACOCK, Staff Nurse.

Alert, comfortable, afebrile. Hydrated; observations within expected range. Abdomen soft with mild suprapubic tenderness only, no guarding or renal angle tenderness. Referral to Community Paediatrics

Patient: K. Richards
MRN: 0744575
Informant: mother, CAICEY MANSFIELD

Dear Community Paediatrics Team,

I would be grateful for assessment of this infant, the patient, aged 7 weeks, with persistent atopic eczema, particularly to advise on management escalation and whether there are contributing environmental or allergic factors.

CAICEY MANSFIELD reports recurrent dry, inflamed skin affecting the cheeks, trunk and flexures, with marked itching and disrupted sleep. The current flare has been worse for 3 days. There has been no fever, reduced feeding or apparent systemic illness. The rash has been treated with regular emollient application and topical hydrocortisone during flares, with incomplete and short-lived improvement. Application technique and avoidance of fragranced products have been discussed.

On review, there were erythematous, excoriated eczematous patches over both cheeks and the antecubital and popliteal areas, with generalised xerosis. No pustules, crusting, vesicles or features to suggest secondary bacterial infection were seen. Hydration and observations were clinically reassuring.

Interpretation: distribution and morphology are consistent with atopic eczema. The principal concerns are inadequate control of pruritus and sleep disturbance, and the need to ensure an appropriate potency and duration of topical treatment. Please review diagnosis, skin-care regimen and trigger avoidance, and consider referral to dermatology or allergy services if the course remains refractory. The family would also benefit from a written eczema action plan and review of treatment adherence.

Yours sincerely,

H. Vickers

Patient: JAMAICA FERGUSON
NHS number: 0003683053
MRN: 0000422
Clinic: Rookwood Hospital
Occupation: Journalist

Respiratory Medicine Outpatient Report

Reason for review: Recurrent episodic headache with associated nausea and photophobia. No respiratory complaint today. The patient describes a unilateral, pulsatile pain lasting several hours, occasionally preceded by visual shimmering. Episodes are aggravated by movement and improve with sleep in a dark room. No persistent visual loss, limb weakness, speech disturbance or altered awareness.

Examination: Comfortable at rest. Chest clear bilaterally with normal air entry; no wheeze or crackles. Cardiovascular examination unremarkable. Neurological screening examination normal, including eye movements, facial symmetry, limb power and gait.

Interpretation: Clinical pattern is most consistent with migraine without evidence of an acute secondary cause. There is no current respiratory finding to account for the headaches, and no indication for chest imaging from this review.

Plan: Continue sumatriptan at onset, with naproxen where required and tolerated. Avoid excessive acute medication use; maintain regular meals, hydration and sleep. A headache diary was advised, including triggers, duration and response to treatment. The patient should seek urgent assessment via A&E for a sudden maximal-onset headache, new neurological deficit or persistent vomiting.

Follow-up in about 13 weeks, with earlier GP review if attacks become more frequent or treatment response deteriorates. The report and management plan have been discussed with Tejinder Bradshaw, consultant clinician, at Rookwood Hospital.

Home address: 168 Verdure Gardens, Winnersh, RG41 1AA

Treatment commenced with oxygen and intravenous furosemide, with fluid balance and urine output monitoring. Symptoms improved after initial diuresis, although ongoing oxygen requirement and peripheral oedema remain. Discussed with SAMM EASTWOOD, who accepts the patient for cardiology admission. Partner updated and understands the plan. Continue telemetry, daily weights, renal profile and medication review on the ward.

Discharge summary – Obstetric Medicine

Patient: Uthra F.
Reason for admission: Persistent vomiting in early pregnancy with reduced oral intake, dehydration and reported weight loss. Current pregnancy documented as 9+4 weeks' gestation. Admitted for intravenous rehydration and symptom control.

Assessment and key results: On arrival clinically dry with postural dizziness and ketonuria. Mild hypokalaemia corrected during admission. Renal function remained satisfactory; liver profile and amylase were unremarkable. Urine culture showed no significant growth. Ultrasound confirmed a single intrauterine pregnancy with cardiac activity, consistent with dates.

Hospital course: Treated with intravenous sodium chloride, initially alongside potassium replacement, and regular cyclizine. Thiamine was given before any dextrose-containing fluid. Vomiting settled over the subsequent 24 hours and oral fluids were reintroduced, followed by small meals. No further ketones documented prior to discharge. Weight stable on repeat assessment. Abdominal examination remained benign, with no vaginal bleeding or pelvic pain.

Problem list:
• First-trimester hyperemesis with dehydration
• Transient hypokalaemia, resolved
• Intrauterine pregnancy, viable on ultrasound

Discharge medicines:
Cyclizine 50 mg orally up to three times daily as needed for nausea. Continue antenatal vitamins if tolerated. No further intravenous treatment required.

Condition at discharge: Alert, haemodynamically stable and tolerating fluids and light diet. Passing urine normally. Discharge home with advice to continue frequent small sips and meals, and to avoid driving if drowsy after cyclizine. Return to the emergency department for inability to retain fluids, reduced urine output, haematemesis, severe abdominal pain or bleeding.

Follow-up: Early pregnancy review with ROYAL INFIRMARY OF EDINBURGH on 25th September 2019. The patient’s sibling, MAXIMUS DREW, from Craigmillar, is aware of the discharge plan. GP to review ongoing antiemetic requirement and hydration; repeat electrolytes if vomiting recurs.

Dear Cardiology Team,
NHS number: 000 520 7895

Re: Huzair

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient’s symptomatic atrial fibrillation, specifically advice on rate control and whether rhythm-control treatment or further cardiac investigation is indicated.

Huzair reports intermittent palpitations with fatigue and exertional breathlessness, currently present for 3 days. There is no reported syncope or chest pain. The emergency contact is aware of the referral and can assist with further history if required.

At review today, the pulse was irregular at 118 beats per minute and blood pressure was 132/78 mmHg. Oxygen saturations were 97% on air. Cardiovascular examination confirmed an irregular rhythm without clinical evidence of fluid overload; chest examination was clear. A 12-lead ECG showed atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response. Recent blood tests showed no significant anaemia or electrolyte disturbance; thyroid function has been requested.

The patient is taking apixaban for stroke prevention and bisoprolol, with only partial symptomatic improvement. Adherence was discussed, and there has been no reported bleeding. I have advised avoiding excess caffeine and seeking urgent assessment via A&E for persistent chest pain, collapse, or severe breathlessness.

Please review the diagnosis and current rate-control strategy, advise on anticoagulation duration and suitability for cardioversion, and consider echocardiography if not already arranged.

A&E Nursing Progress Note

Patient: Priyanshi
DOB: 15/12/1989
Gestation: 9+4 weeks' gestation
Emergency contact: Nashawn Craig

Presentation
Persistent vomiting since yesterday, unable to retain fluids. Reports dizziness on standing and reduced urine output. Documented weight loss from booking history. No abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding reported.

Observations
Alert, pale and dry. Pulse 108 bpm, BP 102/66 mmHg, RR 18, SpO₂ 99% on air, temperature 36.7°C. NEWS2: 1. Urine concentrated; ambulates slowly with supervision owing to light-headedness.

Interventions / response
Cannula inserted. Intravenous sodium chloride commenced as prescribed; cyclizine administered. Oral fluids withheld initially, then sips of water trialled. Nausea eased after medication; no further emesis during observation period. Passed small volume urine.

Medical review
Reviewed by physician Dr Adilah ENGLAND, MBBS. Blood tests sent, including U&E and ketones; results awaited. Continue IV fluids and antiemetic treatment, monitor intake/output and repeat observations.

Risks / escalation
Falls risk discussed; call bell within reach and advised not to mobilise unattended. Escalate persistent vomiting, worsening dizziness, reduced urine output, abnormal blood results or haemodynamic deterioration to covering clinician.

Plan for next shift
Repeat observations in one hour, document emesis and fluid balance, assess oral tolerance. Await blood results and medical decision regarding discharge versus ambulatory admission. Follow-up arranged for 23 Aug 2023.

• Continue good oral fluid intake unless otherwise advised.

Discharge summary
National Insurance number: NT 64 92 61 C

Patient: ishaana howes
Home address: 40 Hermit Seat, Greenlaw, TD10 6AB
Clinical context: a 59-year-old Black female patient
Patient contact: ishaana.howes50@proton.me

Reason for admission
Presented with 18 hours of worsening right lower-quadrant abdominal pain, nausea and loss of appetite. Reviewed in the emergency department at 08:15. Examination supported localised peritonism without haemodynamic instability.

Key results
Blood tests showed raised inflammatory markers and mild neutrophilia. Urinalysis negative for infection. Ultrasound abdomen demonstrated an enlarged, non-compressible appendix with surrounding inflammatory change, consistent with acute appendicitis. No collection identified.

Hospital course
Admitted under general surgery and kept nil by mouth. Treated with intravenous fluids, analgesia and intravenous co-amoxiclav. Underwent uncomplicated laparoscopic appendicectomy. Operative findings were an inflamed, non-perforated appendix; specimen sent for histology. Post-operative recovery satisfactory, with oral intake tolerated and mobilisation independent. Pain controlled with oral paracetamol. Histology result to be followed up by the surgical team.

Problem list
• Acute uncomplicated appendicitis
• Status post laparoscopic appendicectomy
• Post-operative nausea, resolved

Discharge medicines
Paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily as required for pain. Avoid exceeding 4 g in 24 hours. No ongoing antibiotics required.

Condition at discharge
Bright and clinically stable. Afebrile, abdomen soft with expected mild peri-umbilical tenderness; port sites clean, dry and intact. Passing urine and tolerating diet.

Follow-up and advice
Surgical follow-up will be arranged for review of histology and wounds. Keep the dressings clean and dry and avoid strenuous activity until comfortable. Seek urgent medical advice via NHS 111 or A&E for increasing abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fever, wound redness or discharge.

Discharging clinician: Consultant physician

Microbiology Report
NHS number: 000 127 1483

Patient: C. DAVEY
Report/accession ID: 007011721
Reporting laboratory: Green Elms Medical Centre
Specimen: Deep wound swab, plantar ulcer, left foot
Clinical details: Diabetes mellitus with chronic plantar ulceration, reduced protective sensation and local discharge. Specimen collected following wound cleansing; superficial swab interpretation advised with caution.

Culture:
Heavy growth of Staphylococcus aureus.
Moderate growth of Escherichia coli.
Mixed skin and enteric flora also isolated.

Antimicrobial susceptibility:
Staphylococcus aureus: susceptible to flucloxacillin, doxycycline and co-trimoxazole; resistant to penicillin.
Escherichia coli: susceptible to co-amoxiclav, cefalexin and ciprofloxacin; resistant to ampicillin.

Interpretation:
Polymicrobial growth from an ulcer swab. Findings may represent colonisation as well as infection; correlate with erythema, warmth, increasing pain, malodour, systemic features and depth of ulceration. No blood culture result is available with this request. If osteomyelitis is suspected, imaging and tissue or bone sampling should be considered rather than reliance on a superficial swab.

Clinical comment:
Continue local wound care and pressure off-loading. The recorded treatment is co-amoxiclav 625 mg three times daily; review response and renal function in accordance with local antimicrobial guidance. Urgent clinical assessment is indicated for spreading cellulitis, systemic illness, rapidly progressive tissue loss or suspected deep infection. Ensure vascular assessment and diabetic foot multidisciplinary follow-up.

Suggested review appointment: 22nd October 2018

Validated by: Zeyd Kennedy
Laboratory medicine

Iron-deficiency anaemia, clinically stable. Symptoms persisting but no red-flag features.

Continue ferrous fumarate; avoid taking with milk. Encourage iron-containing foods and vitamin C with meals. Repeat blood tests in approximately 4 weeks and review results by telephone or clinic. Reason for admission

Clinical examination was consistent with non-purulent cellulitis of the lower leg. Afebrile throughout admission; haemodynamically stable. Discharged home clinically improved, with reduced redness and tenderness and no systemic features of infection. Keep the leg elevated when resting and maintain good fluid intake. Seek urgent medical advice via NHS 111 or A&E if redness spreads, fever develops, pain worsens, or the leg becomes markedly swollen. Continue or rationalise antimicrobial therapy according to the susceptibility profile and local antimicrobial guidance. Nursing progress note – A&E

Patient: Zalman Hallam
MRN: H3478892
Address: 1 BEXLEY HILL, Downhill
Department: Accident and Emergency
Patient, aged 51 years, attended with friend.

Presenting problem:
Left flank pain with dysuria and rigors. Nauseated on arrival, no vomiting reported. Appears flushed and uncomfortable.

Observations:
08:15 – temperature 38.7°C, pulse 112 bpm, BP 103/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 20, SpO₂ 97% on air. Alert and orientated. Pain 7/10.

Actions:
Cannula in situ. Bloods and blood cultures taken; urine sample sent. IV fluids commenced as prescribed. Cefuroxime administered following medical review; paracetamol given for pain and pyrexia. Encouraged oral fluids as tolerated. Falls precautions in place due to weakness when standing.

Response:
Pain reduced to 4/10 after paracetamol. Temperature remains elevated but rigors settled. Tolerated small amounts of water. Passed urine once, dark and offensive smelling.

Escalation:
Medical team informed of tachycardia and borderline blood pressure. Clinician’s GMC identifier: 0369046. Working diagnosis acute pyelonephritis; awaiting blood results and bed decision.

Plan for next shift:
Repeat observations as per sepsis pathway, monitor urine output and oral intake, review blood/urine results, continue prescribed cefuroxime and analgesia. Escalate recurrent rigors, hypotension, reduced consciousness or increasing pain. Friend updated at bedside with patient’s agreement.

Paediatric Dermatology Clinic

Patient: Alegra
Clinical age: 13 y/o
Home address: 69 Croft Down Road, Skelmersdale, WN8 0AA
Accompanied by aunt, Gal; consent/assent obtained for assessment. Family linked with Brandhall Housing Association for practical support.

Reason for review: Atopic eczema flare, mainly antecubital fossae, neck and hands. Itching worse overnight with broken sleep. Gal reports increased scratching for 3 days after stopping regular emollient use.

History:
Known atopic eczema. No fever, facial swelling or breathing difficulty. No new prescribed medicines. Hydrocortisone used intermittently; application technique reviewed. Teen prefers to manage treatment independently but happy for aunt to support routines.

Examination:
Dry erythematous eczematous plaques in bilateral antecubital fossae and dorsal hands. Excoriations present. Mild lichenification. No crusting, ooze, pustules or cellulitis. Well appearing.

Assessment:
Moderate flare of atopic eczema; sleep disturbance secondary to pruritus. No clinical evidence of bacterial infection today.

Plan:
Regular liberal emollient at least 3–4 times daily and after washing. Hydrocortisone thinly to active areas as previously prescribed, avoiding eyes and broken skin; continue for short flare course, then stop when clear. Soap substitutes advised. Keep nails short. Discussed adherence and treatment privacy with patient and aunt.

Review with GP/dermatology if not improving, or sooner for spreading redness, pain, discharge or fever.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: Luca-Ellis G.
Clinical age: 3 y/o patient
Responsible adult: father, B. Stott
Patient contact: 07700 900067
Admission/discharge date: 7th February 2023
Ward: Paediatrics

Reason for admission
Barking cough, hoarse voice and intermittent inspiratory stridor, worse overnight. Reduced oral intake but passing urine. Father reports no choking episode or suspected foreign body.

Assessment/results
• Afebrile on review; mild coryzal symptoms.
• Stridor at rest initially, improved with settling and treatment.
• No chest recession after observation; air entry equal bilaterally.
• Oxygen saturations maintained in air.
• No investigations indicated; clinical picture consistent with viral croup.

Hospital course
Admitted for respiratory observation. Dexamethasone administered at 08:15 with clear improvement in stridor and work of breathing. Fluids encouraged orally; tolerated drinks before discharge. No nebulised adrenaline required. No antibiotics.

Discharge treatment/actions
• Supportive care: frequent fluids, rest, upright positioning when symptomatic.
• Dexamethasone dose completed in hospital; no further regular medication prescribed.
• Avoid smoke exposure.

Condition at discharge
Alert, settled, drinking, with occasional barking cough but no stridor at rest and no increased work of breathing. Discharged home with father following paediatric review.

Follow-up and advice
GP review if not improving over 48 hours. Return to A&E urgently for stridor at rest, chest recession, blue lips, marked drowsiness or inability to drink. Father verbalised understanding and agreed with the plan.

A&E Medical Assessment

Patient: MUHAMMAD-ZAYN OWEN
Accompanied by spouse, L. Biggs
Referring organisation: Withybush General Hospital

Presenting complaint:
24-hour lower abdominal pain, worse on intercourse. New offensive yellow vaginal discharge. No vomiting or urinary frequency. No PV bleeding reported.

Observations:
T 37.8°C, HR 96, BP 120/80 mmHg, RR 16, SpO₂ 99% RA.

Examination:
Alert, uncomfortable but not toxic. Abdomen soft; suprapubic and bilateral iliac fossa tenderness, no guarding or rebound. Pelvic examination with consent and chaperone: mucopurulent cervical discharge, cervical excitation and bilateral adnexal tenderness.

Investigations:
Urine pregnancy test negative. FBC: mild neutrophilia. CRP 48 mg/L. Urinalysis negative for nitrites. Vaginal/cervical swabs sent for NAAT and microscopy.

Impression:
Clinical pelvic inflammatory disease. No evidence of acute abdomen or haemodynamic compromise.

Management:
Ceftriaxone administered in department. Commenced doxycycline and metronidazole; prescription supplied. Analgesia with oral paracetamol. Advised abstinence until treatment completed and partner assessment arranged through sexual health services.

Disposition:
Suitable for ambulatory treatment. Return to ED if fever, worsening pain, vomiting or collapse. Sexual health review booked for 19/06/2024. GP follow-up advised.

Clinician: Patrik Betts

PAEDIATRIC LABORATORY MEDICINE
NHS number: 0007812257

Patient: Pratik, 9-year-old Hispanic male patient
MRN: 097 202 475
Specimen: Venous blood; fluoride-oxalate plasma and serum
Clinical details: Legal guardian reports increased thirst, frequent urination and recent weight loss. Insulin commenced; home glucose monitoring in use. Current measured weight 28.6 kg.

RESULTS
Plasma glucose: 18.9 mmol/L — high
HbA1c (IFCC): 103 mmol/mol — high
Serum beta-hydroxybutyrate: 1.8 mmol/L — raised
Venous bicarbonate: 19 mmol/L — mildly reduced
Sodium: 134 mmol/L — mildly reduced
Potassium: 4.6 mmol/L — within reference interval
Creatinine: 42 µmol/L — within paediatric reference interval
Urine ketones: 2+
Urine glucose: 4+

INTERPRETATION
Marked hyperglycaemia with substantially raised HbA1c, consistent with diabetes mellitus. Mild ketonaemia and reduced bicarbonate require clinical correlation; results do not alone establish diabetic ketoacidosis.

ACTION
Urgent same-day paediatric diabetes team review advised. Assess hydration, capillary glucose/ketones, respiratory pattern and venous gas; follow local sick-day and insulin guidance. If vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness or worsening ketones, attend emergency department immediately. Please provide medication doses and timing with the clinical referral.

Follow-up appointment: 7th September 2004

Validated and reported by: musammat neal
Laboratory comment: Interpret alongside examination and point-of-care results. Repeat HbA1c is not required for diagnosis confirmation but should be monitored through the diabetes service.

Patient: Lynx Monk
NHS number: 0000089711
MRN: 07100441
Occupation: Lawyer

Seen in general medicine clinic with a five-day increase in breathlessness, wheeze and sputum production. Sputum is now thicker and yellow-green. On examination, alert and speaking in full sentences. Respiratory rate mildly raised, with widespread expiratory wheeze and reduced air entry bilaterally. No focal crackles. Start prednisolone and doxycycline as prescribed today; continue salbutamol inhaler when required and usual maintenance inhalers. Inhaler technique checked and reinforced. Review with the respiratory team at SOLIHULL HOSPITAL in about 4 weeks, or sooner if symptoms fail to improve. Consider pulmonary rehabilitation and vaccination status at review.

Documented by Robynn Downes, General Medicine.

Dear Cardiology Team,
NHS number: 000 043 5059

Re: M. ENGLAND
Home address: 147 KELVIN PARADE, FINNIS
Report/accession ID: 0179754776

I would be grateful for your assessment of recurrent light-headedness and near-falls in this patient with established Parkinson disease, previously assessed by neurology. The episodes occur mainly on standing and have become more frequent over the past month. There has been no reported loss of consciousness, chest pain or sustained palpitations. History today was supplemented by the patient’s friend, who has noticed increased slowness and unsteadiness.

On examination in the surgery, the patient had a resting tremor, bradykinesia and muscular rigidity. Pulse was regular and the cardiovascular examination was otherwise unremarkable. Symptoms were reproduced on standing, without collapse. An ECG showed sinus rhythm. Recent blood tests, including full blood count, electrolytes and thyroid function, were not contributory.

Current medication is co-beneldopa, prescribed in primary care following the established neurological diagnosis. No recent dose change is reported. We have advised slow position changes, adequate fluid intake and a review of other medicines that may worsen postural symptoms. Please assess for orthostatic hypotension or another cardiac contribution, and advise regarding monitoring and management. I would also welcome guidance on whether ambulatory ECG or echocardiography is indicated.

A review appointment has been arranged for 17th February 2021. Please return your recommendations to the surgery, with particular attention to safe multidisciplinary management alongside neurology.

Yours faithfully,

Dr Bertram Norman, MBBS

Patient: BREN THORNTON

Request: Predictive germline testing for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk
Referring organisation: Higher Openshaw Medical Centre
Specimen: Peripheral blood, EDTA
Clinical indication: Significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer; patient requests clarification of inherited cancer risk. No current treatment.

Test performed:
Targeted analysis of the familial BRCA1 variant BRCA1 c.68_69delAG by sequence-specific assay, with appropriate quality controls.

Result:
Familial BRCA1 c.68_69delAG variant detected in the submitted specimen.

Interpretation:
This is a pathogenic BRCA1 variant associated with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome. The finding confirms that the patient has inherited the familial variant and is at increased risk of BRCA1-associated malignancy. The result should be interpreted alongside the detailed family history and genetic counselling assessment; it does not predict whether or when cancer will develop.

Clinical comment:
Please refer to the regional clinical genetics service for post-test counselling, discussion of breast and ovarian risk-management options, and consideration of testing for eligible relatives. Management should follow current UK clinical genetics and oncology guidance. The result is not, in isolation, an indication for treatment, and routine medication review is not required.

A future genetics review is arranged for 2022-05-10. The laboratory can provide variant confirmation documentation if required by the clinical team.

Validated and authorised by:
rudie hardman
Laboratory reporting clinician
Clinical Genetics Laboratory

Paediatric discharge summary

Patient: Ayobami  
Clinical age: 11 y/o  
Home address: 101 CORBRACKY LANE, DUNNAMANAGH  
Father: E. Dickson  
Patient contact: 07700 900515

Admitted with 18 hours of worsening abdominal pain, initially central and subsequently localised to the right lower quadrant, associated with nausea and loss of appetite. E. Dickson provided the initial history. No significant diarrhoea or urinary symptoms reported.

On examination there was focal right iliac fossa tenderness with guarding. Initial blood tests showed raised inflammatory markers. Ultrasound abdomen demonstrated an enlarged, non-compressible appendix with surrounding inflammatory change, in keeping with acute appendicitis. The case was discussed with the paediatric surgical team.

Managed initially with nil by mouth, intravenous fluids, analgesia and intravenous co-amoxiclav. Laparoscopic appendicectomy was undertaken during the admission. Operative findings were consistent with an inflamed, non-perforated appendix; specimen sent for histology. No drain required and no intra-operative complication recorded.

Post-operatively, Ayobami remained haemodynamically stable, tolerated oral fluids and a light diet, and mobilised independently. Pain was controlled with oral paracetamol. At review, abdomen soft with expected mild peri-umbilical port-site discomfort; wounds clean and dry. Current observations include heart rate 92 beats/minute.

Discharge problem list:
• Acute uncomplicated appendicitis, treated by laparoscopic appendicectomy
• Post-operative abdominal pain, improving

Discharge medicines:
Paracetamol as directed on the dispensing label when required for pain. No further antibiotics prescribed.

Plan and advice: keep wounds dry for the first day, then shower normally; avoid strenuous activity until reviewed by the surgical team. GP review if ongoing pain or wound concerns. Return to A&E for fever, persistent vomiting, increasing abdominal pain, abdominal distension, wound redness or discharge, or inability to drink.

Paediatric surgical follow-up arranged in approximately two weeks; histology result to be reviewed by the surgical service. Guardian and patient understood the advice and were discharged home in the care of the father.

NHS number: 0003815910

Date: 13/06/2023
Patient: Jahzari Palmer
Report/accession ID: 036835245

Dear Respiratory Medicine Team,

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient with established rheumatoid arthritis, currently experiencing a flare with pronounced morning stiffness, swollen small joints of both hands and significant fatigue. They report new exertional breathlessness over recent weeks, without chest pain, haemoptysis or infective symptoms. A close friend has accompanied them and provided additional history.

Current treatment is methotrexate 15 mg once weekly, folic acid and naproxen. Methotrexate has otherwise been tolerated, with no recent dose change. The patient has not yet required oral corticosteroids for this episode. Examination in the surgery showed active synovitis at the MCP and PIP joints; chest examination was clear, with oxygen saturation within the expected range at rest. Recent blood tests showed no significant anaemia and stable renal function. A chest radiograph has been requested, but the result is not yet available.

Assessment

Rheumatoid arthritis flare with new exertional dyspnoea. Please assess for interstitial lung disease or other methotrexate-related pulmonary toxicity, while considering alternative respiratory causes.

Plan and request

Please advise on the need for pulmonary function testing, high-resolution CT and any alteration to disease-modifying treatment. Methotrexate will continue pending specialist advice, provided symptoms do not deteriorate. The patient has been advised to seek urgent assessment through A&E if breathlessness becomes severe or occurs at rest.

Yours faithfully,

Siman Clarkson
GP
Queen Elizabeth University Hospital

AKI with oliguria — intake and output chart commenced; strict fluid balance ongoing.

Intravenous sodium chloride running as prescribed; cannula site clean and patent. Temporary medication hold maintained pending review. No nausea or vomiting.

Covering medical clinician informed of urine output and borderline blood pressure; GMC professional identifier GMC-TEST-0206465. Blood tests requested/review planned. Continue observations and escalate reduced consciousness, worsening hypotension or further drop in urine output.

Next shift  
Maintain strict fluid balance, encourage oral intake, repeat observations, check renal blood results when available. Review fluid prescription and medication plan. Follow-up in 18 days.

Clinical Genetics Review

Patient: Hadiyah H.
Occupation: Writer
Employer: Rhodes Town Council
Home address: 31 Lenside Drive, Clacton-on-Sea, CO15 1AA
Patient contact: hadiyah.head65@hotmail.com

Reason for review: Established Parkinson disease with consideration of a hereditary contribution. Information was provided by the patient, with additional observations from a friend.

Clinical history: Resting tremor, bradykinesia and muscular rigidity remain present, with symptoms reported as gradually progressive. The diagnosis was previously assessed by neurology and co-beneldopa has been continued in primary care. No clear multigenerational pattern of parkinsonism was elicited during this consultation. Family history available today is limited; the patient will review this with relatives before the next appointment.

Examination: Mild bilateral bradykinesia and increased tone, more evident in the upper limbs. Intermittent resting tremor observed. Speech was clear and gait was cautious but independent. No dyskinesia or prominent atypical neurological features noted on this assessment.

Interpretation: The clinical picture is consistent with the established diagnosis of Parkinson disease. At present there is insufficient family history or clinical information to define a monogenic syndrome. Genetic testing is therefore not indicated routinely, although this may be reconsidered if a relevant family history emerges, particularly early-onset disease or multiple affected relatives.

Plan: Continue co-beneldopa pending medication review by neurology or the appropriate multidisciplinary team. Obtain a three-generation family history where possible. The patient will contact the service if further relatives are identified with parkinsonism, dementia or unexplained movement disorder. Follow-up in clinical genetics after family-history clarification.

A&E Paediatric Assessment

Patient: KEHLANI-RAE DUNCAN
History from mother, tunisha arif. Generalised convulsion at home during fever, lasting approximately 3 minutes; eyes deviated upwards, no focal jerking. No previous seizures reported. Drowsy afterwards but responding by arrival. No vomiting or breathing difficulty.

Observations: T 39.1°C; heart rate 108 beats/minute; RR 24/min; SpO₂ 98% air.
The patient, aged 4 years, was reviewed with mother present.

Examination: Postictal initially, now alert and interactive. Airway patent, chest clear, CRT <2 seconds. No meningism, focal neurology or rash. Tympanic membranes mildly erythematous. Capillary glucose 5.8 mmol/L.

Impression: Simple febrile seizure, likely viral febrile illness. No indication for neuroimaging or lumbar puncture currently.

Management: Cooling measures, fluids by mouth as tolerated, paracetamol for comfort. Seizure first-aid explained; recovery position and emergency escalation discussed. No antibiotics or anticonvulsant required.

Discharge home with mother once fully back to baseline. GP review if fever persists. Paediatric review booked for 6 January 2036.

Discharging clinician: Abdel Warner

MOLECULAR GENETICS LABORATORY REPORT
NHS number: 000 106 2558

Patient: Jubair
Home address: 158 Widewaters Close, Liverpool, L2 0AA
Report/accession ID: 28/023541
Report date: 29 Jul 1988
Request: Predictive testing for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk
Ordering clinician: Not stated on referral

Specimen
Peripheral blood in EDTA; received for germline analysis. Specimen suitable for testing. No current treatment reported.

Clinical information
Significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer. Jubair requests clarification of inherited cancer risk; cancer-risk concern discussed with partner. Pre-test counselling and consent for analysis documented on the referral.

Result
BRCA1 c.68_69delAG: not detected.

Interpretation
No pathogenic BRCA1 c.68_69delAG variant identified in this specimen. This result substantially reduces, but does not eliminate, the possibility of a hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome. It does not exclude pathogenic variants in other cancer-predisposition genes, variants not detected by the assay, or familial risk unrelated to the tested variant.

Clinical comment
Interpretation should be considered alongside the family pedigree and any known familial result. If the reported family variant is different, targeted testing for that variant should be confirmed before using this result for relatives. Referral to the regional genetics service is appropriate for review of the pedigree, discussion of broader panel testing where indicated, and individualised screening advice.

Authorisation
Validated and reported by: G. Daniel
Laboratory interpretation: result suitable for clinical use within the stated referral context.

General Medicine Clinic Note
NHS number: 000 912 1456

Patient: Haleigh B., 71-year-old Hispanic female patient
MRN: 0538424
Date: 2004-06-16
Patient contact: 07700 900124

Reason for review: Persistent low back pain with left-sided radicular symptoms.

History:
6-week history of central lumbar pain, now shooting down posterior left thigh to calf. Intermittent tingling over lateral calf and dorsum of foot. Worse sitting, driving and bending. Mobilising independently. No reported fall or recent injury. No bowel or bladder disturbance; no saddle sensory change. Emergency contact recorded in demographics.

Pain score: 5/10 currently.
Analgesia: paracetamol and naproxen, partial benefit. Taking naproxen with food. No regular gastroprotection documented.

Examination:
Gait mildly antalgic. Lumbar flexion restricted by pain. Left straight-leg raise positive at approximately 50 degrees. Power 5/5 in both lower limbs; sensation broadly intact. Reflexes symmetrical. No focal spinal tenderness.

Assessment:
Lumbar radiculopathy, likely left S1 distribution. No objective neurological deficit or red-flag features today.

Plan:
Continue paracetamol as directed; review NSAID use and avoid other NSAIDs. Start PPI cover if continuing naproxen, subject to medication review. Refer to physiotherapy for graded exercise and spinal rehabilitation. Consider MRI if progressive deficit, persistent disabling symptoms or failure of conservative treatment. Safety-netting given regarding weakness, saddle numbness or bladder/bowel symptoms; urgent emergency assessment if these occur. Review with GP in 4–6 weeks.

Discharge summary
NHS number: 000 582 3626

Patient: calvin crook
DOB: 1974-07-12
Admission/discharge date: 04/02/2012
Emergency contact: Shasvik Morris, SIX ROAD END

Reason for admission
Presented with several days of lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge and deep dyspareunia. No haemodynamic instability. Pregnancy test negative.

Assessment and hospital course
Pelvic examination was consistent with pelvic inflammatory disease. Vaginal and cervical samples were taken; results were pending at discharge. Blood tests showed a mild inflammatory response, with stable renal and liver function. Pelvic ultrasound did not show a tubo-ovarian abscess. The respiratory medicine review found no respiratory cause for the presenting symptoms and no requirement for respiratory treatment.

Treated initially with ceftriaxone, followed by oral doxycycline and metronidazole. Pain and nausea improved, and oral intake was adequate before discharge. The importance of completing the antibiotic course was discussed. Avoid sexual intercourse until treatment is completed, symptoms have settled and partners have been assessed. Partner notification and sexual health follow-up were advised.

Discharge medicines
Doxycycline and metronidazole as prescribed on the discharge prescription; ceftriaxone course completed in hospital. Avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole and for 48 hours afterwards. Simple analgesia if required, according to the label.

Follow-up and safety net
Please attend the local sexual health service for review, test results and partner management. GP review if symptoms are not clearly improving within 72 hours. Return to A&E urgently for worsening pain, fever, vomiting, fainting or heavy bleeding. Repeat clinical review is planned in about 13 weeks.

Discharged home clinically stable on 04/02/2012.

Patient: Yadav O.
Occupation: Graphic designer
Report/accession ID: 031184053

Thank you for attending the respiratory clinic with your friend. We reviewed the headaches and occasional light-headedness you have noticed recently. Your blood pressure was above the recommended range on several readings, although there were no features to suggest an acute neurological or respiratory emergency today. The chest examination was clear, and your oxygen level was satisfactory.

The overall assessment is essential hypertension. This is not usually caused by a single episode of stress or pain, so we will confirm the pattern with home monitoring and check for factors that may affect treatment. Please record two readings, one minute apart, morning and evening, for seven days, seated and rested. Bring the monitor and the completed readings to your GP surgery if possible.

Continue amlodipine and ramipril as currently prescribed; do not stop either medicine without advice. We discussed reducing salt, moderating alcohol, maintaining regular activity and avoiding excess over-the-counter anti-inflammatory painkillers, which can raise blood pressure. Blood tests for kidney function and electrolytes should be arranged through primary care, with urine testing and an ECG if not already completed.

Seek urgent help via A&E or 999 for sudden weakness, speech difficulty, severe chest pain, marked breathlessness or a sudden severe headache. Otherwise, please arrange a medication and blood-pressure review with your GP within the next few weeks.

Kind regards,

Larsen Wallace
consultant cardiologist
Gstt @ William Harvey Hospital

text:
A&E Cardiology Assessment

Patient: Rishil
History from patient and partner, T. Molloy. Sudden spinning sensation when turning in bed or looking upwards, episodes lasting <1 minute. Nausea, no vomiting. Feels unsteady afterwards but walking independently. No chest pain, palpitations, syncope, headache, diplopia, dysarthria or focal weakness. Prochlorperazine as required; partial relief.

Obs: T 36.7°C, HR 74 regular, BP 120/80 mmHg, SpO₂ 99% air.
Alert, coherent. Cardiovascular: normal heart sounds, no murmur. Chest clear. Neurology: pupils equal/reactive, normal power and sensation, no dysmetria. Gait mildly cautious. No spontaneous nystagmus. Dix–Hallpike positive to right with brief torsional nystagmus and reproduction of symptoms.

ECG: sinus rhythm, no acute ST-T change.
Bloods: FBC, U&E and glucose unremarkable.

Impression: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo; no clinical evidence of central neurological event or cardiac cause.

Treatment: Epley manoeuvre performed with improvement. Prochlorperazine as required. Mobilised safely prior to discharge.

Plan: Discharge home with partner. Written vestibular exercise advice and return precautions given. GP review via University Hospital Llandough if persistent; vestibular physiotherapy review booked for 23rd August 2024. Discussed with senior clinician R. Clarkson.

text:
Dear Clinical Genetics Team,
NHS number: 000 023 7257

Re: Diandra Brook  
MRN: MRN-04209037

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient with persistent iron-deficiency anaemia despite appropriate oral replacement. The specific question is whether an inherited red-cell disorder or other genetic contribution should be considered, particularly in view of a longstanding microcytosis that appears disproportionate to the degree of iron depletion.

The patient reports ongoing tiredness, intermittent dizziness and reduced exercise tolerance. Their spouse has accompanied them and describes reduced stamina over recent months. There is no reported overt gastrointestinal bleeding, and menstrual history has not suggested heavy loss. Previous coeliac serology was negative. Recent blood tests showed haemoglobin 96 g/L, MCV 71 fL and ferritin 8 micrograms/L; renal and thyroid profiles were unremarkable. A blood film showed marked microcytosis and hypochromia without abnormal white-cell morphology.

Treatment has been adherence to ferrous fumarate 210 mg once daily, with only a modest haematological response. The patient has been advised to continue this pending specialist review. We are arranging further gastrointestinal assessment in parallel, given the persistent deficiency.

Assessment: iron-deficiency anaemia with disproportionate microcytosis; possible co-existing haemoglobinopathy or other inherited red-cell trait.

Please review the blood results and advise whether haemoglobin analysis, molecular testing or wider genetic assessment is indicated. If testing is undertaken, counselling regarding implications for the patient and family would be appreciated. Follow-up with the surgery is booked for 2025-07-13.

Yours faithfully,

Falisha Bruce
Royal Victoria Hospital

Patient: Ademola Maynard
MRN: 0344801
Address: 50 Collins Place, Ardminish, PA41 7AA
Clinical area: Respiratory medicine

Review: The patient, aged 55 years, was reviewed on the morning round. Sibling at bedside; history corroborated. Productive cough with yellow sputum, intermittent fever and right-sided pleuritic pain. Breathless on mobilisation, comfortable at rest.

Observations: T 38.1°C; HR 102 bpm; BP 118/67 mmHg; RR 22/min; SpO₂ 94% on air. Alert and orientated. Coarse crackles right base. No acute distress.

Mobility/intake: Mobilised to chair with one assist. Reduced appetite but taking fluids; approximately half of breakfast. Urine passed.

Interventions: Oral amoxicillin administered as prescribed. Paracetamol given for fever and pleuritic pain. Encouraged oral fluids, deep breathing and supported coughing. Sputum pot provided.

Response: Temperature and pain improved on reassessment; breathing settled following rest. No adverse medication effects observed.

Assessment: Community-acquired pneumonia — SNOMED CT 233604007. Falls risk due to weakness and unsteady gait. Pressure areas intact.

Escalation: Respiratory consultant review documented; doctor’s GMC identifier 0305429 recorded in clinical notes. Escalate if increasing oxygen requirement, confusion, hypotension or worsening work of breathing.

Plan: Continue observations, antibiotics and analgesia. Assist with transfers, encourage meals and fluids, repeat respiratory assessment next round. Handover to evening staff.

Patient: Rebbeca Weston
NHS number: 000 028 6371
Occupation: Lawyer
Employer: Talywain Further Education College
Home address: 28 Queen's Avenue, Llanbrynmair, SY19 7AA
Patient contact: rebbeca.weston26@virginmedia.com
Location: A&E ambulatory care

Presenting problem:
Seen following attendance at A&E with several months of fatigue, increased sensitivity to cold and constipation. No chest pain, breathlessness or syncope. Spouse present and contributed to history. Taking levothyroxine regularly; no recent dose change reported.

Examination:
Alert, communicating normally. Skin mildly dry. Pulse regular, no peripheral oedema. Thyroid not enlarged or tender. Abdomen soft, non-tender. No focal neurological deficit.

Results:
A&E bloods suggest under-replacement: TSH raised, free T4 reduced. FBC and U&E without clinically significant abnormality. No acute cause identified for symptoms.

Assessment:
Hypothyroidism, likely suboptimally replaced. Clinically stable for community follow-up; no indication for admission.

Actions:
• Continue levothyroxine at current prescribed dose pending repeat thyroid function tests.
• Blood test requested through GP surgery in 6–8 weeks; take levothyroxine consistently on an empty stomach and separate from iron or calcium preparations.
• GP review after results, with dose adjustment if persistent biochemical hypothyroidism.
• Safety-netted to return to A&E for marked drowsiness, confusion, collapse, chest pain or worsening breathlessness.

Follow-up:
Routine review in about 13 weeks, or sooner if symptoms deteriorate.

Cardiology outpatient review
NHS number: 000 279 4854

Patient: MOLLY-LOUISE SHAHZAD, 62-year-old Latino male patient
MRN: 0369151
Patient contact: 07700 900299

Seen in clinic following referral for intermittent awareness of the heartbeat and chest tightness. Symptoms occur mainly in the evening and during periods of increased stress, without exertional chest pain, syncope or ankle swelling. Previous ECG and routine blood tests were reassuring. The patient describes persistent worry about health, poor sleep with prolonged time to settle, and tightness across the shoulders and jaw. No recent change in caffeine intake or recreational drug use.

Examination today was unremarkable. Heart sounds normal, rhythm regular, chest clear and there was no peripheral oedema. The symptom pattern is not suggestive of a primary cardiac disorder. Overall presentation is consistent with generalised anxiety disorder, with associated palpitations and muscle tension. No indication for further cardiology testing at present.

Medication reviewed. Continue sertraline 50 mg once daily; adherence is good and there have been no significant adverse effects. Discussed allowing several weeks for ongoing benefit and arranging psychological support through the GP surgery. The patient will seek urgent assessment via A&E if sustained chest pain, collapse or severe breathlessness develops.

Plan: discharge from routine cardiology follow-up, with ongoing management in primary care. Review with the GP as planned, including consideration of talking therapy and sleep measures. Cardiology review arranged for 2nd April 2018 only if symptoms persist or the clinical picture changes.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: ASSIM GARRETT
DOB: 2 Dec 1953
Patient contact: 07700 900563
Admission/discharge date: 22nd October 2019

Reason for admission:
Reduced urine output, fatigue and poor oral intake. Spouse Amirat provided collateral history.

Working diagnosis:
Acute kidney injury, felt secondary to dehydration in the context of reduced intake.

Key results:
Initial creatinine elevated from documented baseline; improved with fluids. Urine output increased following intravenous sodium chloride. Urinalysis without significant blood or protein. Renal ultrasound: no hydronephrosis.

Hospital course:
Intravenous sodium chloride administered. Temporary medication hold during AKI; regular medicines reviewed before discharge. Oral intake improved and nausea may improve with hydration. Haemodynamically stable throughout. No evidence of infection.

Discharge condition:
Passing urine, mobilising independently, tolerating oral fluids and light diet. Repeat renal profile improved but requires community follow-up.

Plan:
GP review and repeat U&Es within 3–5 days. Restart held medication only as advised by GP following blood-test review. Encourage regular oral fluids and avoid NSAIDs unless specifically directed.

Safety net:
Return to A&E if urine output falls again, persistent vomiting, increasing lethargy or inability to maintain fluids.

Emergency Department Assessment

Patient: Freddi E.
MRN: 0595610
Patient contact: 07700 900016
Accompanied by friend: MOLOLUWA PATRICK
Referring healthcare organisation: University Hospital Llandough
Arrival/triage time: 08:15

Presenting complaint:
Increasing redness and pain around postoperative wound since yesterday. Purulent discharge noted this morning. No reported rigors, vomiting or collapse.

Initial observations:
Alert, haemodynamically stable. Temperature 37.8°C, pulse 96, BP 128/76, respiratory rate 18, SpO₂ 98% on air.

Focused examination:
Lower abdominal operative wound with approximately 3 cm surrounding erythema, warmth and tenderness. Small amount of thick yellow discharge from the lateral edge; wound edges otherwise intact. No fluctuance, crepitus or spreading cellulitis. Abdomen soft, with local wound tenderness only.

Investigations:
Wound swab sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivities. FBC and CRP requested; venous lactate not raised. Blood cultures not indicated at present in the absence of systemic features.

Assessment:
Likely superficial postoperative wound infection. No clinical evidence of abscess, dehiscence or sepsis requiring admission today.

Treatment/action:
Wound irrigated with sterile saline and covered with a clean dressing. Oral flucloxacillin commenced. Analgesia advised as required. Discussed wound care and the importance of completing antibiotics.

Disposition:
Discharged home with surgical follow-up arranged through University Hospital Llandough. Return to A&E for fever, rapidly extending redness, worsening pain, vomiting, wound separation or feeling acutely unwell.

Paediatric Dermatology Outpatient Report
NHS number: 000 834 6799

Patient: keauna samuel
Clinical age: 18 m/o
MRN: 093012285
Legal guardian: brandyn shaw

Referral reason: Review of recurrent atopic eczema with pruritus, inflamed skin and disrupted sleep.

History: brandyn shaw, the legal guardian, reports increased itching and nocturnal scratching for 3 days, particularly over the antecubital fossae, cheeks and lower legs. Sleep has been unsettled, with several awakenings. No fever, facial swelling, wheeze or reduced oral intake. Existing treatment comprises regular emollient and topical hydrocortisone during flares; application has been intermittent recently because of concern about topical steroid use.

Examination: Comfortable and alert in clinic. Xerosis affecting the trunk and limbs, with erythematous eczematous plaques in both antecubital fossae and scattered excoriated areas over the shins. Mild cheek involvement. No honey-coloured crusting, pustulation, vesicles or lymphangitis. No clinical evidence of eczema herpeticum. Mucous membranes clear.

Impression: Atopic eczema, currently moderately active, with sleep disturbance secondary to pruritus. No convincing evidence of bacterial or viral superinfection today.

Plan: Continue liberal, fragrance-free emollient at least four times daily and after bathing; use as a soap substitute. Apply topical hydrocortisone to active inflamed areas in a thin layer once daily until clear, then stop; avoid application to broken or infected skin. Demonstrated fingertip-unit application and provided written advice. Keep nails short and use cotton nightwear. Review in paediatric clinic if not improving, or sooner via GP/A&E if rapidly spreading redness, blistering, fever or marked deterioration develops.

Report prepared and signed by A. Whittle.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: S. HENRY
MRN: 02366685
Admission area: General medicine
Discharging service: Royal Victoria Hospital
Responsible consultant: General medicine

Reason for admission
Spreading erythema, warmth and tenderness of the lower leg, with progression despite initial oral treatment. No clinical features of sepsis on admission.

Key findings
Inflamed lower leg with well-demarcated erythema; no fluctuance or crepitus. Initial blood tests showed a mild inflammatory response. Blood cultures negative. Ultrasound excluded a deep vein thrombosis.

Hospital course
Treated with intravenous flucloxacillin, then changed to oral flucloxacillin once improving. Erythema receded from the marked margin and pain was controlled with paracetamol. Eating and drinking adequately, mobilising independently. No operative intervention required.

Observations before discharge
BP 120/80 mmHg. Afebrile and clinically euvolaemic. Leg less warm and tender; no new blistering.

Discharge medicines
• Flucloxacillin to complete the prescribed antibiotic course.
• Paracetamol as needed for pain, within the labelled maximum dose.
No other medication changes documented.

Follow-up / actions

Rheumatoid arthritis flare. Reports increased morning stiffness, painful swollen MCP and PIP joints, and marked fatigue for 3 days. Difficulty opening packets and using walking frame. Friend present, history corroborated.

Observations
Alert and orientated. Respirations even at rest, no chest pain or new breathlessness. NEWS2 0. Hands warm; bilateral hand swelling and reduced grip, no skin breaks. Mobilised to bathroom with frame and one staff member; slow but steady. Intake reduced at breakfast, fluids tolerated. Urine passed.

Medication / interventions
Usual methotrexate and folic acid confirmed on medication chart. Naproxen administered with food as prescribed; warm packs applied to hands, rest periods encouraged. Assistance provided with washing and meal set-up. Reassessed after intervention: pain eased slightly, stiffness persists; able to grip cup.

Risk / escalation
Falls risk increased due to fatigue and impaired grip. Call bell within reach, non-slip footwear in place. No acute respiratory compromise. Covering medical team informed of joint swelling and reduced function; review requested regarding flare treatment and analgesia. Check for infection before any immunosuppression change.

Plan for next shift
Repeat pain and joint assessment, encourage oral fluids and assisted mobilisation. Monitor temperature and respiratory status. Confirm rheumatology plan and blood results; withhold methotrexate and escalate if febrile or clinically unwell, following prescription and medical advice.

kosisochukwu nolan

Patient: A. Begum

Reason for attendance  
Presented with four days of persistent vomiting, unable to maintain oral fluids, with dizziness on standing and reported weight loss. No abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding. Partner present; emergency contact locality recorded as Fioscabhaig.

Assessment and investigations  
Clinically dehydrated on arrival with dry mucous membranes and postural symptoms. Urinalysis showed ketones. Blood tests demonstrated mild hypokalaemia and raised urea consistent with reduced intake; inflammatory markers and liver profile were unremarkable. ECG without acute abnormality. Abdominal examination remained soft and non-tender. Pregnancy assessment discussed with the early pregnancy team at Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh; no indication for urgent ultrasound from the A&E assessment, with follow-up arranged.

Received intravenous sodium chloride with improvement in pulse, dizziness and urine output. Cyclizine given intravenously initially, then tolerated orally. Vomiting settled during observation and a trial of oral fluids and plain food was successful. No further weight loss documented during the department stay. Thiamine supplementation given before carbohydrate-containing fluids.

Problem list
• First-trimester hyperemesis with dehydration and ketonuria  
• Mild hypokalaemia, treated with fluids and dietary advice  
• Early pregnancy, 9+4 weeks' gestation

Discharge medicines  
Cyclizine 50 mg orally up to three times daily as needed for nausea. Continue prescribed antenatal vitamins if tolerated. No other medication changes.

Discharge plan  
Discharged home clinically improved with partner. Encourage frequent small amounts of fluid and food; avoid prolonged fasting. Same-day contact with the early pregnancy service at Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh if vomiting recurs or oral intake declines. Return to A&E for inability to keep fluids down, fainting, abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, fever or reduced urine output. GP review for repeat electrolytes if symptoms persist.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY – Cardiology

Patient: NIVIN FRANCIS
Address: 145 LISNAGARVEY DRIVE, KILLINCHY
Patient contact: 07700 900490
Admission reason: Sudden breathlessness, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and tachycardia. Pulmonary embolism confirmed on CT pulmonary angiogram.

Key results
• CTPA: bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli, moderate clot burden; no saddle embolus.
• Echocardiogram: preserved left ventricular systolic function; mild right ventricular strain.
• Troponin mildly raised but stable on repeat. Renal function satisfactory for anticoagulation.
• Lower-limb Doppler: no proximal DVT identified.

Hospital course
Admitted to the cardiology observation ward haemodynamically stable. Required supplemental oxygen initially, weaned to room air before discharge. Apixaban commenced following review of bleeding risk and medication history. No thrombolysis or catheter intervention indicated. Mobilising independently; pleuritic pain improved with simple analgesia. At 08:15, observations remained stable and oxygen saturations were maintained on air.

Discharge medicines
• Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily. Duration to be reviewed by the anticoagulation service.
• Paracetamol as needed for pain.
Avoid NSAIDs unless specifically advised. Seek urgent medical attention for worsening breathlessness, syncope, haemoptysis or significant bleeding.

Follow-up / actions
Anticoagulation clinic referral sent; GP to review within 1–2 weeks. Outpatient respiratory/cardiology review for provoking factors and duration of treatment. Written anticoagulation information supplied.

Condition at discharge: Clinically stable, ambulant, discharged home.

Discharging clinician: Dr Taavi Kavanagh, MBBS, Consultant Physician
GMC: 0843392

Dr Denis-Andrei Plant, MBBS

Patient: 90-year-old Native American female patient — Summer-Jayne
Specimen: Deep swab, plantar diabetic foot ulcer
Collection/report date: 20/06/2035
Report/accession ID: 28/337921

Clinical details:
Diabetes mellitus; plantar ulceration with reduced sensation and local discharge. Wound care in progress. Current treatment: co-amoxiclav 625 mg three times daily.

Microscopy:
Leucocytes: moderate.
Gram-positive cocci: present.
Squamous epithelial cells: few.

Culture:
Heavy growth of Staphylococcus aureus.
Mixed skin flora also isolated.
No anaerobes recovered.

Susceptibility:
S. aureus susceptible to flucloxacillin, co-amoxiclav and clindamycin. Resistant to penicillin. No evidence of meticillin resistance.

Interpretation:
Significant S. aureus growth from an infected diabetic foot ulcer. Result should be interpreted with examination findings and depth of infection; superficial swabs may reflect colonisation.

Clinical comment/action:
Continue prescribed antimicrobial pending clinical review; ensure dose and duration are reviewed against renal function and response. Urgent diabetic foot/multidisciplinary assessment if spreading erythema, systemic upset, increasing pain, necrosis or concern for osteomyelitis. Consider deep tissue specimen if poor response or operative management planned.

Validated by: Kritin ROBERTS
Laboratory medicine clinician

Patient: Pranavan H.
Occupation: Taxi driver
Report/accession ID: 01268027

Thank you for attending review at Ilkeston Hospital Utc. You described a recent worsening of your rheumatoid arthritis, with swollen knuckles and wrists, prolonged morning stiffness and marked fatigue. There was no history of fever or recent infection. You remain able to manage personal care, although dressing and opening jars have become more difficult. Your adult child accompanied you and helped with the history.

On examination, several MCP and PIP joints were visibly swollen and tender, with reduced grip because of pain. No acute joint deformity was noted. Observations were satisfactory and there was no evidence of an intercurrent illness.

The overall picture is of an inflammatory rheumatoid arthritis flare. Please continue methotrexate 15 mg once weekly on the established day, together with folic acid. Continue naproxen with food if required, provided you have no stomach bleeding, worsening indigestion or new kidney problems. Do not take methotrexate on additional days.

We have arranged blood tests, including full blood count, liver profile, renal function and inflammatory markers, and will review the results with the rheumatology team. Please contact the surgery promptly if you develop a fever, mouth ulcers, unusual bruising or breathlessness, as these may require withholding methotrexate and urgent advice. We will discuss whether a short steroid course or adjustment of disease-modifying treatment is appropriate once the results are available.

Signed: osaama rees

Nursing progress note – Neonatal Unit

Patient: raysha blackburn
day 3 of life; mother Daniele WEBBER present and providing history.

Observations: Warm, pink apart from facial/truncal jaundice. RR 46, HR 142, SpO₂ stable in air. Alert briefly to handling, settles readily. No respiratory distress.

Feeding: Sleepy at breast, reduced intake overnight. Assisted by staff with positioning and waking; expressed milk offered by oral syringe. Tolerated small feeds, no vomiting. Wet nappies reported, stool passed.

Treatment: Phototherapy commenced as prescribed; eye protection in place, skin checks completed. Temperature maintained in cot. Feeding support continued, intake/output chart updated.

Escalation: Notify medical team for worsening lethargy, poor feeding, temperature instability or reduced urine output.

Plan: Continue phototherapy and 3-hourly feeds; wake for feeds if required. Repeat observations and bilirubin as requested. Mother to arrange community review in about 12 weeks, appointment dated 2026-01-29.

Documented by J. HOOPER, neonatal nurse.

text:
Discharge summary

Patient: Ahmar
Home address: 171 Brimmond Place, Glasgow, G32 0AA
Report/accession ID: S29-0239280

Dear GP,

Ahmar was admitted with a three-day history of frequent diarrhoea, vomiting and cramping abdominal pain. There was no evidence of a surgical abdomen. A friend accompanied the patient and helped provide the history.

On arrival, the patient was mildly dehydrated but haemodynamically stable; current observations included blood pressure 120/80 mmHg. Blood tests showed a small pre-renal rise in creatinine, which improved after oral and intravenous fluids. Stool culture and viral testing were sent; no concerning pathogen was identified during the admission. No imaging or procedure was required.

The patient was managed with fluid replacement, a light diet as tolerated and anti-sickness treatment. Vomiting settled, oral intake improved and stool frequency reduced before discharge. There was no further abdominal tenderness on review.

Discharge medicines:
• Oral rehydration solution, prepared and taken according to the packet instructions, particularly after loose stools.
• Ondansetron as required for nausea, as prescribed on the electronic discharge prescription.

Please arrange GP review if symptoms have not fully settled within 48–72 hours. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E for inability to keep fluids down, worsening or localised abdominal pain, blood in the stool, fainting, confusion or markedly reduced urine output. Good hand hygiene and avoiding food preparation for others until 48 hours after the last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting were advised.

Discharge condition: clinically improved and safe for home.

Dr Arcadia CROOK, MBBS, GMC number 0046822
Consultant physician, Respiratory Medicine

Haemodynamically stable, suitable for ambulatory PE pathway following senior review. Continue anticoagulation as prescribed, written advice and return precautions provided. Same-day medical assessment arranged. Discharged with sibling.

Referral to Clinical Genetics

Patient: C. WATT
Occupation: Graphic designer
Employer: Lochton Community Centre

Dear Clinical Genetics Team,

I would be grateful for your assessment of C. WATT regarding marked knee osteoarthritis at a relatively young clinical age, with bilateral symptoms and a reported family pattern of early joint problems. The specific question is whether the presentation warrants investigation for an inherited skeletal or connective-tissue disorder, and whether genetic counselling or testing would alter management.

There is a several-year history of progressive bilateral knee pain, morning stiffness and reduced mobility, now limiting walking and work activities. Examination in the surgery showed varus discomfort on loading, crepitus and reduced flexion, without acute effusion or inflammatory skin changes. Current pain score is 5/10. Plain radiographs arranged previously demonstrated medial compartment degenerative change, more pronounced on the right. There has been no history of significant knee trauma.

Management to date has included physiotherapy, activity modification and advice regarding strengthening. Symptomatic treatment is paracetamol and topical ibuprofen, with only partial benefit. No systemic inflammatory symptoms are reported. Festus, the patient’s partner, has helped describe the gradual decline in mobility and increasing difficulty with stairs.

Assessment: clinically significant, progressive knee osteoarthritis with possible familial early-onset pattern; the hereditary basis is uncertain.

I would appreciate your view on eligibility for genetics assessment, any recommended baseline investigations, and whether referral to rheumatology or an inherited musculoskeletal multidisciplinary service would be more appropriate.

Yours sincerely,

Cecelia-Rose Barber

Emergency Department Assessment – Clinical Genetics
NHS number: 0005491801

Patient: Gurpal
Date: 2nd April 2024
Referring service: Glangwili General Hospital
Collateral history: sibling, JERSI PROCTOR

Presenting complaint
Watery diarrhoea, vomiting and intermittent abdominal cramps for 3 days. Several episodes overnight with reduced oral intake. No blood reported. Sibling concerned about dizziness on standing.

Background
Known genetic condition under follow-up; no recent admissions. No recent antibiotic course or overseas travel documented. Medication reconciliation completed.

Examination
Alert, uncomfortable but not distressed. Dry lips and mildly dry tongue. Peripheral perfusion preserved, capillary refill <2 seconds. Pulse regular. Abdomen soft with generalised mild cramping discomfort, no guarding or rebound. No focal neurological deficit.

Observations
Afebrile. Haemodynamically stable at assessment. Passing urine, though less frequently than usual.

Investigations
Urinalysis: concentrated urine, otherwise unremarkable.
Bloods: electrolytes and renal function requested; no immediate biochemical indication for intravenous replacement. Stool sample advised if diarrhoea persists or becomes bloody.

Assessment
Likely infectious gastroenteritis with mild dehydration. No examination evidence of acute abdomen or sepsis.

Treatment / actions
Oral rehydration solution commenced in department, small frequent volumes tolerated. Ondansetron as required for nausea and vomiting. Medication: oral rehydration solution; ondansetron as required. Hygiene advice given and avoid preparation of food for others while symptomatic.

Disposition
