Discharge summary
NHS number: 0006713590

Patient: Bissan Firth
MRN: 00585558
Admitting service: Ulster Hospital

Reason for admission
Admitted with a three-day history of productive cough, fever and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Examination in the emergency department showed focal right basal crackles and reduced air entry. Chest radiograph demonstrated right lower-zone air-space opacity in keeping with community-acquired pneumonia. Coded as SNOMED CT 233604007.

Hospital course
Treated initially with intravenous antibiotics and fluids, then stepped down to oral amoxicillin once clinically improved. Paracetamol given for fever and pleuritic discomfort, with good effect. Oxygen was required briefly on admission but was discontinued following improvement; saturations remained satisfactory on air thereafter. Blood cultures showed no growth. Inflammatory markers and temperature trended down during admission. No evidence of pleural effusion or respiratory deterioration.

Problem list
1. Community-acquired pneumonia, right lower lobe.
2. Fever and pleuritic chest pain, resolved.
3. Reduced oral intake/dehydration, corrected with fluids.

Discharge medicines
Amoxicillin to complete the prescribed course.
Paracetamol as needed for pain or fever.
No other medication changes documented.

Condition at discharge
Alert, mobilising independently and tolerating oral intake. Afebrile, breathing comfortably at rest, with mild residual cough only. Discharged home with advice to complete antibiotics and maintain fluids. Seek urgent medical attention for worsening breathlessness, recurrent high fever, confusion, chest pain not settling with simple analgesia, or inability to keep medication down.

Follow-up
GP review if cough or fatigue persists, and routine clinical review if symptoms have not substantially settled after treatment. Consider follow-up chest imaging if clinically indicated, particularly if respiratory symptoms fail to resolve.

Prepared and authorised by Dr Josia ATKINS, MBBS, consultant physician, GMC number 0692911.

Dear Respiratory Team,

There have been no admissions, but two courses of oral steroids were required through the surgery this year, most recently six weeks ago.

Inhaler technique was reviewed today and improved with a spacer; adherence is reported to be variable, particularly with the preventer. There is no current fever or chest pain. Examination in the surgery showed scattered expiratory polyphonic wheeze, with oxygen saturations of 98% on air and no respiratory distress.

The clinical question is whether control remains poor despite appropriate preventer therapy, and whether treatment should be stepped up or the diagnosis revisited. Please arrange spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility if feasible, and consider FeNO and allergy assessment according to your local pathway. Advice regarding an individualised asthma action plan and trigger reduction would also be helpful.

The family has been advised to seek urgent help via A&E or 999 if breathing becomes severe, speech is limited by breathlessness, or the reliever is not providing sustained benefit. I would appreciate review by a consultant respiratory physician, with recommendations copied back to the GP surgery.

Signed,
Dr Mieka Daley, MBBS

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: Scarlotte
DOB: 1961-03-13
Admission/discharge date: 25/02/2025
Ward: Respiratory Medicine
Reason for admission: Reduced urine output, fatigue and poor oral intake over several days. Admitted with acute kidney injury in the context of dehydration.

Collateral history: Friend, Choi Goldsmith, from BALLYGOWAN, provided additional history by telephone.

Key problems
• Acute kidney injury, likely pre-renal.
• Poor oral intake and clinical dehydration.
• No evidence of acute respiratory infection during admission.

Results
Admission bloods: creatinine 186 µmol/L, urea raised; electrolytes without significant abnormality. Urinalysis bland. Renal ultrasound: no hydronephrosis or obstructive lesion. Chest radiograph without focal consolidation.

Hospital course
Treated with intravenous sodium chloride and encouragement of oral fluids. Urine output improved over 24 hours and renal function began to recover. Temporary medication hold during the acute illness; medicines reviewed before discharge. No oxygen requirement. Mobilising independently and tolerating diet.

Discharge condition
Clinically euvolaemic, passing urine, observations stable. Suitable for discharge home today.

Actions for GP
Repeat U&E and renal function within one week; review medication restart once results available. Monitor hydration and blood pressure. Consider renal referral if kidney function fails to return towards baseline.

Patient advice
Maintain regular oral fluid intake unless otherwise advised. Seek urgent medical attention for worsening breathlessness, vomiting, confusion, markedly reduced urine output or inability to keep fluids down.

A&E emergency assessment

Patient: L. Gale
Age: 75 y/o patient
Accompanied by: relative, emergency contact
Seen at: ROTHERHAM DISTRICT GENERAL HOSPITAL
Document date: today

Presenting complaint:
Vomiting and frequent watery diarrhoea since yesterday, with intermittent central abdominal cramps. Reduced oral intake. Relative reports passing urine, though less than usual. No blood noted in stool or vomit. No recent travel documented.

Observations:
Alert, warm peripherally. Pulse mildly raised; BP maintained. Mucous membranes slightly dry. Capillary refill <2 seconds. Afebrile in department.

Examination:
Abdomen soft, non-distended, mild diffuse discomfort without guarding or rebound. Bowel sounds present. Chest clear. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. No rash.

Investigations:
Capillary glucose normal. Urinalysis: concentrated urine, otherwise unremarkable. No indication for blood tests or imaging at present. Clinical picture consistent with infectious gastroenteritis; no peritonism or evidence of significant dehydration.

Treatment / plan:
Oral rehydration solution commenced in small, frequent amounts. Ondansetron as required prescribed. Tolerated supervised fluids and subsequently settled; no further vomiting in department. Antibiotics not indicated. Relative advised regarding hand hygiene and separate towels.

Disposition:
Discharge home with relative. Continue fluids and light diet as tolerated. Return to A&E if unable to retain fluids, markedly reduced urine, blood in stool, increasing abdominal pain, drowsiness or breathing difficulty. GP review if not improving.

Follow-up: 1 Jul 2026

Clinician: SHALEN WAITE

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report

Patient: charvi lister
Report/accession ID: 0866015383
Report date: 6th May 2035
Clinical context: Rheumatoid arthritis flare with increased morning stiffness, swollen hand joints and fatigue. Current treatment includes methotrexate, folic acid and naproxen. The patient, aged 27 years, was reviewed for pharmacogenetic guidance regarding methotrexate toxicity risk.

Specimen: Peripheral blood, EDTA; received for genomic DNA extraction. Specimen adequate for analysis.

Test performed: Targeted pharmacogenetic panel including MTHFR c.665C>T (p.Ala222Val), TPMT c.460A>G (p.Ala154Thr), TPMT c.719A>G (p.Tyr240Cys), and NUDT15 c.415C>T (p.Arg139Cys).

Results:
MTHFR c.665C>T: heterozygous
TPMT c.460A>G: not detected
TPMT c.719A>G: not detected
NUDT15 c.415C>T: not detected

Interpretation: The detected MTHFR variant is common and, in isolation, does not provide a clinically actionable explanation for the current rheumatoid arthritis flare or indicate a requirement to alter methotrexate treatment. No tested TPMT or NUDT15 reduced-function variant was identified. Genotype does not exclude non-genetic causes of methotrexate intolerance or toxicity.

Clinical comment: Correlate with full blood count, liver function and renal function monitoring, together with disease activity assessment. Continue folic acid as prescribed. Any methotrexate dose change should be made by the treating rheumatology team. Routine clinical review is recommended in about 3 weeks.

Validated and reported by: Ocean-Grace Latham
Clinical Genetics Laboratory

Date: 2045-04-07
NHS number: 000 679 4344
Patient: tia-rae patel, 15-year-old Black male patient
Relative present: Father, AADHYA KEMP
Documented by: Merilin Duncan, Staff Nurse

Situation: Admitted with acute appendicitis. Right lower-quadrant pain, nausea and poor appetite for 3 days. Awaiting surgical review; nil by mouth maintained as prescribed.

Observations: Alert, mildly uncomfortable. Temperature 37.8°C, pulse 104 bpm, respirations 20/min, BP 112/68 mmHg, SpO₂ 99% on air. Pain 6/10 on movement, 3/10 at rest. Abdomen tender in right lower quadrant; no vomiting this shift.

Intake/output: Tolerating small sips of water. No oral food taken. IV fluids running; urine passed independently, amount not measured.

Interventions/result:
- Paracetamol administered as prescribed; pain improved to 3/10 at rest.
- Intravenous co-amoxiclav given, cannula patent with no local inflammation.
- Encouraged rest and assisted mobilisation to bathroom; steady gait, remains independently mobile.
- Surgical team informed of ongoing localised tenderness; review pending.

Risk/escalation: Falls risk low, call bell within reach. Monitor for increasing pain, fever, vomiting, abdominal distension or clinical deterioration. Father updated with patient’s agreement; patient offered opportunity to speak without parent present and assent sought for ongoing care.

Next shift: Continue observations and pain assessment, maintain nil by mouth/IV therapy as prescribed, record urine output, administer analgesia and antibiotics on time. Escalate promptly if observations worsen or pain becomes uncontrolled.

Discharge summary
NHS number: 000 778 1386

Patient: Scott
Discharging service: ROYAL INFIRMARY OF EDINBURGH
Report/accession ID: 06470256

Reason for admission:
Presented via A&E with several days of poor oral intake, fatigue and markedly reduced urine output. Initial blood tests demonstrated acute kidney injury, with creatinine above the patient’s known baseline. No clinical evidence of urinary retention or sepsis.

Hospital course:
Managed with intravenous sodium chloride and close fluid balance monitoring. Urine output improved over the first 24 hours and oral intake subsequently recovered. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis or other obstructive feature. Urinalysis without significant blood or protein. Repeat renal function improved but had not quite returned to baseline at discharge. Potassium remained within acceptable range and no dialysis indication developed.

The case was reviewed with the consultant nephrologist, who advised continued hydration, avoidance of nephrotoxins and repeat blood tests in the community. A temporary medication hold was made during the admission; the patient was advised not to restart the held medicines until reviewed by the GP.

Problem list:
• Acute kidney injury, improving
• Reduced oral intake and oliguria, resolved
• Fatigue, improving

Discharge condition:
Alert and clinically euvolaemic. Passing urine freely, mobilising independently and tolerating oral fluids. No oxygen requirement.

Follow-up and advice:
GP review within 48–72 hours with repeat U&Es, creatinine and medication review. Encourage regular oral fluids unless otherwise instructed. Seek urgent medical attention if urine output falls again, vomiting prevents fluid intake, breathlessness, chest pain or increasing drowsiness develops. A friend in Old Town was updated with the patient’s permission.

Prepared and signed by Shlok Nolan, clinician, following discussion with ROYAL INFIRMARY OF EDINBURGH.

Date: 27th July 2012
National Insurance number: TN 88 24 40 D
To: Clinical Genetics Service

Re: Hadassa Healey
Report/accession ID: 0662721691

Dear Colleague,

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient with diabetes and a plantar foot ulcer, specifically whether the degree of sensory loss and recurrent pressure-related breakdown could indicate an underlying hereditary peripheral neuropathy. The immediate wound problem is being managed in primary care, but the family would value advice on the need for genetic assessment and any implications for relatives.

The patient reports plantar ulceration with reduced sensation and local discharge for 3 days. There is no reported fever or systemic upset. Examination in surgery showed a shallow plantar ulcer beneath the forefoot with surrounding callus and a small amount of serous discharge. Protective sensation was reduced in both feet. Pedal pulses were palpable. The wound was cleansed and dressed, with pressure relief advised; podiatry follow-up has been requested. Co-amoxiclav has been commenced for the local inflammatory change, alongside regular wound care.

An adult child accompanied the patient and described concern about longstanding balance difficulties and sensory symptoms within the family, although no formal diagnosis is known. Please advise whether examination, nerve-conduction studies or genetic testing would be appropriate, and whether family counselling is indicated. There is no known prior neurological review documented in the available records.

Yours faithfully,

E. Singh
For Belfast City Hospital

text:
Accident and Emergency Specialist Assessment

Patient: cate batchelor
MRN: 05188971
Occupation: Police officer
Seen at: Royal Alexandra Hospital

Referral context: Presented with an abrupt episode of pounding palpitations, central chest tightness and intense fear of dying. Symptoms had been present intermittently for 3 days, with the most severe episode occurring at rest and lasting approximately 20 minutes. An adult child accompanied the patient and described marked hyperventilation during the event. No collapse, unilateral weakness or haemoptysis reported.

Examination: Alert and appropriately engaged. Anxious affect with increased respiratory rate, settling during review. Pulse regular on assessment; heart sounds normal, chest clear to auscultation and no peripheral oedema. No focal neurological deficit.

Investigations: Initial ECG showed sinus rhythm without acute ischaemic changes. Troponin and routine blood tests were not suggestive of an acute cardiac or metabolic cause. Clinical observations remained stable during the department stay.

Impression: Presentation is most consistent with a panic attack, with prominent autonomic symptoms and catastrophic fear. There is no current evidence of acute coronary syndrome, significant arrhythmia or respiratory compromise. The patient was advised regarding the benign physiological mechanism of panic symptoms and responded to supervised breathing retraining.

Plan: Breathing retraining commenced and written instructions provided. Avoidance of excess caffeine advised. Follow-up with the GP for assessment of recurrent episodes and consideration of talking therapy. Return to A&E if persistent chest pain, syncope, exertional symptoms or new neurological symptoms develop.

Report prepared and discussed by Dr Nikita WHITING, MBBS, clinician, Royal Alexandra Hospital.

Discharge summary – Cardiology

Patient: Samuela
Home address: 12 ILSE COURT, CASTLEWELLAN
Patient contact: samuela.herbert17@sky.com

Samuela was admitted with sudden breathlessness, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and tachycardia. Her adult child provided collateral history and was kept informed during the admission. Initial observations showed sinus tachycardia with maintained blood pressure and oxygen saturations requiring low-flow supplemental oxygen.

CT pulmonary angiography confirmed bilateral pulmonary emboli, without evidence of right heart strain. Troponin was not elevated. ECG showed sinus tachycardia. Lower-limb Doppler ultrasound did not demonstrate deep vein thrombosis. The likely provoking factors were reviewed; no recent operation or prolonged immobility was identified.

She was treated with supplemental oxygen and commenced on apixaban. Her breathlessness and pleuritic pain improved steadily, and oxygen was discontinued before discharge. At review this morning she was mobilising independently and haemodynamically stable. Current pain score 5/10, improving with simple analgesia.

Assessment: Acute bilateral pulmonary embolism, clinically improving on anticoagulation. No indication for thrombolysis or catheter-directed intervention.

Discharge plan:
Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily. Anticoagulation duration to be reviewed by the GP at three months, with consideration of extended treatment according to bleeding and recurrence risk. Avoid NSAIDs unless specifically advised. Seek urgent medical attention for worsening breathlessness, collapse, haemoptysis or significant bleeding. GP review within one week; anticoagulation clinic referral arranged.

Discharging consultant: Z. Hilton, Cardiology
Professional identifier: 0374625
Discharge destination: Home.

S. Campbell

Patient: waleed stanton
Occupation: accountant
Employer: Tylorstown Town Council
Home address: 65 Craigside Drive, Marloes, SA62 3AA
Patient contact: waleed.stanton39@yahoo.co.uk

Reason for review: Persistent fatigue and cold intolerance, with recent change in bowel habit. The patient reports constipation for 3 days, superimposed on a longer period of reduced bowel frequency. No breathlessness, wheeze, chest pain or nocturnal respiratory symptoms. No recent respiratory infection. Levothyroxine is taken regularly, although the timing varies when work shifts are busy.

Examination: Comfortable at rest. Speech and exercise tolerance preserved. Chest clear bilaterally with normal air entry and no added sounds. Heart sounds normal, with no peripheral oedema. Skin appears dry; pulse regular. No palpable thyroid enlargement or cervical lymphadenopathy.

Interpretation: The respiratory examination is reassuring and there is no evidence of active respiratory disease. The symptom cluster of fatigue, cold intolerance, dry skin and constipation is more consistent with suboptimally treated hypothyroidism than with a pulmonary cause. Medication adherence and administration timing require clarification before dose adjustment.

Plan: Request thyroid function tests, including TSH and free T4, with full blood count, ferritin, renal profile and liver tests. Continue current levothyroxine dose pending results; take consistently on an empty stomach and separate from iron or calcium preparations. Results to be reviewed by the GP, with dose adjustment if indicated. Consider endocrine review if TSH remains abnormal despite reliable administration. Seek urgent assessment if severe abdominal pain, vomiting, marked drowsiness or acute breathlessness develops.

Clinical Genetics referral

Patient: KOHAN DIXON
Occupation: Chef
Employer: Morebattle Sports Club

Dear Clinical Genetics Team,

I would be grateful for your assessment of KOHAN DIXON, who is receiving treatment for a major depressive episode and is concerned that there may be an inherited contribution. The specific question is whether genetic counselling or testing is appropriate in view of a first-degree family history.

The current episode has involved persistent low mood, marked loss of enjoyment and early-morning waking. There are no reported psychotic symptoms or features suggestive of mania. KOHAN DIXON remains engaged with the GP surgery and has been able to continue working, although concentration and motivation are reduced.

The family history is notable for a sibling, Afrina Clarkson, with a confirmed 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. KOHAN DIXON has not previously undergone genetic testing and has asked what this may mean for their own mental health and for other relatives. I have explained that depression is common and may have several interacting causes; a familial condition does not establish that it is the cause of the present episode.

Sertraline is being taken as prescribed, with partial improvement in mood but ongoing anhedonia and sleep disturbance. We will continue primary-care follow-up, monitor response and review risk at each contact. I have arranged a further review in about 6 weeks.

Please advise whether you would offer formal genetic counselling, targeted testing for the familial deletion, or any alternative assessment. EDRIS WELCH

Paediatric outpatient clinic review  
NHS number: 0008372587
Date: 27 January 2018  
Patient: Nimran  
DOB: 01/08/2001  
Patient contact: 07700 900240

Nimran attended with her uncle, muntaz browne, for review of iron-deficiency anaemia. She reports ongoing tiredness and occasional dizziness, particularly when standing quickly, with reduced exercise tolerance compared with usual. She has had a mild viral-type illness with sore throat for 3 days, now improving. No fainting, chest pain, breathlessness at rest or unusual bruising. Menstrual history reviewed; periods are regular but described as heavy on the first two days. Appetite reasonable.

She has been taking ferrous fumarate as prescribed, although admits to missing some doses at weekends because of the taste. No abdominal pain or vomiting. Her uncle feels she is managing school and usual activities, but rests more after exercise. She was comfortable and engaged during the consultation, with appropriate assent and her uncle involved in the discussion. Observations stable. Mild conjunctival pallor; heart sounds normal, no murmur. Abdomen soft and non-tender, with no palpable organomegaly.

Assessment: Iron-deficiency anaemia, symptomatic but clinically stable. Likely contribution from menstrual blood loss and inconsistent iron administration.

Plan: Continue ferrous fumarate and discuss taking it regularly with a vitamin-C-containing drink; avoid taking it alongside tea or milk. Repeat full blood count and ferritin arranged, with review of the response and reticulocyte count if clinically indicated. Discussed menstrual bleeding and advised contacting the GP if this becomes more troublesome. Safety-net advice given regarding collapse, increasing breathlessness, chest pain or marked deterioration. Follow-up in paediatric clinic after blood results.

Discharge summary – Paediatric ward

Patient: M. Atkinson
DOB: 9 July 2019
Admission/discharge date: 27 Aug 2019
Parent present: T. Shaw, from Sgiogarstaigh

M. Atkinson was admitted with cough, increased work of breathing and reduced feeding for 3 days. The history was provided by the parent, who reported fewer wet nappies but no apnoea or colour change.

On assessment, there was mild subcostal recession and bilateral wheeze/crackles consistent with bronchiolitis. Oxygen saturations remained satisfactory in air during observation. No focal chest signs or evidence of bacterial infection. Feeding improved after nasal clearing, and intravenous fluids were not required.

Management was supportive: regular clinical observations, saline nasal drops and smaller, more frequent feeds. No antibiotics, bronchodilators or steroids were indicated. The child is now alert, settled in air and taking adequate oral milk. Work of breathing has returned close to baseline.

Discharge medicines:
• Nasal saline as needed.
• Continue usual milk feeds; offer smaller amounts more frequently if tiring.

Please seek urgent medical help via A&E or 999 if breathing becomes very laboured, there are pauses in breathing, the lips look blue, the child is unusually drowsy, or feeds are markedly reduced. Arrange same-day GP review if wet nappies become much less frequent or symptoms worsen. Bronchiolitis commonly fluctuates over the next few days before gradually settling.

Follow-up: parent to contact the GP surgery if cough or breathing difficulties persist beyond the expected recovery period. No routine paediatric clinic appointment is required. Discharge advice was discussed with T. Shaw, who confirmed understanding.

Discharge summary

Patient: O. Black
MRN: 01784966
Admitting service: Clinical Genetics, Ulster Hospital

Reason for admission
Admitted with a 5-day history of worsening lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge and deep dyspareunia. A friend accompanied the patient and assisted with the history. No haemodynamic instability on arrival.

Assessment and key results
Pelvic examination demonstrated cervical motion tenderness and bilateral adnexal discomfort. Pregnancy test negative. Blood tests showed mildly raised inflammatory markers; renal and liver profiles were satisfactory. Vaginal and cervical NAAT samples were collected, with results pending at discharge. Pelvic ultrasound showed no tubo-ovarian abscess or free pelvic fluid.

Hospital course
Reviewed by the gynaecology team. Clinical diagnosis was pelvic inflammatory disease, with no indication for operative management. Ceftriaxone was administered at 08:15, followed by oral doxycycline and metronidazole. Analgesia was given as required, with improvement in pain and oral intake. The patient remained afebrile and clinically stable throughout observation.

Discharge medicines
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days.
Metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days.
Avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole. Complete both courses unless advised otherwise. Simple analgesia as required.

Advice and follow-up
No sexual intercourse until treatment is completed, symptoms have settled and partners have been assessed. Partner notification and sexual health review were discussed; the patient accepted referral to the local sexual health service. Follow up pending NAAT results will be arranged through Ulster Hospital. Return to A&E if increasing pain, fever, vomiting, faintness or inability to take antibiotics develops. GP review within one week, or sooner if not improving.

Condition at discharge
Comfortable, mobilising independently and tolerating medication. Discharged home with safety-net advice.

Leucocytes: 3+

Protein: 1+  
Glucose: Negative  
Ketones: Negative  
pH: 6.0  
Specific gravity: 1.015

White cells: >100 cells/µL  
Red cells: 18 cells/µL

Significant growth of Escherichia coli, >100,000 CFU/mL. Pure growth.

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report

Patient: S. Kirk
MRN: 0782779
Specimen: EDTA whole blood; received for molecular diabetes assessment
Clinical information: Diabetes with plantar ulceration, reduced sensation and local discharge. Current management includes wound care and co-amoxiclav.

Requested investigation
Targeted hereditary diabetes panel with mitochondrial m.3243A>G analysis. Adjunct biochemical results supplied with request.

Results
HbA1c: 72 mmol/mol (reference target generally <53 mmol/mol) — elevated.
Creatinine: 84 µmol/L (60–110) — within reference interval.
eGFR: >90 mL/min/1.73 m² — preserved renal filtration.
Mitochondrial m.3243A>G: not detected.
Nuclear diabetes panel: no pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant identified.

Interpretation
No reportable molecular cause of diabetes identified on the genes and variant classes covered by this assay. A negative result does not exclude an untested genetic diagnosis or low-level mosaicism. Biochemistry indicates suboptimal glycaemic control, relevant to delayed ulcer healing and infection risk.

Action
Continue coordinated ulcer care, off-loading and antimicrobial review according to the clinical assessment. Correlate with diabetes history and examination; consider genetics review if syndromic features or a strong family history emerge.

Follow-up: genetics review in about 3 weeks, 2024-02-27.

Dr Ensleigh STEAD, MBBS, Consultant Clinical Geneticist

Discharge summary

Patient: erin-may barlow
MRN: 015588455
Responsible clinician: mame rooney, Aberdeen Royal Infirmary

Admitted from A&E with sudden breathlessness, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and tachycardia. CT pulmonary angiography confirmed bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli, without radiological evidence of right heart strain. Troponin was not elevated. ECG showed sinus tachycardia. Oxygen saturations improved with low-flow supplemental oxygen and remained stable on room air before discharge.

The patient was treated initially with therapeutic anticoagulation and supplemental oxygen. There was no haemodynamic compromise, and thrombolysis was not indicated. Lower-limb ultrasound did not demonstrate deep-vein thrombosis. Renal function and full blood count were satisfactory. No bleeding occurred during admission. Observations before discharge included BP 120/80 mmHg, pulse 86, respiratory rate 16 and oxygen saturation 97% on air.

Assessment: clinically stable pulmonary embolism, suitable for outpatient anticoagulation and follow-up.

Discharge medicines:
Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily thereafter. The patient was counselled not to miss doses and to seek urgent medical help for haemoptysis, significant bleeding, collapse or worsening breathlessness. Avoid NSAIDs unless specifically advised. Supplemental oxygen discontinued.

Follow-up: GP review within one week for anticoagulation assessment and review of provoking factors. Haematology or thrombosis clinic referral to be arranged by Aberdeen Royal Infirmary as appropriate, with duration of anticoagulation reviewed at three months. The patient’s spouse, who is based in Millikenpark, was present for the discharge discussion with the patient’s consent. Discharged home in stable condition.

Paediatric Laboratory Medicine Report

Patient: HEERA HASSAN
Patient identifier/MRN: H2115158
Collection/report date: 1988-01-23
Specimen: Venous blood; fluoride oxalate plasma and serum
Request: New presentation with thirst, frequent urination and weight loss for 3 days. History provided by parent. Clinical age group: 10 y/o

Results
Plasma glucose: 24.8 mmol/L (reference interval 3.5–7.8 mmol/L)
HbA1c: 92 mmol/mol (reference interval 20–42 mmol/mol)
Blood ketones: 3.6 mmol/L (reference: <0.6 mmol/L)
Bicarbonate: 15 mmol/L (reference interval 22–29 mmol/L)
Sodium: 133 mmol/L (reference interval 135–145 mmol/L)
Potassium: 4.8 mmol/L (reference interval 3.5–5.0 mmol/L)
Creatinine: 42 µmol/L (paediatric reference interval appropriate for age)
C-reactive protein: 2 mg/L (reference <5 mg/L)
Urine glucose: 4+
Urine ketones: 3+

Interpretation
Marked hyperglycaemia with substantially raised HbA1c, glycosuria and ketonemia. The biochemical findings support newly presenting type 1 diabetes mellitus. Low bicarbonate is concerning for evolving diabetic ketoacidosis; correlate urgently with venous pH, pCO2, clinical hydration and respiratory assessment. Immediate paediatric assessment is required. Do not delay transfer or treatment pending autoantibody results.

Recommended additional testing
Urgent venous blood gas, urea and electrolytes, calcium, phosphate and magnesium. Diabetes autoantibody panel and coeliac screening may be sent after stabilisation. Insulin therapy and glucose monitoring should be initiated under the paediatric diabetes team, with parent education and safeguarding of supervision arrangements.

This report has been validated by Tarell Pope, Laboratory Clinician.

Yours sincerely,

SHANIECE MISTRY

Discharge summary
NHS number: 0005446121

Patient: Locryn D.
Home address: 148 Arnprior Quadrant, Dunbeg, PA37 1AA
Report/accession ID: L29W70179

Admitted with several hours of central chest pressure accompanied by diaphoresis and nausea. Initial ECG showed no ST elevation; serial high-sensitivity troponin demonstrated a significant rise and fall, consistent with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). Chest radiograph without focal consolidation or pulmonary oedema.

Managed on the acute medical ward with telemetry, aspirin, fondaparinux and high-intensity atorvastatin. Symptoms settled promptly and there was no recurrent chest pain or haemodynamic instability. Echocardiogram showed mildly impaired left ventricular systolic function with regional wall motion abnormality. Coronary angiography was discussed with the patient; cardiology advised medical management following review of the clinical picture and angiographic risk.

The cardiology plan is dual antiplatelet treatment with aspirin and clopidogrel for 12 months, unless bleeding or other clinical concerns arise. Fondaparinux was stopped before discharge. Commence bisoprolol and ramipril as tolerated; continue atorvastatin. Avoid non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

Discharge medicines:
Aspirin 75 mg once daily.
Clopidogrel 75 mg once daily for 12 months.
Atorvastatin 80 mg at night.
Bisoprolol 1.25 mg once daily.
Ramipril 1.25 mg once daily.
Glyceryl trinitrate spray as required for chest pain.

Problem list:
• Medically managed NSTEMI
• Mild left ventricular systolic impairment
• Cardiovascular risk-factor modification required

At discharge: comfortable at rest, ambulant, maintaining oral intake; observations stable. Safety-net advice given regarding recurrent or prolonged chest pain, breathlessness, collapse or bleeding—call 999 if severe or persistent.

GP to arrange renal function, electrolytes and blood pressure review within 1–2 weeks, with titration of bisoprolol/ramipril. Cardiology follow-up and cardiac rehabilitation referral requested. Smoking, diet and activity advice provided.

Prepared and signed by SHREESHA BOURNE, consultant cardiologist, GMC: 0525627.

Several days of productive cough, fever and right-sided pleuritic pain with reduced oral intake. Initial oxygen requirement in the emergency department.

Amoxicillin to complete the prescribed course.

GP review if symptoms are not continuing to resolve; consider repeat chest radiograph in approximately six weeks if clinically indicated. Discharge information discussed with the patient and adult child, Tomasina, who lives in Keilarsbrae. Copy sent to GP via Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh.

Patient: Kacie-Jo
MRN: 01222047
Requesting service: Respiratory Medicine, Eversley Medical Centre
Specimen collection date: 13/05/2018
Specimen: Serum, lithium-heparin plasma and EDTA blood

Clinical details: Acute joint pain with swelling and erythema, clinically suspected gout flare. Current treatment includes naproxen and colchicine. Synovial fluid was not received with this request.

Results

Serum urate: 0.52 mmol/L (reference interval 0.18–0.48 mmol/L) – high
C-reactive protein: 86 mg/L (reference interval <5 mg/L) – high
White cell count: 12.8 ×10^9/L (reference interval 4.0–11.0 ×10^9/L) – high
Neutrophils: 10.7 ×10^9/L (reference interval 2.0–7.5 ×10^9/L) – high

Estimated GFR: 68 mL/min/1.73 m²
Alanine transaminase: 24 U/L (reference interval 0–40 U/L)

Hyperuricaemia with neutrophil-predominant inflammation, supportive of an acute gout flare in the stated clinical context. Serum urate may be lower during an acute attack and does not confirm or exclude gout in isolation. If diagnostic uncertainty persists, joint aspiration for crystal analysis is recommended; urgent assessment is required if septic arthritis is suspected.

Renal function is adequate for the reported result but should be reviewed when prescribing or continuing naproxen and colchicine. Consider repeat serum urate after resolution of symptoms and review of long-term urate-lowering strategy with the GP or rheumatology team.

Please apply the emollient generously at least three to four times daily and after bathing. Interpretation: Significant azotaemia with reduced eGFR, compatible with acute kidney injury in the stated clinical context. Mild hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis are present. Comparison with previous creatinine is required to establish baseline and stage the AKI. Results should be correlated with fluid status, urine output and medication history.

Clinical comment: Continue close fluid-balance monitoring and repeat U&E promptly following rehydration. Review nephrotoxic and renally cleared medicines; temporary medication hold should be reviewed by the treating team. If potassium rises, urine output falls further, or there is clinical deterioration, discuss urgently with the renal team.

Date: 1996-03-03

Re: Ashly O'Hara  
DOB: 12th July 1985

Dear Community Paediatrics Team,

I am referring Ashly O'Hara, a school-age child, for assessment of persistent iron-deficiency anaemia and advice on further investigation and management. The specific question is whether the degree and duration of anaemia warrant paediatric review, including consideration of dietary, gastrointestinal or menstrual causes if relevant to development.

Jahan, the patient’s father, reports several months of tiredness, intermittent dizziness and reduced exercise tolerance. There has been no reported fainting, chest pain or persistent abdominal pain. Appetite is variable, with limited intake of iron-rich foods. The family reports good adherence to treatment, although constipation has occasionally made this difficult.

Recent blood tests showed haemoglobin 94 g/L, with microcytosis and low ferritin, supporting iron deficiency. There is no current evidence of acute bleeding. Examination in primary care found the child alert, with mild conjunctival pallor; cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.

Ferrous fumarate has been started and is being given as prescribed, alongside dietary advice. I would be grateful for confirmation of the appropriate dose and duration, review of the response to treatment, and guidance on whether additional blood tests are needed, including coeliac screening or haemoglobinopathy testing if not already completed. Repeat full blood count and ferritin are planned through the GP surgery.

Please assess the child with their father present, while allowing age-appropriate opportunity for the child to contribute. I will continue prescribing and monitoring pending your recommendations.

Yours sincerely,

miron warren

DOB: 22 November 2008

Requesting service: Cardiology
Specimen: Serum, venous blood
Clinical information: Reduced urine output, fatigue and poor oral intake for 3 days. Acute kidney injury under review; intravenous sodium chloride administered and regular medication temporarily held.

Sodium 138 mmol/L (133–146)
Potassium 4.9 mmol/L (3.5–5.3)
Urea 18.6 mmol/L (2.5–7.8) — high

Bicarbonate 20 mmol/L (22–29) — low
Chloride 104 mmol/L (95–108)

Marked azotaemia with reduced estimated glomerular filtration, consistent with acute kidney injury in the stated clinical context. Mild metabolic acidosis. Clinical comment:
Correlate with urine output, fluid balance, blood pressure and recent medication exposure. Repeat U&E after rehydration and medication review. Escalate urgently if worsening oliguria, hyperkalaemia, pulmonary oedema or other clinical deterioration. Consider renal tract imaging if obstruction is suspected.

Respiratory Medicine Clinic Note

Patient: Faridat
MRN: MRN-05478240
Occupation: Lawyer
Seen with spouse.

Faridat describes several months of intermittent chest tightness and a sensation of not getting a satisfying breath, particularly before work meetings and at night. No exertional limitation, wheeze, haemoptysis or infective symptoms. They report persistent worry about health and work, with poor sleep and marked muscle tension through the shoulders and jaw. Symptoms ease with paced breathing and distraction.

Currently taking sertraline, prescribed by the GP surgery. No recent dose change. The spouse feels that reassurance has helped only briefly. No safeguarding concerns identified; the patient engaged appropriately and was able to describe their symptoms and treatment preferences.

On examination, comfortable at rest. Respiratory rate 15, oxygen saturations 99% on air. Chest clear with good air entry bilaterally and no added sounds. Heart sounds normal. No peripheral oedema. Recent spirometry was within expected limits, without a significant bronchodilator response.

Assessment

The pattern is not suggestive of significant airway or parenchymal lung disease. Breathlessness is closely associated with generalised anxiety, persistent worry, poor sleep and muscle tension. No indication for respiratory medication at present.

Plan

Discussed the interaction between anxiety, dysfunctional breathing and chest sensations. Continue sertraline as currently prescribed and arrange review with the GP to consider response and ongoing psychological support. Recommended referral for structured talking therapy and regular breathing exercises. Safety-netted to seek urgent assessment for sustained chest pain, syncope, haemoptysis or rapidly worsening breathlessness.

Respiratory follow-up in about 10 weeks at Brynseiont Hospital. Dictated and signed by Dr Rosaleen O'Sullivan, MBBS.

Discharge summary – Paediatrics
NHS number: 000 352 0600

Patient: Maaya B.
DOB: 3 April 2027
Parent/carer: Dogukan Dale, locality Kings Meadows

Reason for admission:
Vomiting and frequent watery diarrhoea with reduced urine output. Parent reported poor oral intake prior to attendance.

Assessment/results:
Clinical dehydration on arrival; capillary refill 3 seconds, dry mucous membranes. Afebrile during admission. Blood glucose within normal range. No indication for antibiotics. Stool sample not required.

Hospital course:
Admitted for observation and rehydration. Oral rehydration solution given in small, frequent amounts; supportive care only. No further vomiting after initial period. Diarrhoea settling. Passed urine at 08:15 and subsequently had improving intake. Remained alert and interactive. IV fluids not required.

Medication on discharge:
Oral rehydration solution: frequent small sips, increasing as tolerated.
Continue usual diet as tolerated; avoid fruit juice and fizzy drinks.

Condition at discharge:
Clinically hydrated, moist mucosa, settled abdomen, tolerating fluids and light diet. Parent comfortable with home care and return advice. Consent for discharge discussed with parent.

Follow-up/actions:
GP review if ongoing diarrhoea, poor intake or reduced urine output. Paediatric review booked for 29th November 2028.

Return to A&E urgently if unable to retain fluids, no urine, marked drowsiness, blood in stool or breathing difficulty.

Emergency Department Assessment – Clinical Genetics

Patient: Z. Brook, 37-year-old Pacific Islander male patient
Address: 179 Howarth Close, Glais, SA7 0AA
Date: 5th December 2035
Informant: patient; sibling present

Presenting complaint
24-hour lower abdominal pain with abnormal vaginal discharge and dyspareunia. Pain worse on movement. No vomiting or collapse. Sibling concerned regarding reduced oral intake.

Observations
Alert, haemodynamically stable, afebrile. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Mild suprapubic tenderness, no guarding or rebound. Pelvic examination with consent and chaperone: mucopurulent cervical discharge and cervical motion tenderness. No adnexal mass appreciated.

Investigations
Urine pregnancy test negative. Urinalysis: trace leucocytes, no nitrites. FBC and CRP requested; renal and liver profiles satisfactory. Vaginal/cervical NAAT swabs sent for chlamydia and gonorrhoea. Ultrasound not indicated acutely given stable examination.

Assessment
Clinical pelvic inflammatory disease. Differential includes cervicitis and urinary infection; ectopic pregnancy unlikely with negative test and stable observations. No evidence of sepsis or tubo-ovarian abscess currently.

Treatment / actions
Ceftriaxone administered in the department. Discharge medicines: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days and metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days. Advised no sexual intercourse until treatment completed and results reviewed; partner notification discussed. Analgesia with paracetamol as required.

Disposition
Discharged home with written advice. Return to A&E for worsening pain, fever, vomiting or faintness. Sexual health follow-up arranged; GP review if not improving within 48–72 hours.

Clinician: T. Newman

Dear Hypertension Service,

Re: Wang

I would be grateful for your assessment of persistent essential hypertension despite treatment with amlodipine and ramipril. Wang reports intermittent morning headaches and episodes of light-headedness, without syncope, chest pain or focal neurological symptoms. Their adult child has noticed that the headaches are more frequent on days when home readings are elevated.

At review, Wang was comfortable at rest. Blood pressure remained above the practice target on repeat measurement; pulse was regular and there was no clinical evidence of fluid overload. Current headache severity was recorded as 5/10. Medication adherence was discussed, and the patient reports taking amlodipine and ramipril as prescribed. No recent medication changes have been made.

The surgery has advised a structured period of home blood pressure monitoring, with seated readings morning and evening, and reinforced reduction of dietary salt and avoidance of over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medicines. Basic blood tests and urine testing have been requested; results will be forwarded when available.

Assessment: essential hypertension with symptoms and suboptimal control on two agents. Please advise on confirmation of the diagnosis and whether ambulatory monitoring is indicated, together with recommendations for treatment escalation and assessment for secondary causes if clinically appropriate. Advice regarding management of the light-headedness would also be appreciated.

Referring clinician: SARIM DOLAN, GLENOE
Professional identifier: 0657689
Organisation: ROYAL VICTORIA HOSPITAL

Yours sincerely,

SARIM DOLAN

MOLECULAR GENETICS REPORT

Patient: Abdulwahab
Home address: 46 Thorn Street, Biddulph, ST8 6AA
Report/accession ID: 24/652446
Clinical indication: Significant family history of breast/ovarian cancer; predictive testing requested. Cancer-risk concern. No current treatment.

Specimen: Peripheral blood, EDTA
Test: Germline BRCA1 and BRCA2 sequencing with deletion/duplication analysis
Specimen status: Adequate; DNA extracted successfully

Result:
BRCA1 c.68_69delAG — not detected
No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant identified in the genes tested.

Interpretation:
This is a negative result for the familial variant assessed. Residual hereditary cancer risk is not excluded; interpretation depends on the affected relative’s confirmed result and the wider pedigree. If the familial variant is different or unknown, testing strategy should be reviewed by clinical genetics.

Clinical comment:
Please correlate with the family history. Genetic counselling recommended, including discussion of surveillance and risk-reducing options where appropriate. Unaffected predictive testing requires documented informed consent and appropriate pre-test counselling.

Follow-up: Genetics review booked for 26 February 1988. Patient advised to bring any available relative’s molecular report.

Validated and authorised by:
JOHNNY RHODES
Laboratory reporting clinician

Cardiology outpatient report
NHS number: 000 465 6378

Patient: Sofian Blackwell
MRN: 09742071
Patient contact: sofian.blackwell68@talktalk.net

The patient, aged 57 years, was reviewed with their spouse present. They describe brief episodes of rotational vertigo precipitated by turning in bed, looking upwards or rising from a low chair. Associated nausea and transient unsteadiness have been present for 3 days. There is no reported syncope, chest pain, palpitations, persistent visual disturbance or focal limb weakness.

Clinical examination: cardiovascular examination revealed a regular pulse with normal heart sounds and no clinical evidence of heart failure. Blood pressure was stable on standing. Neurological examination was non-focal. Gait was mildly cautious immediately after positional change. Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre reproduced typical vertigo with a brief torsional nystagmus; symptoms fatigued on repetition.

Interpretation: findings are consistent with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, most likely involving the posterior semicircular canal. There is no current clinical suggestion of a cardiac arrhythmia or central neurological cause.

Management: Epley repositioning manoeuvre demonstrated and undertaken in clinic, with advice to repeat this if symptoms recur. Continue prochlorperazine as required for troublesome nausea, avoiding activities requiring rapid positional changes while symptomatic. The patient was advised to seek urgent assessment via A&E if persistent neurological symptoms, collapse, severe headache or continuous vertigo develops.

Follow-up review: 3rd April 2004. Reassess symptom resolution and consider vestibular physiotherapy or ENT referral if positional symptoms persist.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: A. Kay
Discharging service: ROYAL VICTORIA HOSPITAL
Report/accession ID: 07152557
Responsible clinician: ABDULBARR CHARLES, consultant respiratory physician
Professional registration: GMC 0101552

Reason for admission
Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with increased breathlessness, wheeze and purulent sputum. Admitted for bronchodilator treatment, oxygen monitoring and assessment for infective trigger.

Key results
- Chest radiograph: hyperinflation; no focal consolidation.
- Blood tests: inflammatory markers mildly raised, renal function satisfactory.
- Viral respiratory PCR negative.
- Sputum purulent on admission; culture did not identify a significant pathogen.

Hospital course
Responded to nebulised bronchodilators and controlled oxygen therapy. Oxygen requirement resolved; maintaining target saturations on air prior to discharge. No evidence of pneumonia or acute cardiac cause. Partner updated regarding recovery and discharge plan.

Treatment / medication changes
- Prednisolone 30 mg each morning to complete a 5-day course.
- Doxycycline 200 mg on day 1, then 100 mg once daily to complete 5 days.
- Salbutamol inhaler, two puffs as needed, with spacer.
Usual inhalers otherwise continued. Inhaler technique checked.

Condition at discharge
Breathlessness improved, wheeze minimal, mobilising independently and eating and drinking. Afebrile and clinically stable.

Follow-up and advice
GP review within one week; consider respiratory inhaler review and pulmonary rehabilitation referral. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if breathlessness worsens, blue lips, confusion, chest pain or inability to manage inhalers.

Emergency Department Assessment
NHS number: 0007614255

Patient: Katelyn S.
Home address: 83 Yewdall Road, Halesworth, IP19 0AA
Patient contact: katelyn.sweeney25@icloud.com
Report/accession ID: 0036740111
Accompanied by friend, N. Smyth

Presenting complaint:
Sudden onset pounding palpitations with central chest tightness whilst at home. Marked fear of dying, trembling and rapid breathing. No collapse. Symptoms substantially improved on arrival but remains anxious.

Background:
No known cardiac history recorded. Medication: breathing retraining. No recreational drug use disclosed. Friend present and supportive.

Examination:
Alert, distressed initially, speaking full sentences. Pulse regular, no murmur. Chest clear bilaterally. No calf tenderness or peripheral oedema. Abdomen soft and non-tender. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. No focal neurological deficit.

Observations:
Haemodynamically stable; oxygen saturation normal on air. Afebrile.

Investigations:
ECG: sinus rhythm, no acute ischaemic changes.
Capillary glucose within normal range.
High-sensitivity troponin not indicated following senior review given resolved symptoms, reassuring examination and non-ischaemic ECG.

Assessment:
Panic attack with hyperventilation symptoms. No current evidence of acute coronary syndrome, arrhythmia or respiratory compromise.

Treatment/action:
Reassurance and coached slow breathing in the department. Breathing retraining practised; chest tightness resolved. Discussed avoidance of excessive caffeine and arranging GP review for ongoing anxiety assessment and psychological support.

Disposition:
Discharged home with friend. Return to A&E if persistent chest pain, syncope, sustained palpitations or breathlessness. Patient understood advice and agreed with plan.

Date: 29/05/2019
To: Spinal or musculoskeletal specialist
From: ROYAL INFIRMARY OF EDINBURGH
Patient: Murdo Rowley
MRN: 0046118

Dear Colleague,

I would be grateful for your assessment of Murdo Rowley’s persistent low back pain with shooting pain into the right leg and intermittent paraesthesia. The clinical question is whether this represents lumbar radiculopathy requiring spinal imaging, specialist intervention or physiotherapy-led management.

Symptoms began gradually and have continued despite activity modification and simple analgesia. The leg pain is aggravated by prolonged sitting and walking, with occasional tingling over the lateral calf and dorsum of the foot. There is no reported sphincter disturbance, saddle sensory change or progressive loss of power. A friend has assisted with the history and reports that sleep and usual activities are increasingly affected.

On review today, lumbar movement was restricted by pain. Straight-leg raise was uncomfortable on the right. Power was functionally preserved on examination, with no clear foot drop; distal sensation was subjectively altered on the right compared with the left. No systemic features were reported.

Current medication:
Naproxen with food as tolerated
Paracetamol, once daily as needed

The GP has advised continuation of gentle mobilisation and avoidance of prolonged bed rest. Please consider whether MRI of the lumbar spine is indicated and advise on targeted rehabilitation, injection or surgical opinion if appropriate. A review appointment is planned in about 7 weeks, but earlier assessment would be appreciated if neurological symptoms progress.

Yours sincerely,

A. STOKES
Clinician

PAEDIATRIC LABORATORY MEDICINE – FULL BLOOD COUNT / IRON STUDIES

Patient: R. Pollard
Clinical context: aged 11 years reviewed with mother; tiredness, intermittent dizziness and reduced exercise tolerance. Suspected iron-deficiency anaemia.
Collection/report date: 9 May 2020
Report/accession ID: 02882324
Requester: Not stated
Specimen: EDTA blood and serum; adequate, no haemolysis.

Results
Haemoglobin: 96 g/L (115–155) – low
LOINC 718-7: haemoglobin result, 96 g/L
MCV: 68 fL (77–95) – low
MCH: 20 pg (25–33) – low
RBC: 4.80 ×10¹²/L (3.9–5.3)
Platelets: 468 ×10⁹/L (150–450) – mildly raised
Ferritin: 7 µg/L (15–100) – low
Serum iron: 4.1 µmol/L (5.0–25.0) – low
Transferrin saturation: 6% (15–45) – low
CRP: 2 mg/L (<5)

Interpretation: Microcytic, hypochromic anaemia with depleted iron stores. Normal CRP makes significant inflammatory anaemia less likely. Mild reactive thrombocytosis may accompany iron deficiency.

Action: Please correlate with dietary history and reported blood loss; assess for excess cow’s milk intake and gastrointestinal symptoms. Continue prescribed ferrous fumarate, with administration advice reviewed by the clinical team. Repeat FBC and ferritin after treatment interval; investigate further if haemoglobin response is inadequate.

Discharge summary
NHS number: 000 833 9407

Patient: Bertan M.
Home address: 5 Yellowhammer Drive, Tranent, EH33 1AA
Patient contact: 07700 900430
The patient, aged 57 years, was admitted under general medicine with a one-day history of worsening right lower-quadrant abdominal pain, nausea and loss of appetite. There was no reported urinary or respiratory symptomatology. Examination on admission was consistent with localised right iliac fossa tenderness without generalised peritonism.

Initial blood tests showed a raised white cell count and C-reactive protein. CT abdomen and pelvis demonstrated uncomplicated acute appendicitis, with no abscess or perforation. The case was discussed with the on-call surgical team. Given the uncomplicated appearance and clinical improvement, non-operative management was agreed, with safety-netting and outpatient surgical review.

The patient received intravenous fluids, analgesia and intravenous co-amoxiclav. Pain and nausea settled, and oral intake was re-established. There was no fever or haemodynamic instability during the admission. No operation was required.

Assessment at discharge: clinically improved uncomplicated acute appendicitis managed with antibiotics. Abdomen soft, with only mild residual right iliac fossa tenderness; mobilising independently and tolerating diet.

Discharge medicines:
Paracetamol as required for pain, according to the packet instructions. Complete the prescribed oral antibiotic course as supplied by the surgical team.

Plan:
Surgical clinic follow-up in about 6 weeks to review the response to conservative treatment and discuss interval appendicectomy if appropriate. GP review if symptoms do not continue to resolve. Return to A&E urgently for recurrent or worsening abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fever, abdominal distension or inability to tolerate fluids.

Discharging doctor’s professional identifier: 0491916

Discussed with covering medical team; consultant review documented under professional identifier 0976339. Continue IV fluids and antiemetic treatment, repeat observations including postural blood pressure, monitor fluid balance and urine output, and arrange blood tests if vomiting persists. Escalate promptly for worsening tachycardia, reduced urine output, abdominal pain, bleeding or inability to tolerate oral intake. Handover to evening nurse for ongoing review and mobility assistance.

Request: Thyroid function assessment in the context of fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation. Levothyroxine treatment reported.

Thyroid peroxidase antibody: 286 kIU/L (reference interval <34) — positive

Biochemistry supports primary hypothyroidism, with positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies consistent with autoimmune thyroid disease. Results should be interpreted alongside adherence, timing of levothyroxine and recent dose changes. No molecular genetic testing performed on this specimen.

GP/endocrine team to review levothyroxine dose and administration. Repeat TSH and free T4 in about 6 weeks, or sooner if clinically indicated. Follow-up review booked for 2004-04-25.

Please avoid taking levothyroxine with iron or calcium preparations. Further clinical genetics review only if there is a significant family history, syndromic feature or an atypical biochemical course.

Result status: Authorised

Dear Respiratory Medicine Team,

Re: Logan M.

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient, who has longstanding generalised anxiety disorder but is now reporting intermittent chest tightness and a sensation of not being able to take a satisfying breath, particularly at night. The episodes occur without exertion and are often accompanied by persistent worry, marked muscle tension and difficulty settling to sleep. There has been no documented wheeze, haemoptysis or infective illness. I would appreciate your view on whether there is an underlying respiratory disorder, such as asthma, or whether the symptoms are most consistent with anxiety-related dysfunctional breathing.

The patient remains employed by DONAGHCLONEY Housing Association. Their emergency contact is HARRISON-JAY MANNING, who is aware of the current concerns. Examination in the surgery was reassuring: oxygen saturations were normal at rest, chest was clear to auscultation and there was no peripheral oedema. Peak flow readings have been variable, although technique may have contributed. No acute deterioration has been observed.

Management to date has included reassurance, breathing-control advice and discussion of talking therapy. Current medication: sertraline 50 mg once daily. Sleep remains poor despite adherence, and the patient feels that the physical symptoms are reinforcing the anxiety cycle. There is no history of smoking recorded.

Assessment: episodic chest tightness and breathlessness, with anxiety a likely contributor; respiratory cause not yet excluded.

Please could you arrange spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility, or other investigations you consider appropriate, and advise on further management.

Yours sincerely,

Karhys FARROW

Cardiology Referral

Date: 19 Feb 2045
Patient: Jerusha CONNOLLY
Home address: 125 KILFARN ROAD, KILLEAD
Report/accession ID: 0226818036

Dear Cardiology Team,

I would be grateful for your assessment of Jerusha CONNOLLY for persistent reduced exercise tolerance and dizziness in the context of documented iron-deficiency anaemia. The specific question is whether there is an additional cardiac explanation for the exertional limitation, and whether cardiac investigation is indicated before symptoms are attributed solely to anaemia.

They describe increasing tiredness, light-headedness on standing and breathlessness when walking uphill. No syncope, sustained palpitations or chest pain reported. The adult child accompanying the patient reports a noticeable reduction in usual activity over the past several weeks. There has also been a cough for 3 days, without fever or haemoptysis.

Recent primary-care blood tests showed microcytic anaemia with low ferritin, consistent with iron deficiency. Ferrous fumarate has been started and is tolerated apart from mild constipation. There has been modest improvement in dizziness but ongoing exertional limitation. Blood pressure and pulse were stable at review; heart sounds were regular with no audible murmur, and there was no peripheral oedema. Chest examination was clear.

I would appreciate review of the symptoms and consideration of ECG and echocardiography, or other investigation as clinically appropriate. Advice regarding the contribution of anaemia and the need for any cardiac follow-up would be particularly helpful.

Yours faithfully,

J. CROSS

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report
NHS number: 000 897 7349

Patient: Kalonji
MRN: H8375280
Home address: 47 Gatcombe, Maghull, L31 0AA
Specimen/report date: 2nd July 1988
Requesting clinician: Not stated
Laboratory: Clinical Genetics

Clinical details:
Painless lymphadenopathy with night sweats and unintentional weight loss. Hodgkin lymphoma is the working clinical diagnosis; tissue diagnosis and full histopathological classification remain pending. Supportive care pending tissue diagnosis is recorded.

Specimen:
Peripheral blood received for constitutional cancer predisposition assessment. Specimen suitable for DNA extraction. No tumour tissue or formalin-fixed material accompanied the sample; this assay therefore does not establish or exclude a somatic alteration within the lymph node.

Result:
No clinically significant germline variant identified on the tested panel. This is a negative result for the genes and variant classes covered by the assay only. Analytical sensitivity is reduced for low-level mosaicism, deep intronic variants, structural rearrangements and regions with inadequate coverage. A negative germline result does not alter the clinical diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma or replace histological examination, immunophenotyping and staging investigations.

Interpretation:
The result does not provide evidence of an inherited predisposition in the genes analysed. If the pathology is atypical, the family history is concerning, or treatment-related findings suggest an alternative diagnosis, referral back to Clinical Genetics should be considered. Variant interpretation may be revised if relevant new evidence becomes available.

Report validated by:
GOKULAN SHAIKH
Consultant Clinical Geneticist

This report relates to the submitted specimen and should be interpreted alongside the pathology and multidisciplinary team assessment.

Presented following sudden right arm weakness with left facial droop and slurred speech. Symptoms resolved before assessment. Reported cough for 3 days, without associated hypoxia or fever. Sibling attended and contributed to the history.

CT head showed no acute haemorrhage or established infarction. CT angiography demonstrated no large-vessel occlusion or significant carotid stenosis. MRI brain identified no acute diffusion restriction. ECG: sinus rhythm. Routine blood tests satisfactory; HbA1c and lipid profile sent for outpatient review.

Hospital course
Managed as a transient ischaemic attack after discussion with the stroke team. Neurological observations remained stable and there was no recurrence of weakness, facial asymmetry or dysphasia. Swallow assessment passed. No indication for thrombolysis as symptoms had fully resolved on arrival. The clinical genetics team reviewed the family history and advised that no urgent genetic testing was indicated during this admission; outpatient assessment can be arranged if further relevant family history emerges.

Discharge medicines
Aspirin 300 mg once daily for 14 days, then reduce to aspirin 75 mg once daily.
Atorvastatin 80 mg once daily.
Continue usual prescribed medicines.

Problem list
1. Transient ischaemic attack with resolved focal neurological symptoms.
2. Vascular risk assessment required in primary care.
3. Cough, clinically mild; seek review if worsening or persistent.

Follow-up and advice
GP to review within one week, including blood pressure, diabetes and lipid results. Stroke/TIA clinic referral submitted for timely assessment and consideration of prolonged cardiac monitoring. Return immediately to A&E for recurrent facial droop, limb weakness, speech disturbance or sudden visual loss.

Discharged home clinically well. Written advice provided and understood.

Signed: Dr Axon Preece, MBBS, Consultant Physician

MOLECULAR GENETICS LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: crew hickman
MRN: 0331283
Specimen/report date: 17 December 2004
Patient contact: 07700 900978

Clinical indication:
Significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer. Predictive testing requested; patient concerned about inherited cancer risk. No current treatment.

Specimen:
Peripheral blood, EDTA. Received for germline hereditary breast and ovarian cancer panel. DNA extraction and sequencing performed; copy-number analysis included.

Result:
BRCA1: no pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant detected.
BRCA2 and other panel genes: no reportable pathogenic variant identified.
Variant under genetics review: BRCA1 c.68_69delAG. This is recorded as the familial variant of interest; current assay did not confirm its presence.

Interpretation:
Negative result reduces, but does not eliminate, the possibility of inherited cancer predisposition. Residual familial risk may remain, particularly where the affected relative’s molecular result is unavailable or testing has not targeted the confirmed familial variant.

Comment/action:
Discuss result with clinical genetics. Risk management should be based on the full pedigree and verified family reports, not this result alone. Consider testing an affected relative where possible. No treatment indicated from this laboratory result.

Validated and reported by: R. Pearce
Laboratory clinician. Ordering clinician not stated.

Alert and orientated. Reports intermittent central chest pressure, currently 2/10, with associated nausea. Diaphoresis noted during previous episode; no diaphoresis at review. Discharge summary – Respiratory Medicine

Patient: C. CLEGG
MRN: 02436509
Home address: 116 North Pilrig Heights, Barrhead, G78 1AA

Reason for admission
Presented with sudden breathlessness, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and tachycardia. CT pulmonary angiography confirmed bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli, without radiological evidence of right heart strain. No provoking factor identified during this admission; history reviewed for recent surgery, immobility, malignancy and previous venous thromboembolism.

Hospital course
Initially required supplemental oxygen for hypoxaemia, with improvement over the following 24 hours. Oxygen was weaned before discharge and saturations remained satisfactory on room air while mobilising. Troponin was not elevated. ECG showed sinus tachycardia. Renal function and full blood count were suitable for anticoagulation. Lower-limb Doppler did not demonstrate deep vein thrombosis.

Clinical examination at discharge: comfortable at rest, mild residual discomfort on deep inspiration, chest clear, no calf tenderness or significant peripheral oedema. Blood pressure 120/80 mmHg.

Problem list
• Acute bilateral pulmonary embolism
• Pleuritic chest pain, improving
• Transient oxygen requirement

Treatment and discharge medicines
Apixaban commenced for treatment of pulmonary embolism. Take 10 mg twice daily for the first 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily thereafter, unless changed by the anticoagulation service. Supplemental oxygen was discontinued and is not required at home. Avoid non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs unless specifically advised. Medication reconciliation completed with the patient and sibling.

Follow-up and advice
Anticoagulation review arranged through the respiratory/anticoagulation service, with duration to be confirmed after outpatient assessment. GP to review ongoing symptoms and investigate for provoking factors as clinically indicated. Seek urgent medical attention for worsening breathlessness, syncope, haemoptysis or significant bleeding.

Discharging clinician: H. Bowden
GMC professional identifier: 0945692

Increasing breathlessness over 5 days, worse when lying flat. Bilateral ankle swelling and reduced exercise tolerance. Sleeping upright in a chair. No chest pain, fever or productive cough.

Known heart failure. Regular furosemide 40 mg once daily and bisoprolol. Reports compliance. GARBHAN FITZPATRICK notes gradual decline in mobility and appetite.

Acute decompensated heart failure with hypoxia and fluid overload. No convincing evidence of acute coronary syndrome or infection.

Oxygen commenced, target saturations maintained above 94%. IV loop diuretic given; urine output monitored. Fluid and salt restriction advised. Medical registrar reviewed; admit to acute medical unit for ongoing diuresis and echocardiographic review.

Medication reconciliation and heart failure specialist input. Follow-up review arranged for 27 Oct 2024.

At 08:15 the patient was alert and clinically mildly dehydrated, with dry mucous membranes but warm peripheries and a soft abdomen without focal tenderness or guarding. Observations improved following oral fluids. Blood tests showed no significant electrolyte disturbance or inflammatory response. The presentation was felt to be consistent with self-limiting infectious gastroenteritis; there were no features requiring admission or abdominal imaging.

Treatment and progress

The patient tolerated repeated small amounts of oral fluid in the department and had no further vomiting before discharge. Oral rehydration solution was supplied, with ondansetron as required for nausea. Advice was given to take frequent small sips, resume light food as tolerated and maintain hand hygiene. Avoid food preparation for others until 48 hours after symptoms have stopped.

Assessment and plan

Fit for discharge home with adult child. Continue oral rehydration solution and ondansetron as required, according to the dispensing label. Seek urgent medical attention for worsening or localised abdominal pain, blood in the stool, persistent inability to keep fluids down, confusion, reduced urine output or marked weakness. Contact the GP if diarrhoea is not settling.

GP review, if symptoms persist, on 7 Mar 2045. Patient and adult child confirmed understanding of the advice and discharge plan.

Admit under the medical team for fluids, repeat U&Es and renal review. Patient, aged 49 years, and friend understand the plan.

Laboratory Report – Thyroid Function

Patient: maeda dalton
Report/accession ID: 24/670486
Requesting service: Gowerton Medical Centre
Specimen: Serum
Collected: 23/06/2020
Clinical details: Fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation. Patient also reports a cough for 3 days. Current medication: levothyroxine.

TSH: 12.8 mIU/L (reference range 0.27–4.20)
Free T4: 9.1 pmol/L (reference range 12–22)
Free T3: 3.4 pmol/L (reference range 3.1–6.8)
Thyroid peroxidase antibody: 286 IU/mL (reference range <34)

Raised TSH with reduced free T4 is consistent with primary hypothyroidism. Positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies support autoimmune thyroiditis. Results indicate biochemical under-replacement if levothyroxine is being taken regularly.

Please confirm adherence, administration on an empty stomach and any concurrent iron, calcium or antacid treatment, which may impair absorption. If adherence is satisfactory, consider a cautious levothyroxine dose review in primary care, with repeat TSH and free T4 after 6–8 weeks. The short duration cough is not explained by these thyroid results; assess separately if persistent or associated with breathlessness, fever or chest pain.

Discharge summary – General Medicine

Patient: AADVIK WHELAN
Reason for admission: 2-day history of worsening right lower-quadrant pain, nausea and loss of appetite. Admitted via emergency department; clinical assessment consistent with acute appendicitis.

Key results:
• FBC: raised white cell count and neutrophilia.
• CRP elevated. Renal function satisfactory.
• CT abdomen/pelvis: uncomplicated acute appendicitis; no collection.
Report/accession ID: 22/781025
Current observations: BP 120/80 mmHg; afebrile; pain improved.

Hospital course: Reviewed by on-call surgical team. Laparoscopic appendicectomy performed under general anaesthesia. Operative findings of inflamed, non-perforated appendix. No drain required. Tolerated diet post-operatively; mobilising and passing urine. Wounds clean and dry.

Treatment:
• Intravenous co-amoxiclav peri-operatively.
• Paracetamol as required.
• No ongoing antibiotics advised following source control.

Discharge condition: Clinically well, haemodynamically stable, tolerating oral intake. Discharged home with sibling mayzee pitt, who lives in GREYSTEEL.

Follow-up/actions:
• Histology to be reviewed by ROYAL VICTORIA HOSPITAL; patient to contact surgical team if not notified.
• GP review if persistent pain or wound concerns.
• Keep wounds clean and dry; avoid heavy lifting until comfortable.
• Return to A&E for fever, increasing abdominal pain, vomiting, spreading redness or discharge from wounds.

To: Orthopaedic/MSK interface service

Re: CHIMEREYA KIRBY
Report/accession ID: 011400373
Referring organisation: Aberdeen Royal Infirmary

Dear Colleague,

I would be grateful for your assessment of CHIMEREYA KIRBY, seen in the emergency department with progressively troublesome knee pain, morning stiffness and reduced mobility. Symptoms are now limiting walking outdoors and activities of daily living. The patient reports intermittent swelling but no recent injury, locking or giving way. A sibling attended and provided collateral history.

On examination, there was an antalgic gait and reduced active and passive flexion of the affected knee, with medial joint-line tenderness and palpable crepitus. No erythema or significant effusion was identified. The knee was stable on ligament testing, and distal neurovascular examination was intact. Plain radiographs obtained in the department demonstrate medial compartment joint-space narrowing with marginal osteophyte formation, in keeping with osteoarthritis. There is no acute fracture or dislocation.

Initial management has been conservative. Current treatment: paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily and topical ibuprofen, with partial relief only. Advice has been given regarding pacing, use of simple analgesia and maintaining movement within tolerance. The patient has not yet had a structured physiotherapy programme or formal assessment for walking aids.

Please review to confirm the diagnosis and advise on an appropriate non-operative management plan, including physiotherapy, strengthening and weight-bearing support where indicated. If symptoms remain disabling despite these measures, consideration of further interventional options would be appreciated.

Yours faithfully,

Dr Merren MISTRY, MBBS
0286298
Referring clinician, Aberdeen Royal Infirmary

LABORATORY REPORT – WOUND MICROBIOLOGY

Patient: D. Osman
MRN: 065428885
Patient contact: 07700 900645
Specimen: Deep swab from plantar diabetic foot ulcer
Clinical details: Plantar ulceration with reduced sensation and local discharge; symptoms present for 3 days. Wound care in place. Co-amoxiclav currently prescribed.

Specimen received: Adequate; superficial swab, clinical correlation required.

Microscopy:
Pus cells: Moderate
Gram-positive cocci: Few
Gram-negative bacilli: Moderate

Culture:
Heavy growth of Escherichia coli
Moderate growth of Staphylococcus aureus
Mixed skin flora also isolated.

Antimicrobial susceptibility:
E. coli: susceptible to co-amoxiclav; resistant to amoxicillin.
S. aureus: susceptible to flucloxacillin, doxycycline and co-trimoxazole; resistant to penicillin.
Full susceptibility panel available on the laboratory system.

Interpretation:
Growth of potential pathogens from a superficial wound swab may represent colonisation as well as infection. Results support review of the ulcer clinically, including depth, surrounding erythema, malodour, systemic features and evidence of osteomyelitis. No blood culture submitted.

Action:
Continue wound care pending clinical review. Discuss antibiotic choice and duration with the treating clinician; escalate promptly if spreading cellulitis, fever or deterioration. Consider deep tissue sampling if operative debridement is undertaken.

Follow-up wound review: 2nd February 2005

Validated and reported by: Zakariyya Regan

Discharge summary
NHS number: 000 787 1216

Patient: DEVLEEN WOOD
Home address: 12 Muthill Road, Blackford, PH4 1AA
Report/accession ID: LAB-05868049

Reason for admission
Admitted with sudden central chest pressure associated with diaphoresis and nausea. Initial ECG showed dynamic ST-segment depression and serial troponin levels were consistent with a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. He was initially managed on the respiratory medicine ward owing to bed availability, with cardiology input throughout.

Hospital course
Treated with aspirin, fondaparinux and high-intensity atorvastatin. Symptoms settled promptly and there was no recurrent chest pain or haemodynamic instability. Echocardiogram demonstrated mildly impaired left ventricular systolic function with no significant valve abnormality. Coronary angiography showed moderate coronary disease without a lesion requiring PCI; the consultant cardiologist advised medical management.

The renal function remained stable and haemoglobin was unchanged. Fondaparinux was stopped before discharge. The cardiology plan is dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel for 12 months, unless bleeding or other contraindication develops, followed by ongoing aspirin as advised by cardiology. Continue atorvastatin and arrange repeat lipid assessment in primary care.

Assessment at discharge
Clinically stable, ambulant and pain-free. Access sites clean and dry. Discharged home with advice to seek urgent help via 999 if chest pain recurs or is accompanied by breathlessness, collapse or marked sweating.

Follow-up plan
GP review within one week for medication reconciliation and blood pressure assessment. Cardiology outpatient follow-up and referral to cardiac rehabilitation have been requested.

Prepared and signed by Dr Hui Swain, MBBS, consultant cardiologist, GMC number 0741167.
