Date: 12 Aug 2021
NHS number: 0005985049
Report/accession ID: S21-0576990

Dear Cardiology Team,

Re: A. Pritchard
Home address: 14 Kent Avenue, BALLYCLARE

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient’s reduced exercise tolerance and dizziness in the context of iron-deficiency anaemia. The specific question is whether there is any cardiac contribution to the exertional symptoms, or whether these are adequately explained by the anaemia.

They report several months of tiredness, light-headedness on standing and becoming short of breath when walking uphill or carrying shopping. There has been no reported chest pain, palpitations, syncope or ankle swelling. Examination in the surgery showed a soft systolic flow murmur, with otherwise normal heart sounds, clear lungs and no peripheral oedema. Pulse was regular and blood pressure was satisfactory.

Recent blood tests confirmed iron-deficiency anaemia. The patient has started ferrous fumarate 210 mg once daily, with advice regarding adherence and review of tolerance. Repeat full blood count and iron studies are planned through the GP surgery. The cause of the iron deficiency is also being investigated separately, including review of dietary intake and assessment for possible blood loss.

Please consider ECG and echocardiography if clinically indicated, and advise whether any further cardiac investigation or follow-up is required. The patient understands the reason for referral and will seek urgent assessment if chest pain, collapse or marked breathlessness develops.

Yours sincerely,

lacey-rae pope
Referring clinician

Discharge summary – Accident and Emergency

Patient: heidi-mai anwar, 24-year-old Asian female patient  
Home address: 120 HARTSWOOD, MONEYNEANY  
Patient contact: 07700 900136  
Date of attendance: 25 October 2025

Reason for attendance  
You were assessed for cellulitis affecting the lower leg, with spreading redness, warmth and tenderness. Your spouse provided some of the history.

Assessment and treatment  
The leg was examined and the affected area was outlined. There was no evidence of an abscess requiring drainage, and you were clinically stable for treatment at home. Pain at review was 5/10. The first dose of flucloxacillin was given in the department, with paracetamol for discomfort.

Discharge medicines  
• Flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 7 days. Complete the course unless a clinician advises otherwise.  
• Paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily as needed, leaving at least 4 hours between doses; do not exceed 4 g in 24 hours or take other medicines containing paracetamol.

The redness may take a short time to settle, but it should stop spreading within 48 hours. Keep the leg raised when resting, drink normally and avoid rubbing or scratching the skin. Please contact your GP surgery if there is no improvement after two days or if the course is difficult to tolerate.

Return to the emergency department urgently if the redness spreads rapidly, pain becomes severe, you develop fever, vomiting, confusion, marked swelling, or feel faint or significantly more unwell. Seek immediate help for facial swelling or breathing difficulty after taking the antibiotic.

Correlate with baseline renal function and fluid balance; review for obstruction and nephrotoxic exposure. Nausea may improve with hydration.

ACTION
Repeat U&E and creatinine after fluid review, or sooner if urine output falls further. Consider renal tract ultrasound if obstruction is clinically possible. Escalate urgently for worsening hyperkalaemia, acidosis, pulmonary oedema or persistent oliguria.

Follow-up review: 26/07/2035

Wound Microbiology Report

Patient: R. COOKE
MRN: MRN-06746165
Requesting service: Quintin Medical Centre, respiratory medicine
Specimen: Deep wound swab, plantar diabetic foot ulcer
Clinical details: Plantar ulceration with reduced sensation and local discharge. Current management includes wound care and co-amoxiclav.

Specimen quality and data check:
Specimen-date entry 31/04/2025 rejected as an invalid calendar date during laboratory data-quality checking. The sample was nevertheless received and processed; the collection date is therefore not used for interpretive timing.

Microscopy:
Leucocytes: Moderate
Squamous epithelial cells: Few
Organisms: Mixed Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial forms seen.

Culture:
Heavy growth of mixed enteric Gram-negative bacilli and skin flora. No significant anaerobic growth isolated. Result should be interpreted in conjunction with tissue depth, wound appearance and systemic features; superficial swab growth may reflect colonisation.

Antimicrobial susceptibility:
Escherichia coli: susceptible to co-amoxiclav; resistant to ampicillin.
Mixed skin flora: no individual susceptibility testing indicated.

Interpretation and comment:
Findings support polymicrobial colonisation/infection of the ulcer. Correlate with clinical assessment for spreading cellulitis, osteomyelitis or systemic infection. If there is clinical deterioration, obtain a deep tissue or bone specimen following cleansing and debridement, and discuss antimicrobial selection with microbiology. Continue wound care and review off-loading, glycaemic control and vascular status. Co-amoxiclav should be reviewed against the clinical response and local antimicrobial guidance.

Planned clinical review: 28 May 2018

Validated and reported by: Dr Arlo-Jack WATERS, MBBS

Dear Community Paediatrics Team,

Re: BENEAMIN DANIEL, 11 y/o
Home address: 36 DALLAN VIEW, GLENOE

I would be grateful for your assessment of this school-aged child following a recent acute asthma exacerbation, with particular advice on ongoing management and review of inhaler technique. His father, Zeyaan, reports several nights of cough over the past fortnight, wheeze during the day and increased work of breathing during the latest episode. There has been no reported fever or choking event.

He was reviewed at the surgery after using his salbutamol inhaler more frequently than usual. On examination today he is comfortable at rest, with mild bilateral expiratory wheeze and no recession. Air entry is symmetrical. Weight recorded today: 28.6 kg. He is eating and drinking normally and has returned to school, although night-time cough persists.

Salbutamol inhaler remains available as required. Spacer teaching was provided to the child and his father, with technique observed and corrected. The family have been advised to seek urgent assessment through A&E if breathing becomes difficult, speech is limited by breathlessness, or reliever treatment is not providing sustained benefit.

Assessment: recurrent wheeze with a recent acute asthma exacerbation and ongoing nocturnal symptoms. I would appreciate confirmation of the diagnosis, assessment of trigger and control, and advice regarding the need for preventer treatment and a written asthma action plan. Please also review inhaler and spacer technique with the family.

Yours sincerely,

A. Worthington

Patient: B. Hawkes
Occupation: Cleaner
Employer: Caegarw Sports Club
Address: 98 Heath Park Drive, Clarbeston Road, SA63 4AA
Patient contact: 07700 900475

Seen in general medicine clinic with a 5-day history of brief spinning sensations when turning in bed or looking upwards. Episodes last less than a minute and settle if still. Associated nausea and a feeling of unsteadiness, but no vomiting, hearing loss, tinnitus, headache, diplopia, limb weakness or speech disturbance. Also reports a mild cough for 3 days, without fever or breathlessness.

On examination, alert and comfortable at rest. Gait mildly cautious but independent. Cranial nerves grossly intact, with normal limb power, coordination and speech. No spontaneous nystagmus. Right Dix–Hallpike reproduced the characteristic vertigo with a short latency and fatigable torsional nystagmus; symptoms eased on sitting upright. Otoscopy unremarkable. Chest clear.

Assessment: Findings are consistent with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. No features today to suggest a central neurological cause. The cough appears to be a separate, uncomplicated viral upper respiratory symptom.

Plan: Explained the diagnosis and advised slow changes of position, maintaining fluids and avoiding driving or climbing while symptomatic. Epley repositioning manoeuvre demonstrated and written instructions provided. Continue prochlorperazine as required for troublesome nausea, avoiding unnecessary regular use. Return urgently via A&E if persistent vertigo, new severe headache, weakness, altered speech, inability to walk or repeated vomiting. Review with the GP if not improving over the next fortnight; consider vestibular physiotherapy if symptoms persist. Cough management is conservative, with review if fever, chest pain or shortness of breath develops.

Discharge summary – Acute Medical Unit

Patient: Gabriella-Louise  
Clinical age group: 87 y/o  
Relative present: Atay Pike, partner, from CASTLECAULFIELD

Reason for admission  
Admitted following a sudden episode of left arm weakness with facial droop and slurred speech. Symptoms resolved before arrival in the emergency department. Atay Pike reports that the episode began at 08:15 and lasted approximately 20 minutes.

Assessment and key results  
Neurological examination remained normal after admission. CT head showed no acute haemorrhage or established infarction. CT angiography showed no large-vessel occlusion or significant carotid stenosis. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm. Routine blood tests were satisfactory; cholesterol was raised. The overall presentation was felt to be a transient ischaemic attack (TIA).

Hospital course  
Observed overnight with no recurrence of weakness, facial asymmetry or speech disturbance. Reviewed by the stroke team. No indication for thrombolysis or thrombectomy. Swallow assessment was passed and mobilisation was independent.

Discharge medicines  
Aspirin 300 mg once daily for 14 days, then reduce to aspirin 75 mg once daily. Atorvastatin 80 mg at night, newly commenced. Continue other regular medicines as listed on the medicines reconciliation. Do not stop aspirin unless advised by a clinician.

Follow-up and advice  
Stroke clinic review arranged for 14 November 2012. GP to review blood pressure, lipid profile and vascular risk factors. Please seek urgent medical help via 999 if weakness, facial droop, speech difficulty or other sudden neurological symptoms recur, even if they settle quickly.

Condition at discharge: medically stable, symptom-free and discharged home with partner.

Date: 2021-09-26

Situation: Admitted with sickle cell painful crisis. Severe bilateral limb pain and lower back pain on arrival, with poor oral intake and clinical dehydration. Partner, U. Dickson, present and supporting history.

Observations: Alert, pale and uncomfortable. NEWS2 1; temperature 37.2°C, HR 104, BP 112/68, RR 18, SpO₂ 98% on air. Urine concentrated, passed small amount overnight. No chest pain or breathlessness reported.

Actions: IV fluids ongoing as prescribed; cannula patent, site clean and dry. Morphine administered for breakthrough pain; repositioned and encouraged sips little and often. Warm packs offered. Strict fluid balance commenced. Avoiding unnecessary venepuncture.

Response: Pain reduced from 9/10 to 6/10 approximately 30 minutes after morphine, though remains significant on movement. No vomiting. Tolerating small amounts of oral fluid.

Concern/escalation: Medical registrar informed by covering nurse due to persistent pain and tachycardia; review requested if further breakthrough analgesia required. Monitor for fever, hypoxia, chest symptoms or increasing sedation.

Plan for next shift: Continue prescribed analgesia and IV fluids, repeat observations, assess pain and sedation before doses, maintain fluid balance and encourage mobilisation to chair with assistance. Review analgesic plan on ward round. Follow-up arranged in about 11 weeks.

Documented by M. Abbas, registered nurse.

Patient: Dotty-Mae
DOB: 28/02/2023
Informant: mother, BRAMWELL WALSH, who lives in Lunning
Ward: Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh

Admitted with repeated vomiting, loose stools and noticeably reduced urine output. The history was provided by the mother. On arrival the infant was clinically dehydrated, with dry mucous membranes and reduced wet nappies, but remained responsive and consolable. No safeguarding concerns were identified.

Managed with oral rehydration solution in small, frequent amounts and supportive care. Vomiting settled during admission and stools became less frequent. Urine output improved, with a further wet nappy before discharge. No intravenous fluids or antibiotics were required. Observations remained stable and the infant was feeding adequately prior to going home.

Assessment: Acute gastroenteritis with dehydration, now clinically improved following oral rehydration.

Discharge plan:
Continue oral rehydration solution after each loose stool and offer usual milk feeds little and often. Do not dilute formula. No new prescribed medicines. Monitor wet nappies, alertness and ability to keep feeds down.

Follow-up: GP review if symptoms have not settled in about 6 weeks, or sooner if there is concern. Return to the emergency department urgently if the infant becomes difficult to wake, has markedly fewer wet nappies, persistent vomiting, blood in the stool, breathing difficulty or cannot retain fluids. Mother verbalised understanding of the plan and was happy with discharge.

Microbiology Report
National Insurance number: NT 62 31 50 D

Patient: Abubakarr C.
MRN: 0810862
Specimen: Deep wound swab, plantar ulcer
Clinical details: Diabetes mellitus with plantar ulceration, reduced protective sensation and local discharge. Symptoms present for 3 days. Current treatment includes wound care and co-amoxiclav.

Specimen received: Adequate wound swab with clinical details supplied. Culture performed with antimicrobial susceptibility testing where appropriate.

Microscopy:
Moderate polymorphonuclear leucocytes.
Mixed Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms observed.

Culture:
Heavy growth of Escherichia coli.
Moderate growth of Enterococcus faecalis.
Mixed skin flora also isolated.

Antimicrobial susceptibility:
Escherichia coli: susceptible to co-amoxiclav; resistant to trimethoprim; susceptibility to ciprofloxacin reported separately.
Enterococcus faecalis: susceptible to ampicillin; intrinsic resistance to cephalosporins noted.

Interpretation:
The cultured organisms may represent clinically significant infection in the context of discharge from a diabetic foot ulcer. Correlate with ulcer depth, surrounding erythema, systemic features and vascular status. The result does not exclude underlying osteomyelitis; imaging and inflammatory markers should be considered if there is failure to improve or exposed bone.

Clinical comment:
Continue local wound care and review antibiotic choice against the susceptibility findings and renal function. Urgent multidisciplinary diabetic foot assessment is advised if spreading cellulitis, systemic illness, tissue necrosis or ischaemia develops. A repeat deep specimen is preferable to a superficial swab if the clinical response is poor.

Planned clinical review: 05/05/2026

Validated and reported by:
ZARNISH LAWSON, Consultant Clinical Microbiologist
GMC: 0151352

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: R. Cummings
Home address: 19 BLIGH'S LANE, BELTOY
Patient contact: 07700 900293
Admission: Cardiology
Discharge diagnosis: Acute pulmonary embolism

Presentation
Sudden breathlessness, pleuritic right-sided chest pain and tachycardia. Oxygen saturations 89% on air at arrival. At 08:15, pulse 118 bpm; haemodynamically stable.

Key results
CT pulmonary angiogram: bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli, no right ventricular dilatation. Troponin mildly raised but falling on repeat. ECG: sinus tachycardia. Lower-limb Doppler negative for proximal DVT. Routine blood tests satisfactory for anticoagulation; renal function preserved.

Hospital course
Treated with supplemental oxygen initially, weaned to room air before discharge. No hypotension or bleeding. Reviewed by the thrombosis team; outpatient anticoagulation pathway agreed. Partner present for discharge discussion.

Discharge medicines
• Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily thereafter.
• Supplemental oxygen stopped; not required at discharge.

Discharge summary

Patient: Jonathan Roe
DOB: 15 Jun 1977
Patient contact: 07700 900606
Admission/discharge date: 23rd July 2019

Reason for admission
Presented with a 48-hour history of frequent watery diarrhoea, vomiting and cramping abdominal pain. Reduced oral intake with dizziness on standing. K. Foster, the patient’s sibling, provided collateral history.

Assessment and key results
Initially clinically dehydrated, with dry mucous membranes and mild postural symptoms. Abdomen soft, with diffuse mild tenderness and no guarding or rebound. Blood tests showed mild pre-renal biochemical change, which improved following fluids; inflammatory markers not significantly raised. Stool culture and viral PCR were sent, with no result requiring alteration of management at the point of discharge. No evidence of an acute surgical abdomen.

Hospital course
Managed with oral rehydration solution, antiemetic treatment and observation. A short period of intravenous crystalloid was required because of ongoing vomiting, after which oral fluids were tolerated. Vomiting settled and stool frequency reduced. Remained apyrexial and haemodynamically stable. No further abdominal cramps reported before discharge.

Problem list
• Infectious gastroenteritis, clinically improving
• Dehydration secondary to gastrointestinal losses, resolved
• Mild transient pre-renal renal impairment, improved

Discharge medicines
Oral rehydration solution, taken regularly in small amounts and after each loose stool.
Ondansetron as required for nausea or vomiting. Avoid anti-diarrhoeal medication unless advised by a clinician.

Condition at discharge
Alert, mobilising independently and tolerating fluids and light food. Passing urine normally. Discharged home with advice to rest, maintain hydration and follow hand hygiene measures. Seek urgent assessment for persistent inability to keep fluids down, blood in stool, worsening or localised abdominal pain, confusion, or markedly reduced urine output.

Follow-up
GP review if symptoms have not substantially settled in about 3 weeks, or sooner if deteriorating. Outstanding stool results will be reviewed and communicated if they alter treatment.

Treatment to date has included omeprazole and alginate suspension, with partial improvement in the heartburn but little change in the cough. They are taking the medicines as prescribed and have been advised regarding meal timing, avoiding late snacks and raising the head of the bed. Examination in the surgery today was reassuring: chest clear with equal air entry, normal respiratory effort and oxygen saturations. There was no wheeze.

Assessment: reflux-associated cough is possible, but the persistence of symptoms despite acid suppression warrants specialist review.

Please consider spirometry, chest imaging or other investigations as clinically indicated, and advise whether further reflux testing or optimisation of treatment is appropriate. I will arrange primary-care review in about 5 weeks, or sooner if symptoms deteriorate.

Associated drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss. No infective symptoms reported. Eating and drinking adequately, although energy levels are reduced.

Examination demonstrates firm, non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy, with palpable supraclavicular nodes. No overlying skin change. Chest is clear to auscultation; heart sounds normal. Abdomen soft, with no definite hepatosplenomegaly on examination. Performance status remains good.

Investigations reviewed:
Cross-sectional imaging demonstrates extensive cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, radiologically concerning for lymphoma. Blood tests show inflammatory marker elevation; full blood count does not demonstrate significant cytopenia. An image-guided core biopsy has been arranged, with histopathological classification awaited.

Impression:
Clinical and radiological picture is consistent with Hodgkin lymphoma. Tissue diagnosis remains required before definitive staging and treatment selection. The constitutional symptoms are concerning for active disease.

Plan:
Supportive care pending tissue diagnosis, including oral fluids, nutritional support and simple analgesia if required. Avoid corticosteroids unless clinically indicated, as these may affect biopsy interpretation. Expedite biopsy reporting and arrange PET-CT and echocardiography once histology is available. The patient has been advised to seek urgent assessment for rapidly increasing swelling, breathlessness, dysphagia or fever.

Report authored by vedh lea
General Medicine
Chelsea & Westminster NHS Fdn Trust - Weymouth Street Hospital

Patient: RITVIK BARRETT
NHS number: 000 907 1157
MRN: 0654534
Patient occupation: Carpenter
Clinic: Winch Lane Medical Centre

Cardiology review

Thank you for attending clinic with your spouse. You described ongoing tiredness, occasional dizziness when standing, and reduced exercise tolerance. There has been no chest pain, blackouts or sustained awareness of an irregular heartbeat. Your examination today was reassuring, with no clinical evidence of fluid overload. The ECG was sinus rhythm; there was no feature to suggest that a primary cardiac disorder is causing the current limitation.

The overall picture is most consistent with symptomatic iron-deficiency anaemia. Please continue ferrous fumarate as prescribed by your GP. We discussed taking it regularly and reporting troublesome abdominal pain, constipation or nausea. Repeat full blood count and ferritin should be arranged through the GP surgery, with further investigation of the cause of iron deficiency if the results do not improve as expected.

I have not added a cardiac medicine today. Please seek urgent assessment via A&E if you develop persistent chest pain, collapse, severe breathlessness at rest or prolonged palpitations. Otherwise, increase activity gradually according to symptoms and maintain good fluid intake.

We will review your blood results and symptoms in about 10 weeks. If the anaemia has corrected but exercise tolerance remains poor, the need for further cardiac testing can then be reconsidered.

Yours sincerely,

aiyan ibrahim
Cardiology clinician
Winch Lane Medical Centre

Referral to Specialist Service

From: Aberdeen Royal Infirmary
Patient: Jahanzaib H.
Report/accession ID: 25/466923

Dear Colleague,

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient with persistent low back pain and right-sided shooting leg pain, associated with intermittent paraesthesia into the foot. Symptoms began insidiously and have continued despite conservative management. There is no reported bowel or bladder disturbance, saddle sensory change or progressive limb weakness.

On review, lumbar movement is restricted by pain. Straight-leg raise reproduces the leg symptoms on the affected side. Lower-limb power is functionally preserved, with altered light-touch sensation reported distally. Reflexes are not clearly asymmetrical. The clinical picture is most consistent with lumbar radiculopathy; alternative spinal or peripheral nerve pathology should be considered if symptoms persist or progress.

Treatment to date has included activity modification, advice regarding posture and a trial of simple analgesia. Current medication: paracetamol; naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food. Response has been limited. No imaging report is currently available for review.

Please assess the need for spinal imaging and advise on further management, including whether physiotherapy, pain management input or surgical opinion is indicated. The patient has been advised to seek urgent assessment via A&E if new weakness, urinary retention, faecal incontinence or saddle numbness develops.

Yours sincerely,

Amaiah Moss

CT brain showed no acute haemorrhage or established infarction. Carotid Doppler did not demonstrate significant stenosis. ECG was in sinus rhythm and routine blood tests were satisfactory. Neurological examination remained normal throughout admission.

The presentation was felt to be most consistent with a transient ischaemic attack (TIA). No thrombolysis was indicated as symptoms had resolved. Aspirin was commenced and atorvastatin continued for secondary prevention. Please take aspirin once daily and continue atorvastatin as prescribed; these medicines should not be stopped without speaking to your GP or the stroke team. Your GP should review blood pressure, cholesterol and vascular risk factors.

At discharge you were clinically well, mobilising independently and eating and drinking normally. Blood pressure on the ward was 120/80 mmHg.

Follow-up: rapid-access TIA clinic appointment arranged for 18 November 2045. The clinic will review the diagnosis and consider any further cardiac monitoring or treatment. Please attend even if you remain well.

Seek urgent medical help immediately if weakness, facial asymmetry, speech disturbance, visual loss or new severe headache returns, even if it settles within minutes. Do not drive until you have checked the current DVLA advice following a TIA.

Discharge medicines: aspirin once daily; atorvastatin as previously prescribed. Ensure your GP surgery has an up-to-date medication list.

Examination: comfortable at rest. Pulse regular at 76 bpm; blood pressure 128/74 mmHg. Heart sounds normal, with no murmur. Chest clear. No peripheral oedema.

Discharge Summary – Clinical Genetics
NHS number: 0004220740

Patient: N. Ibrahim
Document date: 22nd April 1996
Patient contact: 07700 900049
The patient, aged 29 years, was admitted with a vaso-occlusive sickle cell painful crisis, presenting with severe bilateral limb pain, lumbar back pain and reduced oral intake with clinical dehydration. History was obtained with the patient’s agreement and collateral information from sibling LUNA-LEIGH MITCHELL.

At admission, observations were stable apart from tachycardia related to pain. No hypoxia, chest pain or focal neurological deficit. Examination showed marked tenderness of the limbs and lower back, dry mucous membranes, and no acute chest signs. Initial blood tests demonstrated anaemia in keeping with the patient’s established sickle cell disease; inflammatory markers were not significantly raised. Chest radiograph showed no consolidation.

Problem list:
• Vaso-occlusive painful crisis
• Dehydration, resolved with rehydration
• Sickle cell disease under clinical genetics follow-up

Analgesia was commenced promptly with intravenous morphine, later converted to oral opioid analgesia as pain settled. Intravenous fluids were given initially, followed by encouragement of oral fluids. Regular paracetamol was continued. No antibiotics were required. Thromboprophylaxis was prescribed during reduced mobility. Review at 08:15 confirmed improving pain and normal work of breathing; the patient was mobilising independently by the afternoon.

Discharge condition: comfortable at rest, tolerating diet and fluids, passing urine normally, with pain manageable on oral medication. No evidence of acute chest syndrome or other infective complication during this admission.

Discharge medicines:
• Paracetamol regularly for the next 48 hours, then as required
• Oral morphine solution as required for breakthrough severe pain, reducing and stopping as symptoms improve
Continue usual disease-modifying treatment as previously prescribed.

Follow-up arranged with the clinical genetics/sickle cell service and GP. Return to A&E for fever, chest pain, breathlessness, persistent vomiting, neurological symptoms or uncontrolled pain. Safety-netting and hydration advice discussed with the patient and sibling.

Known heart failure, followed by HORTON GENERAL HOSPITAL. Regular medicines include furosemide 40 mg once daily and bisoprolol. No reported chest pain or infective symptoms.

Alert, speaking in short sentences. RR 26, SpO₂ 92% on air, BP 148/86, pulse 104 irregular, temp 36.7°C. Bibasal fine crepitations to mid-zones, raised JVP and pitting oedema to both shins. ECG: atrial fibrillation with fast ventricular response, no ST elevation. Chest X-ray: cardiomegaly and bilateral interstitial oedema. Bloods sent: FBC, U&E, CRP, troponin, BNP; results pending. Admit to respiratory/cardiology bed for diuresis and monitoring. Escalate urgently for increasing oxygen requirement, hypotension, chest pain or reduced consciousness.

Laboratory Report – Microbiology

Patient: Johnathan DENNIS
Report/accession ID: 0846299075
Specimen: Midstream urine
Clinical details: Flank pain, dysuria and rigors. Acute pyelonephritis suspected. Current treatment: cefuroxime; paracetamol.

Collected: Urine, received in boric acid container
Culture:
• Significant growth of Escherichia coli, >10⁵ cfu/mL
• Mixed growth: not identified
• Appearance: cloudy

Antimicrobial susceptibility:
Cefuroxime – susceptible
Trimethoprim – susceptible
Nitrofurantoin – susceptible
Ciprofloxacin – susceptible
Amoxicillin – resistant

Interpretation:
Significant E. coli bacteriuria with a susceptibility pattern compatible with the reported clinical diagnosis. Correlate with systemic features and renal function. Nitrofurantoin is not appropriate for suspected upper urinary tract infection despite in-vitro susceptibility.

Action:
Continue prescribed cefuroxime if clinically improving; review dose and duration against local antimicrobial guidance and renal function. Seek urgent clinical review if persistent rigors, vomiting, hypotension or worsening flank pain. Repeat urine culture only if symptoms fail to settle or recur.

Follow-up: GP/acute medicine review 11th July 2024, in about 10 weeks.

The patient has also had a dry cough for 3 days, without fever or breathlessness; this appears separate from the episodic symptoms.

On review, the patient was comfortable at rest. Heart sounds were regular, with no audible murmur, and the chest was clear. Resting ECG in the surgery showed sinus rhythm without acute ST-segment changes. Routine blood tests, including full blood count, electrolytes and thyroid function, have been requested; results are pending.

Assessment: episodic palpitations and atypical chest discomfort, with no abnormality captured on the resting ECG. I would appreciate advice on whether ambulatory ECG monitoring and any further cardiac investigation are indicated, and whether sertraline requires any particular cardiac precautions.

Yours faithfully,

Dr Harlow-May Greaves, MBBS

CLINICAL GENETICS LABORATORY REPORT
NHS number: 000 960 9327

Patient: Dexy O.
MRN / patient identifier: 012277671
Home address: 28 Brambling Gardens, Heswall, CH60 0AA
Specimen: EDTA blood, 4 mL; peripheral blood constitutional DNA
Clinical indication: Painless lymphadenopathy, night sweats and unintentional weight loss. Hodgkin lymphoma suspected; tissue diagnosis pending.
Requesting clinician: Not stated

Assay: Germline haematological malignancy predisposition panel, 138 genes; next-generation sequencing with copy-number analysis.
Specimen received: Suitable for analysis.
Mean coverage: 186× (target minimum 100×)
Target bases at ≥20×: 99.1%
Variant classification: ACMG/AMP criteria.

RESULT
No pathogenic or likely pathogenic germline variant identified in the genes analysed.
Variants of uncertain significance: None detected.
Copy-number analysis: No reportable exon-level deletion or duplication.

INTERPRETATION
Negative result. This does not exclude a somatic alteration within the lymph node, a variant outside the assay regions, low-level mosaicism, or a hereditary predisposition not yet characterised. The result does not establish or refute the diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma; histopathology remains required.

Clinical comment: Supportive care pending tissue diagnosis. If lymphoma is confirmed, correlate with the histology and consider tumour-directed molecular testing where clinically indicated. Genetic counselling recommended if family history is significant or if the clinical picture changes.

Action: Result issued to the requesting team; please retain the report with the patient record.
Follow-up genetics review: 1988-10-09

Validated and authorised by:
Dr Poppie-Rose Mustafa, MBBS
Laboratory clinical scientist, Clinical Genetics

Context: The patient, aged 58 years, was reviewed in respiratory clinic regarding fatigue and new inflammatory joint symptoms while receiving methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis. Patient contact: lio.long75@gmail.com

No new cough, wheeze, haemoptysis or exertional desaturation reported. Methotrexate and folic acid have been continued as prescribed; naproxen is being used for symptomatic relief. No recent infection or antibiotic course.

Examination: Comfortable at rest, speaking in full sentences. Chest clear bilaterally with no focal crackles or wheeze. Mild synovitis and tenderness affecting both hands, greatest at the MCP joints. No peripheral oedema. Observations stable in clinic.

The joint disease requires prompt rheumatology review, with consideration of treatment escalation rather than repeated NSAID use alone.

Plan: Continue current methotrexate, folic acid and naproxen pending rheumatology advice; avoid further NSAID escalation without renal and gastrointestinal review. Arrange rheumatology assessment and repeat routine monitoring bloods through the usual pathway. Safety-netted regarding breathlessness, fever or rapidly worsening joint swelling. Discharge summary – Neonatology

Patient: T. Morley
Clinical age: day 3 of life
Father: Shanzey
Report/accession ID: 05703362
Discharging service: Royal Victoria Hospital

Reason for admission
Admitted from the postnatal ward with increasing jaundice for 3 days, sleepy feeding and reduced intake. Father Shanzey reported fewer effective breastfeeds and the baby difficult to rouse for feeds. No fever or respiratory concerns.

Assessment and hospital course
On admission, visibly jaundiced to the trunk but cardiovascularly stable, warm and well perfused. Mildly sleepy, improving with handling. Bilirubin was above the treatment threshold for gestation and postnatal age; serum bilirubin monitored during admission with appropriate downward trend. Blood group and haemolysis screen were reassuring. Glucose remained satisfactory. No clinical evidence of sepsis.

Phototherapy commenced and continued overnight with eye protection. Feeding support provided by the neonatal team and maternity staff: regular breastfeeds encouraged, expressed breast milk offered after feeds where required, with close monitoring of wet nappies and feeding effectiveness. Intake improved during the admission. Weight loss remained within the expected early neonatal range. Phototherapy was stopped following a satisfactory repeat bilirubin, with rebound level below treatment threshold.

Problem list
• Unconjugated neonatal jaundice – responded to phototherapy
• Sleepy feeding/reduced intake – improved with feeding support
• No evidence of infection or hypoglycaemia

Discharge condition and plan
Alert when handled, maintaining temperature in an open cot, settled in air, and feeding more effectively. Passing urine and stools. Discharged home with father after review by the neonatal registrar.

Continue frequent breastfeeds, waking for feeds if needed. Seek urgent medical advice via NHS 111/A&E if increasingly difficult to rouse, refusing feeds, markedly fewer wet nappies, fever, breathing difficulty or worsening jaundice. Community midwife to review feeding and jaundice; GP review if concerns persist.

text:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT ASSESSMENT
NHS number: 000 649 5231

Patient: Laniyah Adamson
DOB: 23rd March 1956
Address: 156 The Gannocks, Crewe, CW1 2AF
Patient contact: laniyah.adamson40@yahoo.co.uk
Accompanied by: partner

Presenting complaint:
Sudden brief spinning episodes since yesterday, brought on by turning in bed and looking upwards. Associated nausea and unsteadiness when walking during episodes. Each spell settles within a minute. No persistent vertigo, syncope, headache, chest pain, hearing loss or focal weakness.

Observations:
Alert, comfortable at rest. BP 120/80 mmHg, pulse regular, respiratory rate normal, afebrile. GCS 15.

Examination:
Speech clear. Pupils equal and reactive; no diplopia or facial asymmetry. Limb power and sensation intact. Finger–nose testing normal. Gait mildly cautious but independent. No truncal ataxia. Dix–Hallpike positive to the right with characteristic brief torsional nystagmus and reproduction of symptoms. Otoscopy unremarkable.

Investigations:
Capillary glucose normal. ECG: sinus rhythm, no acute ischaemic change. No indication for neuroimaging following senior review; presentation consistent with peripheral positional vertigo.

Assessment:
Likely right-sided benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. No clinical features of posterior circulation stroke or other acute neurological process.

Treatment / plan:
Epley repositioning manoeuvre performed with improvement. Prochlorperazine as required advised for short-term nausea/vertigo; avoid driving or hazardous activity while symptomatic. GP follow-up if recurrent, with vestibular physiotherapy consideration.

Disposition:
Discharged home with partner. Return to A&E for continuous vertigo, new weakness, dysarthria, severe headache, collapse or inability to walk.

Seen and discharged by Indrit Butcher, Emergency Department clinician.

Date: 21/10/1996
NHS number: 000 753 1797
To: Respiratory Medicine
From: Queen Elizabeth University Hospital

Re: R. Riley
MRN: 099 238 126

Dear Colleague,

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient with progressive, painless lymphadenopathy, associated drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss. The enlarged nodes were first noted in the left cervical chain and have persisted despite treatment of a presumed intercurrent upper respiratory infection. There is no reported tenderness, erythema or recent vaccination at the site.

On review today, the patient appeared tired but haemodynamically stable. Palpable, firm, non-tender cervical and supraclavicular nodes were present. Chest examination was clear, with no clinical evidence of pleural effusion. The patient reports reduced appetite but is maintaining oral fluids. An emergency contact is recorded in the practice notes.

Initial blood tests showed anaemia and an elevated inflammatory response; peripheral blood film did not provide a diagnostic explanation. Chest radiograph demonstrated mediastinal fullness. The clinical picture is concerning for Hodgkin lymphoma, although tissue diagnosis is awaited.

Assessment
Persistent painless lymphadenopathy with constitutional symptoms and mediastinal widening, requiring urgent specialist investigation.

Plan/request
Please arrange urgent respiratory or haemato-oncology review, cross-sectional imaging and image-guided or excision biopsy as appropriate. Could you advise on the safest route for obtaining tissue and whether staging investigations should be coordinated through your service? Supportive care pending tissue diagnosis is currently in place; no disease-specific treatment has been started.

Yours faithfully,

AVILA GALE
Referring clinician

Date: 19 Nov 2012
NHS number: 0006440488
Patient: G. Bradbury  DOB: 25 April 1965
Ward nursing progress note – cardiology

Reviewed this afternoon following concern regarding the lower abdominal postoperative wound. Patient reports increased local pain since the morning and partner, F. NEEDHAM, noticed yellow discharge on the dressing. Wound edges erythematous with a small amount of purulent discharge; surrounding skin warm and tender. No active bleeding. Temperature elevated at 37.8°C, pulse 92 bpm, respirations 18/min, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, and oxygen saturations 97% on air. Patient alert and conversing appropriately.

Mobilising to the bathroom with supervision owing to discomfort. Taking fluids and a light diet; urine passed. Analgesia given as prescribed with partial relief. Existing dressing removed using aseptic technique, wound irrigated with sterile saline and redressed. Swab obtained as requested and sent to microbiology. Flucloxacillin administered as prescribed; no immediate adverse reaction observed.

Assessment: suspected superficial postoperative wound infection with erythema, purulent discharge and local pain. No evidence of systemic deterioration at present. Patient and partner advised to report worsening pain, spreading redness, fever or feeling unwell.

Covering medical doctor Dr Aurora-Jane McNally, MBBS contacted and reviewed the wound. Continue flucloxacillin and regular observations, monitor the marked edge of erythema, and maintain daily aseptic wound care. Escalate promptly for fever, hypotension, tachycardia, increasing discharge or spreading cellulitis. Handover to the night nurse to reassess the dressing and pain response, encourage oral fluids, and follow up the microbiology result.

PAEDIATRIC MICROBIOLOGY REPORT
NHS number: 000 077 5992

Patient: Darrius Joyce
DOB: 25 August 2018
Report/accession ID: 08090825
Specimen collected: 24 May 2022
Specimen: Midstream urine, clean-catch sample
Clinical details: Parent reports dysuria, urinary frequency and suprapubic discomfort. Current weight: 14.2 kg. Nitrofurantoin commenced by GP pending culture.

URINALYSIS
Appearance: Hazy
Leukocyte esterase: 3+
Nitrite: Positive
Blood: 1+
Protein: Trace
Glucose: Negative

MICROSCOPY
White cells: >100 x 10⁶/L
Red cells: 10 x 10⁶/L
Squamous epithelial cells: Few

CULTURE
Significant growth of Escherichia coli, >10⁵ cfu/mL.
Mixed growth: Not detected.

ANTIMICROBIAL SUSCEPTIBILITY
Nitrofurantoin: Susceptible
Trimethoprim: Susceptible

Consider repeat specimen if persistent symptoms or recurrence.

Discharge summary
NHS number: 0001154720

Patient: 63-year-old African-American male patient, Billie-Anne
Admission reason: Presented with 18 hours of worsening right lower-quadrant abdominal pain, nausea and loss of appetite. Initial assessment supported acute appendicitis; surgical review arranged from the emergency department.

Key findings: Localised right iliac fossa tenderness with guarding. Blood tests showed raised inflammatory markers and neutrophilia. CT abdomen/pelvis demonstrated an inflamed appendix without perforation or collection.

Hospital course: Managed initially with intravenous fluids, analgesia and intravenous co-amoxiclav. Underwent uncomplicated laparoscopic appendicectomy under general anaesthesia. Operative findings were acute suppurative appendicitis without perforation. Appendix sent for histology. Post-operatively tolerated oral fluids and diet, mobilised independently and passed urine. No fever or vomiting; pain controlled with oral medication. Histology result to be reviewed if any unexpected finding is reported.

Discharge medicines:
• paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily when required
• No further antibiotics prescribed.
Avoid exceeding the stated paracetamol dose or taking additional paracetamol-containing preparations.

Wounds: Three small laparoscopic port sites, closed with absorbable sutures and skin adhesive. Keep clean and dry; showering permitted, but no swimming until healed.

Condition at discharge: Clinically well, haemodynamically stable and suitable for discharge home with family. Discharge advice discussed with the patient and adult child, leilan sinclair, who lives in CARNMONEY.

Follow-up: Telephone or surgical review booked for 5 February 2026. GP to review sooner if required. Seek urgent medical attention for increasing abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fever, wound redness or discharge, abdominal swelling, or inability to keep fluids down.

Operation and admission documentation completed; histology will be communicated through the usual surgical pathway.

text:
SITUATION
A&E assessment, 08:15. HITANSH WARD, aged 83 years, brought in by spouse with abrupt palpitations, central chest tightness and intense fear of dying while at home. Symptoms peaked within minutes and had largely settled before review.

BACKGROUND
No known cardiac history reported. No collapse, fever or stimulant use. Spouse present for collateral history; patient consents to discussion. Medication: breathing retraining.

ASSESSMENT
Alert, coherent and visibly anxious initially. Pulse regular; heart sounds normal, chest clear, no focal neurological deficit. ECG: sinus rhythm, no ischaemic changes. Capillary glucose and troponin unremarkable; observations remained stable during department stay. Presentation most consistent with a panic attack; acute coronary syndrome, arrhythmia and respiratory pathology felt unlikely following examination and investigations.

ACTIONS / PLAN
Reassured and coached through slow diaphragmatic breathing and grounding; symptoms resolved without medication. Discussed recurrence plan and avoidance of excess caffeine. No indication for admission. Discharged home with spouse, advised to contact GP surgery for review of anxiety/panic symptoms and psychological support options. Return to A&E urgently for persistent or exertional chest pain, syncope, severe breathlessness or sustained palpitations.

Follow-up with Royal Hampshire County Hospital booked for 8 Feb 2026.
Documented and discharged by eidel beaumont.

Dear Cardiology Team,
NHS number: 000 099 9734

Re: Iqbaal Cannon

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient, who has type 2 diabetes mellitus and increasing thirst, fatigue and frequent urination over the past several weeks. There is no reported chest pain, but the combination of diabetes and reduced exercise tolerance has raised concern about unrecognised cardiovascular disease. I would particularly value advice on cardiovascular risk stratification and whether further cardiac investigations are indicated.

Recent surgery review found the patient haemodynamically stable, with clear chest sounds and no peripheral oedema. An ECG showed sinus rhythm without acute ST-segment changes. Blood tests demonstrated elevated glucose and HbA1c above target; renal function was suitable for continued metformin. Urinalysis was negative for blood and ketones. The patient reports good adherence to metformin and atorvastatin, with no recent medication changes.

Current medication:
Metformin, as prescribed.
Atorvastatin, as prescribed.

Lifestyle measures and diabetic dietary advice have been revisited. The patient’s partner, O. BENSON, is supporting attendance and medication routines. I have arranged repeat diabetic blood tests and asked the patient to seek urgent assessment if chest pain, breathlessness at rest or collapse develops.

Assessment: Type 2 diabetes with suboptimal glycaemic control and possible exertional limitation; cardiovascular risk requires specialist review.

Rohini BOULTON

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report

Patient: thaminah glover
MRN: 04075226
Clinical context: The patient, aged 30 years, reviewed for fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation. Known hypothyroidism. On levothyroxine 75 micrograms once daily.

Specimen: EDTA blood; genomic DNA extracted for targeted thyroid-dysfunction panel.
Request: Investigation of persistent biochemical hypothyroidism; ordering clinician not stated.

Results:
TSH: 8.6 mIU/L (0.27–4.20) — raised
Free T4: 11.2 pmol/L (12–22) — borderline low
Thyroid peroxidase antibody: positive
Thyroglobulin antibody: negative

Genetic analysis: No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant identified in the genes included on the panel. A variant of uncertain significance was detected; this is not diagnostic and should not guide treatment.

Interpretation: Findings support autoimmune primary hypothyroidism. The negative panel does not exclude non-genetic thyroid disease or genetic causes outside the tested regions. Correlate with thyroid function monitoring and clinical history.

Action: Continue management through GP/endocrine team; review adherence, administration and need for dose adjustment. No predictive testing for relatives indicated on this result.

Follow-up review: 2035-03-28

Validated and reported by: Dr Morrigan ENGLAND, MBBS
Laboratory comment: Results authorised for clinical use.

Date: Today’s ward round

Observations:
BP 120/80 mmHg; pulse 104 bpm, regular; respirations 22/min; SpO₂ 94% on 2 L oxygen via nasal cannula; temperature stable. Alert, speaking in full sentences. Mild right-sided pleuritic discomfort, 3/10. No haemoptysis reported.

Mobility/intake:
Mobilised to chair with one staff member; short of breath on exertion. Eating small amounts, fluids tolerated. Urine passed this shift.

Apixaban administered as prescribed; no bleeding, melaena or haematuria observed. Oxygen continued with improved dyspnoea. Chest pain eased following rest and prescribed analgesia.

Discharge summary

Patient: rashika hills
Age/context: aged 6 years
Department: Paediatrics
Responsible service: Aberdeen Royal Infirmary
Informant: mother, benicia black, locality Ormiscaig

Admission
Sickle cell painful crisis with severe limb and back pain, reduced oral intake and clinical dehydration. Mother reported cough for 3 days; no respiratory distress or chest pain.

Key findings
Afebrile on admission. Dry mucous membranes, peripheral perfusion maintained. Oxygen saturations normal in air. Chest clear. No focal neurological deficit or joint swelling.

Results
FBC consistent with known sickle cell disease; haemoglobin below usual baseline, reticulocytosis. U&E satisfactory after rehydration. Blood culture negative. Chest radiograph: no acute chest syndrome or focal consolidation.

Hospital course
Managed on the paediatric ward with intravenous fluids and regular analgesia, including morphine initially, then stepped down as pain improved. Paracetamol and ibuprofen used alongside opioid analgesia. Oral intake and urine output improved. No transfusion, oxygen or antibiotic treatment required. Pain score reduced and mobilising independently before discharge. Mother involved in medication decisions and discharge planning; age-appropriate explanation and assent obtained.

Discharge medicines
Continue regular sickle cell medicines as previously prescribed.
Paracetamol as required for pain.
Ibuprofen as required with food.
No morphine required at discharge.

Plan / actions
GP review within one week; routine sickle cell team follow-up via Aberdeen Royal Infirmary. Encourage regular fluids and early use of the home pain plan. Return to A&E for fever, breathing difficulty, worsening pain, persistent vomiting, unusual drowsiness or inability to drink.

Condition at discharge: clinically stable, pain controlled, tolerating oral fluids.

Please review the diagnosis, clarify any red-flag or syndromic features, and advise on further management, including the appropriateness of genetic counselling or testing. The patient is agreeable to specialist assessment and understands that testing may not identify a causative variant.

A. Smith

Follow-up: GP review in 13 days, with reassessment of nocturnal cough and reflux control. Earlier assessment via urgent services if chest discomfort becomes exertional or is associated with breathlessness, collapse or diaphoresis.

Discharge summary – Paediatrics

Patient: Vasiliki Mitchell
The patient, aged 15 years, was admitted under the paediatric team with a two-day history of wheeze, increased work of breathing and troublesome night-time cough. Mother, Annelie, provided the initial history and remained involved in discussions. Family normally lives in BUSHMILLS.

Admission and assessment
On arrival there was widespread expiratory wheeze with subcostal recession and reduced air entry bilaterally. Oxygen saturations were maintained in air. Chest radiograph was not indicated; viral respiratory PCR was negative. Clinical picture consistent with an acute asthma exacerbation, without evidence of focal pneumonia.

Hospital course
Treated with repeated salbutamol via spacer, followed by a short course of oral prednisolone. Work of breathing and air entry improved over the first day. No oxygen requirement or intravenous therapy. Observed overnight with no further significant deterioration and able to eat and drink normally.

A consultant respiratory physician reviewed the admission and agreed with discharge once inhaler use and safety-netting had been completed. Salbutamol inhaler and spacer technique were demonstrated to the patient and mother, including recognition of poor response and when to seek urgent help.

Problem list
• Acute asthma exacerbation – improved
• Wheeze and increased work of breathing – resolved
• Night-time cough – improving

Discharge medicines
Salbutamol inhaler: 2 puffs via spacer as needed for wheeze or breathlessness. Continue prednisolone to complete the prescribed course. No regular preventer commenced during this admission; this should be reviewed in primary care if symptoms persist or reliever use remains frequent.

Condition at discharge
Alert, clinically stable, speaking comfortably, good oral intake, minimal residual wheeze and no recession.

Follow-up
Discharge today to parental care. GP review within one week, with asthma control assessment and consideration of an individualised asthma action plan. Paediatric follow-up with Ulster Hospital if recurrent exacerbations or diagnostic uncertainty. Return to A&E urgently for severe breathlessness, inability to speak in sentences, exhaustion or poor response to salbutamol.

Urgent diabetic foot referral

Patient: ebonnie emery
Report/accession ID: 041353559
Referring organisation: Queen Elizabeth University Hospital

Dear Diabetic Foot Service,

I am referring this patient for urgent specialist assessment of a plantar ulcer on the left forefoot in the context of diabetes mellitus and reduced protective sensation. The patient’s spouse reports increasing local discharge and difficulty weight-bearing. There has been no documented fever, rigors or systemic deterioration. The accompanying history also notes a cough for 3 days, without chest pain or breathlessness.

Assessment in the emergency department found a superficial-to-moderate plantar ulcer with surrounding erythema and a small amount of purulent discharge. The wound was tender at its margins, although sensation was markedly reduced over both feet. Foot temperature was not substantially different from the contralateral side; dorsalis pedis pulses were palpable. No crepitus or rapidly spreading cellulitis was identified. Plain radiography did not show gas or an obvious radiopaque foreign body.

Initial management comprised cleansing, sterile dressing and advice to avoid weight-bearing on the affected foot. Co-amoxiclav was commenced, and wound care instructions were provided. Please review antibiotic choice and duration, assess ulcer depth and vascular status, and arrange appropriate off-loading, debridement and microbiology if indicated. Osteomyelitis should be considered if the ulcer probes deeply or fails to improve.

The patient and spouse understand the need for prompt review and to return to A&E if there is spreading redness, escalating pain, fever or general deterioration.

Yours sincerely,

pawel rice
GMC-TEST-0242835
Emergency clinician, Queen Elizabeth University Hospital

Presented via the emergency department with profuse watery diarrhoea, vomiting and intermittent abdominal cramps for 3 days. Reduced oral intake and dizziness on standing were reported. Their adult child accompanied them and provided additional history.

Clinically dehydrated on arrival, with dry mucous membranes and mild postural symptoms. Abdomen soft, with generalised cramping discomfort but no guarding or peritonism. No further vomiting after admission; diarrhoea settled to occasional loose stool. No indication for antibiotic therapy. The presentation was felt most consistent with self-limiting infectious gastroenteritis.

• Ondansetron as required for nausea, according to the supplied prescription directions.
Usual regular medicines unchanged.

At discharge
Alert, haemodynamically stable and tolerating oral fluids and food. Passing urine adequately. Abdominal examination benign.

Follow-up and advice
GP review if symptoms have not fully resolved, or sooner for recurrent vomiting, inability to maintain fluids, worsening abdominal pain, blood in stool, fever or reduced urine output. Continue careful hand hygiene and avoid preparing food for others while symptomatic.

Sudden breathlessness with right-sided pleuritic chest pain and palpitations. Tachycardic on arrival; oxygen saturations below target on air.

CT pulmonary angiogram: bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli. No CT evidence of right heart strain.
ECG: sinus tachycardia.

Admitted for observation and anticoagulation. Supplemental oxygen required initially, subsequently weaned; maintaining target saturations on air at discharge. Haemodynamically stable throughout. No bleeding or syncope. Partner updated during assessment.

Alert, ambulant, comfortable at rest. Mild pleuritic discomfort only. No oxygen requirement.

GP review arranged for anticoagulation and provoking-factor assessment. Anticoagulation clinic review in about 5 weeks. Continue apixaban as prescribed; do not stop without medical advice.
Return to A&E for worsening breathlessness, collapse, haemoptysis, chest pain or significant bleeding. Written PE and anticoagulant advice provided.

Patient: KISANET CUMMINGS
MRN: 0903097
Clinic: HATHAWAY MEDICAL CENTRE
Occupation: Paralegal
Informant: patient and partner

Reason for review:
Assessment of possible familial susceptibility to obstructive sleep apnoea. Referred following persistent symptoms despite established treatment.

History:
Partner reports loud snoring and witnessed apnoeas overnight, with gasping and fragmented sleep. Patient describes marked daytime somnolence, particularly during sedentary activities. Continuous positive airway pressure in use, with variable tolerance due to mask discomfort; some improvement when worn throughout the night. No reported cataplexy or sleep paralysis. Separate dry cough for 3 days, without fever or breathlessness.

Family history:
Several relatives described as heavy snorers, although no confirmed genetic diagnoses or sleep-study reports available. No known neuromuscular disorder or syndromic features reported. Three-generation history discussed; further details to be obtained from relatives where possible.

Examination:
Alert in clinic. Speech clear. No dysmorphic features noted. Oropharyngeal examination limited; crowded posterior airway. No focal neurological deficit.

Assessment:
Obstructive sleep apnoea, clinically significant daytime somnolence. Familial clustering possible, but no specific monogenic syndrome evident from today’s assessment.

Plan:
Continue CPAP and liaise with sleep service regarding mask fit and adherence data. Avoid driving if sleepy. Obtain relevant family sleep-study information; review need for genetic testing after records received. Written information provided.

Seen and documented by Dr Surayah Croft, MBBS.

GP review if not clearly improving over the next few days. Return to A&E for persistent vomiting, inability to maintain fluids, blood in stool, worsening abdominal pain, reduced urine output or marked drowsiness. Hand hygiene and avoid food preparation for others while symptomatic.

Date: 18th May 2045
Patient: arzoe kerr
MRN: MRN-06935613
Referring organisation: Altnagelvin Area Hospital

Dear Clinical Genetics Team,

Re: assessment of atrial fibrillation and possible inherited arrhythmia predisposition

I would be grateful for your opinion regarding arzoe kerr, who has recurrent palpitations associated with fatigue and exertional breathlessness. The episodes are intermittent, with no documented syncope. A friend has provided useful collateral history, including concern that symptoms have become more noticeable during routine activity.

Atrial fibrillation has been confirmed on previous ECG recording. Rate control is currently managed with bisoprolol, and anticoagulation is prescribed as apixaban 5 mg twice daily. There have been no reported bleeding complications or recent emergency admissions. Symptoms have persisted despite adherence to treatment, and the patient remains concerned about the significance of the arrhythmia and any implications for relatives.

The available clinical information does not establish a specific inherited syndrome. However, given the recurrent symptomatic arrhythmia and the question of familial susceptibility, specialist review would be helpful. Please assess whether genetic testing or a broader inherited cardiac condition pathway is indicated, and advise on any appropriate screening or counselling for relatives.

Relevant ECG and clinic documentation can be provided through the referring service. I would also welcome recommendations regarding further rhythm assessment and coordination with cardiology if the findings suggest an inherited arrhythmia syndrome.

Yours faithfully,

Dr Chidinma Richardson, MBBS

Please avoid strenuous activity initially and follow the cardiac rehabilitation advice provided. Seek urgent help through 999 if chest pain returns and does not settle promptly with rest, or if you develop severe breathlessness or collapse. Arrange a GP review within one week. Cardiology Outpatient Report

Patient: J. Francis
Occupation: Physiotherapist
Employer: Whitley Bay Public Library
Address: 40 Thornbury Green, City of London, EC2Y 5AG
Patient contact: jacob-scott.francis90@outlook.com

Reason for review: Episodic awareness of heartbeat associated with persistent worry and poor sleep.

History and findings:
The patient describes several months of excessive, difficult-to-control worry, predominantly relating to health and work, with associated muscle tension and fragmented sleep. Episodes of fast heartbeat occur during periods of heightened anxiety and settle with rest. No syncope, exertional chest pain or sustained exercise intolerance. Reports a cough for 3 days, without fever or breathlessness.

Clinical examination today: comfortable at rest; pulse regular, 78 bpm; blood pressure 128/76 mmHg. Heart sounds normal, with no murmur. Chest clear to auscultation. No peripheral oedema. Resting 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm without acute ST-T wave abnormality.

Medication: Sertraline, taken as prescribed. No reported adverse effects. Alcohol and caffeine intake discussed briefly.

Impression:
The symptom pattern and normal cardiovascular examination/ECG are reassuring. Palpitations appear temporally related to generalised anxiety disorder rather than an evident structural or rhythm disorder. Poor sleep and muscle tension are likely maintaining factors. The short respiratory illness does not currently suggest cardiac decompensation.

Plan:
Continue sertraline through the GP surgery and review response and tolerability in primary care. Recommend psychological therapy, preferably structured CBT, with attention to sleep routine and reduction of excess caffeine. Arrange ambulatory ECG only if episodes become prolonged, occur with exertion, or are associated with dizziness or syncope. Return to the GP if the cough persists or worsens. Cardiology follow-up is not routinely required unless symptoms change.

Discharge summary

Patient: MUHAMMAD-ESA MELLOR
Patient contact: 07700 900760
Admission/discharge date: 4th March 2023
Clinical service: Clinical Genetics

75 y/o patient admitted following sudden breathlessness, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and tachycardia. History obtained with the patient; aishleen reid listed as emergency contact and updated during admission.

CT pulmonary angiogram demonstrated bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli with a small peripheral infarct; no central clot. No radiological evidence of right heart strain. ECG showed sinus tachycardia. Troponin was not raised and routine blood tests were satisfactory, including renal function suitable for anticoagulation. Lower-limb Doppler did not identify deep vein thrombosis.

Initially required supplemental oxygen for hypoxia, with rapid improvement over the first 24 hours. Haemodynamically stable throughout; no thrombolysis or invasive procedure required. A consultant respiratory physician reviewed the imaging and advised anticoagulation with apixaban. No provoking factor was identified from the initial history. Thrombophilia and genetic review to be considered as an outpatient if clinically indicated; this admission was not complicated by bleeding.

Discharge medicines:
• Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily, planned for at least 3 months pending review.
• Supplemental oxygen discontinued before discharge; maintaining target saturations on air.
• Continue regular medicines as previously prescribed.

Problem list:
1. Bilateral pulmonary embolism with small pulmonary infarct.
2. Transient hypoxia, resolved.
3. Ongoing assessment of provoking factors.

At discharge, comfortable at rest and mobilising independently. No chest pain or significant breathlessness. Given anticoagulant safety advice, including avoidance of NSAIDs unless agreed with a clinician and urgent assessment for significant bleeding, recurrent breathlessness, collapse or worsening chest pain.

GP to review anticoagulation within 1–2 weeks. Respiratory clinic follow-up arranged for approximately 3 months, with consideration of duration of treatment and further investigations.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: KYLO-JAY RAI
MRN / patient identifier: 01230826
Ward: General Medicine
Discharging organisation: Ulster Hospital
Informant: patient and partner, Adhavan, who lives in BUSHMILLS

Reason for admission
Reduced urine output, marked fatigue and poor oral intake over several days. Acute kidney injury identified on admission.

Key results
Admission creatinine 286 micromol/L, urea 18.4 mmol/L; baseline renal function not recently available. Urinalysis: concentrated urine, no blood or protein. Renal ultrasound: no hydronephrosis or obstructive lesion. Creatinine improved to 142 micromol/L following rehydration; urine output satisfactory before discharge.

Hospital course
Managed with intravenous sodium chloride and monitoring of fluid balance, renal function and electrolytes. Clinical picture consistent with pre-renal AKI secondary to reduced intake. No evidence of sepsis or urinary obstruction. Reviewed with consultant nephrologist; no indication for renal replacement therapy.

Medication changes
• Intravenous sodium chloride completed.
• Temporary medication hold: ramipril and bendroflumethiazide withheld during AKI. Do not restart until reviewed by GP with repeat renal blood tests.
• Paracetamol permitted if required; avoid NSAIDs.

Discharge condition / actions
Mobilising independently, eating and drinking better, passing urine. Discharged home with partner. GP review within 48–72 hours; U&Es and creatinine to be repeated. Encourage regular oral fluids unless otherwise advised. Return to A&E if urine output falls again, vomiting develops, or unable to maintain fluids.

Dear Sleep Medicine Team,

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient following presentation to the accident and emergency department with marked daytime somnolence and concern about sleep-disordered breathing. The patient’s adult child reports several years of loud snoring with recurrent witnessed apnoeas during sleep, followed by restless breathing and morning headache. Daytime concentration and alertness have deteriorated, including an episode of dozing while watching television.

There was no acute cardiorespiratory abnormality identified in the department. Examination showed a crowded oropharyngeal airway; chest was clear, with no clinical evidence of heart failure. The patient is not taking sedative medication or alcohol excessively. Continuous positive airway pressure has previously been tried, but use has been inconsistent because of mask discomfort and reported nasal obstruction. No formal sleep study result is currently available in the referral record.

The specific clinical question is whether obstructive sleep apnoea is present and, if confirmed, whether there is an indication for renewed positive-airway-pressure support, mask fitting and adherence review. Please also consider whether ENT assessment or treatment of nasal obstruction would improve tolerance. The patient has been advised not to drive when sleepy and to arrange primary-care review of cardiovascular risk factors. Follow-up with the GP is planned in about 6 weeks, or sooner if symptoms worsen.

Yours faithfully,

Chelsea-Lea Dyer
Emergency Medicine Clinician

Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). No clinical features suggesting posterior circulation stroke or acute cardiac cause.

Disposition:
Discharged home with sibling. Written positional manoeuvre advice and GP follow-up if persistent. Return to A&E for continuous vertigo, new neurological symptoms, severe headache, inability to walk or recurrent vomiting.

Cranial nerves, limb power, coordination and speech normal. Mobilised cautiously; mild initial unsteadiness, improving. Presentation consistent with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. No current features suggesting acute central neurological event or cardiac cause.

Actions: Discussed findings with Dr Ahmethan Croft, MBBS, clinician at Royal Berkshire Hospital. Epley repositioning manoeuvre performed with partial improvement. Continue prochlorperazine as required; avoid driving or heights until settled. Oral fluids and slow positional changes advised.

Disposition: Suitable for discharge with adult child. GP/vestibular physiotherapy review requested. Follow-up arranged for 1st January 2027. Return urgently for persistent vertigo, new weakness, facial asymmetry, diplopia, severe headache, collapse, chest pain or inability to walk.

Patient: O. Abraham

Clinical referral: recurrent wheeze and acute asthma exacerbation

Dear O. Abraham,

I am referring you to Community Paediatrics for review of your asthma control and support with an agreed action plan. You are an 17 y/o patient with intermittent wheeze, increased work of breathing and night-time cough. The latest episode began with a cough for 3 days and became more troublesome overnight. Your uncle, D. Parkes, reports that you were speaking in shorter phrases and using your reliever more often than usual.

In the surgery, you were alert but visibly short of breath, with widespread expiratory wheeze and prolonged expiration. Oxygen saturation improved after repeated salbutamol via spacer; there was no focal chest sign or evidence of fever. You have since settled, although symptoms remain worse at night. No hospital admission has been required during this episode.

Current treatment: salbutamol inhaler as needed. Spacer teaching was completed with you and your uncle, including slow breaths and checking the inhaler technique. Please bring the inhaler and spacer to the appointment. We have discussed avoiding smoke exposure and seeking urgent help if breathing becomes severe, you cannot speak normally, or the reliever is not lasting.

Your family is also linked with Drumeldrie Housing Association for practical support. Please assess whether preventer treatment is indicated, review inhaler technique and triggers, and consider spirometry when clinically appropriate. A written self-management plan and follow-up after this exacerbation would be helpful.

Yours sincerely,

T. Downes
Referring clinician

Accident and Emergency Clinical Report
National Insurance number: BG413882A

Patient: J. Mills
DOB: 14/12/1931
MRN: 016454331
Patient contact: 07700 900384
Date: 11 October 1988

Reason for attendance: Increasing right knee pain with stiffness and reduced mobility.

History: Reports gradual worsening of right knee pain, particularly on weight-bearing and when climbing stairs. Morning stiffness lasts approximately 20 minutes. No preceding fall or direct trauma. The patient describes intermittent swelling but no locking or true giving way. A friend accompanied the patient and assisted with the history. No fever or systemic upset. Cough for 3 days noted incidentally, without breathlessness or chest pain.

Examination: Mobilising slowly with an antalgic gait. Right knee with mild bony enlargement and small effusion. Medial joint-line tenderness and crepitus through flexion; range of movement restricted by pain, with no fixed deformity. No erythema or increased warmth. Calf soft and non-tender. Distal pulses, sensation and power preserved.

Investigations: Plain radiographs demonstrate medial compartment joint-space narrowing, marginal osteophyte formation and subchondral sclerosis, without acute fracture or dislocation. Findings are consistent with osteoarthritis.

Impression: Symptomatic osteoarthritis of the right knee causing functional limitation. No clinical or radiographic evidence of septic arthritis, acute bony injury or deep-vein thrombosis.

Plan: Continue paracetamol as previously advised and topical ibuprofen to the affected knee, provided the skin remains intact. Encourage pacing of activity, gentle range-of-motion exercise and use of a walking aid if required. GP review recommended for ongoing analgesia and consideration of physiotherapy or musculoskeletal referral. Return to A&E if the knee becomes acutely hot, red or markedly swollen, or if mobility deteriorates suddenly.

Sexual health clinic review and results follow-up arranged. Partner notification discussed. Return to A&E for worsening pain, fever, vomiting or collapse.

Presenting complaint
Sudden onset breathlessness with right-sided pleuritic chest pain while at rest. Palpitations and reduced exercise tolerance since this morning. No syncope or haemoptysis reported.

Alert, speaking in short sentences. Pulse 118 bpm, BP 120/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO₂ 89% on air, temperature 37.2°C. Oxygen commenced via nasal cannula; SpO₂ improved to 95%.

Chest: mild bibasal reduction in air entry, no focal crepitations. Heart sounds normal, tachycardic, regular. Left calf mildly swollen and tender; no skin break. No clinical signs of shock. Abdomen soft.

ECG: sinus tachycardia, no ST elevation.

CT pulmonary angiogram: bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli, greater burden on the right; no central embolus. Right ventricular size mildly increased.

Acute pulmonary embolism with hypoxaemia and tachycardia. Haemodynamically stable; no indication for thrombolysis. Discussed findings and treatment with patient and Irini.

Treatment and plan
Apixaban started as per local VTE protocol. Supplemental oxygen to maintain target saturations. Analgesia administered; avoid NSAIDs. Admitted under general medicine for observation, echocardiography and assessment for provoking factors. VTE and bleeding advice provided.

MOLECULAR GENETICS REPORT

Patient: A. Atkinson
MRN: 0884763
Requesting location: Accident and emergency department
Clinical indication: Significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer. Patient requests predictive testing owing to concern regarding inherited cancer risk. No current treatment.

Specimen: Peripheral blood in EDTA; germline DNA extracted for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk assessment. Specimen suitable for analysis.

Result:
BRCA1 c.68_69delAG — pathogenic variant detected.

Interpretation:
The identified BRCA1 variant is associated with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome. This result is consistent with a significantly increased inherited risk of breast and ovarian cancer. The finding is presumed germline in this blood specimen and should be interpreted in conjunction with the family history and formal genetic counselling.

Clinical comment:
Please arrange referral to the regional clinical genetics service for post-test counselling, discussion of implications for the patient and relatives, and management options including appropriate breast and ovarian surveillance. Predictive testing of adult relatives should be offered through genetics services; relatives should not be tested solely on the basis of this report without counselling. The emergency department should provide routine follow-up arrangements rather than undertake cancer-risk management.

Follow-up: Clinical genetics review booked for 21 Mar 2024. The emergency contact details are held in the requesting record.

Validated and reported by:
R. Francis, Consultant Clinical Geneticist
GMC: GMC 0261911

The patient, aged 26 years, was admitted under General Medicine with persistent vomiting in early pregnancy, poor oral intake, dehydration and associated weight loss. Current pregnancy documented as 9+4 weeks' gestation. Spouse involved in discussions and discharge planning.

Admission blood tests showed mild ketonuria and a raised urea consistent with reduced intake; electrolytes remained within acceptable limits following initial replacement. No abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding or infective symptoms. Urine dip was negative for nitrites and leucocytes.

She received intravenous sodium chloride, antiemetic treatment with cyclizine and gradual reintroduction of oral fluids and food. Clinical hydration improved, urine output was satisfactory and vomiting settled over the latter part of the admission. Repeat blood tests were reassuring. No indication for nasogastric feeding or further inpatient investigation at discharge.

Problems during admission:
• First-trimester hyperemesis with dehydration
• Weight loss secondary to reduced intake
• 9+4 weeks' gestation

Discharge condition: comfortable at rest, tolerating fluids and small meals, mobilising independently. Discharged home with spouse.

Discharge medicines:
• Cyclizine 50 mg orally up to three times daily as needed for nausea

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report

Patient: Honey-Louise Brennan
Report/accession ID: 0979324215
Reporting organisation: Westfield Road Medical Centre
Specimen: Peripheral blood in EDTA
Clinical indication: Diabetes mellitus with plantar ulceration, reduced sensation and local discharge. The ulcer has been present for 3 days. Current management includes wound care and co-amoxiclav.

Test performed:
Targeted next-generation sequencing panel for monogenic diabetes, including HNF1A, HNF4A, GCK, INS and selected syndromic diabetes genes. Copy-number analysis included where technically valid. Variant interpretation undertaken in accordance with current UK clinical genetics laboratory practice.

Result:
No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant identified in the genes analysed. A variant of uncertain significance was not detected. Analytical sensitivity is limited for deep intronic variants, low-level mosaicism, repeat expansions and structural variants below the assay reporting threshold.

Interpretation:
This result does not support a currently recognisable monogenic diabetes diagnosis, but does not exclude a genetic contribution to diabetes or complications. The reported foot ulcer and sensory loss require ongoing multidisciplinary diabetic foot care; this genetic result does not alter antimicrobial or wound-management decisions. Correlation with the diabetes phenotype, age at diagnosis, treatment history and family history remains appropriate.

Recommendation:
Continue clinical management through the diabetes and podiatry teams. Re-referral to Clinical Genetics may be considered if there is atypical diabetes, a strong multigenerational family history, syndromic features, or a significant change in the phenotype. Review appointment requested for 2020-07-05.

Validated and electronically signed by:
MARRISA KERSHAW
