Discharge summary
NHS number: 000 174 9430

Patient: Jihad Da Silva
Home address: 32 DELAMONT PARK, EGLISH
Patient contact: 07700 900704

Reason for admission
Admitted with several days of worsening breathlessness, orthopnoea, ankle swelling and reduced exercise tolerance. Findings were consistent with acute decompensated heart failure.

Key results and hospital course
Chest radiograph showed pulmonary vascular congestion. BNP 2,840 pg/mL. Echocardiography demonstrated impaired left ventricular systolic function. Renal function and potassium were monitored closely during intravenous diuresis, with good symptomatic and weight response. There was no evidence of acute infection or myocardial infarction.

Furosemide was given intravenously initially, then changed to oral treatment once breathing and oedema had improved. Bisoprolol was continued at the established dose. Furosemide has been increased on discharge; please follow the medicines list supplied with this letter and do not take additional doses unless advised by your GP or heart failure team.

Condition at discharge
Comfortable at rest, mobilising on the ward and no longer requiring oxygen. Mild residual ankle oedema only. Please weigh yourself regularly if able and seek urgent help through NHS 111 or A&E if breathlessness becomes severe, you develop chest pain, fainting or rapidly worsening swelling.

Follow-up plan
The heart failure specialist nurse will contact you for an early review, with repeat renal blood tests arranged through your GP surgery after the medication change. Cardiology follow-up will be arranged for ongoing optimisation of treatment.

Prepared and signed by:
M. PRIESTLEY, Consultant Cardiologist
GMC: 0053587

Vomiting and frequent watery diarrhoea with reduced urine output. Admitted for observation and rehydration.

Dry mucous membranes, mildly sunken eyes, tachycardia and delayed peripheral perfusion. Alert, appropriate and able to engage with assessment. No abdominal guarding or focal tenderness.

U&E reassuring apart from mild dehydration-related urea rise; electrolytes remained within acceptable range on repeat testing. Blood glucose normal. No indication for stool sampling during admission.

Variant reviewed: BRCA1 c.68_69delAG — not detected in the submitted specimen.
Analytical sensitivity: Validated for single-nucleotide variants, small insertions/deletions and exon-level copy-number changes within the tested genes. Large rearrangements outside assay design may not be excluded.

Interpretation
Negative predictive result for the familial variant where the familial pathogenic variant is known and documented. If no familial variant has previously been confirmed, this is an uninformative negative result and does not exclude hereditary susceptibility.

Action
Genetic counselling recommended to review the pedigree, limitations and residual risk. Consider testing an affected relative first if the family variant remains unconfirmed. Continue risk assessment through the usual clinical pathway.

Report authorised by: KYEL MATTHEWS
Report date: 19 Sep 2035

Discharge summary

Patient: Sheindel K.
MRN: H4340811
Home address: 102 Cambuskenneth Gardens, Dundee, DD4 0AD
Consultant: O. Kirby
Professional identifier: GMC 0154840

Reason for admission
Admitted via the emergency department with four days of productive cough, fever and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. A friend accompanied the patient and provided collateral history. Chest radiograph showed right lower-zone air-space consolidation, in keeping with community-acquired pneumonia (SNOMED CT 233604007).

Key results
Initial observations: temperature 38.4°C, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturations 93% on air. Blood tests showed raised inflammatory markers (CRP 168 mg/L) with normal renal function. Blood cultures remained negative; sputum culture did not identify a significant pathogen. Repeat chest radiograph demonstrated improving right basal changes.

Hospital course
Treated on the respiratory ward with intravenous antibiotics and oxygen via nasal cannula for the first 24 hours, then stepped down to oral therapy. Fever settled and pleuritic pain improved with simple analgesia. Mobilising independently and maintaining oxygen saturations above 95% on air prior to discharge. No evidence of pleural effusion or cardiac complication.

Discharge medicines
Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily to complete a 5-day course; first outpatient dose due this evening.
Paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily as needed for pain or fever, maximum 4 g in 24 hours.
No regular medicines stopped.

Condition at discharge
Clinically improved, haemodynamically stable, eating and drinking, and suitable for discharge home today.

Follow-up and advice
GP review recommended within one week, with consideration of repeat chest radiograph at 6 weeks if symptoms or radiographic changes persist. Seek urgent medical attention for worsening breathlessness, recurrent fever, confusion, chest pain not settling with paracetamol, or inability to maintain oral intake.

Signed by: O. Kirby

Adrika O'Neill

Specimen: EDTA blood
Clinical details: Tiredness, dizziness and reduced exercise tolerance. Iron-deficiency anaemia under treatment with ferrous fumarate. Partner provided supplementary history.

Haemoglobin: 96 g/L (115–160) — low

Microcytic, hypochromic anaemia with depleted iron stores, consistent with iron deficiency. Mild reactive thrombocytosis may accompany iron depletion. BACKGROUND
Known sickle cell disease; previous admissions for vaso-occlusive pain. Home analgesia taken before arrival with little effect. Assessed with patient and mother; adolescent assent obtained.

Alert, distressed with movement, dry mucous membranes. T 37.1°C, HR 112, BP 118/68, SpO₂ 98% on air. Chest clear, no focal neurology, abdomen soft. Pain 9/10. No fever or acute chest features.

ACTIONS
Cannula inserted. Bloods sent: FBC, reticulocytes, U&E, LFT and group-and-save; results consistent with baseline anaemia, no significant renal derangement. PLAN / HANDOVER
Continue analgesia pathway and reassess pain, sedation, respiratory rate and urine output. Paediatric haematology advice from kady baldwin: admit to short-stay for ongoing analgesia and hydration; no indication for antibiotics currently. Escalate for fever, hypoxia or chest symptoms. Haematology review booked for 2035-03-26, in 12 days.

Potassium: 5.6 mmol/L (3.5–5.3)
Urea: 18.4 mmol/L (2.5–7.8)

Marked creatinine and urea elevation with reduced eGFR, mild hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis. Urgent clinical review required. Assess fluid status, urine output and ECG; repeat U&E after initial treatment and monitor potassium. Intravenous sodium chloride has been commenced. Follow-up: renal function review 18 Jul 2020, in about 10 weeks, if clinically appropriate after recovery.

Laboratory Report – Biochemistry

Patient: EVA-LOUISE SHAIKH
Report/accession ID: 060248201
Collection/report date: 28 Jan 2026
Requesting clinician: unnamed GP
Specimen: Serum, venepuncture
Clinical details: Acute pain, swelling and erythema of the first metatarsophalangeal joint for 3 days. Suspected gout flare. Current treatment includes naproxen and colchicine.

Results

Urate: 0.49 mmol/L (0.18–0.48)
C-reactive protein: 86 mg/L (<5)
White cell count: 11.8 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0)
Neutrophils: 9.4 ×10⁹/L (2.0–7.5)
Creatinine: 104 µmol/L (60–110)
eGFR: 68 mL/min/1.73 m²
Alanine transaminase: 24 U/L (0–40)
Aspartate transaminase: 22 U/L (0–40)

Interpretation

Mildly increased serum urate with raised inflammatory markers and neutrophilia. The findings support an acute inflammatory process and are compatible with the clinical diagnosis of gout, although serum urate may be normal or only modestly raised during an acute attack. Results do not distinguish crystal arthritis from septic arthritis.

Clinical comment

Correlate with examination and temperature. If the joint is unusually hot, rapidly progressive, associated with systemic illness, or the diagnosis is uncertain, urgent assessment and consideration of joint aspiration for microscopy, crystal analysis and culture are advised. Renal function is acceptable for the reported result but should be reviewed when prescribing or continuing naproxen and colchicine.

Validated by: Dr Hinesh Bacon, MBBS, Consultant Chemical Pathologist

Patient: Tosca
Report/accession ID: L20B07588
Clinic: General Medicine, MORRISTON HOSPITAL
Occupation: Office manager

Reason for review:
Follow-up of obstructive sleep apnoea. Ongoing loud snoring and witnessed pauses in breathing reported by sibling. Excessive daytime sleepiness, particularly when sedentary. No recent collapse or driving incident.

History:
Symptoms present for several months; intermittent nasal blockage and dry mouth on waking. Sibling describes restless sleep and occasional choking sounds. No chest pain or exertional breathlessness. Recent cough for 3 days, improving, without fever.

Treatment:
Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) overnight. Uses most nights, generally 5–6 hours; mask occasionally leaks and is removed before waking. No regular medicines otherwise reported.

Examination:
Alert in clinic. Speech clear. Chest clear bilaterally, no peripheral oedema. Oropharyngeal crowding noted. Blood pressure acceptable for this setting.

Results:
Download reviewed: residual respiratory events remain above target with variable mask leak. Report discussed with Dr Tzipora Hadley, MBBS.

Assessment:
Obstructive sleep apnoea, partially controlled on CPAP. Daytime somnolence persists, likely related to suboptimal adherence/interface fit.

Plan:
CPAP mask review and humidification check with sleep service at MORRISTON HOSPITAL. Reinforced nightly use and avoidance of driving if sleepy. Sibling to continue observing breathing pattern and support adherence. Review after download; earlier GP assessment if cough worsens or breathlessness develops.

Signed: Dr Tzipora Hadley, MBBS

Patient: Lillie-Louise, 48-year-old East Asian female patient
Reason for admission: Central chest pressure with diaphoresis and nausea. ECG without ST elevation; serial troponin rise consistent with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI).

Condition: Haemodynamically stable, ambulant, tolerating diet. Discharge home with advice to seek urgent help via 999 for recurrent or persistent chest pain.

Follow-up: Cardiology clinic 3 July 2045, with GP medication review in about 5 weeks. Emergency contact: Jahan, BERAGH.

PAEDIATRIC EMERGENCY ASSESSMENT

Patient: H. Randall
15 y/o patient
Home address: 15 Thatcham Avenue, Swanscombe, DA9 9AA
Accompanied by aunt: NICOLE MOON

Presenting problem:
24 hours of repeated vomiting and watery diarrhoea. Taking only small sips; urine output reduced since yesterday evening. No blood reported in stool. Aunt reports tiredness but responsive and communicating normally.

Background:
No regular medicines recorded. No known drug allergies documented. Consent for assessment obtained; patient involved in history and examination, aunt present with agreement.

Observations:
Alert, mildly dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 2 seconds. Pulse 108, BP 108/68, temperature 37.4°C, SpO₂ 99% air. Abdomen soft, mild diffuse cramping, no guarding or focal tenderness. Chest clear. Peripheral perfusion satisfactory.

Investigations:
Urinalysis: concentrated urine, ketones ++, no nitrites.
Blood glucose normal. No indication for blood sampling at present.

Assessment:
Likely viral gastroenteritis with mild-to-moderate dehydration. No clinical evidence of acute abdomen or sepsis. Nausea may improve with hydration.

Treatment/action:
Oral rehydration solution given in frequent small sips under observation; tolerated 250 mL without further vomiting. Supportive care, continue oral rehydration solution after discharge. Avoid anti-diarrhoeal medication.

Disposition:
Discharged home with aunt after discussion of fluids, urine monitoring and gradual return to usual diet. Return to A&E if unable to retain fluids, becoming drowsy, worsening abdominal pain, blood in stool or no urine.

Seen and authorised by Dr Hasnayn Hassan, MBBS, paediatric emergency clinician.

Patient: elnatan ball
DOB: 23 October 1994
Parent: Forde Ashton
Referring service locality: Semblister

Dear Community Paediatrics Team,

I would be grateful for your assessment of elnatan ball, a young child with an episode of acute otitis media. Forde Ashton, the patient’s parent, reports ear pain, fever and marked irritability. Symptoms have affected sleep and eating, although fluids are being taken and there has been no reported breathing difficulty or rash.

The child has been managed conservatively with paracetamol and supportive care. No antibiotic has been started. I would welcome advice on whether the current presentation requires further examination or treatment, and whether there are factors predisposing to recurrent ear disease or hearing difficulty. The family would also benefit from guidance about when to seek urgent review.

On review today, the child was unsettled but consolable by the parent. Temperature was elevated; work of breathing and hydration appeared satisfactory. Otoscopy was limited by movement, with an erythematous, poorly visualised tympanic membrane on the symptomatic side. There was no post-auricular swelling or neck stiffness.

Please assess hearing and middle-ear function when the acute symptoms have settled, and advise whether community audiology or ENT referral is indicated. The parent understands the proposed referral and will seek urgent assessment via A&E if the child becomes drowsy, develops swelling behind the ear, cannot maintain fluids, or deteriorates otherwise.

We will arrange primary care reassessment in 11 days, sooner if needed.

Yours faithfully,

Jacko Cain

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report

Patient: Narah
MRN / patient identifier: MRN-04041117
Specimen: Peripheral blood EDTA; received for constitutional cancer-predisposition testing
Clinical indication: Painless lymphadenopathy, night sweats and unintentional weight loss. Hodgkin lymphoma confirmed on tissue biopsy. Spouse provided relevant family history at clinic review.
Requesting clinician: Not stated on laboratory request

Test performed:
Targeted next-generation sequencing panel of 84 genes associated with inherited haematological malignancy predisposition, with copy-number analysis.
DNA concentration: 52 ng/µL (laboratory acceptance threshold ≥10 ng/µL)
DNA purity, A260/280: 1.86 (acceptable range 1.8–2.0)
Mean read depth: 486× (minimum validated depth 100×)
Coverage at reportable regions: 99.4% (laboratory target ≥98%)

Result: No pathogenic or likely pathogenic germline variant identified.
Variants of uncertain significance: None detected.
Interpretation: This result does not identify an inherited susceptibility variant on the genes and regions examined. It does not exclude an untested genetic cause or a somatic alteration confined to the lymphoma.

Clinical comment:
Findings should be interpreted alongside histology, treatment history and the wider family history. No change to current supportive care pending tissue diagnosis is advised on the basis of this result alone. Genetic counselling review recommended if further relatives are affected or if the clinical phenotype changes.

Follow-up review: 2004-11-14
Patient contact: narah.ireland86@icloud.com

Validated and reported by: A. Jarvis, Clinical Genetics Laboratory

Discharge summary

Patient: KALP CHAMBERLAIN
Discharging service: Aberdeen Royal Infirmary
Report/accession ID: 07931075

Reason for admission
Presented via A&E with several days of worsening breathlessness, orthopnoea, bilateral ankle swelling and reduced exercise tolerance. Clinical picture consistent with acute decompensated heart failure on a background of chronic cardiac disease.

Key findings
CXR demonstrated pulmonary vascular congestion with small bilateral pleural effusions. ECG showed sinus rhythm with no acute ischaemic change. NT-proBNP elevated. Troponin mildly raised but stable on repeat testing. Renal function remained suitable for diuretic treatment. Oxygen saturations improved with low-flow oxygen, subsequently maintained on air.

Hospital course
Treated with intravenous loop diuretic and fluid balance monitoring. Good diuresis with symptomatic improvement and reduction in peripheral oedema. No evidence of pneumonia or acute coronary syndrome. Mobilising independently on the ward; able to lie flatter overnight before discharge. Weight and renal profile reviewed prior to leaving hospital.

Problem list
• Acute on chronic decompensated heart failure
• Peripheral oedema, improved
• Reduced exercise tolerance, improving

Discharge medicines
• furosemide 40 mg once daily
• Bisoprolol, continue previous dose
• Other regular medicines unchanged as per reconciled prescription

Please arrange GP review within one week, including assessment of breathlessness, oedema, blood pressure and renal function/electrolytes after the diuretic change. Cardiology/heart failure clinic follow-up requested through Aberdeen Royal Infirmary.

Patient advised to monitor for increasing breathlessness, rapidly worsening ankle swelling, chest pain or syncope and to seek urgent medical attention if these occur. Adult child informed; family contact is based in Dalmally.

Discharged home clinically euvolaemic and haemodynamically stable. Discharge plan and medicines discussed with the patient.

A&E Cardiology Assessment

Patient: Tanysha  
MRN: 07679586  
Patient contact: 07700 900168  
Accompanied by friend, JAROME RIMMER.

Presenting complaint: Brief spinning episodes on turning in bed and looking upwards since this morning. Associated nausea and unsteadiness. No syncope, chest pain, palpitations, headache, hearing loss or focal weakness.

Background: No known cardiac history reported. Medication: prochlorperazine as required.

Observations: Afebrile, haemodynamically stable. GCS 15. Capillary glucose normal.

Examination: Alert, speaking normally. CVS HS I+II, no murmur. Chest clear. Neurology: pupils equal, power and sensation intact, normal speech, no limb ataxia. Positive right Dix–Hallpike with brief torsional nystagmus reproducing symptoms. No spontaneous nystagmus.

ECG: Sinus rhythm, no acute ischaemic changes.  
Bloods: FBC, U&E and troponin unremarkable.

Impression: Peripheral positional vertigo, consistent with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. No clinical evidence of acute coronary syndrome or posterior circulation event.

Treatment: Epley manoeuvre performed with improvement. prochlorperazine 5 mg up to three times daily as needed advised for nausea.

Plan: Discharge home with friend. Written positional advice and GP follow-up if persistent. Return to emergency department for continuous vertigo, new neurological symptoms, severe headache, collapse or chest pain.

Seen at The Grange University Hospital.

Laboratory Report
National Insurance number: BG048378B

Patient: Hameeda Gill
MRN: 006 204 103
Requesting service: The Cottage - Horsham Hospital
Specimen/report date: 2022-01-30
Specimen: Venous blood; serum and EDTA plasma. Clinical details: rheumatoid arthritis with increased morning stiffness, swollen hand joints and fatigue. Current medicines include methotrexate, folic acid and naproxen.

Results:
Haemoglobin 122 g/L (115–160)
White cell count 8.7 ×10^9/L (4.0–11.0)
Platelets 412 ×10^9/L (150–400)
CRP 28 mg/L (<5)
ESR 46 mm/hour (1–20)
ALT 31 U/L (5–35)
Albumin 37 g/L (35–50)
Creatinine 74 µmol/L (45–90)
eGFR 82 mL/min/1.73 m² (>60)

Interpretation:
Raised CRP and ESR with mild thrombocytosis support active systemic inflammation, compatible with the reported rheumatoid arthritis flare. No significant anaemia, leucocytosis, renal impairment or transaminitis identified on this sample. Platelet elevation is likely reactive in this clinical context.

The liver profile and renal function are currently acceptable for ongoing methotrexate and naproxen monitoring; interpret alongside dose, adherence, alcohol intake and previous results. Repeat monitoring should follow the established DMARD protocol, with clinical review if symptoms persist or worsen. Rheumatology or GP reassessment is advised in about 9 weeks, or sooner if there is marked functional deterioration.

NHS number: 000 660 2242

Patient: Jibrael Latham
Home address: 11 GULF ROAD, Hilltown
Patient contact: 07700 900121

You were admitted with sudden breathlessness, sharp pain worse on breathing and a fast heart rate. A CT pulmonary angiogram confirmed a pulmonary embolism, with no evidence of right-heart strain. Blood tests showed a raised D-dimer; troponin was not significantly elevated. An ECG showed sinus tachycardia.

You initially needed supplemental oxygen, but this was stopped once your oxygen levels remained satisfactory on air. Your chest pain and breathing improved with treatment. There was no bleeding during admission, and you were able to walk safely before discharge. At 08:15 on the day of discharge, observations were stable.

Discharge medicines:
• Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily. This is an anticoagulant to prevent further clots.
• Paracetamol as needed for residual chest discomfort. Avoid ibuprofen and other anti-inflammatory painkillers unless specifically advised.

Please do not stop apixaban without speaking to a clinician. Seek urgent help via 999 for severe or worsening breathlessness, fainting, coughing up blood, or significant bleeding. Contact your GP or NHS 111 if you develop new leg swelling, increasing chest pain, or problems taking the tablets.

Your GP should review anticoagulation within 1–2 weeks and arrange ongoing follow-up. Please avoid contact sports and tell dentists or other clinicians that you are taking apixaban.

Prepared and signed by Dr Mishkaat Butterworth, MBBS, Cardiology Consultant
Professional identifier: 0837422

Discharge summary
Date: 15th March 1996
Patient: syrah osman
Clinical profile: 50 y/o

You were admitted with worsening breathlessness when lying flat, swollen ankles and a noticeable reduction in exercise tolerance, consistent with decompensated heart failure. Your partner, akvile broughton, was updated during the admission. Please ensure the ward team has your current patient contact: 07700 900664.

On assessment there was peripheral oedema and bibasal crackles. Chest radiography showed pulmonary vascular congestion. Blood tests demonstrated a raised NT-proBNP; renal function remained suitable for continued diuretic treatment. You were monitored on the Model X3 cardiac monitor, with no sustained arrhythmia recorded. Echocardiography confirmed impaired left ventricular systolic function. The clinical genetics team reviewed the family history and advised outpatient review; no acute genetic intervention was required during this admission.

Treatment included intravenous furosemide, followed by conversion to oral therapy once your breathing and fluid balance improved. Bisoprolol was continued. Please take the discharge medicines exactly as listed on the accompanying prescription and do not stop bisoprolol without advice. Monitor your weight regularly and seek help if it rises rapidly, swelling worsens or breathlessness returns, particularly at rest.

At discharge you were comfortable mobilising, able to lie flatter and had improved ankle swelling. Follow-up has been requested with the heart failure team and your GP, with clinical genetics follow-up arranged separately. Blood tests for renal function and electrolytes should be checked in primary care after the medication adjustment. Contact NHS 111 or attend A&E for severe breathlessness, chest pain, collapse or confusion.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: Moad
MRN: 03292017
Admitting service: General Medicine
Treating organisation: Royal Victoria Hospital
Informant/next of kin: sibling, D. Ball, based in COAGH

Reason for admission
Central chest pressure with diaphoresis and nausea. ECG without ST elevation; serial troponin rise consistent with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction.

• Peak high-sensitivity troponin elevated.
• Echocardiogram: mildly impaired left ventricular systolic function, no major valve abnormality.

• GTN spray as required for recurrent angina.

Follow-up/actions
GP medication and blood-test review within 1–2 weeks. Cardiac rehabilitation referral completed. Cardiology reassessment in about 10 weeks.

Patient instructions
Seek emergency help for persistent or worsening chest pain, breathlessness, collapse or marked sweating. Avoid driving until discussed with the GP and insurer. Condition stable at discharge.

text:
Molecular Genetics Laboratory Report
NHS number: 0001231414

Patient: Anaiah CHAN
MRN: H0601339
Specimen: Peripheral blood in EDTA
Test requested: Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk assessment; predictive testing following significant family history. Consent for analysis documented. The patient attended with their spouse and expressed cancer-risk concern.

Methodology: Next-generation sequencing of the BRCA1 and BRCA2 coding regions, with copy-number analysis where technically indicated. Variant interpretation undertaken in accordance with current laboratory and clinical genetics guidance.

Result:
BRCA1 c.68_69delAG — not detected.

No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant was identified in the tested BRCA1/BRCA2 regions. This result does not exclude a familial pathogenic variant outside the regions or genes analysed, nor does it remove risk attributable to the wider family history.

Interpretation:
A negative predictive result is only fully informative where the known familial pathogenic variant has been identified and specifically targeted. If the familial variant is unknown, the result should be regarded as uninformative and individual risk assessment remains necessary. Correlation with the family pedigree and any previous affected-relative results is recommended.

Clinical comment:
Please ensure the laboratory is provided with the familial report, if available, for confirmation that the appropriate variant has been examined. Referral or continued follow-up through the regional clinical genetics service is advised. No current treatment is indicated on the basis of this laboratory result alone.

Planned genetics review: 4th September 2024

Validated and authorised by:
Izabell Richmond, Consultant Clinical Geneticist
Professional identifier: GMC-TEST-0114289

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: Miles Giles
DOB: 09/08/1941
Home address: 151 BEECHLAND PLACE, CRAIGAVAD
Patient email: miles.giles81@proton.me
Admission/discharge date: 25 December 2012
Discharging area: Emergency Department / acute medical unit

Reason for admission
Reduced urine output, fatigue and poor oral intake over several days. Partner provided collateral history. Clinical assessment consistent with dehydration and acute kidney injury (AKI).

Key results
Initial blood tests: creatinine 198 micromol/L, urea 15.2 mmol/L; previous renal function not available at presentation. Urinalysis concentrated, no blood or nitrites. Renal ultrasound: no hydronephrosis or obstructive cause.

Hospital course
Received intravenous sodium chloride with careful fluid balance monitoring. Urine output improved and oral intake tolerated. Repeat creatinine 132 micromol/L before discharge. Haemodynamically stable; no evidence of infection. AKI felt most likely secondary to volume depletion.

Medication changes
• Temporarily withheld regular diuretic and ACE inhibitor during AKI; restart only after GP review and repeat renal profile.
• Avoid NSAIDs until renal function confirmed recovered.
• No new antimicrobial treatment.

Condition at discharge
Mobilising independently, passing urine, clinically euvolaemic. Safety-net advice given regarding recurrent oliguria, vomiting, worsening lethargy or breathlessness.

Follow-up / actions
GP renal profile and medication review in 7 days. Encourage regular oral fluids and gradual return to usual diet. Patient advised to seek urgent medical attention if urine output falls again or unable to maintain fluids. Discharge information discussed with patient and partner.

Reason for admission
Acute asthma exacerbation with wheeze, increased work of breathing and night-time cough for 3 days. Salbutamol required more frequently at home; no fever or vomiting.

• Initial respiratory distress with widespread expiratory wheeze and reduced air entry.

Discharge medicines
• Salbutamol inhaler: 2–4 puffs through spacer as required for wheeze or breathlessness.
• Prednisolone course completed as prescribed.
Spacer technique demonstrated to patient and father; both able to return-demonstrate. Continue usual preventer if prescribed by GP.

Follow-up and advice
GP review within 48 hours, with asthma control and inhaler technique assessment. Paediatric respiratory follow-up if recurrent exacerbations or poor control. Return to A&E urgently for increasing work of breathing, inability to speak or drink, blue lips, drowsiness, or inadequate response to salbutamol.

Condition at discharge: comfortable in air, tolerating fluids, mobilising normally. Safety-netting discussed with AMINOOR PIPER.

Discharge summary – Respiratory Medicine
National Insurance number: ZZ180017C

Patient: JAMIE CHOWDHURY
Date of admission/discharge: 16/05/2025

The patient, aged 62 years, was admitted with a three-day history of profuse diarrhoea, repeated vomiting and cramping central abdominal pain. Their spouse provided additional history and remained involved in discharge planning; spouse’s locality recorded as CRANAGH. At 08:15 on the morning of review, Bahoz reported that there had been no further vomiting overnight and only one loose stool since the previous evening.

Initial assessment was consistent with dehydration secondary to infectious gastroenteritis. Blood tests showed a mild pre-renal acute kidney injury and raised inflammatory markers. Stool culture and viral testing were sent; no result requiring alteration of treatment was available before discharge. There was no peritonism, and abdominal symptoms improved with supportive management. Chest examination remained clear and there was no respiratory compromise.

The patient received intravenous fluids initially, followed by oral rehydration solution once able to tolerate fluids. Ondansetron was given as required, with good effect. Renal function and electrolytes improved on repeat testing. No antibiotics were indicated.

At discharge, tolerating light diet and oral fluids, passing urine normally and mobilising independently. Discharge medicines: oral rehydration solution as directed; ondansetron as required for nausea, in line with the prescription supplied.

Assessment and plan: clinically improved infectious gastroenteritis with resolved dehydration. Continue frequent small volumes of fluid and gradual dietary progression. Maintain hand hygiene and avoid preparing food for others until symptom-free for 48 hours. GP review if symptoms fail to settle; attend A&E for inability to keep fluids down, worsening abdominal pain, blood in stool, confusion or reduced urine output.

Patient: M. Williams
Occupation: Office manager
Employer: Horse Close Secondary School
Address: 156 Doddridge Close, Lanreath, PL13 1AA
Patient contact: 07700 900574

Cardiology review

Thank you for attending cardiology with your sibling. You described abrupt episodes of pounding or racing heartbeat, chest tightness and an overwhelming fear of dying. The episodes settle spontaneously, with no exertional pattern, collapse or persistent chest pain. Your examination today was reassuring: regular pulse, normal heart sounds and clear chest. The ECG showed sinus rhythm without acute ischaemic changes.

Taken together, this presentation is most consistent with panic attacks rather than a heart rhythm or blood-flow problem. The physical sensations are genuine, but the alarm response can then intensify them. We discussed breathing retraining, focusing on a slow, gentle out-breath rather than taking repeated deep breaths. Please practise this when settled as well as during symptoms. Your sibling is aware of the plan and can support you with this.

No cardiac medication is indicated at present. Please seek urgent assessment via A&E or 999 if chest pain is prolonged, clearly brought on by exertion, associated with fainting, or does not improve as usual. Contact the GP surgery if the episodes become more frequent, your mood deteriorates, or you would like support with psychological treatment.

We will arrange a symptom review in about 6 weeks. At that point we can reconsider monitoring or further cardiac investigation if the history has changed.

Dear Respiratory Medicine Team,

Re: Mahvesh K.

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient’s persistent exertional breathlessness and intermittent dry cough, with the specific question of whether there is an underlying respiratory disorder requiring further investigation. Symptoms have gradually worsened over the past three months and are now limiting normal activity. There has been no acute infective illness, haemoptysis or pleuritic chest pain. The patient reports thirst, fatigue and frequent urination in the context of type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Examination in the surgery was stable, with clear breath sounds and no peripheral oedema. Oxygen saturations were satisfactory at rest, although the patient became noticeably short of breath after walking from the waiting area. Chest radiograph has been requested; spirometry would be helpful if appropriate. Recent blood testing showed HbA1c 8.6%, and improving glycaemic control is being addressed separately.

Current medication: metformin and atorvastatin. No inhaler has been prescribed to date. The patient works for COAGH Secondary School. Their friend, Kun, has accompanied them to appointments and can assist with history-taking if required.

Assessment: progressive exertional dyspnoea with cough, without a clear cause on initial primary-care assessment, in a patient with type 2 diabetes.

Plan: please review in the respiratory clinic and advise regarding spirometry, imaging and any further investigations or treatment. The patient has been advised to seek urgent assessment if breathlessness becomes sudden or severe.

Referring clinician: K. WISE
Locality: KILLYBEGS

Nursing progress note – Cardiology
NHS number: 000 363 4435

Patient: DAXSON FISHER
Clinical age: 41 y/o
Date: 26 Apr 1996
Relative present: R. Hudson, partner

Current assessment
Severe bilateral limb and lower back pain consistent with painful sickle cell crisis; pain 9/10 on review. Appears dry, reporting poor oral intake and dark urine. Alert, speaking in full sentences. No chest pain or breathlessness.

Observations
09:20 – BP 120/80 mmHg, pulse 104, respirations 20, temperature 37.2°C, SpO₂ 97% on air. Peripheral perfusion maintained. Urine output reduced overnight; encouraged to use urinal for monitoring.

Interventions / response
Morphine administered as prescribed following pain assessment. Intravenous fluids running via peripheral cannula; site clean and patent. Oral fluids offered little and often. At 10:15 pain reduced to 6/10, able to reposition with assistance. Mobilising only short distance to chair owing to limb and back pain; falls precautions maintained.

Problem / action
Dehydration – continue prescribed IV fluids, strict fluid balance and repeat observations.
Pain – reassess hourly, administer breakthrough analgesia as prescribed, monitor sedation and respiratory rate.
Reduced mobility – two-person assistance as required; pressure-area care completed.

Escalation
Dr Bonni Lister, MBBS (consultant physician) contacted regarding persistent pain and tachycardia; advised ongoing analgesia and hydration, with medical review if pain remains uncontrolled or observations deteriorate. Partner updated at bedside with patient’s agreement.

Next shift
Repeat pain score and observations, review fluid balance, encourage oral intake, and escalate fever, hypoxia, chest symptoms or increasing sedation.

Migraine without documented aura. Family history to be clarified; no current features suggesting a syndromic neurological disorder. Clinical genetics testing not indicated on information available today.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
NHS number: 0003790747

Patient: Khayden Carpenter
MRN: 067450/60
Responsible team: General Medicine, Royal Victoria Hospital
Collateral history: spouse, Maximo, lives in KIRCUBBIN

Reason for admission
Acute worsening breathlessness with orthopnoea, bilateral ankle oedema and reduced exercise tolerance. Admitted with clinical decompensated heart failure.

Key results
- Chest radiograph: pulmonary vascular congestion with small bilateral pleural effusions.
- BNP 2,840 pg/mL.
- ECG: sinus rhythm; no acute ischaemic change.
- Echocardiogram: moderately impaired left ventricular systolic function; no significant valve lesion.

Discharge medicines
- Furosemide, oral dose as on discharge prescription.
- Bisoprolol, continue regular dose.
- Other long-term medicines unchanged; see electronic prescription.

Clinically euvolaemic, comfortable at rest, maintaining oxygen saturations on air. Weight and fluid balance advice discussed with patient and spouse.

Follow-up / actions
- GP review within one week, including renal function and electrolytes.
- Heart failure specialist nurse referral from Royal Victoria Hospital.
- Monitor for increasing breathlessness, rapid swelling or inability to lie flat; seek urgent medical help via NHS 111 or A&E if severe.

Paediatric Emergency Department Assessment

Patient: cheyanna alam
Home address: 105 Gassock Drive, Ponteland, NE20 0AA
Patient contact: cheyanna.alam35@yahoo.co.uk
History from patient and mother, Zunayrah Hubbard.

Presenting complaint: Wheeze and increased work of breathing since this afternoon. Night-time cough for several nights. Salbutamol inhaler used at home with limited benefit. No fever or choking episode reported.

The patient, aged 6 years, was reviewed with mother present. Alert, speaking in short sentences. Intercostal recession with prolonged expiration. Widespread bilateral expiratory wheeze, reduced air entry at bases. No stridor. Capillary refill <2 seconds.

Observations: heart rate 92 beats/minute. SpO₂ 95% in air. RR raised for age. Afebrile.

Assessment: Acute asthma exacerbation, moderate severity. No clinical evidence of pneumonia or foreign body aspiration.

Treatment: Salbutamol via spacer, repeated doses in ED with improved air entry and reduced work of breathing. Spacer teaching completed with patient and mother; technique demonstrated correctly. Oral steroid administered as per paediatric emergency protocol.

Reassessment: Comfortable at rest, speaking normally, mild residual wheeze only. Maintaining saturations in air.

Disposition: Discharge home with mother. Continue salbutamol inhaler via spacer as advised. Written asthma advice supplied. GP review within 48 hours; return to A&E if worsening breathlessness, exhaustion, cyanosis or poor response to inhaler.

Referral to Upper GI Service

Patient: Tasnim
Referring organisation: Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh
Report/accession ID: 047380006

Dear Upper GI Team,

I would be grateful for your assessment of Tasnim, who has persistent symptoms consistent with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease despite treatment in primary care. The main problem is retrosternal burning with acid regurgitation, particularly after meals and when lying down. There is also a night-time cough, reported for 3 days during the recent A&E attendance, although the reflux symptoms have been recurring over a longer period.

At review, the patient was comfortable at rest. Chest examination was clear and there was no focal abdominal tenderness or guarding. No acute cardiopulmonary cause was identified in the emergency department. The patient has been advised about avoiding late meals, remaining upright after eating and reducing recognised dietary triggers.

Current medication:
Omeprazole, taken regularly.
Alginate suspension as needed.

The specific question is whether further investigation, such as upper GI endoscopy or ambulatory reflux monitoring, is indicated given the ongoing regurgitation and associated cough. Please also advise on optimisation of acid suppression and whether an alternative diagnosis should be considered if symptoms continue.

The patient understands that this is an outpatient referral and will seek urgent review for haematemesis, melaena, progressive difficulty swallowing or severe chest pain.

Kind regards,

APRYL MILES
Professional identifier: 0186151
Referring clinician
Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh

Patient: Rafsan Drake
MRN: 02680724
Clinic: Woodside Medical Centre
Occupation: Baker
Seen by: Dr Mikela Glover, MBBS, GP

Presenting problem:
Low back pain for several weeks with intermittent shooting pain into the right buttock and posterior thigh, occasionally to the calf. Tingling over the outer aspect of the right foot. Worse after prolonged sitting and on rising; walking remains possible. No reported bowel or bladder disturbance, saddle numbness or progressive leg weakness.

Medication:
Naproxen with food
Paracetamol as needed

Examination:
Mobilising independently, mildly antalgic. Lumbar flexion restricted by pain. Right straight-leg raise reproduces posterior leg pain. Mild reduction in right ankle reflex compared with left; power preserved in hip flexion, knee extension and ankle dorsiflexion. Peripheral pulses palpable.

Assessment:
Right-sided lumbar radiculopathy, likely nerve-root irritation. No current features of cauda equina syndrome or significant motor deficit.

Plan:
Continue simple analgesia; review naproxen tolerance and avoid additional NSAIDs. Remain active within limits, avoid prolonged bed rest. Physiotherapy referral for graded exercise and spinal rehabilitation. MRI lumbar spine requested if symptoms persist or neurological findings progress. Discussed urgent A&E assessment for new urinary retention/incontinence, saddle sensory change or marked weakness.

Result/action:
Case to be reviewed with consultant neurologist if persistent paraesthesia or worsening reflex asymmetry. Follow-up in primary care after physiotherapy assessment, sooner if deterioration.

Signed: Dr Mikela Glover, MBBS

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: padraic horner
MRN: 0776663
Home address: 139 Coll Gardens, Wishaw, ML2 0AA
Responsible consultant: Doyinsola Cope (GMC number: 0819885)
Specialty: Respiratory medicine

Admission reason
Admitted with three days of poor oral intake, fatigue and reduced urine output, alongside cough for 3 days. Initial blood tests showed acute kidney injury, felt most consistent with dehydration in the context of intercurrent respiratory illness.

Key results
• Creatinine 286 micromol/L on admission; improved to 124 micromol/L following rehydration.
• Chest radiograph: no focal consolidation.
• Urinalysis: concentrated urine, no significant blood or protein.
• Respiratory viral PCR negative.

Hospital course
Treated with intravenous sodium chloride and close fluid-balance monitoring. Urine output improved and oral intake gradually recovered. No oxygen requirement. Renal function stable on repeat testing. The patient’s friend assisted with communication and discharge planning, with consent.

Medication changes
• Temporarily withheld ramipril and ibuprofen during the episode of AKI.
• Restart only following GP review and repeat renal blood tests.
• No new regular respiratory medication commenced.

At discharge
Clinically improved, passing urine, mobilising independently and tolerating oral fluids. Safety-net advice given: seek urgent assessment if urine output falls again, vomiting prevents fluid intake, breathlessness develops or confusion occurs.

Follow-up/actions
GP review within one week, including U&Es and blood pressure. Maintain regular oral fluids unless otherwise advised. Avoid over-the-counter NSAIDs. Discharge information provided and understood.

Documented by: Doyinsola Cope

A&E handover – 18 November 2024

Situation: E. Green attended with abrupt palpitations, central chest tightness and intense fear of dying while at home. Friend Rydal Price present and gave collateral history. Symptoms largely settled by assessment.

Background: No reported previous cardiac diagnosis. No collapse, fever or stimulant use disclosed. Breathing retraining already advised for similar episodes. No regular prescribed medicines reported.

Assessment: Alert, coherent and reassured with support. Airway patent; speaking full sentences. Pulse regular on examination, heart sounds normal, chest clear bilaterally, no calf tenderness or swelling. ECG: sinus rhythm, no acute ischaemic change. Observations stable; capillary glucose normal. Clinical picture most consistent with panic attack; low concern for ACS, arrhythmia or pulmonary embolism at present.

Actions: ECG and observations completed. Supported slow breathing and grounding in department; chest tightness and palpitations resolved without medication. Discussed avoiding excess caffeine and returning if symptoms recur with exertional chest pain, syncope, persistent breathlessness or new neurological symptoms.

Plan: Discharge home with friend. GP review via BRONGLAIS GENERAL HOSPITAL for anxiety/panic management and consideration of talking therapy. Continue breathing retraining. Follow-up planned in about 11 weeks. Safety-net advice understood. Documented by Dr Shaandeep Boyd, MBBS.

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report

Patient: F. Daniel
Report/accession ID: 0125922922
Specimen: EDTA whole blood; peripheral venous sample
Test requested: Monogenic diabetes panel
Clinical details: Type 2 diabetes mellitus. Thirst, fatigue and frequent urination for 3 days. Metformin and atorvastatin treatment. Spouse provided additional history.

Result:
No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant identified in the genes included on this panel.
Variants of uncertain significance: none detected.
Copy-number analysis: no clinically significant deletion or duplication identified.

Interpretation:
The findings do not support a currently recognised monogenic diabetes syndrome. This result does not exclude multifactorial type 2 diabetes mellitus, low-level mosaicism, or a genetic cause not covered by the assay.

Analytical notes:
Sequence coverage satisfactory across reportable regions. Test limitations include variants in poorly covered regions, deep intronic changes and alterations outside the assay design.

Clinical comment:
Interpret alongside phenotype, glycaemic indices and family history. Continue routine diabetes management; review glycaemic control and medication adherence with the GP/diabetes team. Consider further genetics review if diabetes is atypical, strongly familial or difficult to control.

Follow-up: genetics review booked for 2027-01-22.

Validated and authorised by:
K. Lucas, Consultant Clinical Geneticist
GMC professional identifier: 0065835

Nicholai describes repeated unilateral headaches accompanied by nausea and marked photophobia. Episodes have been managed in the community with sumatriptan 50 mg at onset of migraine and naproxen. The specific question for your service is whether the clinical history suggests a familial migraine syndrome and whether genetic counselling or testing would be appropriate. If testing is considered, please discuss its likely benefits, limitations and implications before proceeding. I would also welcome advice on preventive treatment and whether neurology review or brain imaging is indicated.

Urgent assessment is needed for a sudden maximal headache, new weakness, confusion, seizure, fever with neck stiffness or a persistent change in the usual pattern.

Niwaz Boyd

Patient: senada hewitt
MRN: 069163/93
Patient contact: senada.hewitt23@icloud.com
Department: Accident and Emergency

Specialist clinical report

The patient, aged 34 years, was reviewed following an episode of brief positional vertigo associated with nausea and unsteadiness. Symptoms were provoked by turning in bed and looking upwards, with each episode lasting less than a minute. No persistent spontaneous vertigo, new hearing loss, tinnitus, diplopia, dysarthria, limb weakness or sensory disturbance was reported. No recent head injury.

Examination demonstrated normal cranial nerves, full power and intact sensation in all four limbs. Gait was mildly cautious but independent. No limb ataxia. Dix–Hallpike testing reproduced the characteristic vertigo with a short latency and fatigable upbeat-torsional nystagmus on the symptomatic side. There was no concerning truncal instability.

Findings are consistent with posterior-canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. The clinical pattern and examination do not currently suggest a central vestibular cause. Canalith repositioning treatment was performed, with improvement in symptoms afterwards. The patient was advised regarding gradual positional movements and given instruction on home repositioning exercises if symptoms recur.

Medication: prochlorperazine 5 mg up to three times daily as needed.

Return to the emergency department was advised for persistent continuous vertigo, new neurological symptoms, severe headache, inability to walk or repeated vomiting. Routine specialist review is not required if symptoms settle. Follow-up appointment: 14 Dec 2018.

Reason for admission
Admitted via the emergency department with acute diarrhoea, repeated vomiting and colicky abdominal cramps for 3 days. The history was provided by the patient, with additional information from their sibling. No recent antibiotic course or travel was reported.

On admission the patient was mildly dehydrated, with dry mucous membranes and postural dizziness. Abdomen soft, with diffuse mild tenderness and no guarding or peritonism. Clinical genetics reviewed the admission record because of the departmental referral pathway; there was no evidence of a genetic or metabolic cause for this self-limiting illness.

Discharge medicines
• Oral rehydration solution, taken regularly to replace ongoing losses.
• Ondansetron as required for nausea or vomiting, according to the supplied prescription.

Problem list
1. Infectious gastroenteritis, clinically improving.
2. Dehydration, resolved with rehydration.
3. Mild transient pre-renal kidney impairment, resolved.

At discharge the patient was alert, haemodynamically stable, tolerating fluids and passing urine normally. Continue fluids and introduce light food as tolerated. Remain away from work or shared food preparation until 48 hours after the last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting. Seek urgent medical advice for inability to keep fluids down, worsening abdominal pain, blood in stool, reduced urine output or increasing drowsiness. GP follow-up only if symptoms persist or recur.

I would be grateful for your assessment of persistent episodic breathlessness and chest tightness, with the specific question of whether there is an underlying respiratory disorder or whether these symptoms are more consistent with hyperventilation associated with a major depressive episode.

The patient reports several months of low mood, loss of interest and early-morning waking. Sertraline is established treatment, with partial improvement in mood but little change in the breathlessness. There is no reported infective prodrome. Examination in the surgery showed the patient alert and speaking in full sentences; respiratory rate was not elevated, chest expansion was symmetrical and auscultation was clear bilaterally. Oxygen saturation was satisfactory at rest. No peripheral oedema was noted.

Initial primary-care management has included review of inhaler use and advice regarding paced breathing. There is no clear clinical evidence of an acute exacerbation today. Given the ongoing symptoms and their impact on activity, specialist review would be helpful, including consideration of spirometry and further investigations as clinically indicated. Please also advise whether any respiratory treatment or monitoring is required.

The patient has been advised to attend the emergency department if breathlessness becomes severe, occurs at rest, or is accompanied by collapse or significant chest pain. Primary-care mental-health follow-up is planned in about 5 weeks, with review booked for 24 July 2028.

Yours sincerely,

Dr Summa DONOVAN, MBBS

Nursing progress note – Cardiology

Patient: Omarion S.
DOB: 17 April 1974
Home address: 148 DUNYGARTON ROAD, BALLYGAWLEY
Report/accession ID: L27W40438

Situation
Admitted with confirmed pulmonary embolism. Overnight episode of sudden breathlessness with right-sided pleuritic pain; tachycardic on review. Spouse present and assisting with reassurance.

Observations
Airway patent. Respiratory rate 24/min, SpO₂ 94% on 2 L oxygen via nasal cannula, pulse 112 bpm, BP 120/80 mmHg, temperature 37.1°C. Alert and orientated. Mild increased work of breathing, no haemoptysis reported. Chest pain 4/10, worse on inspiration.

Mobility/intake
Mobilised to chair with one staff member; became breathless after short transfer, recovered within several minutes at rest. Oral fluids taken well; light breakfast, no nausea. Urine passed.

Interventions / response
Oxygen continued as prescribed. Apixaban administered; no bleeding noted. Supported upright, paced activity and call bell left within reach. Breathlessness eased at rest, SpO₂ maintained above target range.

Risk/escalation
Falls risk due to exertional dyspnoea. Bleeding precautions maintained. Medical team informed of persistent tachycardia and pleuritic pain; cardiology review documented by doctor, GMC identifier GMC 0833753. No acute deterioration at time of entry.

Plan for next shift
Repeat observations and pain score; titrate oxygen only as prescribed. Assist all mobilisation, encourage rest periods. Monitor for worsening hypoxia, syncope, haemoptysis or bleeding and escalate promptly. Continue anticoagulation and fluid balance documentation.

Specimen: Deep wound swab, plantar ulcer; superficial swab received. Clinical details: diabetic foot ulcer with reduced sensation and local discharge.

Moderate polymorphs. Gram-positive cocci and mixed Gram-negative bacilli seen.

Culture:
Heavy growth of Staphylococcus aureus.

S. aureus sensitive to flucloxacillin and co-amoxiclav; resistant to penicillin. No MRSA detected.

Significant S. aureus growth in the context of ulceration and discharge. Correlate with depth of infection, cellulitis and systemic features. Swab results may not represent deeper tissue infection.

Continue wound care and assess clinically for spreading infection, osteomyelitis or need for urgent diabetic foot review. Antibiotic choice and duration to be reviewed by the treating team; obtain deep tissue/bone specimen if debridement undertaken. Presented with a two-day history of marked itching and burning skin irritation over the upper chest and left shoulder. Rash began after use of a new adhesive dressing; no previous reaction of this type. No facial or tongue swelling, wheeze, vomiting or dizziness. Has used hydrocortisone cream with limited relief and took cetirizine before arrival.

Alert and comfortable at rest. Airway patent, speaking in full sentences. No stridor or wheeze. Chest clear, heart sounds normal. Blood pressure 120/80 mmHg; pulse regular, oxygen saturations satisfactory on air. Patchy erythematous, mildly raised rash with a clear dressing-shaped distribution over the upper chest and shoulder. No blistering, discharge, mucosal involvement or features of cellulitis. No palpable purpura.

Assessment: allergic contact dermatitis, most likely triggered by the adhesive. No evidence of anaphylaxis or secondary bacterial infection.

The adhesive was removed and the area gently cleansed. Advised to continue hydrocortisone cream as previously directed for a short course and cetirizine once daily if required for itch; avoid further contact with the suspected product. Dear Clinical Genetics Team,
NHS number: 0000582310

Re: Love

I am referring this patient from Belfast City Hospital following a recent diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma. The specific question is whether the presentation and family history warrant germline cancer-predisposition testing, and whether relatives should receive any targeted assessment or advice.

The illness began with painless lymphadenopathy, followed by drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss. Examination has demonstrated persistent cervical and axillary nodes without acute airway compromise. Cross-sectional imaging showed lymphadenopathy in more than one nodal region. An excised node has been reviewed by haematopathology and confirms Hodgkin lymphoma. Report/accession ID: 04662357.

Treatment is currently supportive care pending tissue diagnosis; now that the diagnosis has been established, haematology is arranging definitive staging and treatment. No genetic testing has yet been undertaken. The patient has been advised that most Hodgkin lymphoma is not inherited, but that the clinical genetics assessment may still be useful if the wider family history is suggestive or if treatment-related counselling is required.

A close friend has been assisting with appointments and was present for the discussion, with the patient’s agreement. Please review the available pathology and family history, advise whether germline testing is indicated, and provide appropriate counselling regarding implications for relatives. The patient has been given an appointment for follow-up review on 2045-04-07, subject to your service’s advice.

Yours sincerely,

Rakhee Moon

Discharge summary – Paediatrics

Patient: Harmoni Dudley
The patient, aged 7 weeks, was admitted with progressive jaundice, sleepiness during feeds and reduced oral intake. History obtained from parent, Upe Morley. Birth history recorded as born at 39+2 weeks' gestation. No concerns regarding temperature instability or respiratory effort during admission.

On assessment, jaundice was noted to the trunk and limbs. Infant was rousable but initially tired at the breast, with suboptimal intake. Urine output remained satisfactory. Serum bilirubin was above the treatment threshold for the infant’s clinical age and gestation; blood group and haemolysis screen were reassuring. Glucose remained within the expected range. Management and progress:
• Commenced on intensive phototherapy with eye protection.
• Feeding support provided by the neonatal and paediatric nursing team, including assistance with positioning and regular expressed breast milk/top-up feeds as clinically indicated.
• Intake improved during treatment, with the infant more alert for feeds.

Problem list:
1. Unconjugated neonatal jaundice – improved following phototherapy.
2. Sleepy feeding with reduced intake – improved with feeding support.

Discharge medicines: None prescribed. Continue breast or expressed milk feeds regularly; seek advice promptly if the infant becomes difficult to rouse, feeds poorly, has fewer wet nappies, develops fever, or jaundice becomes more pronounced.

Follow-up: GP/health visitor review as arranged locally, with further bilirubin assessment if clinically indicated. Parent received verbal and written discharge advice and demonstrated understanding.

Laboratory Report – Haematology / Histopathology
NHS number: 000 634 8034

Patient: klu vaughan
MRN: 055634612
Requesting service: Respiratory Medicine, University Hospital of Wales
Specimen collected: 17/09/2020
Specimen: Left cervical lymph-node core biopsy and EDTA blood sample

Clinical details:
Painless lymphadenopathy with drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss. Hodgkin lymphoma suspected clinically. Supportive care pending tissue diagnosis.

Results

Full blood count:
Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115–160) – mildly reduced.
White cell count 13.2 ×10^9/L (4.0–11.0) – raised.
Neutrophils 10.1 ×10^9/L (2.0–7.5) – raised.
Platelets 462 ×10^9/L (150–400) – raised.
Absolute eosinophils 0.9 ×10^9/L (0.0–0.5) – raised.
ESR 78 mm/h (1–20) – raised.
Lactate dehydrogenase 318 U/L (120–250) – raised.

Histology and immunohistochemistry:
Lymph-node tissue shows effacement of the nodal architecture by a mixed inflammatory infiltrate containing scattered large atypical cells with prominent nucleoli. The atypical cells are positive for CD30 and weakly positive for PAX5; CD15 is positive. CD20 is negative in the large atypical population. Findings are diagnostic of classical Hodgkin lymphoma.

Interpretive comment:
The biopsy confirms Hodgkin lymphoma. The inflammatory marker pattern and mild anaemia are compatible with the reported systemic symptoms but are not staging tests. Recommend multidisciplinary haematology review for formal staging, PET-CT and treatment planning. Correlate with bone marrow and viral serology results if clinically indicated.

Validated and reported by:
I. Rawlings
Laboratory clinician
Report date: 17/09/2020

A primary care review is planned in about 5 weeks, or sooner if symptoms worsen. The patient and spouse were advised to seek urgent help for vomiting, marked drowsiness, inability to maintain oral intake or rapidly worsening symptoms.

Yours sincerely,

Scarlotte LACEY

Specialist assessment – sleep-related breathing disorder

Patient: oluwafikunmi sinclair
MRN: 0963587
Occupation: Police officer
Seen in the accident and emergency department following concern regarding excessive daytime sleepiness and disrupted sleep.

History
The patient reports longstanding loud snoring, with an adult child describing repeated witnessed apnoeas during sleep. Morning headache and unrefreshing sleep are also reported. Daytime somnolence is most troublesome when sedentary and has affected concentration. No recent chest pain, syncope or acute respiratory infection. Current treatment is continuous positive airway pressure, used on most nights, although tolerance has recently been inconsistent because of mask discomfort.

Examination
Alert and orientated at review. Speech clear. No increased work of breathing; chest clinically clear. Oropharyngeal examination suggests a crowded upper airway. Cardiovascular examination unremarkable. No focal neurological deficit identified.

Interpretation
The history is strongly supportive of obstructive sleep apnoea with residual daytime symptoms, potentially related to suboptimal continuous positive airway pressure adherence or mask/interface problems. There is no clinical evidence today of an acute cardiopulmonary complication requiring admission.

Plan
Continue continuous positive airway pressure pending specialist review; arrange assessment of mask fit, humidification and device-recorded adherence. Avoid driving or operating machinery if sleepy. The patient and adult child were advised to seek urgent assessment for escalating breathlessness, chest pain or collapse. Sleep service review planned in about 7 weeks.

Report prepared and signed by Dr Savleen Andrews, MBBS, Hawthorne Medical Centre.

Discharge summary – acute admission

Patient: D. Turnbull
Admission/discharge date: 12 Nov 1996
Responsible service: ABERDEEN ROYAL INFIRMARY

Reason for admission
Admitted with persistent vomiting in the first trimester, poor oral intake, clinical dehydration and reported weight loss. Current pregnancy documented as 9+4 weeks' gestation. Spouse, Milayah, provided collateral history and remained involved in discharge planning.

Assessment and key results
Initially tachycardic with dry mucous membranes and reduced urine output. Urinalysis showed ketones. Blood tests demonstrated mild hypokalaemia and haemoconcentration; renal function remained satisfactory. No abdominal tenderness or vaginal bleeding. ECG without acute abnormality. Ultrasound confirmed an intrauterine pregnancy with cardiac activity; no acute obstetric complication identified.

Hospital course
Managed with intravenous sodium chloride, antiemetic treatment with cyclizine and gradual reintroduction of oral fluids. Electrolytes corrected with hydration and dietary intake. Vomiting settled over the subsequent day, urine output improved and she tolerated small meals before discharge. Weight loss discussed; dietetic advice given regarding frequent small portions and oral rehydration.

Problem list
• First-trimester hyperemesis with dehydration
• Mild hypokalaemia, corrected
• Weight loss secondary to reduced intake

Discharge medicines
Cyclizine 50 mg up to three times daily when required for nausea. Continue prescribed antenatal vitamins if tolerated. No other medication changes.

Condition at discharge
Clinically euvolaemic, mobilising independently and tolerating oral fluids. Discharged home with spouse to locality of Weem.

Follow-up and advice
Community midwife and GP follow-up arranged through ABERDEEN ROYAL INFIRMARY. Continue frequent sips of fluid and small meals. Return to A&E if unable to retain fluids or medication, passing very little urine, experiencing dizziness or fainting, abdominal pain, fever, vaginal bleeding, or worsening vomiting. Review blood tests and weight with the GP if symptoms recur.

Admission reason
Admitted to the paediatric assessment unit with 2 days of vomiting and frequent diarrhoea, associated with poor oral intake and reduced urine output. Initial assessment was consistent with mild to moderate dehydration. Weight recorded as 54.0 kg.

Hospital course
Managed with oral rehydration solution in small, frequent amounts and supportive care. Antiemetic treatment was given in the unit, with good effect. Urine output improved and oral intake was maintained without further vomiting before discharge. No indication for antibiotics. Abdominal examination remained soft, with no focal tenderness or peritoneal signs.

Investigations
Blood glucose and electrolytes were satisfactory. No significant inflammatory response. Stool sampling was not required as symptoms were improving and there was no blood in the stool or persistent fever.

Clinically well, alert and tolerating fluids. Passing urine normally. Diarrhoea may continue for several days but should gradually settle.

Continue oral rehydration solution after each loose stool and encourage regular sips of water. Offer light foods as tolerated; avoid fizzy drinks and very fatty foods initially. No regular medicines are required. Do not give anti-diarrhoeal medication unless advised by a clinician.

Please seek urgent medical help via NHS 111 or A&E if unable to keep fluids down, becomes unusually drowsy, has severe or worsening abdominal pain, blood in the stool, or markedly reduced urine output. Follow-up with the GP surgery if not clearly improving within 48 hours.

Dear Respiratory Medicine Consultant,

Current management is supportive care pending tissue diagnosis, including advice on hydration, symptom monitoring and prompt review if breathlessness, stridor or rapidly progressive swelling develops. Please arrange specialist assessment, cross-sectional imaging and biopsy as clinically indicated, and advise on onward haematology referral.

A follow-up review is planned for 12 January 2024, subject to the outcome of your assessment. Relevant results and the imaging report will be forwarded through the usual NHS referral pathway.

Yours sincerely,

O. Radford

MOLECULAR GENETICS LABORATORY REPORT
National Insurance number: TN167697C

Patient: ELLIE-BROOKE CAIRNS
MRN: H0705883
Requesting service: Harperbury Hospital
Specimen: Peripheral blood, EDTA
Clinical source: Accident and emergency referral
Clinical indication: Significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer; request for predictive testing and discussion of inherited cancer risk. No current treatment.

Test performed:
Targeted analysis of the familial BRCA1 variant: BRCA1 c.68_69delAG

Result:
Variant detected. Finding is consistent with a pathogenic BRCA1 alteration and should be interpreted in the context of the documented family history and appropriate genetic counselling.

Interpretation:
This result indicates an increased inherited susceptibility to breast and ovarian cancer. It is not diagnostic of current malignancy. Predictive testing and implications for relatives require specialist genetics review; reproductive and surveillance discussions should be individualised.

Action:
Result released to the referring clinical team. Arrange appointment with the regional clinical genetics service and offer counselling before communicating implications to relatives. Confirm family-specific variant documentation if available. No laboratory treatment recommendation.

Follow-up:
Genetics review booked for 25 Nov 2022. Patient advised to discuss the result with the GP and to seek urgent assessment for any acute symptoms; this report does not replace clinical examination.

Validated and reported by:
S. HOLLOWAY
Laboratory genetics clinician

Comment: Testing is limited to the stated familial variant; a negative result would not exclude other hereditary or non-hereditary cancer risks.

Plan and request

Please review promptly in community paediatrics and advise the family regarding feeding support and monitoring. The guardian has been advised to seek urgent assessment via the emergency department if the infant becomes difficult to rouse, stops feeding, develops fewer wet nappies or appears acutely unwell.

Patient: Radin Lees
DOB: 12/04/1960 | MRN: 018882884
Home address: 155 Gegin Road, Caergeiliog, LL65 1AA
Patient contact: 07700 900246

Presented with 2 days of markedly reduced urine output, fatigue and poor oral intake following several days of vomiting. Spouse accompanying and providing collateral history. No chest pain or breathlessness reported.

ASSESSMENT
Alert, tired but coherent. Dry mucous membranes; peripheral perfusion maintained. BP 104/68, pulse 96, afebrile, saturations 98% on air. Chest clear, no peripheral oedema. Abdomen soft, mild suprapubic discomfort, no guarding. Bladder scan 220 mL.

Bloods: creatinine 186 µmol/L, urea elevated, mild hypokalaemia; FBC without significant abnormality. Urinalysis concentrated, no blood or nitrites. ECG sinus rhythm. Working diagnosis: acute kidney injury, most likely pre-renal from poor intake and gastrointestinal losses; obstruction less likely but monitor urine output.

ACTIONS / PRIORITIES
IV sodium chloride commenced; encourage oral fluids as tolerated. Temporary medication hold pending renal recovery and senior review. Strict fluid balance, repeat observations and U&E after fluids. Send urine for culture if symptoms develop. Renal ultrasound if oliguria persists or renal function worsens.

DISPOSITION
Remain in A&E observation for response to treatment; discuss with medical team for admission if urine output remains low or repeat creatinine deteriorates. Safety-net: escalate promptly for hypotension, confusion, worsening pain or no urine.

Admission reason: Fever, productive cough and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Initial oxygen saturation 91% on air; chest radiograph consistent with right lower-zone community-acquired pneumonia.

Diagnosis
• Community-acquired pneumonia (SNOMED CT 233604007)
• Pleuritic chest pain secondary to infection
• Mild hypoxia, resolved

Key results
Chest radiograph: right basal air-space opacity, no pleural effusion.
Blood tests: inflammatory markers raised; renal function satisfactory. Blood cultures negative. ECG without acute ischaemic change; troponin not suggestive of myocardial injury.

Hospital course
Treated with intravenous antibiotics initially, then stepped down to oral amoxicillin once clinically improved. Paracetamol given for fever and pain. Oxygen via nasal cannula for the first night only; subsequently maintaining saturations on air. Afebrile and mobilising independently at discharge. Eating and drinking adequately.

Discharge medicines
Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily to complete the prescribed course.
Paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily as needed for pain or fever.
No other medication changes.

Follow-up / actions
GP review requested if cough or breathlessness persists; repeat chest radiograph to be considered after recovery. Cardiology follow-up appointment: 12th July 2028.

The patient’s adult child, A. Doyle, was updated regarding discharge arrangements and lives in Breich. Written advice provided: seek urgent help for worsening breathlessness, recurrent high fever, confusion or inability to maintain fluids. Condition stable at discharge.

Significant reported family history with concern regarding hereditary breast and ovarian cancer; predictive testing requested. Further pedigree clarification and verification of the reported BRCA1 result are required.

Please assess and counsel S. Karim regarding eligibility for genetic testing, residual cancer risk, surveillance and risk-reducing options. They understand that testing and any subsequent management would follow specialist counselling.

Janvi Sharpe
Paediatric clinician

Symptoms are aggravated by prolonged sitting and bending. No preceding significant trauma. The patient’s spouse attended and provided collateral history regarding reduced mobility at home. Impression: Clinical picture is most consistent with right L5 lumbar radiculopathy. No current indication of an infective, malignant or acute compressive process.

Plan: Continue analgesia within prescribed limits and avoid prolonged bed rest. Arrange physiotherapy focused on graded activity and neural mobility. MRI lumbar spine requested given persistent radicular pain and objective, albeit mild, motor change. Urgent assessment advised for new bladder or bowel dysfunction, saddle numbness or worsening weakness. Review after imaging.

Discharge summary

Patient: DEMARI DREW
Admission/discharge date: 19/04/2045

You were admitted under the respiratory medicine team after several days of poor oral intake, tiredness and reduced urine output, with a cough for 3 days. The patient, aged 41 years, was reviewed with their spouse, O. COLLIER, from GLENARM, present for the discharge discussion.

• Intravenous sodium chloride was given until oral intake and urine output improved.

At discharge you were clinically stable, passing urine and managing food and drinks. Please arrange a GP review and repeat renal blood tests within one week; the results should be reviewed by the surgery. Seek urgent help through NHS 111 or A&E if urine output falls again, you cannot keep fluids down, become confused, develop worsening breathlessness or feel faint.

Discharge destination: home with spouse support.

Discharge summary – Accident and Emergency

Patient: jacquelyn howell
Report/accession ID: 02896675
Discharging service: ROYAL INFIRMARY OF EDINBURGH

Reason for attendance
Presented with several days of poor oral intake, fatigue and reduced urine output. Initial assessment consistent with dehydration-associated acute kidney injury. No chest pain, breathlessness or infective focus identified.

Key findings
At 08:15, clinically dry but haemodynamically stable. Blood tests showed raised creatinine compared with the available baseline, with mild urea elevation; potassium remained within an acceptable range. Urinalysis without significant blood or protein. Bladder scan showed no meaningful retention. Renal tract ultrasound was not indicated following improvement and absence of obstructive symptoms.

Hospital course
Managed with intravenous sodium chloride and monitoring of fluid balance. Oral intake improved during observation and urine output increased. Repeat renal profile demonstrated a clear improvement in creatinine, though not yet fully back to baseline. No indication for admission following senior review. The patient’s friend was updated and can assist with transport and observation at home; friend’s locality recorded as Lybster.

Medication changes
Usual medicines reviewed. Potentially nephrotoxic and/or blood-pressure-lowering medicines were temporarily withheld during the acute illness, with restart to be considered by the GP once hydration and renal function have recovered. Avoid over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medicines unless specifically advised.

Discharge condition
Alert, mobilising independently, tolerating fluids and light diet. Passing urine. No ongoing vomiting or clinical features of fluid overload.

Follow-up and advice
Repeat U&Es and creatinine through the GP surgery within 48–72 hours, with medication review at that point. Maintain regular oral fluids and seek urgent medical attention for inability to keep fluids down, worsening lethargy, confusion, breathlessness, swelling or markedly reduced urine output.

Prepared and electronically signed by I. Bond, on behalf of ROYAL INFIRMARY OF EDINBURGH.

Clinical Genetics Specialist Report
NHS number: 000 491 9247

Patient: Lillee-Mae D., 41-year-old Caucasian male patient  
Patient contact: 07700 900685  
Report/accession ID: 0475841754

Reason for review: Recurrent unilateral headaches associated with nausea and photophobia. Episodes have occurred intermittently over several months, with no reported persistent neurological deficit. Recent cough for 3 days was noted in the accompanying history but is not considered contributory to the headache syndrome.

Clinical findings: Headache is predominantly unilateral and throbbing, with light sensitivity and nausea during attacks. No visual loss, weakness, sensory disturbance or speech disturbance is described between episodes. Examination today is reassuring, with normal gait, cranial nerve assessment and limb neurological examination. No dysmorphic features or other syndromic findings were identified on the limited examination.

Current treatment: Sumatriptan used at the onset of severe attacks, with naproxen when required. The reported response is partial, and medication frequency should be monitored to avoid analgesic-overuse headache.

Interpretation: The phenotype is most consistent with migraine without evidence currently of a recognisable monogenic or syndromic disorder. A clinical genetics referral is not indicated solely on the basis of uncomplicated migraine. Reconsider assessment if there is a strong multigenerational history, atypical aura, progressive neurological change, seizures or developmental concerns.

Plan: Continue headache diary, including triggers, duration and response to treatment. GP review recommended if attack frequency increases or acute treatment becomes ineffective. Emergency assessment for sudden maximal headache or new focal neurological symptoms. Follow-up review arranged for 2021-01-19. The listed emergency contact should be confirmed at the next appointment.
