Discharge summary – Paediatrics
NHS number: 000 795 7603

Patient: ISLA-RAE UNDERWOOD, 13-year-old Caucasian female patient
MRN: 0570960
Informant: Father, Isobell
Responsible clinician: F. HARVEY

Reason for admission
Vomiting and frequent watery diarrhoea with reduced urine output. Admitted for assessment of dehydration and oral rehydration support.

Initial assessment
Dry mucous membranes, tired but rousable, mildly tachycardic; abdomen soft with no focal tenderness. No blood reported in stool. Observations reviewed at 08:15. No features to suggest an acute surgical abdomen.

Investigations
Capillary glucose satisfactory. U&E and inflammatory markers reassuring; no significant electrolyte disturbance. Stool sample not indicated clinically.

Hospital course
Managed with small, frequent volumes of oral rehydration solution and supportive care. Vomiting settled during observation, subsequently tolerating fluids and light diet. Urine output improved. No intravenous fluids or antibiotics required. Father involved in care and given opportunity to ask questions; patient assented to the plan.

Discharge treatment
Oral rehydration solution – continue frequent small sips, increasing as tolerated.
Supportive care only. Paracetamol if required according to the product instructions.

Condition at discharge
Alert, clinically euvolaemic, tolerating oral intake and passing urine. Discharged home with father.

Plan / advice
Continue fluids and gradually resume usual diet. Hand hygiene and separate towels at home; remain away from school until 48 hours after the last episode of vomiting or diarrhoea. Seek urgent medical review if unable to keep fluids down, urine output falls again, severe abdominal pain develops, blood appears in stool, or increasing drowsiness occurs. GP review if not steadily improving.

Signed: F. HARVEY

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report

Patient: Tarique T.
MRN: 037823125
Home address: 96 Ursula Mews, Doncaster, DN1 1AB
Specimen: Peripheral blood, EDTA
Clinical indication: Diabetes mellitus with plantar ulceration, reduced sensation and local discharge; cough for 3 days also reported on request form. Current management includes wound care and co-amoxiclav.

Test requested: Monogenic diabetes gene panel with copy-number analysis.

Specimen assessment:
DNA extracted successfully. Concentration 42 ng/µL; A260/280 ratio 1.9. Sample suitable for next-generation sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis.

Findings:
No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant identified in the genes included on the panel. Sequencing coverage was ≥20× for 99.1% of target bases. A heterozygous variant of uncertain significance was detected in the GCK gene: c.XXXX, p.(XXXX) [classification pending further evidence]. This finding is not sufficient to establish a molecular diagnosis and should not direct clinical management.

Interpretation:
The result does not provide evidence of a recognised monogenic cause for the reported diabetes. A negative panel does not exclude a genetic contribution, including variants outside the tested regions or conditions not represented on the panel. Correlate with the diabetes phenotype, family history and previous investigations. Genetic counselling may be considered if there is a strong familial or atypical presentation.

The reported foot ulcer and sensory loss require ongoing clinical assessment; this molecular result does not alter antimicrobial or wound-care decisions. Please review the laboratory findings at the follow-up appointment on 1988-11-04.

Validated and reported by:
Dr Antonella Said, MBBS
Clinical Genetics Laboratory Scientist/Consultant

Discharge summary – Emergency Department
NHS number: 000 140 5536

Patient: K. Greenwood
Home address: 66 PARKSIDE DELL, MAGHERAMORNE
Patient contact: 07700 900368
Clinical age: 65 y/o

Reason for admission
Presented following a brief episode of left arm weakness with facial droop and slurred speech. Symptoms had fully resolved before assessment. No loss of consciousness, seizure activity or persistent visual disturbance reported.

Assessment and results
On arrival clinically stable; blood pressure 120/80 mmHg. Neurological examination was normal, with no dysphasia, facial asymmetry or limb weakness. Capillary glucose was within range. ECG showed sinus rhythm. Blood tests, including full blood count, electrolytes and glucose, were unremarkable. CT head showed no acute haemorrhage or established infarction. CTA head and neck did not demonstrate a significant large-vessel stenosis or occlusion.

Hospital course
Reviewed by the acute stroke team. Clinical picture considered most consistent with transient ischaemic attack. No thrombolysis or thrombectomy indicated as symptoms had resolved and there was no disabling deficit. Mobilising independently and tolerating diet at discharge.

Problem list
• Transient ischaemic attack – transient arm weakness, facial droop and dysarthria, resolved
• Vascular risk assessment required

Discharge medicines
• Aspirin 300 mg once daily for 14 days, then 75 mg once daily pending stroke clinic review
• Atorvastatin 80 mg at night
Continue usual medicines unless advised otherwise. Avoid driving until discussed with the GP/stroke service and follow current DVLA advice.

Follow-up and advice
Urgent TIA clinic appointment requested for 25 Oct 2012. GP to review blood pressure, diabetes and vascular risk factors. Return immediately to A&E if weakness, facial droop, speech disturbance or other new neurological symptoms recur, even if these settle quickly. Patient discharged home in stable condition with understanding confirmed.

PAEDIATRIC LABORATORY MEDICINE
NHS number: 000 343 9497
Laboratory report – clinical interpretation

Patient: A. Austin
Report/accession ID: 0857911625
Specimen: Venous blood; collected during assessment for vomiting, diarrhoea and reduced urine output. History provided by the patient’s father. The patient, aged 14 years, was clinically assessed in the paediatric setting.

Results
Sodium: 134 mmol/L (133–146)
Potassium: 3.7 mmol/L (3.5–5.3)
Chloride: 98 mmol/L (95–108)
Bicarbonate: 19 mmol/L (22–29)
Urea: 8.9 mmol/L (2.5–7.8)
Creatinine: 86 µmol/L (35–75)
Glucose: 4.8 mmol/L (3.5–6.0)
CRP: 6 mg/L (<5)
White cell count: 11.8 ×10^9/L (4.0–11.0)
Haemoglobin: 148 g/L (120–160)

Interpretation
Mild hyponatraemia with low bicarbonate and raised urea/creatinine, consistent with volume depletion in the reported gastrointestinal illness. Borderline inflammatory marker and leukocytosis are compatible with an acute infective or inflammatory process; results do not by themselves distinguish viral from bacterial gastroenteritis. No hypoglycaemia.

Clinical comment
Correlate with capillary refill, mucosal moisture, weight trend and ongoing urine output. Encourage oral rehydration solution in small, frequent volumes where tolerated; supportive care remains appropriate. Nausea may improve with hydration. Repeat electrolytes and renal profile if oral intake remains poor, urine output falls further or intravenous fluid therapy is required. Escalate for persistent tachycardia, lethargy, bloody diarrhoea or inability to retain fluids.

Follow-up/review date: 08/06/2020

Validated and reported by: MACHAELA NICHOLLS

Dear Colleague,

Re: W. Andrews

I would be grateful for your assessment of persistent iron-deficiency anaemia despite oral replacement, with advice regarding further investigation and management.

W. Andrews reports several months of tiredness, intermittent dizziness and reduced exercise tolerance. There is no reported overt gastrointestinal bleeding, melaena or rectal bleeding. Appetite is maintained, with no unintentional weight loss documented. Menstrual history has been discussed in primary care and does not fully account for the degree or persistence of anaemia.

Renal and thyroid profiles were unremarkable. Examination in the surgery: haemodynamically stable, mildly pale conjunctivae, no jaundice, lymphadenopathy or palpable abdominal mass.

Ferrous fumarate has been prescribed and adherence reviewed. There has been some gastrointestinal discomfort but no significant treatment interruption. Dietary advice has been provided. Repeat testing after treatment has shown only limited improvement, and iron stores remain depleted.

Could you please review the diagnosis and advise whether further investigation, including gastrointestinal assessment where appropriate, is indicated. Guidance on the duration and route of iron replacement would also be appreciated. Please consider whether additional causes of refractory iron deficiency should be excluded.

Referral made by Saavi Houghton, 0268978
Royal Victoria Hospital, BALNAMORE

text:
MOLECULAR GENETICS LABORATORY REPORT
NHS number: 0000980022

Patient: Eliazar S.
Report/accession ID: 0119181602
Request: Predictive germline testing for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk assessment.
Ordering clinician: unnamed respiratory medicine clinician
Clinical information: Significant family history; patient requests predictive testing owing to cancer-risk concern. Partner involved in discussion. No current treatment.

Specimen
Peripheral blood, EDTA. DNA extracted for germline analysis. Specimen suitable for testing; identity and request details concordant.

Analysis
Targeted assessment of BRCA1 and BRCA2 pathogenic variants, including small sequence changes and copy-number abnormalities where technically validated.

Result
BRCA1 c.68_69delAG: not detected.
No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant identified in the tested BRCA1/BRCA2 regions.

Interpretation
This result reduces, but does not eliminate, the possibility of an inherited cancer predisposition. Residual risk may reflect an alteration outside the assay scope, a variant in another susceptibility gene, or limitations of current testing. Interpretation should be integrated with the documented family history and any affected-relative results.

Action
Genetic counselling recommended for discussion of residual risk and options for broader panel testing. Testing an affected relative, if available, may be more informative. No change to treatment indicated on the basis of this result alone; no current treatment.

Follow-up: review appointment 28 March 2026.

Validated and authorised by:
I. Rose, Consultant Clinical Geneticist
GMC number: GMC-TEST-0950321

Discharge summary
NHS number: 000 372 1036

Patient: Ilisha
MRN: 0111506
Clinical area: Paediatrics
Admitting service: Royal Victoria Hospital

Ilisha is 16 y/o and was admitted with a sickle cell painful crisis, with severe bilateral limb pain, back pain and reduced oral intake. His uncle, Reed, remained involved in discussions and supported him during the admission. He was assessed with his assent, with his uncle present for the agreed parts of the consultation.

On arrival he was clinically dehydrated and required intravenous fluids and regular analgesia, including morphine. Initial blood tests were consistent with his known sickle cell disorder, without evidence of significant bacterial infection or acute chest syndrome. Chest examination remained clear and oxygen saturations were maintained in air. No transfusion was indicated.

Pain improved steadily with the inpatient analgesia plan. Fluids were stopped once he was drinking adequately and passing urine normally. At review today he is alert, mobile around the ward and tolerating food and drink. Current pain score is 5/10, but he feels this is manageable with oral treatment and wishes to go home.

Discharge medicines: regular paracetamol and ibuprofen as previously advised; oral morphine solution for breakthrough severe pain only, in accordance with the supplied discharge prescription. Encourage frequent oral fluids and rest. Avoid excess exertion while recovering.

Assessment and plan: suitable for discharge home with his uncle today. Continue the established sickle cell plan and seek urgent medical advice for fever, chest pain, breathing difficulty, increasing lethargy, persistent vomiting or pain not controlled by the prescribed medicines. Follow-up with the sickle cell team at Royal Victoria Hospital and the GP surgery has been requested.

Presenting complaint: 18-hour history of central abdominal pain migrating to right lower quadrant. Nausea and loss of appetite; no diarrhoea. Parent reports reduced oral intake, passing urine normally.

Increasing redness, tenderness and purulent discharge from the left lateral chest wound following recent thoracic surgery. Reports local pain, worse on movement. No pleuritic chest pain or significant breathlessness. Eating and drinking.

Suitable for discharge with written wound-care advice. Return to A&E for fever, spreading erythema, worsening pain, increasing discharge, breathlessness or feeling systemically unwell. Review arranged with surgical service.

Dear Mental Health Team,

I am referring Yashwanth F. following assessment in the emergency department, where they attended with a friend because of several months of persistent worry, poor sleep and marked muscle tension. The worry is present on most days and has begun to affect concentration and day-to-day functioning at work. We have advised Yashwanth F. to seek urgent help through A&E or 999 if they develop immediate safety concerns. Their GP should review progress in about 12 weeks, or sooner if symptoms worsen.

Yours sincerely,

KIANNA-LEIGH DOYLE

Discharge summary – Respiratory Medicine / Acute Medical Unit
National Insurance number: NT861964D

Patient: SHIFAH GRIFFITHS
The patient, aged 63 years, was admitted following sudden left arm weakness, facial droop and slurred speech, resolving completely before assessment. Cebrail, the patient’s adult child from MAGHERAFELT, provided collateral history and was updated during the admission.

On arrival, observations were stable, including blood pressure 120/80 mmHg. Neurological examination was normal after symptom resolution, with no residual weakness, dysphasia or visual field deficit. ECG showed sinus rhythm. Routine blood tests were unremarkable. CT head demonstrated no acute haemorrhage or established infarction. Subsequent MRI brain showed no acute diffusion restriction. Carotid Doppler identified no flow-limiting stenosis. The presentation was discussed with the stroke team and felt most consistent with a transient ischaemic attack.

The patient remained well on the ward, mobilising independently and tolerating diet. No further focal neurological episodes occurred. Swallow assessment was satisfactory. There was no indication for thrombolysis or thrombectomy as symptoms had resolved and imaging showed no acute infarct.

Discharge medicines:
• Aspirin 300 mg once daily for 14 days, then reduce to aspirin 75 mg once daily.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: JAIDA GEASLAND
Reason for admission: Intractable nausea and vomiting during early pregnancy with dehydration and documented weight loss.

Clinical background: Patient is at 9+4 weeks' gestation and presented after several days of persistent vomiting, inability to maintain oral fluids, and reduced urine output. She reported a 3.2-kg weight loss from her pre-pregnancy baseline. There was no vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain, fever, diarrhea, dysuria, or syncope. Her initial evaluation was completed at GEORGE WASHINGTON UNIV HOSPITAL.

Key findings:
- Mild tachycardia on arrival with dry mucous membranes and orthostatic symptoms.
- Serum potassium was mildly decreased; serum bicarbonate was low.
- Urinalysis demonstrated ketonuria without evidence of urinary infection.
- Chemistry findings were consistent with dehydration and starvation ketosis rather than uncomplicated vomiting-related alkalosis.
- Transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound showed a single intrauterine pregnancy with cardiac activity and no acute pelvic abnormality.

Hospital course: The patient received intravenous sodium chloride, electrolyte monitoring, and antiemetic therapy. Doxylamine-pyridoxine was restarted on a scheduled basis after oral tolerance improved. She initially required small-volume intravenous fluids because of recurrent emesis, then advanced from ice chips to clear liquids and a bland diet without further vomiting. Potassium improved with repletion and oral intake. Repeat urine testing showed decreasing ketones. There was no evidence of acute kidney injury or infection.

Discharge medications:
- Doxylamine-pyridoxine: continue as prescribed on a scheduled basis for nausea prevention.
- Prenatal vitamin: resume when able to tolerate.
- No additional prescription antiemetic was required at discharge.

Condition at discharge: Hemodynamically stable, alert, ambulatory, tolerating oral fluids and light food, with improved nausea and adequate urine output. The patient and E. Smurthwaite reviewed return precautions; the relative resides in Washington and will assist with transportation and monitoring at home.

Instructions: Take frequent small sips of fluid and eat small meals containing carbohydrates and protein. Avoid prolonged fasting. Record vomiting episodes and urine output if symptoms recur. Return to the ED for inability to keep liquids down for 8 hours, markedly decreased urination, fainting, abdominal pain, fever, vaginal bleeding, or blood in emesis.

Follow-up: Obstetric follow-up is scheduled for September 28th, 1996. Contact the prenatal care office sooner for recurrent vomiting, worsening weakness, or inability to take doxylamine-pyridoxine. Repeat electrolytes should be considered if oral intake declines or vomiting returns.

Discharge disposition: Home in stable condition.

Emergency Department Note

Patient: Aracelia A., 55 y/o
Home address: 581 S San Miguel St, Hagåtña, GU 96910
Contact: aracelia.aspey48@gmail.com
Report/accession ID: 05466687

Chief Complaint: Shortness of breath and leg swelling.

History of Present Illness: The patient presents with several days of worsening exertional dyspnea, reduced exercise tolerance, and swelling around both ankles. Orthopnea has progressed from using one pillow to needing to sleep partly upright. The patient denies chest pain, syncope, fever, productive cough, unilateral calf pain, or recent immobilization. Furosemide and metoprolol succinate are listed as home medications; the patient reports taking them as prescribed but notes increased urine output has not kept pace with the swelling. No recent medication changes are reported.

On arrival, the patient was speaking in full sentences but became breathless while walking from the waiting area. The Model X3 cardiac monitor was applied, showing sinus rhythm with occasional premature ventricular complexes and no sustained dysrhythmia. Blood pressure was elevated, with otherwise stable vital signs and oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. Examination demonstrated jugular venous distention, bibasilar inspiratory crackles, and two-plus pitting edema to both lower legs. There was no focal wheezing, calf asymmetry, or clinical evidence of cellulitis. Heart sounds were regular without a new murmur. The abdomen was soft and nontender.

Diagnostics: Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy and nonspecific ST-T abnormalities, without acute ischemic changes. Chest radiograph demonstrated cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion, and small bilateral pleural effusions. Laboratory studies showed an elevated natriuretic peptide consistent with volume overload, mild renal dysfunction compared with the available prior result, and normal potassium. High-sensitivity troponin was minimally elevated but stable on repeat testing. Viral respiratory testing was negative.

Medical Decision-Making: Findings are most consistent with acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary and peripheral congestion. Acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, and significant arrhythmia were considered less likely based on the history, examination, serial testing, and imaging. The patient was treated with intravenous furosemide, producing clinically meaningful diuresis and improved breathing. Oxygen was not required after reassessment.

Assessment: Acute on chronic decompensated heart failure with volume overload, orthopnea, and bilateral ankle edema.

Plan and Disposition: Admission was recommended for continued intravenous diuresis, renal-function monitoring, and medication optimization. The patient agreed to hospitalization. The admitting team was asked to review guideline-directed medical therapy, including whether an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and SGLT2 inhibitor are appropriate, while continuing the beta blocker if hemodynamically tolerated. Furosemide dosing will be adjusted to daily weights, urine output, electrolytes, and renal function. The patient left the ED in stable condition for an inpatient bed.

Discharge Summary

Patient: amiee zugg
Attending clinician: jahkeem claybaugh, 072220202
Discharging service: PROVIDENCE SEWARD HOSPITAL

Reason for admission:
The patient presented to the emergency department with progressively worsening right lower-quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and loss of appetite for 3 days. Examination showed focal right lower-quadrant tenderness with guarding but no generalized peritoneal signs. The patient was afebrile and hemodynamically stable on arrival.

Key findings:
Laboratory testing demonstrated mild leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance. Comprehensive metabolic testing was without a clinically significant abnormality. Urinalysis did not suggest urinary infection. CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed an enlarged, inflamed appendix with surrounding inflammatory change, consistent with acute uncomplicated appendicitis. The imaging report was filed under report/accession ID 08780419.

Hospital course:
The patient received intravenous fluids, antiemetic therapy, analgesia with acetaminophen, and empiric intravenous ampicillin-sulbactam. General Surgery evaluated the patient and recommended operative management. After informed consent, laparoscopic appendectomy was performed without complication. The appendix was removed and sent for surgical pathology. Estimated blood loss was minimal, and no drain was required.

Following surgery, the patient advanced from clear liquids to a regular diet without recurrent nausea or vomiting. Abdominal pain improved substantially and was controlled with oral acetaminophen. The patient ambulated independently, voided normally, and remained afebrile with stable vital signs. Incision sites were clean, dry, and intact with no evidence of bleeding or infection. Antibiotics were discontinued after the perioperative course because there was no abscess or perforation.

Assessment and discharge plan:
Acute uncomplicated appendicitis, status post laparoscopic appendectomy, recovering appropriately. The patient is medically stable for discharge home.

Discharge medications:
Continue acetaminophen by mouth as directed on the discharge medication label for postoperative discomfort. No outpatient ampicillin-sulbactam is indicated. Avoid taking more than the labeled daily acetaminophen limit and review other over-the-counter products for duplicate acetaminophen content.

Instructions:
Keep the incision areas clean and dry. Showering is permitted, but do not soak in a bathtub or swimming pool until the wounds are healed. Avoid heavy lifting and strenuous activity until cleared by Surgery. Resume activity gradually as tolerated and maintain adequate oral hydration.

Seek urgent medical attention for fever, worsening or spreading abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, inability to eat or drink, increasing redness or drainage from an incision, abdominal swelling, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

Follow-up:
Follow up with the surgical clinic for postoperative evaluation and pathology review. Arrange routine follow-up with primary care as needed. The discharge plan and return precautions were reviewed with the patient, who verbalized understanding.

Laboratory Medicine Report

Patient: JOHANDRY GRUBY
Report/accession ID: 071857001
Specimen context: Inpatient serum and urine evaluation for reduced urine output, fatigue, and poor oral intake in a patient with suspected acute kidney injury. Ordering clinician not listed on the laboratory request.

Specimens received:
Serum, lithium-heparin plasma, and clean-catch urine. Specimen integrity was acceptable for the assays reported below.

Chemistry results:
Creatinine: 2.1 mg/dL (reference interval 0.60–1.30 mg/dL) — High
Blood urea nitrogen: 38 mg/dL (reference interval 7–20 mg/dL) — High
Estimated glomerular filtration rate, CKD-EPI 2021: 27 mL/min/1.73 m² (reference: ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m²) — Decreased
Sodium: 134 mmol/L (reference interval 135–145 mmol/L) — Slightly low
Potassium: 4.8 mmol/L (reference interval 3.5–5.1 mmol/L) — Within range
Chloride: 99 mmol/L (reference interval 98–107 mmol/L) — Within range
Total carbon dioxide: 21 mmol/L (reference interval 22–29 mmol/L) — Slightly low
Anion gap: 14 mmol/L (reference interval 7–16 mmol/L) — Within range
Glucose: 96 mg/dL (reference interval 70–99 mg/dL) — Within range
Calcium: 8.7 mg/dL (reference interval 8.6–10.3 mg/dL) — Within range
Albumin: 3.6 g/dL (reference interval 3.4–5.0 g/dL) — Within range

Urinalysis:
Specific gravity: 1.018 (reference interval 1.005–1.030)
Protein: 1+
Blood: Trace
Leukocyte esterase: Negative
Nitrite: Negative
Urine sediment: 3–5 red blood cells/high-power field; 0–2 white blood cells/high-power field; no casts identified.

Interpretation:
The increased serum creatinine and BUN with reduced estimated filtration are consistent with clinically significant acute kidney dysfunction in the reported setting. Mild hyponatremia and low total carbon dioxide are also present. The urine concentration is preserved, and the absence of pyuria or nitrites does not support a urinary tract infection. Correlation with prior creatinine values, fluid balance, blood pressure, and medication exposure is recommended to distinguish volume-responsive or other prerenal physiology from intrinsic renal injury or obstruction.

Clinical comment:
The reported poor oral intake and reduced urine output raise concern for a volume-depletion component. Continue close monitoring of urine output and repeat renal function and electrolytes after intravenous sodium chloride, as clinically indicated. The temporary medication hold should be reviewed against all nephrotoxic or renally cleared agents before restart. Consider renal imaging if oliguria persists or obstruction is clinically suspected. Urgent clinical reassessment is warranted for worsening potassium, acid-base status, respiratory symptoms, or further decline in urine output.

Follow-up laboratory review: May 20, 2024

Taison Mcbay, MD, Laboratory Physician

She remained afebrile, tolerated a regular diet, and was able to ambulate without assistance. Abdominal tenderness decreased substantially, and repeat examination showed no guarding or rebound. There was no indication for operative management or drainage.

The patient received counseling regarding completion of therapy, abstinence until treatment is completed and symptoms have resolved, and the need for evaluation and treatment of recent sexual partners. She was advised to use condoms thereafter and to avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole and for at least 24 hours after the final dose. The medication list was reviewed, including doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, which she had already begun before discharge.

- Metronidazole 500 mg twice daily to complete a 14-day course.

LABORATORY REPORT — INFLAMMATION AND CRYSTAL-ARTHRITIS EVALUATION

Patient: JALENA SENEGAL
MRN: 07388074
Home address: 889 Mokapu Saddle Rd, Hawi, HI 96719
Specimen: Serum
Clinical indication: Acute joint pain with swelling and erythema, clinically concerning for gout flare. Current medications include naproxen and colchicine.

Results

Analyte                              Result             Reference interval
Uric acid                            8.9 mg/dL          3.4–7.0 mg/dL
C-reactive protein                   3.8 mg/dL          <0.5 mg/dL
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate       42 mm/hr           0–20 mm/hr
Creatinine                           1.02 mg/dL          0.60–1.30 mg/dL
Estimated GFR                        94 mL/min/1.73 m²   ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m²
White blood cell count               11.6 × 10^3/µL      4.0–10.5 × 10^3/µL
Aspartate aminotransferase           24 U/L             10–40 U/L
Alanine aminotransferase             29 U/L             7–56 U/L

Interpretation

Serum uric acid is elevated. C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and white blood cell count are increased, supporting an active inflammatory process. Renal function and hepatic aminotransferases are within the stated reference intervals. These findings are compatible with the reported acute gout flare but are not, by themselves, diagnostic of monosodium urate crystal deposition.

If synovial fluid is available, definitive laboratory confirmation requires compensated polarized-light microscopy demonstrating intracellular, needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals. Crystal analysis should be performed promptly after collection. A negative serum uric acid result during an acute attack would not exclude gout; in this specimen, the elevated concentration increases suspicion but does not establish the diagnosis. If septic arthritis is clinically considered, synovial fluid Gram stain and culture should be obtained without delaying appropriate evaluation.

Clinical comment

The inflammatory marker pattern is consistent with the patient’s acute joint pain, swelling, and erythema. Correlate with joint examination and response to naproxen and colchicine. The creatinine result does not indicate a current renal dosing limitation, although repeat renal assessment is appropriate if anti-inflammatory therapy continues, oral intake declines, or gastrointestinal symptoms develop. Long-term urate-lowering therapy should be considered after the acute episode according to the treating clinician’s assessment and recurrence history.

A laboratory review appointment is planned for May 22nd, 1988, in about 7 weeks. This interval is appropriate for reassessing symptoms, medication tolerance, and whether a repeat uric acid measurement is clinically useful.

Report status: Final
Validating laboratory clinician: sloka gormus

Discharge Summary

Patient: ASIAH SUTERA
Age: 34 y/o
Encounter date: 10/28/2012

Reason for admission
ASIAH SUTERA was admitted after two days of markedly reduced urine output, fatigue, and poor oral intake in the setting of several days of nausea and intermittent loose stools. The patient denied dysuria, flank pain, chest pain, or shortness of breath. On arrival, the patient appeared mildly volume depleted with dry mucous membranes and orthostatic lightheadedness. Initial blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg.

Key findings
Admission laboratory testing demonstrated acute kidney injury with creatinine 2.3 mg/dL and BUN 41 mg/dL; the patient’s prior creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL. Potassium was 4.6 mmol/L, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L, and sodium 137 mmol/L. Urinalysis showed concentrated urine without significant blood, protein, or pyuria. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis or other evidence of urinary obstruction. A bladder scan showed minimal residual volume. There was no clinical or laboratory evidence of sepsis.

Hospital course
The presentation was felt to represent predominantly prerenal acute kidney injury from dehydration and inadequate intake. The patient received intravenous sodium chloride with close monitoring of urine output, renal function, electrolytes, and daily weights. Oral fluids and nutrition were gradually advanced as nausea resolved. A potentially nephrotoxic and volume-sensitive home medication was temporarily held during the admission; the patient was instructed not to restart it until renal function is reassessed by the primary care clinician.

Urine output improved substantially during the first hospital day. Repeat testing showed creatinine down to 1.4 mg/dL, BUN 27 mg/dL, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, and bicarbonate 24 mmol/L. The patient was ambulatory without dizziness, tolerated a regular diet, and had no further vomiting or diarrhea. No dialysis, urinary catheterization, or other procedure was required.

Discharge diagnoses
1. Acute kidney injury, improving, likely secondary to volume depletion.
2. Dehydration due to poor oral intake and gastrointestinal fluid loss.
3. Fatigue and decreased urine output, improved with hydration.

Medication and self-care instructions
Continue oral hydration throughout the day, unless another clinician has placed a fluid restriction. Resume a regular diet as tolerated. Avoid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, including ibuprofen and naproxen, until cleared by primary care. Do not take the held medication until follow-up laboratory results have been reviewed. No new antibiotic was indicated. Keep a written record of fluid intake and urine output for the next several days if feasible.

Follow-up
Arrange a primary care visit within one week for repeat basic metabolic panel and medication reconciliation. Seek urgent care for inability to keep fluids down, very low or absent urine output for eight hours, worsening weakness, confusion, fainting, chest pain, or shortness of breath. Discharge instructions were reviewed with the patient and with the patient’s relative, Meerab Farster, who resides in Swayzee. Both verbalized understanding of the hydration plan, medication hold, laboratory follow-up, and return precautions.

At discharge, ASIAH SUTERA was clinically stable, euvolemic on examination, and discharged home with outpatient follow-up.

Specimen source: Left plantar diabetic foot ulcer, deep swab submitted in transport medium
Clinical indication: Plantar ulceration with reduced sensation and local discharge; evaluation for soft-tissue infection

SPECIMEN AND QUALITY
Received as a single wound swab with visible purulent material. Specimen is adequate for routine aerobic culture but may not represent deeper tissue microbiology. Gram stain shows moderate polymorphonuclear leukocytes and few gram-positive cocci in pairs. No yeast identified.

RESULTS

• Streptococcus agalactiae: Moderate growth
• Staphylococcus aureus, methicillin susceptible: Light growth

Date: 07/24/2022
Patient: linda homburg
Age: 53 y/o
Report/accession ID: 04749406

Today’s visit addressed episodes of spinning brought on by changes in head position. You described a brief sensation that the room moves when you roll to the right in bed, look upward, or bend over. The episodes last less than a minute and are followed by mild nausea and a feeling of unsteadiness. You have not had fainting, chest pain, new hearing loss, severe headache, double vision, facial droop, weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or persistent vomiting. You have had similar symptoms for 3 days.

Your examination today was reassuring. Blood pressure and pulse were stable. Ear canals and eardrums were clear. Eye movements were intact without spontaneous nystagmus. Strength, sensation, coordination, and walking were normal between symptoms. Positional testing produced brief vertigo with characteristic nystagmus, without other neurologic findings. The pattern is most consistent with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, commonly called BPPV. This is caused by tiny calcium particles moving within the inner ear’s balance canals; it is uncomfortable but usually not dangerous.

Please perform the home canalith-repositioning maneuver demonstrated during the visit once daily for the next several days, stopping if it causes severe or prolonged symptoms. Move slowly when getting out of bed, use a handrail on stairs, and avoid driving, ladders, or other activities requiring reliable balance until the spinning has settled. Maintain fluids and regular meals. Prochlorperazine may be used as required for significant nausea, according to the prescribed directions. It can cause drowsiness, so do not combine it with alcohol or drive after taking it.

If symptoms do not improve within 1–2 weeks, recur frequently, or interfere with normal activities, contact the office so we can arrange vestibular therapy or an ear, nose, and throat evaluation. Seek emergency care immediately for continuous vertigo, inability to walk, severe headache, fainting, new weakness or numbness, trouble speaking, vision loss, chest pain, or repeated vomiting.

Please use linda.homburg85@me.com for routine follow-up communication.

Hematology Consultation Report

Patient: jashua jochim
Occupation: Business Office Manager
Referring clinician: S. Hennefer
Practice: Moberly Regional Medical Center
Report/accession ID: 0941798906

Reason for consultation: Evaluation of progressive, painless lymphadenopathy associated with constitutional symptoms.

Clinical history:
The patient reports several weeks of gradually enlarging, non-tender lymph nodes in the left cervical and supraclavicular regions. There has been no preceding dental infection, pharyngitis, or recent vaccination. The patient also describes drenching night sweats requiring a change of clothing and unintentional weight loss despite no deliberate dietary change. Intermittent fatigue is present, but there is no persistent fever, productive cough, dysphagia, or dyspnea. No prior history of malignancy is reported. Current treatment consists of supportive care pending tissue diagnosis, including hydration, nutritional encouragement, and symptom monitoring.

Examination:
The patient is alert and in no acute distress. A firm, mobile, non-tender cluster of enlarged left cervical lymph nodes is palpable, with an additional smaller left supraclavicular node. No overlying erythema or fluctuance is present. There is no clinically apparent axillary or inguinal adenopathy on today’s examination. Heart rate and rhythm are regular. Lungs are clear bilaterally without wheezes or crackles. The abdomen is soft and nondistended; no definite splenomegaly is appreciated. There is no lower-extremity edema or focal neurologic deficit.

Available findings and interpretation:
The combination of painless progressive lymphadenopathy, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss is concerning for a lymphoproliferative disorder. Hodgkin lymphoma is the leading clinical consideration, although reactive infection, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and less likely metastatic disease remain in the differential diagnosis. Physical examination alone cannot establish histology or disease stage.

Recommendations:
An urgent excisional biopsy of the most accessible abnormal lymph node is recommended rather than fine-needle aspiration alone, with tissue submitted for histopathology, immunohistochemistry, flow cytometry when appropriate, and cytogenetic or molecular studies as directed by pathology. Baseline complete blood count with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, lactate dehydrogenase, and uric acid should be obtained. HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C screening should be completed before any immunochemotherapy. Positron emission tomography/computed tomography is recommended after tissue confirmation for staging and treatment planning.

The patient was advised to report fever, rapidly enlarging nodes, shortness of breath, chest pressure, inability to maintain oral intake, or worsening weakness promptly. Supportive care may continue while diagnostic testing is arranged. Follow-up with hematology is planned after biopsy results are available to review pathology, stage the illness, and discuss treatment options. The findings and need for definitive tissue diagnosis were reviewed with the patient, who expressed understanding.

Electronically signed by S. Hennefer
Hematology consultation, Moberly Regional Medical Center

Maintain regular fluid intake unless another clinician has instructed you to restrict fluids.

Arrange follow-up with your primary care office for reassessment and review of the final culture result. Abnormal thyroid function studies compatible with under-replaced primary hypothyroidism. Positive thyroid peroxidase antibody.

You did not report vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, fever, or painful urination. Your medication reconciliation confirms metformin and atorvastatin. Please continue both as currently prescribed unless we contact you with a change.

Your office blood pressure and heart rate were reassuring, and you appeared well hydrated. Foot examination showed intact skin, palpable pulses, and preserved sensation to monofilament testing. There was no swelling. We discussed that high glucose can pull extra water into the urine, which explains both the thirst and frequent urination. ED Assessment
SSN: 900-41-9464

Patient: A. Crus
Chief complaint: Right flank pain, dysuria, and shaking chills.

History of present illness: Patient reports 2 days of worsening burning with urination and urinary frequency, followed by constant right flank pain and rigors this morning. Nausea without vomiting. No vaginal bleeding, vaginal discharge, chest pain, or shortness of breath. No known history of kidney stones. H. Calma accompanied the patient and provided additional history. Contact detail: (202) 555-0163.

Initial evaluation: At 08:15, temperature 102.8°F, HR 112, BP 108/66, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air. Alert and uncomfortable but nontoxic. Dry mucous membranes. Regular tachycardia without murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft with suprapubic discomfort; marked right costovertebral angle tenderness. No guarding or rebound. No focal neurologic deficit.

Investigations: CBC shows WBC 16.4 K/µL with neutrophil predominance. CMP notable for creatinine 1.0 mg/dL and mild bicarbonate reduction. Lactate 1.6 mmol/L. Urinalysis: positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites, >50 WBC/hpf, moderate blood, and many bacteria. Urine pregnancy test negative. CT abdomen/pelvis without contrast demonstrates right perinephric stranding without obstructing calculus or hydronephrosis. Urine and blood cultures obtained. Report/accession ID: LAB-03161289.

Medical decision-making: Findings support acute right-sided pyelonephritis. No shock, acute kidney injury, abscess, or obstructing stone identified. Sepsis precautions and return-risk discussion completed. The patient tolerated oral intake after treatment and preferred outpatient management with reliable family support.

Treatment: IV fluids, acetaminophen, and cefuroxime initiated in the ED with clinical improvement. Discharge prescription for cefuroxime; continue acetaminophen as directed for fever or pain. Do not exceed the labeled daily dose.

Disposition: Discharged home in stable condition. Follow up with Wilmington Treatment Center within 48–72 hours for reassessment and culture review. Return immediately for persistent vomiting, worsening pain, confusion, fainting, inability to urinate, or recurrent rigors.

LABORATORY MEDICINE REPORT

Patient: iham nappi
MRN: 0794406
Report date: December 20, 2022
Reporting laboratory: Greenfield Area Medical Center
Ordering clinician: Not provided on the submitted requisition

Specimen and clinical context:
Peripheral blood collected for evaluation of painless lymphadenopathy, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss. The clinical indication states concern for Hodgkin lymphoma. The patient is receiving supportive care pending tissue diagnosis. Results below are from the submitted specimen and should be interpreted with the clinical examination, imaging, and planned lymph-node pathology.

Complete blood count:
White blood cell count: 8.7 x10^3/µL (reference range 4.0-10.5 x10^3/µL)
Hemoglobin: 11.2 g/dL (reference range 12.0-16.0 g/dL)
Hematocrit: 34.1% (reference range 36.0-46.0%)
Mean corpuscular volume: 84.8 fL (reference range 80.0-100.0 fL)
Platelet count: 412 x10^3/µL (reference range 150-400 x10^3/µL)
Absolute neutrophil count: 6.3 x10^3/µL (reference range 1.8-7.7 x10^3/µL)
Absolute lymphocyte count: 1.2 x10^3/µL (reference range 1.0-4.8 x10^3/µL)

Chemistry:
Sodium: 138 mmol/L (reference range 135-145 mmol/L)
Potassium: 4.3 mmol/L (reference range 3.5-5.1 mmol/L)
Chloride: 101 mmol/L (reference range 98-107 mmol/L)
Carbon dioxide: 24 mmol/L (reference range 22-29 mmol/L)
Blood urea nitrogen: 14 mg/dL (reference range 7-20 mg/dL)
Creatinine: 0.82 mg/dL (reference range 0.60-1.10 mg/dL)
Glucose: 96 mg/dL (reference range 70-99 mg/dL)
Calcium: Not measured
Phosphorus: Not measured
Uric acid: 5.8 mg/dL (reference range 3.4-7.0 mg/dL)
Lactate dehydrogenase: 286 U/L (reference range 120-250 U/L)
Aspartate aminotransferase: 22 U/L (reference range 10-40 U/L)
Alanine aminotransferase: 19 U/L (reference range 7-56 U/L)
Total bilirubin: 0.6 mg/dL (reference range 0.1-1.2 mg/dL)

Interpretation:
Mild normocytic anemia, borderline thrombocytosis, and increased lactate dehydrogenase are present. These findings are nonspecific and may occur with inflammation, malignancy, or other systemic illness. The CBC does not establish or exclude Hodgkin lymphoma; definitive classification requires tissue examination with appropriate immunophenotyping.

No evidence of hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, or acute kidney injury is present in the reported results. Phosphorus and calcium were not measured, so spontaneous tumor lysis cannot be fully assessed. If clinically indicated, obtain phosphorus, calcium, repeat renal function testing, and serial uric acid and potassium measurements, particularly before cytotoxic therapy.

Validated and electronically reported by Sayyid Heraty, MD.

Nursing Progress Note

Date: May 28, 2023
Patient: SHIA HIL, a 31-year-old Latino female patient
Gestational age: 9+4 weeks' gestation
Attending clinician: Q. Kramper

Patient remains admitted for first-trimester hyperemesis with ongoing nausea, recurrent vomiting, dehydration, and recent weight loss. She reports four episodes of emesis overnight and one small episode this morning, primarily clear fluid with scant food contents. She denies hematemesis, abdominal pain, fever, dysuria, vaginal bleeding, or pelvic cramping. Her sister, Lorie, was present during morning rounds and assisted with communication regarding the home medication schedule.

At 0800, patient was awake, oriented, and tired-appearing. Oral mucosa was dry. Skin was warm with slightly decreased turgor; capillary refill was approximately 2 seconds. Heart rate was mildly elevated while upright and improved after fluids. Blood pressure remained stable. Abdomen was soft and nondistended with mild epigastric discomfort after vomiting, without guarding or rebound. She reports lightheadedness when standing but denies syncope. Urine output was low overnight, with dark yellow urine documented. Weight is down from her reported pre-pregnancy baseline, and daily weight will continue to be monitored.

A peripheral IV remains patent in the left forearm without redness, swelling, or tenderness. Intravenous sodium chloride was continued per order. Doxylamine-pyridoxine was administered as scheduled, and the patient reported reduced nausea approximately one hour later. She tolerated several ice chips, 4 ounces of oral rehydration solution, and a few bites of crackers after medication. No further emesis was observed during the remainder of the morning assessment. Mouth care was provided, and the patient was encouraged to take small, frequent sips rather than large volumes.

Assessment: Persistent first-trimester nausea and vomiting with clinical evidence of mild volume depletion and inadequate oral intake. No current bleeding, acute abdominal findings, or signs of infection. Fall risk is increased because of weakness and orthostatic lightheadedness.

Plan: Continue IV hydration and scheduled doxylamine-pyridoxine. Maintain strict intake and output documentation, daily weight, and orthostatic vital signs as tolerated. Offer bland foods and fluids in small, frequent amounts. Assist with ambulation and reinforce use of the call light before getting out of bed. Notify the provider for recurrent uncontrolled vomiting, inability to tolerate oral intake, worsening dizziness, reduced urine output, abnormal vital signs, abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, or blood in emesis. The next shift should reassess hydration status, emesis frequency, urine output, medication response, and readiness to advance oral intake.

Nursing signature: Q. Kramper

Primary Care Follow-Up Note
SSN: 666 09 5278

Patient: E. Wiblin
DOB: Sep 8, 1971
MRN: 0028832

The patient presents for follow-up of essential hypertension and reports intermittent headaches and light-headedness over the past several weeks. The headache is described as a dull pressure, usually occurring late in the day, without visual loss, focal weakness, speech difficulty, syncope, chest pain, or shortness of breath. Current pain is 5/10. Light-headedness is brief and most noticeable when standing quickly. There has been no fall.

The patient is taking amlodipine and lisinopril but acknowledges missing occasional evening doses. No medication side effects are reported, including no ankle swelling, cough, or facial swelling. Home blood pressure readings have generally been in the 130s to 140s systolic, although the patient did not bring the log today. Salt intake has been reduced, and the patient is walking several times weekly. Alcohol use is limited. The patient denies tobacco or illicit drug use.

On examination, the patient is alert, conversant, and in no acute distress. Blood pressure is 146/88 in the right arm while seated, with a repeat reading of 140/84 after five minutes. Pulse is 76 and regular. Orthostatic measurement does not show a significant drop. Heart has regular rate and rhythm without murmur. Lungs are clear bilaterally. There is no peripheral edema. Neurologic examination is nonfocal, with normal gait, strength, sensation, and coordination.

Assessment and Plan

1. Essential hypertension, above goal in the office. Inconsistent evening dosing may be contributing to the elevated readings. Continue amlodipine and lisinopril at the current prescribed doses. The patient will use a pill organizer and set an evening alarm, rather than increasing medication today. Continue home blood pressure checks several times weekly and bring the log to the next visit. Continue a low-sodium diet and regular physical activity.

2. Headache and intermittent light-headedness. No red-flag findings on today’s examination. Encourage hydration and slow position changes. The patient was instructed to seek emergency care for sudden severe headache, persistent vomiting, fainting, new neurologic symptoms, chest pain, or severe shortness of breath.

Basic metabolic panel and urinalysis were ordered to monitor renal function and electrolytes while taking lisinopril. The patient will send the preferred pharmacy contact detail through the portal at emmerich.wiblin50@outlook.com if medication reconciliation changes are needed. Follow-up blood pressure review is scheduled for 2024-03-20.

Discharge Summary
SSN: 000-70-6281

Patient: Kyrese E.
MRN: 022 883 860
Discharging facility: Meadville Medical Center

Reason for admission:
Kyrese E. was admitted after sudden onset of right arm weakness, left facial droop, and slurred speech witnessed by a family member. The focal deficits began while the patient was at home and improved substantially before arrival in the emergency department. The patient also reported a mild headache for 3 days, without fever, neck stiffness, loss of consciousness, or seizure activity. Because the presentation was concerning for an acute cerebrovascular event, stroke alert evaluation was initiated.

Key evaluation:
Initial neurologic examination showed subtle right pronator drift and mildly slowed speech, with no persistent facial asymmetry by the time of hospital assessment. The remainder of the examination was nonfocal. Noncontrast CT of the head showed no acute hemorrhage or established infarction. CT angiography of the head and neck demonstrated no large-vessel occlusion or hemodynamically significant carotid stenosis. MRI of the brain did not show an acute infarct. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed preserved left ventricular systolic function and no intracardiac thrombus identified. Telemetry remained in sinus rhythm without atrial fibrillation.

Hospital course:
The patient was not treated with thrombolytic therapy because neurologic symptoms had resolved and the patient was outside the treatment decision window at the time of evaluation. Symptoms remained absent during observation, and serial neurologic examinations were normal. Swallow screening was passed, and the patient tolerated a regular diet. Physical and occupational therapy found independent mobility without an assistive device. Speech therapy noted no persistent dysarthria or language deficit.

The overall presentation was most consistent with a transient ischemic attack. Risk-factor counseling was provided, including the importance of blood pressure monitoring, a heart-healthy diet, regular physical activity as tolerated, and avoidance of tobacco exposure. The patient and Breana Mochrie, who lives in Huntington Mills, were instructed to seek emergency care immediately for recurrent weakness, facial droop, speech difficulty, vision loss, severe new headache, imbalance, or confusion.

Medication changes:
• Start aspirin 81 mg by mouth daily.
• Start atorvastatin 40 mg by mouth nightly.
• Continue other home medications as reviewed on the discharge medication reconciliation.
• Do not stop aspirin or atorvastatin without discussing the change with a clinician.

Condition at discharge:
Stable, alert, fully oriented, hemodynamically stable, and neurologically at baseline. The patient was able to ambulate independently and verbalized understanding of the medication plan and stroke warning signs.

Follow-up:
Follow up with primary care for vascular risk-factor management and medication review. Outpatient neurology follow-up is recommended for completion of TIA evaluation and consideration of extended rhythm monitoring if clinically indicated. Return to the emergency department immediately for any recurrent neurologic symptoms, even if they resolve before arrival.

Discharging clinician: ____________________
Healthcare organization: Meadville Medical Center

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT ASSESSMENT
SSN: 931-48-8980

Patient: tomas ogden
The patient, age 72, was reviewed in the ED for worsening abdominal pain.

Chief Complaint:
Right lower-quadrant abdominal pain with nausea and loss of appetite.

History of Present Illness:
Pain began around the umbilicus and migrated to the right lower quadrant, becoming constant and sharper with walking or coughing. The patient reports nausea and minimal oral intake but no vomiting. No diarrhea, dysuria, hematuria, chest pain, or shortness of breath. No prior abdominal surgery is reported. Last oral intake was earlier today. At 08:15, nursing documentation noted persistent pain despite initial acetaminophen.

Examination:
Appears uncomfortable but alert and cooperative. Temperature 100.4°F, heart rate 104, blood pressure 128/76, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Mucous membranes mildly dry. Abdomen is soft with focal right lower-quadrant tenderness, guarding, and pain with percussion; no diffuse rigidity. Positive focal tenderness at McBurney point. No costovertebral angle tenderness. Cardiorespiratory examination is unremarkable.

Investigations:
CBC demonstrates leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance. Comprehensive metabolic panel shows preserved renal function and no significant electrolyte abnormality. Serum lactate is normal. Urinalysis has concentrated urine without convincing evidence of infection. CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast demonstrates an enlarged fluid-filled appendix with surrounding inflammatory stranding, consistent with acute uncomplicated appendicitis; no abscess, perforation, or bowel obstruction.

Medical Decision-Making:
Findings are most consistent with acute appendicitis. Differential considerations included ureteral stone, urinary infection, gastroenteritis, and gynecologic pathology where clinically applicable, but imaging and examination favor appendicitis. The patient remained hemodynamically stable without evidence of perforation or sepsis.

Treatment:
IV fluids initiated. Acetaminophen administered for pain, with antiemetic therapy as needed. Ampicillin-sulbactam given after review of allergies and renal function. The patient was kept NPO. General surgery was consulted through NEWPORT HOSPITAL, and operative management was recommended.

Disposition:
Admit to the surgical service for laparoscopic appendectomy evaluation and continued IV antibiotics. Return precautions and the anticipated inpatient course were reviewed with the patient. Follow-up with surgery is arranged for January 21, 2027 if discharge occurs before that review.

Signed electronically by Heily Metellus, MD, Emergency Medicine.

Referral to Gastroenterology

Patient: Westen Donnan
MRN: 0423144
Referring organization: MCLEOD REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER-PEE DEE

Dear Gastroenterology Service,

I am referring Westen Donnan for evaluation of persistent symptoms consistent with gastroesophageal reflux disease, with a specific question of whether additional testing or upper endoscopy is needed because symptoms continue despite initial treatment.

The patient describes retrosternal burning several times each week, acid regurgitation after meals and when lying down, and a night-time cough that can interrupt sleep. The cough has been present for 3 days and is not associated with fever, wheezing, shortness of breath, or hemoptysis. There is no reported difficulty swallowing, painful swallowing, vomiting, vomiting of blood, black stool, or unintentional weight loss. Appetite remains stable.

Current treatment is omeprazole taken before breakfast and alginate suspension as needed after meals and at bedtime. The patient reports taking the omeprazole consistently but has had only partial relief. We reviewed practical measures, including avoiding meals close to bedtime, raising the head of the bed, limiting foods that clearly trigger symptoms, and avoiding tobacco and excess alcohol. The patient has not reported regular use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

At the most recent primary care assessment, the patient was comfortable and speaking in full sentences. Abdominal examination showed a soft, nondistended abdomen without focal tenderness, guarding, or rebound. There was no clinical evidence of dehydration. The night-time cough appears temporally related to reflux symptoms, although an upper-airway or pulmonary contributor should be considered if it persists after better acid control.

Please assess the ongoing reflux symptoms and determine whether endoscopy, ambulatory pH monitoring, or esophageal manometry is appropriate. I would also appreciate recommendations regarding medication timing, dose adjustment, and the duration of acid-suppression therapy. If symptoms remain uncomplicated and improve with optimized treatment, guidance on follow-up in primary care would be helpful.

The patient understands the reason for referral and agrees with the proposed evaluation. Please send your recommendations back to our office.

Sincerely,

ramzi brilliant
Referring clinician
Professional identifier: 073573181
MCLEOD REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER-PEE DEE

LABORATORY MEDICINE INTERPRETIVE REPORT

Patient: Neeley Abrante
Age: 41 y/o
MRN: 03773476
Specimen context: Inpatient evaluation of reduced urine output, fatigue, and poor oral intake. Patient is receiving intravenous sodium chloride; temporary medication hold is documented. Ordering clinician not specified in this laboratory report.

Specimen received: Serum and urine specimens obtained during the current acute-care evaluation. Results below are interpreted with the available clinical context. Hemolysis index was not significant. Specimen integrity was acceptable for analysis.

CHEMISTRY

Analyte                         Result             Reference interval
Sodium                          133 mmol/L         135–145 mmol/L
Potassium                       4.8 mmol/L         3.5–5.1 mmol/L
Chloride                        98 mmol/L          98–108 mmol/L
Total carbon dioxide            21 mmol/L          22–29 mmol/L
Blood urea nitrogen             48 mg/dL           7–20 mg/dL
Creatinine                      2.36 mg/dL         0.60–1.30 mg/dL
Estimated GFR                   31 mL/min/1.73 m²  ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m²
Glucose                         104 mg/dL          70–99 mg/dL
Calcium                         8.7 mg/dL          8.5–10.5 mg/dL
Albumin                         3.8 g/dL           3.5–5.0 g/dL
Aspartate aminotransferase      22 U/L             10–40 U/L
Alanine aminotransferase        18 U/L             7–56 U/L

URINALYSIS

Appearance: Concentrated, clear
Specific gravity: 1.025
pH: 5.5
Protein: 1+
Blood: Negative
Leukocyte esterase: Negative
Nitrite: Negative
Microscopy: 0–2 RBCs/hpf; 0–2 WBCs/hpf; rare hyaline casts; no granular casts identified

Urine sodium: 18 mmol/L
Fractional excretion of sodium: 0.5%

INTERPRETATION

The serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen are elevated, with a reduced estimated GFR, consistent with acute kidney injury in the stated clinical setting. Concentrated urine, low urine sodium, and a fractional excretion of sodium of 0.5% support a renal hypoperfusion component, such as volume depletion associated with poor oral intake. Urinalysis does not show significant hematuria, pyuria, or active sediment to suggest a primary glomerular or interstitial inflammatory process.

The mildly decreased sodium and total carbon dioxide should be reassessed with serial chemistry testing. Potassium is currently within the laboratory reference interval but warrants continued monitoring because kidney function is impaired. Correlation with prior creatinine values, cumulative intake and output, blood pressure, and medication exposure is recommended. Renal ultrasound may be considered if renal function fails to improve or if obstruction is clinically suspected.

CLINICAL COMMENT

Continue careful volume assessment and documentation of urine output while intravenous sodium chloride is administered. The temporary medication hold should be reviewed against the outpatient medication list, with particular attention to agents that may worsen renal perfusion or require renal dose adjustment. Repeat basic metabolic testing is appropriate after initial management and sooner for worsening oliguria, hyperkalemia, acidemia, or hemodynamic instability.

A laboratory review is planned in about 7 weeks, with follow-up appointment date August 24th, 2035. Earlier testing is recommended if creatinine does not trend toward baseline.

Validated and electronically signed by kainat hojnicki, laboratory medicine clinician.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: E. Mortenson
Home address: 651 200 West St, Logan, UT 84321
Admission diagnosis: First-trimester hyperemesis with dehydration and weight loss
Discharge diagnosis: First-trimester hyperemesis, improved

Reason for admission
The patient, at 9+4 weeks' gestation, presented after several days of persistent vomiting with inability to tolerate fluids or prescribed oral medications. She reported decreased urine output, dizziness when standing, and unintentional weight loss. She denied vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain, fever, diarrhea, or urinary symptoms.

Key findings
Initial examination was notable for dry oral mucosa and mild orthostatic symptoms without abdominal tenderness or peritoneal signs. Urinalysis showed concentrated urine with ketones. Serum chemistry demonstrated mild hypokalemia and bicarbonate reduction consistent with volume depletion; creatinine remained within the expected range. CBC showed no significant anemia or leukocytosis. Quantitative pregnancy testing was appropriate for the reported gestational duration. Obstetric ultrasound confirmed a single intrauterine pregnancy with cardiac activity and no acute abnormality identified.

Hospital course
The patient received intravenous sodium chloride, electrolyte replacement, and thiamine before dextrose-containing fluids. Antiemetic therapy was given initially by intravenous route, then transitioned to oral therapy as vomiting subsided. Doxylamine-pyridoxine was restarted on a scheduled basis. Oral intake advanced from ice chips to bland solids without recurrent emesis. Urine output and orthostatic symptoms improved, and repeat metabolic testing showed correction of the potassium abnormality.

Laboratory report/accession ID: 0151886867

Discharge medications
• Doxylamine-pyridoxine: continue as prescribed on the discharge medication reconciliation.
• Oral electrolyte-containing fluids in small, frequent amounts.
• Avoid nonprescribed antiemetics or herbal products unless reviewed by the prenatal clinician.

Instructions and follow-up
Eat small meals every 1–2 hours, emphasizing protein-containing foods as tolerated. Take fluids in frequent sips rather than large volumes. Return to the emergency department for inability to keep fluids down for 12 hours, fainting, blood in vomit, severe abdominal or pelvic pain, fever, vaginal bleeding, or markedly decreased urination.

Follow up with the prenatal care office for reassessment of hydration, weight, electrolytes, and medication response. The patient was discharged home ambulatory, hemodynamically stable, tolerating oral intake, and understanding the return precautions.

Discharging clinician: M. Odell, professional ID 051048399

ED Evaluation

Patient: jolie mira, Age: 27 y/o. Contact detail: jolie.mira71@hotmail.com
Home address: 99 State Rte 103, Westford, VT 05494

Chief complaint: Persistent vomiting in early pregnancy.

HPI: Presents with 5 days of near-continuous emesis and inability to keep down fluids or prenatal vitamins. Reports approximately 6-lb weight loss over 1 week, lightheadedness when standing, and decreased urine output. No hematemesis, abdominal pain, fever, dysuria, vaginal bleeding, or syncope. Current gestational age 9+4 weeks' gestation. Taking doxylamine-pyridoxine with minimal relief.

Your family history suggests that an inherited cancer-predisposition condition should be considered. The information available today is not enough to determine your personal risk with certainty, and a negative result would not eliminate the need for routine age-appropriate screening. Discharge Summary

Patient: heysell torresgonzalez
Admission/discharge date: March 8, 2021

68-year-old Asian male patient admitted with two days of worsening right flank pain, dysuria, urinary frequency, fever, and rigors. On arrival, temperature was 38.7°C, heart rate 112, and blood pressure 104/66 mmHg. The patient reported a current pain score of 5/10. Examination showed right costovertebral angle tenderness without peritoneal signs. There was no nausea, vomiting, or concern for pregnancy documented.

Initial urinalysis demonstrated moderate leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, numerous white blood cells, and moderate blood. White blood cell count was 14.8 K/µL with neutrophil predominance. Serum creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL, and lactate was 1.6 mmol/L. A urine culture was obtained before antibiotics and subsequently grew greater than 100,000 CFU/mL of a susceptible gram-negative organism. Blood cultures remained negative. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis or visible obstructing stone.

Hospital course

The patient received intravenous fluids, ceftriaxone, and acetaminophen with improvement in fever, tachycardia, and flank discomfort. No procedure was required. After clinical improvement and review of culture susceptibility results, therapy was transitioned to oral cefuroxime. The patient tolerated oral intake, remained hemodynamically stable, and had no recurrent rigors. At discharge, flank pain was mild, dysuria was substantially improved, and the patient was able to ambulate independently.

Assessment and plan

Acute pyelonephritis, improving with antimicrobial therapy. Complete cefuroxime as prescribed for the full course, even if symptoms resolve early. Acetaminophen may be used for pain or fever according to the discharge bottle instructions; do not exceed the recommended daily amount or combine it with other acetaminophen-containing products. Encourage adequate oral fluids unless another clinician has instructed otherwise.

Return to the emergency department for recurrent high fever, shaking chills, worsening flank or abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, confusion, fainting, inability to urinate, rash, facial swelling, or difficulty breathing. Follow up with primary care within one week to confirm continued recovery and review the final urine culture. If symptoms have not clearly improved within 48–72 hours, seek medical reassessment sooner.

The patient’s discharge instructions and medication changes were reviewed verbally, and understanding was confirmed. The patient requested electronic follow-up communication at heysell.torresgonzalez47@gmail.com. Home mailing address on file: 356 Missle Rd, Wyarno, WY 82845. Condition at discharge is stable.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: Christ
Discharge date: Dec 9, 2028
Admitting service: Medicine
Treating organization: COMMONWEALTH HEALTH CENTER

Reason for admission:
Christ was admitted for approximately 2 days of frequent watery diarrhea, several episodes of nonbloody vomiting, and intermittent lower abdominal cramps. Oral intake had been poor, with associated weakness and lightheadedness when standing. The patient denied recent antibiotic use, hematemesis, melena, chest pain, or urinary symptoms. A relative, Johnthomas Pettit from Saipan, assisted with the history and discharge planning.

Initial evaluation:
On arrival, the patient was mildly tachycardic with dry oral mucosa but remained normotensive and afebrile. The abdomen was mildly diffusely tender without guarding, rebound, or focal peritoneal findings. There was no clinical evidence of sepsis or acute surgical abdomen. Laboratory testing showed mild hemoconcentration and borderline hypokalemia consistent with gastrointestinal fluid loss. Liver tests and lipase were unremarkable. Renal function remained preserved; creatinine 1.1 mg/dL was documented during the evaluation. Stool testing was negative for Clostridioides difficile toxin and did not identify a bacterial enteric pathogen. Viral gastroenteritis was considered most likely based on the acute course and unrevealing infectious studies.

Hospital course:
The patient received intravenous isotonic fluids, electrolyte replacement, and ondansetron for nausea. Vomiting resolved during the first hospital day, and abdominal cramping improved without narcotic medication. Diarrhea gradually decreased in frequency, with no blood noted at any point. The patient was advanced from clear liquids to a bland, low-fat diet and tolerated oral intake before discharge. Repeat metabolic testing showed improvement in the potassium level and stable renal function. No antibiotics were indicated.

A brief episode of dizziness with standing resolved after additional fluids. Orthostatic symptoms were absent on reassessment, and the patient was ambulatory without assistance. There were no cardiopulmonary complications, fever, or altered mental status.

Discharge diagnoses:
1. Acute infectious gastroenteritis, improving
2. Volume depletion due to vomiting and diarrhea, resolved
3. Mild hypokalemia, corrected
4. Nausea and abdominal cramping, improved

Medications at discharge:
• Oral rehydration solution: Drink frequent small amounts throughout the day and replace fluid after each loose stool.
• Ondansetron as required for nausea, according to the prescribed label instructions.
No new antibiotic, antidiarrheal, or opioid medication was prescribed. The patient was advised to avoid alcohol, greasy foods, and dairy products until symptoms have fully settled. Resume other routine medicines as previously directed.

Condition at discharge:
Stable, tolerating oral fluids and food, with substantially improved nausea and diarrhea. The patient verbalized understanding of the medication plan, hydration instructions, and warning signs. Discharge teaching was reviewed with Johnthomas Pettit as requested.

Follow-up and return precautions:
Arrange follow-up with a primary care clinician after recovery, or sooner if symptoms fail to continue improving. Return to the ED for inability to keep fluids down, fainting, confusion, severe or localized abdominal pain, bloody or black stools, persistent fever, markedly reduced urination, or worsening weakness. Wash hands carefully, avoid preparing food for others while diarrhea persists, and remain home from work or school until at least 24 hours after the last episode of vomiting or diarrhea.

To the Hereditary Cancer Genetics Team,

I am referring Kirkland for formal hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk assessment and counseling. The specific clinical question is whether her family history meets criteria for germline testing and, if so, which testing strategy would provide the most useful information for her and her relatives.

Kirkland reports a significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer across more than one generation. She is understandably concerned about her own future cancer risk and has requested predictive testing. During our discussion, I explained that a genetic result may be positive, negative, or indeterminate, and that a negative result does not always eliminate risk when the family history remains strong. We also reviewed the possible effects of testing on screening recommendations and the value of testing an affected relative first, when that option is available.

The family history currently includes a relative with a previously reported BRCA1 c.68_69delAG variant under genetics review. The source documentation and laboratory report should be obtained and confirmed before using this result to guide testing. If the familial variant is verified, targeted analysis may be appropriate; otherwise, please advise whether a multigene hereditary cancer panel is preferable.

She has no current treatment and is not taking prescription or over-the-counter medications for this concern. No breast or ovarian cancer symptoms were reported at this visit. The examination was nonacute, with no reported breast mass, nipple discharge, abdominal distention, or pelvic pain. This referral is for risk assessment rather than evaluation of an active cancer diagnosis.

Please provide pretest counseling, review the pedigree in detail, confirm the reported familial variant, and discuss the benefits, limitations, and potential insurance or privacy implications of testing. If testing proceeds, I would appreciate recommendations for individualized breast screening and consideration of risk-reducing options based on the final result and updated family history. Please also clarify whether cascade testing should be offered to relatives.

I am sending this referral through Alaska Native Medical Center from Anchorage. The referring clinician is H. Allegrezza, professional identifier 098247515. Please return your consultation findings and testing recommendations to our office so that we can review them with Kirkland and coordinate follow-up.

Discharge Summary

Patient: Arron M.
MRN: 018526105
Discharging organization: RIO GRANDE HOSPITAL
Attending clinician: N. Botwinick, Professional ID: 081746655

You were admitted to RIO GRANDE HOSPITAL after developing central chest pressure with sweating and nausea. Your initial evaluation and serial heart tests were consistent with a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), meaning that part of the heart muscle was not receiving enough oxygen even though the electrocardiogram did not show the classic ST-elevation pattern.

During your stay, you were monitored on a cardiac unit. Repeat cardiac enzyme testing showed a rise and subsequent decline consistent with a recent heart injury. The ECG did not show persistent ST elevation. Your chest discomfort improved, and you did not have recurrent symptoms after treatment. A heart ultrasound showed mildly reduced pumping function without a major valve problem. Kidney function and blood counts remained acceptable for discharge.

You received aspirin, fondaparinux, and high-intensity atorvastatin in the hospital. The cardiology team reviewed your results and recommended medical management with close outpatient follow-up. Please continue the following discharge medications exactly as listed on your medication bottle or final medication list:

• Aspirin, as directed, and do not stop it unless the prescribing clinician tells you to.
• Atorvastatin, as directed, preferably at the same time each evening.
• Any additional heart medicines provided on your final medication list.

Fondaparinux was used during hospitalization and is not to be continued at home unless specifically prescribed separately. Do not take ibuprofen, naproxen, or other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs unless a clinician confirms they are safe for you. Bring all medication bottles to your follow-up visit.

Your blood pressure before discharge was 120/80 mmHg. Walk slowly at first, avoid heavy lifting until cleared, and follow the heart-healthy eating plan discussed with the team. Do not smoke or use nicotine products. Arrange follow-up with your primary care clinician and cardiology as directed by RIO GRANDE HOSPITAL.

Call 911 immediately for chest pressure, shortness of breath, fainting, new severe weakness, or sweating with nausea, especially if symptoms last more than a few minutes or return after resting. Do not drive yourself to the emergency department.

At discharge, you were alert, able to walk safely, and tolerating food and medications. The discharge plan, warning signs, and medication instructions were reviewed with you, and your questions were answered.

Signed by N. Botwinick, Professional ID 081746655
