DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: Airy V.
The patient, age 79, was admitted for worsening shortness of breath when lying flat, bilateral ankle swelling, and a marked decline in exercise tolerance. Symptoms had progressed over approximately two weeks despite taking outpatient furosemide and bisoprolol. Vianney, the patient’s adult child and designated emergency contact, participated in medication reconciliation and discharge teaching; the family plans to assist from Burt.

Admission findings were consistent with acute on chronic decompensated heart failure. The patient was hypertensive on arrival, with blood pressure 164/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. Bibasilar crackles and 2+ lower-extremity edema were present. A subsequent stable outpatient-style reading of 120/80 mmHg was documented before discharge. Chest radiograph showed pulmonary vascular congestion and small bilateral pleural effusions. Electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus rhythm without acute ischemic changes. Initial laboratory testing showed elevated natriuretic peptide, creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, and mildly elevated liver enzymes consistent with congestion. Serial troponins were negative.

The patient received intravenous furosemide with strict intake and output monitoring, daily weights, sodium restriction, and fluid restriction. Urine output increased appropriately, and breathing improved over the first 48 hours. Supplemental oxygen was weaned to room air. Edema decreased to trace at the ankles, and the patient was able to walk in the hallway without significant dyspnea. Renal function remained stable, with discharge creatinine 1.1 mg/dL and potassium 4.0 mmol/L. Echocardiography showed reduced left ventricular systolic function with an estimated ejection fraction of 35%, global hypokinesis, and no hemodynamically significant valvular disease. No invasive procedure was required.

Problem list:
1. Acute on chronic systolic heart failure exacerbation, improved after diuresis.
2. Reduced left ventricular ejection fraction, 35%.
3. Hypertension.
4. Medication and dietary education needs.

Medication reconciliation was completed with the patient and family. Discharge medications are:
• Furosemide 40 mg by mouth every morning. This replaces the prior outpatient dose of 20 mg daily.
• Bisoprolol 5 mg by mouth every evening; continue.
• Lisinopril 5 mg by mouth every morning; start at discharge.
• Potassium chloride extended-release 20 mEq by mouth every morning; start at discharge while taking the increased furosemide dose.
• Aspirin 81 mg by mouth daily; continue.
• Acetaminophen 650 mg by mouth every 6 hours as needed for pain, not to exceed 3,000 mg in 24 hours.
The prior furosemide 20-mg regimen is discontinued. No other home medications were identified during reconciliation, and no unlisted medications should be restarted without review. Avoid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs unless specifically approved.

At discharge, the patient is afebrile, hemodynamically stable, euvolemic on examination, and appropriate for home. Follow up with primary care on December 21, 2025 for medication review and repeat basic metabolic panel. Cardiology follow-up should occur within two weeks. Obtain earlier evaluation for worsening shortness of breath, chest pain, fainting, confusion, inability to lie flat, or rapidly increasing swelling.

Weigh every morning after using the restroom and record the result. Call the care team for a gain of more than 2 pounds in one day or 5 pounds in one week. Follow a low-sodium diet, limit fluids to 1.5 liters daily unless otherwise directed, elevate the legs when sitting, and take medications exactly as listed. Do not stop bisoprolol, lisinopril, or furosemide without medical guidance.

The patient, age 65, presented to Centracare Health - Monticello with 2 days of watery diarrhea, four episodes of nonbloody emesis, and intermittent periumbilical abdominal cramps. Symptoms began after a shared meal. No fever, hematemesis, melena, dysuria, chest pain, or dyspnea. Tolerating only small sips. Took oral rehydration solution at home and ondansetron as required with partial relief.

Vitals: BP 108/72, HR 96, RR 18, Temp 99.1 F, SpO2 99% RA.

Low concern for appendicitis, obstruction, pancreatitis, or surgical abdomen. Given 1 L lactated Ringer’s IV and ondansetron 4 mg ODT; no further emesis in ED and tolerated oral fluids.

Disposition: Discharge home. Continue oral rehydration solution, small frequent sips, bland foods as tolerated. Ondansetron as required. Return for worsening pain, persistent vomiting, bloody stool, syncope, or inability to hydrate. Primary care follow-up in about 7 weeks, scheduled for Jun 18, 2026.

Reviewed by RENNY SAUSEN.

Referral Consultation: Asthma Evaluation

Dear Pulmonary Medicine Consultant,

I am referring Shterna for specialist assessment of recurrent wheezing and incomplete control of asthma symptoms. The specific clinical question is whether the current regimen should be stepped up and whether additional testing is indicated to clarify the severity and phenotype of the disease.

The patient reports intermittent expiratory wheeze, shortness of breath with exertion, and a dry night-time cough that has occurred for 3 days. Symptoms are more noticeable with cold air and during upper-respiratory illnesses. There has been no hemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, syncope, or documented fever. The patient has visited the emergency department once in the past year for breathing difficulty but was not admitted and has never required intubation. Family history is notable for asthma in a first-degree relative, Koa.

Current medications are an albuterol inhaler, two puffs by inhalation every 4 to 6 hours as needed, and a beclomethasone inhaler, two puffs twice daily. The patient reports using the controller medication on most days but acknowledges inconsistent adherence during periods of feeling well. Inhaler technique was reviewed in the office, including use of a spacer, slow inhalation, and breath holding after actuation. There is no reported tobacco or vaping exposure.

On examination today, the patient was speaking in full sentences without accessory muscle use. Respiratory rate was 18/min, oxygen saturation was 97% on room air, and pulse was 86/min. Mild bilateral expiratory wheezes were present, without crackles. Cardiac examination was regular, and there was no peripheral edema. Peak expiratory flow measured 320 L/min, approximately 72% of the patient’s personal best. After supervised albuterol administration, wheezing improved and peak flow increased to 360 L/min.

The clinical pattern is consistent with asthma with current variable airflow limitation and suboptimal symptom control, likely influenced by inconsistent inhaled corticosteroid use. I have advised continuation of beclomethasone twice daily, albuterol as the rescue medication, and avoidance of known triggers. The patient was instructed to seek urgent care for worsening breathlessness, inability to speak comfortably, cyanosis, or inadequate response to rescue therapy.

Please perform spirometry with bronchodilator response and assess whether fractional exhaled nitric oxide, allergy evaluation, or escalation to combination inhaled therapy is appropriate. Please also provide an individualized written asthma action plan and recommendations regarding follow-up frequency.

Referring clinician: LOVA REMM
Service locality: North Carrollton
Professional identifier: 069379857

Sincerely,

LOVA REMM

Discharge Summary

Patient: Ashawn L.
MRN: M9258100
Discharging clinician: achsah knaack
Healthcare organization: Renown South Meadows Medical Center

Admission reason
Presented with sudden breathlessness, pleuritic right-sided chest pain, and persistent tachycardia. Initial oxygen saturation was reduced on room air. CT pulmonary angiography demonstrated acute bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli without CT evidence of right-heart strain. Lower-extremity venous ultrasound showed no proximal DVT.

Hospital course
The patient was admitted for monitoring and anticoagulation. Apixaban was started after review of renal function and hemoglobin. Supplemental oxygen was required initially at low flow and was discontinued before discharge; oxygen saturation remained acceptable with ambulation. Troponin was negative, BNP was not elevated, and echocardiography showed normal right ventricular size and function. Chest pain and dyspnea improved substantially. No bleeding occurred.

Blood pressure was stable throughout the stay, including a reading of 120/80 mmHg. The patient remained afebrile and hemodynamically stable. No procedure was required.

Discharge medications
• Apixaban 10 mg by mouth twice daily to complete the initial treatment phase, then 5 mg twice daily as directed.
• Supplemental oxygen: not required at discharge.

Medication counseling included strict adherence, avoidance of NSAIDs unless specifically approved, and prompt evaluation for bleeding. The patient was instructed to seek emergency care for worsening shortness of breath, syncope, severe chest pain, coughing blood, black stools, or uncontrolled bleeding.

Follow-up
Follow up with primary care and the pulmonary/thromboembolism clinic associated with Renown South Meadows Medical Center for anticoagulation management and evaluation of treatment duration. Review age-appropriate cancer screening and potential provoking factors at outpatient follow-up. No driving or strenuous activity until symptoms have continued to improve.

The patient’s relative, who resides in Sparks, was included in discharge teaching by phone. At discharge, the patient was ambulatory, breathing comfortably without supplemental oxygen, tolerating oral intake, and verbalized understanding of the medication plan and return precautions.

Signed,
achsah knaack

Emergency Department Assessment

Patient: KARMA HOLZUM
DOB: April 25, 1984
Home address: 157 W Hollis Rd, Grafton, NH 03240
Contact detail: (617) 555-0118

The patient is an adult woman presenting with three days of gradually worsening lower abdominal pain, now more prominent on the right and left pelvic sides. She reports increased yellow-gray vaginal discharge with an unpleasant odor and pain during intercourse. She denies vaginal bleeding, fever, vomiting, diarrhea, dysuria, flank pain, or syncope. Her last menstrual period was not associated with unusual bleeding. She has taken acetaminophen with partial relief; current pelvic pain is 5/10. No medication allergies are documented.

On arrival, she is awake, conversant, and mildly uncomfortable but not toxic appearing. Temperature is 99.1°F, heart rate 92, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The abdomen is soft with mild suprapubic and bilateral lower-quadrant tenderness, without guarding or rebound. Pelvic examination demonstrates moderate mucopurulent discharge from the cervical os, cervical motion tenderness, and bilateral adnexal tenderness without a palpable mass. There is no significant vaginal bleeding. No costovertebral angle tenderness is present.

Urine pregnancy testing is negative. Urinalysis shows trace leukocyte esterase but no convincing evidence of urinary tract infection. CBC shows no leukocytosis and hemoglobin is within the expected range. Comprehensive metabolic testing is unremarkable. Vaginal testing is positive for bacterial vaginosis; trichomonas testing is negative. Gonorrhea and chlamydia nucleic acid testing was collected and remains pending at discharge. Report/accession ID: 08822318.

Assessment and medical decision-making: The clinical findings are most consistent with pelvic inflammatory disease with concurrent bacterial vaginosis. The patient has no peritoneal signs, hemodynamic instability, pregnancy, tubo-ovarian mass on pelvic ultrasound, or other finding requiring admission. Ovarian torsion and ectopic pregnancy are considered less likely given the gradual bilateral symptoms, negative pregnancy test, and reassuring examination and imaging. Appendicitis is also not supported by the current presentation.

Treatment and disposition: Ceftriaxone was administered in the ED. She was prescribed doxycycline and metronidazole and instructed to complete the full course, avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole, and abstain from sexual activity until treatment is completed, symptoms have resolved, and partners have been evaluated and treated. Acetaminophen or ibuprofen may be used as directed for discomfort. She was advised to notify recent sexual partners and to obtain repeat STI testing through primary care or the local health department.

She was discharged in stable condition with strict return precautions for worsening pain, fever, vomiting, fainting, heavy bleeding, or inability to tolerate medications. Follow-up with primary care or gynecology was recommended within 48–72 hours and when pending test results are available.

March 28th, 2012

Dear Endocrinology Consultation Service,

I am referring mynor maclauchlan for evaluation and management of persistent primary hypothyroidism despite reported adherence to levothyroxine. The specific question is whether the current replacement dose is inadequate or whether an absorption or administration issue is contributing to the ongoing biochemical abnormality.

Over the past several months, the patient has described daily fatigue, increased sensitivity to cold, and constipation occurring approximately every two to three days. There has been no chest pain, palpitations, tremor, unexplained weight loss, dysphagia, or neck pressure. The patient reports taking levothyroxine each morning with water, although breakfast and coffee may follow within 15 to 20 minutes. Calcium-containing supplements are taken later in the day. There is no reported use of amiodarone, lithium, or biotin.

On examination today, the patient was alert and in no acute distress. Blood pressure and heart rate were within the patient's usual range. The thyroid was not visibly enlarged, and I did not appreciate a discrete nodule or cervical lymphadenopathy. Skin was mildly dry. There was no peripheral edema, tremor, or proximal muscle weakness. Cardiac and pulmonary examinations were unremarkable, and the abdomen was soft without focal tenderness.

Recent laboratory testing showed TSH 8.2 mIU/L. Free T4 was at the low end of the reference range. The associated accession identifier is 051493804. A repeat TSH and free T4 have been ordered, along with a basic metabolic panel and CBC to assess other contributors to fatigue. No medication changes have been made pending confirmation of the results and specialist input.

Current medication is levothyroxine at the previously prescribed daily dose. The patient denies missed doses but acknowledges that the timing relative to breakfast has not been consistent. We reviewed taking the medication on an empty stomach with water and separating it from calcium, iron, and fiber supplements by at least four hours.

Assessment

Persistent symptomatic hypothyroidism with elevated TSH while taking levothyroxine. Inconsistent administration timing may be contributing, although dose adjustment or another cause of impaired absorption should be considered.

Requested action

Please assess the appropriate levothyroxine dose, review administration and absorption factors, and advise whether additional testing is indicated, including thyroid peroxidase antibodies or evaluation for gastrointestinal malabsorption. Please return recommendations to Shore Medical Center.

Sincerely,

Alexiana Haddox, MD

Primary Care Clinic Note

Date: April 4, 2020
Patient: Niran R.
Age: 30 y/o
Contact: (202) 555-0184

Niran R. presents for evaluation of worsening asthma symptoms. The patient reports intermittent wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath, particularly at night and with brisk walking. A dry cough has been present for 3 days and is now waking the patient several times overnight. There has been no fever, chills, sore throat, productive sputum, hemoptysis, or known sick contact. The patient has been using the albuterol inhaler more frequently than usual, with temporary relief. Beclomethasone inhaler is being taken as prescribed, although the patient admits occasionally missing the evening dose.

No recent emergency department visits, hospitalizations, oral steroid courses, or intubations were reported. The patient denies chest pain, syncope, leg swelling, or symptoms suggestive of reflux. There is no tobacco or vaping use. The patient reports that symptoms are often worse during spring pollen exposure and when cleaning a dusty room.

On examination, the patient is alert and speaking in complete sentences without apparent distress. Temperature and oxygen saturation are normal on room air. Mild expiratory wheezes are heard bilaterally, without rales or focal diminution of breath sounds. Cardiac examination shows a regular rhythm without murmur. There is no peripheral edema, and the oropharynx is clear. Peak flow in the office is reduced from the patient’s reported usual baseline. Report/accession ID: S23-0838920.

Assessment:
Asthma with mild acute worsening, likely related to environmental triggers and inconsistent controller use. No current findings to suggest pneumonia, acute heart failure, or respiratory failure.

Plan:
The patient was advised to continue beclomethasone inhaler twice daily every day, with a review of rinsing the mouth after each use. Albuterol inhaler may be used as a rescue medication for wheezing or shortness of breath, with instructions to seek care if it is needed more often than every four hours or provides inadequate relief. Inhaler technique was demonstrated and corrected, including use of a spacer.

Environmental measures were discussed, including reducing dust exposure, keeping windows closed during high-pollen periods, and washing bedding regularly. The patient will monitor nighttime symptoms and rescue-inhaler frequency. Follow-up is recommended in approximately four weeks for reassessment and consideration of spirometry if control remains suboptimal. Emergency precautions were reviewed for severe shortness of breath, inability to speak comfortably, blue lips, confusion, or poor response to albuterol.

SSN: 999609875

Date: February 6th, 2022
Patient: Nikola
Report/accession ID: 0364504853

Chief Complaint
Increasing redness, drainage, and pain at a recent surgical incision.

History of Present Illness
Nikola presents with approximately 2 days of worsening tenderness and redness around a postoperative wound. The patient noticed thick yellow drainage this morning and reports localized pain with movement. No measured fever, shaking chills, vomiting, chest pain, or shortness of breath. The patient has been changing the dressing at home and has not taken antibiotics before arrival. L. Pomije, identified as the patient’s relative, is present and assists with the history.

Past Medical/Surgical History
Recent surgery with an incision at the affected site; operative details were reviewed in the available record. No additional history provided today.

Medications and Allergies
Home medications reviewed. No current antibiotic therapy. No medication allergy was reported during this encounter.

Focused Examination
Triage vital signs reviewed and within acceptable range. Patient is alert, conversant, and nontoxic appearing. The surgical incision has surrounding erythema and warmth with mild induration. A small amount of purulent discharge is expressed from the superficial wound edge. Local pain is present with palpation. No wound dehiscence, crepitus, fluctuance extending beyond the incision, lymphangitic streaking, or neurovascular deficit is identified. Abdomen is soft and without diffuse tenderness. No evidence of systemic toxicity.

Investigations
- CBC without leukocytosis or significant anemia.
- Basic metabolic panel without clinically important electrolyte or renal abnormality.
- Wound drainage sent for culture; Report/accession ID: 0364504853.
- Bedside ultrasound demonstrates superficial inflammatory change without a drainable fluid collection.

Medical Decision-Making
Findings are most consistent with a localized postoperative wound infection and superficial cellulitis. There is no current evidence of necrotizing infection, deep abscess, wound disruption, or sepsis. The case was discussed with the surgical service at Adena Fayette Medical Center, which recommends outpatient treatment, local wound care, and close reassessment. Wound culture results will be reviewed when available.

The wound was cleansed and irrigated with sterile saline, then covered with a clean dressing. Dicloxacillin was initiated, with dosing and completion instructions reviewed. 2023-10-03

Referral: Evaluation of Lumbar Radiculopathy

Patient: Dafny C.
Address: 596 S Ripley Rd, Nashoba, OK 74558
Occupation: Journalist

Dear Spine Specialist,

I am referring Dafny C. for specialist assessment of persistent low back pain with right-sided shooting leg pain and intermittent paresthesia. The clinical question is whether the patient has a compressive lumbar nerve-root process that would benefit from advanced imaging, targeted injection, or surgical consultation.

Symptoms began gradually and have continued despite conservative treatment. The pain is centered in the lower lumbar region and radiates through the right buttock and posterior thigh toward the lateral calf. The patient describes intermittent tingling in the same distribution, without reported saddle anesthesia, bowel or bladder incontinence, or progressive foot drop. Current pain is rated 5/10. Prolonged sitting, bending, and lifting worsen the symptoms; brief walking and position changes provide partial relief. Sleep is occasionally interrupted by leg discomfort.

Current medications are naproxen and acetaminophen, used as directed for pain. The patient has also attempted activity modification, home lumbar stretching, and heat application with incomplete improvement. No opioid medication is being used. There is no reported recent trauma, fever, unexplained weight loss, or history suggestive of active malignancy or infection.

On examination, the patient was alert and ambulatory with a mildly antalgic gait. Lumbar flexion was limited by pain, while extension was less restricted. Right straight-leg raise reproduced posterior leg pain at approximately 50 degrees; the left side was negative. Mild right ankle dorsiflexion weakness was noted compared with the left, although the patient was able to heel-walk. Patellar reflexes were symmetric, and the right Achilles reflex was slightly reduced. Light-touch sensation was diminished over the right lateral calf and dorsum of the foot. There was no clonus. Hip range of motion was preserved bilaterally, and peripheral pulses were intact.

The pattern of radiating pain, sensory change, provocation with straight-leg raise, and subtle focal motor and reflex findings is concerning for lumbar radiculopathy, most likely involving the right L5 or S1 distribution. The duration and functional impact, together with incomplete response to medication and home therapy, support further evaluation. Please obtain or review lumbar spine MRI as clinically indicated and advise whether formal physical therapy, epidural steroid injection, electrodiagnostic testing, or surgical evaluation is appropriate. Please also provide guidance regarding medication optimization and activity restrictions.

Thank you for evaluating this patient. I will continue primary care follow-up and reassess promptly for any new weakness, gait deterioration, or bowel or bladder symptoms.

Sincerely,

K. Malnory
Referring Physician

Primary Care Follow-Up

Patient: JEWELZ VASCONCELOS
MRN: 0569508

Dear JEWELZ VASCONCELOS,

Today we reviewed the symptoms that have been bothering you, including ongoing fatigue, feeling unusually cold, and constipation. Taken together with your history, these concerns remain consistent with hypothyroidism. You do not report chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting, or new swelling. Your appetite is stable, and there has been no recent unexplained weight change.

Your office examination was reassuring. You were alert and conversant, with normal heart rhythm and clear breath sounds. The thyroid was not visibly enlarged or tender. There was no lower-extremity swelling, and your neurologic screening was normal. Your blood pressure and pulse were within the expected range for this visit.

Please continue levothyroxine 75 micrograms once daily. Take it with water on an empty stomach, ideally 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast. Avoid taking calcium, iron, antacids, or a multivitamin during the four hours after the dose, since these products can reduce absorption. If you miss a dose, take it when remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose; do not double the next dose.

We will obtain a thyroid-stimulating hormone level and free T4 to determine whether your current dose is adequate. The blood draw does not require fasting. Because symptoms often improve gradually, please allow several weeks after any dose adjustment before judging the full effect. Continue regular fluids and add fiber gradually through vegetables, fruit, beans, and whole grains to help with constipation. Gentle daily activity may also help with energy and bowel regularity.

Occupation: Journalist

Contact the office sooner if you develop palpitations, tremor, severe diarrhea, marked worsening of fatigue, confusion, or difficulty breathing. Otherwise, we will review the laboratory results and contact you if a medication change is needed. Please schedule a follow-up visit in approximately 6 to 8 weeks, or earlier if symptoms worsen.

Sincerely,

C. Farkash
Primary Care Clinician
Westerly Hospital

LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: Chelsie
Home address: 267 US Hwy 82 Bus, Coolidge, TX 76635
Report/accession ID: 096926719
Specimen collection/report date: May 19, 1988

Clinical indication:
Evaluation and staging support for Hodgkin lymphoma in the setting of painless lymphadenopathy, drenching night sweats, and unintentional weight loss. Current management is supportive care pending tissue diagnosis.

Specimens:
Peripheral blood collected in EDTA and serum separator tubes. Specimen received for testing on the reported date. Sample integrity was acceptable, with no significant hemolysis or clotting identified.

Complete blood count:
White blood cell count: 11.8 x10^3/µL (reference range 4.0–10.5 x10^3/µL) — High
Hemoglobin: 10.9 g/dL (reference range 12.0–16.0 g/dL) — Low
Hematocrit: 33.4% (reference range 36.0–46.0%) — Low
Mean corpuscular volume: 84.6 fL (reference range 80.0–100.0 fL)
Platelets: 462 x10^3/µL (reference range 150–400 x10^3/µL) — High
Absolute neutrophil count: 9.2 x10^3/µL (reference range 1.8–7.7 x10^3/µL) — High
Absolute lymphocyte count: 1.4 x10^3/µL (reference range 1.0–4.8 x10^3/µL)

Chemistry and inflammatory markers:
Creatinine: 0.78 mg/dL (reference range 0.60–1.20 mg/dL)
Aspartate aminotransferase: 22 U/L (reference range 10–40 U/L)
Alanine aminotransferase: 19 U/L (reference range 7–56 U/L)
Albumin: 3.2 g/dL (reference range 3.5–5.0 g/dL) — Low
Lactate dehydrogenase: 286 U/L (reference range 120–246 U/L) — High
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 68 mm/hr (reference range 0–20 mm/hr) — High
C-reactive protein: 7.8 mg/dL (reference range <0.5 mg/dL) — High

Interpretation:
The results demonstrate a mild normocytic anemia with neutrophilic leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminemia, and elevated inflammatory markers. This pattern is compatible with an active inflammatory or lymphoproliferative process and may be seen in Hodgkin lymphoma. The elevated lactate dehydrogenase is nonspecific but supports correlation with disease burden and imaging findings.

Peripheral blood flow cytometry shows no immunophenotypically aberrant B-cell or T-cell population. This finding does not exclude nodal Hodgkin lymphoma, which is generally diagnosed by excisional or core lymph-node biopsy with appropriate immunohistochemical studies. Recommend correlation with tissue pathology, cross-sectional imaging, and oncology evaluation. Results should be interpreted with the clinical examination and staging workup.

Validated and reported by:
Destyn Siepker, MD

Review of systems is otherwise negative for fever, chest pain, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, urinary retention, or constipation requiring medication.

On examination, the patient is alert, conversant, and in no acute distress. Speech is slightly soft but clear. There is a low-amplitude resting tremor of the right hand that lessens with action. Facial expression is mildly reduced. Bradykinesia is present with finger tapping and rapid alternating movements, right greater than left. Mild muscular rigidity is noted at both elbows, also greater on the right. Strength is 5/5 throughout, sensation is intact, and gait is slow with decreased right arm swing. The patient turns in several small steps but remains steady without assistance. No freezing is observed in the office.

Assessment: Parkinson disease with resting tremor, bradykinesia, and rigidity. Current response to carbidopa-levodopa is partial, without significant adverse effects.

Plan: Continue carbidopa-levodopa at the current prescribed dose and timing; take doses consistently and avoid taking them immediately with a high-protein meal if this appears to reduce benefit. The patient will keep a brief log of medication times, mobility, tremor, and wearing-off symptoms. Fall-prevention measures were reviewed, including removing loose rugs, improving lighting, and using handrails. Regular walking and gentle stretching were encouraged as tolerated. Referral to physical therapy for gait and balance training was discussed. Neurology follow-up will be arranged for medication adjustment and ongoing management. Return to primary care sooner for falls, fainting, hallucinations, abrupt worsening, or medication intolerance.

There is no hemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, leg swelling, syncope, or known sick contact. The patient denies measured fever but describes fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance. Oral intake remains adequate.

Past pulmonary history is notable for COPD with a similar flare last winter. The patient is not on home oxygen and has not required hospitalization or intubation for COPD. Current medications were reviewed, including albuterol inhaler, prednisone, and doxycycline. The patient has started prednisone 40 mg once daily for 5 days and doxycycline as prescribed, with the first doses taken this morning. No medication allergy was reported during the visit.

On examination, the patient was alert, speaking in full sentences, and mildly dyspneic after walking from the waiting area. Temperature was 98.6°F, blood pressure 136/78, pulse 92, respiratory rate 20, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Nasal mucosa was mildly congested. Cardiac examination showed a regular rhythm without murmur. Lung examination demonstrated diffuse expiratory wheezes and mildly prolonged expiration, without focal crackles or rhonchi. There was no peripheral edema or calf tenderness.

Assessment: Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, with increased breathlessness, wheezing, and purulent sputum. Current oxygenation and examination do not suggest acute respiratory failure or focal pneumonia requiring emergency transfer.

Plan: Continue prednisone 40 mg once daily for 5 days and complete the doxycycline course. Continue albuterol inhaler, two puffs every four to six hours as needed for wheezing or shortness of breath. The patient was advised to rest, maintain hydration, and avoid smoke and other inhaled irritants. A chest radiograph will be obtained if symptoms fail to improve or if fever, pleuritic pain, or focal respiratory findings develop. Maintenance inhaler therapy and pulmonary function testing will be revisited after this flare has resolved.

Strict ED precautions were reviewed for worsening breathlessness, inability to speak in full sentences, cyanosis, confusion, chest pain, or oxygen saturation persistently below 90% if checked at home. Follow-up in the office was recommended within one week, sooner for deterioration.

Discharge diagnosis: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, medically managed coronary artery disease, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia

Cardiology evaluated the patient on arrival. The attending cardiologist recommended an ischemia-guided strategy after discussion of risks and benefits. Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated mildly reduced left ventricular systolic function with an estimated ejection fraction of 50%, mild inferior wall hypokinesis, and no significant valvular disease.

Coronary angiography was performed through right radial access. It demonstrated moderate multivessel coronary artery disease without a focal lesion requiring immediate intervention. No stent was placed. The radial compression device was removed without bleeding, hematoma, or neurovascular deficit. Renal function remained stable after contrast exposure. Potassium and magnesium were replenished during the admission, and telemetry showed no clinically significant arrhythmia.

By discharge, the patient was walking independently, tolerating meals, and breathing comfortably on room air. Examination showed clear lungs, regular heart sounds without new murmur, and a clean, dry radial access site. There was no peripheral edema. - Cardiovascular: Positive for palpitations and exertional dyspnea. No chest pressure or syncope.
- Pulmonary: No cough or wheezing.

Vital signs:
BP 128/76, pulse 92 and irregular, respirations 16, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Weight stable from prior visit.

Alert, comfortable appearing, and speaking in full sentences. Cardiovascular examination reveals irregularly irregular rhythm without murmur, rub, or gallop. Lungs clear bilaterally with normal work of breathing. No jugular venous distention. Trace symmetric ankle edema. Neurologic examination grossly nonfocal.

Assessment:
1. Atrial fibrillation with intermittent symptomatic palpitations, fatigue, and exertional breathlessness. Rate is borderline controlled in the office. No evidence of acute heart failure, ischemia, or thromboembolic event today.
2. Chronic anticoagulation; currently tolerating therapy without reported bleeding.

Plan:
- Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily. Reinforced adherence and bleeding precautions.
- Continue bisoprolol at the current dose pending cardiology review; check home pulse and blood pressure once daily and bring log to follow-up.
- Obtain CBC, CMP, TSH, and magnesium. Arrange transthoracic echocardiogram and ambulatory rhythm monitoring.

- Return to primary care after testing, or sooner for worsening symptoms.

Patient: arjay lichtman
The 69-year-old Middle Eastern female patient presents with 24 hours of frequent watery diarrhea, four episodes of nonbloody vomiting, and intermittent, cramping periumbilical abdominal pain. Symptoms began after a shared meal at home. No fever, chest pain, dyspnea, dysuria, recent antibiotics, or known sick contacts. The patient reports decreased oral intake and urination but denies syncope. Oral rehydration solution was attempted at home. Ondansetron was taken as required with partial relief of nausea.

Home/contact information reviewed: 318 Piestewa Fwy, Second Mesa, AZ 86043. Preferred patient contact detail: (617) 555-0137.

EXAMINATION

Alert and cooperative, mildly uncomfortable but nontoxic. Oral mucosa is slightly dry. Temperature is 99.1°F, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 16, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Abdomen is soft and nondistended with mild diffuse tenderness, greatest in the periumbilical region. No guarding, rebound, focal right lower quadrant tenderness, or costovertebral angle tenderness. Bowel sounds are increased. No calf swelling; neurologic examination is grossly nonfocal.

INVESTIGATIONS

Point-of-care glucose is normal. CBC shows no leukocytosis or anemia. Comprehensive metabolic panel demonstrates preserved renal function and electrolytes without clinically significant abnormality. Lipase is normal. Urinalysis shows concentrated urine without infection. Pregnancy testing is negative when applicable. No indication for abdominal imaging at this time given the benign serial examinations and absence of peritoneal findings.

MEDICAL DECISION-MAKING

Presentation is most consistent with acute infectious gastroenteritis with mild volume depletion. There is no current evidence of appendicitis, bowel obstruction, pancreatitis, gastrointestinal bleeding, or sepsis. The patient received oral ondansetron in the ED followed by an oral rehydration challenge, which was tolerated without recurrent emesis. Abdominal discomfort improved, and repeat examination remained soft without guarding.

Treatment and discharge plan:
• Continue frequent small sips of oral rehydration solution.
• Use ondansetron as required for nausea according to the discharge prescription instructions.
• Advance from bland foods as tolerated; avoid alcohol and high-fat foods temporarily.
• Follow up with primary care if symptoms are not clearly improving within 48–72 hours.
• Return immediately for inability to keep fluids down, markedly decreased urination, bloody stool, persistent severe or localized pain, fainting, or fever.

DISPOSITION

Discharged home in stable condition with return precautions understood. Treating clinician: bexten dicosmo.

Caring clinician: A. Podowski

Patient was received resting in semi-Fowler position with oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula. She was awake, attentive, and able to answer questions appropriately, though she appeared fatigued after speaking in full sentences. She reports worsening shortness of breath when lying flat for 3 days, along with bilateral ankle swelling and reduced exercise tolerance. She denies chest pain, dizziness, fever, or new cough. Her relative, A. Husman, was updated at the bedside with the patient’s permission.

At assessment, respirations were 22/min and mildly labored with activity. Oxygen saturation was 94% on 2 L/min and 89% on room air during a brief repositioning trial; oxygen was reapplied with prompt improvement. Lung sounds were diminished at the bases with fine bibasilar crackles. Cardiac rhythm was regular on the monitor. Bilateral lower-extremity edema was 2+, extending from the ankles to the mid-shins. Skin was warm and intact, with no open areas noted. The patient denied calf pain. Blood pressure remained within the ordered parameters, and she had no acute change in mental status.

Assessment: Findings remain consistent with volume-overloaded heart failure. Respiratory status is improved at rest on low-flow oxygen but remains exertion-limited. The patient is at increased risk for falls because of weakness, dyspnea, and frequent toileting after diuretic therapy.

Plan for next shift: Continue oxygen as ordered, elevate the lower extremities when tolerated, maintain fall precautions, and assist with all transfers. PEDIATRIC LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: RISHAN MISRA
MRN: 00738841
Specimen: Plasma and urine
Ordering clinician: Not provided
Laboratory service: Pediatrics
Collection context: Outpatient evaluation for thirst, fatigue, and frequent urination in a 72-year-old Native American male patient. The specimen was received in acceptable condition.

RESULTS

Hemoglobin A1c: 8.7% (reference interval 4.0–5.6%)
Interpretation: Elevated; consistent with diabetes mellitus when correlated with clinical findings.

Glucose, plasma: 214 mg/dL (reference interval 70–99 mg/dL fasting)
Interpretation: Elevated. Fasting status was not documented.

C-peptide: 2.8 ng/mL (reference interval 1.1–4.4 ng/mL)
Interpretation: Detectable endogenous insulin production.

Beta-hydroxybutyrate: 0.18 mmol/L (reference interval 0.02–0.27 mmol/L)
Interpretation: Within reference interval.

Sodium: 137 mmol/L (reference interval 135–145 mmol/L)
Potassium: 4.3 mmol/L (reference interval 3.5–5.1 mmol/L)
Bicarbonate: 23 mmol/L (reference interval 22–29 mmol/L)
Creatinine: 0.62 mg/dL (pediatric reference interval varies by age and laboratory method)
ALT: 31 U/L (reference interval 7–40 U/L)
AST: 25 U/L (reference interval 10–40 U/L)

Urinalysis:
Specific gravity: 1.025 (reference interval 1.005–1.030)
Glucose: 3+
Ketones: Negative
Protein: Trace
Blood: Negative
Leukocyte esterase: Negative
Nitrite: Negative

INTERPRETIVE COMMENT

The elevated plasma glucose and hemoglobin A1c support diabetes mellitus. Detectable C-peptide, absence of ketonuria, normal beta-hydroxybutyrate, and preserved bicarbonate do not suggest diabetic ketoacidosis in this specimen. The overall pattern is compatible with the documented clinical diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus, although diabetes classification remains a clinical determination. If the phenotype or course is atypical, pancreatic autoantibody testing may be considered.

The mild urinary protein finding should be reassessed on a first-morning urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio after glycemic stabilization. Liver enzymes and creatinine are not elevated by the laboratory’s stated intervals. Results should be interpreted with examination findings, medication adherence, nutritional history, and home glucose data. Current medications include metformin and atorvastatin as documented by the ordering service.

Recommend pediatric diabetes follow-up, nutrition counseling, and review of glucose-monitoring technique. The family should seek urgent assessment for vomiting, abdominal pain, deep or rapid breathing, confusion, inability to maintain hydration, or moderate-to-large urine ketones. Repeat metabolic and glycemic testing is planned in about 7 weeks, with follow-up scheduled for Apr 13, 2035.

deckard hansberger

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT ASSESSMENT

Patient: JAZPER TAMILIO
The 46-year-old Native American female patient presented to the ED with abrupt shortness of breath and right-sided pleuritic chest pain beginning approximately two hours before arrival. The pain is sharp, worse with deep inspiration, and not exertional. She reports a racing heartbeat and mild lightheadedness but denies syncope, hemoptysis, fever, productive cough, or leg trauma. She has been taking apixaban as prescribed; no missed doses were reported. Supplemental oxygen was started during triage.

Home/contact information: 204 Temple St, West Dennis, MA 02670; jazper.tamilio94@outlook.com
MRN: 04163505

Initial vital signs: temperature 98.4°F, heart rate 126 bpm, respiratory rate 28/min, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, oxygen saturation 88% on room air. After 3 L/min oxygen by nasal cannula, saturation improved to 95%.

Focused examination:
- Alert, anxious, speaking in short sentences but protecting the airway.
- Tachycardic and regular rhythm without murmur.
- Increased respiratory effort with clear breath sounds bilaterally; no wheezing or crackles.
- No unilateral calf tenderness, edema, or palpable cord.
- Abdomen soft and nontender. No focal neurologic deficit.

Diagnostics:
ECG showed sinus tachycardia at 124 bpm with nonspecific ST-T changes and no STEMI pattern. Portable chest radiograph showed no focal infiltrate, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax. CT pulmonary angiography demonstrated acute bilateral segmental and subsegmental pulmonary emboli, greatest in the right lower lobe, without saddle embolus. There was mild right ventricular enlargement concerning for early strain.

Laboratory testing showed troponin I mildly elevated at 0.08 ng/mL, BNP 214 pg/mL, lactate 1.7 mmol/L, hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, platelets 238 K/µL, and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. Pregnancy testing was negative. Repeat blood pressure remained stable.

Medical decision-making:
Findings are consistent with acute pulmonary embolism with hypoxemic respiratory failure and biomarker evidence of right-heart strain. She remained normotensive without shock, making immediate systemic thrombolysis unnecessary. The case was discussed with the hospitalist and pulmonary/critical care teams. Because she is already taking apixaban, anticoagulation adherence and dosing will be reviewed before any adjustment. No evidence of active bleeding.

Disposition:
Admit to telemetry for oxygen support, serial troponins, echocardiography, and continued anticoagulation management. Continue supplemental oxygen and cardiac monitoring. Return precautions and admission plan reviewed with the patient, who verbalized understanding.

At discharge, she was tolerating a regular diet, drinking adequately, ambulating independently, and reporting manageable pain on oral medication.

Jocelyn Millender,
SSN: 985210445

Today we reviewed your blood pressure and the symptoms you have noticed, including intermittent headache and light-headedness. Your DOB is 1961-01-09, and your MRN is 032715623. At the visit, your blood pressure remained above goal on repeat measurement, while your heart rate and oxygen level were normal. Your heart and lung examination was reassuring, and there were no new neurologic findings such as weakness, facial droop, speech trouble, or loss of coordination.

The overall pattern is most consistent with essential hypertension. Headache and light-headedness can occur when blood pressure is not well controlled, although these symptoms can also have other causes. Please seek emergency care for chest pain, severe shortness of breath, fainting, sudden severe headache, new confusion, or one-sided weakness or numbness.

Continue amlodipine at your current prescribed dose. Continue lisinopril as prescribed as well; do not stop either medication without contacting the office. Take both medicines at approximately the same time each day. If you develop swelling of the lips or tongue, trouble breathing, or a widespread rash, stop lisinopril and seek urgent medical attention. Mild ankle swelling can occur with amlodipine; report persistent or worsening swelling.

For the next two weeks, check your blood pressure once in the morning and once in the evening, after sitting quietly for five minutes. Record the reading, pulse, and whether you had a headache or light-headedness. Bring the log and your home cuff to the next visit so we can compare it with our office equipment. Limit excess sodium, choose more fresh foods when possible, stay physically active as tolerated, and avoid frequent use of ibuprofen or naproxen unless we have discussed it, because these medicines may raise blood pressure or affect kidney function.

We will obtain a basic metabolic panel to monitor kidney function and potassium while you are taking lisinopril. Please also continue routine preventive care. The attending cardiologist’s prior recommendation was reviewed as part of today’s medication discussion; no urgent cardiology evaluation is indicated based on today’s examination.

Your follow-up appointment is scheduled for March 11, 2026. Please send questions through jocelyn.millender96@outlook.com, and contact the office sooner if your home readings are repeatedly above 180/120 or if the light-headedness becomes persistent.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
SSN: 947067588

Patient: markon hallatt
MRN: M7776576
Attending clinician: KYNLIE GOODROAD
Treating organization: Mercy Hospital of Buffalo

Reason for admission
markon hallatt was admitted for an acute sickle cell painful crisis characterized by severe bilateral limb pain, low back pain, poor oral intake, and clinical dehydration. The patient reported that the pain had progressed despite home measures and was limiting ambulation and sleep. There was no reported chest pain, shortness of breath, focal neurologic deficit, or recent trauma.

Key findings
On presentation, the patient appeared uncomfortable with dry oral mucosa and diffuse tenderness of the arms, legs, and lumbar paraspinal region without erythema, swelling, or focal joint findings. Initial oxygen saturation was normal on room air. Chest examination remained clear throughout the admission. Laboratory testing showed anemia consistent with the patient’s known sickle cell disease, reticulocytosis, and mild leukocytosis without a clear infectious source. Kidney function and electrolytes remained acceptable after hydration. Urinalysis did not suggest urinary infection. Chest imaging showed no acute infiltrate.

Hospital course
The patient received intravenous crystalloid fluids and intravenous morphine with close reassessment for sedation, respiratory depression, and constipation. Pain gradually improved, and treatment was transitioned to oral analgesia as oral intake increased. Antiemetic medication was available as needed, though nausea was limited. Incentive spirometry was encouraged while awake. There was no fever, hypoxia, acute chest syndrome, or evidence of bacteremia during the stay. The patient remained hemodynamically stable and did not require transfusion.

By the day of discharge, the patient was drinking adequately, voiding without difficulty, and walking independently. Pain had decreased substantially and was rated 5/10 at the time of the final assessment, with the patient reporting that this was manageable on the oral regimen. Examination showed improved hydration and no respiratory distress.

Discharge problem list
1. Sickle cell painful crisis, improved.
2. Dehydration, resolved with intravenous and oral fluids.
3. Chronic sickle cell anemia without indication for transfusion during this admission.
4. Opioid-associated constipation risk.

Medication changes
Continue the established home sickle cell medications as previously prescribed. Use the prescribed oral opioid only for breakthrough pain and do not combine it with alcohol, sleep medications, or other sedating drugs. Continue nonopioid pain measures when effective, including acetaminophen if permitted by the outpatient clinician. Maintain regular fluid intake. A bowel regimen was recommended while using opioid medication. No new antibiotic was indicated.

Follow-up and instructions
Follow up with the hematology team at Mercy Hospital of Buffalo and with primary care after discharge for reassessment of pain control, hydration, preventive care, and disease-modifying therapy. The patient was advised to seek emergency care immediately for fever, chest pain, shortness of breath, new weakness or confusion, inability to drink, persistent vomiting, markedly worsening pain, or symptoms not controlled by the discharge plan.

The patient verbalized understanding of the medication precautions, hydration goals, return precautions, and follow-up plan. Discharged home in stable condition with family support available in Saint Albans. Signed by KYNLIE GOODROAD.

Patient is awake, anxious, and speaking in full sentences. Skin is cool and diaphoretic. Cardiac rhythm regular without audible murmur. Lungs clear bilaterally with no increased work of breathing. Abdomen soft and nontender. No calf tenderness or peripheral edema. Radial pulses symmetric. Neurologic examination is nonfocal.

Investigations
ECG shows sinus rhythm with subtle ST-segment depression in the lateral leads and no ST-elevation. Repeat tracing is similar. Initial high-sensitivity troponin is elevated at 86 ng/L, increasing to 214 ng/L on repeat testing. CBC without significant anemia or leukocytosis. Basic metabolic panel notable for creatinine 0.9 mg/dL; potassium 4.1 mmol/L. Portable chest radiograph shows no focal infiltrate, pulmonary edema, or pneumothorax.

Medical Decision-Making
Presentation, dynamic troponin elevation, and ischemic ECG changes are consistent with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. No evidence currently supports STEMI, pulmonary embolism, aortic catastrophe, or acute heart failure. Cardiology was contacted for inpatient management and consideration of early coronary angiography.

Treatment
Aspirin loading dose administered in the ED. Fondaparinux initiated after confirming preserved renal function. Atorvastatin given. Sublingual nitroglycerin was offered; pressure improved without hypotension. Continuous cardiac monitoring maintained, with serial ECG and troponin ordered.

Disposition
Admit to telemetry under cardiology service for NSTEMI. Keep NPO after midnight pending procedural planning. Continue antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy per inpatient protocol. Patient and Blakeleigh were updated regarding the diagnosis, treatment plan, bleeding precautions, and need to report recurrent pain immediately.

text:
HEREDITARY CANCER RISK ASSESSMENT
Pediatric Molecular Genetics Laboratory Report

Patient: Erikson S.
Report/accession ID: 097844291
Collection/report date: 03/23/2020
Reporting laboratory: Sioux Falls Specialty Hospital
Ordering clinician: Not provided on the submitted requisition

Specimen and methodology

Peripheral blood collected in an EDTA tube was received for familial-variant analysis. DNA was extracted and analyzed by targeted next-generation sequencing with confirmatory bidirectional Sanger sequencing for the specified BRCA1 variant. The laboratory was asked to determine whether the familial pathogenic variant BRCA1 c.68_69delAG is present in the submitted specimen.

Result

BRCA1 c.68_69delAG: Not detected.

No pathogenic or likely pathogenic alteration involving the requested familial BRCA1 variant was identified in this specimen. This result is negative for the specific variant evaluated and does not exclude other sequence changes, copy-number changes, mosaicism below the assay detection threshold, or a hereditary cancer predisposition attributable to another gene.

Interpretation

The finding substantially reduces the likelihood that the patient inherited the known familial BRCA1 c.68_69delAG variant. If the familial variant has been independently confirmed in an affected relative, this result is generally considered a true negative for that familial alteration. Management should nevertheless be guided by the complete pedigree, documentation of the relative’s laboratory result, and the patient’s personal and family history.

This testing was requested because of significant family history, cancer-risk concern, and a request for predictive testing. The patient’s parent or legal guardian participated in the pretest discussion. Age-appropriate assent should be obtained when clinically appropriate, and the family should be counseled that predictive cancer testing in a minor is ordinarily considered when results are expected to affect care during childhood. No current treatment was reported.

Limitations and recommendations

This assay is designed for the specified BRCA1 familial variant and is not a comprehensive hereditary cancer panel. A negative targeted result should not be used to eliminate risk-based surveillance if the familial variant is uncertain, the family history is strongly suggestive, or another pathogenic variant is suspected. Genetic counseling is recommended to review the pedigree, confirm the relative’s reported variant, discuss residual familial risk, and determine whether additional testing is medically appropriate. Testing of an affected family member, if not already completed, may provide greater diagnostic yield.

Clinical correlation is required. The laboratory recommends retention of the original family test report for comparison and review with the patient’s genetics or oncology care team as the family history evolves.

Validated and electronically signed by:
camri capron
Laboratory Reporting Clinician

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
SSN: 666 82 8006

Patient: HAYZE ZULEGER
Age: 70 y/o
Encounter date: December 4th, 2023
Discharge diagnosis: Acute pyelonephritis

Reason for admission
The patient presented to the ED with 2 days of dysuria and urinary frequency followed by worsening left flank pain, fever, and rigors. Oral intake was reduced because of nausea, but there was no vomiting, chest pain, shortness of breath, or vaginal bleeding. Maiia Cedillo participated in medication and discharge teaching by the patient’s request.

Key findings
Initial temperature was 39.1°C with mild tachycardia. Examination showed left costovertebral angle tenderness without peritoneal signs. Urinalysis demonstrated large leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, numerous white blood cells, and moderate blood. WBC count was 15.8 K/µL with neutrophil predominance. Serum creatinine remained at baseline, and lactate was normal. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis or visible obstructing calculus. Urine culture grew greater than 100,000 CFU/mL of a susceptible gram-negative organism. Blood cultures remained without growth during the hospitalization.

Hospital course
The patient received IV fluids, ceftriaxone, and acetaminophen in the ED, followed by continued IV antibiotic therapy and antiemetic treatment on the medical floor. Pain and fever improved over the next 24 hours, and flank tenderness substantially resolved. The attending nephrologist reviewed the renal imaging and agreed that there was no indication for urgent urologic intervention. The patient tolerated a regular diet, ambulated independently, and remained hemodynamically stable on room air. Antibiotics were narrowed to oral cefuroxime after culture susceptibilities were available.

Discharge medications
• Cefuroxime 500 mg by mouth twice daily to complete a 10-day total course; take with food.
• Acetaminophen 650 mg by mouth every 6 hours as needed for pain or fever. Do not exceed 3,000 mg in 24 hours.
• Stop any unused empiric antibiotics from prior illnesses unless specifically restarted by a clinician.

Condition at discharge
Improved and afebrile. No current rigors, vomiting, or respiratory symptoms. Discharged home with reliable oral intake and understanding of the treatment plan.

Follow-up and instructions
Follow up with primary care within 3–5 days for clinical reassessment and review of the final culture report. Continue hydration and complete the entire cefuroxime course. Return to the ED for recurrent rigors, fever, worsening flank pain, inability to keep medications down, confusion, fainting, or decreased urine output.

Patient: shire obias
Seen at Rutland Regional Medical Center for persistent vomiting at 9+4 weeks' gestation. She reports 10 days of worsening nausea with frequent nonbloody emesis, inability to tolerate solids, and only small sips of fluid. She estimates a 7-lb weight loss since symptoms began. No abdominal pain, fever, diarrhea, dysuria, vaginal bleeding, or syncope. Mahya Quilling accompanied her and confirms reduced oral intake.

Initial vital signs: BP 104/68, HR 108, RR 18, T 98.4°F, SpO2 99% on room air. Weight is 58.2 kg by triage measurement. Alert but tired appearing; mucous membranes dry. Cardiopulmonary exam is unremarkable. Abdomen soft, nondistended, and nontender without guarding. No focal neurologic deficit.

Bedside ultrasound demonstrates an intrauterine pregnancy with fetal cardiac activity; no free fluid.

Discharged in stable condition with continuation of doxylamine-pyridoxine, small frequent meals, electrolyte-containing fluids, and return precautions for inability to keep liquids down, decreased urination, abdominal pain, fever, syncope, or vaginal bleeding. Follow up with obstetrics at Rutland Regional Medical Center on 05/22/2024. ED care and discharge plan reviewed with wanya fraughton.

Referral for hematology evaluation

Dear Hematology Consultant:

I am referring KACEON MAGETTE for evaluation of persistent iron-deficiency anemia with symptomatic tiredness, intermittent dizziness, and reduced exercise tolerance. The clinical question is whether the anemia is adequately explained by nutritional deficiency and menstrual blood loss or whether additional evaluation for occult gastrointestinal bleeding, malabsorption, or another hematologic process is indicated.

The patient reports gradually worsening fatigue over approximately three months and becoming short of breath with stairs or brisk walking, without chest pain, syncope, melena, hematochezia, fever, or unintentional weight loss. There is no reported history of chronic kidney disease, inflammatory bowel disease, bariatric surgery, or known bleeding disorder. Nikolaos Clampet, the patient’s relative, accompanied the visit and confirmed that the dizziness has been more noticeable when standing quickly. Menstrual periods are described as regular but heavy during the first several days.

Recent office testing showed hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, hematocrit 29.8%, mean corpuscular volume 72 fL, and red cell distribution width 18.1%. Ferritin was 7 ng/mL, serum iron 24 mcg/dL, total iron-binding capacity 438 mcg/dL, and transferrin saturation 5%. Platelet count was mildly elevated at 468,000/mcL, with a normal white blood cell count. The basic metabolic panel and thyroid-stimulating hormone were unremarkable. There was no evidence of hemolysis on the available testing. Vital signs were stable in the office, and examination showed conjunctival pallor without jaundice, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, or focal neurologic deficit.

Treatment with oral iron was started, and the patient has been taking ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily with food because of nausea when taken on an empty stomach. Adherence has otherwise been consistent. Afton Housing Authority has been supportive of the patient’s need to adjust work duties during periods of marked fatigue. We discussed taking iron with vitamin C-containing food, avoiding simultaneous calcium supplementation, and reporting worsening dizziness, syncope, chest pain, or shortness of breath at rest.

Assessment: Microcytic iron-deficiency anemia, symptomatic, with low ferritin and low transferrin saturation. The degree of anemia and incomplete clinical response to initial oral therapy warrant specialist input.

Plan: Please assess the need for additional laboratory evaluation, intravenous iron, and investigation for sources of blood loss or impaired absorption. Guidance regarding the appropriate pace of hemoglobin monitoring and indications for endoscopic evaluation would also be appreciated. I will repeat a complete blood count and iron studies after the next treatment interval and forward the results.

Sincerely,

Aryel Kishi
Primary care clinician
Center Cross

Patient: T. Leonen
Admitting service: Internal Medicine

Healthcare organization: Washakie Medical Center

Reason for admission:
The patient was admitted with four days of worsening shortness of breath, increased wheezing, and thicker yellow-green sputum despite frequent use of an albuterol inhaler. There was no chest pain, hemoptysis, syncope, or known sick contact. A relative, Prapti Cannito, participated in discharge teaching and will assist with medication organization at home in Saratoga.

Hospital course:
On arrival, the patient was tachypneic with diffuse expiratory wheezes and borderline oxygenation on room air. Blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg. Chest radiograph showed hyperinflation without focal infiltrate, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax. Viral respiratory testing was negative. Laboratory evaluation showed mild leukocytosis without significant renal or electrolyte abnormality. Report/accession ID: LAB-01897383.

The presentation was consistent with an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, likely triggered by a respiratory infection. The patient received scheduled nebulized bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroid therapy, and doxycycline. Supplemental oxygen was used briefly during the first night, then discontinued after resting and ambulation oxygen levels remained acceptable on room air. Breathlessness and wheezing improved steadily, and sputum production decreased. No evidence of pneumonia, acute heart failure, pulmonary embolism, or acute coronary syndrome was identified.

Assessment and plan:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with acute exacerbation, improved after inpatient treatment. Complete the prescribed prednisone course and doxycycline course. Continue albuterol inhaler as directed for acute symptoms. The patient was instructed to use the inhaler with a spacer if available and to review inhaler technique with primary care or pulmonary staff. Maintenance inhaler therapy should be reassessed after recovery, particularly if rescue inhaler use remains frequent.

Condition at discharge:
The patient is alert, hemodynamically stable, eating and drinking adequately, and able to walk without significant respiratory distress. Mild scattered expiratory wheeze remains, but there is no increased work of breathing. Discharge is appropriate with family support.

Follow up with Washakie Medical Center through primary care within one week for reassessment of breathing, oxygenation, and long-term COPD management. Seek emergency care for severe or rapidly worsening shortness of breath, bluish lips, confusion, fainting, chest pain, inability to speak in full sentences, or inadequate response to albuterol. ED HANDOVER NOTE

Patient: Keeran Dyre, a 45-year-old Pacific Islander male patient
Home address: URB San Patricio, 195 Pr- 682, San Juan, PR 00901
Preferred contact: keeran.dyre20@outlook.com

Priority 1 – Pelvic pain / suspected pelvic inflammatory disease
Presented with 2 days of worsening bilateral lower abdominal pain, abnormal yellow vaginal discharge, and pain with intercourse. No syncope, heavy bleeding, vomiting, dysuria, or known pregnancy. Reports one sexual partner recently; contraception use unclear. Current pain 5/10. Afebrile and hemodynamically stable.

Focused examination: Mild suprapubic and bilateral adnexal tenderness without guarding or rebound. Cervical motion tenderness and mucopurulent discharge on speculum examination. No vulvar lesions. Abdomen otherwise soft. No costovertebral angle tenderness. Patient uncomfortable but nontoxic.

Investigations
Urine pregnancy test negative. CBC without leukocytosis; hemoglobin stable. CMP unremarkable. Urinalysis without convincing urinary infection. Vaginal testing sent for gonorrhea, chlamydia, trichomonas, bacterial vaginosis, and yeast; results pending at handoff. HIV and syphilis screening offered. Pelvic ultrasound without tubo-ovarian abscess or torsion.

Treatment / decision-making
Clinical picture supports uncomplicated pelvic inflammatory disease. No current evidence of ectopic pregnancy, appendicitis, sepsis, or surgical abdomen. Given ceftriaxone in the ED and first doses of doxycycline and metronidazole. Tolerated medications without reaction. Discussed abstinence until treatment is complete, partner evaluation/treatment, and barrier protection. Patient instructed not to drink alcohol while taking metronidazole.

Disposition
Appropriate for outpatient management. Discharge medications: doxycycline and metronidazole for the prescribed course; complete all doses. Follow up with primary care or gynecology within 48–72 hours and review pending STI results. Return immediately for fever, escalating or one-sided pain, fainting, persistent vomiting, heavy bleeding, or inability to take medication.

Care plan and return precautions reviewed with the patient. Treating clinician: A. Neesmith.

REFERRAL: Chronic knee pain and reduced mobility

Patient: Mackenley P.
Referring organization: United Medical Center
Report/accession ID: 06976094

Clinical question
Please evaluate for specialist management of symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, including whether injection therapy, formal physical therapy, bracing, or surgical consultation is appropriate.

History
Mackenley P. has persistent knee pain with morning stiffness and progressive limitation in walking, stair climbing, and rising from a chair. Symptoms are most pronounced after activity and following periods of inactivity. There has been no reported acute injury, fever, or constitutional symptom. Conservative treatment with acetaminophen and topical diclofenac has provided incomplete relief. The patient is not currently taking an oral NSAID.

Current findings
Office examination shows an antalgic gait and reduced knee flexion because of pain. There is palpable joint-line tenderness with crepitus on active range of motion. No erythema, warmth, or appreciable effusion is present. Distal pulses and sensation are intact. The contralateral knee is less symptomatic.

Prior evaluation and management
Plain knee radiographs were reviewed and are consistent with degenerative osteoarthritis, with medial compartment joint-space narrowing and osteophyte formation. The patient has been advised to continue acetaminophen within labeled dosing limits, use topical diclofenac as directed, and avoid activities that reliably exacerbate symptoms. Home range-of-motion and quadriceps-strengthening exercises were discussed. Despite these measures, pain continues to interfere with routine mobility.

Requested action
Please assess the patient and recommend next steps, including supervised physical therapy, an appropriately fitted brace or assistive device, and the risks and benefits of intra-articular corticosteroid or other injection treatment. Please comment on whether additional imaging or orthopedic surgical evaluation is warranted. Follow-up with primary care is planned in about 5 weeks, or sooner for rapidly worsening pain, swelling, or inability to bear weight.

Sincerely,

N. Kowallis
089957381
Referring clinician, United Medical Center

LABORATORY REPORT
SSN: 000-04-1699

Patient: Seleah Orantes
MRN: 02988492
Patient contact: (671) 555-0117
Specimen: Serum
Ordering clinician: Not listed
Clinical indication: Known hypothyroidism; fatigue, cold intolerance, and constipation while taking levothyroxine.

THYROID FUNCTION TESTING

Analyte                         Result       Reference interval
TSH                             8.2 mIU/L    0.40–4.50 mIU/L
Free T4                         0.8 ng/dL    0.8–1.8 ng/dL
Free T3                         2.6 pg/mL    2.3–4.2 pg/mL
Thyroid peroxidase antibody     186 IU/mL    <9 IU/mL

Interpretation

TSH is elevated with free T4 at the lower limit of the adult reference interval. In the current clinical context, this pattern is compatible with under-replacement or inconsistent administration of levothyroxine. Positive thyroid peroxidase antibody supports an autoimmune thyroid process. Free T3 is within the stated interval and should not be used alone to assess adequacy of replacement.

Clinical comment

The reported symptoms are concordant with biochemical evidence of persistent mild primary hypothyroidism. Confirm the prescribed levothyroxine dose, daily adherence, and administration technique. The medication should generally be taken with water on an empty stomach, separated from calcium, iron, antacids, and high-fiber supplements; review of interacting medications and recent dose changes is recommended. If adherence and administration are appropriate, the treating clinician may consider a cautious dose adjustment based on the complete clinical picture. Repeat TSH and free T4 testing is reasonable after approximately 6–8 weeks following any dose change.

Additional laboratory considerations

• Biotin-containing supplements may interfere with some thyroid immunoassays; document supplement use and hold biotin before repeat testing when clinically appropriate.
• Results should be interpreted with pregnancy status, acute illness, pituitary disease, and assay-specific factors in mind.
• No evidence of overt thyrotoxicosis is identified in this specimen.

Follow-up review: September 12th, 2004

Validated and electronically signed by:
vonn radgowski
Laboratory reporting clinician

Emergency precautions reviewed for syncope, dyspnea at rest, chest pain, or black/bloody stools.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: MAGDALENE HAENLEIN
Home address: 769 Chalan Santa Lourdes, Saipan, MP 96950
Report/accession ID: LAB-02152804

Admission reason
Admitted for acute central chest pressure with diaphoresis and nausea. Initial ECG showed nonspecific ST-T abnormalities without ST-segment elevation. Serial high-sensitivity troponins rose and then began to decline, consistent with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI).

Hospital course
The patient was placed on telemetry and treated with aspirin, fondaparinux, and high-intensity atorvastatin. The Model X3 cardiac monitor was used during the encounter; no sustained ventricular arrhythmia was observed. Chest discomfort resolved without recurrent ischemic symptoms. Echocardiogram demonstrated mildly reduced left ventricular systolic function with an estimated ejection fraction of 45% and regional hypokinesis of the inferior wall. Cardiology evaluated the patient and recommended coronary angiography. Catheterization showed obstructive coronary artery disease managed medically; no intervention was required. Renal function and hemoglobin remained stable. The patient ambulated independently and tolerated oral intake before discharge.

Discharge diagnoses
1. Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction
2. Coronary artery disease
3. Hyperlipidemia

Discharge medications
• Aspirin 81 mg by mouth daily.
• Atorvastatin 80 mg by mouth nightly.
• Fondaparinux discontinued after completion of the inpatient course.
• Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg sublingually as needed for chest pain, up to 3 doses; call 911 if pain persists after the first dose.

Follow-up and instructions
Follow up with primary care within 1–2 weeks and cardiology within 2–4 weeks. Continue a heart-healthy, low-sodium diet and avoid tobacco. No heavy lifting until cleared by cardiology. Return to the ED immediately for recurrent or worsening chest pressure, shortness of breath, fainting, palpitations, or unusual bleeding.

Condition at discharge
Hemodynamically stable, chest-pain free, and discharged home.

Discharging clinician: Naylani Voruganti, 029763840

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT ASSESSMENT
SSN: 666-52-8548

Patient: JAMIRAH WISCO
MRN: 00004410
Contact: jamirah.wisco88@outlook.com
Healthcare facility: Dale Medical Center

Chief complaint: Worsening redness and pain of the left lower leg.

History of present illness: Patient reports a small abrasion near the left shin several days ago, followed by progressive redness, warmth, and tenderness extending toward the ankle. No known puncture wound or animal bite. Denies fever, chills, chest pain, dyspnea, calf cramping, numbness, or weakness. Took acetaminophen with partial relief. Has started dicloxacillin as prescribed but notes continued spread of erythema. Relative Barbara is present and confirms symptoms have worsened since yesterday.

Exam: Afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Alert, conversant, and in no acute distress. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Left distal lower leg with diffuse, blanching erythema and increased warmth, extending from the mid-shin to the ankle. Moderate tenderness without fluctuance, crepitus, bullae, drainage, or lymphangitic streaking. No pain out of proportion. Ankle and knee range of motion preserved. Dorsalis pedis pulse 2+; sensation and motor function intact. No asymmetric edema of the thigh.

Investigations: CBC without leukocytosis. CMP notable for normal renal function and glucose. Lactate normal. Venous duplex ultrasound negative for deep venous thrombosis. Tibia/fibula radiographs show no acute osseous abnormality or soft-tissue gas.

Medical decision-making: Findings support uncomplicated cellulitis without abscess, sepsis, necrotizing infection, or DVT. Persistent erythema after limited outpatient therapy does not by itself indicate treatment failure. Patient is appropriate for continued outpatient management with close reassessment.

Treatment and disposition: First dose of oral antibiotic administered in the ED; continue dicloxacillin as previously directed and acetaminophen as needed, within labeled dosing limits. Leg elevated when resting. Border of erythema marked; return immediately for fever, rapid progression, severe pain, vomiting, weakness, or color change. Follow up with primary care within 24–48 hours. Discharged ambulatory in stable condition.

Date: Jun 30, 2021
SSN: 000882265

Endocrinology Consultation Request

Re: Jennings

Dear Endocrinology Consultant:

I am referring this patient for evaluation of persistent symptoms and biochemical hypothyroidism despite ongoing thyroid hormone replacement. The specific question is whether the current levothyroxine dose is adequate and whether an alternative explanation for the continued fatigue, cold intolerance, and constipation should be pursued.

Jennings reports approximately eight months of gradually worsening low energy, increased sensitivity to cold, and bowel movements occurring every three to four days. There has been no neck pain, dysphagia, odynophagia, tremor, palpitations, or unexplained weight loss. The patient denies recent use of amiodarone, lithium, biotin supplements, or over-the-counter “thyroid support” products. Medication reconciliation confirms levothyroxine 75 micrograms once daily, taken before breakfast with water. The patient occasionally takes calcium carbonate within two hours of the thyroid medication and has been counseled to separate these products by at least four hours.

At the most recent primary care evaluation, blood pressure was 128/76 mmHg, pulse 64 beats/minute, temperature 97.7°F, and body mass index 27.4 kg/m². The patient appeared well but mildly fatigued. There was no proptosis, tremor, or diaphoresis. The thyroid was smooth and nontender without a palpable dominant nodule. Heart rhythm was regular, and there was no peripheral edema. Neurologic examination showed normal strength and intact reflexes, with mildly delayed relaxation at the ankles.

Recent laboratory testing showed TSH 8.62 mIU/L, free T4 0.8 ng/dL, hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, sodium 139 mmol/L, creatinine 0.86 mg/dL, and alanine aminotransferase 19 U/L. Thyroid peroxidase antibody was positive at 146 IU/mL, supporting autoimmune thyroiditis. A lipid panel demonstrated total cholesterol 218 mg/dL and LDL cholesterol 139 mg/dL. There is no known history of coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, osteoporosis, bariatric surgery, or inflammatory bowel disease.

The patient has been advised to take levothyroxine consistently on an empty stomach and to avoid calcium or iron during the absorption window. No dose escalation has yet been made pending specialist input. Please assess adherence and absorption, recommend an appropriate replacement dose and monitoring interval, and advise whether thyroid ultrasound or additional testing is indicated. Guidance regarding management of the associated constipation and lipid elevation would also be appreciated.

Thank you for evaluating this patient.

Sincerely,

Myier Alkhatib
Referring Clinician

Patient: TYSEAN GALLATY
Report/accession ID: 02516805
Reporting laboratory: Kingman Regional Medical Center
Specimen: Venous blood and clean-catch urine
Clinical indication: Essential hypertension with intermittent headache and light-headedness. Current medications reported as amlodipine and lisinopril.

RESULTS

Basic metabolic panel
Sodium: 139 mmol/L (reference interval 135–145 mmol/L)
Potassium: 4.3 mmol/L (reference interval 3.5–5.1 mmol/L)
Chloride: 103 mmol/L (reference interval 98–108 mmol/L)
Carbon dioxide: 25 mmol/L (reference interval 22–29 mmol/L)
Blood urea nitrogen: 16 mg/dL (reference interval 7–20 mg/dL)
Creatinine: 0.88 mg/dL (reference interval 0.60–1.20 mg/dL)
Estimated GFR: 89 mL/min/1.73 m² (reference interval ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m²)
Glucose: 96 mg/dL (reference interval 70–99 mg/dL)
Calcium: 9.4 mg/dL (reference interval 8.5–10.5 mg/dL)

Complete blood count
White blood cells: 6.8 x10^3/µL (reference interval 4.0–10.5 x10^3/µL)
Hemoglobin: 13.9 g/dL (reference interval 12.0–16.0 g/dL)
Hematocrit: 41.8% (reference interval 36.0–46.0%)

Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio

Renal function and serum electrolytes are within the stated reference intervals.
