If symptoms occur with hypotension, bradycardia, focal neurologic findings, chest pain, or acute visual change, prompt clinical assessment is recommended.

FOLLOW-UP

Repeat a basic metabolic panel after clinically indicated medication changes and continue routine blood pressure monitoring. A laboratory review is planned for 2022-04-13, in about 8 weeks, or sooner if symptoms worsen.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: K. Abkarian
Age: 82 y/o
Home address: 283 Silver Dr, Egnar, CO 81325
Contact: (617) 555-0117
Discharge date: January 16, 2025

Reason for admission:
The patient was admitted after several days of worsening shortness of breath, increased wheezing, and a change in sputum to thick yellow-green secretions. Symptoms were present despite more frequent use of the albuterol inhaler. There was no reported chest pain, hemoptysis, leg swelling, or known sick contact.

Hospital course:
The patient was hospitalized for four days for an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Initial examination showed tachypnea, diffuse expiratory wheezes, and diminished air movement at both lung bases. Oxygen saturation was below the patient’s usual baseline on room air and improved with low-flow nasal cannula oxygen. Blood pressure during the stay included a reading of 120/80 mmHg. Chest radiograph showed hyperinflation without focal air-space consolidation or pleural effusion. Viral respiratory testing was negative, and laboratory studies did not demonstrate significant leukocytosis or acute kidney injury.

Treatment included scheduled nebulized bronchodilators, as-needed albuterol, systemic corticosteroid therapy, and doxycycline for suspected bacterial contribution given the purulent sputum. The patient received prednisone during the admission and completed supportive pulmonary hygiene measures, including incentive spirometry and assisted ambulation. No invasive procedure was required. Oxygen was gradually weaned as respiratory effort improved.

During the first 48 hours, wheezing and breathlessness decreased, sputum became less purulent, and the patient tolerated walking in the hall without significant desaturation. By the fourth hospital day, the patient was breathing comfortably at rest and near baseline with exertion. The patient was afebrile, eating and drinking adequately, and able to use the inhaler correctly after review with respiratory therapy.

Discharge problem list:
1. Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, improved.
2. Acute hypoxemia, resolved without need for supplemental oxygen at discharge.
3. Tobacco exposure history; cessation counseling provided.
4. Deconditioning related to acute illness, improving with activity.

Discharge medications:
• Prednisone: continue the prescribed short course and take with food.
• Doxycycline: complete the remaining prescribed doses; do not stop early unless directed because of a significant adverse reaction.
• Albuterol inhaler: use as directed for wheezing or shortness of breath. The patient demonstrated proper inhaler technique before discharge.
No other medication changes were made during this hospitalization.

Condition at discharge:
Stable for discharge home on January 16, 2025. Lung examination showed markedly improved air movement with only mild scattered end-expiratory wheeze. The patient was alert, ambulatory, and able to maintain oral intake. Return precautions were reviewed.

Follow-up and instructions:
Arrange follow-up with primary care within one week for reassessment of breathing, medication completion, and long-term COPD management. Seek emergency care for severe or worsening breathlessness, blue lips, confusion, chest pain, inability to speak in full sentences, fainting, or failure of the rescue inhaler to provide relief. Continue hydration, avoid smoke and other respiratory irritants, and resume activity gradually with rest breaks.

Lower abdominal pain for 3 days, gradually worsening, with new abnormal yellow-white vaginal discharge and deep dyspareunia. Reports mild nausea but no vomiting. Denies syncope, urinary frequency, flank pain, or measured fever. No known pregnancy. Hemodynamically stable on arrival; blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, pulse 96, temperature 99.4°F, respirations 16, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.

Focused examination
Alert, uncomfortable but nontoxic. Abdomen soft with suprapubic and bilateral lower-quadrant tenderness; no guarding or rebound. Given ceftriaxone intramuscularly in the department. Start doxycycline and metronidazole as prescribed for the full treatment course; reviewed dosing, avoidance of alcohol with metronidazole, and photosensitivity precautions. Acetaminophen or ibuprofen may be used if safe. No indication for admission, emergent surgery, or IV antibiotics at this time.

Discharge home in stable condition. Abstain from sexual activity until treatment is complete, symptoms have resolved, and partners have been evaluated and treated. Referral: Rheumatology

Patient: Jairus P.
Reason for referral: Suspected rheumatoid arthritis flare with persistent synovitis despite current treatment.

Clinical history
Jairus P. reports 6 weeks of worsening morning stiffness, now lasting approximately 90 minutes, with swelling and aching in both wrists, MCP joints, and several PIP joints. She also describes increased fatigue and difficulty opening jars and performing work tasks. No recent fever, rash, ocular symptoms, or gastrointestinal illness. Her sister, bowman schwagerl, has noticed that hand swelling is most pronounced in the morning.

Current treatment
Methotrexate weekly with folic acid supplementation and naproxen as needed. She reports adherence and denies mouth sores, unusual bruising, dyspnea, or heavy alcohol use. No recent corticosteroid course. Occupation: elementary school teacher. She remains employed by Lewes Youth Services.

Findings
Office examination shows visible swelling and tenderness of both wrists, the second and third MCP joints bilaterally, and the right second and third PIP joints. Grip strength is reduced by pain. No nodules or large-joint effusion. Skin is clear, and cardiopulmonary examination is unremarkable.

Recent testing
CBC and comprehensive metabolic panel were acceptable for continued methotrexate monitoring. ESR and CRP are elevated above prior baseline. Hand radiographs show periarticular osteopenia without definite new erosions. Pregnancy is not clinically suspected.

Clinical question and request
Please evaluate for active rheumatoid arthritis and advise whether escalation to combination conventional DMARD therapy or a biologic/targeted agent is indicated. Guidance on interim anti-inflammatory management and monitoring would be appreciated. I have advised her to continue methotrexate, folic acid, and naproxen only as previously directed, and to seek urgent care for fever, shortness of breath, or a hot acutely painful joint.

Follow-up with primary care is planned in about 6 weeks, sooner if symptoms worsen.

Discharge Summary

Patient: A. Noffsinger
Admitting service: Obstetrics
Discharging facility: Eastern Idaho Regional Medical Center

Reason for admission: A. Noffsinger was admitted for persistent vomiting during early pregnancy with inability to tolerate fluids or oral medications, dehydration, and approximately 6% weight loss from her reported prepregnancy baseline. She is currently 9+4 weeks' gestation. There was no vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain, fever, diarrhea, hematemesis, or urinary complaint.

Initial evaluation showed dry mucous membranes, mild orthostatic tachycardia, and ketonuria. Serum sodium was 134 mmol/L, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L, and creatinine 0.8 mg/dL. Potassium was 3.5 mmol/L and was repleted orally after vomiting improved. Liver enzymes and lipase were normal. Urinalysis showed concentrated urine with moderate ketones and no evidence of infection. Obstetric ultrasound demonstrated a single viable intrauterine pregnancy consistent with the stated gestational duration.

Hospital course: She received intravenous sodium chloride, thiamine, and antiemetic therapy. Doxylamine-pyridoxine was restarted on a scheduled basis, with metoclopramide available as needed during the admission. Her nausea and vomiting gradually decreased, and she advanced from ice chips to clear liquids and then to small portions of a regular diet without recurrent emesis. Orthostatic symptoms resolved, urine output remained adequate, and repeat metabolic testing showed improvement in bicarbonate and normalization of potassium. No procedure was required.

Assessment at discharge: First-trimester hyperemesis with dehydration and weight loss, improved after IV hydration and medication therapy. She is hemodynamically stable, tolerating oral intake, and appropriate for discharge home. Her sister, Suhaavi, who lives in Jerome, was present for medication teaching and transportation planning.

Discharge plan: Continue doxylamine-pyridoxine exactly as prescribed, taking it on a scheduled basis rather than waiting for severe nausea. Use metoclopramide only as directed for breakthrough symptoms. Drink frequent small amounts of fluid, consider oral rehydration solutions, and eat small meals containing carbohydrates and protein. Avoid prolonged fasting and advance the diet as tolerated. Intravenous sodium chloride was discontinued at discharge because she is now maintaining hydration by mouth.

Follow-up is arranged with prenatal care at Eastern Idaho Regional Medical Center on June 8th, 1996. She should call the obstetric office promptly for inability to keep liquids down for 12 hours, markedly decreased urination, dizziness or fainting, abdominal pain, fever, vaginal bleeding, or blood in the vomit. She was instructed to return to the emergency department for severe symptoms or concern for worsening dehydration. Discharge instructions and medication precautions were reviewed with the patient, who verbalized understanding.

Referral for Hematology Consultation

Dear Hematology Consultant,

I am referring Y. Burnum for evaluation and management of persistent iron-deficiency anemia. The specific clinical question is whether additional diagnostic evaluation is indicated beyond presumed nutritional or chronic blood-loss causes, and whether intravenous iron or another treatment strategy should be considered because of ongoing symptoms despite oral supplementation.

The patient reports several months of tiredness, intermittent dizziness, and reduced exercise tolerance. There is no reported syncope, chest pain, melena, hematochezia, or abnormal uterine bleeding in the available history. Dietary intake has been limited in iron-rich foods. The patient has been taking ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily and reports generally good adherence, although occasional gastrointestinal discomfort has made the medication difficult to tolerate. No other current medication is documented in the referral record.

Recent primary care testing demonstrated a microcytic, hypochromic anemia. Hemoglobin was 9.8 g/dL, hematocrit 30.7%, mean corpuscular volume 72 fL, and red cell distribution width 18.6%. Ferritin was 6 ng/mL, serum iron 24 mcg/dL, total iron-binding capacity 426 mcg/dL, and transferrin saturation 6%. The reticulocyte count was not elevated. Vitamin B12 and folate levels were within reference range, and the creatinine level was normal. These results support iron deficiency rather than isolated anemia of chronic inflammation.

On examination in the referring office, the patient appeared tired but was alert and in no acute distress. Mucous membranes were mildly pale. Heart rate was regular; no murmur was heard. Lungs were clear bilaterally, and there was no peripheral edema. Orthostatic vital signs did not show a significant blood pressure drop. The reported dizziness and reduced exercise tolerance may reasonably be attributable, at least in part, to the degree of anemia.

Please assess the patient for an underlying source of iron loss or impaired absorption, including the need for gastrointestinal evaluation or additional testing based on your assessment. I would also appreciate recommendations regarding oral iron dosing and duration, laboratory monitoring, and criteria for intravenous iron if symptoms or laboratory abnormalities persist. Repeat complete blood count and iron studies are planned after a treatment interval, with earlier reassessment for worsening dizziness, dyspnea, chest discomfort, syncope, or evidence of bleeding.

Thank you for evaluating this patient. This referral is submitted through MEMORIAL HOSPITAL AND HEALTH CARE CENTER in Fort Wayne.

Sincerely,

eryss sesti
Professional ID: 020956744

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: Azorah B.
MRN: 075220/77
Discharging organization: Abbeville General Hospital
Discharging clinician: Dhana Pashby, MD, professional ID 035432222

Reason for admission:
Azorah B. was admitted from the emergency department for acute pyelonephritis with several hours of worsening flank pain, dysuria, fever, and rigors. Oral intake was reduced because of nausea, although there was no persistent vomiting. The patient denied chest pain, shortness of breath, vaginal bleeding, or other new focal symptoms.

Hospital course:
On arrival, the patient was febrile and mildly tachycardic with left costovertebral angle tenderness. Initial laboratory testing showed leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance and a mild creatinine elevation that improved after intravenous fluids. Urinalysis demonstrated pyuria, positive leukocyte esterase, microscopic hematuria, and bacteriuria. Urine culture grew a susceptible urinary pathogen. Blood cultures remained without growth. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis or visible obstructing stone.

The patient received intravenous crystalloid, antiemetic therapy as needed, acetaminophen for fever and pain, and empiric intravenous ceftriaxone. Flank discomfort and rigors resolved during observation, and the patient remained hemodynamically stable without hypotension or recurrent high fever. Antibiotics were transitioned to oral therapy after clinical improvement and review of the culture susceptibility profile. The patient tolerated oral fluids and medications and was able to ambulate independently before discharge.

Discharge diagnoses:
1. Acute pyelonephritis, improved
2. Dysuria and flank pain secondary to urinary tract infection, improved
3. Mild dehydration, resolved
4. Transient creatinine elevation, resolved with hydration

Discharge medications:
- Cefuroxime 500 mg twice daily. Complete the prescribed course even if symptoms resolve sooner.
- Acetaminophen as directed on the package for pain or fever. Do not exceed the labeled daily maximum and avoid combining it with other acetaminophen-containing products.
- Continue usual home medications unless otherwise instructed.

The patient was specifically instructed to take cefuroxime 500 mg twice daily with food when possible and to maintain adequate oral hydration. Return immediately for recurrent rigors, fever that does not improve, worsening flank or abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, inability to keep antibiotics down, confusion, fainting, reduced urine output, or any other rapidly worsening symptom. Emergency evaluation is also advised for new shortness of breath or chest pain.

Follow-up:
Follow up with a primary care clinician within one week for reassessment and review of the final urine culture result. A repeat urinalysis and renal function panel may be obtained if symptoms persist or recur. The patient should seek prompt evaluation for recurrent urinary symptoms after completing treatment. No procedure was required during this admission.

Condition at discharge:
Stable, afebrile, tolerating oral intake, voiding without difficulty, and ambulatory. Discharge instructions, medication administration, warning signs, and follow-up recommendations were reviewed with the patient, who verbalized understanding.

Signed by Dhana Pashby, MD, professional ID 035432222

The patient, age 45 years, was reviewed during the shift for acute infectious gastroenteritis. Spouse at bedside provided additional history. Ongoing loose stools with intermittent abdominal cramping; one episode of emesis reported after attempting solid food. No blood or mucus observed. Patient denies chest pain, dyspnea, or urinary symptoms.

Contact precautions maintained, with dedicated equipment and reinforcement of handwashing using soap and water. Oral rehydration solution offered regularly. Ondansetron administered per existing order: ondansetron 4 mg every 8 hours as needed. Nausea improved on reassessment, and patient tolerated crackers without recurrent vomiting. Spouse instructed not to share food or drinks and to notify staff after each stool or emesis episode.

Fall precautions continued because of weakness and postural lightheadedness. Covering provider notified of reduced intake and orthostatic symptoms; plan is to reassess hydration status and consider laboratory testing or IV fluids if oral intake declines. Escalate immediately for persistent vomiting, worsening abdominal pain, blood in stool, confusion, syncope, or inability to maintain fluids.

Next shift plan:
Continue stool and emesis documentation, strict intake and output, contact precautions, assisted bathroom transfers, and oral hydration trial. Recheck vital signs and abdominal findings after the next episode.

Emergency Department Follow-Up Clinical Report
SSN: 965639297

Patient: Manvi
Occupation: Real Estate Administrative Assistant
Employer: Kerrick Community Center
Home address: 709 Co Hwy 14, Taylors Falls, MN 55084
Contact: (312) 555-0117

Reason for evaluation: Persistent fatigue, cold intolerance, and constipation in the setting of known hypothyroidism.

History and collateral:
Manvi presents for outpatient follow-up after emergency department evaluation of several weeks of reduced energy, increased sensitivity to cold, and bowel movements occurring less frequently than usual. The patient’s adult child provided supplemental history and reports no syncope, chest pain, shortness of breath, confusion, or focal weakness. There has been no recent febrile illness. Medication reconciliation confirms levothyroxine use, although the patient is uncertain whether doses have occasionally been taken with breakfast or other medications. No new over-the-counter thyroid products were reported.

Examination:
Patient is alert, conversant, and in no acute distress. Blood pressure and pulse are clinically stable. Skin is mildly dry without jaundice. No periorbital edema is observed. Thyroid is not visibly enlarged, and no discrete neck mass is palpable. Heart rhythm is regular without murmur. Lungs are clear bilaterally. Abdomen is soft and nontender, with mildly decreased bowel sounds. There is no pretibial edema. Neurologic examination shows normal attention, speech, gait, and gross strength.

Assessment and interpretation:
The symptom cluster is compatible with suboptimally treated or inconsistently absorbed primary hypothyroidism. Differential considerations include anemia, medication effect, sleep disturbance, and metabolic disease; current examination does not suggest myxedema crisis or another acute endocrine emergency. The emergency department record was reviewed, including the recommendation for outpatient thyroid-function testing. The attending endocrinologist’s prior assessment is referenced in the available history, but the current medication dose cannot be changed safely without updated laboratory data.

Plan:
Continue levothyroxine at the previously prescribed dose pending results. Take it consistently with water on an empty stomach and separate it from calcium, iron, and fiber supplements. Obtain TSH and free T4; consider CBC and comprehensive metabolic panel if symptoms persist. Increase fluids and dietary fiber gradually for constipation, with polyethylene glycol as needed if approved by the primary-care clinician. Arrange follow-up after laboratory review. Return to the ED for confusion, marked weakness, fainting, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: tysir beabout
Residence: 749 Washington Ave, Shannon, MS 38868
Contact: tysir.beabout42@yahoo.com
Service: Internal Medicine
Discharging clinician: Professional identifier LIC71888170

Admission reason
81-year-old multiracial male patient admitted from the emergency department for 3 days of productive cough, fever, chills, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Chest radiograph showed a right lower lobe air-space opacity consistent with community-acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis is coded as SNOMED CT 233604007.

Key findings
Initial oxygen saturation was mildly reduced on room air and improved with low-flow nasal cannula. White blood cell count was elevated with neutrophil predominance; lactate remained normal. Respiratory viral testing was negative. Blood cultures showed no growth, and sputum culture did not identify a bacterial pathogen. Renal function remained stable.

Hospital course
The patient received intravenous fluids, supplemental oxygen, and empiric ceftriaxone with azithromycin during the first hospital day. Fever resolved, pleuritic pain improved, and cough became less frequent. Oxygen was discontinued before discharge, with stable saturation during ambulation. No evidence of sepsis, parapneumonic effusion, or acute cardiac process was identified.

Discharge medications
• Amoxicillin 1,000 mg by mouth three times daily to complete the prescribed course.
• Acetaminophen 650 mg by mouth every 6 hours as needed for fever or discomfort; do not exceed 3,000 mg in 24 hours.
• Stop inpatient intravenous antibiotics after the final hospital dose.

Condition at discharge
Hemodynamically stable, afebrile, tolerating oral intake, and breathing comfortably without supplemental oxygen. The spouse participated in medication and return-precaution teaching and will assist with transportation and home monitoring.

Follow-up and instructions
Follow up with primary care within one week. A repeat chest radiograph should be considered in 6–8 weeks if symptoms persist or based on primary care assessment. Seek emergency care for worsening shortness of breath, chest pain, confusion, inability to maintain hydration, recurrent high fever, or bluish discoloration of the lips. Encourage fluids, rest, and gradual return to usual activity.

Patient: I. Wallingsford
Clinical age group: 74 y/o
Home address: 260 Alvarado Ave, Valley Park, MO 63088
Emergency contact: relative listed in chart.

Priority problem: Sudden, brief spinning episodes triggered by rolling in bed and looking upward, with associated nausea and persistent mild unsteadiness. No syncope, chest pain, dyspnea, headache, diplopia, hearing loss, focal weakness, facial droop, or speech difficulty. No recent head trauma reported.

Focused assessment: Awake, cooperative, and mildly uncomfortable with position change. Hemodynamically stable; oxygen saturation normal on room air. Lungs clear bilaterally. Cardiac rhythm regular. No nystagmus at rest. Right-sided positional testing reproduces vertigo with a brief torsional nystagmus; symptoms fatigue on repeat testing. No limb ataxia or pronator drift. Gait cautious but independent. Glasgow Coma Scale 15.

Investigations: Point-of-care glucose normal. ECG without acute ischemic change or arrhythmia. No indication for emergent neuroimaging at this time given reproducible positional symptoms, normal neurologic examination, and absence of red flags.

Clinical impression: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, likely right posterior canal. Low concern for stroke, cardiopulmonary cause, or intracranial hemorrhage.

Treatment/plan: Epley maneuver performed with improvement. Oral fluids encouraged. May use prochlorperazine as required for nausea; avoid driving, ladders, and rapid head movement until steady. Vestibular exercises reviewed. Discharge home with relative available for observation.

Safety net: Return immediately for continuous vertigo, inability to walk, severe headache, weakness, numbness, confusion, new hearing loss, chest pain, or shortness of breath. Primary care/vestibular therapy review scheduled for April 18, 2035.

Signed: Z. Lebrecht

Patient: Lumine C.
Home address: 894 Merrill Ave, Hungry Horse, MT 59919
Occupation: Pastry Baker
Employer: Bozeman Public Library

Dear Cardiology Team,

I am referring Lumine C. for evaluation and management of symptomatic atrial fibrillation, with particular concern regarding persistent exertional symptoms despite rate-control therapy. The specific clinical questions are whether rhythm-control treatment should be considered, whether additional cardiac testing is indicated, and whether the current anticoagulation and beta-blocker regimen remains appropriate.

The patient reports intermittent rapid, irregular palpitations accompanied by fatigue and breathlessness when walking uphill or carrying groceries. The patient’s partner has also noticed reduced activity tolerance and occasional nighttime awareness of a racing heartbeat. There is no reported syncope, pleuritic chest pain, focal neurologic deficit, melena, or clinically significant bleeding. Medication adherence has been reported as consistent.

Atrial fibrillation was previously documented on office electrocardiography, and the patient has been managed in primary care with apixaban and metoprolol succinate. No medication changes were made today. The patient denies use of over-the-counter decongestants and reports limited alcohol intake. There is no known history of heart failure documented in the available chart.

At today’s visit, blood pressure was 128/76 mmHg and pulse was irregular at 92 beats/minute. Oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. Cardiac examination demonstrated an irregular rhythm without audible murmur, gallop, or peripheral edema. Lungs were clear bilaterally. The patient appeared comfortable at rest but became mildly breathless after walking in the hallway. Recent basic metabolic panel and thyroid testing were without a clear reversible trigger; a current complete blood count and transthoracic echocardiogram have been requested.

Please assess ventricular rate control, stroke and bleeding risk, left atrial and ventricular structure, and candidacy for cardioversion or an antiarrhythmic strategy. Guidance regarding duration of anticoagulation and peri-procedural management would be appreciated. The patient will continue apixaban and metoprolol succinate as prescribed pending your recommendations and will seek urgent care for sustained severe dyspnea, chest pain, syncope, or neurologic symptoms.

Follow-up with primary care is planned in about 3 weeks, or sooner if symptoms worsen.

Sincerely,

Sunnee Mesen, MD

Date: 2004-11-19
Patient: Cillian K.
Contact: (202) 555-0160
Report/accession ID: 04347674

You were seen today for recurrent migraine. Your adult child joined the visit, and you provided the history directly. Your chart lists you as 86 y/o. The current pattern remains consistent with migraine without a concerning change in character: one-sided headache followed by nausea and sensitivity to light. You did not describe fever, fainting, new weakness, trouble speaking, persistent vision loss, or a sudden “worst headache” onset.

Please continue sumatriptan 50 mg at onset of migraine. Take it as soon as you recognize the usual migraine symptoms; do not use it more than directed on the prescription. Naproxen may be used with food for pain if you normally tolerate anti-inflammatory medicines. Avoid combining naproxen with other over-the-counter NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen. Limit acute headache medicines to no more than 2 to 3 days per week when possible, since frequent use can create medication-overuse headaches.

For prevention, keep a simple headache diary noting the date, duration, possible triggers, menstrual or sleep-related pattern if relevant, medicines taken, and response. Regular meals, adequate fluids, consistent sleep, and limiting excess caffeine may reduce attacks. During an episode, rest in a quiet, dark room and reduce screen exposure.

Seek emergency care for a sudden maximal headache, new neurologic symptoms, confusion, seizure, fever with neck stiffness, repeated vomiting with inability to keep fluids down, or a headache after significant injury. Contact the office if attacks become more frequent, last longer than usual, require repeated rescue medication, or interfere with work or daily activities. At follow-up, we can review the diary and discuss preventive treatment if the current plan is not sufficient.

Internal Medicine Follow-up Note

Discharge Summary

Patient: Valentino
DOB: 1956-05-19
Service: Pulmonary Medicine

Reason for admission: Valentino was admitted for progressive redness, warmth, and tenderness of the lower leg concerning for nonpurulent cellulitis. The erythema had extended beyond the area first noticed at home, without preceding trauma, drainage, or known animal bite. noheli heinsen, a friend who assisted with the history, reported no confusion or fainting. The patient provided consent for this collateral history.

Hospital course: On arrival, the patient was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Examination showed a warm, tender erythematous area of the lower leg without fluctuance, crepitus, bullae, or pain out of proportion to examination. Distal pulses and sensation were intact. Laboratory evaluation showed a mild leukocytosis with preserved renal function. Blood cultures remained without growth, and ultrasound did not demonstrate a drainable fluid collection or deep venous thrombosis.

The patient received initial intravenous antibiotics with clinical improvement in pain and reduction in the advancing erythema. There was no evidence of sepsis, necrotizing soft-tissue infection, or osteomyelitis. No procedure was required. The patient remained ambulatory and tolerated oral intake before discharge.

Discharge assessment and plan: Cellulitis of the lower leg, improving on antibiotic therapy. Continue dicloxacillin 500 mg four times daily to complete the prescribed course. Acetaminophen may be used for discomfort according to the bottle instructions; do not exceed the labeled daily maximum. Keep the leg clean and dry, elevate it when resting, and avoid scratching or applying unapproved topical products.

Return immediately for fever, rapidly spreading redness, new drainage, severe or escalating pain, numbness, skin discoloration, dizziness, vomiting, or difficulty walking. Follow up with primary care on October 28, 2012 for reassessment and medication review. The patient may contact noheli heinsen in Alloway for transportation or support if needed.

At discharge, the patient was alert, comfortable, ambulatory, and clinically improved. Discharge instructions and return precautions were reviewed, and the patient verbalized understanding.

Admitted for an acute sickle cell painful crisis with severe bilateral limb pain, diffuse low back pain, and poor oral intake with clinical dehydration. History was obtained from the patient and legal guardian. The patient assented to the treatment plan; guardian consent was obtained for inpatient care and medication administration.

Hospital Course
Pain was initially treated with intravenous morphine with reassessment after each dose, then transitioned to oral analgesia as symptoms improved. Hemoglobin was near the patient’s documented baseline, with reticulocytosis consistent with the underlying hemoglobinopathy. Electrolytes and renal function remained acceptable. Pain decreased from severe to mild with oral medication, and the patient tolerated fluids and meals before discharge. Guardian was present for medication teaching and return precautions.

Discharge Medications
• Morphine by mouth for breakthrough severe pain only, using the dose listed on the medication reconciliation.
• Acetaminophen and ibuprofen as directed on the discharge medication list, unless otherwise instructed by hematology.
• Continue home sickle cell disease medications without interruption.

Condition at Discharge
Stable, alert, breathing comfortably on room air, adequately hydrated, and ambulatory. Discharged home with legal guardian.

Instructions and Follow-Up
Encourage frequent oral fluids, rest, warmth, and gentle activity as tolerated. Seek emergency care for fever of 101°F or higher, chest pain, shortness of breath, increasing sleepiness, persistent vomiting, inability to drink, new weakness, or pain not controlled by the prescribed plan. Follow up with the hematology clinic in about 6 weeks, or sooner for recurrent or worsening symptoms.

LABORATORY REPORT
SSN: 666 21 5700

Patient: B. Toops
MRN: 012110/84
Clinical service: Internal Medicine
Specimen: Venous blood and random urine
Collection context: Outpatient evaluation of thirst, fatigue, and frequent urination for 3 days. Patient reports taking metformin and atorvastatin as prescribed.

Results
- Hemoglobin A1c: 9.2% (reference range 4.0–5.6%); high
- Estimated average glucose: 217 mg/dL
- Glucose, serum: 248 mg/dL (reference range 70–99 mg/dL fasting); high
- Creatinine: 0.86 mg/dL (reference range 0.60–1.30 mg/dL)
- Estimated GFR: 106 mL/min/1.73 m² (reference value ≥60)
- Sodium: 136 mmol/L (reference range 135–145)
- Potassium: 4.3 mmol/L (reference range 3.5–5.1)
- Bicarbonate: 24 mmol/L (reference range 22–29)
- Urine albumin/creatinine ratio: 18 mg/g (reference value <30); normal
- Urine ketones: Negative
- Urine glucose: 3+; abnormal

Interpretation
Findings are consistent with inadequately controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus. Renal filtration and urine albumin excretion are preserved. Normal bicarbonate and negative urine ketones provide no laboratory evidence of ketoacidosis in this specimen.

Clinical comment
The elevated A1c indicates sustained hyperglycemia rather than an isolated serum glucose abnormality. Review adherence, meal pattern, home glucose readings, and metformin tolerance. Consider diabetes medication intensification through the treating primary care clinician, with nutrition counseling and hydration guidance. The patient should seek urgent evaluation for vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, inability to keep fluids down, or marked worsening of polyuria.

Recommended follow-up
Repeat glycemic assessment and medication review at the follow-up appointment on 07/18/2026. Consider annual retinal examination and continued lipid management with atorvastatin. Any treatment change should account for home glucose trends and hypoglycemia risk.

Initial ECG showed nonspecific ST-segment and T-wave abnormalities without ST-segment elevation. • Aspirin 81 mg by mouth daily.

• Metoprolol succinate 25 mg by mouth daily.
• Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg sublingually as needed for chest pain, up to three doses.

Instructions and follow-up
Call 911 for chest pressure, shortness of breath, fainting, or pain not relieved after the first nitroglycerin dose. Avoid heavy exertion until cleared. Follow up with primary care within 1 week and cardiology within 2 weeks; referral to cardiac rehabilitation was placed.

Stable, chest-pain free, and discharged home with sibling support.

LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: Cobie C.
MRN: 0618818
Contact: (212) 555-0175
Specimen: Serum
Collection context: Outpatient evaluation for fatigue, cold intolerance, and constipation in a patient receiving levothyroxine. Fasting status was not required. Specimen received without hemolysis or lipemia sufficient to affect reported results.

Results:
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH): 8.62 mIU/L
Free thyroxine (free T4): 0.71 ng/dL
Total triiodothyronine (T3): 74 ng/dL
Thyroid peroxidase antibody: 186 IU/mL
Thyroglobulin antibody: 22 IU/mL
Hemoglobin: 12.9 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume: 89.4 fL
Ferritin: 48 ng/mL
Vitamin B12: 512 pg/mL
Sodium: 139 mmol/L
Potassium: 4.2 mmol/L
Creatinine: 0.82 mg/dL
Alanine aminotransferase: 19 U/L

Reference interpretation:
TSH: 0.40–4.50 mIU/L
Free T4: 0.8–1.8 ng/dL
Total T3: 76–181 ng/dL
Thyroid peroxidase antibody: <9 IU/mL
Thyroglobulin antibody: ≤1 IU/mL

Interpretive comment:
TSH is elevated with mildly decreased free T4 and low total T3, consistent with biochemical under-replacement or insufficient thyroid hormone exposure in the setting of known hypothyroidism. Positive thyroid peroxidase antibody supports an autoimmune thyroiditis pattern. The normal hemoglobin, ferritin, vitamin B12, renal function, electrolytes, and alanine aminotransferase do not identify an alternative laboratory explanation for the reported fatigue.

Correlation with the prescribed levothyroxine dose, adherence, timing relative to food, and use of calcium, iron, antacids, or other absorption-interfering agents is recommended. Dose adjustment should be determined by the treating clinician rather than from laboratory findings alone. Repeat TSH and free T4 after a clinically appropriate interval is advised; a follow-up review is scheduled for April 14, 2004, in about 11 weeks.

Discharge Summary

Patient: A. Robards
Admission/Discharge Date: December 10th, 2019
Service: Emergency Department
Emergency contact/partner: Laylarose Nassery
Patient contact: alinur.robards62@icloud.com

Reason for visit:
The patient, age 33 years, presented to the emergency department with two days of worsening right flank pain, dysuria, urinary frequency, chills, and rigors. The patient reported nausea without persistent vomiting and denied chest pain, shortness of breath, vaginal bleeding, or testicular symptoms. The partner provided additional history and remained available during the evaluation.

Evaluation:
Initial examination showed right costovertebral angle tenderness and mild suprapubic discomfort without peritoneal signs. The patient was alert, ambulatory, and clinically euvolemic. Current vital signs included blood pressure 120/80 mmHg. Urinalysis demonstrated pyuria, positive leukocyte esterase, bacteriuria, and microscopic hematuria. CBC showed mild leukocytosis. Renal function and electrolytes were reassuring, and lactate was not elevated. A urine culture was obtained before antibiotics. CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast showed inflammatory changes about the right kidney and proximal ureter without obstructing stone or hydronephrosis.

Hospital course:
The patient received intravenous fluids, acetaminophen for pain and fever, antiemetic therapy, and an initial dose of cefuroxime in the ED. Rigors resolved, flank pain improved, and oral intake was tolerated before discharge. There was no hypotension, persistent tachycardia, altered mental status, or evidence of septic shock. Given clinical improvement, stable renal function, absence of obstruction, and reliable outpatient follow-up, admission was not required. The patient and partner were counseled regarding the diagnosis, anticipated recovery, medication use, and return precautions.

Discharge diagnoses:
1. Acute right-sided pyelonephritis.
2. Dysuria and flank pain secondary to urinary tract infection.
3. Nausea, improved.

Discharge medications:
• Cefuroxime, continue the prescribed outpatient course and complete all doses, even if symptoms improve.
• Acetaminophen as directed for pain or fever. Do not exceed the labeled daily maximum and avoid combining it with other acetaminophen-containing products.
• Maintain hydration as tolerated. Avoid NSAIDs unless approved by the primary care clinician, particularly if vomiting or dehydration recurs.

Follow-up and instructions:
Follow up with primary care within 48–72 hours. The urine culture will be reviewed, and antibiotic therapy may be adjusted if resistance is identified. Return to the ED immediately for recurrent rigors, worsening flank pain, inability to keep medications or fluids down, fainting, confusion, reduced urination, or fever that persists despite treatment. The patient left in stable condition with written instructions and verbalized understanding.

Emergency Department Note
SSN: 666 22 8106

Patient: Cataliyah
MRN: 08998244
Contact: (212) 555-0123
Accompanied by spouse, Yuritzy

Presenting concern: Itchy rash and skin irritation.

Cataliyah presents with two days of progressively itchy, red patches along the sides of the neck, upper chest, and forearms. The patient reports using a new scented laundry detergent earlier this week and denies new prescription medications, foods, or insect exposure. There has been no fever, facial swelling, throat tightness, wheezing, vomiting, blistering, or drainage. The spouse confirms that the rash has remained localized and that the patient has been otherwise acting normally. Prior records from St Croix Regional Medical Center were reviewed, including the current medication list of hydrocortisone cream and cetirizine.

On examination, the patient is comfortable and speaking in full sentences. Temperature and other vital signs are within acceptable limits. Skin examination shows scattered, sharply demarcated erythematous papules and thin plaques over areas corresponding to clothing and detergent contact. There is mild excoriation without warmth, fluctuance, vesicles, bullae, petechiae, mucosal involvement, or skin sloughing. The face, lips, and tongue are not swollen. Lungs are clear bilaterally without stridor or wheezing. Cardiovascular examination is unremarkable. Glasgow Coma Scale 15.

No laboratory or imaging studies are indicated based on the benign localized examination and absence of systemic symptoms. The presentation is most consistent with allergic contact dermatitis, likely related to the newly introduced scented detergent. There is no clinical evidence of anaphylaxis, cellulitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, or disseminated infection.

Treatment and plan: The patient was advised to stop using the new detergent, wash recently exposed clothing and bedding with a fragrance-free product, avoid scratching, and use cool compresses. Continue cetirizine as previously directed and apply hydrocortisone cream in a thin layer to affected nonfacial areas as directed; avoid application to broken skin or near the eyes. Return immediately for breathing difficulty, facial or oral swelling, blistering, fever, rapidly spreading redness, or skin pain.

Disposition: Discharged home in stable condition with primary care follow-up if symptoms do not improve.

Pulmonary Medicine Referral
SSN: 666 79 6028

Re: Gabrielly

Dear Pulmonary Medicine Colleague,

I am referring Gabrielly for evaluation of suspected obstructive sleep apnea and recommendations regarding ongoing management. The specific clinical question is whether formal sleep testing and adjustment of positive airway pressure therapy are indicated given persistent symptoms despite current use of continuous positive airway pressure.

The history was obtained from the patient and the patient’s sibling, Infinite Hoemann. Over the past several months, the family has noticed loud snoring and recurrent pauses in breathing during sleep, followed by gasping and repositioning. The patient reports unrefreshing sleep, morning dry mouth, and daytime somnolence with difficulty maintaining attention during meetings at Baggs Senior Center. There has been no reported syncope, nocturnal chest pain, or witnessed seizure activity. The patient has experienced nasal congestion for 3 days but denies fever or significant shortness of breath.

The patient uses continuous positive airway pressure most nights, although adherence is inconsistent because of mask discomfort and intermittent nasal obstruction. The device download was not available for review today. The patient is not taking sedative-hypnotic medication and reports no regular alcohol use near bedtime. There is no known history of chronic lung disease. Examination in the office showed the patient in no acute distress, with clear breath sounds, regular heart rhythm, and no lower-extremity edema. Oropharyngeal examination suggested a crowded airway. Resting oxygen saturation was 96% on room air.

Assessment: Symptoms and witnessed events remain strongly suggestive of obstructive sleep apnea, with possible inadequate positive airway pressure adherence or settings. Nasal symptoms may be contributing to mask intolerance.

Plan: Please assess whether repeat polysomnography or home sleep apnea testing is appropriate, review available device adherence and residual-event data, and advise on pressure settings and mask/interface options. Recommendations for treatment of nasal obstruction and any additional cardiometabolic risk evaluation would also be appreciated. The patient was asked to bring the device, mask, tubing, and recent medication list to the consultation.

Referring clinician: R. Fioritto
Service locality: Yoder

MRN: 041 818 265
Reporting organization: Hospital Menonita De Cayey
Collection/report date: June 4, 2022
Specimen: Plasma, venous blood; received for chemistry testing. Ordering clinician: not listed.

Results
Creatinine: 2.4 mg/dL (reference 0.6–1.3)
BUN: 46 mg/dL (reference 7–20)
eGFR: 28 mL/min/1.73 m² (reference ≥60)
Sodium: 137 mmol/L (reference 135–145)

CO2: 21 mmol/L (reference 22–29)
Glucose: 108 mg/dL (reference 70–99 fasting)
Calcium: 8.7 mg/dL (reference 8.5–10.5)

Interpretation
Creatinine and BUN are elevated with reduced estimated filtration, consistent with acute kidney injury in the appropriate clinical setting. Mildly decreased CO2 may reflect developing metabolic acidosis. Potassium is currently within the laboratory reference interval.

Clinical context and comment
The clinical history notes reduced urine output, fatigue, and poor oral intake for 3 days. Findings may represent volume-responsive/prerenal kidney injury, although obstruction and intrinsic renal disease cannot be excluded from these results alone. Correlate with baseline renal function, fluid balance, urinalysis, and renal imaging if oliguria persists.

Intravenous sodium chloride and temporary medication hold are documented. Continue close monitoring of urine output, electrolytes, and repeat renal function after treatment; avoid nephrotoxic exposures when feasible. Urgent clinical reassessment is appropriate for worsening oliguria, dyspnea, confusion, or hyperkalemia.

Patient: Rohnan Krasinski
MRN: 099 730 847
Occupation: Hairdresser
Department: Emergency Department
Genetics consultation location: Guam Memorial Hospital

Your visit today focused on hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk. You shared a significant family history of cancer and requested predictive genetic testing because of ongoing concern about your own future cancer risk. You do not currently have symptoms requiring treatment, and you are taking no current treatment.

We reviewed that an inherited cancer-risk change can be passed through a family, but a positive result does not mean that cancer is present or certain to develop. A negative result may be reassuring but does not always remove risk when the family history remains concerning. The most informative person to test is often a relative who has had a related cancer, if testing is available and that relative is willing.

With your permission, we will obtain and review available family medical records and pathology information before finalizing the testing plan. Genetic counseling will include discussion of possible positive, negative, and uncertain results; insurance and privacy considerations; and the effects of testing on relatives. The laboratory panel may include BRCA1 c.68_69delAG and other genes associated with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer. This variant will be interpreted in the context of the full laboratory report and your family history.

No blood draw was completed during this encounter. After the family-history review, the genetics team will contact you to confirm whether you wish to proceed with a saliva or blood test and to discuss the expected turnaround time. Until results are available, continue routine preventive care and age-appropriate breast and gynecologic screening with your primary care clinician. Seek urgent evaluation for new breast mass, persistent nipple or skin change, unexplained bleeding, or other acute symptoms.

Please contact Guam Memorial Hospital with questions about records, consent, or test results. This assessment was completed by Kelley Nostrand, MD, who recommends formal genetic counseling and shared decision-making before predictive testing.

CLINICAL GENETICS LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: Grayson C.
Clinical context: The patient, age 42 years, was referred for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk assessment because of a significant family history, concern regarding future cancer risk, and a request for predictive testing. The family history was reviewed with the patient and includes a previously identified familial BRCA1 variant. The patient reports no current treatment and is not taking prescription medications.

Report/accession ID: LAB-07292954
Specimen: Peripheral blood submitted in an EDTA tube for germline hereditary cancer testing. Specimen integrity and quantity were adequate for analysis.

Testing performed: Targeted analysis for the familial BRCA1 variant BRCA1 c.68_69delAG. Sequencing and confirmatory analytical procedures were completed according to laboratory protocol. The assay is designed to detect the specified familial sequence change and is not a comprehensive evaluation of all possible pathogenic variants in BRCA1, BRCA2, or other cancer-predisposition genes.

Result: NEGATIVE for BRCA1 c.68_69delAG in the submitted specimen.

Interpretation: The familial BRCA1 variant was not detected. This result substantially reduces the likelihood that the patient inherited this specific familial variant; however, it does not eliminate hereditary cancer risk from other variants or from a different familial mechanism. The result should be interpreted in conjunction with the patient’s complete pedigree, the affected relative’s laboratory report, and the testing methodology used in the family.

Clinical comment: If the affected relative’s report has not been independently verified, comparison with that report is recommended before using this result for definitive family counseling. Cancer screening should continue to reflect the personal and family history rather than this negative targeted result alone. A genetics professional should review whether broader multigene testing is indicated, particularly if the family history includes early-onset breast cancer, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, metastatic prostate cancer, or multiple related cancers.

Follow-up: Genetic counseling follow-up is recommended for review of the result, residual risk, and screening options on October 19th, 2035. The ordering clinician was not identified on this laboratory report.

Validated and reported by: lauretta watry, Clinical Genetics Laboratory.

Elevate the leg, outline the redness, and return immediately for fever, rapid progression, severe pain, weakness, or vomiting. Follow up with primary care within two days. Laboratory Medicine Report
SSN: 000-63-1940

Patient: newt grigson
MRN: 02708068
Reporting laboratory: Norwalk Hospital
Department: Emergency Department
Specimen: Peripheral blood, EDTA whole blood and serum
Clinical indication: Painless lymphadenopathy with drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss; evaluation for suspected Hodgkin lymphoma. Supportive care pending tissue diagnosis.

Hematology
White blood cell count: 12.8 × 10^9/L (4.0–10.5 × 10^9/L) — High
Hemoglobin: 10.9 g/dL (12.0–16.0 g/dL) — Low
Hematocrit: 33.1% (36.0–46.0%) — Low
Platelet count: 468 × 10^9/L (150–400 × 10^9/L) — High
Absolute neutrophil count: 9.7 × 10^9/L (1.8–7.7 × 10^9/L) — High
Absolute lymphocyte count: 1.6 × 10^9/L (1.0–4.8 × 10^9/L)

Chemistry
Sodium: 137 mmol/L (135–145 mmol/L)
Potassium: 4.2 mmol/L (3.5–5.1 mmol/L)
Creatinine: 0.84 mg/dL (0.60–1.20 mg/dL)
Albumin: 3.1 g/dL (3.5–5.0 g/dL) — Low
Lactate dehydrogenase: 312 U/L (120–246 U/L) — High
C-reactive protein: 74 mg/L (0–8 mg/L) — High
Uric acid: 6.8 mg/dL (3.4–7.0 mg/dL)

Peripheral blood smear
Mild normocytic anemia and reactive neutrophilia are present. Platelets are increased in number with unremarkable morphology. No circulating blasts or definitive atypical lymphoid population is identified.

Interpretation
The findings demonstrate an inflammatory pattern with mild anemia, thrombocytosis, elevated C-reactive protein, and increased lactate dehydrogenase. These abnormalities are nonspecific but may accompany an active lymphoproliferative process, including Hodgkin lymphoma. Peripheral blood findings do not establish or exclude the diagnosis. Definitive classification requires excisional or core lymph-node biopsy with histopathology and immunophenotyping. Consider flow cytometry if clinically indicated; a negative peripheral-blood study would not exclude tissue-limited disease.

Clinical comment
Correlate with cross-sectional imaging and surgical or interventional radiology consultation for tissue sampling. Monitor CBC, metabolic panel, and uric acid if tumor burden is substantial or systemic therapy is anticipated. The patient is receiving supportive care pending tissue diagnosis. Follow-up review is scheduled for 2018-08-31.

Neonatology Outpatient Consultation Report

Patient: Cyriah
Clinical age: 2 wk old
Legal guardian: Deshae
Contact: (202) 555-0175

Reason for consultation: Evaluation of neonatal jaundice with sleepy feeding and reduced intake.

History: Deshae, the patient’s legal guardian, reports progressive yellow discoloration of the skin and eyes. The newborn has been more difficult to arouse for feeds and is taking less at each feeding than usual. No reported fever, apnea, cyanosis, bilious emesis, bloody stool, or abnormal movements. Urine output is present, and stools remain pigmented. Phototherapy and feeding support have been provided, with modest improvement in alertness during feeds. No medication exposure other than the documented neonatal treatment has been reported.

Examination: The infant is arousable with handling but fatigues during examination. Mild scleral icterus and jaundice are visible to the trunk. Mucous membranes are moist. Anterior fontanelle is soft and level. Respirations are unlabored, with clear bilateral breath sounds. Cardiac examination demonstrates regular rate and rhythm without murmur. Abdomen is soft and nondistended; liver edge is not appreciably enlarged. Extremities are warm with brisk capillary refill. Neurologic examination shows symmetric tone and spontaneous movement of all extremities. No bruising or petechiae is identified.

Interpretation: The clinical appearance is most consistent with unconjugated neonatal hyperbilirubinemia associated with suboptimal intake. The infant is currently hemodynamically stable without examination findings suggesting sepsis, significant dehydration, cholestatic disease, or acute neurologic dysfunction. Ongoing feeding fatigue remains clinically important because inadequate intake may increase enterohepatic bilirubin circulation and impair bilirubin clearance.

Plan: Continue phototherapy according to the established neonatal treatment protocol and maintain frequent assisted feeds. Offer expressed breast milk or formula supplementation when direct feeding is ineffective, with intake and output documented by the guardian. Obtain repeat fractionated bilirubin and serum chemistry testing through the treating nursery team; escalation should occur for worsening lethargy, inability to feed, fever, pale stools, dark urine, or decreased urine output. No new outpatient medication is recommended today.

Neonatology follow-up is scheduled for June 5, 2020, in about 6 weeks. The family was advised that the planned interval should not delay earlier evaluation if feeding or alertness worsens.

Discharge Summary

Patient: Gautham M.
Admission/Discharge Date: Sep 29, 2028
Service: Cardiology
Healthcare organization: LINCOLN COUNTY HOSPITAL

Reason for admission: The patient presented to the emergency department with several hours of central chest pressure accompanied by diaphoresis and nausea. Initial electrocardiogram showed nonspecific ST-segment and T-wave abnormalities without ST elevation. Serial high-sensitivity troponin levels rose and then began to decline, consistent with a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction.

Hospital course: The patient was admitted to telemetry and treated with aspirin, therapeutic enoxaparin, and high-intensity atorvastatin. Symptoms resolved without recurrent chest pain. Cardiology evaluated the patient, and coronary angiography demonstrated significant coronary atherosclerotic disease without an indication for urgent surgical intervention. The cardiology team recommended medical management, with outpatient reassessment for further ischemic evaluation and risk-factor modification. Renal function and hemoglobin remained stable, and there was no clinical bleeding while receiving anticoagulation.

At discharge, the patient was hemodynamically stable and ambulatory, tolerating oral intake, and breathing comfortably on room air. Most recent vital signs included blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg. Cardiac examination was regular without a new murmur, and lungs were clear bilaterally.

Assessment and plan: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, clinically improved after medical treatment. Continue aspirin 81 mg daily and atorvastatin 80 mg nightly. Enoxaparin was stopped at discharge. In accordance with the cardiology plan, begin clopidogrel 75 mg daily after the inpatient loading dose and continue dual antiplatelet therapy for the duration specified by cardiology, unless bleeding or another contraindication develops. The patient was instructed not to stop aspirin or clopidogrel without speaking with cardiology.

Follow-up: A cardiology appointment should be arranged promptly through LINCOLN COUNTY HOSPITAL, with primary care follow-up for blood pressure, lipid management, diabetes screening, and tobacco counseling as applicable. Return immediately for recurrent or worsening chest pressure, shortness of breath, fainting, significant palpitations, black stools, vomiting blood, or other evidence of bleeding.

The patient identified I. Roban in Cedar as the emergency contact and received medication and return-precaution instructions before leaving the hospital.

CARDIOLOGY AND VASCULAR LABORATORY REPORT
SSN: 666-19-9655

Patient: Ramadan
MRN: 059481660
Reporting organization: MERCY ST FRANCIS HOSPITAL
Specimen: Venous blood and wound-associated laboratory evaluation
Clinical indication: Plantar ulceration with reduced sensation and local discharge in the setting of diabetes mellitus. Current management includes wound care and amoxicillin-clavulanate.

Results

Hemoglobin A1c: 8.7%
Reference interpretation: Above the usual diabetes treatment goal for many nonpregnant adults; correlate with individualized glycemic targets and recent treatment changes.

Glucose, serum: 164 mg/dL
Reference interval, fasting: 70–99 mg/dL

Creatinine: 0.92 mg/dL
Estimated GFR: 96 mL/min/1.73 m²

White blood cell count: 10.8 x10^3/µL
Reference interval: 3.8–10.8 x10^3/µL

C-reactive protein: 18.6 mg/L
Reference interval: <8.0 mg/L

Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 42 mm/hr
Reference interval: 0–20 mm/hr

Wound culture: Mixed skin and enteric flora recovered; no single predominant pathogen isolated. Susceptibility testing was not performed because the culture did not yield a clinically actionable predominant isolate.

Specimen quality and limitations

The wound specimen was received in an appropriate transport medium. A superficial wound culture may not represent organisms in deeper tissue or bone. Results should be interpreted with the ulcer depth, probe-to-bone findings, vascular examination, imaging, and clinical response to therapy.

Interpretation

The elevated hemoglobin A1c indicates suboptimal recent glycemic control, which may impair ulcer healing. Mild inflammatory marker elevation is compatible with localized inflammation or infection but is not specific for osteomyelitis. The normal creatinine and preserved estimated GFR do not suggest a current renal limitation to standard medication dosing. The white blood cell count is at the upper end of the reference interval.

Clinical comment

Continue local wound care and the prescribed amoxicillin-clavulanate pending clinical reassessment. Prompt podiatry or wound-care evaluation is recommended, with vascular assessment if pulses are diminished or healing is delayed. Escalate urgently for spreading erythema, fever, increasing drainage, tissue necrosis, systemic symptoms, or rapidly progressive pain. Glycemic management should be reviewed with the treating diabetes clinician.

Follow-up laboratory and wound review appointment: Feb 24, 2020

M. Ghalib was seen in the pediatric outpatient clinic with father present for follow-up of iron-deficiency anemia. Father reports that tiredness has improved somewhat since starting ferrous sulfate, although the patient still becomes dizzy after standing quickly and tires sooner than expected during active play. There has been no fainting, chest pain, shortness of breath at rest, vomiting, abdominal pain, blood in the stool, or unusual bruising. Appetite is fair. Father states the medication is given with water and is separated from milk when possible. No missed doses were reported this week.

The patient was alert, cooperative, and appropriately interactive. Conjunctivae remain mildly pale. Oral mucosa was moist without lesions. Heart had regular rate and rhythm without murmur, and lungs were clear bilaterally. Abdomen was soft and nontender, without palpable hepatosplenomegaly. Gait was steady, and there was no focal weakness. Orthostatic symptoms were not reproduced during the office examination.

Assessment:
Iron-deficiency anemia with gradual clinical improvement on oral iron. Residual fatigue and intermittent positional dizziness may reflect incomplete hematologic recovery. No concerning cardiopulmonary or neurologic findings today.

Plan:
Continue ferrous sulfate as currently prescribed. Give with a source of vitamin C when tolerated and avoid administering it with milk. Reviewed expected stool darkening and the importance of keeping the medication secured because accidental ingestion can be dangerous. Encourage iron-rich foods, regular fluids, and gradual activity advancement based on symptoms. Repeat CBC, reticulocyte count, ferritin, and iron studies before the next visit. Father will call sooner for fainting, breathing difficulty, marked weakness, persistent vomiting, or worsening dizziness.

Follow-up is planned in about 7 weeks, after laboratory testing, to review response and determine the duration of supplementation. Both patient and father voiced understanding and agreed with the plan.

History of Present Illness
The patient, age 22 years, was brought to the ED by a friend for progressive tiredness and markedly reduced urination. The patient reports minimal fluid intake because of nausea but denies persistent vomiting, diarrhea, chest pain, dyspnea, flank pain, dysuria, or recent contrast exposure. The friend reports no confusion, syncope, or witnessed seizure. Medication reconciliation identified a recently used over-the-counter anti-inflammatory; exact duration is unclear.

Focused Examination
Afebrile, heart rate 96, blood pressure 104/66, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Appears fatigued but alert and cooperative. Oral mucosa dry. Lungs clear bilaterally. Regular cardiac rhythm without murmur. Abdomen soft and nontender, without suprapubic fullness or costovertebral angle tenderness. No peripheral edema. Extremities warm with intact distal pulses.

Investigations
Basic metabolic panel notable for creatinine 2.4 mg/dL and BUN 39 mg/dL; prior baseline was not available at initial review. Potassium 4.8 mmol/L, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L. Urinalysis shows concentrated urine without significant blood or leukocyte esterase. CBC without leukocytosis. ECG demonstrates sinus rhythm without acute ischemic changes. Bladder scan shows low post-void residual. Renal ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis.

Medical Decision-Making
Findings are most consistent with acute kidney injury, likely related to volume depletion and medication effect. No evidence of obstructive uropathy, urinary infection, pulmonary edema, or emergent hyperkalemia. Cardiology was consulted because of the department pathway; no cardiac admission indication was identified.

Treatment and Disposition

Discharge Summary

Patient: Karasi S.
Service: Cardiology
Discharging clinician: A. Drewery
Treating organization: MUSC Health Columbia Medical Center Downtown

Reason for admission: The patient was admitted after developing sudden breathlessness, right-sided pleuritic chest pain, and a rapid heartbeat. Initial oxygen saturation was reduced on room air, and CT pulmonary angiography demonstrated acute bilateral pulmonary emboli without evidence of right ventricular strain. The associated report/accession ID was 035611055.

Hospital course: The patient received supplemental oxygen and therapeutic anticoagulation with apixaban. Lower-extremity venous ultrasound did not show deep vein thrombosis. Troponin was minimally elevated initially and subsequently down-trended; echocardiography showed normal right ventricular size and function. There was no hypotension, syncope, or need for thrombolysis. Oxygen was gradually weaned, and the patient maintained acceptable saturation on room air with ambulation. Pleuritic discomfort improved from 5/10 on admission to mild intermittent pain at discharge. Acetaminophen was effective, and no opioid was required.

Assessment: Acute pulmonary embolism with transient hypoxemia, clinically improving on anticoagulation. The event appears appropriate for treatment with a direct oral anticoagulant. The duration of therapy should be reassessed in follow-up after review of provoking factors, bleeding risk, and any pending age-appropriate screening.

Discharge medications:
- Apixaban 10 mg by mouth twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily.
- Acetaminophen as needed for pleuritic discomfort.
- Supplemental oxygen is not required at rest or with ambulation at discharge.

The patient is hemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably, and ambulates independently. Discharge instructions included strict avoidance of NSAIDs unless specifically approved, reporting unusual bleeding or black stools, and avoiding activities with a substantial risk of trauma. The patient should return to the ED immediately for worsening shortness of breath, fainting, new chest pain, coughing blood, or marked unilateral leg swelling.

Follow-up is requested with MUSC Health Columbia Medical Center Downtown and primary care within one week to review anticoagulation tolerance and treatment duration. The patient’s sibling was informed of the plan and will assist with transportation from Pawleys Island.

Patient: C. Mclennan
The patient, age 7 weeks, was admitted for cough, increased work of breathing, and reduced feeding in the setting of an acute viral bronchiolitis illness. Viral testing was positive for respiratory syncytial virus; testing for influenza and SARS-CoV-2 was negative. Chest imaging was not indicated. The clinical presentation and examination were consistent with bronchiolitis without evidence of focal bacterial pneumonia.

2. Reduced oral intake, improved and adequate for discharge.
3. Nasal congestion, responsive to saline and suctioning.

At discharge, the infant was alert and consolable, breathing comfortably on room air, and taking oral feeds with a clear improvement from admission. The father demonstrated appropriate nasal suction technique and verbalized understanding of warning signs.

Discharge medications:
• Nasal saline drops as needed, followed by gentle bulb suctioning.
• No new prescription medications.

Instructions were reviewed with F. Zehms. Offer frequent smaller feeds and monitor wet diapers. Patient: arzoey hemmert, 87 y/o
Date: Today

The patient presented with approximately 18 hours of abdominal pain that began near the umbilicus and has migrated to the right lower quadrant. There has been no vomiting, diarrhea, urinary discomfort, vaginal bleeding, or prior abdominal surgery. The sibling reports no known sick contacts. On examination, the patient is alert, uncomfortable with movement, and not toxic appearing. Temperature is mildly elevated, with otherwise stable vital signs. Mucous membranes are slightly dry. There is no costovertebral angle tenderness. Peripheral perfusion is intact.

Laboratory testing shows leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance. Comprehensive metabolic panel is without clinically significant electrolyte or renal abnormality. Urinalysis does not suggest urinary infection. Pregnancy testing was obtained when clinically applicable and is negative. Ultrasound demonstrates a noncompressible, enlarged appendix with surrounding inflammatory change, consistent with acute appendicitis; no drainable abscess is identified.

Assessment and Plan

Findings are most consistent with acute uncomplicated appendicitis. Ovarian or testicular pathology, urinary infection, gastroenteritis, and perforation were considered, but the examination and imaging favor appendicitis. The patient received intravenous fluids, analgesia, antiemetic therapy, and ampicillin-sulbactam. Symptoms improved somewhat, but right lower-quadrant tenderness persists. The patient remains hemodynamically stable and is kept NPO.

The case was discussed with the surgical service at Evergreenhealth Medical Center. The patient will be admitted for operative evaluation and management. The patient and sibling understand the diagnosis, treatment options, and need for continued monitoring. Follow-up with primary care is recommended after hospitalization on 2026-11-25.

Patient: J. Belgum
Occupation: elementary school teacher
Clinic: Asociacion Hospital Del Maestro, Inc
Report/accession ID: 015145371

Reason for visit: Follow-up of brief positional vertigo with nausea and unsteadiness.

History: Patient reports several short episodes of room-spinning dizziness when turning in bed, looking upward, or rising from a low position. Episodes last less than a minute and resolve when still. Nausea occurs during the spinning but there has been no vomiting. Patient denies hearing loss, tinnitus, ear pain, headache, diplopia, dysarthria, focal weakness, syncope, chest pain, or recent head injury. A friend accompanied the patient and confirms increased caution with stairs. No falls. Prochlorperazine as required has helped nausea but has not changed the positional trigger.

Exam: Alert and conversant. Otoscopic examination normal bilaterally. Extraocular movements intact without spontaneous nystagmus. Strength and sensation grossly symmetric. Gait mildly cautious; tandem gait produces slight unsteadiness. Dix-Hallpike maneuver on the right reproduces brief vertigo with fatigable torsional nystagmus. No persistent nystagmus or focal neurologic deficit.

Assessment: Findings are most consistent with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, likely right posterior canal. Current examination does not suggest a central process.

Plan: Right-sided canalith repositioning maneuver performed in clinic with improved symptoms afterward. Reviewed home Epley maneuver and fall precautions; avoid driving during active episodes. Continue prochlorperazine as required, using the lowest effective amount and avoiding alcohol or other sedatives. Seek ED care for persistent vertigo, new severe headache, weakness, speech difficulty, fainting, or inability to walk. Follow up in 20 days if symptoms persist or sooner for worsening.

Signed by: LEELAND MCMAKEN

• Continue prenatal vitamin as tolerated; take with food or hold temporarily if it worsens vomiting.

Improved and hemodynamically stable. Ambulating without significant dizziness and tolerating oral intake. Discharge instructions were reviewed with the patient and spouse, including return precautions.

Arrange prompt follow-up with the established prenatal care clinician for reassessment of hydration, weight trajectory, and medication response. Follow-up appointment: 1996-12-09

Discharge Summary

Patient: yetzel eufemia
MRN: 083108776
Admitting service: Internal Medicine
Discharging service: Internal Medicine

yetzel eufemia was admitted for three days of profuse diarrhea, recurrent vomiting, and crampy abdominal pain with inability to maintain oral intake. The patient’s spouse, Nelle Radey, provided additional history and remained involved in discharge planning. Initial examination showed mild volume depletion with dry mucous membranes and diffuse, nonfocal abdominal tenderness without guarding or rebound.

Laboratory studies demonstrated mild prerenal azotemia and hypokalemia, both of which improved with treatment. Lactate was normal. Stool testing was negative for Clostridioides difficile and for the common bacterial and viral pathogens included on the inpatient panel. Blood cultures showed no growth. Abdominal imaging was not indicated because the pain remained diffuse, the abdominal examination stayed benign, and symptoms improved promptly with supportive care.

Hospital course: The patient received intravenous crystalloid, electrolyte replacement, and antiemetic therapy. Oral rehydration solution was introduced gradually and tolerated before discharge. Vomiting resolved, abdominal cramps substantially improved, and stool frequency decreased. There was no fever, hypotension, bleeding, or evidence of an acute surgical abdomen. At 08:15 on the day of discharge, the patient was tolerating a light diet, drinking fluids independently, and ambulating without dizziness.

Assessment and plan: Acute infectious gastroenteritis with associated dehydration and transient hypokalemia, clinically improved with supportive care. No antibiotics are recommended at this time given the negative testing and continued improvement.

Discharge medications:
• Oral rehydration solution by mouth frequently while diarrhea continues.
• Ondansetron as required for nausea, using the prescribed instructions.

The patient should advance the diet as tolerated, avoid alcohol and very fatty foods until fully recovered, and wash hands carefully after using the bathroom. Follow up with primary care through Mat-Su Regional Medical Center within one week, or sooner if symptoms recur. Return to the emergency department for inability to keep fluids down, fainting, worsening or localized abdominal pain, bloody stools, fever, confusion, or markedly reduced urination. The spouse will assist with transportation and monitoring at home; Nelle Radey resides in Gambell.

Condition at discharge: Stable, clinically euvolemic, and appropriate for discharge home.

Patient: dkhari rafacz

Reason for admission:
dkhari rafacz was admitted from the emergency department for an acute asthma exacerbation with diffuse wheeze, increased work of breathing, and several nights of cough. solvei budniewski, the patient’s parent, reported that symptoms had worsened over the preceding two days despite intermittent use of the albuterol inhaler. There was no fever, vomiting, choking episode, or known foreign-body aspiration.

Hospital course:
On arrival, the patient was alert but tachypneic with suprasternal retractions and expiratory wheezing. Oxygen saturation remained acceptable on room air, and supplemental oxygen was not required. Chest radiograph showed mild peribronchial thickening without focal pneumonia or pneumothorax. Viral respiratory testing was negative for influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, and SARS-CoV-2. At 08:15, the patient received an albuterol nebulizer treatment with improved aeration and reduced work of breathing. A systemic corticosteroid was administered in the ED, with a second dose planned after discharge per the asthma action plan.

During observation, albuterol was spaced from frequent treatments to every four hours without recurrence of respiratory distress. The patient tolerated oral fluids and food, remained afebrile, and had no further nighttime cough while monitored. Nursing staff provided inhaler and spacer teaching to the patient and solvei budniewski. Return demonstration showed appropriate technique after coaching.

Discharge problem list:
• Acute asthma exacerbation, improved
• Wheezing and increased work of breathing, resolved
• Need for controller therapy assessment in primary care

Discharge medications and instructions:
Continue albuterol inhaler, two puffs with spacer every four hours while awake for the next twenty-four hours, then use every four to six hours as needed for cough or wheeze. Complete the prescribed corticosteroid course. Use the spacer with every inhaler treatment. Avoid tobacco smoke, vaping aerosols, and other known triggers. The family was given a written asthma action plan and instructed to seek emergency care for blue lips, inability to speak or drink because of breathing difficulty, marked retractions, unusual sleepiness, or inadequate response to albuterol.

Condition at discharge:
Stable on room air, speaking comfortably, drinking, and without significant retractions or wheeze after treatment.

Follow-up:
See the primary care clinician within two business days for reassessment and discussion of daily inhaled corticosteroid therapy if symptoms remain frequent or nighttime cough recurs. ED Assessment

Patient: kalo swyers
DOB: 01/18/1964
Home address: 528 W Nine Mile Rd, Hawthorne, FL 32640
History obtained from patient and friend. Presents with 2 days of pruritic erythematous rash and burning skin irritation across the anterior neck, upper chest, and bilateral forearms. Symptoms began after using a new scented laundry detergent. No dyspnea, wheezing, throat tightness, facial swelling, fever, mucosal lesions, or vomiting. No similar prior episode. Friend reports no recent medication changes.

Vitals: BP 120/80 mmHg, HR 78, RR 16, Temp 98.4 F, SpO2 99% room air.

Exam: Alert, nontoxic. Oropharynx clear without edema. No stridor or respiratory distress. Blanching erythematous papular plaques with mild excoriation in areas of clothing contact; no vesicles, pustules, drainage, fluctuance, or cellulitic streaking. Lungs clear. Cardiovascular exam regular.

Medical decision-making: Findings most consistent with allergic contact dermatitis. Low concern for anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, bacterial cellulitis, or disseminated infection. No indication for epinephrine or laboratory testing.

Treatment: Advised immediate discontinuation of the new detergent, gentle fragrance-free skin care, cool compresses, and avoidance of scratching. Continue hydrocortisone cream to affected areas as directed and cetirizine for pruritus. Return precautions reviewed for breathing difficulty, oral swelling, fever, blistering, or rapid progression.

Disposition: Discharged home in stable condition. Primary care follow-up scheduled for Oct 5, 2035. Discharge instructions reviewed with patient and friend.

Signed: INCI MONASMITH, ED clinician

Date: May 22, 2045
SSN: 000498509
Patient: M. Wiechec
