Address: 554 Louis Sead Rd, Bronwood, GA 39826

Referral question
Please evaluate M. Wiechec in Clinical Genetics for possible inherited predisposition to essential hypertension and advise whether genetic testing is indicated. The patient has persistent blood pressure elevation despite treatment with amlodipine and lisinopril.

History
The patient reports intermittent headaches and light-headedness, without syncope, chest pain, palpitations, focal neurologic symptoms, or visual loss. A friend accompanying the patient provides supplemental history and notes that home readings have remained above the office goal despite reported adherence. Current medications are amlodipine and lisinopril; no over-the-counter decongestant or stimulant use is reported. Family history is concerning for hypertension affecting multiple first-degree relatives, although the available history is incomplete.

Current assessment
In the office today, blood pressure remains elevated on repeat measurement. Cardiac and pulmonary examinations are unremarkable. There is no peripheral edema. Neurologic examination is nonfocal. The patient rates the current headache 5/10. Basic metabolic testing and urinalysis obtained through primary care were reportedly unrevealing, with no documented hypokalemia or proteinuria. Renal ultrasound has not shown structural abnormality.

Prior management
Lifestyle counseling, home blood pressure monitoring, and medication adherence review have been addressed. Primary care is continuing amlodipine and lisinopril while the diagnostic evaluation proceeds.

Requested action
Please assess the pedigree, review the available laboratory and blood pressure records, and determine whether testing for a monogenic hypertension syndrome or referral to another specialty is appropriate. Recommendations regarding additional biochemical testing and medication management would be appreciated.

Sincerely,
aarion freiermuth

Patient: J. Ali
Occupation: Paralegal
Report/accession ID: A28U39170
Clinic: Morrison Community Hospital
Seen by: CALEY INNIS

Dear J. Ali,

Today we reviewed your concern about inherited cancer risk and your request for predictive genetic testing. You report a significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer, and you would like to understand whether you inherited a familial risk that could affect your own screening or future treatment decisions. You are not taking any current medications, and no treatment is being started today.

We discussed that genetic testing is most informative when a known family variant is available. The family result under review is BRCA1 c.68_69delAG. A positive result would indicate an inherited predisposition, but it would not mean that cancer is present or certain to develop. A negative result may be reassuring but can have different implications depending on whether the family variant has been confirmed and whether the test is able to detect it.

Before testing, the genetics team should review the family history, confirm the specific familial result, and explain possible outcomes, limitations, privacy considerations, and effects on relatives. Testing may be performed from a blood or saliva sample after informed consent. We also reviewed that results can be positive, negative, or uncertain, and that an uncertain result generally does not guide preventive surgery or intensified screening by itself.

Plan:
• Refer to the hereditary cancer genetics program at Morrison Community Hospital for counseling and confirmation of the familial variant.
• Obtain available records documenting the relative’s genetic test before selecting the patient’s assay.
• Continue routine preventive care while testing is arranged; no cancer-directed medication is indicated from today’s visit.
• Contact the clinic if you develop a new breast, ovarian, or other concerning symptom, although this visit does not suggest an active malignancy.
• Discuss results with the genetics clinician and consider testing for appropriate adult relatives if a pathogenic familial variant is confirmed.

CALEY INNIS
Pulmonary Medicine / Genetics Risk Assessment Clinic

Discharge Summary
SSN: 666-75-6052

Patient: Haydee B.
Home address: 797 McCullum, Lamar, IN 47550
Contact: (212) 555-0174
Encounter date: May 14, 2012
Clinical age: 62 y/o

Reason for admission: The patient was brought to the emergency department after sudden right arm weakness, left facial droop, and slurred speech witnessed by the patient’s emergency contact. Symptoms resolved before completion of the initial evaluation. There was no persistent numbness, vision loss, chest pain, or loss of consciousness.

Hospital course: Stroke alert evaluation was completed. Noncontrast head CT showed no acute hemorrhage or established infarct. CT angiography of the head and neck did not demonstrate large-vessel occlusion or hemodynamically significant carotid stenosis. Brain MRI showed no acute ischemic lesion. Telemetry remained in sinus rhythm without atrial fibrillation. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed preserved left ventricular systolic function and no obvious intracardiac thrombus. Laboratory testing was notable for elevated LDL cholesterol; renal function and blood counts were stable.

The neurologic examination remained normal throughout observation. At the time of discharge, blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg, and the patient was speaking clearly, ambulating independently, and tolerating a regular diet. The presentation was most consistent with transient ischemic attack rather than completed stroke.

Assessment and plan: Continue aspirin 81 mg once daily and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. The patient was counseled regarding medication adherence and vascular risk-factor reduction, including a heart-healthy diet, tobacco avoidance, and follow-up of blood pressure and cholesterol with primary care. Cardiology recommends outpatient rhythm monitoring if recurrent events occur or if palpitations develop; neurology follow-up is also advised for completion of secondary stroke-prevention evaluation.

Discharge medications:
Aspirin 81 mg by mouth once daily.
Atorvastatin 40 mg by mouth nightly.

Return immediately for recurrent weakness, facial asymmetry, speech difficulty, sudden vision change, severe headache, chest pain, or trouble walking, even if symptoms resolve before arrival. Do not drive yourself during a recurrent episode. Follow up with primary care within one week and arrange neurology follow-up after discharge. The patient verbalized understanding of the discharge instructions and was released home in stable condition.

Emergency Department Handover – Acute Pyelonephritis

Patient: Jens Cupka
MRN: M3852859
Home address: 457 18th Ave, Grandview, IA 52752
Contact: (202) 555-0157
Collateral: adult child, J. Kohlwey

Priority: Suspected acute right-sided pyelonephritis. Presents with two days of dysuria and urinary frequency, followed by worsening right flank pain, nausea, and shaking rigors overnight. No reported pregnancy risk. Adult child provided collateral history; patient remains able to answer questions appropriately.

At 08:15: febrile and uncomfortable, mildly tachycardic, blood pressure maintained, oxygenation normal on room air. Dry mucous membranes. Right costovertebral-angle tenderness without peritoneal signs. No focal neurologic deficit. No rash.

Investigations: urinalysis positive for leukocyte esterase, nitrites, and blood. CBC with leukocytosis and neutrophil predominance. Creatinine not significantly above available baseline; lactate normal. Blood and urine cultures obtained before antibiotics. Renal ultrasound without hydronephrosis or visible obstructing stone.

ED treatment: IV fluids, acetaminophen for fever and pain, and initial IV cefuroxime. Symptoms and heart rate improved during observation; tolerating oral fluids. No hypotension, altered mental status, or evidence of septic shock.

Assessment: complicated urinary infection with upper-tract involvement; obstruction and infected stone currently less likely based on imaging. Continue cefuroxime per local susceptibility guidance, transition to oral therapy when clinically stable, and review culture results within 48–72 hours. Avoid NSAIDs until renal function and hydration are reassessed.

Disposition: Observation admission for continued IV antibiotics and serial vitals is recommended given rigors and systemic features. Escalate urgently for recurrent hypotension, confusion, persistent vomiting, worsening flank pain, or reduced urine output.

Referral to Gastroenterology
SSN: 915 69 9230

Patient: ELIYANNAH PATLOLLA
Occupation: software developer
Employer: Roxbury Community College
Emergency contact: Athena

Dear Gastroenterology Consultant,

I am referring ELIYANNAH PATLOLLA for evaluation of persistent gastroesophageal reflux disease despite initial primary care and emergency department management. The specific question is whether additional diagnostic testing, including upper endoscopy or ambulatory reflux monitoring, is indicated and whether the current acid-suppression strategy should be modified.

The patient reports several months of retrosternal burning with frequent acid regurgitation and a night-time cough that is most noticeable after lying down. Symptoms occur despite avoidance of late meals and reduction of coffee, spicy foods, and alcohol. There is no reported dysphagia, odynophagia, hematemesis, melena, unexplained weight loss, or persistent vomiting. Athena has accompanied the patient to prior visits and reports that the cough sometimes interrupts sleep. The patient remains able to eat and drink without difficulty.

At the most recent emergency department assessment, vital signs were stable. Examination showed a well-appearing patient without respiratory distress. Cardiac examination was regular, lung fields were clear bilaterally, and the abdomen was soft and nontender without guarding. An electrocardiogram did not show acute ischemic changes, and chest radiography was without an acute cardiopulmonary process. The presentation was felt to be most consistent with reflux-related symptoms rather than an acute cardiopulmonary disorder.

Current medications are omeprazole and alginate suspension. The patient reports taking omeprazole before breakfast and using alginate suspension after symptomatic meals and at bedtime. Lifestyle measures have provided only partial relief. There has been no prior upper endoscopy, esophageal pH study, or documented evaluation for hiatal hernia.

Please assess for refractory gastroesophageal reflux disease, alternative causes of chronic cough, and any alarm features requiring expedited investigation. Recommendations regarding medication timing, dose optimization, duration of therapy, and the need for endoscopic or physiologic testing would be appreciated. If symptoms improve with the current plan, primary care follow-up is reasonable in about 9 weeks, with earlier reassessment for dysphagia, gastrointestinal bleeding, progressive pain, or inability to maintain oral intake.

Sincerely,

brynleigh holliness
Emergency Department Clinician

Patient: hollin arcouette
Occupation: Commercial Baker Helper
Employer: Fort Fairfield Public Library
Home address: 585 Detroit Rd, Topsham, ME 04086
Contact: hollin.arcouette85@hotmail.com

Dear hollin arcouette,

Today we reviewed your worsening breathing over the past several days. You described more breathlessness with routine activity, increased wheezing, and sputum that has changed from clear to thick yellow-green material. Your partner has noticed that you are stopping more often to catch your breath but has not seen confusion, fainting, or blue discoloration. You denied chest pressure, new leg swelling, coughing up blood, or fever.

In the office, you were able to speak in complete sentences. Breathing was mildly labored after walking, with diffuse expiratory wheezes and no focal crackles. Heart rhythm was regular, and there was no significant ankle edema. Oxygen saturation remained acceptable at rest and with brief office ambulation. This pattern is most consistent with an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Because you also have cardiac risk factors, seek emergency care for persistent chest discomfort, severe or rapidly worsening shortness of breath, inability to speak normally, fainting, or oxygen readings that remain below your usual target if you monitor at home.

Treatment plan:
• Start prednisone as prescribed for the short course; take it with food and do not extend the course without contacting us.
• Start doxycycline as prescribed because of the increased sputum purulence. Finish the course unless a serious reaction occurs.
• Use your albuterol inhaler for wheezing or shortness of breath according to the prescription. If you need it much more often than directed, call the office rather than repeatedly increasing the dose.
• Continue maintenance inhalers and avoid cigarette smoke, vaping, and other respiratory irritants. Drink fluids as tolerated.

An attending pulmonologist’s input may be helpful if symptoms do not return to baseline or if exacerbations continue. Please arrange follow-up with primary care within one week, sooner for worsening symptoms. We will also review inhaler technique and whether pulmonary testing or cardiac reassessment is needed at follow-up.

Sincerely,

Cardiology Clinic

Discharge Summary
SSN: 000 92 9635

Patient: KOBIE KVETON
MRN: MRN-04249369
Healthcare organization: Community Medical Center
Legal guardian: CUYLER VANGALDER

Reason for admission: The patient, age 17 years, was admitted from the emergency department with worsening right lower-quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and loss of appetite for 3 days. The legal guardian provided collateral history, and the patient participated in the history and assented to examination and treatment discussions as developmentally appropriate.

Evaluation showed localized right lower-quadrant tenderness with guarding but no diffuse peritoneal signs. Laboratory testing demonstrated leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance. Abdominal ultrasound was concerning for an enlarged, noncompressible appendix with surrounding inflammatory change. The pediatric surgery team reviewed the findings and recommended operative management.

Hospital course: The patient received intravenous fluids, acetaminophen for pain, and ampicillin-sulbactam before surgery. After discussion of risks, benefits, and alternatives with the patient and CUYLER VANGALDER, the patient underwent uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy. Operative findings were consistent with acute, nonperforated appendicitis. There was no abscess or drain placement. Recovery in the post-anesthesia unit was uneventful.

By discharge, the patient was tolerating a regular diet, drinking adequately, walking independently, and voiding without difficulty. Pain was controlled with oral acetaminophen. Incision sites were clean, dry, and intact without erythema or drainage. The patient denied recurrent vomiting, worsening abdominal pain, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

Discharge medications:
• Acetaminophen by mouth as directed on the discharge medication list for surgical pain.
• No additional antibiotic course is required because the appendix was nonperforated and source control was achieved.

Assessment and plan: Acute appendicitis, status post uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy. The patient is clinically stable for discharge home with the legal guardian. Patient and guardian received return precautions for fever, increasing abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, inability to maintain hydration, redness or drainage from an incision, or other concerning change.

Follow-up is arranged with pediatric surgery through Community Medical Center. Keep the incisions clean and dry as instructed, avoid strenuous activity until cleared, and resume school and routine activities gradually according to comfort and the surgical team’s guidance.

An adult child accompanied the patient and confirms that the cough is most noticeable overnight. There is no exertional chest pressure, shortness of breath, diaphoresis, syncope, fever, vomiting, black stool, or trouble swallowing. The patient has been using omeprazole and alginate suspension with partial relief, although the timing of the omeprazole has been inconsistent.

Review of systems is otherwise negative for abdominal tenderness, wheezing, or recent respiratory illness. No new prescription, tobacco, or alcohol exposure was reported.

Exam: Patient is alert, comfortable, and speaking in full sentences. Heart has regular rate and rhythm without murmur. Lungs are clear bilaterally with no wheezes or crackles. Abdomen is soft and nontender, without guarding or distention. Oropharynx is moist. No calf tenderness or peripheral edema is present.

Assessment: Symptoms are most consistent with gastroesophageal reflux disease with acid regurgitation and reflux-associated night-time cough. The benign cardiopulmonary and abdominal examination is reassuring, and the history is not suggestive of acute coronary syndrome, pneumonia, or gastrointestinal bleeding at this visit.

Plan: Continue omeprazole daily, taken before the first meal, and continue alginate suspension as directed for breakthrough symptoms. Avoid lying down for at least three hours after eating, and reduce late meals, large portions, caffeine, alcohol, peppermint, and spicy or fatty foods. Elevate the head of the bed if feasible. Follow up with primary care for reassessment and consideration of testing or gastroenterology referral if symptoms persist. Emergency precautions were reviewed for new exertional chest pain, breathing difficulty, fainting, vomiting blood, black stools, or worsening symptoms.

The patient remained hemodynamically stable and had no recurrent weakness, facial asymmetry, or language difficulty during observation. At 08:15, nursing staff documented that the patient was ambulatory without assistance and speaking in complete sentences.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed no acute hemorrhage or established infarct. CT angiography of the head and neck demonstrated no large-vessel occlusion or clinically significant carotid stenosis. Brain MRI showed no acute diffusion restriction. Telemetry did not reveal atrial fibrillation. Transthoracic echocardiography showed preserved left ventricular systolic function without an intracardiac thrombus or significant valvular abnormality. Routine laboratory testing was reassuring, including stable blood counts, electrolytes, renal function, and glucose. The presentation was reviewed with neurology and felt most consistent with transient ischemic attack.

The patient received aspirin during the admission and was started on high-intensity atorvastatin for secondary cerebrovascular prevention. Blood pressure was monitored without need for acute intravenous treatment. Swallow screening was passed, and physical, occupational, and speech therapy found no ongoing functional deficit. The patient and sibling were counseled regarding stroke warning signs and the need to call 911 for recurrent symptoms. The sibling’s locality is documented as Ulysses for discharge communication purposes.

Discharge problem list:
• Transient ischemic attack with resolved arm weakness, facial droop, and dysarthria
• Vascular risk reduction
• No acute infarct identified on MRI

Discharge medications:
• Aspirin, continue as directed on the medication list.
• Atorvastatin, continue nightly as directed on the medication list.
Medication reconciliation was completed, and the patient was advised not to stop aspirin without speaking with a clinician.

Condition at discharge:
 neurologically intact, tolerating diet, ambulating independently, and appropriate for discharge home with family support.

Follow-up and instructions:
Follow up with primary care within one week and neurology as arranged for further risk-factor assessment and consideration of prolonged cardiac rhythm monitoring. Seek emergency care immediately for recurrent weakness, facial droop, speech difficulty, vision loss, severe headache, imbalance, or confusion.

Emergency Department Assessment

Patient: Darleth Kumro
Clinical age: 48 y/o
Presenting concern: Brief episodes of spinning dizziness

Darleth Kumro presented to the ED with several episodes of room-spinning vertigo triggered by rolling onto the right side in bed and looking upward. Each episode lasted less than a minute and was followed by nausea and transient unsteadiness. There was no persistent dizziness at rest, headache, neck pain, diplopia, dysarthria, unilateral weakness, numbness, syncope, chest pain, palpitations, hearing loss, or recent head injury. A sibling provided collateral history and confirmed that the patient remained alert and interactive between episodes.

Initial vital signs were stable, including blood pressure 120/80 mmHg. The patient was afebrile, comfortable at rest, and speaking in full sentences. Pupils were equal and reactive, extraocular movements were intact without spontaneous nystagmus, and facial symmetry and speech were normal. Strength and sensation were symmetric in all extremities. Finger-to-nose testing was accurate, gait was mildly cautious, and there was no truncal ataxia. Right-sided Dix-Hallpike testing reproduced brief vertigo with fatigable torsional nystagmus; symptoms resolved when the patient returned to a seated position.

An ECG showed normal sinus rhythm without acute ischemic changes. Point-of-care glucose was within the expected range. Given the brief, reproducible positional symptoms and reassuring neurologic examination, the presentation is most consistent with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. Posterior circulation stroke, arrhythmia, metabolic disturbance, and vestibular neuritis were considered less likely. Emergent neuroimaging was not indicated based on the absence of persistent neurologic findings or other central red flags.

The Epley maneuver was performed with substantial improvement. Oral fluids were tolerated, and nausea improved after prochlorperazine as required. The patient was discharged ambulatory with instructions to change position slowly, avoid driving or climbing until symptoms have resolved, and return immediately for persistent vertigo, new weakness, severe headache, fainting, chest pain, trouble speaking, or inability to walk.

Assessment and Plan: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, improved after canalith repositioning. Continue supportive care and prochlorperazine as required. Follow up with Rhode Island Hospital on Jul 9, 2026 for reassessment and consideration of vestibular therapy.

Discharging clinician: PRIMO GUTT

Referring service locality: Beaufort

Reason for referral:
Please evaluate Yesica Sinnema for a possible inherited predisposition to asthma and related airway disease. The specific clinical question is whether the patient’s respiratory pattern, together with a notable family history of asthma and atopy, warrants genetic counseling, targeted testing, or broader evaluation.

Clinical history:
The patient reports episodic wheeze, night-time cough, and shortness of breath, particularly with viral upper-respiratory infections, seasonal allergens, and exertion. Symptoms have increased in frequency despite adherence to an albuterol inhaler for rescue use and a beclomethasone inhaler as controller therapy. The patient denies tobacco exposure and has not reported occupational inhalational exposures. The partner, W. Lefere, confirms intermittent nocturnal coughing and has observed increased work of breathing during recent flares.

No known congenital anomalies, developmental concerns, unusual infections, or features suggestive of a primary immunodeficiency have been documented. The patient has not previously undergone genetic testing.

At the most recent primary care assessment, the patient was comfortable at rest, with bilateral expiratory wheeze and no focal crackles. Oxygenation was clinically acceptable, and there was no evidence of acute respiratory distress. Inhaler technique was reviewed, adherence was reinforced, and avoidance of known triggers was discussed. The patient has been advised to seek urgent evaluation for severe dyspnea, inability to speak in full sentences, cyanosis, or inadequate response to rescue medication.

The presentation is clinically consistent with asthma, but the familial clustering and persistent symptoms raise the question of a heritable susceptibility rather than a recognizable single-gene syndrome. Please assess the pedigree, clarify the family history, and advise whether genetic counseling or testing is medically indicated. Recommendations regarding additional immunologic or pulmonary evaluation would also be appreciated. Primary care follow-up is planned in about 10 weeks, or sooner for worsening control.

Presented to the ED with sudden breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, and tachycardia. Initial oxygen saturation was reduced on room air, with improvement after supplemental oxygen. CT pulmonary angiography demonstrated acute bilateral segmental and subsegmental pulmonary emboli without CT evidence of right-heart strain. Take apixaban consistently and do not stop it without medical guidance. Seek emergency care for worsening shortness of breath, fainting, new or severe chest pain, coughing or vomiting blood, black stools, or uncontrolled bleeding. Avoid activities with substantial injury risk and notify clinicians before procedures or dental work.

Follow up with primary care within 1 week and with hematology or pulmonary medicine to determine anticoagulation duration and assess provoking factors. The patient’s spouse, who is currently in Glendale, received discharge teaching by telephone.

Repeat TSH and free T4 after a clinically appropriate interval following any dose change. Follow-up review scheduled for 03/19/2018.

Clinical Genetics Consultation Report

Patient: AZARIUS WHEELINGTON
Occupation: Hospital Pharmacist
Employer: Pago Pago School District
Home address: 465 Fagatogo Road, Pago Pago, AS 96799
Contact: azarius.wheelington62@hotmail.com

Reason for consultation: Evaluation of recurrent itching, erythematous rash, and skin irritation with concern for a possible inherited susceptibility to dermatitis.

History: The patient reports episodic pruritic eruptions affecting the hands, forearms, and neck. Symptoms worsen after contact with fragranced personal-care products and during periods of increased occupational exposure to cleaning materials. The current episode has improved but not fully resolved with hydrocortisone cream and cetirizine. There is no reported blistering, mucosal involvement, fever, joint swelling, or systemic illness. The patient’s spouse participated in the history with the patient’s permission. No clear family pattern of severe eczema, blistering disease, or syndromic skin findings was identified.

Examination: The patient is well appearing and in no acute distress. Examination shows faint, poorly demarcated erythematous patches with mild scale on the dorsal hands and flexural forearms. There is excoriation without ulceration, vesiculation, crusting, or drainage. No nail dystrophy, palmoplantar keratoderma, alopecia, unusual facial features, or other findings suggestive of a recognizable inherited dermatologic syndrome are present. No cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy is appreciated.

Interpretation: The clinical pattern is most consistent with allergic contact dermatitis, likely related to exposure to fragranced or occupational products. At this visit, the distribution and examination do not support a monogenic skin-barrier disorder or other inherited condition requiring genetic testing. A genetic etiology cannot be excluded solely by examination, but testing would not be expected to change current management.

Plan: Continue cetirizine as previously directed for pruritus and use hydrocortisone cream only as instructed for limited flares. Avoid fragranced products, harsh detergents, and identified cleaning agents; use protective gloves with a cotton liner when appropriate. Dermatology referral for patch testing is recommended if symptoms persist or recur despite avoidance measures. The patient was advised to seek prompt evaluation for facial swelling, breathing difficulty, extensive blistering, mucosal lesions, or signs of infection.

Follow-up: Return to Clinical Genetics in about 7 weeks for reassessment, or sooner if new syndromic features or a significant family history emerges.

Patient: brayzen graves

Referring location: Anderson

Clinical question: Please evaluate suspected obstructive sleep apnea, confirm severity, and advise on positive-airway-pressure management. I would also appreciate recommendations regarding persistent daytime sleepiness despite reported use of continuous positive airway pressure.

History and current concerns:
The patient reports several years of loud snoring with progressively disruptive nighttime breathing. The spouse has observed recurrent witnessed apneas followed by gasping and repositioning during sleep. Morning headache and nonrestorative sleep are also reported. Daytime somnolence is most problematic during sedentary activities and has begun to interfere with concentration at work. The patient denies syncope, exertional chest pain, or resting dyspnea. There is no reported history of chronic lung disease.

Continuous positive airway pressure was previously prescribed and is being used on most nights, although the patient is unsure whether the mask remains in place throughout the night. Nasal congestion and occasional dry mouth have limited tolerance. No sedative-hypnotic medication is reported. Counseling has included avoidance of alcohol near bedtime, side sleeping, and not driving when drowsy.

Examination in the primary care office:
The patient was alert and conversant, with no respiratory distress at rest. Nasal examination showed mild mucosal congestion without purulent drainage. Oropharyngeal examination demonstrated a crowded posterior airway. Lung fields were clear bilaterally, and cardiac rhythm was regular without a murmur. There was no peripheral edema. Blood pressure and oxygen saturation were recorded in the office but are not included here because the principal concern is sleep-related breathing rather than daytime cardiopulmonary instability.

Assessment and requested action:
The history is strongly suggestive of obstructive sleep apnea with clinically significant daytime impairment. Please arrange diagnostic reassessment, preferably with review of prior sleep-study data and a download of the continuous airway pressure device, including adherence, residual apnea-hypopnea burden, and leak. If indicated, repeat polysomnography or home sleep apnea testing may clarify current severity and treatment response. Please assess mask fit, humidification, nasal symptoms, and whether bilevel or alternate therapy is warranted.

I will reassess symptoms in about 12 weeks after pulmonary recommendations are implemented.

Sincerely,

M. Warns

Emergency Department Specialist Report

Patient: Chikamso K.
Encounter date: February 26th, 2004
Contact: chikamso.klix44@yahoo.com
Report/accession ID: 0455114516
Clinical age: 19 y/o

Reason for evaluation: Acute low back pain with radiation into the leg and associated paresthesia.

History of present illness:
The patient reports approximately 5 days of midline and left lower lumbar pain beginning after routine lifting at home. Pain is described as aching at rest with intermittent shooting pain extending through the left buttock and posterior thigh toward the calf. Tingling is present over the lateral calf and dorsum of the foot. Symptoms worsen with prolonged sitting, forward flexion, and coughing. Naproxen and acetaminophen have provided partial, temporary relief. No fall, direct trauma, fever, unexplained weight loss, active malignancy, intravenous drug use, or recent spinal procedure is reported. The patient denies saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, urinary incontinence, fecal incontinence, and progressive leg weakness.

Examination:
The patient is alert, conversant, and ambulatory with an antalgic gait. Lumbar paraspinal tenderness and reduced flexion are present without midline step-off or palpable deformity. Straight-leg raise reproduces radiating pain on the left at approximately 45 degrees. Motor testing is 5/5 for bilateral hip flexion, knee extension, ankle dorsiflexion, and great-toe extension. Sensation is mildly diminished to light touch along the left lateral calf compared with the opposite side. Patellar and Achilles reflexes are symmetric. Distal pulses are intact, and the feet are warm. No focal abdominal tenderness or costovertebral angle tenderness is identified.

Interpretation:
The presentation and examination are most consistent with uncomplicated left lumbar radiculopathy, likely from nerve-root irritation related to degenerative or discogenic disease. There is no current evidence of cauda equina syndrome, spinal cord compression, fracture, epidural infection, or other emergent compressive process. Emergent imaging is not indicated in the absence of red-flag findings or objective progressive deficit.

Plan:
Continue naproxen with food if tolerated and acetaminophen within labeled daily limits; avoid combining naproxen with other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Gentle activity and short walks are encouraged, while heavy lifting and prolonged bed rest should be avoided. The patient was advised to arrange primary-care follow-up for reassessment and consideration of physical therapy. Return immediately for new weakness, inability to walk, saddle numbness, loss of bladder or bowel control, fever, or rapidly worsening pain. If symptoms are not substantially improving, outpatient reassessment is recommended in about 12 weeks.

Discharge Summary
SSN: 666-33-4186

Patient: joscelyn belrose
MRN: 01104812
Service: Pulmonary Medicine
Admission diagnosis: Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

joscelyn belrose was admitted for several days of worsening breathlessness, increased wheezing, and purulent sputum despite increased use of the albuterol inhaler. A friend provided collateral history and assisted with transportation and medication review. At presentation, the patient was tachypneic with diffuse expiratory wheezes and an oxygen saturation below the usual baseline on room air. There was no focal chest pain, hemoptysis, or unilateral leg swelling.

Chest radiograph showed hyperinflation without focal air-space consolidation or pleural effusion. Viral respiratory testing was negative. Initial laboratory testing showed mild leukocytosis; renal function remained adequate for the prescribed treatment. Sputum was thick and yellow-green, without a clinically significant organism identified. The patient did not require noninvasive ventilation or intensive care.

Treatment included scheduled nebulized bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroid therapy, and doxycycline for suspected bacterial contribution to the exacerbation. Supplemental oxygen was titrated to the patient’s established target range and discontinued before discharge. By the morning of discharge, the patient was walking in the room with substantially less dyspnea, had improved air movement, and was able to speak in full sentences. At 08:15, oxygen saturation was stable on room air at rest.

Problem list:
• Acute COPD exacerbation, improved
• Purulent sputum, treated empirically with doxycycline
• Tobacco exposure counseling provided; cessation was encouraged
• Deconditioning related to acute illness

Discharge medications:
• Prednisone with completion of the prescribed short taper
• Doxycycline to complete the remaining course
• Albuterol inhaler, two puffs every 4 to 6 hours as needed for wheezing or shortness of breath
• Continue the patient’s other home medications unless otherwise directed

The patient received inhaler-use teaching, return-demonstration instructions, and an action plan for worsening respiratory symptoms. Seek emergency care for severe or rapidly increasing shortness of breath, blue lips, confusion, inability to keep down medications, or chest pain. Arrange follow-up with primary care and pulmonary medicine after discharge to reassess symptoms, inhaler technique, oxygen needs, and preventive therapy. Pulmonary rehabilitation and vaccination status should be reviewed at follow-up.

Discharge condition: Improved and medically stable for home discharge with friend support. Home address: 59 4100 North Rd, Salmon, ID 83467.

Chief complaint: Three days of worsening lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge, and pain with intercourse. Denies syncope, chest pain, dyspnea, vomiting, or urinary retention. Emergency contact: camilo dellangelo.

History: No reported fever at home. No prior pelvic surgery. Last menstrual period is not documented. Pregnancy possibility discussed; patient consents to pelvic examination and testing.

Return immediately for fever, worsening pain, vomiting, fainting, or inability to take medication. Follow up with gynecology in about 9 weeks, on Mar 14, 2024, or sooner for persistent symptoms.

Evaluation of painless lymphadenopathy with night sweats and unintentional weight loss. Hodgkin lymphoma is under consideration. The patient’s partner reports no current antimicrobial or antineoplastic therapy. Medication history indicates supportive care pending tissue diagnosis.

White blood cell count: 12.8 x10^3/µL (reference range 4.0–10.5 x10^3/µL) — High

Discharge Summary

Discharge date: February 6, 2045
Service: Cardiology observation

Patient: Dillan
Home address: 354 State Rte 820, Thibodaux, LA 70310
Contact: (212) 555-0137

32-year-old Hispanic female patient presented to the emergency department with two days of frequent watery diarrhea, several episodes of nonbloody vomiting, and crampy periumbilical abdominal discomfort. A friend provided additional history and confirmed reduced oral intake but no syncope, chest pain, dyspnea, recent antibiotic exposure, or known sick contacts. The patient was admitted to the cardiology observation service because of tachycardia and lightheadedness with standing, felt to be related to gastrointestinal fluid loss.

Initial evaluation showed mild volume depletion with dry mucous membranes and orthostatic symptoms. Electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. Serial troponins were negative. Basic metabolic testing showed mild hypokalemia and a modest increase in serum creatinine from the expected baseline; both improved after treatment. The abdomen remained soft without guarding or rebound. Stool testing was not indicated because there was no blood, high fever, recent hospitalization, or persistent severe abdominal pain.

Hospital course: The patient received intravenous crystalloid, electrolyte replacement, and antiemetic therapy with good response. Vomiting resolved, and diarrhea became less frequent. The patient tolerated clear liquids followed by a bland solid diet, ambulated without dizziness, and maintained stable blood pressure and heart rate without supplemental oxygen. No evidence of acute coronary syndrome or another cardiac cause for the presenting symptoms was identified.

Assessment and plan: Acute infectious gastroenteritis with dehydration, resolved/improving. Discharge home today with oral rehydration solution taken in frequent small amounts and ondansetron as required for nausea. Advance the diet gradually, avoiding alcohol, greasy foods, and dairy until symptoms have settled. Wash hands carefully and do not prepare food for others while diarrhea continues.

Follow-up is recommended with primary care in about 12 weeks, or sooner if symptoms recur or fail to fully resolve. Return to the emergency department for inability to keep fluids down, fainting, blood in the stool or vomit, severe or localized abdominal pain, confusion, or markedly decreased urination. At discharge, the patient was alert, comfortable, ambulatory, and able to repeat the medication and return-precaution instructions.

There is no chest pain, exertional pressure, syncope, palpitations, orthopnea, or leg swelling. The patient has not had fever, vomiting, or recent illness. Medication reconciliation confirms metformin 500 mg twice daily with food and atorvastatin; the patient reports taking both as directed without significant adverse effects.

The patient has been drinking more water because of persistent thirst and is waking during the night to urinate. Fatigue is present most days but has not prevented usual activities. Dietary intake includes frequent refined carbohydrates, and exercise has been inconsistent. Home glucose readings were reviewed qualitatively; no log was available for today’s visit.

On examination, the patient is alert and in no acute distress. Heart rate and rhythm are regular without audible murmur. Lungs are clear bilaterally. There is no peripheral edema. Skin is warm and dry, and distal pulses are palpable.

Assessment:

Plan:

Emergency Department Assessment — CIBOLA GENERAL HOSPITAL
SSN: 959 01 9745
Date: 2026-12-10

Patient: J. Shikany
The patient, age 68 years, presented with 36 hours of worsening pain, swelling, and redness at the right first metatarsophalangeal joint. The patient reports that the pain began overnight and is now severe with any contact or attempted walking. There was no fall, puncture wound, recent procedure, or other injury. The patient denies fever, chills, numbness, calf pain, chest pain, or shortness of breath. A relative is listed as the emergency contact.

Past history is notable for prior gout episodes with similar symptoms. Home medications include naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food and colchicine; the patient states that the current flare developed despite taking the usual medication. No recent antibiotic use or immunosuppressive therapy was reported.

On examination, temperature is 98.6°F, blood pressure 142/84, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The patient is uncomfortable but nontoxic. The right first metatarsophalangeal joint has marked tenderness, warmth, erythema, and soft-tissue swelling. Passive range of motion is severely painful. There is no fluctuance, drainage, streaking erythema, crepitus, or open wound. Sensation and distal perfusion are intact. The calf is soft and nontender.

Assessment: Findings are most consistent with an acute gout flare. Septic arthritis and cellulitis were considered because of the erythema and intensity of pain, but the patient is afebrile, well appearing, and without an infectious portal or systemic symptoms. Plain radiographs show no acute fracture or dislocation. Arthrocentesis was discussed; given the classic recurrent presentation and absence of systemic features, it was deferred with instructions to return promptly for any change.

The patient received oral analgesia and a dose of colchicine in the ED with partial improvement. Treatment options, medication precautions, hydration, rest, and elevation were reviewed. The patient was advised to continue naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food only as directed and not to combine it with other NSAIDs.

Disposition: Discharged home in stable condition with follow-up through primary care and CIBOLA GENERAL HOSPITAL. Return immediately for fever, spreading redness, drainage, worsening pain, inability to bear weight, or other concerning symptoms.

Electronically signed by Taleyah Popeck, MD.

Elizajane P. has a previously established diagnosis of Parkinson disease assessed by neurology. Current motor manifestations include a resting tremor, bradykinesia, and muscular rigidity. The patient remains on carbidopa-levodopa, prescribed through primary care after specialist assessment. Over recent weeks, the patient and partner report brief episodes of dimming vision, unsteadiness, and a sensation of impending faint when rising from a chair or standing for prolonged periods. There has been no reported loss of consciousness, exertional chest discomfort, sustained palpitations, or focal neurologic deficit. The partner has not observed seizure-like activity.

In the office, the patient was alert and able to provide a coherent history, with the partner contributing collateral information. A resting tremor and slowed initiation of movement were evident. Cardiac examination demonstrated a regular rhythm without an audible murmur, and the lungs were clear. Peripheral pulses were palpable, with no clinically significant edema. Symptoms were reproduced during supervised positional change, although the patient recovered after sitting. A formal orthostatic blood pressure series and medication reconciliation are requested; no home blood pressure log was available for review.

The differential includes autonomic dysfunction associated with Parkinson disease, volume depletion, and adverse hemodynamic effects from dopaminergic therapy. Arrhythmia and structural heart disease should be excluded given the near-syncope. Please obtain an electrocardiogram, ambulatory rhythm monitoring if indicated, and echocardiography based on your examination. Consider tilt-table testing or autonomic reflex testing if initial cardiac evaluation is unrevealing.

Please advise regarding safe blood pressure targets, compression and hydration measures, and whether medication timing or dose adjustment should be coordinated with neurology. A multidisciplinary medication review would be helpful before adding any agent for orthostatic symptoms.

Thank you for evaluating this patient.

Referring clinician: Mayline Niederhofer

Clinical indication:
Evaluation of fatigue, cold intolerance, and constipation in a patient with established hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. The patient reports worsening constipation for 3 days. No family history information was submitted with the specimen.

Specimen:
Peripheral blood, EDTA. Sample received in acceptable condition for genomic DNA extraction. Testing performed using a targeted thyroid-disease gene panel with sequence analysis and deletion/duplication assessment for the validated regions included in the assay.

Results:
• TSH: 8.6 mIU/L (reference interval 0.40–4.50 mIU/L) — high
• Free T4: 0.8 ng/dL (reference interval 0.8–1.8 ng/dL) — low-normal
• Thyroid peroxidase antibody: 186 IU/mL (reference value <9 IU/mL) — positive
• Thyroglobulin antibody: 42 IU/mL (reference value ≤1 IU/mL) — positive
• Targeted genetic panel: No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant identified in the genes analyzed.
• Variants of uncertain significance: None detected.

Interpretation:
The biochemical pattern is consistent with under-replacement or suboptimal control of primary hypothyroidism. Positive thyroid autoantibodies support an autoimmune etiology. The negative targeted panel does not exclude genetic contributions outside the assay’s coverage or multifactorial thyroid disease.

Clinical comment:
Correlation with medication adherence, administration timing, recent dose changes, and interacting agents is recommended. Levothyroxine is best taken consistently on an empty stomach, separated from calcium, iron, and certain antacids. Repeat TSH and free T4 after the treating clinician’s usual dose-adjustment interval; earlier review is reasonable if symptoms progress. Genetic counseling is not routinely indicated on the basis of this negative panel alone unless the personal or family history suggests syndromic thyroid disease.

Patient: Kourtnee S.
Contact: kourtnee.sayeed49@gmail.com
Report/accession ID: 0153971406
Visit type: Internal medicine follow-up

Dear Patient,

The patient, age 36 years, was reviewed today for several weeks of painless swelling in the left side of the neck, drenching night sweats, and unintentional weight loss. There has been no choking, difficulty swallowing, persistent cough, or recent dental infection. Examination shows firm, nontender cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes without overlying redness. Heart and lung examinations are reassuring, and the abdomen is soft without a clearly palpable spleen.

The working diagnosis is Hodgkin lymphoma. This is a serious but commonly treatable lymphoma, and the next essential step is obtaining tissue so hematopathology can confirm the subtype and guide treatment. The current report/accession identifier is 0153971406. Imaging has been requested to assess the chest, abdomen, and pelvis for additional lymph-node involvement. Blood testing will include a complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, lactate dehydrogenase, HIV testing, and hepatitis B and C screening before any potential chemotherapy.

For now, continue supportive care pending tissue diagnosis. Maintain fluids, small frequent meals, and a written record of temperature and night sweats. Do not start steroid medication unless directed by the oncology team, because steroids can affect biopsy interpretation. Seek emergency care for trouble breathing, rapidly increasing neck swelling, inability to swallow fluids, fever of 100.4°F or higher, chest pain, or severe weakness.

An urgent referral to hematology/oncology and surgical consultation for lymph-node biopsy will be placed. Please bring a complete medication and supplement list to those visits. We will review the pathology and imaging as soon as available, with follow-up scheduled for 10/23/2020. A support person may attend if desired.

Return to the ED for fever, chest pain, shortness of breath, worsening pain, inability to drink, fainting, or new weakness. Condition at discharge: stable, improved, and discharged home with family support.

Emergency Department Assessment
SSN: 000-38-2626

Patient: E. Shackleton
Report/accession ID: A29A06590
Presenting concern: Persistent vomiting in early pregnancy

The patient presents with five days of frequent vomiting and inability to keep down fluids or most food. She reports continued nausea despite doxylamine-pyridoxine and estimates unintentional weight loss over the past week. She denies abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, dysuria, diarrhea, fever, chest pain, or shortness of breath. Current pregnancy is documented as 9+4 weeks' gestation. Her adult child, iliyana makowiec, is present with the patient’s permission and helps provide the medication history.

On arrival she appeared tired and mildly volume depleted, with dry oral mucosa and delayed capillary refill. Blood pressure was 104/68 mmHg, heart rate 108 beats/minute, respiratory rate 18/minute, temperature 98.4°F, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Cardiac examination showed regular tachycardia without murmur. Lungs were clear. The abdomen was soft and nontender without guarding. No focal neurologic deficit was identified.

Urinalysis showed concentrated urine with ketones and no evidence of infection. Basic metabolic panel demonstrated mild hypokalemia without significant renal dysfunction or acidosis. Serum glucose was normal. Complete blood count showed no leukocytosis. Quantitative pregnancy testing was consistent with the reported gestational duration. An ECG obtained for persistent tachycardia showed sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. Report/accession ID: A29A06590.

Assessment: Findings are most consistent with first-trimester hyperemesis with dehydration and starvation ketosis. There is no current evidence of ectopic pregnancy, urinary infection, acute abdomen, or cardiopulmonary disease.

Treatment and disposition: Intravenous sodium chloride was administered with clinical improvement in heart rate and oral moisture. Antiemetic therapy was given in the ED, and the patient tolerated oral electrolyte solution and crackers before discharge. She was advised to continue doxylamine-pyridoxine as prescribed, take small frequent sips and meals, and return immediately for inability to keep fluids down, fainting, abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, fever, or reduced urination. Obstetric follow-up was arranged with Dallas Regional Medical Center for Aug 9, 2022.

A friend accompanying the patient provides additional history and confirms reduced appetite but no confusion, syncope, hemoptysis, vomiting, or leg swelling. The outpatient amoxicillin regimen was reviewed, and an additional antibiotic was prescribed for broader coverage.

Please arrange follow-up with the primary care office in about 8 weeks, or sooner if symptoms are not improving. Bring this summary and the current medication list to that visit.

LABORATORY REPORT
SSN: 000-95-5041

Patient: Lillien R.
MRN: 029 441 691
Reporting laboratory: Usa Health University Hospital
Ordering clinician: Not provided
Specimen: Peripheral blood, serum and EDTA whole blood
Clinical indication: Rheumatoid arthritis with increased morning stiffness, swollen hand joints, fatigue, and symptoms present for 3 days. Current medications include methotrexate, folic acid, and naproxen. Sibling provided additional history.

Collection context: Outpatient pulmonary medicine evaluation. Results are interpreted with the clinical examination and prior disease activity measurements.

RESULTS

Complete blood count
White blood cell count: 7.8 x10^3/uL (reference range 3.8-10.8)
Hemoglobin: 11.6 g/dL (reference range 11.7-15.5)
Hematocrit: 35.1% (reference range 35.0-45.0)
Platelet count: 412 x10^3/uL (reference range 140-400)
Absolute neutrophil count: 5.6 x10^3/uL (reference range 1.5-7.8)
Absolute lymphocyte count: 1.4 x10^3/uL (reference range 0.85-3.90)

Comprehensive metabolic panel
AST: 24 U/L (reference range 10-35)
ALT: 19 U/L (reference range 6-29)
Alkaline phosphatase: 79 U/L (reference range 31-125)
Creatinine: 0.78 mg/dL (reference range 0.50-1.10)
Albumin: 3.8 g/dL (reference range 3.6-5.1)

Inflammatory markers
C-reactive protein: 18.6 mg/L (reference range <8.0)
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 42 mm/hr (reference range 0-20)

Rheumatoid factor: 186 IU/mL (reference range <14)
Anti-CCP antibody: >250 units (reference range <20)

INTERPRETATION

Mild normocytic anemia and thrombocytosis are present. Elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate support active systemic inflammation. Strongly positive rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibody results are consistent with the established rheumatoid arthritis diagnosis but do not independently quantify joint activity. Hepatic transaminases and creatinine are within reference limits, with no laboratory evidence of current methotrexate-associated hepatotoxicity or renal impairment.

CLINICAL COMMENT

The inflammatory profile is compatible with a rheumatoid arthritis flare in the reported clinical setting. Correlate with joint examination and functional status. Continue medication review, including methotrexate monitoring and folic acid adherence; reassess naproxen exposure if gastrointestinal or renal risk factors are present. Consider rheumatology-directed adjustment of disease-modifying therapy rather than relying on anti-inflammatory treatment alone. Follow-up laboratory and clinical review is scheduled for October 27, 2020.

Noah Leverington

Plasma and serum obtained during evaluation for increased thirst, frequent urination, and weight loss. The patient’s mother reports several days of increased drinking and nighttime urination. Insulin therapy and home glucose monitoring are documented medications/management measures.

Results are consistent with new or poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus in this school-age patient. MRN: 0143288
Occupation: Physiotherapist
Referring facility: Adventhealth Deland
Consulting clinician: B. Grosinger

Reason for consultation:
Evaluation of several weeks of progressive fatigue, increased sensitivity to cold, and constipation in a patient with known hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine.

History of present illness:
Brianny reports reduced energy despite adequate sleep and describes feeling chilled in environments previously tolerated comfortably. Bowel movements have become less frequent, without abdominal pain, vomiting, hematochezia, or melena. The patient’s partner confirms gradual onset and no acute confusion, syncope, chest pain, dyspnea, or focal neurologic symptoms. No recent neck procedure, iodinated contrast exposure, or medication interruption is reported. The current medication list includes levothyroxine 75 micrograms once daily. Adherence is described as consistent, although the medication is occasionally taken with breakfast rather than on an empty stomach.

Examination:
Patient is alert, cooperative, and in no acute distress. Speech is clear, and mentation is appropriate. Skin is mildly dry without diaphoresis. No periorbital edema or obvious thyroid enlargement is appreciated. Heart rhythm is regular, lungs are clear to auscultation, and the abdomen is soft and nontender without palpable masses. There is no tremor, clonus, or focal weakness.

Diagnostic interpretation:
The symptom cluster is compatible with suboptimally controlled primary hypothyroidism or impaired levothyroxine absorption related to administration with food. There is no current clinical evidence of myxedema crisis, acute abdomen, cardiopulmonary instability, or an emergent neurologic process. Differential considerations include anemia, sleep disorder, mood disorder, and metabolic disturbance.

Plan:
Obtain TSH and free T4, with CBC and comprehensive metabolic panel to assess alternative contributors and treatment safety. Continue the current levothyroxine dose pending laboratory results; take it with water on an empty stomach, 30–60 minutes before breakfast, and separate calcium or iron supplements by at least 4 hours. Increase dietary fiber and fluids gradually for constipation if tolerated. Primary-care follow-up is recommended after results are available, with dose adjustment based on laboratory findings rather than symptoms alone. Return precautions include worsening somnolence, confusion, hypothermia, syncope, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

Referral to Cardiology/Vascular Medicine

Patient: Tadashi Bigford
MRN: 0510208
Referring organization: Cascade Medical Center

Clinical question: Please assess lower-extremity perfusion and cardiovascular risk in this patient with a persistent diabetic plantar foot ulcer, reduced protective sensation, and local discharge. I would appreciate recommendations regarding vascular testing and whether additional vascular or multidisciplinary intervention is indicated.

The patient has a plantar ulcer beneath the forefoot that has not fully healed despite regular wound care. A friend has helped provide the recent history and reports intermittent drainage from the wound, without a known episode of syncope or chest pain. The patient describes diminished sensation in both feet and limited awareness of pressure or minor trauma. There has been no reported fever, rigors, or rapidly spreading redness.

On today’s examination, the ulcer had a clean-appearing base with a small amount of serous-to-cloudy local discharge. Surrounding erythema was limited, and there was no obvious fluctuance or crepitus. Pedal pulses were difficult to appreciate clinically, and the foot was slightly cool compared with the proximal leg. Capillary refill was delayed. Reduced sensation was present to light touch in a stocking distribution. These findings raise concern for impaired arterial supply in addition to diabetic neuropathy, although infection remains a consideration.

The patient is receiving local wound care and has been taking amoxicillin-clavulanate for the local discharge. I advised pressure relief, daily inspection of the foot, clean dressings, and urgent evaluation for fever, worsening pain, spreading redness, foul odor, tissue discoloration, or systemic illness. No medication changes were made pending specialist input.

Please consider ankle-brachial indices or toe pressures, arterial duplex imaging, and review of overall cardiovascular risk management. If significant ischemia is identified, guidance on expedited vascular referral would be helpful. I would also welcome recommendations for coordinated wound care, diabetes management, and off-loading. Follow-up with primary care is planned in about 6 weeks, or sooner if the wound deteriorates.

Sincerely,

Malikye Holiday

Clinical Laboratory Interpretive Report

Patient: sigourney sengchanh
Collection/report date: Apr 14, 2004
Report/accession ID: 0899611812
Patient contact: (617) 555-0122
Ordering clinician: Not listed

Specimen context:
Plantar ulcer swab submitted for culture and susceptibility testing in the setting of diabetic foot ulceration, reduced protective sensation, and local discharge. Specimen received in appropriate transport medium; superficial swab limits assessment of deep tissue infection.

Results:
Gram stain: Moderate polymorphonuclear leukocytes; few gram-positive cocci.
Aerobic culture: Moderate growth of Staphylococcus aureus, methicillin susceptible.
Mixed skin flora: Scant.
Anaerobic culture: No anaerobes isolated at 48 hours.
C-reactive protein: 18 mg/L (reference <8 mg/L), elevated.
Hemoglobin A1c: 8.7% (reference 4.0–5.6%), elevated.

Susceptibility:
S. aureus susceptible to oxacillin, cefazolin, clindamycin, doxycycline, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Inducible clindamycin resistance not detected.

Interpretation:
Findings support local bacterial involvement but do not distinguish colonization from invasive infection. Correlate with ulcer depth, erythema, warmth, pain, systemic symptoms, and vascular status. Bone exposure or failure to improve should prompt imaging and deep tissue or bone sampling rather than repeat superficial swab.

Clinical comment:
Continue wound care and off-loading. The current medication instruction is amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily; antibiotic selection and duration should be reviewed against clinical severity and susceptibility results. Urgent evaluation is appropriate for spreading erythema, fever, ischemic change, or suspected osteomyelitis.

Validated by: ZAKYRIE TROPIANO

Patient: Kaito Dones
MRN: 062462303
Home address: 355 S State Rd 263, Manilla, IN 46150
The patient, age 31 years, was received in the ED with sudden onset shortness of breath and sharp right-sided chest pain that worsens with inspiration. The patient reports feeling generally unwell for 3 days, but states the breathing difficulty became markedly worse today. Spouse is present at bedside and provides additional history. No reported syncope, hemoptysis, or recent fever. The patient appears anxious but remains alert and oriented, answering questions appropriately.

Initial assessment showed tachycardia with a regular rhythm, increased work of breathing, and oxygen saturation below the ordered target on room air. Supplemental oxygen was applied by nasal cannula with improvement in saturation and visible reduction in respiratory distress. Pleuritic pain remains present but is tolerable at rest. Skin is warm and dry. Peripheral pulses are palpable, and there is no acute change in mental status. The patient reports mild unilateral calf discomfort; the extremity is warm with intact sensation and movement.

Provider evaluation and diagnostic imaging are consistent with pulmonary embolism. The patient was placed on continuous cardiac and pulse-oximetry monitoring. Apixaban was administered as ordered after medication and bleeding-risk review. The patient and spouse were instructed to report worsening chest pain, increased shortness of breath, dizziness, coughing blood, or any bleeding. Fall precautions are in place because of dyspnea and anticoagulant therapy. The patient was assisted to a position of comfort and advised not to ambulate without staff assistance.

Assessment: Pulmonary embolism with tachycardia, pleuritic chest pain, and hypoxemia responsive to supplemental oxygen. Hemodynamics are currently stable. No active bleeding noted.

Plan for next shift: Continue oxygen and telemetry, repeat vital signs per protocol, reassess pain and respiratory effort, monitor for bleeding or clinical deterioration, and maintain IV access. Escalate immediately for hypotension, increasing oxygen requirement, altered mentation, or worsening chest pain. Await final disposition and continue education regarding apixaban precautions.

Discharge Summary
SSN: 958-55-2533

Patient: tyleigh houzenga
Clinical context: The patient, age 13 years, was admitted to the pediatric service for approximately one day of worsening right lower-quadrant abdominal pain with nausea and loss of appetite. History was obtained from the patient and the patient’s uncle, ADVAY WOLFFORD, who remained involved in discussions and discharge planning. The patient denied urinary symptoms, diarrhea, or prior abdominal surgery.

On arrival, the patient was uncomfortable but alert and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal examination showed focal right lower-quadrant tenderness with guarding but no diffuse rigidity. At 08:15, the patient reported increased pain with movement. Laboratory testing demonstrated leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance; electrolytes, renal function, and liver enzymes were within acceptable limits. Ultrasound showed a mildly enlarged, noncompressible appendix with periappendiceal inflammatory change, consistent with acute uncomplicated appendicitis. Report/accession ID: 073290508.

Hospital course: Pediatric surgery evaluated the patient and recommended operative management. After discussion of risks, benefits, alternatives, assent from the patient, and consent from the appropriate guardian, laparoscopic appendectomy was performed. The appendix was inflamed without perforation, abscess, or gross peritonitis. No drain was required, and estimated blood loss was minimal. The patient received intravenous fluids, analgesia with acetaminophen, and perioperative ampicillin-sulbactam. Antibiotics were discontinued after the operative findings confirmed uncomplicated disease.

Following surgery, the patient advanced from clear liquids to a regular diet without recurrent nausea or vomiting. Pain improved with oral acetaminophen, and the patient ambulated and voided independently. Incision sites remained clean, dry, and intact with expected mild tenderness. There was no fever or postoperative complication.

Discharge problem list:
1. Acute uncomplicated appendicitis, status post laparoscopic appendectomy.
2. Postoperative abdominal discomfort, improving.
3. Decreased oral intake, resolved.

Discharge medications:
• Acetaminophen by mouth as directed on the package or surgical instructions for pain.
• No antibiotics are required after discharge unless specifically directed by the surgical team.

Instructions and follow-up: Keep the incision areas clean and dry and follow the surgeon’s activity restrictions. Avoid strenuous activity, heavy lifting, and contact sports until cleared. Return promptly for fever, worsening abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, inability to drink, increasing redness or drainage from an incision, or other concerns. Follow up with pediatric surgery in approximately two weeks. Primary care follow-up should occur as needed.

The patient was discharged home in stable condition with the uncle and guardian understanding the medication plan, wound care, warning signs, and follow-up instructions.

Discharging clinician: Kamau Kazan, MD

SSN: 666583381

Patient: K. Kreilkamp
Report/accession ID: 057981445
Reporting laboratory: Millinocket Regional Hospital
Specimen: Peripheral blood in EDTA
Test: Germline hereditary breast and ovarian cancer panel
Ordering clinician: Not specified on requisition

Clinical indication:
Predictive testing requested because of a significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer and ongoing cancer-risk concern. The patient is an adult child of an individual with a documented familial BRCA1 finding.

Results:
BRCA1 c.68_69delAG — NOT DETECTED

No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant was identified in the analyzed genes. Internal quality metrics met laboratory acceptance criteria. This assay evaluates germline sequence and selected copy-number changes; limitations include variants outside interrogated regions, low-level mosaicism, and alterations not detectable by the methods used.

Interpretation:
The negative result substantially reduces, but does not eliminate, the possibility of an inherited cancer-predisposition variant. If the affected relative’s specific result is confirmed to be BRCA1 c.68_69delAG, this patient’s negative result is consistent with absence of that familial variant and is generally considered a true negative. If the familial report is unavailable or the affected relative was not tested, residual hereditary risk remains and cannot be determined from this result alone.

Clinical comment:
Please correlate with the family pedigree and obtain the affected relative’s original laboratory report when possible. Genetic counseling is recommended for discussion of residual risk and screening based on personal and family history. No treatment is indicated from this laboratory result alone. Genetics follow-up is planned for 2022-02-19.

Validated by:
Liliani Slosky, MD
Laboratory geneticist

Emergency Department Referral: Hematology/Oncology
SSN: 666322817

Patient: Airam L.
Occupation: State Highway Police Officer
Employer: Lambert Public Library
Referring clinician: J. Lafosse
Collateral history: Dominico Fattorini, sibling

Clinical question: Please evaluate this patient for suspected Hodgkin lymphoma and advise on definitive tissue diagnosis, staging, and treatment planning.

The patient presented to the emergency department with approximately several weeks of progressively enlarging, painless lymph nodes in the left neck and supraclavicular region. The patient also reports drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss despite no intentional dietary change. Dominico Fattorini confirms that the change in appetite and clothing fit has been noticeable at home. There is no reported fever, productive cough, dysphagia, or focal infectious source. No recent travel or known tuberculosis exposure was reported.

On examination, the patient is alert and hemodynamically stable. Multiple firm, mobile, nontender left cervical and supraclavicular nodes are palpable, without overlying erythema or drainage. No axillary or inguinal adenopathy was appreciated on the emergency department examination. Breath sounds are clear bilaterally, and there is no clinical evidence of airway compromise. The abdomen is soft, with no definite palpable splenomegaly.

Initial laboratory testing demonstrated mild normocytic anemia and elevated inflammatory markers. The comprehensive metabolic panel showed preserved renal and hepatic function. Chest imaging demonstrated mediastinal fullness concerning for additional lymphadenopathy. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and chest showed bulky left cervical and mediastinal adenopathy without an acute pulmonary process. These findings, together with the constitutional symptoms, are concerning for Hodgkin lymphoma. Tissue confirmation is required before assigning stage or initiating therapy.

The patient received intravenous fluids, antiemetic therapy as needed, and analgesia in the emergency department. Current treatment is supportive care pending tissue diagnosis. The patient was discharged with expedited specialty follow-up instructions and return precautions for fever, increasing shortness of breath, difficulty swallowing, bleeding, or rapidly progressive swelling.

Please arrange prompt hematology/oncology consultation and image-guided or surgical excisional biopsy as clinically appropriate. Further recommendations regarding PET-CT staging, baseline echocardiography, pulmonary assessment, fertility counseling, and venous access can follow once pathology is available.

Respectfully,

J. Lafosse

Three days of markedly reduced urine output, fatigue, dizziness on standing, and poor oral intake. Medication reconciliation incomplete.

Alert but tired. Dry oral mucosa, delayed capillary refill, no peripheral edema. Lungs clear bilaterally; heart regular without murmur. Potential nephrotoxic and blood-pressure-lowering medications placed on temporary medication hold pending repeat renal function. Avoid NSAIDs and additional contrast. Repeat metabolic panel after hydration shows partial improvement, but urine output remains below goal.

Disposition and safety net:
Admit to medicine for continued fluids, serial creatinine/electrolytes, urine studies, and medication review. Escalate urgently for worsening oliguria, hypotension, dyspnea, confusion, or hyperkalemia. Friend updated regarding plan.

Specimen: Peripheral blood, EDTA
Test requested: Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk assessment
Clinical indication: Significant family history, request for predictive testing, and cancer-risk concern. Ordering clinician not listed on this laboratory copy.

RESULT SUMMARY

BRCA1/BRCA2 sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis:
• BRCA1 c.68_69delAG: Not detected
• Pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant: Not detected in the genes included in this panel
• Variants of uncertain significance: None identified

INTERPRETATION

No clinically actionable germline variant was identified by the assay. This negative result does not exclude a hereditary cancer predisposition caused by a variant outside the assay’s validated regions, a gene not included on the panel, mosaicism below the assay detection threshold, or an alteration not currently recognized as disease-associated.

The familial risk assessment remains dependent on the documented pedigree and the testing history of affected relatives. If the reported familial variant is known and was not included in the submitted requisition, targeted analysis may be appropriate. A negative predictive result is most informative when an affected relative has first undergone comprehensive testing.

SPECIMEN AND QUALITY

The specimen was suitable for analysis. Internal quality-control metrics met laboratory acceptance criteria. Results apply to germline DNA from the submitted blood specimen and should not be interpreted as tumor profiling.

CLINICAL COMMENT

No current treatment is indicated on the basis of this laboratory result alone. The patient should review the result with a genetics professional or the referring clinical team, including individualized breast, ovarian, pancreatic, and prostate cancer screening recommendations based on personal and family history. Testing of an affected relative may clarify residual familial risk.

Laboratory medicine interpretation: Correlate with the complete test requisition, pedigree, and prior family-member results.

Patient: Kaheem L.
DOB: Jun 3, 2004
Report/accession ID: 081942087
Treating facility: Sanford Hillsboro
Service: Pediatrics

You were admitted for a sickle cell painful crisis with severe pain in both limbs and your back, along with dehydration. Your aunt, Iksha, stayed involved in your care with your permission. You were also included in discussions about treatment and discharge planning.

During this admission, you received intravenous fluids and morphine for pain control. Your pain improved steadily, and you were able to drink fluids and take medicine by mouth before leaving. Blood testing showed anemia consistent with your known sickle cell disease but no evidence of a new bacterial infection. Chest imaging did not show acute chest syndrome. Your oxygen level remained stable without supplemental oxygen, and you had no breathing difficulty.

At discharge, your pain is manageable on the oral plan, you are eating and drinking, and you are walking safely. Your current pain score before discharge was 5/10. Continue your home sickle cell medicines exactly as previously prescribed. Use the prescribed oral pain medicine only as directed and do not combine it with alcohol, sleep medicines, or another opioid. Drink fluids regularly, rest, and use warmth for painful areas. Avoid strenuous activity until your pain has resolved.

Call your hematology team or primary care office promptly for pain that is not improving, fever, worsening fatigue, vomiting, or inability to drink. Go to the emergency department immediately for trouble breathing, chest pain, severe headache, new weakness or numbness, confusion, fainting, or severe abdominal pain. A temperature of 101°F or higher requires urgent evaluation; do not wait for the fever to go away.

Please arrange follow-up with your sickle cell/hematology team and primary care clinician after discharge. Bring your medication list and note how often you need breakthrough pain medicine. You may request private time with your clinician for questions that you do not wish to discuss in front of family.

Mild increased work of breathing without accessory muscle use. Crackles and bronchial breath sounds are present at the right base, with mild right basilar pleuritic discomfort; no wheezing. Heart rhythm regular. Abdomen soft and nontender. No unilateral calf tenderness or edema.

Investigations:
Chest radiograph demonstrates patchy right lower-lobe air-space opacity consistent with pneumonia; no pleural effusion or pneumothorax. CBC shows mild leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance. Basic metabolic panel is without clinically significant abnormality. Viral respiratory testing is negative for influenza and SARS-CoV-2. The diagnosis was documented with SNOMED CT 233604007.

Medical Decision-Making:
Findings support community-acquired pneumonia. Pulmonary embolism and acute coronary syndrome are less likely given the infectious syndrome, focal radiographic infiltrate, and reproducible pleuritic symptoms. Oxygenation remained stable during ambulation, and there is no indication for ICU-level care.

Treatment and Disposition:
Amoxicillin was discontinued as inadequate monotherapy. The patient received the first dose of oral doxycycline in the ED and was discharged with doxycycline to complete the prescribed course, acetaminophen as needed, fluids, rest, and strict return precautions for worsening shortness of breath, persistent fever, confusion, or inability to maintain hydration. Primary care follow-up was advised.

Signed: Ajwa Manche, MD
