Clinical Genetics Referral
SSN: 666-22-9445

Patient: sabrina meltzer

Dear Clinical Genetics Team,

I am referring sabrina meltzer for advice regarding recurrent inflammatory polyarthritis and whether the pattern warrants evaluation for an inherited immune or connective-tissue disorder. The current episode is characterized by several hours of morning stiffness, painful swelling of the MCP and PIP joints bilaterally, and marked fatigue. Symptoms have worsened despite adherence to the established treatment plan.

The patient has a prior diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis and has been followed in primary care with rheumatology involvement. Current medications include methotrexate 15 mg once weekly, folic acid, and naproxen as needed. Recent examination showed visible swelling and tenderness of the wrists and several hand joints without overlying cellulitis. No fever or weight loss was reported. Nuaym Fujiwara, the patient’s spouse, reports that multiple relatives have had “arthritis,” although the specific diagnoses and ages at onset are not known.

Given the recurrent flares and reported family history, please advise whether genetic assessment, targeted testing, or additional immunologic evaluation is appropriate. I would also appreciate recommendations for coordinating genetics with rheumatology and for reviewing the current disease-modifying regimen. Until specialist guidance is available, the patient will continue the existing medications and obtain monitoring laboratories through rheumatology.

Referring clinician: Ramier Polum
Practice locality: Washington
Professional ID: LIC54213995

Thank you for your assessment.

Sincerely,

Ramier Polum

Situation: barbie teteak, a 68-year-old multiracial male patient admitted with suspected infectious gastroenteritis. MRN: 0996903. Home address on file: 126 Usvi Hwy 30, Charlotte Amalie, VI 00802.

Background: Ongoing diarrhea and intermittent vomiting with abdominal cramps. Friend at bedside provides support. Oral rehydration solution encouraged; ondansetron as required per MAR.

Current assessment: Alert, fatigued, answers appropriately. Two loose stools and one small emesis this shift. Abdomen mildly crampy, soft, no guarding. Current pain 5/10. Oral intake limited but tolerating small sips; urine output decreased, amber, no dysuria. Afebrile this shift. Peripheral IV patent; maintenance fluids infusing per order.

Pediatric Discharge Summary
SSN: 997-90-6811

Patient: Daleiza, 10 m/o
Legal guardian: Daijah Marder
Guardian locality: Saipan
Discharging service: Commonwealth Health Center
Weight: 6.4 kg

Admission reason
Vomiting, frequent watery stools, and reduced urine output. Guardian reported fewer wet diapers and limited oral intake before presentation. No blood noted in stool.

Key results
Initial exam consistent with mild-to-moderate dehydration: dry mucous membranes, decreased tears, delayed capillary refill. Electrolytes without clinically significant abnormality. Urine output improved during observation. Abdomen soft, nondistended, without focal tenderness.

Hospital course
Treated with oral rehydration solution in small, frequent volumes. Vomiting resolved; tolerated successive feeds and oral fluids. Diarrhea decreased in frequency. No IV fluids required. Supportive care only. Remained afebrile and hemodynamically stable on room air.

Discharge medications
• Oral rehydration solution by mouth after each loose stool and between feeds.
• Continue usual age-appropriate feeds as tolerated.
• No antibiotics or antidiarrheal medication.

Condition at discharge
Alert, consolable, moist mucous membranes, improved urine output, tolerating oral intake. Guardian demonstrated understanding of rehydration plan.

Home instructions / follow-up
Continue fluids and monitor wet diapers. Follow up with primary care within 1–2 days. Return to the ED for inability to keep fluids down, markedly decreased urine output, blood in stool, lethargy, breathing difficulty, or worsening symptoms.

Discharge disposition: Home with legal guardian.

Date: May 14th, 2045
To: Movement Disorders Service

Re: phaedra floresgarcia
Referring organization: FAIRBANKS MEMORIAL HOSPITAL
Report/accession ID: 0937805754

Dear Specialist,

I am referring phaedra floresgarcia for movement-disorders consultation regarding progressive motor symptoms despite ongoing carbidopa-levodopa therapy. The patient was evaluated in the emergency department on May 14th, 2045 after presenting with worsening resting tremor, slowed movement, and increased muscular rigidity. There was no acute focal neurologic deficit, fever, or recent medication interruption identified during the visit.

Parkinson disease was previously assessed by neurology, and prescribing has subsequently been continued through primary care. Current treatment is carbidopa-levodopa; the exact outpatient schedule was reviewed with the patient and emergency contact, although adherence and timing in relation to meals may be contributing to variable benefit. The patient reports greater difficulty initiating gait and completing instrumental activities of daily living. No recent falls were reported during this encounter.

Examination showed asymmetric resting tremor, bradykinesia on finger tapping and rapid alternating movements, increased tone in the upper extremities, and a short-stepped gait. Strength was grossly preserved. Emergency department laboratory testing and ECG did not identify an acute medical precipitant.

Please reassess diagnosis and treatment response, advise whether medication timing or dose adjustment is appropriate, and consider referral for physical therapy, occupational therapy, and speech therapy. A medication reconciliation and multidisciplinary management plan would be appreciated.

Sincerely,

Andro Jarzab, MD
Emergency Department Clinician

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: cathryn teaters
Service: Clinical Genetics
Admit diagnosis: Acute pyelonephritis

Reason for admission:
Presented with 2 days of dysuria, right flank pain, fever, and rigors with poor oral intake. Urinalysis showed positive leukocyte esterase, nitrites, and pyuria. Renal ultrasound demonstrated mild right pelviectasis without obstructing stone or perinephric collection.

Hospital course:
Treated initially with IV ceftriaxone and fluids. Urine culture grew susceptible Escherichia coli; blood cultures remained negative. Symptoms and oral intake improved over the next 48 hours, with resolution of rigors and decreasing flank tenderness. Creatinine remained at baseline. The attending nephrologist reviewed the imaging and recommended completion of oral therapy without additional intervention. No evidence of an infected obstructed system.

At discharge, afebrile and hemodynamically stable, ambulating independently and tolerating diet. Mild residual right costovertebral angle discomfort only.

Discharge medications:
- Cefuroxime 500 mg by mouth twice daily to complete a 7-day total antibiotic course.
- Acetaminophen 650 mg by mouth every 6 hours as needed for pain or fever.
Medication reconciliation completed; no other changes.

Follow-up and instructions:
Follow up with primary care within 1 week. Return to the ED for recurrent rigors, worsening flank pain, vomiting, inability to take antibiotics, confusion, or fever not improving with treatment. Maintain oral hydration. Genetic counseling follow-up may be arranged through the outpatient clinical genetics service if clinically indicated.

Contact information:
Home address: 846 N 168th Ave, Paonia, CO 81428
Phone: (202) 555-0106

Discharging clinician: Gypsy Wilbanks, 087513882
Condition at discharge: Stable.

Clinical indication: Essential hypertension with intermittent headache and light-headedness; current therapy includes amlodipine and lisinopril. Symptoms reported for 3 days.

Results:
CYP11B2: No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants identified.
KCNJ5: No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants identified.

WNK1, WNK4, CUL3, KLHL3, and related panel genes: No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants identified.

Negative for a disease-causing variant in the genes analyzed. This result reduces, but does not eliminate, the possibility of a monogenic cause of hypertension. A negative panel does not exclude acquired secondary hypertension or genetic mechanisms not represented by this assay.

Continue routine management of hypertension through the treating clinician. Correlate with serum potassium, bicarbonate, creatinine, and urine albumin when clinically indicated. Genetic counseling is recommended if there is early-onset disease, persistent hypokalemia, multiple affected relatives, or a strong family history of hypertension.

Patient: SAVIO RENERT

Home address: 308 S Shore Rd, Libby, MT 59923

Clinical Genetics Referral

Dear Clinical Genetics Team,

I am referring SAVIO RENERT for evaluation of possible inherited susceptibility contributing to persistent gastroesophageal reflux disease and associated upper-airway symptoms. The specific question is whether a heritable connective-tissue or motility disorder should be considered in the setting of ongoing retrosternal burning, acid regurgitation, and night-time cough despite medical therapy.

Symptoms have been present intermittently, with the current flare ongoing for 3 days. Omeprazole has been used as directed, with alginate suspension for breakthrough symptoms. There has been partial improvement in the burning, but recurrent regurgitation continues, particularly after meals and when supine. No dysphagia, gastrointestinal bleeding, persistent vomiting, or unintentional weight loss is reported. Examination today was reassuring: well appearing, normal cardiopulmonary findings, soft nontender abdomen, and no focal neurologic abnormality.

Prior management has included dietary trigger reduction, avoidance of meals close to bedtime, head-of-bed elevation, and continuation of acid suppression. Given the persistent symptoms and the patient’s concern about a possible familial condition, I would appreciate your assessment of whether genetic evaluation is clinically indicated. Please advise regarding any relevant family-history documentation, additional testing, or referral to gastroenterology and/or a specialized motility service.

Thank you for reviewing this consultation request.

Sincerely,

karmani goodman

LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: M. Stiegemeier
Report/accession ID: 025973662
Collection/report date: 2035-12-09
Specimen: Deep tissue swab from plantar foot ulcer; received in aerobic transport medium.
Clinical information: The patient, age 37 years, with diabetes mellitus and peripheral sensory loss, has plantar ulceration with local discharge for 3 days. Current management includes wound care and amoxicillin-clavulanate.

Microbiology
Aerobic culture:
Moderate growth of Staphylococcus aureus, methicillin susceptible.
Scant mixed skin flora.
No Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolated.

Susceptibility:
Oxacillin: Susceptible
Clindamycin: Susceptible
Doxycycline: Susceptible
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole: Susceptible

Gram stain: Few polymorphonuclear leukocytes; rare gram-positive cocci in pairs and clusters.

Inflammatory markers:
C-reactive protein: 38 mg/L (reference interval <8 mg/L)
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 54 mm/hr (reference interval 0–20 mm/hr)

Interpretation: Culture demonstrates methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus with limited mixed skin flora. Findings support bacterial involvement of the sampled ulcer; interpret with wound depth, tissue viability, vascular status, and clinical examination. A superficial swab may not represent deep tissue or bone infection.

Clinical comment: Continue local wound care and assess response to current amoxicillin-clavulanate regimen. Persistent drainage, progressive erythema, systemic symptoms, exposed bone, or failure to improve should prompt urgent reassessment, consideration of imaging for osteomyelitis, and repeat deep tissue sampling if clinically indicated.

Discharge Summary – Pediatrics

Patient: Stephan Visocky
DOB: October 16, 1982
Legal guardian: Yanelli, emergency contact in Hammon

Reason for admission: Admitted for vaso-occlusive sickle cell painful crisis with severe bilateral limb pain, low back pain, and reduced oral intake with clinical dehydration. Yanelli provided history and remained involved in care; adolescent patient assented to treatment.

Hospital course: Initial examination notable for pain-limited ambulation, dry mucous membranes, and tachycardia that improved with hydration and analgesia. No fever, hypoxia, focal neurologic deficit, or acute chest findings during admission. CBC and reticulocyte count were consistent with the patient’s known sickle cell disease; no transfusion indication. Chest radiograph without acute infiltrate. Blood cultures remained negative, and antibiotics were not required.

Managed with IV fluids, scheduled acetaminophen, and IV morphine followed by transition to oral analgesia as pain improved. Encouraged incentive spirometry, oral fluids, and activity as tolerated. No procedure performed. Weight documented at 54.0 kg.

By discharge, tolerating oral intake, voiding normally, afebrile, breathing comfortably on room air, and ambulating with pain controlled on oral medication. Guardian and patient reviewed return precautions and medication plan.

Discharge problem list:
1. Sickle cell vaso-occlusive pain episode — improved.
2. Dehydration — resolved after intravenous fluids.
3. Chronic sickle cell disease — continue established hematology care.

Medications at discharge: Continue home sickle cell regimen. Oral pain medication as directed on the discharge medication list; avoid duplicate acetaminophen-containing products. Maintain hydration. No remaining IV therapy.

Follow-up: Pediatric hematology review scheduled for March 24th, 1996. Primary care follow-up recommended after discharge. Seek emergency care for fever, chest pain, shortness of breath, persistent vomiting, increasing pain not relieved by the prescribed plan, confusion, or inability to drink.

Admitting diagnosis: Acute pyelonephritis

Abigal was admitted with 3 days of right flank pain, dysuria, fever, and rigors. - Acute right-sided pyelonephritis, improving on antibiotics
- Dysuria and flank pain, improved
- Transient sinus tachycardia associated with febrile illness

At discharge, afebrile and hemodynamically stable, ambulatory, tolerating diet, and voiding without difficulty. Return precautions reviewed for recurrent fever, worsening flank pain, vomiting, confusion, inability to keep medications down, or decreased urine output.

Follow-up: Primary care visit within 1 week to review culture results and clinical response. Follow up with Ozarks Community Hospital of Gravette if symptoms recur or additional evaluation is recommended. A friend in Fouke was listed as the emergency contact and received discharge-update instructions with the patient’s permission.

- Cefuroxime 500 mg twice daily; complete course

Patient: A. Marabito
Occupation: Clinical Pharmacist
Report/accession ID: 06814423
Clinic: Sarasota Memorial Hospital - Venice

Your family history raises a meaningful concern for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk. Today we reviewed the pattern of cancer in your relatives, your questions about predictive testing, and what a positive or negative result could—and could not—tell us. You are not taking any prescription medications at this time.

The next step is genetic counseling with review of the most informative person in the family to test, if that individual is available. Testing a relative who has had breast or ovarian cancer may provide clearer information than testing an unaffected family member first. We will also review possible results, insurance considerations, and implications for relatives before you decide whether to proceed. Testing remains your choice.

The family variant listed for genetics review is BRCA1 c.68_69delAG. This notation will be confirmed against the available family records and laboratory documentation; it should not be used by itself to determine screening or treatment.

Plan:
• Obtain prior genetic test reports and relevant pathology records from the family, when available.
• Refer for formal genetic counseling and discuss predictive testing after informed consent.
• Continue routine age- and risk-appropriate breast and ovarian health care with your primary care clinician and gynecology team.
• Return to this clinic after counseling or sooner for questions about the testing process.

Sincerely,

Lexon Watjen, MD
Cardiology clinician
Sarasota Memorial Hospital - Venice

Referral: Pediatric Endocrinology

Patient: Kenslie C.
Referral question: New-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus; request diagnostic confirmation, insulin plan, and diabetes education.

5-year-old Hispanic male patient seen in community pediatrics with 2 weeks of increased thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, and unintentional weight loss. No vomiting or abdominal pain. Legal guardian, Anthonny Barrier, provides history and confirms consent for referral. Family receives support through Stonewall Transit Authority.

Exam: Alert, mildly fatigued; mucous membranes slightly dry. Afebrile. No respiratory distress. Abdomen soft, nontender.

Point-of-care glucose elevated. Urine positive for glucose and ketones. Basic metabolic panel obtained; no current clinical evidence of severe dehydration. Family instructed to proceed to the ED for vomiting, worsening lethargy, abdominal pain, or rapid breathing.

Management to date:
- Insulin initiated per weight-based pediatric protocol.
- Finger-stick glucose monitoring before meals and at bedtime.
- Guardian taught hypoglycemia treatment and glucose log use.
- Dietitian and diabetes educator referral placed.

Please evaluate promptly for outpatient versus hospital-based management, finalize basal/bolus dosing, and arrange continuous glucose monitoring if appropriate. Please include the attending endocrinologist in multidisciplinary follow-up.

Sincerely,

Izar Flaa, MD

Pulmonary Medicine

Up to bathroom with standby assist. Gait slow but steady. Tolerating small amounts of oral fluids and soup; appetite reduced. Urine output adequate per patient report.

Cough remains productive, breathing easier after rest. Fall risk related to weakness and exertional dyspnea; call light within reach. Monitor for increasing oxygen requirement, confusion, worsening chest pain, or inability to maintain oral intake.

Friend Wilbert Golisano updated by patient request. Covering provider notified of persistent fever; continue current plan and reassess overnight.

Repeat respiratory assessment and temperature. Assist with ambulation, document intake, administer scheduled medications, and escalate respiratory decline promptly.

Follow-up pulmonary review scheduled for January 21, 2026.

Documented by: KANARY TRANGSRUD

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: B. Aebi
Service: Clinical Genetics
Discharging organization: TRIDENT MEDICAL CENTER

Reason for admission:
Admitted for acute infectious gastroenteritis with frequent diarrhea, vomiting, and crampy periumbilical abdominal pain. Initial concern was volume depletion after poor oral intake.

Hospital course:
Received IV crystalloid in the ED, followed by oral rehydration solution as tolerated. Ondansetron as required controlled nausea, and vomiting resolved during observation. Stool testing was consistent with an infectious gastroenteritis pattern; no indication for antibiotic therapy. Abdominal examination remained benign without guarding or rebound. No procedure required.

At discharge, tolerating clear liquids and advancing diet, urinating normally, and reporting substantially improved cramping. Vital signs stable; most recent blood pressure 120/80 mmHg. Electrolytes remained acceptable after rehydration, with no acute kidney injury. kaylanni orlove, the patient’s adult child, was updated and will assist with transportation and monitoring at home in Edgemoor.

Problem list:
1. Infectious gastroenteritis, improving.
2. Dehydration secondary to gastrointestinal losses, resolved with rehydration.
3. Nausea and vomiting, resolved.

Discharge medications:
- Oral rehydration solution: frequent small amounts while diarrhea continues.
- Ondansetron as required for nausea or vomiting, per discharge prescription.
- Resume other home medications unless otherwise directed.

Disposition/condition:
Discharged home in stable condition. Advance from bland foods as tolerated; avoid alcohol and foods that worsen symptoms. Seek urgent care for inability to keep fluids down, fainting, blood in stool or emesis, worsening abdominal pain, or markedly reduced urination.

Follow-up:
Primary care review recommended within one week. Follow up with TRIDENT MEDICAL CENTER on February 28th, 2029 for reassessment and review of any pending results. Contact adult child kaylanni orlove if assistance is needed.

LABORATORY REPORT – THYROID FUNCTION TESTING
SSN: 000 40 3290

Patient: K. Astley
MRN: 090472836
Patient address: 101 Ranch Rd 155, Wiergate, TX 75977
Ordering clinician: Not provided
Specimen: Serum, venous draw
Clinical indication: Fatigue, cold intolerance, and constipation; known hypothyroidism on levothyroxine.

Results
TSH: 8.62 mIU/L (reference range 0.40–4.50 mIU/L) — High
Free T4: 0.71 ng/dL (reference range 0.80–1.80 ng/dL) — Low
Total T3: 74 ng/dL (reference range 76–181 ng/dL) — Slightly low
Thyroid peroxidase antibody: 286 IU/mL (reference range <9 IU/mL) — Positive

Specimen and data-quality review
Specimen received in serum separator tube; sample adequate for analysis. The submitted specimen-date field “04/31/2025” is invalid and was rejected during data-quality checking. Testing was released based on the verified collection record in the laboratory information system.

Interpretation
The elevated TSH with low free T4 is consistent with biochemical primary hypothyroidism and may explain the reported fatigue, cold intolerance, and constipation. Positive thyroid peroxidase antibody supports an autoimmune etiology. Correlate with levothyroxine adherence, administration timing, dose, and recent medication changes. No acute laboratory evidence of thyrotoxicosis.

Clinical comment
Recommend review by the treating clinician before adjusting levothyroxine; repeat TSH and free T4 approximately 6–8 weeks after any dose change. Follow-up appointment: September 16, 1988.

Date: 04/30/2019
SSN: 000 21 3911
To: Pulmonary Medicine Sleep Clinic
From: Summersville Regional Medical Center
Report/accession ID: 02149477

Re: Ainoah

I am referring Ainoah for evaluation and management of suspected obstructive sleep apnea. The specific question is whether formal sleep testing is indicated and, if confirmed, whether continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) remains the best treatment.

The patient reports loud snoring and waking with a dry mouth. An adult child has observed repeated pauses in breathing followed by gasping during sleep. Daytime somnolence is now affecting concentration and routine activities, although there has been no reported drowsy-driving incident. The patient has not previously used CPAP and has not had a documented sleep study.

At today’s visit, the patient was alert and in no acute respiratory distress. Lung examination was clear, with regular heart rhythm. Blood pressure was reviewed in the office and is being followed by primary care. No sedative medication use was reported. We discussed avoiding alcohol or other sedating substances near bedtime and not driving when sleepy.

Please arrange sleep-medicine consultation and appropriate diagnostic testing, preferably home sleep apnea testing if clinically suitable, with in-laboratory polysomnography if the initial study is nondiagnostic or another sleep disorder is suspected. If obstructive sleep apnea is confirmed, please advise on CPAP initiation, mask fitting, adherence monitoring, and alternatives if CPAP is not tolerated. Primary care follow-up is planned in about 10 weeks.

Sincerely,

lorilei terreri

Dear Bryson,
SSN: 000 21 8750

You were seen in Clinical Genetics to review your type 2 diabetes mellitus and whether your family history suggests an inherited contribution. The patient, age 49 years, was reviewed with an adult child present. You described increased thirst, fatigue, and frequent urination for 3 days. These symptoms can occur when blood glucose is above goal, although they are not specific to diabetes.

Please continue metformin and atorvastatin as currently prescribed. Arrange a prompt glucose check with your primary care office, along with hemoglobin A1c, comprehensive metabolic panel, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, and lipid panel if these are not up to date. Drink water regularly. Seek urgent care for vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, severe weakness, or inability to keep fluids down.

We discussed that most type 2 diabetes reflects a combination of inherited susceptibility and environmental factors. Genetic testing is not routinely useful for typical adult-onset type 2 diabetes, but testing may be reconsidered if the family pattern, age at diagnosis, treatment history, or examination suggests a monogenic form. Please bring any available family medical records, particularly information about relatives with diabetes, kidney disease, vision loss, or diabetes diagnosed unusually early.

Your patient identifier is 03372699. For scheduling or questions, use (312) 555-0152. Follow-up genetic counseling is planned for March 24th, 1988, with primary care follow-up sooner for glucose review and medication management.

Discharge Summary – Pediatrics

Patient: Rosilee, age 15 years
Admitting service: Pediatrics
Treating facility: Logan Health - Whitefish
Informant: Patient and father, Susie Forder

Reason for admission:
Presented with approximately one day of worsening abdominal pain, initially periumbilical and later localized to the right lower quadrant, with nausea and loss of appetite. No prior abdominal surgery reported.

Hospital course:
Initial examination showed focal right lower-quadrant tenderness with guarding but no diffuse peritoneal signs. Ultrasound demonstrated a noncompressible, enlarged appendix with surrounding inflammatory change, consistent with acute appendicitis. The patient received IV fluids, acetaminophen, and ampicillin-sulbactam. Pediatric surgery evaluated the patient, and assent was obtained with parental consent.

Laparoscopic appendectomy was performed without complication. Operative findings were an inflamed, nonperforated appendix. Pathology was consistent with acute appendicitis. Postoperatively, diet was advanced from clear liquids to regular food without recurrent nausea or vomiting. Pain was controlled with oral acetaminophen. Ambulating independently and voiding normally by the morning of discharge. At 08:15, incision sites were clean, dry, and intact; abdomen soft with expected mild incisional tenderness.

Discharge problem list:
1. Acute appendicitis, status post uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy.
2. Postoperative abdominal pain, improved.

Discharge medications:
- Acetaminophen by mouth as needed for pain, following the labeled pediatric dosing instructions.
- No further antibiotic therapy required after completion of perioperative ampicillin-sulbactam.

Disposition and instructions:
Discharged home in stable condition with father. Keep incisions clean and dry; no soaking until cleared. Resume activity gradually and avoid strenuous activity or heavy lifting until surgical follow-up. Return for fever, worsening abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, redness or drainage from an incision, or inability to tolerate fluids.

Follow-up:
Pediatric surgery clinic at Logan Health - Whitefish in approximately 1–2 weeks. Father reports residence in Deer Lodge and understands the follow-up plan.

Dear Cardiology Team,

Re: K. Kaai
Referring organization: Saint Rose Dominican Hospitals - San Martin Campus
Report/accession ID: 0003132950

I am referring this patient for assessment of intermittent palpitations occurring in the setting of generalized anxiety disorder. The specific question is whether additional cardiac evaluation is indicated and whether the episodes are consistent with an arrhythmia rather than anxiety-related autonomic symptoms.

The patient reports persistent worry, poor sleep, and diffuse muscle tension. Over the past week, there have been several brief episodes of a rapid, forceful heartbeat, without syncope, exertional chest pain, or sustained dyspnea. The most recent episode occurred for 3 days as intermittent symptoms, with no clear exertional trigger. A friend accompanied the patient and assisted with the history.

Current medication: sertraline; adherence reported as consistent. No recent medication changes documented. In primary care today, pulse was regular, and cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable. Office ECG showed sinus rhythm without acute ST-T abnormalities. Basic laboratory testing, including CBC, electrolytes, and thyroid studies, was not suggestive of a secondary metabolic cause.

Given the recurrent symptoms and associated concern, please advise regarding ambulatory rhythm monitoring, echocardiography, or other testing. Recommendations on safe continuation of sertraline and management of palpitations would also be appreciated. The patient has been advised to seek emergency care for syncope, persistent chest pain, or sustained shortness of breath.

Sincerely,

jones pluhar, 075426236

Patient: Ozias Folk
DOB: 1977-12-06
MRN: 0836570
Contact: (202) 555-0138

Pulmonary Medicine Clinic

Your recent evaluation is most consistent with iron-deficiency anemia contributing to tiredness, dizziness, and reduced exercise tolerance. Your breathing examination today was reassuring, without wheezing or signs of fluid buildup. The anemia can make ordinary activity feel harder even when the lungs themselves are functioning reasonably well.

Continue ferrous sulfate as currently prescribed. Take it consistently; if stomach upset or constipation develops, contact the office rather than stopping it on your own. We will repeat a complete blood count and iron studies before the next review. Please also follow up with primary care to look for the source of iron loss and to confirm that age-appropriate gastrointestinal evaluation is up to date.

For now, pace activity and maintain regular fluids. Seek urgent care for fainting, chest pain, severe shortness of breath at rest, black or bloody stools, or rapidly worsening dizziness.

A follow-up appointment is scheduled for December 18, 2004. This is in about 12 weeks, with laboratory testing completed beforehand. Bring an updated medication list to that visit so we can assess response to treatment and decide whether additional pulmonary testing is needed.

Pulmonary Medicine Clinic

History obtained from the patient and adult child. The patient reports four days of brief spinning episodes triggered by rolling to the right in bed, looking up, or rising from a low chair. Episodes last less than a minute and are followed by mild nausea and a sense of unsteadiness. No syncope, chest pain, palpitations, new hearing loss, severe headache, focal weakness, or speech change. The adult child notes the patient has been walking more cautiously but has not fallen.

Medication review completed. Uses prochlorperazine 5 mg up to three times daily as needed for nausea; has taken one dose with partial relief. No recent medication changes.

Patient was alert and conversant. Gait mildly cautious but stable without assistance. Extraocular movements intact; no spontaneous nystagmus. Dix-Hallpike on the right reproduced brief vertigo with torsional nystagmus. Strength and sensation were grossly symmetric. No dysmetria.

Assessment:
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, right-sided, without findings suggesting an acute central neurologic process.

Plan:
Reviewed the diagnosis and demonstrated the right Epley maneuver, with written instructions for home use. Continue hydration and rise slowly until symptoms improve. Prochlorperazine may be used only as directed for significant nausea; discussed sedation and fall precautions. Referral to vestibular physical therapy through Adventist Health Ukiah Valley if symptoms persist or recur. Emergency evaluation advised for persistent vertigo, inability to walk, new weakness, severe headache, or speech difficulty.

Follow-up with primary care in two weeks or sooner as needed. Seen and documented by CYPHER ABAR.

Discharge Summary
SSN: 666610215

Patient: C. Inkster
Service: Pulmonary Medicine
Reason for admission: The patient, age 20 years, was admitted for increasing erythema, local pain, and purulent drainage from a postoperative chest incision. No hemodynamic instability or respiratory distress during admission.

Initial wound culture was obtained before antibiotics. Gram stain showed mixed skin flora; final culture did not identify a resistant organism. Chest imaging showed expected postoperative changes without pleural collection or pneumothorax. Laboratory studies remained stable, with no significant leukocytosis.

Hospital course: The incision was opened slightly at the draining area and irrigated at bedside. No operative debridement was required. Serial examinations showed decreased erythema and drainage, with improved tenderness. The patient remained afebrile and maintained adequate oxygenation on room air. Pulmonary hygiene and activity as tolerated were continued.

Antibiotics were transitioned to oral dicloxacillin 500 mg four times daily to complete the prescribed course. Medication reconciliation was reviewed; no other new discharge medications. Keep the wound clean and covered with a dry dressing, change dressing if saturated, and continue local wound irrigation as instructed by the nursing team. Avoid soaking the incision until fully healed.

Condition at discharge: Stable, ambulatory, tolerating diet, pain controlled with the existing home regimen. Partner DEZIRAE LEVOY participated in wound-care teaching and will assist at home in Colorado Springs.

Problem list:
- Postoperative wound infection, improving after irrigation and oral antibiotics
- Incisional pain, improved
- No evidence of deep collection or acute respiratory complication

Follow-up with the surgical/pulmonary clinic is scheduled for November 23, 2025. Return to the ED for fever, spreading redness, worsening pain, recurrent purulent drainage, shortness of breath, or inability to take the antibiotic.

Stable for discharge home with spouse. Emergency contact locality: Driggs.

Keep incisions clean and dry; showering is permitted unless otherwise directed. No lifting greater than 10 pounds until cleared. PEDIATRIC LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: Cici B.
MRN: M1021519
Specimen/report date: 2004-02-28
Clinical context: 4 m/o infant with acute vomiting, watery diarrhea, and reduced urine output. History provided by father. Oral rehydration solution and supportive care reported.

Specimen: Venous blood and urine, collected for evaluation of dehydration.

Results
Basic metabolic panel:
Sodium:  is not available
Potassium: 4.3 mmol/L (reference interval 3.5–5.5)
Chloride: 104 mmol/L (reference interval 98–107)
CO2: 19 mmol/L (reference interval 18–25)
BUN: 18 mg/dL (reference interval 5–18)
Creatinine: 0.3 mg/dL (pediatric reference interval 0.2–0.4)
Glucose: 78 mg/dL (reference interval 60–100)

Urinalysis:
Specific gravity: 1.030 (reference interval 1.005–1.030)
Ketones: 2+
Blood: negative
Leukocyte esterase: negative
Nitrite: negative

Interpretation
Mildly increased BUN-to-creatinine relationship, concentrated urine, and ketonuria support reduced oral intake with mild volume depletion. CO2 is low-normal and compatible with gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss. No laboratory evidence of hypoglycemia or urinary tract infection in this specimen. The sodium result is unavailable; correlate with clinical assessment and repeat testing if symptoms or poor intake persist.

Clinical comment
Findings are consistent with gastroenteritis with dehydration in an infant. Continue frequent oral rehydration solution in small amounts as tolerated; urine output may improve with hydration. Emergency evaluation is appropriate for inability to retain fluids, worsening lethargy, bloody stool, or continued oliguria.

Validated by: Adore Zakharov
Pediatric Laboratory Medicine

- Atorvastatin 80 mg by mouth nightly.

Enoxaparin was discontinued at discharge. Medication reconciliation completed.

Condition:
Discharged home in stable condition, ambulatory, tolerating diet, and free of active chest discomfort. Avoid heavy exertion until cleared. Call 911 for chest pain that is severe, persistent, or associated with shortness of breath, fainting, or recurrent diaphoresis.

Discharge Summary

Patient: Madina
Parent present: S. Tunson
Report/accession ID: 010573464
Treating facility: ROY LESTER SCHNEIDER HOSPITAL

Madina, the patient, age 3 years, was admitted to pediatrics after repeated vomiting and watery diarrhea with fewer wet diapers than usual. S. Tunson provided the history and participated in the discharge discussion.

At presentation, examination was consistent with mild-to-moderate dehydration. Current measured weight was 14.2 kg. There was no respiratory distress or focal abdominal tenderness. Blood glucose and basic electrolytes were reassuring; no imaging was needed. The clinical picture was most consistent with viral gastroenteritis.

During the stay, vomiting settled and urine output improved after small, frequent amounts of oral rehydration solution. No IV fluids or antibiotics were required. Supportive care was continued, with a gradual return to usual foods as tolerated. The child remained alert, was able to drink, and had no recurrent concerning abdominal pain before discharge.

Discharge plan:
• Continue oral rehydration solution in frequent small sips, especially after each loose stool or episode of vomiting.
• Resume usual diet gradually; avoid forcing food.
• Do not give antidiarrheal medicines unless specifically directed by the child’s clinician.
• Arrange follow-up with the primary care office if symptoms are not clearly improving within the next couple of days.

Return to the emergency department for inability to keep fluids down, markedly reduced urination, unusual sleepiness, blood in vomit or stool, severe belly pain, breathing difficulty, or any rapid worsening. Parent verbalized understanding and agreed with the plan.

Medical decision-making: Findings are concerning for acute kidney injury, most consistent with volume depletion from poor intake. No evidence of obstructive uropathy or emergent hyperkalemia. Intravenous sodium chloride was started, with urine output monitored. Potentially nephrotoxic and blood-pressure-lowering medications were placed on temporary medication hold pending reassessment. Internal medicine accepted the patient for continued fluids, repeat metabolic panel, medication review, and renal monitoring.

Assessment/Plan: Acute kidney injury with oliguria and dehydration. Admit to internal medicine at LBJ Tropical Medical Center in stable condition. The patient and friend were updated regarding the need for inpatient treatment.

Triage stable, afebrile. Left lower leg with diffuse anterior erythema, increased warmth, moderate tenderness, and mild edema. No crepitus, bullae, drainage, or fluctuance. Distal pulses and sensation intact; ambulates with pain. No calf asymmetry beyond involved erythema.  
08:15 — CBC without leukocytosis; basic metabolic panel unremarkable. Venous ultrasound negative for DVT. Lactate normal.

ACTIONS / CONCERN  
IV access obtained. Given IV cefazolin and acetaminophen; borders marked. Presentation consistent with nonpurulent lower-leg cellulitis, without current evidence of abscess, necrotizing infection, or DVT. Discussed with ED attending and Kahuku Medical Center infectious disease service; recommend outpatient therapy if reassessment remains stable.

PLAN  
Observe response, then discharge on oral antibiotic regimen if pain and erythema do not worsen. Return immediately for fever, rapid spread, severe pain, weakness, or new drainage. Primary care review scheduled for Sep 7, 2022.

SSN: 000499481

Patient: yousef faithful
Report/accession ID: S28-0605794
Specimen: Peripheral blood, EDTA
Department: Clinical Genetics
Indication: Hodgkin lymphoma with painless lymphadenopathy, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss. Supportive care pending tissue diagnosis.

Test performed:
Hereditary hematologic malignancy panel; sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis of 84 genes.

RESULT
No pathogenic or likely pathogenic germline variant identified.

Variants of uncertain significance:
None detected.

Technical notes:
Mean sequencing depth 286×; 99.1% of targeted bases covered at ≥20×. Copy-number analysis limited to reportable exon-level events. This assay does not evaluate tumor-acquired variants and does not establish or exclude a somatic cause of Hodgkin lymphoma.

INTERPRETATION
Negative germline result. The finding does not eliminate inherited susceptibility because some alterations may be outside the assay’s detection range or not yet clinically characterized. Testing of an affected relative may be considered if tissue diagnosis and family history support additional evaluation.

Problem / Result / Action
Problem: Hodgkin lymphoma.
Result: No reportable germline predisposition variant.
Action: Correlate with pathology and oncology assessment; no predictive cascade testing based solely on this report.

Follow-up review: March 14th, 2004
Patient contact: (617) 555-0187

Medelyn Dauis, MD

SSN: 924 99 4944

Patient: Nazayla A.
Service: Internal Medicine
Discharging facility: PENN HIGHLANDS DUBOIS
Admission diagnosis: Pelvic inflammatory disease with lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge, and dyspareunia.

Key results
- Pelvic examination: cervical motion tenderness and bilateral adnexal tenderness; no tubo-ovarian mass appreciated.
- Pregnancy test negative. CBC without leukocytosis. Urinalysis not consistent with urinary infection.
- Gonorrhea/chlamydia nucleic acid testing pending at discharge; HIV and syphilis screening nonreactive.

Treated empirically with ceftriaxone in the emergency department, followed by doxycycline and metronidazole. Follow-up
Primary care and gynecology follow-up within 1 week. Patient may receive results by phone. Sibling Jianna in Leck Kill listed as emergency contact.

Condition at discharge: Stable, ambulatory, discharged home. Return for fever, worsening pain, vomiting, syncope, or inability to take medications.

Discharge Summary

Patient: Feliciana
MRN: 004783611
Caregiver present: ROXIE DEVIZIO, mother

Feliciana is a 2-year-old Black male patient who was admitted to pediatrics for vomiting, watery diarrhea, and reduced urine output. At 08:15 on arrival, the child was tired but responsive, with dry lips and decreased tears. The history was provided by the mother.

Evaluation was consistent with viral gastroenteritis with mild-to-moderate dehydration. No focal abdominal tenderness or signs of a surgical abdomen were found. The child remained afebrile during observation. Blood glucose was normal, and no concerning electrolyte abnormality was identified.

Oral rehydration solution was given in small, frequent amounts with good tolerance. Vomiting stopped during observation, urine output improved, and the child became more active. IV fluids were not required. No antibiotics were prescribed because the presentation was most consistent with a self-limited viral illness.

Discharge plan:
• Continue oral rehydration solution, offering small sips every few minutes and increasing as tolerated.
• Resume usual foods gradually; avoid heavy or greasy foods until appetite returns.
• Supportive care only. Do not give over-the-counter diarrhea medicines unless directed by the child’s clinician.
• Arrange follow-up with the primary care pediatrician within 1–2 days.

Return to the ED for inability to keep fluids down, no urine for 8 hours, blood in the stool, worsening abdominal pain, unusual sleepiness, trouble breathing, or other significant concern.

Condition at discharge: stable, drinking, interactive, and with improving hydration.

Discharging clinician: E. Lobiondo

Current management includes subcutaneous insulin and glucose monitoring. The aunt reports that doses have been given as instructed, although meal-related glucose values remain variable. There has been no reported vomiting or inability to tolerate fluids.

Type 1 diabetes mellitus is strongly suspected based on the symptom pattern, hyperglycemia, ketonuria, and weight loss. The patient is clinically stable at this visit, but requires prompt pediatric endocrinology assessment for confirmation, insulin regimen optimization, diabetes education, and screening for associated autoimmune disease. Please assess sick-day management, hypoglycemia prevention, carbohydrate counting, and access to supplies. School-based support and an updated diabetes care plan will also be needed.

The family has been advised to seek emergency care for persistent vomiting, abdominal pain, deep or rapid breathing, worsening lethargy, or inability to maintain hydration. Follow-up with primary care is planned in about 10 weeks, or sooner after specialist review.

Sincerely,

Fynlee Akinleye

Situation: ANZEL WALTON evaluated for 3 days of productive cough, fever, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Increased work of breathing overnight; no syncope or hemoptysis. Emergency contact Areyah Dekock at bedside and updated.

Assessment: Febrile, tachycardic, mildly tachypneic on room air. Alert, speaking full sentences. Coarse crackles and reduced air entry at the right base; no wheeze. Abdomen soft, nontender. No peripheral edema.

Actions/results: IV access obtained. CBC with mild leukocytosis; lactate normal. Chest radiograph shows right lower lobe air-space opacity, no effusion or pneumothorax. Blood cultures obtained before antibiotics. Given IV fluids, acetaminophen, and first ED antibiotic dose per pulmonary medicine guidance. Working diagnosis: community-acquired pneumonia; SNOMED CT 233604007.

Concern/plan: Reassess temperature, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation after treatment. Admit to LOYOLA GOTTLIEB MEMORIAL HOSPITAL for continued antibiotics and observation due to persistent tachycardia and oral intake concerns. Escalate for increasing oxygen requirement, hypotension, confusion, or worsening chest pain.

Attending: Destyn Filoramo, MD

Internal Medicine Consultation Report
SSN: 931630166

Patient: COLIBRI FAYA
Occupation: Children's Librarian
Report/accession ID: 013277896
Referring organization: RUSSELL COUNTY HOSPITAL
Consulting clinician: Caiyah Rancifer, MD

Reason for consultation: Progressive bilateral knee pain, greater on the right, with morning stiffness and reduced mobility.

History and interpretation:
The patient describes gradual worsening of weight-bearing pain, particularly with stairs, prolonged standing, and rising from a chair. Morning stiffness lasts approximately 20 minutes and improves with movement. No recent fall, fever, locking episode, or acute joint swelling. Acetaminophen provides partial relief; topical diclofenac is used intermittently. The patient’s spouse assists with transportation and reports that walking tolerance has declined over recent months.

Examination:
Antalgic gait. Mild varus alignment of both knees. Right greater than left medial joint-line tenderness and palpable crepitus with flexion and extension. Active flexion mildly reduced by pain. No appreciable effusion, erythema, or warmth. Distal strength and sensation preserved. No calf tenderness.

Assessment:
Clinical findings are most consistent with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, right worse than left. There is no examination evidence of an acute inflammatory arthropathy or septic process.

Plan:
Continue acetaminophen within labeled daily limits and topical diclofenac as directed, avoiding application to broken skin. Begin low-impact strengthening and range-of-motion therapy; referral to physical therapy placed. Discussed use of a cane in the contralateral hand and activity pacing. Knee radiographs will be obtained if symptoms fail to improve or mechanical symptoms develop. Consider corticosteroid injection or orthopedic evaluation for persistent functional limitation.

Follow-up: in about 9 weeks, sooner for marked swelling, fever, inability to bear weight, or rapidly worsening pain.

Signed: Caiyah Rancifer, MD

Discharge Summary
Patient: A. Schlossberg
Date: 09/18/2045

The 59-year-old White male patient was admitted to Pulmonary Medicine for community-acquired pneumonia with productive cough, fever, and right-sided pleuritic pain. Initial chest imaging showed a focal air-space opacity consistent with pneumonia. Respiratory viral testing was negative, and oxygen saturation remained acceptable on room air after the first hospital day.

The patient received IV fluids and empiric ceftriaxone plus azithromycin, with clinical improvement in temperature, breathing, and oral intake. No procedure was required. Blood cultures showed no growth. The diagnosis is recorded as community-acquired pneumonia (SNOMED CT 233604007).

At discharge, complete amoxicillin as prescribed until the course is finished. Acetaminophen may be used as needed for fever or discomfort, following the discharge medication label. No medication allergies were reported during this admission. Avoid strenuous activity until energy and breathing have returned to baseline; fluids and regular meals are encouraged.

Condition at discharge: afebrile, hemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably without supplemental oxygen, and tolerating oral medications.

Follow-up with primary care is recommended within one week, with consideration of repeat chest imaging if symptoms do not fully resolve. Return to the ED for worsening shortness of breath, persistent fever, confusion, inability to keep fluids down, chest pain that is not pleuritic, or bluish discoloration.

Discharge instructions were reviewed with the patient and sibling rehema briggle, who is available in Pierre Part.

SSN: 666 06 9072
Occupation: Building Carpenter
Employer: Wilmont Youth Services
Home address: 655 S Sibley Ave, Ellsworth, MN 56129
Contact: (202) 555-0133

Today we reviewed your low back pain and the shooting pain traveling down your leg. The tingling you describe is consistent with lumbar radiculopathy, meaning irritation of a nerve root in the lower back. Your symptoms have been present for 3 days. On examination, movement of the lower back reproduced the leg pain, but strength was preserved and there was no concerning change in bowel or bladder control.

Continue naproxen with food as directed on the bottle, provided you are not having stomach bleeding, kidney problems, or an allergy to anti-inflammatory medicines. You may use acetaminophen between doses if needed, staying within the package maximum and avoiding other products that contain acetaminophen. Gentle walking is encouraged; avoid bed rest, heavy lifting, and repeated bending for now. Heat or ice may be used for short periods.

Please arrange follow-up with primary care if the pain is not improving over the next 2–4 weeks. Physical therapy may be appropriate if symptoms persist. Seek urgent evaluation for new leg weakness, numbness in the groin or saddle area, loss of bladder or bowel control, fever, or rapidly worsening pain.

Continue your usual work restrictions as discussed, and contact the office if your employer needs updated documentation.

Sincerely,

E. Spigener

Situation: Keilyn, DOB 05/26/1991, admitted with infectious gastroenteritis. Ongoing loose stools, intermittent emesis, and cramping; telemetry in place for volume-depletion monitoring.

Clinical Genetics Consultation Note

Patient: Auriela Alabi
Encounter date: Oct 26, 2035
Contact: auriela.alabi32@comcast.net
Report/accession ID: 037083020
Clinical age group: 70 y/o

Reason for consultation: Evaluation of episodic positional dizziness and consideration of an inherited neurologic disorder.

History: The patient describes brief spinning episodes triggered by rolling in bed, looking upward, or bending forward. Associated nausea and mild unsteadiness have occurred for 3 days. Episodes resolve within approximately one minute when still. No syncope, focal weakness, sensory loss, persistent headache, hearing loss, or family history suggestive of a progressive ataxia. Spouse provided corroborating history. Prochlorperazine as required has reduced nausea but has not altered the positional trigger.

Examination: Alert and appropriately interactive. Extraocular movements full without spontaneous nystagmus. Dix-Hallpike maneuver produced transient vertigo with fatigable upbeat-torsional nystagmus on the right. No dysarthria or limb dysmetria. Gait mildly cautious; tandem gait intact. Remaining neurologic examination nonfocal.

Interpretation: Findings are most consistent with right posterior-canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. The short latency, fatigability, and positional reproducibility are not suggestive of a genetic episodic ataxia or other inherited vestibular syndrome at this time. Genetic testing is not indicated based on the current phenotype.

Plan: Canalith repositioning maneuver performed and home instructions reviewed. Continue prochlorperazine as required only for significant nausea. Vestibular therapy referral if symptoms persist or recur. Return promptly for continuous vertigo, new neurologic deficit, severe headache, or inability to walk. Follow up with primary care; genetics follow-up as needed.

Discharge Summary

Patient: MAYTTE CORINO
MRN: 006 074 702
Admitting service: Emergency Department, Warm Springs Medical Center
Discharging clinician: BALDEMAR SPILKER, Professional ID 040247274

Reason for visit: Acute onset watery diarrhea, recurrent vomiting, and intermittent cramping abdominal pain. History obtained from the patient with spouse present. No recent hospitalization or antibiotic exposure reported.

ED evaluation showed mild volume depletion with dry mucous membranes but stable hemodynamics. Abdominal examination remained soft and nondistended, with diffuse mild cramping and no focal tenderness, guarding, or rebound. CBC without clinically significant leukocytosis. Basic metabolic panel reassuring; renal function preserved. Lipase normal. Respiratory viral testing negative. Stool studies were not obtained because symptoms improved and there was no blood, persistent fever, or recent travel risk requiring inpatient evaluation.

Treatment included oral rehydration solution in small, frequent amounts and ondansetron as required, with successful oral challenge before discharge. Vomiting resolved during observation; diarrhea decreased in frequency, and abdominal cramps improved. The presentation is most consistent with uncomplicated infectious gastroenteritis. Symptoms may improve with hydration.

Problem list:
1. Acute gastroenteritis with diarrhea and vomiting.
2. Mild dehydration, resolved after oral fluids.
3. Abdominal cramping, improved.

Discharge medications:
• Oral rehydration solution: frequent small sips, advancing diet as tolerated.
• Ondansetron as required for nausea or vomiting, according to the prescription instructions.

Condition at discharge: Stable, tolerating oral fluids, ambulatory, and appropriate for outpatient management.

Instructions reviewed with the patient and spouse: continue fluids, use bland foods initially, and avoid alcohol until fully recovered. Return to the ED for inability to keep fluids down, fainting, worsening or localized abdominal pain, blood in stool or vomit, confusion, or reduced urination. Follow up with primary care if symptoms are not clearly improving over the next several days or if diarrhea persists.

Signed electronically by BALDEMAR SPILKER, Warm Springs Medical Center.

Patient: AVELYNN GREMO, a 64-year-old Hispanic male patient
Home address: 63 Keaau Pahoa Bypass Rd, Princeville, HI 96722
Contact: (312) 555-0182
Emergency contact: on file

Chief complaint: Right great toe pain and swelling.

History of present illness: Sudden worsening pain at the right first metatarsophalangeal joint since yesterday morning, with redness and difficulty bearing weight. Similar episodes in the past, previously diagnosed as gout. No trauma, fever, chills, open wound, or recent procedure. Has been taking naproxen at home without adequate relief. Medication list also includes colchicine, which the patient reports using during prior flares. No known kidney disease or anticoagulant use.

Exam: Afebrile and nontoxic. Right first MTP markedly tender with erythema, warmth, and moderate swelling. Range of motion limited by pain. No fluctuance, drainage, proximal streaking, or crepitus. Dorsalis pedis pulse palpable; sensation intact. No calf tenderness.

ED course: Received oral colchicine and naproxen with partial improvement. Crutches provided for comfort. Advised rest, ice, elevation, hydration, and avoidance of additional NSAIDs beyond directed dosing.

Assessment: Acute gout flare involving the right first MTP joint.

Plan: Continue colchicine and naproxen as prescribed, with food. Follow up with primary care in about 9 weeks for urate-lowering therapy discussion. Return immediately for fever, spreading redness, drainage, or worsening pain.

Discharged ambulatory in stable condition. Attending: Luigi Kronstedt, MD

To: Pulmonary Medicine Specialist

Re: M. Schouest
Referring organization: St Luke's Wood River Medical Center
Report/accession ID: 0640404749

I am referring this patient for evaluation of progressive painless lymphadenopathy with associated night sweats and unintentional weight loss. Recent chest imaging shows bulky mediastinal and right hilar adenopathy, with mild narrowing of the adjacent bronchus but no current oxygen requirement. The patient reports intermittent dry cough and exertional shortness of breath; no hemoptysis or acute respiratory distress.

The working diagnosis is Hodgkin lymphoma. Tissue confirmation is still pending, and the patient is receiving supportive care pending tissue diagnosis. Initial laboratory testing showed mild normocytic anemia and elevated inflammatory markers. The spouse has been present for discussions and understands that a biopsy is needed before oncology treatment can be selected.

Please assess the airway and determine the safest and highest-yield method for tissue sampling, including whether endobronchial ultrasound-guided biopsy is appropriate. If bronchoscopy is planned, please advise on anesthesia risk and any need for additional pulmonary function testing. We would appreciate expedited coordination with hematology/oncology once an adequate specimen is obtained.

The patient has been advised to seek emergency care for worsening shortness of breath, chest pain, inability to swallow, or rapidly increasing neck swelling. Please send your recommendations and procedure results back to our office.

Sincerely,

SAKIRA LOUGHRIN

Laboratory Report – Cardiology Laboratory
SSN: 000-28-0768

Patient: ADELINE DEVULAPALLI
Report/accession ID: 07169813
Specimen: Deep wound swab from plantar foot ulcer
Clinical information: Diabetes mellitus with plantar ulceration, reduced sensation, and local discharge. Spouse reports ongoing wound care and current treatment with amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily.

Microbiology
Gram stain: Moderate polymorphonuclear leukocytes; few gram-positive cocci.
Aerobic culture: Moderate growth of Staphylococcus aureus.
Susceptibility: Methicillin susceptible. Susceptible to oxacillin, cefazolin, clindamycin, doxycycline, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Resistant to penicillin.
Anaerobic culture: No anaerobes isolated.

Inflammatory markers
C-reactive protein: 38 mg/L (reference range <8 mg/L) – elevated.
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 62 mm/hr (reference range 0–20 mm/hr) – elevated.

Hematology
WBC: 11.8 × 10^3/µL (reference range 4.0–10.5 × 10^3/µL) – mildly elevated.
Hemoglobin: 12.9 g/dL (reference range 13.5–17.5 g/dL) – mildly decreased.
Platelets: 342 × 10^3/µL (reference range 150–450 × 10^3/µL).

Interpretation
Culture demonstrates methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus with laboratory evidence of active inflammation. Correlate with wound depth, vascular status, glycemic control, and clinical examination for assessment of cellulitis or underlying osteomyelitis. Culture results should be reviewed by the treating clinician; antibiotic selection and duration require clinical correlation.

Patient contact detail: (202) 555-0127

Sincerely,

A. Blackadar

The patient and adult child were instructed to return promptly for fever, spreading redness, increasing pain, malodor, or systemic symptoms.

Please evaluate wound depth and perfusion, determine whether debridement or advanced imaging is indicated, and recommend an off-loading and dressing plan. Please also advise on diabetes-related foot surveillance and follow-up frequency.

Sincerely,

Aristides Dodwell

Service: Internal Medicine
Treating organization: BON SECOURS ST FRANCIS MEDICAL CENTER

You were admitted after several days of poor oral intake, fatigue, and reduced urine output. Initial testing showed acute kidney injury, including creatinine 2.1 mg/dL. Your blood pressure and electrolytes were monitored closely, and a bladder scan did not show significant retention.

You received intravenous sodium chloride, with gradual improvement in urine output and kidney function. The likely contributors were dehydration and temporary medication effects. At discharge, you were eating and drinking better, walking safely, and urinating without assistance. Your kidney function was improving but had not yet returned fully to baseline.

Discharge plan:

• Do not restart the held medication(s) until reviewed by your primary care clinician.
• Avoid ibuprofen, naproxen, and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs unless specifically approved.
• Arrange repeat kidney blood tests with primary care within one week.
• Seek urgent care for worsening weakness, inability to keep fluids down, very little or no urine, confusion, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

Your partner, Cashtyn Parisano, who is based in Port Republic, may help review the medication instructions and follow-up plan. Bring this summary and your complete medication list to the next appointment.

Patient: Avanoelle
Home address: 195 Main Princess Rd, Charlotte Amalie, VI 00802
Report/accession ID: 001673118

Dear Clinical Genetics Team,

I am referring Avanoelle for assessment of recurrent migraine with a unilateral headache, nausea, and photophobia. Episodes occur approximately twice monthly and may last most of the day when untreated. The family is particularly concerned because a sibling has also experienced disabling headaches, although no formal syndromic diagnosis has been established.

Sumatriptan is used at the onset of more severe attacks, with naproxen when additional analgesia is needed. This combination has reduced the duration of some episodes, but breakthrough headaches continue to interfere with work and routine activities. There is no reported history of seizures, progressive neurologic deficit, developmental regression, or persistent visual loss. Prior primary care examination was nonfocal. DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: delante tabuena
Age/clinical context: the patient, age 17 years, was reviewed with mother HENSON KEAT present
Service: Pediatrics
Healthcare organization: Decatur County Memorial Hospital
Report/accession ID: S26-0043415

Reason for admission:
Vomiting, frequent loose stools, and reduced urine output for 3 days. Poor oral intake at home.

Admission findings:
Mild dehydration with dry mucous membranes and tachycardia. Abdomen soft, nontender, no guarding. No respiratory distress.

Key results:
Electrolytes reassuring; glucose normal. CBC without clinically significant leukocytosis. Urinalysis concentrated, no evidence of infection. Stool testing not indicated.

Hospital course:
Received oral rehydration solution in small, frequent amounts with improvement in nausea and oral intake. Urine output increased during observation. No IV fluids required. No further emesis after arrival; diarrhea decreased. Remained afebrile and hemodynamically stable.

Discharge condition:
Alert, interactive, tolerating fluids, benign abdominal examination. Mother verbalized understanding of hydration plan and return precautions. Adolescent participated in discharge discussion and agreed with plan.

Discharge medications:
• Oral rehydration solution: frequent small sips; continue after each loose stool.
• Supportive care only. No antibiotics or antidiarrheal medication.

Follow-up:
Primary care follow-up within 2–3 days, sooner for worsening symptoms.

Return to ED for inability to keep fluids down, no urine, bloody stool, severe abdominal pain, confusion, or new breathing difficulty.

Cardiology Referral

Patient: Fruma
Address: 469 State Hwy 115, Custer, MI 49405
Occupation: Hospital Pharmacist
Employer: Rapid River School District

Dear Cardiology Colleague,

I am referring Fruma for assessment of persistent fatigue and low resting heart rate noted in primary care. The patient reports several months of reduced energy, increased sensitivity to cold, and constipation. There is no exertional chest pain, syncope, or known history of coronary disease. The referral question is whether the degree of bradycardia and fatigue warrants cardiac evaluation in addition to ongoing thyroid management.

Hypothyroidism is being treated with levothyroxine 75 micrograms once daily. Medication adherence is reported as consistent, and there have been no recent dose changes. Examination in the office showed a regular bradycardic rhythm without murmur, clear lungs, and no peripheral edema. An office ECG demonstrated sinus bradycardia without acute ST-T abnormalities. Recent thyroid testing is being repeated; prior results were reportedly improved but not fully available for review today.

The patient’s adult child has helped provide the medication history and is concerned that fatigue is limiting usual activities. I would appreciate your evaluation, including consideration of ambulatory rhythm monitoring and echocardiography if clinically indicated. Please advise whether the symptoms appear disproportionate to the thyroid disorder and whether any cardiac treatment or follow-up is recommended.

Thank you for seeing this patient.

Sincerely,

Reginald Rivetti, MD

Patient: MUSLIM EDUARDO
Occupation: Clinical Pharmacist
Report/accession ID: 066622343

Your evaluation today is reassuring overall. The spinning sensation is brief and is brought on by turning in bed, looking up, or changing position. The nausea and unsteadiness fit benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), rather than a heart rhythm problem or ongoing inner-ear infection. Your partner’s observations were also helpful during the visit.

Heart rate and rhythm were regular, and there was no chest pain, fainting, or shortness of breath. Positional testing reproduced the vertigo without concerning neurologic findings. We reviewed that BPPV results from movement of small inner-ear particles and is usually treatable.

Plan:
• Perform the home Epley maneuver as demonstrated, once or twice daily until symptoms settle.
• Use prochlorperazine as required for troublesome nausea or vertigo; avoid driving, ladders, and other fall-risk activities while dizzy.
• Rise slowly and keep a handhold nearby until your balance improves.
• Continue routine medications and hydration.

Please seek urgent care for new weakness, facial droop, trouble speaking, severe continuous headache, fainting, chest pain, or vertigo that does not let up. Contact The Queens Medical Center if symptoms worsen or are not improving. We will reassess in about 6 weeks, sooner if needed.

Sincerely,

B. Bolon
Cardiology clinician

Patient: Elek S.
Encounter date: 04/23/2012
Clinical age: 79 y/o
Service: Pulmonary Medicine

Reason for admission: Presented with several hours of worsening right lower-quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and loss of appetite. CT abdomen/pelvis was consistent with acute uncomplicated appendicitis. General Surgery evaluated the patient and recommended operative management.

Hospital course: The patient received IV fluids, ampicillin-sulbactam, and symptom control with acetaminophen. Laparoscopic appendectomy was performed without complication. Operative findings showed an inflamed, nonperforated appendix. No drain was required. Postoperatively, the patient tolerated advancement from clear liquids to a regular diet, ambulated independently, and voided without difficulty. Pain was controlled with oral medication. Incisions remained clean, dry, and intact.

Assessment at discharge: Acute appendicitis, status post uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy. Hemodynamically stable for discharge home.

Discharge medications:
- Acetaminophen by mouth as needed for pain.
- Resume other home medications as previously prescribed.
No further antibiotic therapy is planned unless directed by Surgery.

Instructions: Keep the incision sites clean and dry; avoid soaking until healed. No heavy lifting until cleared at follow-up. Return for fever, worsening abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, redness or drainage from an incision, or inability to tolerate fluids.

Follow-up: Surgical clinic visit arranged in about 12 weeks for postoperative review and pathology discussion. The patient’s sibling, M. Brah, from South Dennis, was updated with the patient’s permission. Discharged home in stable condition.

Emergency Department Assessment
Date: Jun 26, 2024
Patient: A. Zolecki
Emergency contact: DEILANY DEAGUIAR

Patient presented with approximately 90 minutes of central chest pressure associated with diaphoresis and nausea while at rest. No syncope or reported trauma. Past history and outpatient medication list reviewed; no known medication allergy documented. Initial vital signs notable for BP 158/92 and pulse 96. Patient was uncomfortable but speaking in full sentences. Lungs clear bilaterally, no peripheral edema. Heart regular without audible murmur. Abdomen soft and nontender. Glasgow Coma Scale 15.

ECG showed sinus rhythm with mild ST-segment depression in the lateral leads and no ST-elevation. Initial high-sensitivity troponin was elevated at 86 ng/L, with repeat increasing to 214 ng/L. Chest radiograph showed no focal infiltrate, pulmonary edema, or pneumothorax. Basic metabolic panel and CBC without an acute abnormality requiring intervention.

Assessment: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Presentation and dynamic troponin change are concerning for acute coronary syndrome; aortic dissection and pulmonary embolism felt less likely based on examination and history.

Aspirin was administered, followed by therapeutic enoxaparin and high-intensity atorvastatin. Sublingual nitroglycerin improved the pressure. Cardiology at Columbia Memorial Hospital was consulted by the ED team and accepted the patient for monitored admission and possible coronary angiography. Patient remained hemodynamically stable without recurrent severe pain.

Disposition: Admit to telemetry. Risks, treatment, and need for cardiology evaluation discussed with the patient and DEILANY DEAGUIAR. Documented by DUTCH MALMQUIST.

Serum urate may be normal during an acute attack; the elevated value supports, but does not independently establish, gout. Results do not exclude septic arthritis. If joint aspiration is clinically feasible, synovial fluid crystal analysis and Gram stain/culture are recommended before escalation of treatment.

Renal and hepatic indices are within the stated reference intervals, providing no laboratory contraindication to the reported short-term naproxen or colchicine regimen; correlate with dose, hydration, and comorbidities.

Follow-up: Primary care review scheduled for 04/23/2026.

Discharge Summary

Patient: Seidy
Encounter date: February 9th, 2019
Contact: (312) 555-0182

Reason for admission: A 76-year-old East Asian female patient presented to the emergency department with approximately 18 hours of worsening right lower-quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and loss of appetite. Friend V. Didia accompanied the patient and provided collateral history. No prior abdominal surgery reported.

ED course and key findings: Afebrile and hemodynamically stable on arrival. Focal right lower-quadrant tenderness with mild guarding; no diffuse peritoneal signs. CBC showed leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance. CMP without clinically significant abnormality. Urinalysis negative for infection. CT abdomen/pelvis demonstrated an enlarged fluid-filled appendix with periappendiceal inflammatory change, consistent with acute uncomplicated appendicitis. Surgical service evaluated the patient at 08:15.

Hospital course: Received IV fluids, acetaminophen for pain, antiemetic therapy, and ampicillin-sulbactam. Underwent laparoscopic appendectomy without complication. Operative findings consistent with acute suppurative appendicitis without perforation or abscess. Tolerated advancement from clear liquids to regular diet. Ambulating and voiding independently; pain controlled with oral medication. Incisions clean, dry, and intact with expected mild tenderness.

Discharge diagnoses:
• Acute uncomplicated appendicitis, status post laparoscopic appendectomy
• Postoperative abdominal pain, improved

Discharge medications:
• Acetaminophen by mouth as needed for pain, according to the discharge medication list
• No further antibiotics required after completion of perioperative ampicillin-sulbactam

Condition at discharge: Stable for discharge home. Follow up with general surgery in approximately 1–2 weeks for postoperative review. Keep incisions clean and dry; no heavy lifting until cleared. Return to the ED for fever, worsening abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, inability to tolerate fluids, spreading redness, or drainage from an incision.

ED treatment/action:
- Aspirin administered.
- Enoxaparin given for anticoagulation.
- Atorvastatin started.
- Nitroglycerin relieved pressure; repeat ECG without ST elevation.

Cardiology consulted; admit to telemetry for invasive versus medical management decision. Hemodynamically stable at handoff. Cardiology follow-up arranged in 12 days after discharge.

• Consider a Parkinson disease multigene panel after consent and insurance review.
• Genetic counseling follow-up scheduled for November 23rd, 2004.
• Return sooner for medication intolerance, falls, or rapid functional decline.

Data reviewed: CBC demonstrates mild normocytic anemia with preserved leukocyte and platelet counts. Comprehensive metabolic panel without significant hepatic or renal abnormality. CT neck/chest reviewed and shows bulky cervical and mediastinal adenopathy. The pattern, together with night sweats and weight loss, is concerning for Hodgkin lymphoma.

Impression: Lymphoproliferative malignancy suspected; tissue confirmation required before definitive treatment selection.

Plan: Arrange expedited image-guided or surgical excisional biopsy of the most accessible node. Obtain PET/CT and baseline LDH after pathology is available, with pregnancy testing when clinically applicable before imaging or systemic therapy. Continue hydration, nutritional support, and acetaminophen as needed for discomfort. Avoid corticosteroids unless clinically necessary, as they may reduce diagnostic yield. Return visit after pathology review; emergency evaluation advised for dyspnea, rapidly progressive neck swelling, or inability to swallow.

Seek urgent evaluation for chest pain, shortness of breath, fever, rapidly progressive swelling, or inability to bear weight.

Jaison Cell

LABORATORY REPORT – HEMATOPATHOLOGY

Patient: Albus Wons
Collection date: June 23, 2018
Report/accession ID: 055225063
Reporting laboratory: LBJ Tropical Medical Center
Specimen: Left cervical lymph node, excisional biopsy; peripheral blood submitted for correlation.

Clinical information: Painless lymphadenopathy with drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss. Clinical diagnosis: Hodgkin lymphoma. Supportive care pending tissue diagnosis.

Findings:
Excisional lymph node demonstrates partial architectural effacement by a mixed inflammatory infiltrate containing scattered large atypical cells with prominent nucleoli, morphologically compatible with Reed-Sternberg cells. Immunohistochemical stains show the atypical cells positive for CD30 and weak PAX5, with variable MUM1 expression; negative for CD45 and CD20. EBER in situ hybridization is negative. Background small T cells are present. Flow cytometry identifies no monotypic B-cell population and no aberrant T-cell population in the submitted sample.

Peripheral blood, complete blood count:
WBC 8.7 x10^3/uL (4.5–11.0)
Hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL (12.0–16.0)
Platelets 362 x10^3/uL (150–400)
Absolute neutrophils 6.2 x10^3/uL (1.8–7.5)

Interpretation:
Findings support classic Hodgkin lymphoma, favoring nodular sclerosis subtype in the appropriate clinical and morphologic context. Final classification should incorporate full excision review and radiographic staging. Correlate with oncology evaluation; consider PET/CT and baseline chemistry testing before treatment planning.

Electronically validated by Brightly Melsness, laboratory clinician.

• Seek urgent care for inability to keep fluids down, markedly reduced urine output, confusion, fainting, chest pain, or worsening weakness.

Condition at discharge: stable. The discharge medication list and laboratory follow-up instructions were reviewed before leaving.
