Dear Community Pediatrics Colleague,

I am referring KYAIRAH GENTEMAN, a 3-year-old African American male patient, for evaluation of recurrent ear pain and guidance regarding further management of acute otitis media. History was obtained from the legal guardian, JAYSHON PROEUNG, who reports two days of pulling at the right ear, intermittent fever, poor sleep, and increased irritability. Oral intake remains adequate, and there has been no ear drainage, vomiting, or breathing difficulty.

On examination today, the child was alert but fussy and consolable by the guardian. Temperature was elevated. The right tympanic membrane appeared erythematous and bulging with decreased mobility; the left tympanic membrane was partially obscured by cerumen but without obvious drainage. Mild nasal congestion was present. No mastoid swelling or neck stiffness was noted.

The family has also been connected with Wichita Youth Services for practical support during the child’s illness. The guardian has been giving acetaminophen and supportive care, with partial relief of discomfort. Given the examination findings and persistent fever, I would appreciate your assessment of treatment need, confirmation that there are no complications, and recommendations for management if symptoms recur.

Assessment: Acute otitis media, right greater than left, with fever and irritability.

Plan: Continue fluids, rest, and acetaminophen according to the labeled pediatric dosing instructions. Please evaluate the child and advise whether antimicrobial therapy or hearing follow-up is indicated. The family will arrange reassessment in about 5 weeks, or sooner for worsening pain, persistent fever, drainage, poor intake, or lethargy.

Sincerely,

Kashdyn Meneese

Assessment: Clinical findings are consistent with an active rheumatoid arthritis flare without evidence of an acute infectious or traumatic process.

Please assess promptly for adjustment of disease-modifying treatment, need for a short corticosteroid bridge, and monitoring recommendations for methotrexate. Please also advise regarding interim analgesia and follow-up timing.

Sincerely,

aviel kriehn

Date: Oct 30, 2012
Patient: Jasier
MRN: 036501692
Address: 177 State Rte 331, Jasonville, IN 47438

Dear Clinical Genetics Team:

I am referring Jasier for evaluation of persistent microcytic anemia and consideration of an inherited hemoglobin disorder or other genetic cause of impaired red-cell production.

The patient reports several months of tiredness, intermittent dizziness, and reduced exercise tolerance. There is no reported overt gastrointestinal bleeding, melena, heavy menstrual bleeding, or recent major illness. An adult child provided additional history and is concerned that similar anemia has occurred in other relatives, although family records are not available for review.

Recent primary care testing showed hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, MCV 72 fL, ferritin 8 ng/mL, and transferrin saturation 9%. The pattern is consistent with iron deficiency, but the degree of microcytosis has persisted despite treatment. Peripheral smear noted microcytosis and hypochromia without blasts. Renal function and thyroid testing were unremarkable. Celiac screening was negative.

The patient has been taking ferrous sulfate. Medication reconciliation: ferrous sulfate 325 mg by mouth once daily. Tolerance is acceptable, with mild constipation. Gastrointestinal evaluation has been requested through primary care, and adherence and dietary iron intake were reviewed. Follow-up laboratory testing is planned in about 3 weeks to assess hematologic response; this interval is not intended as a continuation instruction for medication.

Please assess whether hemoglobin electrophoresis, molecular testing, or broader inherited anemia evaluation is indicated, particularly if iron repletion does not normalize the indices. Please advise regarding testing of relatives and recommended monitoring.

Sincerely,

Keimari Horng, MD

Episodes begin without exertional trigger and peak rapidly; most recent event occurred while at home. Reports similar symptoms for 3 days. Adult child provided additional history by phone. No syncope, sustained exertional chest pain, or known cardiac history reported.

Exam: Alert, speaking comfortably. Pulse regular in office; heart sounds normal, no murmur. Lungs clear bilaterally. No peripheral edema.

Testing: Office ECG reviewed—normal sinus rhythm without acute ischemic changes. Symptoms not reproduced during visit.

- Reviewed reassuring examination and ECG.
- Continue breathing retraining; practiced paced breathing during visit.

Discharge Summary

Patient: Ravilucca V.
DOB: 1993-08-18
Admission diagnosis: Transient ischemic attack

Presented to the ED after sudden right arm weakness, left facial droop, and slurred speech noted at home. Symptoms resolved before neurologic evaluation. Partner, ELENORA KORNICK, provided additional history and will assist with medications after discharge; emergency contact locality: Nashville.

Initial CT head showed no acute hemorrhage or established infarct. CTA head and neck without large-vessel occlusion or hemodynamically significant carotid stenosis. MRI brain showed no acute ischemia. Telemetry remained in sinus rhythm. Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated preserved systolic function without intracardiac thrombus. Laboratory testing notable for elevated LDL; hemoglobin A1c in the nondiabetic range. No recurrent weakness, facial asymmetry, or dysarthria during observation.

Hospital course: Neurology evaluated the patient and felt the episode was most consistent with TIA. No thrombolysis or thrombectomy indicated because deficits had resolved and imaging showed no target lesion. Started aspirin and high-intensity atorvastatin. Patient tolerated oral intake, ambulated independently, and had a nonfocal examination at discharge. A cough was also reported for 3 days; chest radiograph was clear, with no oxygen requirement or evidence of pneumonia.

Discharge medications:
Aspirin 81 mg by mouth once daily.
Atorvastatin 40 mg by mouth nightly.
Continue other home medications as reconciled in the after-visit medication list.

Problem list:
1. Transient ischemic attack, resolved.
2. Hyperlipidemia.
3. Acute cough without radiographic pneumonia.

Follow-up: Primary care and neurology review on May 20, 2045. Arrange outpatient cardiac rhythm monitoring if not completed. Return immediately for recurrent weakness, facial droop, speech difficulty, vision loss, severe headache, chest pain, or shortness of breath. Condition stable; discharged home with partner.

Treatment: IV access obtained. Intravenous fluids started; morphine administered with reassessment and substantial pain improvement. Oral fluids tolerated.

Disposition: Discharged home with mother after observation. Continue prescribed home pain plan and hydration; return for fever, breathing difficulty, worsening pain, or inability to drink. Follow up with hematology.

Attending: HELIX SONKSEN

Assessment: Symptoms and course are most consistent with a panic attack. No evidence of an emergent cardiopulmonary process at this time.

Plan: Guided breathing retraining was completed in the department with good response. Discussed recognition of early symptoms, reduction of caffeine, and follow-up with primary care for ongoing anxiety assessment and possible behavioral-health referral. No medication was administered.

Discharged home in stable condition with friend present. Return precautions reviewed for persistent chest pain, fainting, severe shortness of breath, or new neurologic symptoms.

S: Cardiology floor handoff—Tao Fabry, DOB 03/01/1972, home address 84 New Main St, Gloversville, NY 12078. Admitted with cellulitis of the lower leg; erythema extending beyond prior skin marking.

B: Receiving dicloxacillin per MAR and acetaminophen as needed. Report/accession ID: 0793138404. Adult child updated at bedside.

Assessment: Awake, oriented, conversant. Left lower leg red, warm, edematous, and tender; margins outlined at 1900. Current pain 5/10. Afebrile this shift, hemodynamically stable. No drainage noted. Ambulates short distances with standby assist; gait guarded due to tenderness. Tolerated dinner and fluids.

Actions: Leg elevated on pillows. Area cleansed, skin kept dry. Dicloxacillin administered as ordered; acetaminophen given for discomfort with partial relief. Encouraged call light before ambulation. Monitor erythema border and neurovascular status.

Concerns/escalation: Notify covering provider for fever, hypotension, rapidly advancing redness, new drainage, increased pain, numbness, or change in mentation. Reassess response to antibiotics overnight; consider provider review if redness extends beyond marked border.

Next shift: Continue scheduled medications, pain reassessment, intake/output, mobility assistance, and q4h vital signs. Document erythema progression and maintain leg elevation.

Documented by RN, professional ID 073862279.

Discharge Summary
SSN: 666739281

Patient: Dayana E.
Address: 455 Montague Ave Exd, Marion, SC 29571
Patient contact: (312) 555-0122
The patient, age 64 years, was admitted to Internal Medicine for acute pyelonephritis with flank pain, dysuria, fever, and rigors. Spouse was present during discharge teaching and participated in medication review.

Admission urinalysis showed pyuria, positive leukocyte esterase, and bacteriuria. Urine culture grew a susceptible urinary pathogen. Blood cultures remained negative. Initial leukocytosis and mild creatinine elevation improved with treatment. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis or obstructing stone.

Hospital course: Received IV fluids and empiric ceftriaxone, then transitioned to oral cefuroxime after clinical improvement and culture review. Flank pain and rigors resolved; dysuria substantially improved. Tolerated oral intake and remained hemodynamically stable without supplemental oxygen. No procedure required.

Problem list:
1. Acute pyelonephritis — improved on antibiotics.
2. Dehydration/acute kidney injury — resolved with IV fluids.
3. Pain and fever — controlled with acetaminophen.

Discharge medications:
- Cefuroxime, complete the prescribed antibiotic course as directed.
- Acetaminophen as needed for pain or fever; do not exceed the labeled daily maximum.
Medication reconciliation completed. Avoid using leftover antibiotics. Maintain oral hydration unless otherwise instructed.

Condition at discharge: Stable, ambulatory, tolerating diet, voiding without difficulty. Discharged home with spouse.

Follow-up: Primary care reassessment in about 6 weeks, or sooner for persistent urinary symptoms. Seek urgent care for recurrent rigors, worsening flank pain, vomiting, confusion, inability to keep medications down, or fever that returns.

Reason for consultation: Evaluation of type 2 diabetes mellitus with recent thirst, fatigue, and frequent urination.

History: Patient reports increased thirst and urinary frequency over the past several weeks, accompanied by reduced energy. No acute infectious symptoms reported. Current medications include metformin and atorvastatin; adherence reviewed. A friend accompanied the patient and assisted with the history.

Findings: Patient appears clinically stable and is conversant. Oral mucosa mildly dry. Heart rate regular; lungs clear to auscultation. No focal neurologic deficit identified. Foot examination shows intact skin without ulceration; distal pulses palpable bilaterally. Laboratory results associated with report/accession ID 076828900 demonstrate hyperglycemia consistent with the reported symptoms. Renal function and urine albumin assessment should be confirmed on the final laboratory panel.

Arrange follow-up after laboratory results. An attending endocrinologist was requested for medication optimization and diabetes education if glycemic control remains above goal.

Discharge Summary

Patient: FLORIAN SURREY, a 75-year-old South Asian female patient

You were admitted after developing central chest pressure with diaphoresis and nausea. Initial ECG showed no ST-segment elevation, but serial troponin levels were elevated, consistent with a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). Chest radiograph showed no acute pulmonary process. Kidney function and blood counts remained stable.

You were treated with aspirin, therapeutic enoxaparin, high-intensity atorvastatin, and symptom-directed care. Cardiology reviewed the case; the attending cardiologist recommended medical management rather than urgent catheterization because symptoms resolved, the ECG remained stable, and your overall risk was acceptable. No procedure was performed. Enoxaparin was stopped before discharge.

Discharge medications:
• Aspirin 81 mg by mouth daily
• Clopidogrel 75 mg by mouth daily, planned for 12 months unless cardiology changes this
• Atorvastatin 80 mg by mouth nightly
• Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg under the tongue for chest pain as directed; call 911 if pain persists after the first dose or returns

Do not stop aspirin or clopidogrel without speaking with cardiology. Avoid strenuous activity until cleared. Follow a heart-healthy, low-sodium diet and keep a current medication list.

You are discharged home in stable condition, without recurrent chest pain or shortness of breath. Follow up with cardiology on August 21, 2025 and with primary care afterward. Your sibling, L. Pensyl, in Saint Charles, was listed as an emergency contact. Return to the ED immediately for recurrent chest pressure, fainting, severe shortness of breath, or new neurologic symptoms.

Dear Podiatry and Wound Care Team,

I am referring jandiel sinicropi for urgent evaluation of a plantar diabetic foot ulcer with concern for deeper infection and impaired healing. The ulcer developed beneath the forefoot and has persisted despite local wound care. The patient reports reduced sensation in both feet and increasing local discharge over the past several days. No systemic symptoms were reported in the ED.

Examination showed a plantar ulcer with a granular base, surrounding callus, moderate serous-purulent discharge, and localized erythema. Tenderness was limited, consistent with peripheral sensory loss. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were present. No crepitus or rapidly progressive soft-tissue change was identified. Plain radiographs did not show an acute osseous abnormality. Wound culture was obtained; results are pending.

Prior management has included off-loading advice, dressing changes, and wound care. Amoxicillin-clavulanate was started in the ED, with instructions to continue as prescribed. The patient was advised to avoid weight-bearing on the affected area as much as practical and to return for fever, spreading erythema, or worsening drainage.

Clinical question: please assess ulcer depth, need for debridement and advanced off-loading, and whether MRI or admission for intravenous antibiotics is indicated. Please also evaluate vascular status and coordinate diabetes management with the patient’s primary clinician and the attending endocrinologist.

Thank you for your assessment and treatment recommendations.

Sincerely,

raelle plenert

The wound was irrigated at bedside and gently packed. A wound culture was obtained; results were pending at discharge. MRN: 095777262
Referring organization: University of MD Shore Medical Center at Easton

Dear Cardiology Service,

I am referring this patient for assessment of recurrent episodic unilateral headache accompanied by nausea, photophobia, and intermittent awareness of a rapid heartbeat. The clinical question is whether the associated palpitations represent a cardiac rhythm disorder or are occurring as part of the patient’s established migraine episodes.

Headaches have been occurring approximately twice monthly, generally lasting several hours and improving in a dark, quiet room. There has been no reported syncope, exertional chest pain, focal weakness, or persistent visual loss. The patient describes the heartbeat as “fluttering” during some attacks, without documented heart rate measurement. Office cardiovascular examination today was regular, with no murmur; lungs were clear. Blood pressure was within the patient’s usual range. Neurologic screening examination was nonfocal.

Current medications:
• Sumatriptan as needed for acute migraine
• Naproxen as needed for acute migraine

The patient reports partial relief with the current regimen but remains concerned about the palpitations. Please consider ECG and ambulatory rhythm monitoring as clinically indicated, and advise whether any cardiac precautions or medication changes are recommended. I would also appreciate guidance regarding the safety of continuing sumatriptan pending assessment.

Primary care follow-up is planned in about 5 weeks, or sooner if symptoms worsen. Please forward your findings and recommendations to our office.

Sincerely,

LES KOLLURU, 002652540
Referring clinician

Current medications: methotrexate, folic acid, naproxen. Adherence reported as consistent. No recent medication changes.

Findings: Alert, nontoxic patient with symmetric swelling and tenderness of several MCP and PIP joints, reduced grip secondary to pain, and morning stiffness lasting approximately 90 minutes. Plan: Continue folic acid and naproxen as currently prescribed pending rheumatology review. Do not increase methotrexate without specialist direction. Obtain CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, inflammatory markers, and chest radiograph. Consider pulmonary function testing and high-resolution CT if cough persists, dyspnea develops, or imaging is abnormal. Expedite rheumatology follow-up for disease-modifying therapy adjustment. Go to the ED for worsening shortness of breath, chest pain, or hemoptysis.

SSN: 000-17-8681

Patient: Adiline
Report/accession ID: 03820692
Collection/report date: 2035-06-17
Specimen: Neonatal serum, heel-stick sample
Clinical context: a 4-month-old Black female infant evaluated for jaundiced skin, sleepy feeding, and reduced intake. Parent reports the infant was born at 39+2 weeks' gestation.

Results
Total bilirubin: 17.8 mg/dL
Direct bilirubin: 0.4 mg/dL
Indirect bilirubin: 17.4 mg/dL
Hemolysis index: 8, no significant interference
Serum glucose: 68 mg/dL

Reference interpretation
Direct bilirubin is not elevated. The indirect hyperbilirubinemia is clinically significant and should be interpreted with the infant’s postnatal age in hours, gestational age, rate of bilirubin increase, and presence of neurotoxicity risk factors. The reported total bilirubin may meet treatment criteria depending on the applicable phototherapy nomogram and current clinical age.

Interpretive comment
Pattern is consistent with predominantly unconjugated neonatal hyperbilirubinemia. Correlate promptly with feeding adequacy, hydration status, weight trend, and physical examination. Continue phototherapy and feeding support as clinically indicated. Repeat total and direct bilirubin after treatment initiation or sooner if intake declines, lethargy progresses, or jaundice extends to the lower extremities. Consider CBC, reticulocyte count, blood type/DAT, and evaluation for hemolysis if the bilirubin rise is rapid or the clinical course is atypical.

Discharge Summary

Patient: Z. Parcell
Admission/discharge date: Aug 7, 1996
Service: Cardiology, Eastern Oklahoma Medical Center

Reason for admission:
Presented to the ED with new central chest pressure associated with diaphoresis and nausea. Initial ECG without ST-segment elevation. Serial high-sensitivity troponins rose and subsequently peaked, consistent with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction.

Hospital course:
Treated promptly with aspirin, therapeutic enoxaparin, telemetry monitoring, and high-intensity atorvastatin. Chest discomfort resolved without recurrent ischemic symptoms. Echocardiogram showed mildly reduced left ventricular systolic function with regional wall-motion abnormality in the inferior territory. Coronary angiography demonstrated significant coronary artery disease without a lesion requiring immediate intervention; cardiology recommended medical management. Renal function and hemoglobin remained stable. No sustained arrhythmia or heart failure during observation.

Medication changes at discharge:
• Aspirin 81 mg by mouth daily.
• Clopidogrel 75 mg by mouth daily after inpatient loading dose; continue dual antiplatelet therapy as directed by cardiology.
• Atorvastatin 80 mg by mouth nightly.
• Metoprolol succinate 25 mg by mouth daily, if tolerated.
• Sublingual nitroglycerin for recurrent chest discomfort as instructed.
Enoxaparin discontinued at discharge.

Condition:
Hemodynamically stable, ambulatory, tolerating diet, and free of chest pain at discharge. Discharge instructions reviewed with the patient and sibling Japheth Tartaglia, who provided collateral history and will assist with medication organization. Family contact is based in Calumet.

Follow-up:
Cardiology follow-up requested with Eastern Oklahoma Medical Center and primary care for blood pressure, lipid, and medication review. Cardiac rehabilitation referral placed; reassessment planned in about 5 weeks. Return to the ED for chest pressure lasting more than a few minutes, dyspnea, syncope, or symptoms not relieved by prescribed nitroglycerin. Avoid stopping aspirin or clopidogrel unless directed by cardiology.

Emergency Department Specialist Report

Patient: A. Waco
Occupation: Pastry Baker
Employer: Vader Housing Authority
Home address: 181 E 3rd Ave, Edwall, WA 99008
Patient contact: aman.waco32@outlook.com

Reason for evaluation: Plantar ulceration of the right forefoot with reduced sensation and local discharge in the setting of diabetes mellitus.

History: Patient reports several days of drainage from a callused area beneath the first metatarsal head. Denies fever, rigors, or proximal streaking. No recent trauma reported. Emergency contact information is documented in the registration record.

Examination: Hemodynamically stable and nontoxic appearing. Plantar ulcer measuring approximately 1.2 cm with a clean-appearing base and scant seropurulent discharge. Surrounding erythema extends less than 1 cm from the wound margin. No fluctuance, crepitus, exposed bone, or necrotic tissue. Reduced protective sensation on monofilament testing of both feet. Dorsalis pedis pulse palpable; foot warm with preserved capillary refill.

Interpretation: Findings are consistent with a diabetic foot ulcer with limited local cellulitis. No current clinical evidence of deep-space infection, acute ischemia, or systemic infection. Plain radiographs show no radiopaque foreign body or cortical destruction.

Treatment/Plan: Wound irrigated and dressed in the ED. Begin amoxicillin-clavulanate as prescribed; continue local wound care and off-loading of the affected forefoot. Keep dressing clean and dry. Close follow-up with podiatry and primary care arranged. An attending endocrinologist should review glycemic management and risk-factor control. Return immediately for fever, spreading redness, increasing pain, malodor, or change in foot color.

Patient: SHIRLEE ZAAGMAN
Address: 349 State Hwy 116, Greybull, WY 82426
Occupation: Front Desk Receptionist
Employer: Dayton Senior Center

Dear Sleep Medicine Colleague,

I am referring SHIRLEE ZAAGMAN for evaluation of suspected obstructive sleep apnea and guidance regarding treatment. The patient’s spouse reports several months of very loud snoring with repeated pauses in breathing during sleep, followed by gasping. The patient also describes significant daytime somnolence, including difficulty staying alert during routine work activities. There has been an intermittent dry cough for 3 days, without fever or reported chest pain; this appears separate from the sleep-related concern.

Nocturnal symptoms have not improved with changes in sleep position. The patient has not yet completed a formal sleep study. Continuous positive airway pressure has been discussed but is not currently being used. Office examination today showed a regular heart rhythm, clear lungs, and no peripheral edema. Blood pressure was mildly elevated, and the patient was advised to continue home monitoring through primary care.

Assessment:
Symptoms and spouse-observed apneas are concerning for clinically significant obstructive sleep apnea. Daytime somnolence raises concern for impaired alertness and cardiovascular risk. Cardiology would appreciate sleep evaluation given the possible relationship between untreated apnea and blood pressure control.

Plan:
Please arrange diagnostic polysomnography or an appropriate home sleep apnea test and assess candidacy for continuous positive airway pressure. Recommendations regarding equipment, adherence monitoring, and follow-up would be appreciated. The patient was advised not to drive when drowsy.

Sincerely,

LES PROTSMAN

Discharge Summary

Patient: Aela Quisenberry
The patient, age 81 years, was admitted for progressive shortness of breath with orthopnea, bilateral ankle swelling, and reduced exercise tolerance consistent with acute decompensated heart failure.

On arrival, oxygen saturation was mildly reduced on room air with bibasilar crackles and dependent edema. Chest radiograph showed pulmonary vascular congestion and small bilateral pleural effusions. BNP was elevated. Troponins remained flat without evidence of acute coronary syndrome. Echocardiogram demonstrated reduced left ventricular systolic function with no significant valvular obstruction. Cardiology, including the attending cardiologist, reviewed the case.

Hospital course: Treated with IV furosemide, then transitioned to oral therapy after improvement in respiratory status and edema. Renal function and electrolytes were monitored; potassium was replaced once during diuresis. Metoprolol succinate was continued. No invasive procedure performed. Oxygen was weaned before discharge, and the patient ambulated on the ward without significant dyspnea.

Problem list:
- Acute on chronic systolic heart failure, improved after diuresis
- Orthopnea and peripheral edema, resolved/improving
- Reduced exercise tolerance
- Risk for recurrent volume overload

Discharge condition: Hemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, tolerating diet, ambulatory. Mild residual ankle edema.

Discharge medications:
- Furosemide, continue oral dose per medication reconciliation; daily weights requested
- Metoprolol succinate, continue
- Potassium supplementation only as listed on the finalized medication list
Medication reconciliation completed; “attending cardiologist” remains documented as the consulting specialty role, not a medication or diagnosis.

Instructions: Limit excess dietary sodium, follow prescribed fluid guidance, record weight each morning, and call primary care for rapid weight gain or worsening swelling. Seek emergency care for severe shortness of breath, chest pain, syncope, or inability to lie flat.

Follow-up: Primary care and cardiology review scheduled for January 30, 2013. Sibling J. Littlebird, who resides in Charlotte Amalie, was updated with the patient’s permission.

Patient: M. Dunderdale
Referring clinician: D. Fangman
Service locality: Saipan

Dear Clinical Genetics Team,

I am referring M. Dunderdale for assessment of lumbar radiculopathy with persistent low back pain, shooting pain into the right leg, and intermittent paresthesia. The specific question is whether an inherited neurologic, connective-tissue, or skeletal disorder could contribute to the patient’s recurrent symptoms and apparent multilevel degenerative changes at a relatively early stage.

Symptoms worsened for 3 days after routine lifting activity. Examination in the office showed antalgic gait, reduced lumbar flexion, and positive right straight-leg raise. Strength was 5/5 at the hips, knees, and ankles; sensation was mildly reduced along the lateral calf, with no bowel or bladder symptoms reported. Lumbar imaging was reviewed and showed degenerative changes with foraminal narrowing, without acute fracture. No dysmorphic features or significant joint hypermobility were identified on today’s limited examination.

Management to date has included activity modification, home stretching, and conservative analgesia with naproxen and acetaminophen. Physical therapy is being arranged. The patient’s adult child, Eastlynn, attended the visit and provided additional history regarding longstanding intermittent back and leg symptoms in the family; the available family history remains incomplete.

Please review the clinical history and imaging, advise whether genetic evaluation or testing is indicated, and recommend any appropriate multidisciplinary assessment. A genetics consultation would also help clarify whether further family-history documentation or targeted examination is warranted.

Sincerely,

D. Fangman

Patient: juandavid ylitalo

I am referring juandavid ylitalo for urgent assessment of a plantar diabetic foot ulcer with reduced sensation and local discharge. There was no reported fever or systemic illness, but the wound requires specialist review to assess depth, ischemia, and possible osteomyelitis.

Sincerely,

Emil Colpoys

Patient: TENNESSEE TRESCO, 61-year-old White female patient
MRN: 0827595
Patient contact: tennessee.tresco66@icloud.com
Referral reason: Episodic autonomic symptoms concerning for panic attacks.

History and findings:
The patient reports abrupt episodes of palpitations, chest tightness, and intense fear of dying. Symptoms have occurred intermittently, with chest tightness noted for 3 days before today’s visit. Episodes are not associated with syncope, seizure-like activity, focal neurologic deficit, or a persistent exertional pattern. The patient’s spouse provided corroborating history and describes visible hyperventilation during events. No known family pattern of sudden unexplained death, cardiomyopathy, or a recurrent neurogenetic syndrome was identified during this interview.

Interpretation:
The symptom cluster and observed respiratory pattern are most consistent with panic attacks and autonomic hyperarousal. The available history does not establish a recognizable inherited disorder, and genetic testing is not indicated solely for these symptoms. Cardiac and metabolic contributors should remain excluded through routine primary-care evaluation as clinically appropriate.

Plan:
Continue breathing retraining, emphasizing slow diaphragmatic breaths at the earliest warning of an episode. Recommend follow-up with primary care for review of cardiac risk, medication/substance triggers, and consideration of behavioral-health treatment. Emergency evaluation remains appropriate for sustained chest pain, syncope, or symptoms unlike the established episodes. No genetic testing ordered today.

LABORATORY REPORT – Wound Culture / Inflammatory Assessment
SSN: 942685797

Patient: Shreeyansh S.
MRN: 020405976
Ordering service: Mainehealth Franklin Hospital, Cardiology
Collection date: October 25, 2022
Specimen: Deep swab from plantar ulcer, left foot
Clinical indication: Diabetic foot ulcer with reduced sensation and local discharge; drainage for 3 days.

Results
- Gram stain: Few gram-positive cocci; no polymorphonuclear leukocytes seen.
- Aerobic culture: Moderate growth of Staphylococcus aureus.
- Susceptibility: Methicillin susceptible; susceptible to amoxicillin-clavulanate, cefazolin, clindamycin, doxycycline, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Resistant to penicillin.
- Anaerobic culture: No anaerobic growth at 48 hours.
- C-reactive protein: 18 mg/L (reference <8 mg/L), elevated.
- Hemoglobin A1c: 8.7% (reference 4.0–5.6%), elevated.

Interpretation
Culture supports a superficial bacterial component in the setting of diabetic foot ulceration. Results should be correlated with depth of infection, perfusion, and clinical examination; swab cultures may not represent deep tissue pathogens.

Treatment / Action
Continue prescribed amoxicillin-clavulanate and local wound care pending clinical response. Assess ulcer depth, erythema progression, pedal pulses, and need for debridement. Consider deep tissue culture if not improving. Urgent evaluation for fever, spreading cellulitis, ischemic change, or concern for osteomyelitis.

Validated and reported by: Liesl Lendo, MD
Laboratory comment: No blood culture specimen received.

Patient: C. Vanhulle

Employer: Stowe Transit Authority
Home address: 894 Grand Ave, Danville, VT 05828
Patient contact: (617) 555-0124

Thank you for meeting with Clinical Genetics today with your adult child. We reviewed your current major depressive episode, including low mood, loss of interest, and early-morning waking. You report that sertraline has been prescribed and is being taken as directed. You also mentioned a cough for 3 days; please arrange primary-care review if this persists or worsens.

At this visit, we discussed that depression usually reflects several contributing factors rather than a single inherited gene. Genetic testing is not recommended at this time as a routine diagnostic test for major depressive episode. A detailed three-generation family history may still be helpful, particularly if relatives have had recurrent depression, bipolar disorder, psychosis, suicide attempts, or unusually early symptoms. Your adult child may help confirm family details, with your permission.

Plan:
• Continue sertraline through the prescribing clinician; do not stop abruptly.
• Follow up with primary care or behavioral health to assess response, sleep, and adverse effects.
• Seek urgent help through the ED or 988 for suicidal thoughts, inability to remain safe, or new manic symptoms such as markedly reduced need for sleep, racing thoughts, or risky behavior.
• Genetics follow-up is not required unless additional family history becomes available or your treating clinician identifies a specific inherited condition to evaluate.

Sincerely,

Clinical Genetics Clinic

The familial BRCA1 c.68_69delAG pathogenic variant was identified. This result is consistent with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer predisposition. Refer to genetics and appropriate cancer-risk management service. Cascade testing should be discussed with adult relatives.

Result requires review in the context of the family’s known variant and documented genetic counseling.

Pediatric Hematology Consultation Report
SSN: 000 23 4360

Patient: Alizon Smolarski
Clinical age: 14 y/o
Parent present: LIGIA CAALIM
Patient contact: alizon.smolarski93@gmail.com

Reason for consultation: Tiredness, intermittent dizziness, and reduced exercise tolerance. History obtained from the patient with parent input; private adolescent discussion completed with assent.

Findings: Appears mildly fatigued but not acutely ill. Conjunctivae pale. Heart rate regular without murmur. No respiratory distress. Abdomen soft, without hepatosplenomegaly. No reported melena or hematochezia. Menstrual history reviewed confidentially; no acute gynecologic concern reported. Diet is low in iron-rich foods. Taking ferrous sulfate with inconsistent adherence because of gastrointestinal discomfort.

Laboratory review: Hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL, hematocrit 31.6%, MCV 72 fL, RDW 18.4%. Ferritin 6 ng/mL and transferrin saturation 8%, consistent with depleted iron stores. Platelet count mildly elevated, compatible with reactive thrombocytosis. Findings do not suggest an acute blood-loss syndrome or marrow failure.

Impression: Iron-deficiency anemia, symptomatic but hemodynamically stable. Reduced exercise tolerance and dizziness are likely anemia-related.

Plan: Continue ferrous sulfate as prescribed, preferably with vitamin C-containing fluid and separated from calcium-containing foods. Discussed adherence strategies and expected stool changes; take with food if nausea occurs. Increase dietary iron intake. Repeat CBC, reticulocyte count, and ferritin after treatment interval. Return sooner for syncope, chest pain, dyspnea at rest, or bleeding. Pediatric hematology follow-up scheduled for 03/05/2027, in about 12 weeks. Parent and patient verbalized understanding.

Start clopidogrel 75 mg by mouth once daily; continue for the cardiology-directed duration unless bleeding or another contraindication develops.

Atorvastatin 80 mg by mouth nightly.
Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg sublingual for chest pain, repeat every 5 minutes for up to 3 doses; call 911 if pain persists or is severe. Enoxaparin discontinued at discharge.

Condition and follow-up
Discharged home in stable condition with spouse, E. Saurage, whose locality is Howell. Patient: B. Castonia
Encounter date: Jun 1, 2035
Clinical age: 24 y/o
Report/accession ID: A26K71667
Patient contact: (212) 555-0165

Reason for consultation: Evaluation of persistent upper gastrointestinal symptoms and consideration of a hereditary connective-tissue or gastrointestinal motility disorder.

History and findings: The patient reports retrosternal burning with intermittent acid regurgitation, most noticeable after meals and when supine. Night-time cough occurs several nights weekly. Symptoms have improved but not fully resolved with omeprazole and alginate suspension. No reported dysphagia, food impaction, unexplained weight loss, recurrent vomiting, or gastrointestinal bleeding. Family history provided today does not suggest a recognized familial pattern of severe reflux disease, early gastrointestinal malignancy, or syndromic hypermobility.

Physical examination: Well appearing and in no acute distress. Oral mucosa moist. No appreciated craniofacial dysmorphism or abnormal skin fragility. Cardiopulmonary examination unremarkable. Abdomen soft and nontender without palpable organomegaly. Joint examination does not demonstrate clinically significant generalized hypermobility on today’s focused assessment.

Interpretation: Current findings are most consistent with uncomplicated gastroesophageal reflux disease. There is insufficient phenotypic or family-history evidence at this visit to support germline genetic testing. The night-time cough may reflect reflux-related laryngeal irritation; pulmonary or allergic contributors should be considered if it persists despite symptom control.

Plan: Continue current treatment through primary care and reinforce reflux precautions. Consider gastroenterology referral if symptoms remain refractory or alarm features develop. Genetics follow-up in about 5 weeks for review of interval symptoms and any additional family history.

Reason for consultation: Episodic wheeze, night-time cough, and exertional shortness of breath.

History: History obtained from the patient with additional observations from the patient’s sibling. Cough has been present for 3 days, with intermittent chest tightness and audible wheeze, worse overnight and with outdoor activity. No reported fever, hemoptysis, pleuritic pain, or recent emergency department visit. Current medications include albuterol inhaler and beclomethasone inhaler; adherence to the controller inhaler is inconsistent. No prior intubation reported.

Examination: Alert and speaking in full sentences. Respiratory rate normal. Mild expiratory wheeze at both lung bases, without crackles or accessory muscle use. Cardiac rhythm regular. No peripheral edema. Oxygenation is clinically stable at rest.

Findings and interpretation: The pattern of variable wheeze, nocturnal cough, and exertional dyspnea is most consistent with asthma with suboptimal symptom control, likely related in part to inconsistent inhaled corticosteroid use. There is no current examination evidence of pneumonia or acute respiratory distress.

- Prenatal vitamin as tolerated.

Instructions: Take frequent small sips of fluid and eat small, carbohydrate-containing meals as tolerated. Track urine output and ability to keep liquids down. Return to the ED for inability to retain fluids, fainting, worsening abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, fever, or markedly decreased urination.

Internal Medicine Consultation Note
SSN: 666 74 7340

Patient: Yahri B.
MRN: 046 026 678
Referring/treated by: P. Kosic
Healthcare organization: Mount Carmel New Albany Surgical Hospital
Occupation: Geriatric Physical Therapist

Reason for consultation: Acute right first metatarsophalangeal joint pain with swelling and erythema.

History: Patient reports abrupt onset of severe right great-toe pain beginning overnight, with progressive swelling and redness. A friend provided additional history and reports no recent trauma. Similar but less intense episodes have occurred in the past. No fever, rigors, open wound, or drainage reported. Current pain score is 5/10 after partial relief with naproxen. Medication list also includes colchicine.

Examination: Afebrile-appearing and nontoxic. Right first metatarsophalangeal joint markedly tender with limited active and passive range of motion. Focal warmth, erythema, and soft-tissue swelling present. No fluctuance, ulceration, or proximal streaking. Distal perfusion and sensation intact. No other acutely inflamed peripheral joint identified.

Findings and interpretation: The abrupt monoarticular inflammatory presentation, characteristic first-toe distribution, and prior similar episodes are most consistent with an acute gout flare. Septic arthritis is less likely clinically but remains an important exclusion if systemic symptoms develop or the examination worsens. Cellulitis is not favored in the absence of skin disruption or spreading erythema.

Plan: Continue anti-inflammatory treatment with naproxen as previously tolerated; take with food and avoid additional NSAIDs. Colchicine may be continued according to the established prescription. Rest, elevation, and local ice advised. Reassessment recommended for persistent symptoms, fever, spreading redness, inability to bear weight, or drainage. After the flare resolves, review serum urate and discuss preventive urate-lowering therapy if recurrent attacks continue.

Signed: P. Kosic

Patient: Leodan H.

To Cancer Genetics,

I am referring this patient for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk assessment. The specific question is whether the reported family history meets criteria for germline testing and, if so, which testing approach and screening recommendations are appropriate.

The patient reports multiple blood relatives with breast and ovarian cancer, with limited access to some relatives’ pathology and genetic records. A close friend accompanied the patient and helped clarify the family history. The patient is understandably concerned about personal cancer risk and requests predictive testing. No current treatment is being taken for this concern.

The patient has no known personal cancer diagnosis and is seeking counseling before any testing is ordered. We reviewed that a documented affected relative’s result, when available, may help guide interpretation and that a negative result in an unaffected person can be less informative when no familial variant is known. The patient understands that testing may identify a pathogenic variant, a negative result, or a variant of uncertain significance.

Please obtain a three-generation pedigree, verify available records, and provide pretest counseling regarding potential medical, family, and insurance implications. If testing is indicated, please arrange appropriate germline analysis and return recommendations for breast and ovarian risk management. The family has specifically mentioned BRCA1 c.68_69delAG as a variant under genetics review; its laboratory documentation and relationship to this family should be confirmed rather than assumed.

Please send your assessment and testing plan to our office. Follow-up with primary care is planned for August 23, 2028.

Sincerely,

kaspen nielander

CLINICAL GENETICS LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: Kalissi
MRN: 02439008
Reporting organization: Lawrence & Memorial Hospital
Specimen: Peripheral blood, EDTA
Test: Hereditary hematologic malignancy panel, germline DNA sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis
Clinical indication: Painless lymphadenopathy, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss; Hodgkin lymphoma under evaluation. Supportive care pending tissue diagnosis.

RESULTS
• DNA concentration: 42 ng/µL; purity acceptable
• Sequencing coverage: 98.7% of reportable coding regions at ≥100×
• Pathogenic/likely pathogenic germline variants: None identified
• Variants of uncertain significance: None detected
• Copy-number analysis: No reportable exon-level deletion or duplication

INTERPRETATION
No clinically actionable germline variant was identified in the genes analyzed. This negative result does not exclude a somatic alteration in the lymph node or other involved tissue and does not rule out a hereditary predisposition outside the assay scope.

CLINICAL COMMENT
Findings should be interpreted with pathology, flow cytometry, imaging, and family history. For suspected Hodgkin lymphoma, testing of affected tissue may be more informative than germline blood testing. Genetic counseling is recommended if the family history includes multiple hematologic malignancies, early-onset cancer, or unusual tumor patterns.

ACTION
• Correlate with excisional lymph node pathology.
• Consider tumor-directed molecular studies per hematopathology.
• Genetics follow-up: April 1st, 2018
• Validated and released by J. Manzoni, laboratory clinician.

Patient: Nekoda Immediato, 62-year-old White male patient  
SSN: 000 99 2949
MRN: 079339568  
Patient contact: (212) 555-0171  
Date: 01/06/2024

Today’s evaluation supports benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). Your brief spinning episodes are triggered by changes in head position, with associated nausea and mild unsteadiness. The examination did not suggest a persistent neurologic deficit, and there is no report of fainting, chest pain, or new hearing loss. You also mentioned a mild cough for 3 days; this appears separate from the positional dizziness and can be monitored.

I reviewed that BPPV is usually caused by displacement of small inner-ear particles. Symptoms commonly occur when rolling in bed, looking up, or standing after bending. Please perform the home Epley maneuver as demonstrated, once daily until the positional symptoms have resolved. Move slowly, use a stable surface, and have your sibling nearby the first few times because brief worsening of dizziness may occur.

Medication: prochlorperazine as required for significant nausea. Avoid driving, ladders, and operating machinery while dizzy or after taking this medicine. Maintain fluids and rise gradually from bed or a chair.

Please contact the office if symptoms are not improving within 1–2 weeks, recur frequently, or interfere with walking. Go to the ED for continuous severe vertigo, inability to walk, fainting, severe headache, weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or new vision changes. A vestibular therapy referral can be arranged if home treatment is unsuccessful.

Problem list:
1. Gastroenteritis with dehydration, improved.
2. Vomiting and diarrhea, improving.
3. Reduced urine output, resolved with hydration.

Follow-up with the primary care office after discharge if symptoms persist. Return to the ED for inability to keep fluids down, no urine for 8 hours, bloody stool or emesis, severe or localized abdominal pain, fainting, confusion, or worsening weakness.

Admission diagnosis: Acute pyelonephritis with flank pain, dysuria, and rigors.

Initial urinalysis showed pyuria and positive leukocyte esterase; urine culture subsequently grew a susceptible urinary pathogen. CBC demonstrated leukocytosis. Renal function remained stable, and renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis or obstructing calculus.

- Cefuroxime, continue the prescribed oral course through completion.
- Acetaminophen as needed for pain or fever; follow package directions and do not exceed the recommended daily amount.

Instructions: Maintain hydration and complete all cefuroxime doses. Return to the ED for recurrent rigors, persistent vomiting, worsening flank pain, confusion, inability to urinate, or fever that does not improve. Follow up with primary care for reassessment and review of the final culture result. DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: aby okan
Clinical age: 28 y/o
Patient contact: (617) 555-0102
Emergency contact: Aaleeyah

Reason for admission:
Presented to the emergency department with approximately 1 day of worsening right lower-quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and loss of appetite. Exam showed localized right lower-quadrant tenderness with guarding but no diffuse peritoneal signs.

Evaluation:
CBC showed leukocytosis. CT abdomen/pelvis demonstrated an enlarged inflamed appendix with surrounding inflammatory change, consistent with acute uncomplicated appendicitis; no abscess or perforation identified. Pregnancy testing was not indicated based on the clinical history.

Hospital course:
Received IV fluids, analgesia, antiemetic therapy, and ampicillin-sulbactam. General Surgery evaluated the patient and recommended operative management. Laparoscopic appendectomy was completed without complication. Operative findings were consistent with acute appendicitis without perforation. Appendix submitted to pathology. Diet advanced from clear liquids to regular diet with good tolerance. Ambulating and voiding independently; pain controlled with oral medication. No postoperative fever, emesis, or wound concern.

Discharge medications:
- acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed
- Ibuprofen as directed on the discharge medication list
- No further antibiotics required unless specifically directed after pathology review

Condition at discharge:
Stable, afebrile, tolerating oral intake, with clean and dry laparoscopic sites. Discharged home with emergency contact aware of the plan.

Instructions:
Keep incisions clean and dry; shower permitted per surgical instructions. Avoid heavy lifting until cleared. Return for fever, worsening abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, spreading redness or drainage from an incision, or inability to tolerate fluids.

Follow-up:
Postoperative surgical clinic review scheduled for 2019-11-21. Pathology results will be reviewed at follow-up or communicated through the patient portal. Contact the surgery office for increasing pain or wound concerns.

Report/accession ID: 02000175

Specimen context: Plantar ulcer swab and venous blood; specimen submitted for assessment of local discharge and glycemic control. Ordering clinician not specified.

Results

Hemoglobin A1c: 8.7%
Reference: <5.7% normal; 5.7–6.4% increased risk; ≥6.5% consistent with diabetes.

White blood cell count: 10.8 ×10^3/µL
Reference: 4.0–11.0 ×10^3/µL

Reference: <8.0 mg/L

Creatinine: 1.02 mg/dL

Estimated GFR: 86 mL/min/1.73 m²

Wound culture: Moderate growth of Staphylococcus aureus. Susceptibility testing performed separately. No anaerobic growth identified.

Hemoglobin A1c is above usual treatment target and indicates suboptimal recent glycemic control. Mildly elevated C-reactive protein supports localized inflammatory activity. White blood cell count is within the laboratory reference interval. Renal function is preserved on this specimen.

Culture findings should be interpreted with wound appearance, depth, perfusion, and clinical examination. Continue prescribed wound care and amoxicillin-clavulanate pending susceptibility review and clinical reassessment. Urgent evaluation is warranted for spreading erythema, fever, increasing pain, tissue necrosis, or exposed bone.

Legal guardian: DEZMON BOMMAREDDY
Receiving facility: Landmark Medical Center
Arrival: 08:15

Chief complaint: Burning with urination and frequent small voids since yesterday. Suprapubic discomfort. No flank pain, vomiting, vaginal bleeding, or reported fever.

Urinalysis: positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites; moderate blood.
Urine microscopy: WBCs elevated, bacteria present.

Treatment: First dose of nitrofurantoin given in ED; tolerated without reaction. Oral hydration encouraged. Discharge medication: nitrofurantoin as prescribed.

Disposition: Discharged home with legal guardian. Patient and guardian understand medication use, return precautions, and need for reassessment if fever, flank pain, vomiting, or worsening symptoms.

Follow-up: Primary care review on November 12, 2026. Culture sent; family to be contacted for significant resistance or change in therapy.

Discharge Summary

Patient: RENARD TIECHE
MRN: 0302549
Home address: 181 W Midway Ln, Logan, UT 84322

Reason for admission: Presented with several days of markedly reduced urine output, fatigue, and poor oral intake, with cough for 3 days. Initial laboratory testing showed acute kidney injury with creatinine 3.1 mg/dL, elevated from the available baseline. Mild orthostasis was noted; no respiratory distress.

Hospital course: Pulmonary evaluation found no focal infiltrate on chest radiograph and no evidence of acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. Viral respiratory testing was negative. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis or obstructing lesion. Urinalysis was concentrated without significant hematuria or proteinuria. Nephrology agreed the presentation was most consistent with volume depletion and medication-associated kidney injury.

The patient received intravenous sodium chloride with strict intake/output monitoring. Urine output improved over the next 48 hours, and creatinine decreased to 1.4 mg/dL before discharge. Oral intake and energy level improved. No dialysis indication developed. Home NSAIDs and the outpatient diuretic were held during recovery; the primary care team should reassess need for restart after repeat renal testing.

Discharge medications:
- Continue prescribed maintenance medicines except those specifically held above.
- Avoid NSAIDs until cleared.
- Maintain oral hydration.
- No new antibiotic indicated.

Condition at discharge: Hemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, ambulatory, tolerating diet, and voiding without difficulty.

Follow-up: Repeat basic metabolic panel with primary care within 3–5 days. Pulmonary clinic follow-up if cough persists or worsens. Return to the ED for inability to keep fluids down, recurrent oliguria, confusion, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

Discharging clinician: asenet stodola, Professional ID: LIC07270594

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT LABORATORY REPORT
SSN: 000-91-6389

Patient: G. Bontempo
MRN: 0278413
Reporting organization: CONFLUENCE HEALTH HOSPITAL
Collection/report date: January 11th, 2018
Specimen: Left plantar ulcer swab; collected before antibiotic dose. Clinical history: diabetic foot ulcer with reduced sensation and local discharge for 3 days. Wound care and amoxicillin-clavulanate reported.

RESULTS
CBC:
WBC 12.8 x10^3/µL (4.0–10.5) — high
Hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL (12.0–16.0)
Platelets 326 x10^3/µL (150–400)

Inflammatory markers:
CRP 6.8 mg/dL (0.0–0.5) — high
ESR 48 mm/hr (0–20) — high

Chemistry:
Glucose 214 mg/dL (70–140) — high
Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL (0.6–1.3)
Lactate 1.4 mmol/L (0.5–2.2)

WOUND CULTURE
Moderate growth of methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. Mixed skin flora also present. No Pseudomonas isolated. Susceptibility: susceptible to amoxicillin-clavulanate, cephalexin, doxycycline, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

INTERPRETATION/ACTION
Leukocytosis and elevated inflammatory markers support active soft-tissue infection. Lactate not elevated. Culture result is consistent with the reported diabetic foot ulcer; correlate with depth of ulceration and imaging findings. Continue local wound care and prescribed amoxicillin-clavulanate pending ED reassessment. Urgent surgical evaluation if exposed bone, advancing erythema, systemic symptoms, or concern for osteomyelitis.

Patient: E. Mcmurtrie
DOB: 01/23/1987
Home address: 43 State Hwy 59, Moose, WY 83012

You were admitted for several days of lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge, and pain with intercourse. Pelvic examination and testing supported pelvic inflammatory disease. Your symptoms improved, and you remained able to eat, drink, and walk without assistance.

Discharge condition: stable; pain improved; no fever at discharge.

Please schedule follow-up with primary care or a gynecology clinic in 19 days, appointment date May 30, 2021. Return to the emergency department for worsening or one-sided abdominal pain, fever, vomiting, fainting, heavy bleeding, or inability to take medications. A friend may accompany you and help with transportation or medication reminders.

Medication reconciliation:
Ceftriaxone — administered in hospital.
Doxycycline — continue as directed.
Metronidazole — continue as directed; no alcohol.

Keep your patient contact information current with the outpatient clinic so pending test results can be communicated.

Acute atraumatic right first MTP pain with swelling and erythema, onset overnight. Unable to tolerate shoe. No fever or systemic symptoms.

Known gout; prior flares treated outpatient. Home medications include colchicine and naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food. No recent injury or procedure reported. Emergency contact: AMIRI MARBAKER.

Discharge Summary

Patient: avayla verdery
Service: Clinical Genetics
Discharge diagnosis: Cellulitis of the lower leg

avayla verdery was admitted for progressive redness, warmth, and tenderness of the left lower leg despite initial outpatient observation. The patient remained afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Examination showed spreading erythema with local warmth and leg tenderness; no fluctuance, crepitus, or drainage was identified. Current pain score 5/10.

Laboratory evaluation showed mild leukocytosis without other significant abnormality. Ultrasound did not demonstrate a drainable collection or deep venous thrombosis. Blood cultures remained without growth during the admission. The case was reviewed with the inpatient team at Commonwealth Health Center, and the clinical picture was felt to be consistent with uncomplicated nonpurulent cellulitis.

Treatment and course: Received intravenous antibiotics with improvement in erythema and tenderness. No procedure was required. Transitioned to oral dicloxacillin once able to tolerate oral intake. Acetaminophen may be used for discomfort.

Discharge medications:
• Dicloxacillin, complete the prescribed course.
• Acetaminophen, as needed for pain or fever.

Condition at discharge: Stable, ambulatory, and tolerating diet. The borders of erythema were marked before discharge, with instructions to seek urgent care for extension beyond the markings, fever, worsening pain, drainage, vomiting, or new weakness.

Follow-up is arranged with primary care on April 1st, 2028. The patient’s sibling, Kayior Hoopaugh, who resides in Saipan, was identified as an emergency contact and participated in discharge planning. Keep the leg elevated when resting, maintain hydration, and avoid manipulating the affected skin.

Please provide specialty assessment and recommendations regarding daily inhaled corticosteroid therapy, an individualized asthma action plan, trigger evaluation, and spirometry when clinically feasible. Dear Cardiology Colleague,

I am referring Laurelin P. for evaluation of persistent reduced exercise tolerance, dizziness, and fatigue despite treatment for iron-deficiency anemia. The patient reports becoming short of breath and lightheaded with routine activity, without syncope, chest pain, palpitations, orthopnea, or leg swelling. A sibling accompanied the patient and confirms that these symptoms have been more noticeable recently.

Recent primary care testing showed microcytic anemia with low ferritin, consistent with iron deficiency. There is no reported overt bleeding, and the patient denies black or bloody stools. Oral replacement was started, with partial improvement in tiredness but ongoing exertional limitation. Current medication: ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily.

Patient: Yelitza P.
Patient contact: (617) 555-0138
Report/accession ID: S29-0075546

Patient presented with abrupt shortness of breath and sharp right-sided chest pain that worsens with inspiration. Spouse, sherry frinks, reports the patient became visibly winded while walking and complained of a racing heartbeat. No syncope or hemoptysis. The patient is followed by FREEMAN NEOSHO HOSPITAL for a known clotting disorder.

On arrival, tachycardic at 124 bpm with oxygen saturation 89% on room air. Respiratory rate 26/min, blood pressure stable, afebrile. Patient appears anxious and mildly distressed. Lungs with decreased breath sounds at the right base but no wheezing. Regular rapid rhythm without murmur. No unilateral leg erythema; mild right calf tenderness. Awake and answering appropriately.

ECG showed sinus tachycardia without ST-segment elevation. Chest radiograph without focal infiltrate or pneumothorax. CTA chest demonstrated acute bilateral pulmonary emboli with a segmental burden greater on the right; no CT evidence of right-heart strain. Troponin was negative, and basic metabolic testing was acceptable for anticoagulation.

Treatment: Supplemental oxygen applied, with improvement in saturation to 96%. Medication reconciliation confirms apixaban 5 mg twice daily; patient reports adherence and no bleeding. Given stable blood pressure, negative biomarkers, and absence of right-heart strain, systemic thrombolysis is not indicated. ED attending discussed the case with the covering pulmonary clinician, who recommends continued anticoagulation and close follow-up.

Assessment: Acute pulmonary embolism with hypoxemia and pleuritic chest pain, hemodynamically stable.

Plan: Admit to monitored medical service at FREEMAN NEOSHO HOSPITAL for oxygen weaning, observation, and anticoagulation management. Patient and spouse understand the plan and return precautions.

Patient: pericles jangda, 56-year-old Asian female patient
Location: Emergency Department, Cibola General Hospital

Chief complaint: Vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps

History: Acute onset yesterday after shared meal. Spouse reports 6 loose stools and 3 episodes of nonbloody emesis. Cramping periumbilical pain; nausea may improve with hydration. No syncope, chest pain, or dysuria. No recent antibiotics.

Exam: Mildly dry mucous membranes. T 99.1°F, BP 108/70, HR 96, RR 18, SpO2 99% RA. Abdomen soft, nondistended, mild diffuse tenderness; no rebound or guarding. Alert, nontoxic.

Workup:
CBC without leukocytosis. CMP: Na 136, K 3.8, CO2 21, Cr 0.9. Lipase normal. Urinalysis with concentrated specific gravity, no infection.

ED treatment: Oral rehydration solution tolerated after ondansetron as required. Repeat abdominal exam benign; no indication for CT.

Assessment: Infectious gastroenteritis with mild volume depletion. Low concern for appendicitis, obstruction, or acute surgical abdomen.

Disposition: Discharged home. Continue oral rehydration solution, bland diet, return for worsening pain, bloody stool, inability to keep fluids down, or syncope. Follow up with primary care. Attending: Malasia Petrakos

Patient: Mizuki
SSN: 000634492
Occupation: Auto Electrician
Employer: Dellroy School District
Home address: 320 N Gay St, Spencer, OH 44275
Patient email: mizuki.gefre10@proton.me
Department: Clinical Genetics

Today’s visit focused on worsening breathing. You described increased breathlessness, wheezing, and thicker yellow-green sputum for 3 days. This is consistent with an acute exacerbation of your established chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. There was no report of chest pain or coughing blood. Your emergency contact remains listed in the chart.

Plan:
• Start prednisone as prescribed for the flare.
• Start doxycycline because of the change to purulent sputum.
• Continue albuterol inhaler for wheeze or shortness of breath according to the medication instructions.
• Use your maintenance inhalers consistently if prescribed; bring all inhalers to follow-up so technique can be checked.
• Avoid tobacco smoke and other respiratory irritants, and maintain fluids as tolerated.

Please seek urgent evaluation in the ED for severe or rapidly worsening breathlessness, blue lips, confusion, inability to speak in full sentences, or poor response to albuterol. Call the office if symptoms are not clearly improving within 48–72 hours or if fever develops.

Follow-up with primary care is recommended after this episode for COPD maintenance review, vaccination status, pulmonary function testing if not current, and assessment of oxygen needs. The clinical genetics team can coordinate with primary care if there is a relevant family history or concern for an inherited contribution to lung disease.

Spouse/contact: Jahaan Soderlind
Patient contact: azurii.foux30@hotmail.com
Date: September 28th, 1996

Reason for visit: Persistent vomiting with poor oral intake, dehydration, and reported weight loss during early pregnancy. Current pregnancy documented as 9+4 weeks' gestation.

ED evaluation showed mild tachycardia and dry mucous membranes. Urine was concentrated with ketones. Basic metabolic panel showed mild hypokalemia without significant renal impairment. No abdominal tenderness or vaginal bleeding. Bedside ultrasound confirmed an intrauterine pregnancy with cardiac activity. Findings were consistent with first-trimester hyperemesis without evidence of a surgical abdomen or hemodynamic instability.

Treatment/course: Received intravenous sodium chloride and antiemetic therapy with improvement in nausea. Tolerated oral fluids and crackers before discharge. Doxylamine-pyridoxine was started for scheduled home use. She was counseled to take small, frequent sips and bland foods as tolerated.

Assessment: First-trimester hyperemesis with dehydration and weight loss, improved after ED treatment.

Discharge medications:
Doxylamine-pyridoxine as prescribed.
Continue prenatal vitamin if tolerated.

Follow-up: Contact obstetric care for reassessment within 24–48 hours and medication adjustment if vomiting persists. Return to the ED for inability to keep fluids down, fainting, worsening abdominal pain, fever, vaginal bleeding, decreased urination, or other concerning symptoms. Patient and spouse verbalized understanding of the discharge plan.

Please assess promptly for depth, vascular status, culture needs, and definitive wound-care and glycemic-management recommendations.

Pediatric Laboratory Medicine Report

Patient: Isak K.
Report/accession ID: 0464271020
Clinical context: The patient, age 14 years, was reviewed with a parent for thirst, frequent urination, and recent weight loss. Type 1 diabetes mellitus under evaluation. Insulin therapy and home glucose monitoring reported.

Specimen: Venous blood, collected in EDTA and serum tubes. Specimen adequate for analysis.

Results:
Glucose: 286 mg/dL (reference interval 70–99 mg/dL fasting)
Hemoglobin A1c: 11.8% (reference interval 4.0–5.6%)
Estimated average glucose: 292 mg/dL
C-peptide: 0.32 ng/mL (reference interval 1.1–4.4 ng/mL)
Beta-hydroxybutyrate: 1.7 mmol/L (reference interval <0.6 mmol/L)
GAD-65 antibody: Positive, 186 IU/mL (negative <5 IU/mL)
IA-2 antibody: Positive, 42.6 U/mL (negative <7.5 U/mL)
Insulin autoantibody: Negative

Interpretation: Marked hyperglycemia with substantially elevated A1c, low endogenous insulin secretion, and positive pancreatic islet autoantibodies. Findings strongly support autoimmune type 1 diabetes mellitus in the appropriate clinical setting. Mildly increased beta-hydroxybutyrate warrants correlation with venous blood gas, electrolytes, hydration status, and symptoms; these results alone do not establish diabetic ketoacidosis.

Clinical comment: Prompt pediatric endocrinology management is recommended, including insulin regimen review, ketone precautions, and continued glucose monitoring. Parent and patient should receive age-appropriate diabetes education. Repeat laboratory review is planned in about 7 weeks, with follow-up appointment on 07/19/2020.

Validated and reported by: JAQUON SHILOW
Pediatric Laboratory Medicine

Date: 06/20/1996
To: Cancer Genetics Clinic

Re: Samaad A.
MRN: 0520203

Referral reason: Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk assessment; review of significant family history and consideration of predictive genetic testing.

Dear Cancer Genetics Team,

I am referring Samaad A. from Syringa General Hospital for formal cancer-risk assessment and genetic counseling. The patient is concerned about a reported familial pathogenic BRCA1 variant and would like to discuss predictive testing. History was reviewed with the patient and spouse present. The family history includes breast and ovarian cancer in multiple relatives on the same side of the family; the available pedigree is incomplete, and ages at diagnosis and prior pathology reports are not currently confirmed.

The patient has no personal history of breast, ovarian, pancreatic, or prostate cancer and is not receiving current treatment. No cancer-directed medications are reported. There are no acute symptoms prompting this referral. The patient understands that testing may have implications for relatives and wishes to review potential outcomes, limitations, insurance considerations, and recommended surveillance before proceeding.

A family laboratory record reportedly identifies BRCA1 c.68_69delAG. Please verify the original report and determine whether targeted familial-variant testing is appropriate. If the familial result cannot be confirmed, broader multigene testing may be considered based on the completed pedigree and counseling assessment.

Requested action: genetic counseling, construction of a three-generation pedigree, verification of the reported variant, and recommendations for risk-based screening and family communication. Please send your assessment and testing recommendations back to our office.

Sincerely,

D. Loughead
Referring Clinician
Syringa General Hospital
